A.translation: For verdigris eats away the [367] ulcerated flesh, being a hot and pungent drug; whereas the cerate is mild and non-biting, but instead of new flesh it breeds filth upon the ulcers. How this too is mixed together with the other, and likewise all the other drugs that are compounded in the same manner from contraries, has already been stated by me also in the third book of the therapeutic treatise, and now too the exercise in particular cases will be set out with an example for each affection. [What one who intends to compose drugs well must know in addition.] Concerning the power of simple drugs it has been said in another treatise that one must know the power of each, not only according to kind, as some have written, saying merely that it heats or cools or dries or moistens, but in a determinate and articulated way, namely of which order it is, as we have shown. For some drugs produce each of the aforesaid effects altogether faintly, some clearly, some strongly, just as others do completely.

It is therefore not sufficient to know that this [368] drug heats or cools, but one must further determine to what degree it heats and cools. For all the resins heat, and this is common to them, but they possess the more and the less in heat to no small extent. Many juices also heat, differing from one another by no small difference in the more and the less. For if you were to compare the juice of panax with the Cyrenaic and the Median, this will seem to you to be nothing in comparison with those. And why need one carry the argument far afield, when we can recall the difference among the very things we take daily? Dill, at any rate, and rue and onion, though all of them heat, differ greatly from one another, so that in treatments too we shall apply to the part that has been considerably chilled the drug that heats considerably, to the part that has been altered only slightly from its natural state the drug that heats moderately, just as to the part that has been thoroughly chilled the drug that heats most vehemently.

Reasonably, then, we established four orders among the heating drugs, distinguishing from those that heat slightly those that do this clearly, those that heat very much, and those that heat intensely together with [369] burning. And in each of the four differentiae some drugs are, as it were, of the differentia as it begins, some of it as it ends and approaches the one after it, and some in between. At any rate, among the drugs that draw by means of heat, just as among those called septic, some display their own power as soon as they are applied to the body, while others require two or three or four hours; and some a whole day, or even the night after it, or even several in succession. These things, then, as in the case of heating drugs, so also in the case of cooling drugs, must be known by anyone who is going to compound a drug; and likewise also in the case of moistening and drying ones. The materials of drugs are some from plants, some from metals, and some from animals; and you have learned all of them, distinguished, in the treatise on simple drugs.

For this discourse of mine is addressed above all to my companions, who have asked me now to write these things a second time, after the loss of the earlier ones. And just as it was proper for you to know accurately the powers [370] of all the simple drugs, so that in every place you might easily compound, from what is at hand, the things that are beneficial to the bodies in need of treatment, so too [you should know] the differences of all the conditions contrary to nature, [on which you have] a treatise; a second is the one on the differences of the symptoms, and a third after these, in which I go through the causes that produce diseases; and in addition to these, three others on the causes in the symptoms. You also have my writing On Plethora and that On the Differences of Fevers; and after these, the books of the Therapeutic Method, through which you learned the conditions by which activity is harmed, and that treatment is of these first, just as, conversely, prophylaxis is of the causes that produce them.

Heras, however, deserves to be praised for having written both the professed virtues of the drugs [431] and the modes of their use, which Andromachus omitted altogether in the case of the white plasters, only rarely adding the professed virtue alone; nor indeed did he write how one ought to boil the drug. But perhaps one would not blame him on this count, since he was writing for those already trained in the medical art, not for laymen. Yet not adding the professed virtues or the general powers is no small fault. For what will anyone say in his defence? Perhaps that these things have been written for those who know the powers of the simple drugs. And yet none of those has any need of Andromachus, since he is himself able to compound in like manner. [White plaster of Heras for hydrophobes.] So let us come back again to Heras, who, after the Attalic plaster, writes another white one, in these very words: White plaster for those bitten by rabid dogs. It acts precisely also for hydrophobes; for it delivers them at once from the danger when applied to the wound.

For those, however, who are very much overpowered, one should also make from it a pill the size of a Pontic nut and give it, and [432] do this for forty days. It changes its colour, however, on the compresses and becomes black. It is effective also for human bites, dog bites, abrasions, and wounds hard to cicatrize; it also removes bruises under the eyes, one keration, and glues wounds together. It is effective also for phymata and fissures. It is also an emollient pessary. One must, however, undo it every other day and sponge off the blackness that forms on the ulcers, and do this until the blackness no longer appears. The same plaster is also cicatrizing and good for all things. Having said these things first, Heras next wrote the proportion of the plaster in the following words: White. Take: of white Pontic wax, two pounds; of litharge chrysitis, one pound; of white lead, one pound; of myrrh, two ounces; of deer marrow, two ounces; of uncut frankincense, one ounce; of old oil, one xestes. This, then, is the proportion of the ingredients composing the plaster. Next he wrote the boiling thus: boil the litharge in oil, and when it seems to become glutinous in consistency, [add] the wax; then sprinkle in the white lead and stir.

When it has become unified and no longer stains, remove the [433] charcoal fire and add the marrow. After cooling it, add the myrrh and the frankincense, and when you have softened it, use it. In this respect too, then, one must praise Heras, for not leaving it up to us to boil the plaster in whatever way we might wish, but himself adding the instruction in writing. For the obvious course was to boil the ceruse together with the litharge straightaway from the beginning, as in the case of the other white plasters, and we ourselves are for the most part accustomed to do this, and indeed he himself has prescribed it in the case of others. But in the case of this one at least he orders it to be thrown in later, not indeed adding in writing the cause on account of which it is better to do this, yet nevertheless indicating that there is not one single manner of boiling that is equally useful in all cases, but that in some it is possible to carry out even two or three, altering not only the colour but also the power of the drugs. Just so, in the case of the one now before us, he did not wish the ceruse to be boiled together with the litharge, knowing that it both fails to preserve its exact whiteness when boiled down and lays aside the astringency which it possesses together with its cooling property.

And it is quite evident that, in the case of inflamed parts, one must cure the inflammation [499], while in the case of parts whose flesh is dyscratic, one must render it eucratic; and since it becomes dyscratic in four simple modes and in four other composite ones, the cure will be effected by means of the opposite qualities. But these matters will be discussed again later; next I shall speak about the strongly cleansing drugs. [On the strongly cleansing drugs.] That these belong to the same genus as those previously mentioned, which, by cleansing moderately and without biting at all, were applied to hollow, clean, uncomplicated ulcers, has been said before. But those which remove abundant filth have the cleansing power intensified, so that some of the green drugs mentioned differ from the simply flesh-producing ones in one thing only, the quantity of verdigris; and some differ also by the admixture of other ingredients, such as cleanse vigorously, as for instance the one called Isis and that of Machairion, and the one which we habitually use, called 'oily' (elaiōdes) on account of its use.

For where it is our task to produce flesh in a sinus, we melt it in a large quantity of oil and pour it in through a horn bored straight through, in the manner of a clyster [500] attached to a pig's bladder; we also use the so-called pus-drawers (pyoulkoi) for this purpose, for of these too, those which have a wider bore are useful for such a service. It is obvious that we render the foul sinus clean by using the drug in a more undiluted form, that is, by mixing it with less oil, whereas [we treat] the clean one with the drug moistened to a greater degree through the admixture of more abundant oil. If, then, there should be some suspicion that a still slight inflammation is mingled with the sinus, let the drug by all means be melted in rose-oil; but if it is free of inflammation, in olive oil, and if it tolerates without biting the admixture of old oil, let the drug be melted in that. Suitable for such use is not only this drug, but also that of Machairion and the isis, and all the others which those before me have written become flesh-producing for hollow ulcers when mixed with cerate.

For all these, without being mixed with cerate, are melted in oil and rose-oil and injected into sinuses, because the consistency called 'emmoton' (suited for lint-dressings) cannot be injected into sinuses; just so, indeed, in the case of the dry drug made from burnt papyrus [501] too, we mix it with much rose-oil and pour it into them. And just as sinuses need the more liquid drugs, since the thicker ones cannot be injected, so those of the hollow ulcers that lie on the surface require a thicker drug, because the liquids flow off them quickly and the lint-plugs are left dry. Reasonably, then, in such cases we mix cerate with the strongly detergent drugs, whereas in the case of sinuses we mix in a very great quantity of oil or rose-oil. These drugs that are detergent in this way are in every case also discutient, and for this reason also strongly desiccative, and there arises a certain common kind of them, which they call 'polychreston' (of many uses). Beyond this kind lies that of the very acrid plasters, such as those called 'through salts' (di' halōn), which one must not apply where we wish to produce flesh in some part. For, in addition to their other properties, salts have this too as peculiar to them: that they are astringent rather than detergent.

Of this same kind as cedar oil [569] is also the so-called strained lye. And of this very lye, whichever is produced from a fine-particled material that has been burnt surpasses cedar oil in power. So it is from the apple tree and the fig tree, and still more the wild fig, which they call erineos, and from the spurges, when burnt, that we prepare such a lye. The best of the spurges is the one called charakias. Among the seeds called cereal seeds, the most fine-particled is bitter vetch, without heating noticeably; darnel, with clearly heating; barley does not heat at all. Of intermediate material among them are those that are bitter in their qualities, falling short of the very fine-particled ones, but having nothing thick-particled. Some of them have departed slightly from the intermediate, some in the direction of heating, others in the direction of cooling; the materials of all of these I went through in the treatise on simple drugs, just as also those of the tree-fruits, among which are the bitter almonds and the pistachios.

Of the material derived from plants I make no mention at present, for I wish to go back to the beginning and to recount when and [570] how I made use of each of the things that were devised. For from this I think the naturally gifted among the young will be encouraged to come to know the material of drugs by becoming eyewitnesses of it themselves, not once or twice, but many times. For the recognition of perceptible things is perfected through continuous viewing, and the greatest proof of this is the case of twins, who seem to us to be indistinguishable but are not indistinguishable to those familiar with them, so that they do not pass unnoticed (παραδραμεῖν). Now the material from herbs, shrubs and trees it is best to examine, before it is taken up out of the earth, at the stages of fruiting—impending, beginning, advancing and at full maturity. For this continuous viewing of them will teach you at what season above all one would do well to gather them and, placing them in dry rooms, to preserve them, neither baked by the rays of the sun nor moistened by damp from the roof or the walls. This would come about if the rooms are neither underground nor προσχόρων (adjoining the ground?), nor under tiles, having, however, their windows turned toward the south. But let the drugs at any rate not be stored near these.

And I urge my companions [571] to imitate me in this respect too, at least if they wish to perform well the works of the art. For you know how the finest drugs are conveyed to me from each of the nations every year, because the wretched sellers of petty wares (ῥωποπῶλαι) corrupt them in every possible way. But it is perhaps better to blame not these alone, but much more than them the merchants who transport them, and still more than those the men who are called root-cutters, but who bring down from the mountains to the cities no less than roots also juices and saps and fruits, flowers and shoots; for these are the first of all to practise villainy upon them. Whoever, then, wishes to have an abundance of remedies from every source, let him become experienced in all the material from plants, and in all that from animals and from metals, and in all the earthy bodies which we bring into medical use without mining, so as to distinguish among them the genuine and the spurious; and after this let him exercise himself in my treatise in which I wrote about the power of simple drugs.

Such, in addition to those already mentioned, are maron and amarakos and polion, argemone and chamaipitys and centaury, and all the others which I went through in my teaching on simple drugs, as also the roots of all the aristolochias and of drakontion and of wild cucumber and of bryony and of althaia and of iris, and of akoron and meon and asaron and phou and gentian [635] and panax; for you have the material on all such things in the commentaries on simple drugs. It is necessary not only to know how, when pounding both the roots and the whole herbs, to sift them accurately through fine-meshed sieves, but also to triturate them again carefully, like the dry collyria, until they become dust-like. For what is coarse-particled is of no benefit to those with wounded nerves, who need, as has been said, fine-particled drugs. Let what has been sifted (διατμηθέν) and triturated be taken up in some cerate-like substance, in a proportion having the ratio previously stated in the case of euphorbium. For as much as there is in that of the two-year-old euphorbium, so much in these must be put of dittany and meon and akoron, and of all the others that are similarly hot to the taste as these; and as much as there is in those of the three-year-old, so much in these of aristolochia, iris and drakontion and gentian, and of all the others that are bitter in a manner comparable to these. [On the expensive preparations of drugs for those with wounded nerves.] It would not be useless to know such drugs too.

For a need of them does sometimes arise, [636] though more rarely, just as a need of the cheap ones arises often. For where a man possessing not more than five hundred myriads, a lover of drugs and a lover of medicine, did not think fit to use any of the cheap ones, much more will either some rich man or even a monarch wish to have such a drug, one that is at once fragrant and prepared at a great cost of silver. The rich man whose story I recounted in the first book of the work On Prognosis by the Pulses I have mentioned without a name, as also now; what sort of man he was you will learn from two such deeds of his as these. He himself was attempting to treat the malignant ulcer of a household slave. But when he accomplished nothing, he handed the man over to me, and on seeing him cured he asked for the prescription of the drug, not knowing that there are many differences among malignant ulcers and many among drugs, but thinking that one drug could cure them all. At any rate, not even (μὴ γοῦν μήτε) when the one who applied it did not use it skilfully, when he heard of what ingredients it was composed, and they were all cheap, 'this,' he said, 'keep for beggars; but teach me one of the more costly ones.'

And moreover, when a slave-boy had a chronic condition in the ears [637], since he himself, with the many drugs which he had employed without method, had done no good at all, he ordered that boy too to be brought to me to be treated. And later, when he learned that it had been cured by means of one of the ordinary ones, he did not think it worth while to take the prescription of the drug. This man, then, having himself seen many cases of those wounded in the nerves, with fingers cut off and putrefied, and some even dying or being maimed, and then having learned that none of those treated by me had come into danger, but all had quickly become healthy, asked to receive from me some drug that was at once fragrant and costly, with which he would be able to treat those wounded in the nerves. Now I had already on many occasions given to companions and to physician friends many improvised prescriptions according to the Method written above, in order that the reasoning behind their composition might be confirmed by the outcomes. But a costly one, such as that man wanted, I would not have given to poor people, since I considered it better that cures be effected by means of easily procured materials.

And you must also bear in mind, in the composition, this point too, which is neglected by most physicians and in which some even go wrong through ignorance. [703] For they trust the dealers in petty wares who profess to supply old oil, not knowing how they produce what they hand over: they melt old pig's fat, once they have thoroughly stripped it of its fibres, and mix it with common oil. For in this way it appears thick to those who look at it and foul-smelling to those who smell it, like the old oil. The foul smell, then, is similar, but to one who remembers each of the two precisely the difference is clear. For the peculiar character of the smell of fat is one thing, that of old oil another. And the thickness of the adulterated oil itself is not continuous nor homoeomerous, as is that of the unadulterated, but it also becomes thicker toward the bottom of the vessel, while what is on the surface is thinner; which is why those who have counterfeited it also stir it up when giving it to the buyers. But even if the oil is truly genuine, without any such knavery, it has indeed this name 'old', but its potency is not close—that of the three-year-old compared with the thirty-year-old, or that of the four-year-old compared with the fifty-year-old. For both oil and fat acquire in addition a certain bitingness with time, when they have grown old.

But this is very great, [704] and greatest is the alteration in respect of power. For both oil and fat become most discutient when they have aged. And having had experience of this, because by some chance I had very old oil and fat, my father having kept them for a long time, I myself in turn laid down both in abundance, when I was quite young, so that I might be able to use them as they grew old, after having used up my father's. But also after this I again, not seldom, stored away both to be aged. And now I have so great a quantity of them as to suffice even if I live a hundred years. And so the drug under discussion, having received oil and fat of forty years, has always in my hands benefited the most malignant of long-standing ulcers, beyond expectation. Such are those ulcers in which the affected part itself has come into so great a cachexia that, even if the blood arriving at it for the sake of nourishment is well-concocted, it alters and corrupts it; or in which what flows in is cacochymous to such a degree that, even if the part had suffered nothing, it would be eaten away by that alone.

It has been said in what precedes that the austere quality is necessary for malignant ulcers, and especially [771] when they are rheumatic. To all these, then, which I have mentioned, litharge and resin and frankincense were mixed in, in order that the drug might become plaster-like. But litharge belongs to the intermediate material, while frankincense is concoctive and pus-producing, for those who take the well-tempered nature as the reference. For it was shown that for moister bodies it is flesh-producing, and moreover that of the concoctive drugs, which indeed also possess the so-called suppurative power, none is strongly discutient, just as none is acrid either. For such things heat moderately, and moreover they soften rather than dry. Rightly, then, some frankincense too was mixed into the composition of the plaster before us, so that it might have something soothing and mild as well. And the oil too is evidently of the same power, mixed in, according to the primary reason, for the sake of the boiling of the plaster, but carrying along with it two powers, the soothing one and the one that blunts the strong drugs, whether these be of an acrid or of an austere power.

Ampelitis earth both dries and disperses, [772] having nothing clearly acrid. And for this reason it is suitable for malignant ulcers, even if you should triturate it by itself and sprinkle it on. Galbanum too was itself mixed into the present composition because it is concoctive and emollient and soothing and anodyne, frankincense also having the same powers, but weaker than in the case of galbanum, since the latter is stronger in respect of both. Terebinth resin too, along with its detergent and discutient quality, has something concoctive of such conditions. As for bitumen, we know that it is of a drying power together with a heat that is not very vehement. To all these, then, the one who composed the plaster mixed in a drug of attractive power, propolis, since he wished it to be a polychreston (of many uses). And all drugs that are of many uses must necessarily have the most varied powers, so that they may treat a greater number of conditions. So too he mixed in no small amount of honey, knowing that it dries and disperses and is most appropriate for parts that are putrefying.

For it too, in turn, belongs among the things that do not putrefy, and it keeps the things mixed with it such, [773] except for those that are in the highest degree disposed to putrefaction, which are both moist and hot. And the one who composed the drug put in honey in greater quantity than the other ingredients. For apart from the three that need to be boiled, asphalt, litharge and ampelitis earth, it exceeds the others; and to these very ingredients, the asphalt, the litharge and the ampelitis, he mixed as much oil as will be suitable for the boiling, taking into estimate also the other dry ingredients that are put into the drug. And moreover, when all had been completely boiled, he required that the myrrh and the aloe be added on top, both of which dry without biting, but differ in that the aloe is astringent, whereas the myrrh is more fine-particled and more drying. I do not know what it was that led Heras to decide to write this panacea with smaller proportions, when it has been written by others with larger ones. For some wrote it as having everything doubled, and some quadrupled.

Of galbanum, at any rate, Heras wrote six drachms and one and a half obols, whereas others wrote ten and a half drachms, just as others again [774] wrote twenty-five, having increased the other ingredients proportionally as well, so that nowhere in the proportion is an obol or a half-obol mentioned. You must therefore pay attention, when comparing the panaceas written by the others with this one, whether they have everything doubled or quadrupled, and if everything has been increased proportionally, not to suppose that those are different from this one. [The Isis, called by some that of Epigonus.] There is a drug of many uses (polychrēston), which they call Isis, praised by all. I shall now set out what Heras wrote about it, which runs word for word as follows. The one called by some that of Epigonus, by others Isis, effective for every wound and for those in the head accompanied by cuttings-through of the bones. It heals without surgical removal (anaskeuē), and is effective also for punctures, splinters, human bites, dog bites, and it draws out the venoms of viper, scorpions, sea-dragons and stingray, and is good for fractures of the limbs with a wound.

[840] Another. Take oak-galls 4 dr., white lead 8 dr., myrrh 4 dr., litharge 8 dr., dross of lead 4 dr.; use finely ground. The remedy of Maia, good for condylomata and rhagades. Take oak-gall 8 dr., molybdaena 8 dr., myrrh 4 dr., white lead 4 dr.; use finely ground. Onetor, for all purposes. Take iris in place of the molybdaena; put in two parts of litharge, and of the remaining ingredients one part each. Septic dry powder of Lecanius Areius. Take orpiment 1 litra, quicklime 2 dr.; grind in water for 30 days, changing the water twice a day, in the sun; then, having dried it, use it. Sitz-bath for haemorrhoids, that of Phanias. Chalkanthos, split alum, chalcitis, raw misy, sandarach, 4 dr. each; have them all finely ground. At the time of use, put old, stale urine of a single man, 2 xestai by measure, into an earthenware basin, and 12 dr. of the drug; keep pouring in urine, so that the two xestai are always maintained. Use this, sitting in it, for 7 days; for within these it takes effect. And when it becomes glutinous at the sediment, smear it around the anus. And just as to these three plasters written out above he added a note—to some that [909] he himself uses them, to others that it is anodyne—so too he bears witness to others, naming them theriacs. At any rate the third from the beginning is written word for word thus: "Theriac which I use." And after this another again, whose heading is as follows: "Eupatorian theriac." But about the theriacs we shall speak in what follows. Now, however, I wish to speak further about the grey plasters written by Andromachus, blaming him because he omitted to state both their professed uses and their preparations. At any rate, one of my physician friends used the one written first of all, and it accomplishes very many things. For it is cicatrizing for ulcers difficult to cicatrize, and especially when callused and hard lips surround the ulcer. It is suitable also for putrefactions and for fistulas and sinuses and large wounds, and in general it is a polychreston (of many uses). The proportion of the drugs composing it has been written as follows: ℞ litharge, 144 drachmas; oil, 5 cotylae; quicklime, 48 drachmas; frankincense, 48 drachmas; burnt copper, 48 drachmas; terebinth, 48 drachmas; aristolochia, 48 drachmas.

of pitch ninety-six drachmas, of wax ninety-six drachmas, of ammoniac [910] ninety-six drachmas. Thus Andromachus wrote it. It is also possible for you to prepare it in a smaller proportion, mixing in a fourth part of each of the ingredients mentioned. For the composition will be as follows: Take litharge, 36 dr.; of quicklime, burnt copper, frankincense, terebinth and aristolochia, a third of each by weight relative to the litharge, that is, 12 dr.; then of pitch, wax and ammoniac incense, of each double the amount of the five drugs mentioned (πέμπτων), I mean the aristolochia, terebinth, frankincense, burnt copper and quicklime. The lime must evidently be unslaked and fresh; in this way the drug becomes useful also against putrefactive conditions. But since Andromachus wrote all the drugs in drachmas, he would have done better to mention the oil also according to the same proportion, stating that what is put in weighs so many drachmas; or, if not this, at any rate he certainly ought to have mentioned the Roman pound.

But as it is, he writes a kotyle, leaving us the customary [911] ambiguity about this measure, whether he wants the kotyle to be of nine measured ounces or of twelve. In my judgement the complete proportion should take the six ounces by weight, because the Roman litra weighs twelve ounces; and if you prepare it at the quarter, the proportion is quite evident. It is also quite evident if someone says that 480 drachms are to be taken for the complete proportion, because the weight-ounce weighs eight drachms. ...is written; and clearly it is possible to prepare it in two ways, knowing that the larger quantity of vinegar makes [912] the drug most powerful. [362] GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK I. A treatise had already been written by me earlier, two of the first books of it having been published, but left behind in the storehouse on the Sacred Way together with the others, when the whole precinct of Peace was burned, and the great libraries on the Palatine as well.

For at that time the books of many others perished, and of mine all those that were lying in that storehouse, since none of my friends in [363] Rome acknowledged having copies of the first two. Since, then, my companions pressed me to write the same treatise again, it seemed necessary to me to make a declaration about the previously published ones, so that no one who had earlier come across them might ever seek the reason why I have treated the same matters twice. In those, then, I made my argument from the beginning of the first book against those who sophistically do away, as far as they can, with the professed virtues of compound drugs, and who also abuse some of the simple ones, at the same time mocking those who have written about them, on the ground that some benefit the liver, others the spleen, others the kidneys or bladder or head or lung. 'For does someone,' they say, 'standing over them give them orders, as in the tragedy: "You, go to the streams of Inachus; and you, proceed around Cadmean Thebes"?

So here: 'you go to the gates at the liver, and you to the bladder or indeed the two kidneys' — or is what has been swallowed into the belly distributed to the liver and from there carried to every part [364] of the body? But this jest at any rate shows that those who say these things are so inexperienced in the power of drugs as not to know that by the sea-hare the lung alone of all the parts in the body is ulcerated, and the bladder alone, in turn, by cantharides, and that by other drugs the stones in the kidneys are broken up, and by yet others the expectorations from the lung and the thorax are made easy, just as by others still other effects are brought about distinctively in some one part. I worked out this argument in many forms in the first of the treatises already written by me before, as I said, just as again in the second I worked out another, since some think that in composition the powers of the simple drugs that are contrary to one another are entirely destroyed. For if, they say, you mix the hottest water with the coldest, neither of the things mixed will remain such as it was before, but some one third thing will come to be, different from both.

But here too they were shown to be talking idle nonsense, because they did not know that some of the things applied to the body act according to their innate powers, others according to their acquired [365] qualities. For who does not know that hemlock or poppy-juice are cooling? And yet, if you heat them strongly and apply them to the body of an animal, you will produce an ulcer much as a cautery does. Just as, again, if you grind mustard in cold air, with very cold water, in the season of winter, and apply it suddenly to a loose-textured and weak body, it will shiver no less than if snow or ice had touched it. But if it remains in contact with the body of an animal for a longer time, it will first produce a sensation of slight heat, then of more, then of so much that one seems to be burned by fire. Conversely, hemlock and poppy-juice applied hot, if they remain in contact with the body for a longer time, will produce so great a cooling that the bodies become insensible, even if they were previously most sensitive.

Since, then, all such matters have been defined by us in the commentaries On the Power of Simple Drugs, which are eleven in number, I shall now turn to the useful teaching itself, in which, once someone has exercised himself, even if he carries about with him no written formulae at all of the many-ingredient preparations, he will not be at a loss for the remedies suitable for each [366] affection, provided that he, as I said, is experienced in the material of simple drugs. Incidentally, this discourse also demonstrates the contentiousness of the Empiricist physicians, who refer nearly all compound drugs to dreams and chance and accidental encounter, except for some very few, which they say they have discovered according to the reasoning common to all human beings, which they themselves call epilogismos. As when we mix with one another (μίξωμιν, read μίξωμεν) drugs that have displayed through experience the same action, but one having acted better or worse on one body and another on another: "it seemed reasonable to us," say some of the Empiricists—for certainly not all of them—"to compound several such drugs together, so that at least one of them might be found to be appropriate to the nature of the body being treated." This, they say, is what happened in the case of this very novel drug called the "cephalic", all those ingredients having been mixed in it which are known, even singly, to produce flesh in wounds. But by what rationale verdigris, when mixed with a simple cerate, produces a flesh-producing drug, though neither of the ingredients mixed produces flesh, they no longer say.

You learned also that the first indication of the treatment is discovered from the morbid conditions, and that the nature of the affected part gives a joint indication together with these, along with the mixture of the air that surrounds us; and many of the best physicians consider in addition the constitution (of the atmosphere), age, season and region, as well as pursuits and habits, [371] about which some things will be said now too, wherever there is need of them. All these things, then, you must thus hold in memory ready to hand, if you wish in every place to be well supplied with drugs, both simple and compound; and further, in addition to these, that sometimes one single naturally occurring simple drug is sufficient to cure the condition contrary to nature, while sometimes there is need of a compound one; and why indeed we do this must be stated next. [What the use of compound drugs is.] If it were possible to cure all the conditions contrary to nature by means of simple drugs alone, we would never have needed a compound drug; but as it is, this is not the case. For often, wishing the body to be heated through up to a certain degree, we have no simple of that sort. For the drug that treats must be proportionate to the condition being treated. If, then, the condition is cold, standing removed from the natural one by four numbers, it is obvious to everyone that the drug which is to treat it must be hotter than the well-proportioned by an equal quantity.

[372] But when sometimes no such simple is available, if we have at hand two, of which the one is hotter by five degrees and the other by three, by mixing them we shall produce the mean, which exceeds the well-tempered state by four degrees. Some of the simples, moreover, cannot even be brought into use without mixture with something else, as for instance when we wish to apply an emplastic drug to someone; for none of the simples is suitable for such a use. Neither asphalt, then, nor wax nor resin, just as neither pitch nor propolis nor ladanum, and still less verdigris and white lead or litharge or molybdaena or any of the other metallic drugs. In the same way neither can herbs by themselves make an emplastic drug. Reasonably, therefore, those who first compounded emplastic drugs devised the plan of boiling the metallic substances with an admixture of oil, of melting the meltable ones, and of adding to them also dry herbs, pounded and sifted.

In other conditions, again, there is need of one single drug from among the naturally occurring ones, but we mix something in with it, sometimes [373] intending to blunt the vehemence of its power, sometimes to mitigate its unpleasantness, just as Hippocrates said in the work On Regimen in Acute Diseases in the following passage: 'If the pain is beneath the diaphragm and gives no sign toward the collarbone, one must soften the belly either with black hellebore or with peplion, mixing with the black (hellebore) daucus or seseli or cumin or anise or some other of the fragrant things, and with peplion the juice of silphium.' In this passage Hippocrates clearly indicated that there is need of the purging drug, but that its unpleasantness in the drinking and in the belly alone requires a sweetening agent. For indeed many of the drugs that are drunk are so unpleasant to those who take them that the stomach is upset and they are vomited at once, while some, even if they are able to remain for a short time in the belly, are nonetheless afterwards vomited, having stirred up foul eructations.

And just as, for the purgatives, such drugs as those which Hippocrates mentioned are, as it were, sweeteners, so too for the drugs called anodynes there are others that mitigate their vehemence, as when we administer poppy juice [374] or henbane seed or the bark of mandrake root; so that this too is a need for the composition of drugs. But the greatest need is in the case of affections that require opposite powers at the same time, such as repellent and discutient, or detergent and smoothing, or thickening and at the same time thinning of humours; and accordingly the most widely useful and the best drugs have the opposite powers in them, as we shall show. But there is also this need for the composition of drugs, when we wish to have a single drug suitable against many of the venomous beasts or deadly drugs—a need which produced the antidote called Theriac, and in addition to it the Mithridatium and many others. There are also certain other needs, lesser than those mentioned, but nevertheless often compelling us to have recourse to the composition of drugs, all of which you will learn in this treatise. For now I shall at once begin on the matters proposed, mentioning first a plaster drug of the widest usefulness composed by me.

[375] [On the plaster-drug made with chalcitis.] As to the reasoning by which I composed the plaster made with chalcitis, which I call phoinikine (the date-plaster) — agglutinative of wounds and cicatrising them, and curative of inflammations, whenever, once melted, it has the consistency of a liquid cerate — leave the Empiricists to confess their own ignorance, and stand apart also from the followers of Thessalus, who are ignorant of the finest of the drugs discovered by physicians, those composed out of opposite powers; and exercise your reasoning so as to be able to compose drugs, using the same methods as I do, in order that you yourselves may be persuaded by actual practice that the drugs discovered by our predecessors were all composed by reasoning, the 'chance encounter' of the Empiricists being nonsense. So now the rationale of the composition of the drug before us must be stated. Old oil and fat have a discutient power, while chalcitis and the juice of the date have a repellent and astringent power.

From these, then, I composed a drug which you know very many people already use, [376] because it has been judged better than all those of the same kind, having been tested by the works themselves. For reason discovers the composition, but experience judges the excellence of what has been discovered, so that things composed with art are trusted even by those inexperienced in rational methods. And I mixed in with the drugs just mentioned litharge, which is able to contribute nothing great either to those that repel what flows in or to those that disperse what is already fixed in the inflamed parts; for it is of a drying faculty, yet not a strong one; but I mixed it in as a drug suitable for the composition of a plaster, for it is boiled together with the aforesaid until a consistency that does not stain. The fat must be unsalted and as old as possible, and the oil likewise old. For you have learned, I think, that oil and the fat of pigs are of a faculty similar to one another, the fat being slightly more emollient and hotter in its faculty.

You also learned that as they grow old they become finer in their parts and more discutient, and for this reason the new ones are more soothing for painful inflammations, [377] while the old ones are more beneficial for those that are not such. And the more chronic and hard to resolve the inflammation is, the more useful are the old ones, and they alone are sufficient to cure it, when nothing is any longer flowing into the affected part. But if something is flowing in, the power of the drug too must be mixed, such as is that of the one composed by me. For this reason, at any rate, I mixed chalcitis and palm with the discutient drugs, knowing that there are altogether few inflammations that become chronic in which nothing flows in; for it is because of the humours flowing into them that they are accustomed to become chronic. But when inflammations are beginning and increasing, the power of the astringent and cooling drugs ought to predominate, and for this reason, when melted down to the thickness of a liquid cerate, this emplastic drug becomes quite a polychreston (of many uses), sometimes taking in addition wine or vinegar or water, and sometimes being melted with oil of unripe olives (omotribes) or with one of those that have astringency, such as the Spanish and the Istrian, or with one of the sweet ones without astringency, or with old oil.

And [378] I have often melted the drug in myrtle oil and in quince oil, in those cases where there is need of a stronger astringency. This composition of the drug, then, is made according to the following proportion. Of the old fat, which those who sell it call axoungion, let there be 2 litrai; of the old oil, 3 litrai; and of litharge, 3 litrai; and of chalcitis, 4 ounces. One must boil them in the following manner. Having removed the membranes of the fat and crushed the remainder so that it becomes easy to melt, after this melt it over a fire, then take a strainer and strain it, so that it becomes pure, containing nothing of membrane, drawing in weight the aforesaid two litrai; then you will mix the 4 ounces of chalcitis, finely ground, together with the three litrai of oil, with the fat, adding in also the 3 litrai of litharge, and having united everything in a mortar, put it into the cauldron, stirring with a stick of palm-wood. A single branch of the large ones will suffice for you, so as to use the thick part of the wood for stirring, in the function of the so-called spathe; for thus they name that with which they stir the things being prepared, and we, holding to clarity, shall call it the same as they do.

But the part [379] continuous with the thick part of the branch you should clean all around, and, having rubbed off the thin outgrowths on either side, cut it up, having first scraped off the bark all round, so that the pieces, when thrown into the drug, may impart to it the juice within themselves. Now it is proper to use the spatula straightaway from the beginning, but to throw in the thin pieces of the palm when the drug has come to a consistency like that of a cerate. For if you throw them in from the beginning, the juice of what has been thrown in, which we wish to remain, will be consumed through the boiling. And as for the spatula itself, with which you stir the drug from the beginning, when the part that is being soaked in the cauldron becomes dry, so that it no longer has its own juice, cut it off and throw it away and use the remainder. And again likewise, if it should happen that the part being soaked in the drug has dried out, cut it off again. It is evident that the branch of the palm must not have been cut from the tree many days beforehand, for in time it dries out and becomes juiceless. So, if it is winter, let it be removed on the previous day; but in summer the branch must be removed from the tree on that very day on which you boil the drug.

But when the drug, being boiled in this way, [380] has become non-staining (ἀμόλυντον), you will use it as a plaster both upon ulcers that are hard to cicatrize and upon fresh bleeding wounds; and, melting it down with oil, upon inflamed parts, in podagra, in arthritis, in buboes, in phymata, in burns, in chilblains, in fractures, in contusions, and in all the so-called rheumatic conditions. Indeed, many of those who operate on hernias also apply it immediately after the surgery, carrying through the treatment with it together with the affusions and the poultices. If, however, you add six ounces of chalcitis, which is half a pound, the drug will be for you more agglutinative of large wounds and more cicatrizing of ulcers that are hard to cicatrize. But in this respect there are also other drugs of the same power; whereas, when it has been melted with oil, one should trust it more than all the others in the rheumatic conditions. At any rate in Rome, where very many such conditions occur, nothing has won such approval.

It is suitable, as I said, also for podagra and arthritis at every time [381] at which there are no violent pains requiring affusions and soothing cataplasms. When, then, such conditions (διαθέσεως) are beginning and still increasing, once you have melted the drug, having let it cool and scraping it with a spatula-probe, throw what has been scraped into a mortar, pouring in wine and rubbing it with the hands against the mortar, so that it takes up the wine. Let this wine be from the more austere ones, middling in age, not thick in consistency, but as far as possible rather transparent. For such wine, being of finer parts, sinks into the depth of the bodies. Pour it onto the melted drug up to this point, rubbing with the hands, until it takes it up and it is mixed in, and the liquid does not float alongside unmixed with the drug that is being rubbed and softened. And even without cooling it beforehand and scraping it, one will be able to mix in the wine by pouring it into the melted drug while it is still hot. At the beginnings of inflammations, then, the repellent power ought to prevail, but during the increases one should take away something of it and add some of the discutient power.

But when the swelling of the inflammation [382] has arrived at its proper peak, the faculties—the repellent and the discutient—must be comparable to one another, unless indeed some violent pain requires a soothing drug. And as the inflammation declines, the discutient faculty should prevail, so that at that time no wine whatsoever is mixed in. And moreover, also in the melting itself, where we wish the astringent quality to prevail considerably, it is fitting to put in Spanish oil, or Istrian oil, or that called omphakinon and omotribes (oil of unripe olives). But where we wish both faculties to be comparable, to melt it with sweet oil that is neither fresh nor old. And when we wish to make it discutient, old oil or castor oil (kikinon) is suitable. And let the proportion of the emplastic drug in the melting be as follows: let the oil be for you a little more than the drug, and more, obviously, in summer, so that there are ten ounces of the drug, while of the oil one would sufficiently put in one pound (litra).

It is quite evident that it becomes more active when it contains more of the drug, but more soothing [383] and more pain-relieving the more liquid it becomes when melted with rose-oil. It takes on the consistency of a cerate for anointing when one litra of the drug is melted in half a litra of oil. Such a preparation is useful in the declines of inflammations. And nothing so benefits the inflammatory swellings that arise spontaneously in the seat and in the rectum. At that time it must have been melted with a greater quantity of oil, so that it can be injected through a straight-bored horn having a pig's bladder fastened to it, as we are accustomed to use in such cases. And in these cases I have often melted it with rose-oil, with a cauldron placed beneath the vessel in which it is melted, the cauldron containing hot water and set upon glowing coals or over a smokeless flame. When, however, it has been melted in the aforesaid proportion, so as to have the consistency of a liquid cerate, it benefits also the ulcers on the genitals and those on the seat, and not least all the others too, even down to ulcerated chilblains and burns. For it quickly renders them all free of inflammation and clean, and it fills them with flesh, and firm flesh at that, especially when it contains more chalcitis.

It is quite evident [384] that wine too must be mixed into the drug that is to accomplish this. And if it takes in addition some vinegar, it is best for burns, applied both at once and afterwards at every stage, whether the burn already has blisters or not. And it is obvious that even if someone is scalded by boiling water, this affection too is called a burn (pyrikauton). But if someone applies the drug before inflammation has set in, nothing so prevents the formation of inflammation, so that, as I said, some of those who operate on hernias use it immediately, without even having first moistened the wound. And for contusions and fractures and parts struck in any manner whatever it is most suitable when applied in liquid form. And when it is held in place with bandages in the manner of a fracture bandaging, it is of wonderful benefit to all oedemas and emphysemata (windy swellings). But when the body is full of bad humours or also excessively sensitive, one must, when applying it at the beginning to the bruised and struck parts, mix with it fresh [juice] of henbane.

But if you should be at a loss for fresh (juice), on account of the season of the year [385] or the locality, you will have no less (benefit) by adding in that which was put away during the summer, such as is the kind brought to us at Rome from Crete every year. And still more than this, by mixing in the juice of mandrake you will make the drug anodyne. Know that this too is brought from Crete, of the finest quality, in earthenware cups. It suffices to mix one ounce of the juice to a pound of oil of the plaster that is being melted; and at times you may put in more, and at times less, according to the need of the condition. In the case of such bodies it also contributes that the drug be melted in rose-oil. As for those parts of the body that have been bruised from a fall, or struck with wood or stone, even if some ecchymoma arises, one must at the very beginning immediately apply the melted drug, as has been said, with wine mixed in. But it is fitting on the third day, or at all events the fourth, if the part should be free of inflammation, to remove the wine and to melt the plaster with old oil. For if the ecchymomata are astringed further, they become difficult to disperse.

I use this drug also for erysipelata, and especially [386] those of a phlegmonous character, and still much more for erysipelatous phlegmonai. At the beginning, then, I apply it after melting it in rose-oil prepared from oil of unripe olives (omotribes) and unsalted; for such oil is best for erysipelata. And when it has been thus melted, let there be mixed with it in the mortar, kneaded in and thoroughly soaked through whole and entire, juice of strychnos, or, if this is not available, of psyllion. And when it is summer, also the juice of unripe grape (omphax) together with that of purslane or houseleek. For the juice of unripe grape by itself astringes more than is needed; and astringency of such a degree harms erysipelata, for it shuts in their heat by condensing the skin. Conversely, the juice of purslane cannot even be pressed out by itself because of its viscosity. It is best, therefore, after pressing out the juice of unripe grape, to pour it upon the purslane that has been pounded in a mortar, and so to pound it again; then, when the mixture of both has been thoroughly unified, to press out the juice. In the same way you will also press out the juice of houseleek; for on its own it is not possible to press out an abundant quantity from this either, just as not from kotyledon.

And if you also press out fresh juice from the apples of the mandrake [387] when they are at their peak, you will make the drug more suitable. But if it should not be the season, one must at any rate mix in some of that which is brought from Crete or from some other such region. I am also accustomed to mix henbane juice with it, and sometimes mekoneion as well; this is the name given to the sap of the poppy. It is better, together with this, also to add in some glaukion. Much weaker than these, but easily procured, is the juice of thridakine (lettuce), both that of the wild kind and that of the cultivated, which all the Greeks of today call not thridakine but thridax, naming only the wild one thridakine. Weaker than these for cooling are the juices of seris (endive), of polygonon (knotgrass), of triphyllon (trefoil) and of mouse-ear; nevertheless these too cool, and more than they does the duckweed (phakos) from the marshes. If none of these is at hand, mix in vinegar and water. And all such drugs should have their acquired qualities cold, the vessels being set in very cold water or in snow.

And let the phoinikine drug itself likewise be cooled when it is applied [388] to erysipelata, until their very fiery character has ceased. It is quite evident that the things which benefit erysipelatous conditions through an acquired cold quality must be changed continually, and especially when the erysipelas is exact, without being mixed with phlegmone. When, however, the very fiery character has ceased, or when from the outset there was no exact erysipelas at all, but either an erysipelatous phlegmone or a phlegmonous erysipelas, we no longer have any need of the acquired cooling; rather, we shall also abstain from the strongly cooling juices, mixing the moderately cold ones with the melted drug. And after these let us now also mix in juice of linseed and of chamomile; and after this we shall use the melted drug by itself alone, mixing in nothing else.

But if at some point the erysipelas has already become livid, from the power of the cooling agents, one ought no longer even to call such a thing erysipelas; and at that time it is fitting to abstain not only from the admixture of wine, but also from rose-oil and the astringent oils, for phoinikine alone, melted in old oil, is sufficient to disperse what has become livid [389], and at that time the affected parts are fomented with hot water and scarified. And if it should ever seem good to you to do this, one must at once apply the liquid drug of the melted phoinikine containing wine, and after one day remove the wine. But if we take over an erysipelas already cooled to a greater degree by physicians who have cooled it immoderately, so that it is already even turning black, we shall make greater use of the fomentation and the scarification. And apart from these, we shall mix some unslaked lime into the liquid drug; but if the affected parts are soft-fleshed, we shall mix in washed lime. Good at that time also is the juice of coriander mixed into the drug. This indeed, even with rose cerate, is of great benefit; and for these, namely such conditions, many other drugs as well will be described in the following discussion, some having a power similar to phoinikine, others even more active.

For rheumatic conditions this is the best drug of all, and one that has often accomplished something beyond hope. [390] Thus once, when a thigh had suppurated near the groin, the inflammation that occupied the whole of it being unconcocted, the leg was positioned by us so that the ichors would flow out toward the groin. Through the ulcer that formed—this having happened over a rather long time—the flux that had settled into the thigh was indeed evacuated, but a certain fistulous condition arose beneath the skin throughout the whole thigh, so that I wished to divide it near the kneecap, in order that on either side there might be an outlet for the ichors, and an easy passage for the liquid drugs that were injected to pass through further. But when the thigh was unbound on the following day, on which I had resolved to cut it, everything was found to have fallen together, dry and without moisture. It is clear, then, that on that day too it was reasonable to use the drug, and likewise on the next, and on the following days, since on each of them the part became better-coloured and as a whole healthier.

So, when the youth had been cured in this way, I afterwards treated many rheumatic conditions with the drug, ones which had a single opening, [391] but whose interior was unagglutinated and fistulous. One must not desist from its use, even if it appears to bring no perceptible benefit for many days. For later, at some point, in a single day it displays a very great benefit all at once; so use it with confidence always in rheumatic conditions, when a soft-fleshed person or some child or woman is affected, adding, in accordance with the aforesaid proportion, four ounces of chalcitis; but when the affected body is strong and hard, adding in proportion either one ounce or two, so that there are five or six ounces of chalcitis, three pounds of each of the two, the old oil and the litharge, and two of the old fat, which I said those who sell it call axoungion. And in rheumatic conditions let it be diluted with sweet oil that is neither fresh nor old, and let it take in addition the austere wine, this being of middle age.

This drug has refuted the nonsense of Thessalus, since it displays a most effective benefit while being composed of ingredients opposite in their faculties, of which, if you remove [392] the one, it will accomplish none of the things mentioned. For neither, from the astringents alone without the relaxants, will it accomplish anything noteworthy in rheumatic conditions, or in general in inflammations that are beginning and increasing—for it will not have the soothing quality—nor, from the relaxants alone, will it have the discutient quality, when it is made without astringency, relaxants to which it belongs to soften what is becoming hard. It would, however, be thoroughly relaxant and moderately emollient, if it had the oil and the fat not very old. At any rate the drug which Mnaseas compounded has the oil, the litharge and the fat in equal amounts to one another, and it is most contrary to inflammations that are beginning and increasing. Clearly this drug of ours, too, has all the things that Mnaseas' drug has: the litharge, the fat and the oil. But if it takes in none of the astringents—?

it makes the parts effeminate and dissolves their tone, for which reason they also become rheumatic; for you have learned that it is not always through much heat, as some suppose, that the parts of the body are afflicted with flux, but this happens to them [393] rarely. Rather, it is the weakness of the parts that produces the rheumatic conditions, a weakness which for the most part is brought about in accordance with a cold dyscrasia. If, then, one moistens and warms them with relaxing drugs, they become completely slack and feeble. Conversely again, one who strongly astringes the swellings in rheumatic conditions will seem at the beginning to accomplish something, but will render the residue itself hard to dissolve and scirrhous. And for the most part such conditions do not even tolerate the application of excessively astringent agents, being pained and tensed by them. And every pain exacerbates inflamed parts and becomes a cause of fluxes, even if the affected person does not have a rheumatic dyscrasia.

But it is no wonder that Thessalus, being inexperienced in the works of the medical art and unable to discover the conditions by reasoning, is ignorant of everything that pertains to the cures of inflammations; but you, who have often observed the most evident benefit, in many conditions, both of this phoenicine plaster and of other drugs composed of opposite powers, must yourselves also attempt, whenever you are at a loss [394] for those already compounded, to compound drugs according to the same method, from the materials readily available in that locality—when an inflammation is expected to occur, or has even already begun, drugs having more astringency; during the increases themselves, less; and during the acmes and declines, drugs having more of the relaxing and discutient power. Always, however, let both be mixed, the repellent and the discutient, except if at some time, when the influxes have already completely ceased and the body is empty, one might without danger proceed to the discutient powers, just as in the first onsets to the repellent ones. [On the plasters prepared with litharge.] Since, in the composition of my phoenicine plaster, I said that the discutient power lies in the old fat and in the oil, and the contracting and repellent power in the chalcitis and in the date, and these cannot without litharge produce an emplastic drug, for this reason it seemed good to me to go through next the matter of the use of litharge.

For with respect to the power of the phoinikine plaster [395] one must suppose that it neither counteracts it in any way nor contributes to it, but has only the status of a material suitable for the making of an emplastic drug. It therefore seemed to me reasonable to go through the account of such drugs with litharge as an example. There are not a few of them that contribute either no power or a very small one to what is being prepared, but which supply the service of a material toward the drug's becoming emplastic or cerate-like. For litharge, neither clearly heating, just as it is neither cooling nor moistening, has a slight drying power, at the first remove from the things that are exactly intermediate, in this respect, namely moistening and drying; nor indeed is it of a pore-blocking power, just as it is not of a de-obstructing one, and likewise it is neither detergent, just as it is not clearly befouling, but it has departed somewhat gently from the intermediates toward the thicker-in-parts. But in the course of more prolonged boiling it lays aside even this, being melted and altered by the power of the fire. Alone and by itself, raw, it benefits chafings of the thighs arising from walking, from which it is also clear that it dries slightly.

And that it has [396] neither a pungent or sweet quality, nor a sour or bitter or harsh or astringent or, in general, styptic one, taste is a sufficient witness, as are also the ulcers, which are neither bitten by it nor heated nor cooled nor cleansed nor filled with flesh, nor, when they have grown excess flesh, reduced. It is therefore open to us to use litharge for many purposes, sometimes carrying out its boiling with oil and water until a plaster-like consistency is reached, sometimes in oil and vinegar, and sometimes in oil and wine. In whichever of these it is boiled, the drug becomes better when boiled for a longer time. And this will be achieved by the quantity of the liquids mixed in. For litharge too is among the meltable drugs, being wholly fused, just like resin and wax, but not immediately upon touching the fire; hence it escapes the notice of many, and they think that it is not fused at all.

When boiled with vinegar-and-oil (oxelaion), then, it melts more quickly, just as it also does with verdigris (ios), verdigris itself obviously being of a nature to be fused, as are chalcitis [397] and misy. Of these, chalcitis undergoes this most quickly, litharge most slowly; and in between these are verdigris and misy. Sory too is fused, in a longer time, for it is more earthy and more stony than chalcitis and misy. But about these things it will be spoken again later. As for litharge, if you boil it in vinegar-and-oil you will melt it more quickly, in water-and-oil (hydrelaion) more slowly; nevertheless it is fused even so, provided that each of the liquids is double its quantity. I myself have often mixed in even more than double, as will be said a little later. It is better to mix the three together straightaway from the start in a mortar, the litharge, the water and the oil. And if you are concerned that the drug should come out white, put in oil that is purer and more transparent, and water likewise pure and clear, and let it be boiled in an open-air spot exposed to the sun. For murky air blackens the drug, whereas clear air contributes greatly to whiteness, just as does the water sprinkled over it in such air.

Beware also of carrying out the boiling over wood, or over charcoals that are just beginning to burn through, [398] for the smoke easily blackens it. So burn the charcoals through beforehand, and when they are thoroughly glowing, then begin to boil. And if these should not suffice to complete the boiling, prepare charcoals in the same way on another hearth and set them under that cauldron. As regards the drug becoming white, then, what one must guard against has been stated sufficiently. It becomes more adhesive to the degree that it contains more of the liquid, as has been said; so that if you put in one litra of each of the three, it will be hard to fall off (δυσαπόπτωτον). And indeed the litharge remains unmelted, and this very thing is the chief cause of its easily falling off, just as, conversely, of its staying on for longer, if the litharge, having been boiled, has been fused and altered. It will be whiter and will be boiled more quickly if two litrai of water are put in to three of each, of litharge and of oil. And this I customarily use for small ulcers. The power of the drug boiled with water is evident to us if we remember what was said in the treatise on simple drugs.

[399] [On the plaster prepared from litharge and water-and-oil (hydrelaion).] Water always moistens and cools according to its own proper substance; but when it has taken on an acquired heat, it warms for as long as it retains that heat, and when it has become cold it cools. The oil, for its part, if it is fresh, does not work against the drug, for it remains both moist and moderately cold, which is precisely what soft-fleshed bodies and those full of bad humours most require. Women, then, and children, and those among adults who have a soft habit of body — and these are also white in colour — need drugs of this kind. Boiled, as has been said, with a larger quantity of oil and water, it becomes so hard to fall off that it does not even run off when they bathe. And indeed it is beneficial for wounds that are cicatrizing that the drug remain in place for several days in succession, for in this way they cicatrize both better and more quickly.

It is evident that such a drug is suited to scratches and abrasions and, in a word, to small ulcers, for which the cerate called "moist" (parhygros) and certain other similar ones are more useful [400] than those having a strong power, such as we apply to large wounds. Concerning the general power of all of these it has been written in the third book of the Therapeutic Method, in which I went through the generic and common accounts, which they call universal, for each difference of ulcer, showing of what sort the powers of the drugs that are to cure them ought to be; here, however, I go through the particular materials, both defining the proportions of the ingredients mixed and showing the manners in which, when prepared, they will turn out best. Litharge, then, prepared with water-and-oil (hydrelaion), as has been said, makes the plaster at once most agreeable to the touch and hard to fall off, and moreover white in appearance, having a moderate cooling power, by the use of which it both prevents anything from flowing to the ulcerated parts and drives back again toward the surrounding places what has already flowed in, so that the matter becomes such as when we make a sponge soaked in cold water and apply it to some part of the body.

For that [sponge] makes the whole place wrinkled and contracted, not [401] only repelling what flows in, but also squeezing out what is contained within it toward the neighbouring parts. And the plaster now mentioned in our account would be said to dry not by its primary power, but accidentally. For properly and primarily it is the things that disperse and those that alter the temperaments toward the drier that are called drying; but accidentally also those that, through cooling, check what flows in and squeeze out what is contained. In general, none of the moistening things, whether primarily or accidentally, is beneficial for ulcers, as has been shown in the third book of the Therapeutic Method. [On the plaster prepared from litharge and vinegar-and-oil.] Concerning litharge prepared with water-and-oil (hydrelaion), then, this too is sufficient. It is now time to pass on to the one compounded with vinegar-and-oil (oxelaion). The drug becomes moderately drying if each of the two, the oil and the vinegar, is double the litharge. And if the oil is also old, it dries still more.

[402] But if more than double of each of them is put in, it makes the drug stronger, so that it heals even fistulas, as many as do not yet have a hard callus. One part of litharge is put in, and two and a half of each of those. And indeed, having sometimes mixed in triple of each, I boiled the drug through a whole day. It became black, but shining like fine asphalt. This has a most drying power, and it treats ulcers hard to heal and fistulas such as I mentioned, and it is agglutinative of bloody wounds. In a word, it is drying without biting. For this reason, therefore, it also treats all the other ulcers, both the greater and the smaller, up to cicatrization. It is worth going through some other of its works as well, which one would perhaps not even expect, so far as concerns the contemptible character of the material. For when someone in a fever had reached a crisis through a parotid swelling that suppurated, a small fistula was left behind, which was shown to me in the country six months after its beginning.

For the boy was a farmer's son, about fifteen years of age; having given him, to be applied, as much of this plaster [403] as I had with me, I myself returned to the city, and, being caught up in a good many medical engagements, I forgot about the one who had received the drug. But after two months he came back healthy, though I had not at all expected this to happen. For when we passed a pig's bristle through the little fistula, it appeared to advance as far as the articulation. By chance, however, a few days later another boy was shown to me, of the same age as the previous one and having a similar condition; I applied some of the plaster, and it came about that he too was completely restored to health. After this I cured not a few persons of the same condition with this drug—children and women and young men. If, then, you too wish to use it for such cases, put in the oldest oil and the sharpest vinegar, one made, clearly, from wine alone, not as some prepare it by mixing in water. And let the vinegar be as pure and transparent as possible.

For thus it would be more fine-particled and better for [404] the purposes we require. With this drug I have also often cured muscles that had become hardened. [On the plaster prepared from litharge and oinelaion (wine-and-oil).] It remains, then, for me to go through the litharge prepared with oinelaion, which in the matter of proportion has the same features as those already described, and correspondingly has the excesses of its power according to the quantity of the liquids. For I have prepared it putting in the three in equal amounts, and with each of the liquids double the litharge, and adding a further half beyond the double, and sometimes even triple. And I once prepared it also in the following way. In the summer season, in hot sun, each day the litharge was triturated with Falernian wine, and this went on for fifteen days, with me pouring in wine again if the previous wine happened to have been dispersed. After the said days the drug, once boiled, became sufficiently drying. I have also used it against rheumatic conditions in the same way as the phoinikine, melting it down with oil, just as has been said before in the case of that one.

And I also cured with it a thigh that had long been hardened, and I applied it to [405] bleeding wounds, and it was most excellent for everything. Accordingly, in its case, even if one does not have Falernian ready to hand, let there be another wine, tawny in colour but thin in consistency, so as to be translucent. Such is the Ariousian, cultivated on Chios, and the very fragrant Lesbian, which is produced in small quantity at Mitylene, but at Eresos and Methymna is at once both more abundant and better, and the Tmolite, which resembles the Falernian. This too is very thin and translucent, tawny in colour, moderately sweet and very fragrant. When it has been aged it is possible to use it for all the purposes for which the Falernian too is used. And there is also another Tmolite wine, similar to it in colour and consistency, but neither sweet nor fragrant; it has a certain astringency, but falls far short of the sweet one. These, then, are the drugs that are produced when the litharge is boiled. [On the use of raw litharge.] Without boiling, by itself, as I said, it is useful for chafings (παρατρίμματα).

But if it has been prepared beforehand by being ground with vinegar or wine and dried, it becomes a remedy for ulcers that are hard to cicatrize [406] on account of moisture. And if indeed you should wish it to be non-biting, you will use it washed. [How one should wash litharge and the remaining metallic substances.] It is washed easily, since on account of its innate heaviness it quickly settles in the liquids in which it is levigated. Now it becomes most completely non-biting when washed with water; but to sensitive bodies it brings a slight sensation of bitingness when it has been washed with vinegar or wine. One must, having first levigated it sufficiently with the liquid through a whole day, let it settle during the night; then on the following day, at dawn, pouring off the liquid, pour on another in its place; then again grind in the same way, and pour off again on the following day, and do this as long as some sort of fine scum of the litharge appears together with the liquid. But when nothing any longer floats on top, it is no longer fitting to pour off either; it is better, however, to grind for several more days, even if nothing floats on top. And do this in hot sun; for in this way the drug becomes more drying.

It is quite evident that it is better to do this in the summer season, not only in the case of litharge but also of the [407] others, all those which are prepared in this manner. For cadmia and the scale of copper and burnt copper, and further, in addition to these, the so-called diphryges and white lead and misy and sory and stimmi and all the stones, and besides these lime, are, in the same way as litharge, both washed and levigated with one of the liquids mentioned. Sometimes I also carry out their preparation with sea-water; about these things more will be said again as the discourse proceeds. For at present my task is to go through the emplastra, which the more recent physicians both write and pronounce with the rho in the last syllable, just as all are accustomed to do in the case of the kentrion and the melotris. For in the case of these too the original imposition of the names seems to have taken place without the rho, the kentrion having been named from kentein (to prick), its final syllable not having the rho, and the melotris being compounded from mele (probe) and ous (ear). Now, however, since nearly everyone pronounces them with the rho, one would not err in uttering them in the same way as they do, and especially kentrion.

For it has been shown [408] by me, in my writings against those who censure people who commit solecisms, that the Attic men themselves too followed the prevailing usage. For it has been shown also by others before me that a manifold change of the Attic dialect itself has taken place, and that all those whose reputation among the Greeks for skill in speech is greatest follow the custom of their own time. And so we too, since we now find all the books on drugs having the name of the emplastron written with the rho, shall ourselves also follow the prevailing usage. [On the drugs prepared with molybdaena.] It has been said by me also earlier that the use of molybdaena is closely similar to that of litharge. For everything that is compounded with litharge can also be prepared with molybdaena. In their power they differ from one another to this extent, that the substance of molybdaena is more coarse-particled and colder, while that of litharge is more fine-particled and intermediate between hot and cold.

But with respect to the colours of the drugs that are prepared by means of them, there is a certain difference [409] in it, inasmuch as molybdaina leads the colours toward the greyer. For this reason too, of the white plasters that contain not only white lead but also litharge, none is prepared with molybdaina; for when it has been mixed in, the white colour becomes ash-coloured. The properties of the power, however, not only are not lost—at least in the case of the white plaster prepared with water-and-oil (hydrelaion)—but even become better, and especially in the case of those with soft flesh. But when we wish to disperse something, litharge is better than molybdaina. So too with all the other drugs which have been recorded as being compounded with litharge: if one puts in molybdaina, both the colour of the drug and its power undergo alteration to the degree that has just been shown by me.
