[On the white plasters prepared with litharge and white lead.] Either for the sake of the colour physicians prepare the white plasters by mixing white lead with the litharge, or for the sake of adding some astringency and cooling to the drug; and seeing that such a drug also turns black [410] when it is boiled for too long, and especially when over wood—and that perhaps not even smokeless—and not in clean air, they are compelled to remove it quickly from the fire, and for this very reason to mix in neither abundant water nor oil. They therefore reasonably devised adding resin to it, so that it might be ductile and cohesive, acquiring a certain viscosity, and especially when the liquid resin is mixed in. But the drug becomes worse through such a mixture, since resin too has something biting, while its drying property is not at all vigorous—and you have learnt that ulcers have especial need of this. Some resins, then, are even very biting, and all of them will be discussed again later. The gentlest among them are two: first the terebinth, and second the one called larch. It is better, then, to mix in some of these when one wishes to prepare such a plaster. And all become much more pleasant to the touch, both those prepared with resin when they take on some wax, and those prepared with wax when resin is mixed in with them. One must therefore add wax too along with the resin.

And in order that the colour of the plaster [411] may be preserved white, the wax ought to be white. Naturally white is the so-called Pontic wax—for it is now customarily so named even if it comes from some other region, because white wax is produced in the greatest quantity in Pontus and in the least in other regions. Not naturally white is the wax named Tyrrhenian. This one, then, has no evident acridity; but some of the naturally white kinds are acrid, and these must first be washed. Their washing is done by melting them over a fire, then throwing them into clean spring water, and stirring them about there and rinsing them thoroughly. In the same way pitch and resin and what is called physema must also be washed; about these a more precise account will be given later. But now, since I am writing the composition of the white plaster, I shall relate in order the remainder of what I mentioned.

For when wax has been added, together with the resin, to the white lead and the litharge that have been boiled beforehand, until the drug becomes thoroughly non-staining, you would now have a white plaster, if you wish, sometimes adding water to it, sometimes oil alone, and this sometimes [412] new, sometimes old. For you have already heard beforehand what power water and old oil have. And you know also that both omphacine oil and that cultivated in Iberia, which they now call Hispania, impart something of astringency to the drug. The Istrian oil has not only slight astringency but also bitterness. The preparations made with the astringent oils will therefore have a difference from those made with the sweet oil, insofar as at the beginning and at the end of ulcers all those that have something of astringency are better, but in the middle stages the sweet ones. For at the beginnings ulcers need the repellent drugs, so that they may not even begin to become inflamed; and thereafter the more relaxing ones: if inflammation does not occur, for the sake of transpiration; but if it has already occurred, also on account of that, so that it may be resolved more quickly. It is quite evident that the account concerns a small inflammation. For a great inflammation cannot supervene upon small ulcers, for which we use these white plasters, when no error has been committed in addition.

And that the astringent quality is also beneficial when the ulcers are already cicatrizing, [413] no one is unaware. It is therefore now time to state the proportion of the drugs compounded into the most useful white plaster. [The weighing of the plaster.] Let there be an equal part of each of the two metallic substances, the white lead and the litharge, and this, if you wish, let the weight be one litra of each; and of oil, a measure equal to both together, or, as the Romans name it, two litrae; and of wax let there be half a litra, and of terebinth half of that, that is, a weight of three ounces. And if you should also mix in frankincense, you will make the drug more pain-relieving and more concoctive of small ulcers that are inflamed, but weaker, at any rate, with respect to cicatrization. For you will produce excess flesh, since frankincense belongs among the flesh-producing drugs, as you have also learned in the third book of the Therapeutic Method. It is therefore better to add also a little alum, both for the sake of cicatrization and for another reason, since relaxing drugs, when applied to plethoric bodies and to bodies full of bad humours, incite the affected parts to be subject to fluxes.

The drug composed of all these will be able to disperse swellings [414] contrary to nature in persons of tender flesh, such swellings as are neither very large nor painful, and especially when it receives frankincense in abundance. The frankincense would be abundant, in relation to the ingredients mentioned above, if it is equal in weight to the terebinth. But if the frankincense were half of the resin, the drug will be less discutient, but more cicatrizing than the one containing double the frankincense. And if you should wish to make it somewhat more discutient, add also a little white pepper, since it is able to do no harm to the cicatrization of the ulcers. Accordingly, let the weight of the alum be an ounce (γο.), and that of the pepper half. It is reasonable, then, that three drachms of the latter be put in, and six of alum. And since the alum called split (σχιστή), white in colour, is better than the other alums, it is fitting to put in this kind.

[White plaster, the one made with white pepper, as Attalus and Heras give it.] It benefits the ulcers of old men and of those with tender skin, and it heals every ulcer, those that are rather moist and hard to cicatrize, and abrasions (ἀποσύρματα), such that the skin hangs loose, sometimes [415] turning black, on the elbow and the shin and the knee, in which places there is not even flesh, but only the periosteal membrane lies beneath. So then, for one who enumerates everything in order, the drug has turned out to be composed of the following: of litharge and white lead, a litra of each by weight, and two litrai of oil by measure. For among the Romans the litra weight of solid bodies is called by the same name as the litra measure of liquids, which is very common throughout the whole city, being made of horn material. In addition to these, half a litra of wax by weight, three ounces of terebinth resin, of frankincense either half of this or an amount equal to it, and six drachmas of alum and three of pepper. The boiling is obvious: from the beginning the metallic ingredients are boiled in the sun, until it becomes completely non-staining (ἀμόλυντον) or even a little harder; then at that point wax and resin are thrown in, and then, when everything has been unified, first the frankincense, and after it the alum and the pepper.

One must put in the white lead called Rhodian, if one wishes the [416] plaster to come out very white. But also in the city formerly named Dicaearchia and now Puteoli, some of those who prepare white lead are accustomed to make it white in the same way as the Rhodian. That one must prepare the plaster in the sun, and mix in water, so that it becomes at once whiter and more cooling, has been stated earlier. But if someone wishes to make it more cicatrizing, no water at all is to be mixed in, but it is to be prepared with old oil alone, putting in two and a half ounces (γο β΄ ἥμισυ), or even three. This drug is not one of those first composed by me, but already many years ago by Attalus, who was king of us Pergamenes, a man who devoted himself to drugs of every kind; and it is composed according to the rationale stated above, and we would be astonished if any of the drugs of the same kind could be composed better than it. Heras too mentions it in his book of drugs, which some entitle Narthex, others Tonos of Remedies (τόνον δυνάμεων), judging that the oil should be old, and that water equal to it, or half as much, be mixed with it.

As for the rest of the proportions, [417] they are as I have written them, except that he wrote kotylai, not litrai, of the water and of the oil, without indicating of how many ounces he wants the kotyle to be, whether weight-ounces or measure-ounces. For the weight-ounces judge the heaviness of bodies, the measure-ounces their bulk. Now in saying that this drug treats the ulcers of old men and of those with tender skin he speaks the truth; but he grants it more than he ought, when he asserts that it heals every ulcer. For it treats those that are rather moist and for that reason hard to cicatrize, but none of the malignant ones, just as it treats none of the bleeding wounds either; yet he says it treats all these too. However, in saying that it treats abrasions (aposyrmata, cases where the skin has been torn away) he speaks the truth; for often, when the skin had been torn away on someone in such a way that it hung off together with the underlying flesh, I applied the drug and saw the torn-away part united with it, and—what is greater than this—sometimes when it was already turning black.

And again another case, still greater than this one, on the olecranon, the shin and the knee, in which not even flesh, but only the periosteal membrane or a broad tendon lies beneath; so that against abrasions [418] you would have this drug as the best, but for sinuses and abscesses it is neither the best of all nor second in excellence to the best, but in cases of these affections that are moderate in size, in people of soft skin, in women, children and old men, it is a good drug; so that here too Heras has testified more than he should on behalf of the drug. And much more so when he praised it, saying that it is suitable for all bites. For what does the 'all' added to the statement mean? Does he mean it even if the biter were a venomous beast, or only the bites of all human beings? And yet each alternative is false. In the case of venomous beasts, plainly so: for what is treated only with difficulty by powerful drugs, no one would say could be set right by means of this one; and if he is speaking of human beings, even so the statement is so undefined as to harm rather than benefit those who hear it. At any rate someone persuaded one of the physicians to apply this plaster to a young man who had been bitten on the index finger in the pankration, who was in such a bad state that the whole bitten part was in danger of rotting away, putrefaction having supervened upon it.

and only with difficulty, [419] after being treated over a longer period, was it agglutinated. Since this bite had been made not into a nerve but into flesh, it is nothing remarkable that it was cured by a drug of this kind. For the bites of human beings are similar to other ulcers, unless the one who bit should be exceedingly full of bad humours, or have been fasting for a longer time, or be enraged, so that both his whole body and the parts around the teeth have been filled with bile. Yet not even in these cases will the drug be seen to do anything noteworthy of that sort; rather, it will suffice for the one who uses it immediately that no harm be done, before one of the drugs specifically suited to such cases is applied to the bitten part—concerning which we shall speak again later. For now it will be enough to say this much: that in those cases where the biter was either a human being of the kind we described, or an ape, or a dog, or some other such animal.

[Explanation and composition of the Attalic white plaster of Andromachus, showing that it harms less those bitten by rabid dogs and those wounded in the nerves.] The white plasters prepared with fresh oil and water, without taking in the pepper and the [420] frankincense, greatly injure the bitten parts, even if the saliva of the animal that bit has the very slightest venomous quality. But the Attalic is naturally less harmful than all of those, because the terebinth is put into it, and the old oil and the frankincense and the pepper. In the same way, in the case of those wounded in the nerves also, the other white plasters are more harmful, whereas the harm from this one is much less, since it contains old oil and does not contain water; and still more so if it contains the whole three ounces of frankincense and not the half. For I have said before as well that, even if we prepare it in this way, in such white plasters the alum turns out to the detriment of the drug. For it requires not astringents but things that sufficiently draw outward what is causing trouble in the depth, both the punctured nerves and the venomous saliva of animals. And Heras says that this plaster also heals burns, when loosened with rose-oil or myrtle-oil or myrrh-oil. But here too it falls far short of the drugs that treat burns well, about which also it will be spoken later.

For on these the other [421] white plasters, which contain neither frankincense nor resin, are better. But these too fall very far short of the drugs that properly cure burns, just as I said that the one compounded by me cures them completely when vinegar is added to it. For that one is useful at every stage, whereas the white plaster with pepper is useful for burns that have been stripped of their skin. So when the burn is being brought to a scar it is useful, but before that it is useless on its own, though when dissolved in myrtle oil it is useful, yet not with strength equal to the drugs that are properly suited to burns. Heras also says that it is suited to bites. But here too there is need of a distinction. For in the case of hard bites and those difficult of concoction the drug is rather weak, but in the case of the more moderate ones it is sufficient, and especially in old men, children and women, and, to speak summarily, in the soft-fleshed. The drug is also useful for ionthoi, as Heras wrote this too truthfully, but he pronounced without distinction concerning exanthemata.

For of these too it treats those that are moderately somewhat hard, but those that have advanced further in heat or have something inflammatory about them it exacerbates, [422] and especially at the beginning. Following on what has been said, Heras wrote word for word as follows: "It was effective also in a case of a hardness of three months' standing, which had formed as a result of childbirth, and dispersed it" — saying nothing impossible. But he ought to have added in writing of what part the hardness was: whether of the whole uterus itself, or in the neck only, or the orifice, or in the horns, or in one of the bodies lying externally upon it. Heras also praises this plaster for fistulas more highly than its nature warrants, both all the others and especially those occurring in the anus (daktylios); for he himself used this term, declaring that it cures it. Similarly Heras is also praising the plaster under discussion for podagra and carbuncles, epinyctides and condylomata, leprai and lichens and bruises under the eyes (hypopia). If, then, he supposes that someone using it, when the better drugs are not available to him, would benefit moderately, he has supposed truly; but if he supposes it to be the best drug for these conditions, he is manifestly in error, since there are many others that are better. At any rate, at the end of his praises of it he wrote thus, in these very words.

[423] Use it especially whenever an ulcer is being broken down and becoming inflamed again under the action of acrid drugs and of those for bleeding wounds, and in the case of abscesses around the knee. Here too it ought to have been added, in the account of the abscesses, that it is for the soft-fleshed and children and women and old men, and in the case of the ulcers, their kinds, as we shall do in the discussion of malignant ulcers. For the plaster under consideration in the present discussion is cicatrizing for none of the ulcers that are malignant in this way. But a distinction is needed between those that are hard to cicatrize and the malignant ones; for not all the malignant ones are hard to cicatrize. And clearly there will be a discussion, as the account proceeds, both of their difference and of the drugs which are of a nature to benefit each of the two. And it is also possible for a white plaster to be prepared from the metallic substances alone, as I was saying a little earlier in the case of litharge boiled by itself.

For if white lead is added to the litharge, then twice as much of oil and of water, of each, is mixed in, and one carries out the boiling, as I said just now, over charcoals burnt through beforehand, in clear air, [424] the drug will be both adhesive and white in colour, and more cooling than the one prepared from litharge alone. For just as molybdaena is of a more cooling and thicker-parted nature, even if one sets it beside litharge, so too is white lead, or even more so than molybdaena. And if the oil put in is also old, this drug too will have no little viscosity, so as not to fall off readily from the body to which it happens to have been applied. But if you wish the plaster to turn out white, put in the purest and clearest oil possible, for many oils are not of this kind. And the drug will be soothing and pain-relieving if one also adds fat to it, as I myself am accustomed to do. Let the fat be goose fat, or, if this is not available, fowl's fat; and if we have not even this, let us put in pig's fat, knowing that goose fat has no small superiority over the others, but making use also of the inferior ones when we lack the best; for indeed, when cinnamon is not at hand, we resort to the best cassia.

And it suffices, with the proportion stated above, [425] to mix in of the fat half a part of the weight of each of the metallic substances, so that there is one part each of litharge and white lead, double that of oil and double that of water, or even a little more (πλεῖστον ὀλίγῳ), and of the fat half a part. In what sense I speak of the things measured as double, half and equal to the things weighed on a balance, I showed a little earlier, when I explained the homonymy of the Roman litra of weight with the litra of measure. I have prepared this drug in many forms: for having mixed the four in equal amounts, I put into them half a part of fat, and sometimes also one and a half parts of each of the liquids. By way of example, the proportion will be as follows: of litharge, 1 litra; of white lead, 1 litra; of the oil and of the water, half a litra of each (λίτρας ἥμισυ); and of the remaining ingredient, the fat, half a litra; and sometimes I also put in a third of a litra, just as also one litra of the water.

But what laymen, and those physicians who resemble such people, are often accustomed to say — guard against ever saying it: namely, as they put it, that such-and-such a drug becomes better if it takes in addition some such-and-such ingredient, [426] whatever they may name. Some of them, for their part, admit that they do not know, but ask us which of the compositions and preparations is the finest, not recognizing that a different one is more useful for a different condition, and that none is best simply and without distinction. For this reason, then, I require you to know accurately the powers of the simple drugs; for it is not possible to use the compound drug well when these are unknown. To take an immediate instance, in the case of the white plaster under discussion in the present account, fresh fat, when mixed in, will make the drug more pain-relieving, so that even if the ulcer is somewhat inflamed it benefits it, but it will make it worse for cicatrization. The one without the fat, on the other hand, is more cicatrizing, but not equally pain-relieving. It was also said earlier that when it takes in water in addition it becomes more cooling, and with old oil more discutient. He, then, who is able to recognize which of these the ulcer has more need of, will both himself compound drugs best and make best use of those already compounded.

And you have often seen me, using the drugs of the physicians who had called me in for consultation, [427] treat many of the cases that were baffling to them. So then, a drug is called best not without qualification, but among those that profess to do some particular thing, just as I said the phoinikine is best for rheumatic conditions, when one uses it according to the distinctions stated above. [On the other white plasters.] The white plasters mentioned above, then, were prepared of old according to the rationale I have stated. But after these, others of many kinds were compounded, the physicians who came afterwards removing certain things, adding others and substituting others; and about these too it is better to speak, for the sake of your being exercised in varied ways in the composition of drugs. Accordingly, it has been written by Andromachus, in the book which he entitles Remedies for External Conditions, roughly as follows, in these very words: "The white plaster which I use: litharge, one mina; white lead, one mina; wax, a quarter; resin, a quarter; oil, three kotylai; water, two kotylai." This is what Andromachus wrote, neither adding for what cases it is suited nor going through its boiling.

Some, then, [428] say that the mina has twenty ounces, others sixteen. And the drug could be prepared in either way; yet it does not seem to me correct to put in an equal amount of resin and of wax. For the Attalic one is better composed, taking twice as much wax as resin. And it is obvious that if the resin is put in equal to the wax, the plaster would become more adhesive, but not equally agreeable to the ulcers, but having something acrid. And moreover, in not making clear what kind of resin he wants to be put in, he did not act correctly. But we, knowing that the terebinth resin is better in every respect than the Colophonian and the so-called roasted (phrykte) resin, shall put in that one. And if we should also have a good supply of larch resin, nothing prevents us from using it, for they are somewhat similar. As for the oil, I think that he writes three Attic kotylai, or else he would certainly have written litrai. And yet one might wonder how, while residing in Rome, he named kotylai instead of litrai; for these are the local names: that of the litra, that of the xestes, and that of the ounce.

From many drugs written up long ago, before the affairs of the Romans had grown to so great [429] a degree of power, I have conjectured that what those authors call a kotyle is equal to nine of the ounces that make up the litra now in use in Rome. Can it be, then, that Andromachus too thinks the three kotylai should be put in on the understanding that each of them is of nine ounces, and by the same reckoning also the two of water? Since we, then, know beforehand the power of each of the simples, in whatever way you prepare it you will be able to use it for the purposes which the manner of the composition promises, leaving it to others to inquire which of the compositions is best. For they are all both best and not best, as has been demonstrated by me earlier. For indeed, next after this one too Andromachus writes another, as follows. [Another white one.] Take litharge, 160 drachmas; white lead, 200 drachmas; wax, 50 drachmas; terebinth resin, 24 drachmas; oil, half a kotyle; water, 6 kyathoi. This plaster, then, having more white lead than litharge in comparison with the former one, would be whiter and more cooling, at least in this respect.

but one that falls off easily, even if we suppose the kotyle [430] to contain sixteen and two-thirds ounces, as some say. The admixture of the terebinth, however, helps it in this respect, so that the drug does not become brittle, since otherwise it would have been entirely fat-free and dry, having little oil and water. And in the case of this one too Andromachus added neither the boiling nor the indication. [Another white.] Next after this he writes a third, which has in all other respects all the same ingredients as the Attalic one made with white pepper. But these two are added to it: of the orchis plant, 8 drachms; of soapwort, two ounces; and water he does not put into this drug at all; and of frankincense he requires putting in twenty-five drachms, without having added in writing, as Heras is accustomed to do. Some, however, put in twelve and twenty; of oil, at any rate, here too he mixes in two kotylai, leaving us the same obscurity which I mentioned earlier. One might greatly fault him for not having added in writing the indications of the drugs. For surely the one written second does not have the same potency as the first and the third.

Perhaps, then, someone will also ask why the man who first compounded the drug, whoever he was, although he wished it to be discutient, [434] nevertheless tried to preserve the white lead raw within it. It seems to me that he came to such a preparation for this reason, in order that the drug might have something also of the repellent faculty. For those drugs that have none of this kind are not safe for plethoric bodies. So that it might be suitable for these too, it is likely that the white lead was mixed in raw. It is quite evident that the drug before us makes great promises, from its having taken on in addition both myrrh and deer marrow, since in other respects it has the same ingredients as these common plasters. We have learned that myrrh is a strongly drying drug and sufficiently fine-parted, while the marrow is inferior to none of the so-called emollients. This faculty has been discussed, as have all the other secondary ones too, in the fifth book of the treatise On Simple Drugs.

It seems, however, that the man who composed the drug placed his confidence not in these alone, but also in the white Pontic wax, as having a medicinal power, and for this reason put in a very large quantity of it. [435] And I think that Heras has in mind the Roman xestes. For among the Athenians there existed neither the measure nor this name. But now, from the time when the Romans have held sway, the name of the xestes is in use among all the peoples who employ the Greek language, but the measure itself is not equal to the Roman one; for different people use a different xestes-measure. Among the Romans, at any rate, the xestes contains one litra and a half and a sixth, so that the ounces in all are twenty; and these they for the most part measure with the horns, which are incised on the outside with certain circular lines. Some, however, have falsely supposed that the Roman xestes contains eighteen measure-ounces. It seems, then, that Heras too, whenever he writes 'kotyle', means half of a xestes; but whether they indicate the nine ounces from the litra-horn or the ten, this is unclear. And whether the drug is also suitable for those bitten by rabid dogs, whether taken by mouth or applied externally, it is not possible to know by reasoning.

For it has been shown by us that drugs of this kind have their activity by the whole peculiarity of their substance and are for [436] this reason judged by experience. But I never dared to make trial of this drug, as to what power it displays in those bitten by rabid dogs, because I have a drug that cures reliably, the one made from crabs, and, when this is not at hand, certain others that have never failed. Accordingly, to abandon the reliable remedies in so dangerous an affection and to betray the safety of the bitten person for the sake of an officious experiment seemed to me terrible and unjust. Concerning those bitten by rabid dogs, then, let this much suffice to have been said. As for the other things written by Heras about this plaster, just as in the case of the Attalic one, some of them, I say, are true, while some are exaggerated beyond the mark. For it is a most excellent drug, as plasters go, for the so-called bruises under the eyes (hypopia), but as an agglutinative of bleeding wounds it is not among the first and best. And in general, concerning this class of plasters, I find that very many physicians, not only those of the present day but also those who have written treatises, have produced praises greater than the truth, about which matters an account will be given in the discourse following this one.

But now, having come to the plaster before us, [437] we shall examine again what has been said by Heras. For he says that it cures phymata, without adding any of the distinctions which I wrote about concerning the phoinikine. For some of the phymata are very hot and violently erupting, while others are both cold and dry. And very many others lie between these, some exactly in the middle between those mentioned, some departing a little from the mean in either direction, and some likewise further toward either side, and some near the extremes or somehow midway, at an equal distance from both the middle ones and the extremes; for all of which it is impossible for this plaster to be suitable, unless indeed one should wish to melt it with certain liquids, so that many modes of use arise, which he ought to have stated, just as he did in the case of others. Wherefore I say that it is just to praise him for the things he wrote in this way, but to blame Andromachus.

But as for this plaster's being suitable for the bites of humans and the bites of dogs, consider that you are hearing from me the same arguments which I also stated concerning the Attalic plaster, and likewise concerning the other things which he attests of the [438] drug, since just as in the case of that one so also in the case of this one I say that the drug is a good one, but falls far short of those which act best for each of those conditions, so that one may use it with confidence when none of the best ones is at hand. And this too is no small matter in drugs, just as also in regimens and in everything pertaining to the art — a thing which I at first disdained, so as to think it not even worthy of Hippocrates when he exhorts us to do everything in the art in such a way as to help, or not to harm. But later I recognised that it has the greatest power, when I saw some of the physicians who, with drugs by which they had earlier succeeded so as to be admired, later failed with these same drugs on other patients so as to be laughed at. And for this reason I have always tried to use such remedies in which the hope of benefit sometimes admits of doubt, but the fact that no harm will result admits of exact knowledge. So then, the things for which Heras praised the Attalic plaster and this one are, as I said, not great.

But when those which accomplish these things in a great degree are not at hand, [439] one who uses these will not produce any manifest harm, even if he does no benefit. If, however, someone wishes to use this drug for phymata, he will himself discover, from what I said in the case of the phoinikine, how to melt it in different ways at different times. The whole care of phymata, too, will be spoken of at greater length in what follows, through which I hope you will possess an accurate and complete method concerning the drugs that are able to benefit phymata. And let this plaster be called by you the white plaster for those bitten by rabid dogs, just as the one made with white pepper is called the Attalic. Next after this one Heras also writes another plaster, in the following words: "The white Ariobarzanian, with which Xenocrates dispersed the abscess around the tarsus when it had already undergone change." Then, having stated the proportion of the ingredients put into it and after that the boiling, he added at the end, word for word, as follows: "It is effective especially for malignant, spreading and hard-to-heal ulcers, and in general for every ulcer."

But the proportion itself of the ingredients that compose the drug he wrote down, I know not how, at a third part, whereas it has been written in full by others [440] in the following manner. (X) Of litharge 200 drachms; of wax 50 drachms; of old oil 3 kotylai; of white lead 80 drachms; of terebinth 32 drachms; of burnt whelks 10 drachms; of frankincense 19 drachms; of water 12 kyathoi. All these drugs which I have just listed Heras wrote at a third part: Take of litharge 66 drachms 4 obols; of wax 16 drachms 4 obols; of old oil 1 kotyle; and of white lead 26 drachms and four obols; and of terebinth resin 10 drachms and four obols; of burnt whelks 3 drachms and two obols; and of frankincense 6 drachms and two obols; of water 4 kyathoi. Then next he writes the boiling as follows. Grind the litharge and the white lead with the water and the oil, then boil in a new pot over a gentle fire, stirring carefully with an iron spatula, so that it does not burn. When it is half-boiled, add wax, and when that has melted, resin and frankincense, and boil until it becomes to some degree such that it does not stain; then, when it seems to be near to being in good condition, add the whelks and boil together for the remaining time.

And when it has become thoroughly compacted, pour it out into a mortar with a little water [441] placed in it beforehand, and after kneading it, use it. This drug has been prepared so as to disperse without biting, since it contains only a little white lead in proportion to the litharge, and this is boiled together with the litharge from the beginning, and it is a strongly drying drug on account of the burnt whelks. The same power belongs in some way also to purple-shells and to burnt oysters. It is quite evident that the shells of these animals are burnt without their flesh. Now Heras wrote one book of powers (dynameis); but Asclepiades, surnamed Pharmakion, wrote ten, apart from those on the theriacs and on women's remedies, he too adding the profession of each drug, and in the case of many also the boiling, and in the case of some also the manner of its use. Andromachus, for his part, collected many powers, nearly no fewer than those in the ten books of Asclepiades Pharmakion; and he comprised them in three books: one in which he writes the drugs that are applied externally, a second in which he writes those taken into the interior of the body, and a third, that concerning the eyes.

But one might fault him, as I said, for not adding the preparations, [442] nor the modes of use, nor the powers, nor the professions of the drugs. [The white plasters written by Asclepiades.] Passing now, then, to Asclepiades, I shall set out the white plasters written by him at the end of the third book of the external remedies. He himself entitles these books the first Marcella, and the second, third, fourth and fifth, just as he entitles the other five, those of the internal remedies, the first Mason, and the second, third, fourth and fifth. In the third Marcella, towards the end, he wrote down white plasters: one whose profession he says is for burns and abrasions and tender skins, which he says is called akesis. He says to boil the four ingredients together, litharge, white lead, oil, water, all in equal amounts; and it is clear that this drug turns out crumbly and without greasiness, so that it cannot even remain on the skin without bandaging. For unless, as I said before, the metallic ingredients are boiled for a longer time, the plaster must necessarily turn out of such a kind.

[443] But they are boiled for longer when they have a greater share of the liquids in the mixture. Next after this one Asclepiades wrote another white plaster, which has the same promise but not the same composition. For he neither puts in an equal weight of the metallic substances, but the white lead at one and a half times the litharge, and he adds in addition calf's fat, making the whole proportion as follows: Take of white lead 120 drachmas, of litharge 80 drachmas, of calf's fat 30 drachmas, of wax 25 drachmas, of oil 2 cotylae. This drug contains little oil in relation to the proportion of the metallic substances, if one assumes that the cotyle holds nine Roman ounces, those marked off on the customary horn measures of a pound (κέρασι λιτραίοις). And since the white lead has been increased in it, and for this reason it was becoming more astringent than the one written before, the man who composed it mixed in the fat. And knowing that the fat of oxen is hotter and more discutient than that of pigs, he took care not to put in the fat of a full-grown ox. For in every kind of animal the young have fat that is moister and less hot than the full-grown.

This composition too, then, would be more elaborate [444] than the simple white plaster previously written down by him, while having nothing more by way of benefit. And he wrote a third, another white one, a cicatrizing one, from white lead equal to the litharge, and wax a fourth part, or in proportion to these (ἢ κατὰ ταῦτα), and the terebinth in turn from a half part of the wax. The oil has been put in very nearly equal to both metallic substances together, and the water in turn equal to this itself. For the one who composed the drug wished 100 drachms of each of the white lead and the litharge to be put in, 25 drachms of wax and 12 of terebinth, and of oil and water two cotylae each. If, then, you call to mind the Attalic plaster, which has the metallic substances in the same way as this one, as also the oil together with the water, but the wax double that in this one, and the terebinth likewise, you will know clearly what difference the drugs have in relation to one another. For to those were added also frankincense and alum and pepper. And indeed Asclepiades too mentions that Attalic plaster, not naming it Attalic, nor indeed putting in the pepper.

But all the rest he wrote in the same way, word for word thus: "White [plaster] called that of Mnasaeus; it works also for chronic and hard-to-heal [conditions]. Take litharge, white lead, 100 drachms each; wax, 8 drachms; terebinth, frankincense, 25 drachms each; split alum, 12 drachms; oil, 2 cotylae." Do not think, however, that it makes a difference if you find somewhere 100 drachms written instead of one litra; rather, consider this, whether the one who wrote the 100 drachms mixes with them half [that amount] of wax, and then half of that of terebinth, so that there are 50 of wax and 25 drachms of terebinth, or whether he makes some other proportion. For if it is the one just stated, he will differ in no way from one who says a litra and half a litra and three ounces. For the litra contains ninety-six drachms, and the half litra, evidently, forty-eight, just as half of this again is twenty-four; so that the same ratio is preserved, it making no great difference whether the two cotylae of oil are mixed with the 100 drachms of the metallic [ingredients] or with the ninety-six. In this respect, then, the drugs will not differ whether a litra is named or 100 drachms.

But in this respect the drug written by Asclepiades [446] differs from the Attalic plaster: in that the Attalic has six drachms of split alum and three of white pepper, whereas the one written by Asclepiades does not contain the white pepper, but has double the weight of split alum. And it is quite clear that the drug of Asclepiades will be somewhat more astringent and for this reason more cicatrizing, while the Attalic will be more discutient; so that, as I also said before, those who inquire which of the two is better do not know how to use drugs. For with a view to cicatrization the drug of Asclepiades is better, but with a view to discussion the Attalic. In a word, one must bear in mind what was written by Hippocrates in On Nutriment, that it is in relation to something that the bad and the not-bad are spoken of, and evidently also the harmful and the beneficial.

For on another account you might say that the Attalic plaster is better than this plaster, in that the former is of more manifold use; indeed Asclepiades himself, when writing next after the one just mentioned that very plaster with white pepper, does not call it Attalic but Pamphileion, being ignorant, as [447] I think, of the one who first discovered it, and having added instead the name of the man who used it and gave it to him. At any rate he wrote its profession word for word thus: Another, called Pamphileion, a successful drug. It is effective for old and hard-to-heal ulcers, carbuncles, epinyctides, achores, scabby conditions; it glues together sinuses; it is effective for abscesses, condylomata, and the drug is more or less of more manifold use. He says it is composed of white lead and litharge and wax and terebinth and the two kotylai of oil, in the same way as in Heras, and in addition to these also of split alum and white pepper; but he makes no mention of water in the preparation, nor indeed of frankincense at all. Some, however, do not put in twenty-five but half that amount; and indeed likewise concerning the water: for having written that two kotylai of old oil are put in, after this he added in writing two kotylai of water, or one kotyle.

I myself have very often prepared the drug even without water, and it appears to turn out better for all other purposes, except in the case of those with tender skin; for in these cases the one that has taken on water is better, and especially when [448] the ulcers are somewhat inflamed. Asclepiades also describes, along with the white plasters already mentioned, another one which professes to treat those bitten by rabid dogs, just as the one written in Heras also had this profession. This one too takes in addition, beyond the simple white plaster composed of litharge, white lead, frankincense and wax, further, from outside, deer marrow and myrrh. He puts into it forty drachms of litharge, thirty drachms of white lead, ten drachms of frankincense and an equal amount of myrrh, of deer marrow two less than ten, fifty drachms of white wax, and one xestes of old oil. But first of all those he mentioned Asclepiades wrote the one which he names Rhodian, as being discutient and curing the hardnesses on the breasts, composed of the following: of litharge and Pontic wax he orders one litra each to be put in, of white lead and of worked pig's fat half a litra, that is six ounces of each, of myrrh four ounces, of roasted eggs two yolks, and one and a half kotylai of oil.

He says that this one is also good for the seat, [449] not having written beforehand with what he wishes the drug to be melted, but leaving it to us, perhaps, to conjecture that at one time it should be melted with rose oil, at another with myrtle oil, at another with one of the oils. [How one ought to compound white plasters for ulcers that are hard to cicatrize and malignant.] Which of the ulcers I call hard to cicatrize and which malignant, it is the moment to distinguish, since the distinction will prove useful not only for what is at present but also for what is going to be said. Those, then, that arise from an influx of humours, either abundant or acrid, without the affected place having already acquired such a condition that, even if what flows in is good, it nonetheless corrupts it, I call hard to cicatrize; those that already have the aforesaid condition I name, in the special sense, malignant.

Now then, since those before me have recorded certain of the white plasters as cicatrizing well the ulcers that are hard to cicatrize, for this reason I too write up white plasters which I composed both for all the hard-to-cicatrize ulcers and for some of the malignant ones, [450] as many as do not have an altogether bad constitution; for in the case of those the suitable drugs will be stated later. First, here too, I shall state the method according to which you will learn to compose many plasters of this kind. Its aim is twofold: the one common to all drugs composed according to method, the other particular, namely that which concerns the colour of these. Accordingly, recall all those drugs which you came to know in the treatise on simple drugs as drying without biting yet very strongly. And it is altogether fitting that they, besides not biting or astringing manifestly, be able also to cleanse. For indeed most of such ulcers appear hollow, as having arisen from erosion by malignant humours and for this reason needing to be filled with flesh. And it has been demonstrated in the third book of the Therapeutic Method that all flesh-producing drugs possess a cleansing power. Now many other drugs too have a dry power curative of such ulcers.

But now let us recall those which are able either to preserve the whiteness of the compounded [451] plaster or at any rate not to harm it much. Such are cadmia and pompholyx and lime, burnt oyster-shells and purple-shells and whelks (kerykes) and the bone-like part of the cuttlefish. Nor would the scale of copper much spoil the colour, nor that part of burnt chalcitis which is not reddish-yellow but ash-coloured or whitish. How one ought to prepare such a thing will be stated later in the account of the theriac antidote. Each of the things mentioned, if it is washed, becomes entirely non-biting, as do also the wax, which one must mix into the drug as it is being prepared, and the resin. It has been stated that the wax called Tyrrhenian or Pontic is suitable for the preparation of the white plaster. Of the resins, the one called larch and the terebinth are more beneficial for the more malignant of ulcers. And it is fitting also to add some portion of frankincense, in order that the condition of malignant ulcers may be concocted and brought to suppuration.

One must not only wash each of the aforementioned drugs, but also triturate the metallic ones, at any rate, for a very long time in a sunny place with water [452] or vinegar or sea-water or wine. And let each of these be pure and white and exactly transparent, so as to contribute something to the whiteness of the drug. And concerning the white lead too it has been said before, and concerning the oil and the manner of the boiling and the surrounding air and the fire, how each of them might contribute something to the whiteness. And just as in the case of the others, so too in the case of these, one must, knowing the powers of water and vinegar and sea-water and the whitest wine, mix into the composition that which is most useful for the condition being treated. For in the case of ulcers with raised, bank-like edges, whose lips are thick and hard and in need of much thinning, the substances triturated with vinegar and sea-water are more useful than those triturated with water; but in those cases where the fluid carried in the ulcers is acrid and biting, each of the metallic substances should rather have been triturated in water, just as, again, rather in wine in those cases where the fluid that flows in to the ulcers appears abundant.

So then, each of these substances which I mentioned, having been levigated in each of the aforementioned liquids for several days, I threw in [453] on each occasion into the drugs made with white lead and litharge, and I found by experience that all of them cicatrized most excellently. I also gave some written recipes to friends who were in need of such drugs, and when brought to trial by them as well, the drugs plainly made good their promise. So then, when the litharge has first been boiled, as has been said, together with the white lead, and the drug has come near to a non-staining consistency, one must add some of the larch or terebinth resin together with white wax, and when these have been well united, throw in the metallic substances in addition, in the following proportion. Of litharge and white lead, according to the usual practice, let one litra of each be boiled with two litrai of oil, while often also throwing in half a litra of water; for in this way the litharge melts more quickly, and the boiling consumes the water, so that it manifestly contributes nothing toward moistness in the drug. Three ounces of resin and twice that quantity of wax are sufficient. Nevertheless, even if at some time you throw in two of resin and four of wax, you will find that even so the compositions differ in no great respect.

And one and a half ounces of frankincense [454] is also sufficient, put in after the wax and the resin. And after these, three ounces of the other ingredients, which is twenty-four drachms. You will put in two, three, more, or all of those I have mentioned, according to whichever of them you happen to have in good supply. For example, if you have them all, you will put in an equal amount of each — I mean cadmia and pompholyx, and burnt whelks or oysters, and flakes of copper; and there will be six drachms of each, making up the three ounces. But if you also mix in washed lime, five drachms of each will be put in. And if burnt chalcitis too, four drachms of each, so that, when all six come together, the three ounces are made up. Let the burnt chalcitis be washed and, obviously, ash-coloured in hue, not such as most of those who burn it make it, pale-yellow (ὠχρόξανθον), as one might say. And if someone has only some two of these, let him put in three ounces from both, that is, one and a half of each. These things suffice for you to know for the present concerning the composition of white plasters for ulcers that are hard to cicatrize.

And white [455] and moist (parhygros) cerates are also prepared by means of the same ingredients, differing from the plasters in that the litharge and the white lead are not boiled, and in that fat is added—either goose fat or hen's fat or pig's fat or calf's fat. And if at any time you have a supply of wine or of vinegar, you will add the whitest and most transparent of them in place of water. [Damocrates on the white plaster.] Since the compositions of drugs written down in metre are easy to remember and preserve their proportions exactly, it seemed to me better to make mention of these too. Since, then, Damocrates has written other white plasters, and indeed also a white one which he praises, I shall set out the recipe in the very verses written by him, in the metre called trimeter. Together with these, lovers of the medical art must have a fine white plaster for abrasions, and for burns, and for ulcers that arise on the surface without any evident cause. It is prepared as follows.

a pound of white lead, [456] and of litharge, especially the soft kind now (in use), one pound and a third part of a pound, of pure Pontic wax five ounces, and of terebinth, the purest, one ounce, of frankincense manna or of frankincense five ounces, and of white oil, good and fresh, two and a half pounds, and one xestes of water. Boil the oil, white lead, litharge and water over a gentle fire, stirring constantly with the spathe. And when all the water has been thoroughly boiled away, and you see the drug smooth and white, soft, not staining, then you add the terebinth, then the wax, and then the frankincense last. Lift the pot from the fire and stir it, and when the drug has cooled moderately, pour it into the mortar and take it up. And in the case of women or of delicate children, and in the case of old men or of young persons in a cachectic condition,

[457] With this mix in a third part of the alum plaster, the plaster which we set out a little earlier, and use it for all wounds, including freshly inflicted ones. Mix into it, once it has been melted, rose-oil and a little wax, pouring in a little white astringent wine, and you will have a fine emollient (liparan). The composition of the alum plaster which he mentioned is in the fifth book of this treatise.

[458] GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK II. Since the present treatise has, together with its other aims, also this one, namely that if we should ever lose the book in which we have the compositions of the drugs we use written down, we ourselves should be able to compound drugs closely similar to those that have been lost, it is necessary, first, that we should have learned some general outline of a method by which we shall discover what we have set out to find.

and second, to have been trained along this [459] path in many of the particular cases, knowing that without having trained oneself in such an exercise none of the works is accomplished correctly. Terrible too is what has already befallen certain persons whom I know, two physicians: for the one, wasted away by grief at the loss of such writings, died, while the other withdrew from medical practice. But those who have been trained, as I say, possess, in addition to being able to compose useful drugs, also the capacity to be discriminating judges of what has been written by the physicians before us, and to make suitable use both of everything written by them and of whatever one may oneself discover according to the method that is going to be taught. Now it is better to use the drugs already tested through experience, having learned the method of their use; but, as I said, necessity often overtakes us, so that we must use even untried ones, improvising. In the book before this one, then, it has been stated how one may prepare plasters from litharge alone, sometimes mixing in oil only, sometimes vinegar or wine or some of these together, and from what proportion of them a white plaster can be produced when properly boiled.

And we said that of these plasters [460] some turn out to be cicatrizing, some also agglutinative of bloody wounds, some curative of small inflammations, and that some of them also treat the ulcers that are hard to cicatrize, so far as these are not malignant, and that some of them disperse tumours contrary to nature, so far as these are neither large nor scirrhous. There was also written in it, not long after the beginning, the plaster compounded by me, which I call phoinikine. In this book, the one now before us, there will be discussion of the green plasters and the quince-yellow and the tawny and the grey and the reddish ones, among which are also those called two-coloured, and between these others, some of them bearing names, such as the whitish-quince-yellow and the blackish-green and the dirty-coloured and the sky-blue-tinged and the dark-blue-tinged, while some are altogether nameless. Now, to write one after another those that are similar in power is useful for enabling one who meets with several of them, or who reads the book, to choose the one most suitable for the body and the affection that is being treated.

But to record those that are alike in colour is not the practice of people who look to likeness according to the art; [461] rather, since some of the very powerful men sometimes order us to make for them a quince-yellow plaster that is agglutinative of wounds, or cicatrizing, or emollient of parts that are becoming hardened, or able to effect something of this sort, some of the more recent physicians have been compelled, in writing one after another those that are alike in colour, to add to each its proper professed effects. I, then, shall try to make my instruction a mixed one, beginning from the more technical arrangement. For I write first the flesh-producing plasters for hollow ulcers, most of which are green in colour, indicating which of these are agglutinative as well, and which are curative of ulcers that are turning malignant, and which are able to accomplish something else of this kind. Second, the agglutinative ones, not only for recent wounds but also for sinuses, among which there are also many that lead right up to cicatrization. And of all these I shall make one series of the quince-yellow ones, another of those called barbarian, another of the grey ones, and likewise for the other colours.

And I shall also state, in one other book [462] without similarities of colour, all those that treat the wounds that are hard to cicatrize, which they also call Chironian. And after this, in yet another book, all those that treat both these and certain other things, being both called and actually being polychrēsta (of many uses). And after all these I shall try to go through by method whatever remains to be known of the plasters according to their powers. These things, then, have been said beforehand as a kind of common preface to all the plasters that are going to be written up hereafter; and I shall pass over to those written in this book, having set before them a certain common account, as if nothing had already been said beforehand by me. Compositions of a very great many drugs worthy of praise were written, first of those I know, by Mantias the Herophilean, whose pupil Heraclides of Tarentum appears to imitate him not only in the use of drugs but also in the dietetic part of the art. After whom certain others (wrote) in several books, just as both Mantias and Heraclides did.

There are also those who made their record of them in only one or two books, as Heras the Cappadocian did, who neither wrote down any drug that is not approved, nor [463] left out their preparations, and went through all their particular uses. Musa, Asclepiades and Criton have written up many drugs carefully in several books. Andromachus wrote in one book the medical drugs for the parts outside the body, and in another single one those for the parts within, there being also a third, smaller than these, on eye-remedies. For very few of them, however, is the preparation and the use not added. But neither any of these men nor anyone else wrote the reasoning behind the composition of each of the drugs, and for this reason those of the empirical school make their pronouncements with greater boldness, even though what they say is inconceivable, for they refer the discovery of compound drugs to chance encounter. They have taken courage from the fact that none of the dogmatic physicians has written out in articulated form the method of their composition.

For when those who dogmatize, on being asked the rationale by which each of the drugs they use is composed, have nothing to say, and, if they have lost their written recipes for them, are unable to improvise other compositions, they are themselves deservedly despised, and they make the Empiricists [464] bolder in contradiction. But if they understood the nature of each affection among those they treat, and knew a method such that from it they could discover both the aim of the treatment and the power of each of the simple drugs, they would not be ignorant of the rationale of the composition. For example, to begin with, let it be set before us to consider how one might heal a hollow uncomplicated ulcer (for it is no worse that we too should name it thus, as some call it, for the sake of concise teaching), as if no drug suitable for it had yet been discovered. For having been taught by reason that the healing of hollow ulcers comes about when other flesh is generated in place of that which has been lost, sprouting evidently from the underlying flesh itself, we realized that it is impossible for this to happen when filth or much moisture lies in the ulcer. But the detergent drugs remove the filth, while the drying ones disperse the moisture.

It is necessary, then, to know the materials of such drugs, not simply by kind, as Dioscorides wrote in a different manner, but as we did in the books on simple drugs, [465] writing not only that this particular drug heats or cools or produces some other such effect, but also that the drug is of such a kind at the first remove from the mean, or the second or the third or the fourth; and often, indeed, that it is at the middle of each of these, or at its beginning or its end, so that there are twelve orders of the drugs that are spoken of according to any predominance whatsoever. For sometimes we need one that heats or dries moderately, and sometimes one that is able to do any of these things most vehemently. But he who knows simply that the part needs to be heated will no more choose pepper and mustard than frankincense. These things, then, have been said by us before, and have been said also in the third book of the Therapeutic Method. Taking it that they are already known together with the appropriate demonstration, I shall lead the present discourse forward to what remains, beginning from here.

Since it has been shown that those ulcers which are to be filled with flesh require a drug that dries and cleanses moderately, without bitingness, one must recall what the material of such drugs [466] is. It has been shown in the treatise on the power of simple drugs, together with the appropriate rank of each also having been stated. For this, as I said, is the most useful thing: so that, if ever someone needs a stronger drug, he knows to which one he will pass over; but when none of the simples is at hand, we come to the compound. And first let it be supposed that we have wax and verdigris, but nothing else of the things directly suited to a hollow ulcer—I mean frankincense and iris and aristolochia, and the flour of bitter vetch and the root of panax, and whatever other such things there are. Knowing, then, that if wax alone is applied the ulcer will be found sordid, inasmuch as wax is able neither to cleanse nor to dry, whereas if verdigris is applied it will be bitten and eaten away and will become inflamed, we shall decline each of these, and shall make from both another, intermediate one, weaker than verdigris but stronger than wax. But since wax falls short only a little of what would be usefully applied, whereas verdigris exceeds it by much, we shall mix a little verdigris with much wax. How much, then, with how much?

[467] For this is the next thing to state: it is not possible to find exactly the quantity of each before trial, but it is possible to make a conjecture and to judge and to compound at the first attempt a drug that will have no failure worth mentioning, just as I myself once did in a certain village, in which I neither had any drug with me myself, nor was anyone else among the people there well supplied, and I found, of the things suitable for compounding, only verdigris and wax. Taking up both and melting the wax over a fire together with rose oil, so that a liquid cerate came about, I mixed into a litra of the cerate one ounce of verdigris, that is, the twelfth part. For I had in mind to mix in either the tenth or the twelfth part, suspecting the greater amount as likely to prove more pungent than the wax, and the lesser as likely to be weaker. When we came to a trial of what had been compounded, both the tenth and the twelfth proved to be correctly mixed according to the differences of bodies. For it was indicated to us—which is also attested through experience—that strong bodies tolerate stronger drugs, whereas weaker ones do not bear the application of such drugs.

By stronger bodies I mean [468] those that are drier in their temperaments, such as are those of farmers, sailors and hunters; by weaker, those that are softer by nature or by habit, such as those of women, eunuchs and children, and all who are moist by nature in their temperaments, having a white and soft body. Hard bodies, then, are made to grow flesh when more verdigris is mixed with the cerate, soft bodies when less. Hence, as has often been said, it is impossible for one drug to suit all bodies; rather, the drug must be intermediate, as being fitted to the intermediate temperament, and must be led in either direction, being judged by its use on each day. For if it appears to have accomplished what is needed, it is proper to continue with it; but if it falls somewhat short, to increase its power, just as also to reduce it, whenever it has acted beyond what is proper.

For example, in the case of the drug now before us, the one made from cerate and verdigris, one must consider whether the ulcer has been filled with flesh, or whether flesh was not generated but the ulcer was found foul and full of moisture, or whether, in addition to its not having been filled with flesh, [469] some sensation of biting arose in the patient and the ulcerated part appeared hotter, or at any rate redder. If, then, it appears weaker, you will increase its power by the admixture of honey or verdigris; but if stronger, you will mix in olive oil or rose-oil, softening the drug that is to be taken up on the lint pledgets. On an occasion of need, then, cerate and verdigris are mixed in this way, just as I said they were once mixed by me. But let those who practise medicine have in readiness a prepared plaster, the one they name 'green' from its colour, which is sufficient also to treat fresh wounds, those that are not large, and which can also be melted with rose-oil to the consistency of a drug of intermediate (ἐμμέσου) character. It will also need to contain some resin, either the one called Colophonian and 'roasted' (φρυκτῆς), or terebinth. It has been said that the resin called larch is somewhat similar to terebinth. Here too the quantity in which they are mixed is a matter of conjecture.

For if we mix in more resin than is appropriate, while it is being softened by the hands it appears soft, but once spread on a linen cloth it will a little later be hard like leather, [470] easily falling off the body. But if less resin than the due proportion is mixed with the wax, it will not have that quality which is called echekollon ("glue-holding"), so as to be stretched further when it is drawn out; and it is evident that even if it is applied to some part, it will adhere poorly and quickly fall off it. What, then, is the well-proportioned mixture, with a view to a plaster-like consistency? If you would be persuaded by me, an equal amount of each. And let neither the wax be dry and old, nor the resin. For in this way the consistency of what is mixed from them becomes best, if both are taken fatty and soft. But if one of the two should exceed, it is always better for the resin to predominate, so that some even mix in a double quantity with the wax when it is melted (staktos). [Preparation of the simple green plaster of Andromachus, and an exposition concerning its power.] And the green plaster—for so they themselves call it—some have made from a double quantity of the resin, putting in two litrai of it, one of wax, and two kyathoi of oil.

Of verdigris, some add two, others three ounces to such a mixture [471] of wax and resin. But also in the preparation, some work the verdigris into the meltable ingredients once they have been melted, while others, having cooled them and then scraped them, make the mixture in the mortar. Those, however, who wish to make the drug more agglutinative of bloody wounds first triturate the verdigris in a mortar with vinegar and add it while scraping in the cerate. If, then, anyone asks you which of these green plasters is best, remember what is often said by me, and answer that all are best for the one who knows the conditions to which each is suited, just as all are also bad for the one who does not know. For my part, it is for me to say that the one which takes in vinegar in addition dries more vigorously. And it is quite evident that the one containing more verdigris is both strong and more drying and more cleansing of foul ulcers. The limit of it is that it should effect these things without biting.

For what is so strong that it already even bites when applied to clean ulcers will never make them grow flesh, and will, in a different manner, render them moist and foul, in much the same way as those [drugs] that dry and cleanse insufficiently; but in the case of the more acrid ones the ulcer becomes hollower, redder [472] and hotter. And there are times when the patient himself also perceives its bitingness. Do not, then, simply praise some drug without adding the condition for which it is praised, neither in the case of any other drug nor in the case of those now before us. Those, therefore, who, in writing up the green plasters one after another, did not shrink from defining the conditions for which they are suitable, err less than those who did not even do this. But those who have written without distinctions, prescribing at their transitions, 'another green one', produce a most faulty teaching—if indeed one ought to call such writing teaching at all. Andromachus, at any rate, in the book which he entitles 'Of External Remedies', a little after the beginning wrote first the grey [plasters], then the red, and after these the black; then, turning to the green ones, he made the beginning of his teaching as follows: having written as heading 'Green ones', he wrote the first of them all in these very words. Green plaster of Gallus. Rx: pine-cone resin, 300 drachmas; wax, 100 drachmas; scraped verdigris, 50 drachmas.

of frankincense [473] 25 drachms, of vinegar a sufficient quantity. He ought perhaps, then, to have said something also about the preparation, whether he wishes the frankincense too to be ground fine together with the verdigris while the vinegar is poured on, or only the verdigris. For either way is possible; and in many compositions some have written it the one way, others the other. But in this case it is possible to divine his intention, namely that he wishes both to be triturated with vinegar, the frankincense and the verdigris. For which affections, however, the drug is to be used ought by all means to have been made clear. Perhaps, then, since before this one he had written two plasters, to the former of which he prefixed "for gangrenes and putrefactions and old and malignant spreading sores", and to the second "for spreading sores, the one I use, and many other things", for this reason he wrote this green one next, without any addition, indicating that it is suited to the same conditions. But again, writing another one next, he said simply "green plaster of Potamon", then another, a third green one, and a fourth green one, "which I use", and a fifth, another, and a sixth after these and a seventh and an eighth and a ninth and a tenth, an eleventh

[474] and a twelfth and a thirteenth and a fourteenth and a fifteenth and a sixteenth, prefixing to each of them only this one word, "another", writing them all as differing from one another in power, yet not all of them suitable for putrefactions and spreading sores and gangrenes, as can be recognised from their material. From which it is also clear that he wrote them together with one another according to similarity of colour, not according to similarity of power. We, then, shall state the power of each of them, taking our starting-point from the nature of the simple drugs. For this will be most useful to those who wish not only to understand in general the method of the composition and use of such drugs, but also to be able, by this means, to improvise and to discern, in the case of things written by the older authors without distinction, of what sort of power they are. So we shall examine the one which Andromachus wrote first, taking up and considering each of the simples of which it is composed. First, then, in it he mentions pine-cone (strobiline) resin.

This is, as was said in the books on the power of simple drugs, the most heating [475] of the resins, just as the terebinth is the most moderate of all in both respects. For all resins both heat and dry, but some of them do these things more, others less. The strongest, then, is the strobilos resin, and the most moderate, as I said, the terebinth. And indeed the strobilos resin dries most quickly, as does what is called by its own particular name 'pine physema' (πιτύϊνον φύσημα), which is itself also a resin in kind, drying and heating; but while in drying it does not fall short of the strobilos resin, in heating it falls short by not a little. These, then, are without fattiness when they have dried, and for this reason they cannot produce plasters pleasant to the touch, as the viscous and moist ones do. Between the pine physema and the strobilos resin stands the fir resin, at least as regards heating; it however remains moist for a longer time, just as does the frankincense-like (λιβανίζουσα) variety of the Colophonian—and some call this alone Colophonian—having something pleasant in its smell, like the fir resin, and heating moderately, like that one. It is produced in very small quantity, and for this reason it is costly.

The most moist of all, however, is the one variety of the resin called [476] larch. For this too is in a way twofold: the one kind is closely similar to the terebinth in all respects, while the other is more pungent than it and τερμοτέρα and more moist, and more unpleasant in smell and more bitter in taste and hotter. The liquid resin that settles at the bottom of the earthenware vessels containing pine resin exactly resembles the terebinth in consistency and colour, but differs in smell and taste, being more unpleasant in smell, as also more pungent, and more biting in taste; wherefore it is also better to mix the terebinth into all the drugs that are to heal ulcers well, since the first and best aim among them is that what is applied be non-biting. Let us return, then, to the plaster before us, into which Andromachus orders that three hundred drachmas of stone-pine resin be put, mixed with the hundred drachmas of wax, neither he himself nor whoever composed it having aimed accurately at either its consistency or its power.

For it will not be adhesive, and it will become acrid; and he rightly provided it with a remedy against both by mixing in frankincense, but, [477] relative to the quantity of those ingredients, he mixed in little, and especially because he puts in fifty drachms of verdigris, and these are an eighth part of the four hundred that are made up from the wax and the resin. But this one would not fault in someone whose aim is to produce a sufficiently drying drug, since for one wishing to make it flesh-producing and agglutinative for moderate wounds, the fifty drachms would be well mixed in. And in this way it would become milder and more flesh-producing, more adhesive and more widely useful. One must praise the admixture of frankincense, which helps towards a plaster-like consistency; for it is both pain-relieving and concoctive. If, then, he had mixed in a weight of it equal to the verdigris, that is, the fifty drachms, he would, as I said, have made the drug both more adhesive and milder. But since he mixed in twenty-five, wishing to preserve the drying strength of the verdigris, he has made the plaster suitable both for the agglutination of larger wounds and for the cure of ulcers that are hard to treat. And that he intended it to become such is shown also by the admixture of vinegar.

It is therefore in our power to make it both more vigorous and milder [478], by mixing in either more or less vinegar, and likewise more acrid or less biting. For from the admixture of the more acrid vinegar, as also of a greater quantity of it, the drug will be more drying, and more agglutinative of bloody wounds, when wine-like vinegar has been mixed in. It is better, in the composition, to grind the verdigris with sharp vinegar for several days in a hot sun; for its biting quality will be mitigated, while nothing of its power will be diminished. The frankincense, however, it is not necessary to mix in from the beginning; rather a single day suffices for this. For I think you remember this too, which has often been said, that in the case of the strong drugs, such as verdigris, misy, chalcitis, sory, scale and chalcanthum, when they are ground in vinegar for several days, the bitingness is blunted while the virtue is increased. For all the metallic drugs, being by nature of coarser parts, do not extend their powers to the depth of the bodies being treated.

In order, then, that they may become more fine-particled, one must add to them the working-up by means of trituration and vinegar; for having been thoroughly refined through this, they sink down [479] as far as the depth. And there accrues also another benefit in such preparations of drugs: for having been thoroughly worked up, they pass through the pores in the body, being held back nowhere on their journey, and for this reason, even if they are hotter by nature, they act without biting. And so too of the humours themselves that are generated in the body, the thin ones are easily dispersed by transpiration without bitingness, whereas the thicker ones, being retained and wedged in, cause distress, when they are biting. The same account holds also for the burnt metallic drugs; but those retain something biting from their contact with the fire, which they lay aside in the washings and become entirely non-biting. Whereas those which, instead of the fire, undergo something similar to burning in the trituration with vinegar in the sun do not acquire in addition even the heat that comes from the fire. Indeed, even the burnt ones, when levigated in vinegar, become much better. These things, then, which are common to many drugs, are necessary to be known, and likewise what concerns their use, which is different in the case of different affections.

and in the case of hollow ones, when, taken up [480] on lint-pledgets (motoi), they are inserted. The plaster before us, at any rate, if you melt it with rose-oil and use it, will be useful on foul and moist ulcers, but biting on those that are free of complicating circumstances, and for this reason it will be necessary to mix with it a moist cerate made from wax and resin, melted either with rose-oil or with olive oil. There might sometimes also be need of myrtle-oil, and one must also know some method for the mixing of these. Of olive oil, at any rate, there is one name, but not one quality and power. For the omphakion is colder, while that from ripe olives is hotter; and if it is aged, it will increase its power of heating. So too the oil containing salt, to the extent that it has taken a share of it, is more heating and more drying than that which has not received any; while the oil with tender shoots of olive, which they call thalloi, is more astringent.

The more useful choice is dictated to you by both the form of the ulcer and the nature of the body being treated, the ulcer being treated by its contraries, the ulcerated body by its similars; so that you will also melt with myrtle oil the drug that is going to be applied on lint, whenever the flesh being generated appears to you to be more flabby than is proper [481], and all the more whenever the ulcer is near to cicatrization; just as, whenever some small remnant of inflammation is left in the surrounding parts, it is best to melt the drug with rose oil. And you have learned that the best rose oil is that which has been made from roses alone, many of them steeped for a considerable time in oil prepared without salt. If, then, one keeps these things always ready to hand in memory and is mindful, as I said, of the power of all the simple drugs, he will both compose green plasters of many kinds himself and make the best use of each of those already compounded. At any rate, the plaster set forth up to this point in our discussion, which Andromachus wrote first among the green ones, can be remodelled in many ways: on the one hand by putting in some other resin in place of the strobilos (pine-cone) resin, on the other by increasing the frankincense or putting in along with it one of the dry flesh-producing drugs, such as iris, aristolochia, bitter-vetch meal, and whatever others are of this kind. And indeed one may also vary the composition by mixing in something emollient for the hardened lips of the ulcer.
