On the basis of this notion some mixed in ammoniac incense [482] and galbanum, and some stag's marrow or calf's marrow or fat, just as, again, others mixed in one of the repellent drugs, wishing to check the influxes. On this account, at any rate, some put in schist alum, others the round kind, and others omphacine gall-nut. Others mixed in ladanum, which has both powers, the emollient and the repellent, so that the lips might be softened and nothing might flow in from the parts lying above. And indeed all those who also wished to treat ulcers hard to heal, so that the drug should be a polychreston (of many uses), mixed with the aforesaid ingredients chrysocolla or diphryges or burnt copper or scale, some of copper, some of steel (stomoma) or of iron. And nearly all the things just mentioned preserve the colour of the green plasters, whereas others, though of the same powers, destroy it if they are mixed in. This is why I too did not mention all the drugs under each power, but only those which will preserve the colour of the plaster being compounded.

For it was proposed not simply to speak about agglutinative or flesh-producing plasters, but with the condition that they be green ones, so that both these just mentioned and chalcanthum [483] and raw chalcitis, when mixed in a small measure, preserve the colour of the drugs that are the subject of the discussion. Concerning the composition of such drugs, then, enough has been said; but concerning their use, this too ought to have been added in writing by Andromachus. Since, however, it has been omitted by him, we shall add it ourselves, first stating one general account bearing on the use of such drugs. This account is necessary; and then, having stated the universal method, it is fitting to make the particular [applications] rest with those who have learned it. But such a thing is the task of dialectical men (διαλεκτικῶν), to write the particular [uses] for them in the case of all [the drugs], as Heras and Criton and Asclepiades and many others do. And indeed there is also a third kind of teaching, which we ourselves practise, neither writing the use in the case of all the particular drugs, nor yet entrusting the whole to the universal, common teaching of the method alone, but teaching this first, and after it writing one, or a second, or even a third example for the sake of clarity and of the exercise of the learners.

[484] just as, indeed, we are also now demonstrating these things in practice, as we have already done them also in the preceding books. For having discovered, from the power of the ingredients that compose it, to what degree the drug attains in drying and cleansing, from this we shall also discover the condition for which it will be useful. For where there is much moisture and filth in abundance, there one must apply a drug that dries and cleanses to a considerable degree; but where there is the so-called uncomplicated (aperistaton) ulcer, which needs the production of flesh, there the most moderate of the drying and cleansing drugs. And the less and the more in this it is fitting to discover from the nature of the person being treated. For to harder bodies, whether through natural temperament or through age or through region or pursuits, one must apply drugs that dry more, and to moister bodies those that dry less. The first use, then, of each of the drugs called emmota is taken by conjecture from the indications just mentioned; the second, as I also said before, from the signs that appear in the body being treated.

For if the hollow ulcer is found to be free of inflammation and [485] clean, one should make no innovation; but if it is moister or fouler, one should intensify the drying and cleansing drug; and if it is more hollow than before, one should relax it. Now it is intensified by the admixture of honey, and it is mitigated by that of oil and cerate or of one of the oily substances, such as rose-oil and myrtle-oil and henna oil prepared simply, without the astringent thickening ingredients (stymmata) which people add either for the sake of fragrance or so that the preparations remain unaffected for a longer time. And if one of the lovers of fault-finding should charge us with leading the argument, contrary to what was set out from the beginning, towards the uses of the drugs, when we had promised to speak about their composition, let him consider that a kind of composition also takes place in the course of use, and hold his peace. For the first composition in it is that of the drugs mixed with the cerate, and the second lies in adding rose, myrtle, henna or rush oil, or honey. And of these things enough; we shall now proceed to the record of the plasters which have already given sufficient proof by experience.

These, then, are the drugs that Andromachus [486] wrote down, worthy of note for those who know how to use them. Since they are of this sort, one must select those composed of fewer or more easily procured simples, those of more numerous uses (the more polychrēsta), and those that most closely adhere to the aim in hand. What I am saying would become clearer by an example. Let the example, then, be a hollow ulcer, free of complications, in a healthy body. Such an ulcer will be treated by the so-called plain green plaster, melted together with rose-oil. They call "plain" the one made of verdigris, wax and resin. I, as I said, mix an equal amount of each of the two, and of verdigris a tenth or a twelfth or an eighth. It is evidently a twelfth if we mix a pound of wax and a pound of resin, and two ounces of verdigris; a tenth, if to the two ounces of verdigris we mix twenty of both together, the resin and the wax, that is, if ten of each. And indeed, even if we mix an eighth part of verdigris with the cerate made of wax and resin, it will be fine this way too. For such a drug will be more pungent and more detergent, yet not useless; for it will be suitably applied to hard bodies.

[487] But a finer composition will result if one mixes the eighth part of verdigris with the composition made from wax and resin, having first triturated the verdigris for several days with the most acrid vinegar. And it would be finer still if we also mixed in frankincense, in half the amount relative to the verdigris. Of oil you will mix in, whenever you prepare the drug without vinegar and frankincense, cyathi equal in number to the ounces of verdigris; but whenever you mix in frankincense and vinegar, if the phryktē (roasted resin) is somewhat fattier and softer and you are preparing it in summer, you will mix in none; but when it is hard and it is winter, one cyathus. It is also possible for you, by mixing one of the liquid resins with the wax, to have no need of oil at all. You will mix in, of the most liquid resin, a third of the weight of the wax, and of the less liquid, a half. The composition will evidently turn out to be something like this: having melted the wax and the resin and cooled them, mix them with a part of verdigris, sometimes an eighth, sometimes a tenth, sometimes a twelfth, knowing that for hard bodies the first proportion is suitable, for soft ones the third, and for intermediate ones the intermediate.

[488] You will triturate the verdigris with vinegar. And if you should wish to make the drug milder, you may add a weight of frankincense half of that which you used for the verdigris. And if someone [wishes it] milder than this, you will mix the verdigris in a quantity equal to the frankincense. And also without scraping, having cooled the resin together with the wax, we melt them and pour them onto the verdigris and the frankincense, which have been triturated in a mortar with vinegar. These, then, are the first compositions of the green plaster, which is agglutinative of bloody wounds, those that are not large, and which is able to heal the others as far as cicatrization and to produce flesh, if it is melted with some oily liquid. By oily I mean rose-oil, which it is most fitting to use, prepared in the manner I have described, and after this myrtle-oil and henna-oil and mastic-oil, and oil itself: in those cases where you wish to add some heat to the drug being melted you will mix in this common oil; where cooling, the so-called omotribes (oil of unripe olives); where astringency, myrtle-oil.

and in those cases where you want something of a mixed faculty, one that has something concoctive and yet also something repellent, rose-oil; and in those where you want slight astringency together with more heat, henna-oil [489] and mastic-oil. There will also be many other compositions, as I said, for the simple drugs just mentioned, when there are mixed in either the flesh-producing or the emollient or the astringent ones, or those that heal the ulcers which are hard to cure. Some have also mixed in discutient ones, just as also cicatrizing ones. Certain others, by mixing everything together, have either produced a useless hotchpotch (καρύκη) or have had the good fortune to work up a drug of many uses (polychrēston); and knowing the materials of these, you yourselves will be able both to use those already discovered and to compound others in like manner. I too shall append some of the reputable ones, beginning again from those which Andromachus wrote. There are, then, following the one written above, some thirty; but I shall set down only those praised by him. The fourth from the first is written thus: Green plaster, which I use. Take: scraped verdigris, 9 drachms; chrysocolla, 9 drachms; terebinth resin, one mina of sixteen ounces; wax, half a mina; a little vinegar.

As I also said before, Andromachus did not append to each of the plasters its profession, but from the material of the simple drugs out of which he composes the one before us [490] it is not unclear that it is able both by itself, before being melted, to treat ulcers, and, once melted, to become a lint-dressing (ἔμμοτον). And one should put in the mina of sixteen ounces; for the mina of twenty is large in relation to the equal measure of the chrysocolla and the verdigris. After this one, having written three others in succession, he again writes another, verbatim as follows. "Another, which I use. Take scraped verdigris, one pound; manna, 10 ounces — I, 1 pound; wax, 5 pounds; roasted resin, 5 pounds; liquid resin, 5 pounds; oil, 1 cyathus; vinegar, a sufficient quantity. And I [add] also ammoniac incense, 10 ounces." With these words Andromachus stopped. But it is quite evident, if we remember anything of what has been said before, that this plaster itself too has a power similar to the one written before it. Next after the one written before, Andromachus, writing another, began thus: "Another, mallow-coloured (μολοχίνη)." And after this he subjoined the proportion of the simple drugs from which he composes it, thus: Take scraped verdigris, 1 pound; pitch, 2 pounds; manna, 1 pound; wax, 2 pounds; resin, 2 pounds; oil, 1 pound; vinegar, a sufficient quantity.

This one, [491] then, is similar to the preceding ones. And it is quite clear that the verdigris and the manna, one litra of each, must be ground fine together with the vinegar, while double the amount of each of these of the wax and the pitch and the resin, that is two litrai of each, must be melted together with the litra of oil, and in this way mixed with the ingredients that have been ground fine with the vinegar, as has often been said by us, after one has cooled them and scrapes them rather than pours them on top, so that it does not happen, when the surrounding air is cold, that the so-called enkerides (lumps of wax) form. Next after this he wrote another approved plaster, thus. Green hundred-drachm plaster. Take ammoniac incense, 8 drachms; scale of copper, 12 drachms; manna, 8 drachms; dry resin, 12 drachms; verdigris, 8 drachms; calf's suet, 14 drachms; terebinth resin, 8 drachms; wax, 30 drachms; oil, a quarter of a cyathus; vinegar, a sufficient quantity. This one is able both to glue together large wounds and to cleanse the foul among ulcers, and, having taken on cerate in the melting, to produce flesh. But before being melted it is able also to heal the thick-lipped among ulcers, to bring together sinuses, and in general to disperse and to repel.

[492] For it is mixed from opposite powers. And the green plaster written next after it is of similar power and use, having this proportion: Take terebinth, 1 mina; herb of serapias, 25 dr.; scraped verdigris, 10 dr.; calf's fat, 25 dr.; wax, 25 dr.; frankincense, 12 dr.; henna oil for the dry ingredients. And the one which is called by others Isis he himself wrote, without this appellation, thus: Green plaster of Epigonus. Although all make mention of it, I shall nonetheless now too write out the proportion of the simple drugs according to this author, since some differ in them. For he orders one to put in burnt copper, ammoniac salt, copper scale, verdigris, ammoniac incense, aristolochia and frankincense, an equal amount of each, 8 dr., that is 1 ounce; but of aloe, myrrh and galbanum one and a half times these, of each, that is 1½ ounces, which is the same as saying 12 (ounces) and a half; of round alum 6 dr. He also mixes in 200 dr. of Colophonian resin and half as much wax, that is 100.

[493] and of oil half a kotyle. He says that some mix in a quarter, and a sufficient quantity of vinegar, and of dracontium root half an ounce, which is 4 drachms. He added this at the end, since it is not carried in the recipe of the Isis; for Epigonus added it, and in this respect the Isis of Epigonus differed. Next after those previously recorded, Andromachus wrote a green plaster of Pasion in the following proportion: Colophonian resin 300 drachms, wax 150 drachms, verdigris 8 drachms, round alum 8 drachms, scale of copper 12 drachms, frankincense 16 drachms, burnt copper 8 drachms, ammoniac salt 8 drachms, half a kyathos of oil, vinegar a sufficient quantity. This drug, because it has taken in addition the ammoniac salts, has become more attractive and more discutient and more cleansing than the preceding ones; in all other respects it is similar. Stronger than the one previously recorded and more widely useful is the one Andromachus wrote after one intervening recipe, which he names the green plaster of Alcimion, in the following proportion: terebinth resin 200 drachms, wax 150 drachms, scale of copper 18 drachms, scraped verdigris 16 drachms, round alum 16 drachms, galbanum 16.

[494] frankincense 10; ammoniac salt 12 dr.; burnt copper 16 dr.; aristolochia 10 dr.; Indian aloe 12 dr.; myrrh 16 dr.; ammoniac incense (gum ammoniac) 18 dr.; galbanum 12 dr., though some say 8; of oil half a kotyle; of vinegar half a kotyle. Next after this one he writes another, called Athena, as he himself added in writing at the end. The proportion of the simple drugs from which it is composed is as follows. ℞ wax 250 dr.; terebinth 200 dr.; roasted resin (φρυκτῆς) 100 dr.; calf's suet 50 dr.; galbanum 24 dr.; manna 24 dr.; ammoniac salt 12 dr.; burnt copper 12 dr.; aloe 12 dr.; copper scale 24 dr.; round alum 12 dr., and split alum 8 dr.; chalkanthos 8 dr.; misy 8 dr.; opopanax 8 dr.; scraped verdigris 6 dr.; ammoniac incense 6 dr.; Sinopic red earth (miltos) 3 dr.; of vinegar 3 kotylai; of oil 2 kotylai. Put in the red earth at the beginning. It is called Athena; this drug too, as I said, is a polychreston (of many uses), and how one must use the polychresta will be shown in the discussion devoted to them. After this one he wrote another green plaster, word for word as follows: Green plaster through henna oil, of Aphrodas.

[495] ♃ Wax, 24 dr.; dry resin, 12 dr.; scraped verdigris, 8 dr.; Aphrodas (?), 12 dr.; manna, 8 dr.; henna oil, an eighth of a kotyle. It is pounded together with it (?), and it is able to be suitable for the ulcers that are hard to treat; and for this reason he wrote this one down, as being compounded from few ingredients and able to be sufficiently useful. Since Andromachus goes on to write many other green plasters, both of many ingredients and polychrēsta (of many uses), it seemed good to me to leave them aside, mentioning only the plain ones (litai), as they themselves call them. He himself writes, then, word for word thus: another green plain plaster, which I use. ♃ Resin, twelve pounds; wax, 8 pounds; scraped verdigris, two pounds; calf's fat, two pounds; vinegar, one pound; but I put in one pound of manna. It is quite evident, then, that he wants the vinegar to be triturated together with the two pounds of verdigris and the pound of frankincense, just as I said before, and then the meltable ingredients to be mixed with these. I mean the eight pounds of fat, together with the eight of wax and the 12 of resin.

This plaster would have been strictly simple (λιτή), had it taken neither the fat nor the [496] manna. For in that case the verdigris would have been a tenth part of the two together, the resin and the wax. And if the resin were hard, surely some oil too would have been mixed in, as has been said before. But since it has taken the calf's fat, it is no longer strictly simple, having acquired in addition an emollient and concocting drug. And much more so indeed if it should also take the manna, for that is concocting and suppurative and has something flesh-producing in it. [A general account of plasters of the same colour.] That the grouping together of drugs in the written record of them ought to be made not according to similarity of colour but according to that of their power is surely quite clear. At any rate, just as Andromachus does, so too certain others write out in sequence one after another not only the green plasters, but also the quince-yellow ones and the grey ones and the white ones. How, then, the white ones are made, I have stated in the first of these treatises; and how the green ones are made has been said before as well, and I shall now recall it.

[How green ones come about.] Verdigris is put into them in no small quantity, but so much as to prevail over the colour of the other [497] ingredients and to make the whole like itself. The one compounding such a plaster must take aim, besides the quantity of the verdigris, also at the colour of the things mixed with it and at the manner of the boiling: in the case of the things mixed, guarding against the colours that are hard to shift, such as are those of the yellow and reddish and black drugs. I mean by yellow and reddish such as is that of melite (μηλίτου) and that of burnt chalcitis, of arsenic and of sandarach; by black, such as are those of pitch and asphalt and ampelitis earth and gagates stone. And in the boiling the verdigris must not be put in together with the things being united over the fire, but be mixed with them, once united, in the mortar, if you wish the drug to remain green in colour. But if you wish to make the plaster quince-yellow, you must know that in the boiling the verdigris changes first into this colour, and later into the tawny, so that what is called the two-coloured plaster comes about. For in the time after the boiling, after a few days, the greyer part forms on its surface, while the tawny runs together into the depth of the drug.

But since what is appropriate has been said about their colour, [498] I shall pass again to the discussion of their powers, having recalled the point from which I first set out in this book. I set out, if we remember, to speak about the flesh-producing drugs, whose aim with respect to their power lies in cleansing and drying moderately and without biting; but the compositions according to species are different, being varied according to the materials of the simple drugs. It is evident that those properly and primarily called flesh-producing are flesh-producing for uncomplicated ulcers, that is, those which are hollow but do not have filth or inflammation attending them, and still less an influx of bad humours, nor dyscratic flesh in the hollow ulcer. For if any of the things mentioned is combined with the hollowness, that must be treated first. And the aims of their treatment are, in the case of the filthy ones, the drugs capable of cleansing; in the case of those arising from an influx of humour, drying and repelling that which flows in; and if it should be abundant and hard to overcome, to cut off the cause of the influx first.

For as regards drying, at least, they are in no way inferior to aphronitron and nitron; but those two have no share in the astringent power, just as neither does [502] the flower of the stone of Asia, and for this reason they are able both to disperse and, when mixed with cerates, to cleanse foul ulcers. Salts, however, do not possess this, on account of their astringency. Accordingly, for you who bear these things in mind and have heard the method both of the composition and of the use of all such drugs, I shall write in what follows those drugs that have been approved by experience on the part of the physicians renowned for their knowledge of the best drugs. Mantias and his pupil Heraclides of Tarentum were the first to write down many drugs, which, having come to the test of experience among those who followed them, were sorted out (διωρίσθη); and the best among them these men in turn wrote down again, while those that seemed to act less effectively than the others they left aside. Reasonably, therefore, I too make the fuller mention of those who came after them. Among these, those who seem most to have achieved success in the experience of drugs are Petronius Musa and Heras and Andromachus, and Asclepiades and Criton. Not a few drugs have been written down also by Archigenes and Philippus and their circle.

And there is also one book of Menecrates entitled [503] 'Autokrator hologrammatos (The Emperor, written out in full letters) of noteworthy drugs'. So then, whatever finest drugs have been written down by these men and are praised by them, and all those of which we ourselves have experience, both from these very ones that have been written down and from those which our teachers used, and if anything has been discovered in addition by us as well, this I shall write in what follows, explaining of what kind (genos) each of them is. But now, since I have gone through the green ones, next after these I shall write the quince-yellow ones. [Quince-yellow plasters.] Just as most of the green plasters become such because of the verdigris predominating, and especially the better-coloured among them, in the same way also the quince-yellow ones. But the green ones contain the verdigris unboiled, whereas the quince-yellow ones contain it boiled, but moderately; since if you boil it further, you will produce the ones called by some 'two-coloured' and by others 'tawny'. It is the custom of physicians to call simply green and quince-yellow and tawny those which both glue together wounds that are not very large and bring to cicatrisation ulcers which physicians are accustomed to call 'uncomplicated' (aperistata), and which fill up hollow ones with flesh when melted with rose oil.

Polychrēsta (of many uses), however, [504] among them are those for which the professed virtues are more numerous. Some, again, do not have many professed virtues, but one that is noteworthy: either to be suited to the malignant ulcers, or to disperse pus or melicerides, or to soften hardnesses, or something of that sort among the things that are neither to be lightly regarded nor easy to treat. Andromachus, then, wrote fourteen quince-yellow ones, of which five contain verdigris, while the others have been made without verdigris. Of those containing verdigris, one is the one written first of the fourteen, another is the fourth, and one after it the sixth, and after that one the seventh and the tenth. Those, then, to which he has added nothing special, all of these both glue ulcers together and cicatrize them; and if one wishes, when melted with rose oil they also produce flesh. They also treat moderate inflammations, just as they also soften moderate hardnesses; and those do this more which contain ammoniac incense, and among these themselves more so those that contain more of it, in proportion to the other ingredients. In the case of some he himself added 'tender' (ἁπαλή), that is, evidently, suited to tender skins.

And in the one to which is added "drawing" and "squeezing out" (ἐξιπωτικὴ), [505] he indicates that it is suited to intense pain and synanche and pain of the side. Or, when he says that it disperses the internal abscesses, he attests something more for these than for those written without qualification. Accordingly I shall set them all down below in order. [Quince-yellow plasters of Andromachus.] A quince-yellow plaster which I use. Take litharge 104 drachmas, oil in summer 1 kotyle, in winter half a kotyle, wax 48 drachmas, Colophonian resin 48 drachmas, ammoniac incense 24 drachmas, scraped verdigris 8 drachmas, galbanum 8 drachmas, myrrh 8 drachmas. Another. Take litharge 100 drachmas, oil 3 kyathoi or half a kotyle, Colophonian resin 64 drachmas, ammoniac incense 40 drachmas, white lead 24 drachmas. Another. Take litharge 40 or 50 drachmas, white lead 6 drachmas, Tyrrhenian wax 16 drachmas, dry pine resin 16 drachmas, ammoniac incense 2 drachmas, oil 1 kotyle. Another. Take litharge 100 drachmas, Colophonian resin 64 drachmas, but others 48, wax 84 drachmas, galbanum 8 drachmas, myrrh 8 drachmas, verdigris 8 drachmas, opopanax 6 drachmas.

of oil, in summer one kotyle [506], in winter half a kotyle or three kyathoi. Another. Take litharge 100 drachmas, pine resin 100 drachmas, wax 12 drachmas, oil half a kotyle or three kyathoi, Falernian wine half a kotyle. The litharge is ground fine with the wine until it has dried, then it is boiled. Another. Take litharge 100 drachmas, old oil 70 (?) or 2 kotylai, wax 100 drachmas, scolex verdigris 25 drachmas, black chamaeleon 12 and a half drachmas, chrysocolla 40 drachmas. Another. Take litharge 200 drachmas, old oil 3 kotylai, wax 168 drachmas, ammoniac incense 100 drachmas, myrrh 4 drachmas, verdigris 8 or 20 drachmas, Colophonian resin 128 drachmas, galbanum 20 drachmas, black chamaeleon 8 drachmas; but some use propolis, 8 or 20 drachmas, instead of the chamaeleon. Another. Take old oil in which chamaeleon, as much as possible, has been boiled down, one xestes; litharge one litra. Having brought it to the boil, sprinkle in the litharge and boil. Another, for spreading sores (nomai). Take sandarach 3 drachmas, split alum 4 drachmas, frankincense 4 drachmas, myrrh 4 drachmas, ammoniac incense 18 drachmas, wax 18 drachmas, terebinth resin 6 drachmas, pig's fat 2 drachmas, honey one sixteenth of a kotyle.

[507] Another. ♃ Litharge, 108 or 120 drachms; wax, 108 or 120 drachms (in another copy, 100); ammoniac incense, 50 drachms; terebinth, 40 drachms; aristolochia, 25 drachms; root of zeia (spelt), 8 or 20 drachms; verdigris scolex, 16 drachms; split alum, 16 drachms; old oil, 2 cotylae. Another, simple. ♃ Litharge, 100 drachms; axungia (lard), 75 drachms; old oil, 75 drachms. For those of tender skin, and it disperses. Another, called aphra, the emollient quince-yellow plaster of Diophantus, drawing and expressive, by which joints have been treated. ♃ Worked birdlime (ixos), 1 litra; wax, 1 litra; terebinth resin, 1 litra; galbanum, 3 ounces. Melt and use. Another, Salome, for every excessive pain and for synanche together with a cupping-glass, and for pain of the side. ♃ Litharge, 2 litrae; old oil, 8 ounces. Boil together. [Another quince-yellow plaster from Heraclides, dispersing the internal abscesses without pain.] ♃ Litharge, 100 drachms; white lead, 100 drachms; wax, 80 drachms; dry resin, 60 drachms; ammoniac incense, 50 drachms; galbanum, 16 drachms; old oil, 2 cotylae. But according to Rusticus, the pupil of Isidorus: ♃ litharge, 50 drachms;

[508] of white lead 50 drachms; of ammoniac incense 50 or 40 drachms; of wax 25 drachms; of dry resin 30 drachms; of elm, the part in the little pouches, 15 drachms; of galbanum 8 drachms; of old oil half a kotyle or one and a half kotylai. Of none of these plasters did Andromachus write the boiling; but I have stated earlier what is decisive for their colour, namely that the verdigris must be neither raw, as in the green ones, nor boiled for a very long time, as in those called two-coloured and tawny. Rather, when the cauldron is already close to being about to be taken off the fire, the verdigris is to be added; then, when it changes and becomes quince-yellow, it is to be lifted from the fire, if the drug is by then already non-staining. If not, one should allow a little additional time over the gentlest fire and then remove it in that way; for over the most violent fire it readily changes toward the tawny. For this reason I shall also append two other celebrated quince-yellow plasters, the one called that of Menoetus, the other that of Serapion, whose boilings too many have written down, and you will have a model for the preparation of those written by Andromachus.

[509] [Quince-coloured plaster of Menoetus.] Take: litharge, 4 pounds; oil, 3 pounds; transparent terebinth, 2 pounds; wax, 1 pound; verdigris, frankincense, galbanum, 4 ounces each; ammoniac incense, 6 ounces. Boil the litharge and the oil until it thickens considerably, then add the resin and the wax. And when these have dissolved well, set the cauldron down and let it cool well, then add the verdigris, and having stirred it while it is down, boil again over a gentle fire until it becomes quince-like in colour; then, having triturated the galbanum and the frankincense and having poured [the mixture] out into a mortar, where the ammoniac has previously been triturated in vinegar so as to be glutinous, and having kneaded it, take it up at once, and having poured on a little vinegar, leave it until the following day, and then, having kneaded it again, store it away. [Quince-coloured plaster of Serapion, for wounds and dissolving, for boxers (πυκτική), useful for everything.] Take: litharge, 100 drachmas; ammoniac incense, 28 drachmas; wax, 56 drachmas; Cyprian verdigris, 9 drachmas; myrrh, 1 drachma; Colophonian resin, 56 drachmas; galbanum, 9 drachmas.

of oil [510] half a kotyle, in summer one and a quarter kotylai. Boil the litharge and the oil; when it changes, [add] the ammoniac, then the wax, and having taken it down [from the fire] put in the galbanum, the verdigris and the rest, and boil gently. Such boilings of the quince-yellow plasters that have been written down were described by many of those before me, and from these, by analogy, you will be able to boil the other quince-yellow ones as well. One must put in the litharge first, then the resins and the ammoniac, then the galbanum and the verdigris; then, if it takes either frankincense or myrrh or aloe — for these, when the drug is lifted from the fire, must be added on top, since they do not tolerate the boilings. It has also been said before that it must be boiled gently, especially when the verdigris has been put in; and indeed also that one must put the latter in after setting the cauldron down on the ground and letting it cool a little, and all the more if the vessel in which the boiling takes place is small. For when the verdigris has been added to what has been boiled beforehand at the very moment it is seething, it has often caused the drug to overflow the vessel.

And in the first quince-yellow plaster of Menoetus, the one called the 'pugilistic' plaster, because boxers in particular use the drug, we have also [511] learned beforehand that the ammoniac can be ground with vinegar in the mortar, all the other ingredients having been mixed together in the cauldron, and then it is poured in. [Quince-yellow plasters of Heras.] Of Heras, for scrofulous swellings. The ones written by Heras, word for word, as follows. A quince-yellow plaster for old sinuses, even if they have been perforated through into the hollow spaces. The same plaster also disperses scrofulous swellings that have recently formed in children; it is effective also for wrenched joints. Take: litharge chrysitis, 100 drachms; dry pine resin, 100 drachms; Pontic wax, 12 drachms and four obols; oil, half a kotyle; Falernian wine, half a kotyle. The litharge is ground with the wine until it is dried out; then, in that state, it is boiled with the oil until it changes, and then the resin and the wax are mixed in, and it is boiled until it no longer stains. The gold-coloured plaster of Menoetius, effective for those with tender skin, and especially eunuchs. It is suitable for abrasions and for every wound, old and fresh, and for burns.

It is a malagma; it disperses phymata, parotid swellings, scrofulous swellings, hardnesses [512] of every kind; it is also effective against fissures and condylomata; it is exceedingly good. Take: litharge, 100 drachms; old oil, 100 drachms; dry pine resin, 50 or 100 drachms; wax, 50 drachms. Boil the litharge and the oil until it begins to thicken together, and add the resin finely ground, and when this has melted, the wax. When it is in good condition, pour it out into a mortar previously smeared with oil, and having worked it thoroughly, take it up. It is adhesive and does not stain. The plaster of Hygieinos, of good colour, serviceable for many things, effective in cases of ulcers that are hard to cicatrize and in cases of paronychiae. There is no plaster better than this. Chrysitis litharge, 1 mina; wax, 1 mina; root of black chamaeleon, 36 drachms; scraped verdigris, 18 drachms; chrysocolla, 40 drachms; old oil, 3 kotylai. Boil the litharge and oil over a gentle fire until it begins to boil up, then sprinkle in the verdigris, having lifted it off the fire, and stir, boiling again until it takes on its proper colour; then the wax. When it is in good condition, the chrysocolla and the chamaeleon; and having poured it out into a mortar, sprinkle vinegar over it.

[513] For the aforementioned conditions, then, it works even with the chrysocolla mixed in. Without this, however, it is most soothing and works supremely well for punctures of the nerves and wherever something needs to be brought up to the surface from muscles or nerves. Of these three plasters which Heras wrote, the first is both prepared with wine and called "the one through wine". And many of our teachers and friends use it, prepared, evidently, without verdigris; it has been written also by Andromachus and by nearly all who have composed various plasters. Now most people, by preparing it carelessly, make the drug contemptible. But it is excellent if, as it is written, it is prepared with Falernian wine. When this is not available, one must put in a tawny wine, old, thin in consistency, in so far as it is at all possible for this to be tawny (καθόλου ἐγχωρεῖ κιῤῥὸν τοῦτον ὑπάρχειν); for transparency is a property peculiar to the white wines.

The finest tawny wines among us in Asia are the one called Tmolites, the Lesbian, and the one most renowned among the ancients, the Ariusian, which is produced in Chios, which everyone used to use for the finest of the drugs and especially [514] for the antidotes, just as now they use the Falernian. If, then, we put such a wine into the litharge during the burning heat under the Dog-star, or otherwise in a hot sun, and then triturate it, or even without sun triturate it for a long time, so that the liquid is dried off and the litharge itself is left behind either completely free of moisture and dry or something close to this, the drug becomes excellent. One of my teachers used to prepare it, after the litharge had been prepared dry, having been triturated in Falernian wine, in some such way as this. Heating the oil in one vessel and the wine in another, he poured (κατέχει) little by little upon the litharge, sometimes going first to the wine, and after pulverizing it well and mixing it in, he added some of the oil; sometimes, beginning from the oil, he passed over to the wine. Doing this alternately many times he used up each of the two, and so, having poured it out from the mortar into a cauldron, he added the pine resin, which they specifically call physema, thoroughly pulverized, then the wax, and he boiled (ἥψει) it gently until it did not stain.

He used it also for sinuses (kolpoi), smearing beforehand with the blood of a pigeon, not of the domestic ones, [515] but of those called by some boskades (the 'grazing' ones), which go into the towers that people in our country construct in the fields. Some call these wild. Likewise in the case of large fresh wounds, smearing over with the blood of such a pigeon, he applied the drug, trusting in it very greatly. Of the wine he put in one and a half kotylai, not, as Heras and Andromachus do, only half a kotyle; and in this respect the drug became much better. If you wish to make it fragrant, you will mix in half an ounce of opopanax, which is 4 drachms. And for the sake of good colour put in the white Pontic wax. This drug also brings ulcers well to cicatrization. [Crito's quince-yellow drugs.] Concerning the quince-yellow ones about which Crito wrote, which he himself names boxwood-coloured (pyxinai). Boxwood-coloured plaster for freshly inflicted wounds. The same one both cicatrizes and draws. ♃ Of litharge 4 litrai, of wax 4 litrai, of terebinth 8 ounces, of verdigris 8 ounces, of old oil 2 xestai.

half a xestes of vinegar. Boil the litharge, oil, verdigris and vinegar together over a gentle [516] fire. When it is about to thicken, put in the resin and the wax, and having united them use it, especially on fresh wounds. Criton also wrote another before this one, which he calls boxwood-coloured (pyxine), simple as far as the number of ingredients mixed in goes, but great in what it promises; at any rate he writes about it verbatim as follows: "The one made with chamaeleon, which does the same things as the Tyrian. It is most cicatrising for ulcers that are hard to heal, callous and chronic, and it also heals fissures in the anus, condylomata and indurations. Take litharge 1 mina, wax 6 minae, verdigris 4 minae, chamaeleon 8 minae, oil 1 mina. Boil the oil and the litharge, stirring with a spatula, until it sets and becomes quince-yellow. When this has happened, sprinkle on the verdigris, then add the wax, and having melted it carefully and taken it off the fire, sprinkle on the chamaeleon. When it has been united, pour it out into a mortar and, having kneaded it, take it up."

Criton has also written certain other plasters in the fourth book of his Drugs, 'boxwood-coloured' as he himself names them, but 'quince-yellow' according to the [517] others; but some of them are compounded without verdigris, while others do take verdigris but will be discussed under another kind of drugs, according to the similarities of their power: the cicatrizing ones among the cicatrizing, those made with juices among those made with juices, and among the emollient ones all those whose nature it is to soften, as is also the plaster of Mnaseas, which is prepared in many forms by him in the book before us. Now then it is already time to pass on to the agglutinative plasters, which differ in colour both from one another and from the quince-yellow ones. [On the tawny plasters, which they call two-coloured.] Some are composed of the same material as the quince-yellow plasters that contain verdigris, as I also said before, differing in one thing only, in having been boiled for longer. For all those that are green on account of the raw verdigris become quince-yellow when it has been boiled moderately, and tawny when boiled more. It is evident, then, that the quince-yellow and the tawny ones must necessarily contain more oil than the green ones, even if they should have all the other ingredients the same.

And for this reason it is proper to put into the cauldron first [518] the litharge, which is to be boiled until it reaches a glutinous consistency, next the verdigris, and after it, if any of the metallic substances is being put in, such as burnt copper and its scale, and when it has thickened, at that point wax and resin, if the drug takes these too, and at the end frankincense and myrrh and aloe and whatever other such things, as in the case of the most renowned of the tawny plasters, which they call the one 'through dittany', it too being one of those named 'sacred', like the Isis, since they say that they were brought from the temples in Egypt. This one, then, is a polychrēston (of many uses), and for that reason it will be written up in the following discourse together with the polychrēsta. But for now I shall make my account concerning the other tawny plasters, both those that are strictly simple and those that lie between these and the polychrēsta. Just as, then, the simple green ones were composed of wax and resin and oil and verdigris, according to the proportion stated in its case, so the tawny ones have their composition with the addition of litharge and of more oil than the green ones.

If, then, you wish the plaster to be boiled for a longer time, [519] you will increase the oil, and you will have the drug more desiccative, and for this reason more agglutinative of bloody wounds; but if you wish it boiled moderately, it suffices for the measure of oil to be as much as the weight of the litharge. For having measured out the Roman litra of oil by measure, we shall put it in to the litra of litharge by weight. But if we wish the drug to be boiled for a longer time, we shall put in not only one and a half litrai of oil, but even two and more. More desiccative than the tawny plasters prepared in this way are those which have no resin and wax at all, but are composed solely of the so-called metallic substances, just as certain others among earlier writers have recorded such plasters, and the one which I always use, composed by me and boiled in the following manner. Having first boiled the litharge with the oil, I add the metallic substances triturated with vinegar, and thus I boil until it no longer stains. I put in four litrai of oil—and the older it is, the better it will be, and all the more if it is Sabine—and three litrai of litharge.

and of the most acrid vinegar [520] two pounds; and three metallic substances, these: scale of black copper, verdigris and chalcitis, an equal weight of each, two ounces apiece, which is sixteen drachmas. But when the oil is old and thick because of its age, you may put in four and a half pounds; and I once even put in five, for this reason also, it being winter. For we know that more oil is put in in winter than in summer. You will, of course, boil the litharge beforehand to a glutinous consistency. And if you also have castor oil (kikinon), put that in instead of the old oil. This drug glues bleeding wounds readily, and more so on hard bodies than on soft and womanish ones and those of children, of which sort also those of eunuchs are; and when loosened with castor oil (kikinon) or old oil and applied as a lint-dressing, it is wonderful how it concocts the most difficult-to-cure of ulcers, those which produce no pus at all. It also glues together sinuses, and reduces fistulas and dries them and closes them completely.

And when indeed you wish it to accomplish these things well, triturate the metallic substances in the most acrid vinegar for several days, and preferably [521] in the sun. And having likewise triturated and dried the litharge, then, having mixed it with the oil, boil it in the manner that has been stated. For the ulcers that are hard to cicatrize, however, it is not necessary that the metallic substances and the litharge be worked up in this way in the trituration; for even without these it becomes more cicatrizing. But in that case add to it also an ounce of diphryges and an ounce of chrysocolla. These are not put in together with the scale and the verdigris, nor yet when the drug is already completely boiled, but at the intermediate time. For such drugs require just so much boiling as to be precisely united with the ingredients already present, which comes about through a moderate interval of time, neither very long before the removal of the cauldron nor close to it. And so this plaster by itself is sufficient to glue together fistulas and sinuses and large wounds. But a new sponge, not a hard one, soaked in old wine, also assists it. And the bandaging in the case of sinuses should be done from the bottom, with the bandage arriving at the mouth, as will be shown more clearly in the discussion on fistulas.

[522] [On cicatrizing drugs.] Whether you wish to call the plasters that produce a scar "epulotic" (cicatrizing) or "synulotic" (scar-closing), and likewise also the other drugs, both the powders sprinkled on and those applied by the use of lint-pledgets, makes no difference at all with regard to the cures they effect, provided you keep in mind the faculty which it is fitting that such drugs possess, which was stated together with all the others in the books of the Therapeutic Method. For by as much as the agglutinative plasters were shown to be more drying than the flesh-producing ones, by so much are the cicatrizing ones more drying than the agglutinative. For our aim in these is to make into skin the flesh that has been generated in hollow ulcers. Hence such a class of drugs must also be astringent, whether it be something smeared on or something sprinkled on (ἐπίσπαστον). But our purpose here is to mention only those plasters; for indeed the drugs applied by means of lint-pledgets come about when these plasters are melted in rose-oil or myrtle-oil. And myrtle-oil is in fact more useful than rose-oil, by as much as it is also more astringent.

But if you have neither of these, one must melt them in henna oil and mastic oil and [523] quince oil; and if you have none of these, in oil of unripe olives (omotribes) or that from Iberia, which they call Spanish. And when you do not have even this, you will crush tender shoots of olive trees and throw them into some other of the oils that happen to be at hand. And if you are without these as well, it is better to melt in old oil; at any rate you would have from this the result that the drug becomes more drying. Now most physicians abandon the drugs which from ancient times have given sufficient proof of themselves to all the best physicians and for this reason have become renowned, in order that they themselves may seem to have something better than their predecessors. But one must know that, of the renowned drugs which have been praised among all, the drug made with cadmia and the one made with ladanum are best for cicatrization. The proportion of the simple drugs that are mixed, however, is not agreed upon among all physicians. For this reason, then, I decided to write down the proportions that satisfy each of those who wrote them, beginning from those written by Asclepiades in the third book of the external remedies, which he entitles Marcellas.

[524] [On cicatrizing plasters Asclepiades writes as follows.] For ulcers in the particular parts which, without any other condition, are already inclining toward a scar, one must use the preparations written below. The cicatrizing plaster through cadmia. Lucius the Teacher used this. Take: of cadmia burnt and prepared with wine, of roasted chalcitis, 16 drachms each; of wax 80 drachms; of Colophonian pitch 8 ounces; of Italian wine a sufficient quantity. Grind the chalcitis and the cadmia with wine, so as to have the thickness of a liquid cerate. Having broken up the wax and the resin and put them into an earthenware vessel, and having added to these 1 litra of myrtle oil, set it upon charcoals, stirring continuously. And when it has melted, remove it from the fire, allow it to cool, and having scraped it off, add it to the ground ingredients, and having mixed and taken it up, use it, diluting it with myrtle oil. Let the blend be suited to the condition. Another through cadmia. Take: of roasted cadmia, of roasted chalcitis, of diphryges, 16 drachms each.

of wax, of roasted resin, of myrtle oil, half a litra each, of Italian wine as much as suffices; prepare as has been stated above, and use the drug at one time [525] diluted, at another undiluted. Another. Take litharge, white lead, cadmia, diphryges, resin, 8 drachms each; chalcitis, 2 drachms; wax, 8 drachms; myrtle oil, a sufficient quantity; Aminaean wine, as much as suffices. Another, of Euphranor. Take diphryges, roasted misy, 8 drachms each; roasted chalcitis, molybdaena, 2 drachms each; cadmia, 1 drachm; wax, 6 drachms; Colophonian resin, 3 ounces; myrtle oil, 6 litrai; Italian wine, a sufficient quantity. Another, the one made with ladanum, a well-proven drug, not only cicatrizing but also cutting away calluses and setting right the deficiencies of treatment (λειπουργίαι). Take chalcitis, litharge, ladanum, 24 drachms each; bitumen, 8 drachms; wax, 72 drachms; myrtle oil, one kotyle (others say 18 drachms); wine, one kotyle. Prepare in the proper manner. In use, employ it both as a splenion and diluted. Another. Take litharge, 100 drachms; pitch, 50 drachms; ladanum, 25 drachms; scraped verdigris, burnt copper, 8 drachms each; myrtle oil, 2 litrai; copper scale, 4 drachms. Prepare and use. Another, the one called the burn-plaster (pyrikautos), from the Attalic formularies, a well-proven drug.

[526] Take: oil, 1 kotyle; split alum, manna, frankincense, litharge, galbanum, 1 drachm each; wax, 24 drachms; alkanet, 8 drachms; deer's marrow, pig's fat, verdigris, white lead, 2 drachms each; the yolk of three eggs. The meltable ingredients are poured over the dry ones, and use the drug sometimes diluted, sometimes undiluted. Another, a successful drug; it works for old and hard-to-heal sores. White lead, litharge, split alum, manna, galbanum, frankincense, deer's and calf's marrow, 4 drachms each; wax, alkanet, egg yolks, 8 drachms each; oil, 4 kotylai. Pound the marrows carefully and melt them together with the meltable ingredients, stirring with the alkanet so that it takes on colour; then, having taken it off the fire and strained it into another vessel, let it cool, and having scraped it off, add it to the dry ingredients, and having taken it up, use it. The one called white Magne, a successful drug. It works also for chronic wounds and those which cicatrise only with difficulty; it works also for scabby conditions. It is also a good one for the seat, when diluted with rose-oil or myrtle-oil. Take: litharge, 100 drachms;

[527] of wax 50 drachms, of white lead 100 drachms, of terebinth resin 25 drachms, of frankincense 25 drachms, of split alum 12 drachms, of oil 2 kotylai. Compound in the usual manner and use it, sometimes as a plaster, sometimes with the drug diluted. Another, called the Pamphileios, for the aforesaid conditions; it also agglutinates sinuses and removes the callus from fistulas. It works for the rheumatic kinds of ulcers and for chronic ulcers and those hard to cicatrize; it also cures scabies (psora) and removes bruises under the eyes (hypopia). It works also for those suffering from headache and for fluxes of the eyes when applied upon the forehead. It is also good for the seat when diluted with rose oil or myrtle oil. The particulars of the preparation are as follows. ♃ of litharge 100 drachms, of wax 50 drachms, of terebinth resin 25 drachms, of frankincense 25 drachms, of white lead 100 drachms, of split alum 16 drachms, of white pepper 3 drachms, of old oil 2 kotylai. Melt together in the usual manner, using the drug sometimes diluted, sometimes spreading it on as a plaster.

For in the case of achores on the head, or roughnesses about the face, or the so-called epinyctides, or conditions about the seat, [528] it is smeared on with the drug dissolved in myrtle oil or mastic oil. Another, of Telamon, a successful drug; it works also against carbuncles, dries up sinuses when injected and infused, and is also a good cicatrizing agent. Take pine resin, wax, quicklime, litharge, 50 drachms each; white lead, 25 drachms; oil, half a kotyle. Boil the litharge and the oil until it sets, then the wax, then the resin. Grind the quicklime and the white lead fine and add the melted ingredients to them. In use, place oil over hot ashes and add some of the drug after crushing it; and when it has been warmed, put it into a mortar and beat it up diligently until it becomes of the consistency of gloios (an oily paste), and having stored it away, use it as a very great drug, sometimes smearing it on with feathers, sometimes infusing it. In the case of the so-called carbuncles, spread it on a linen cloth and apply. Another, of Moschion, well known, for whatever you wish to free from callus and to cicatrize; it is also good for the seat. Take litharge, white lead, quicklime, 8 drachms each; deer marrow, wax, 16 drachms each; myrtle oil, a sufficient quantity.

the melted ingredients over the dry ones, [529] and having kneaded it carefully make troches. At the time of use it is first dissolved in water or milk, as much as you wish, so as to have the thickness of strigil-grease (gloios); then a sufficient amount of rose-oil or myrtle oil is added, and having beaten it up carefully and taken it up into a leaden box, use it as has been said before. [Cicatrizing plasters of Andromachus.] Take cadmia 1 pound, burnt chalcitis one pound, wax 1 pound, dry resin 3 pounds, myrtle oil 3 pounds, wine for the dry ingredients. Another, the one with ladanum. Take litharge 40 drachms, ladanum 32 drachms, chalcanthum 8 drachms, split alum 12 drachms, wax 100 drachms, scale (of copper) 8 drachms, asphalt 32 drachms, myrtle oil a quarter of one kotyle, Falernian wine for the dry ingredients. Otherwise, as Alcimion has it, which I prepared. Take ladanum 8 drachms, hyssop 4 drachms, propolis 8 drachms, asphalt 8 drachms, litharge 4 drachms, scale of copper 4 drachms, raw misy 4 drachms, wax 24 drachms, myrtle oil 8 minae. The one with barley. Take white lead 50 drachms, litharge 50 drachms, burnt unground barley 1 xestes, wax 50 drachms, oil 1 xestes.

[530] the barley last. Another cicatrizing plaster. ♃ Of cadmia 2 ounces; of chalcitis, of wax, of terebinth resin, 4 ounces each; of hyssop 1 ounce; of myrtle oil 4 ounces; of chalcanthum 4 ounces; wine for the dry ingredients. Another cicatrizing plaster. ♃ Of dry resin 18 drachms; of diphryges 4 drachms; of litharge 16 drachms; of wax 10 drachms; of oil 4 cotylae. Following these Andromachus wrote six other plasters, curative of ulcers that are hard to cicatrize, which I have decided not to add here now; for they will be stated together with those that cure the hard-to-heal ulcers in the fourth of these commentaries. But since Andromachus, in the same place of the book, before the cicatrizing plasters just written, also wrote certain others without having set down in a heading for them that they are cicatrizing plasters for uncomplicated ulcers, and especially in the case of children and women and eunuchs and, in general, those who have soft flesh, I have decided to add these too here, bearing in Andromachus the title taken from their colour. For he wrote about them thus, word for word: White cicatrizing plasters of Andromachus. The white one which I use.

♃ Litharge, [531] 1 mina; white lead, 1 mina; wax, 4; resin, 4; oil, 3 cotylae; water, 1 cotyle. Another. ♃ Litharge, 160 drachms; white lead, 200 drachms; wax, 50 drachms; terebinth, 24 drachms; old oil, half a cotyle; water, 6 cyathi. Another. ♃ Litharge, 100 drachms; white lead and wax, 50 drachms each; terebinth, 25 drachms; split alum, 6 drachms; white pepper, 3 drachms; the plant orchis, 8 drachms; soapwort, 2 drachms; manna, 25 drachms. Another. ♃ Litharge, 70 drachms; white lead, 100 drachms; wax, 50 drachms; old oil, 2 cyathi—otherwise, 2 drachms; water, 2 cotylae. Another. ♃ Litharge, 25 drachms; wax, 57 drachms; pig's fat, 37 drachms; myrrh, 2 drachms; yolks of boiled eggs, 4—some say of raw ones. The "Excellence" (ἡ ἀρετή). ♃ Pure gloios, 12 cotylae; litharge, 3 minae; scale (of copper), 6 drachms—others, 16 drachms; Colophonian resin, 6 minae—others, 50 drachms; wax, 1 mina—others, 45 minae; sea-water, 3 cotylae. [Panacea of Andromachus.] ♃ Litharge, 150 drachms; wax, 40 drachms; terebinth, 53 drachms.

of old sea-water, or rather [532] of old wine, 2 cotylae; of gloios (bath-scrapings), 6 cotylae; of scale (of copper), 16 drachms; of castor oil, 2 cotylae; of white lead, 80 drachms; of ammoniac incense, 24 drachms; of calf's fat, 80 drachms; of quicklime, 24 drachms; of aristolochia, 25 drachms. Boil as you know how. [The white plaster of Telephanes.] ℞ Of litharge, 80 drachms; of white lead, 120 drachms; of myrrh, 3 drachms 2 obols; of sagapenum, 5 drachms; of frankincense, 6 drachms and four obols; of oil, 2 ½ cotylae. Boil all together. Another. ℞ Of white wax, 1 litra; of myrrh, 1 ounce; of frankincense, 1 ounce; of deer's marrow, 2 ounces; of hyena's fat, 2 ounces; of deer's rennet, 2 ounces, or of kid's; of nitre, 2 ounces; of galbanum, 1 ounce; of ammoniac incense, 4 ounces; of litharge, 1 ½ litrae; of white lead, 6 drachms; of old oil, 1 ½ cotylae; of sea-water, half a cotyle. It is called the Caunian. Another. ℞ Of litharge, 200 drachms; of wax, 52 drachms; of oil, 3 cotylae; of white lead, 80 drachms; of terebinth resin, 32 drachms; of burnt whelks (kerykes), 10 drachms; of frankincense, 19 drachms; of water, 1 sextarius. Another. ℞ Of fresh pig's fat, 88 drachms;

of white [533] wax 48 drachmas, of white lead 12 drachmas, of litharge 12 drachmas. Another, for herpetes, anthrakes (carbuncles), condylomata, rhagades (fissures), extremely non-inflaming, as Heras the Cappadocian gives it. Now in the case of this one he did rightly in not writing simply 'wax' but adding 'white' as well; for thus it would come out, as he wishes, white in colour. But afterwards, in writing another, he added neither 'white' for the wax nor 'white' for the wine; rather we must add it, if indeed we wish to make the plaster white. Its composition has been written down by Andromachus himself word for word as follows. [White plaster with wine, of Publius.] ♃ Of cadmia 1 pound 9 ounces, of litharge 2 pounds, of white lead 2 pounds, of Greek wine 2 xestai, of rose oil 5 pounds, of wax 3 pounds, raw eggs 12 in number, of frankincense 3 ounces; boil. The boilings of white plasters I went through in the first book, at the same time also showing the method not only of their boiling but also of their composition. And perhaps nothing at all was still left to be added to the teaching concerning such plasters. But since this

[534] book taught the account not only of the flesh-producing plasters, which are for the most part green, but also of all the agglutinative and cicatrizing ones, those at least which cicatrize ulcers that are without malignancy, and I went through also the quince-yellow and the tawny ones, for this reason it seemed good to me to write in addition in this book the white plasters too, of which I have made no account in that book. And so that nothing may be lacking in the present book, I shall also add the plasters named by them cephalic and fracture plasters, which are agglutinative of large wounds and sinuses, and, when they are loosened so as to become lint-dressings, also flesh-producing. [On the fracture and cephalic plasters.] Those who wrote the most numerous and finest drugs, whom I went through earlier by name, called a certain kind of plasters cephalic and fracture plasters, assigning the appellation to them chiefly from the fractures in the head.

Such plasters are of a detergent, discutient and drying [535] power. Most authors, however, mixed into them a little of the astringent drugs, for two needs, as has been said: both to repel that which flows in to the affected parts, and to guide the power of the detergent drugs down to the depth. And it was said by us earlier that if the astringent drugs are not worked up by grinding until they become dust-fine, they will themselves furnish harm rather than benefit to those drugs that have the attractive power. And I said that the best working-up of them comes about when they are triturated in sharp vinegar. I shall therefore now begin the writing-out of such drugs from those written by Asclepiades. [On the fracture plasters written by Asclepiades.] The first he wrote in the third book of the External Drugs, verbatim as follows. Black fracture plaster, 'the Best'. I used this drug in the case of fractures in which many bones were floating loose, and when all were advising me to lift out the floating ones, 'the Best' accomplished something resembling a marvel.

For it held the floating fragments, which had been separated from the other bones, so firmly [536] that they formed callus together with the others. It is as follows. ♃ Of litharge, of asphalt, 200 drachmae each; of dry pitch, of wax, 100 drachmae each; of terebinth resin 50 drachmae; of split alum, of propolis, 30 drachmae each; of ammoniac incense 24 drachmae; of verdigris 10 drachmae; of oil 4 xestai. Prepare as described before. Asclepiades wrote others of the same kind as the one set down above in the same book, word for word as follows. Another, the fracture-plaster of Pythion. Helenus used this. It is effective also for wounds resulting from a blow; and at its removal one must loosen the splenion with a sponge soaked in hot water, for the drug is strongly adhesive. The same drug is effective also for scrofulous swellings and fistulas. And in the case of fistulas and sinuses one must cut out the splenion, that is, over the mouth, so that the fluid being discharged has a place to go. One must also bathe with the drug on. The particulars of its preparation are as follows. ♃ Of Judaean asphalt 5 litrai 4 ounces; of dry Bruttian pitch the same amount; of roasted resin 8 litrai; of wax 4 litrai; of frankincense 4 litrai.

of red scale (lepis) one pound, [537] four ounces; of oil, in summer one pound, in winter one and a half pounds; of vinegar one kotyle. Melt the meltable ingredients; grind the frankincense and the scale with vinegar and add them to the rest, taking care that it does not boil over, and after stirring pour it down into a mortar, and having beaten it up and softened it, take it up and use it. In another copy I found: of red scale one and a half pounds. It is quite evident that the preparation which has received the greater quantity of scale becomes more active. The fracture-plaster of Moschion, a drug well suited to freshly inflicted wounds and cuttings-through of the nerves and divisions accompanied by contusion; it is effective also for fractures accompanied by a wound. For it both helps the wounds and forms callus on the bones when applied together with the requisite bandaging, and also for incipient dropsical patients. It is effective also for contusions of the testicles, and it shrivels the protrusions around the seat. It is effective also for fissures when diluted with butter; it is effective also for bronchoceles; it dissolves every hardness. It is effective also for chafings and sprains.

It is effective also against the callus-like outgrowths on the feet and hands, which we call "nails" (hēloi), so as to remove them without ulceration; [538] and in general it is a drug of the very widest use (polychrēstotaton), and it is effective also against incipient dropsies. The details of its preparation are as follows. Of litharge, one mina; and the mina, in the case of this drug, contains 160 holkai (drachms). Of liquid pitch, 160 drachms; of calf's fat, 160 drachms; of terebinth resin, 80 drachms; of manna of frankincense, 80 drachms; of wax, 40 drachms; of verdigris (ios), 8 drachms; of opopanax, 8 drachms; of galbanum, 8 drachms; of castor oil (kikinon), one kotylē; of vinegar, the same amount; of juice of the sycamine, one kotylē; of liquid pitch, half a kotylē. Put the litharge, ground as fine as possible, and the castor oil into an earthenware or bronze vessel, set it over the fire and boil it. And when it boils up, add the fat and the manna, stirring continuously. And when it has thickened together, add the pitch, the wax, the resin, and having boiled it until it no longer stains, sprinkle in the galbanum, then the verdigris and the opopanax dissolved in vinegar.

The juice of the sycamore-fig and the liquid pitch we put into another vessel and boil, and when it has thickened we add it to the first drug, and setting it again upon the fire we boil until it no longer stains, [539] and having poured it out into wine we leave it for three days; then, kneading it, we use it, spreading it upon a linen cloth. At the application of the drug one must soak a small bandage in wine, squeeze it out, and then put it around over the drug. As our teacher Lucius prepared it, it goes thus: we first melt the fat and the oil, and when it has dissolved we sprinkle in the manna, very finely ground, and the litharge; and when it has thickened we do what follows. Both in the case of this drug and in that of the one written next after it he says that the mina has 160 drachmas. It is quite evident, then, that he means the Alexandrian mina, which has 20 ounces, so that each of the ounces has 8 drachmas; for thus it will come about that the mina has 160 drachmas. Another, of Claudius Philoxenus, inscribed "of Apellus" (ἀπελοῦς), for bleeding wounds and for fractures. It works also against the aforementioned conditions. Take litharge, one mina, that is 160 drachmas; calf's fat, 160 drachmas; frankincense, 80 drachmas; opopanax, terebinth resin, 80 drachmas each; wax, 40 drachmas.

of verdigris, of split alum, [540] of chrysocolla, of galbanum, 12 drachms each; of castor oil, 1 kotyle; of vinegar, as much as suffices. Last of all add the frankincense and the verdigris and the opopanax and the alum and the chrysocolla and the like, first dissolving them in vinegar and triturating them carefully. In another recension it reads thus: Take litharge, 160 drachms; pitch, 160 drachms; calf's suet, 160 drachms; terebinth resin, 80 drachms; manna of frankincense, 80 drachms; wax, 40 drachms; opopanax, scraped verdigris, 16 drachms each; chrysocolla, split alum, 12 drachms each; ammoniac incense, 6 drachms; castor oil, 1 kotyle; vinegar, the same. Compound in the same way as the fracture plasters. Oinanthe fracture plaster, a successful drug. It acts upon the aforementioned conditions. Take litharge, 160 drachms; wine-pitch, 160 drachms — this we take as it flows off from the Italian earthenware jars (κεραμείων); terebinth resin, 80 drachms; frankincense, 80 drachms; worked calf's suet, 80 drachms; worked deer marrow, 80 drachms; wax, 40 drachms; dried oinanthe, comfrey root, centaury foliage, 1 litra each; scraped verdigris, opopanax, 8 drachms each; poppy juice, myrrh, aloe, galbanum, 8 drachms each.

[541] of vinegar 3 kotylai, of castor oil 1 kotyle. Having chopped the comfrey, the oinanthe and the centaury into coarse pieces and thrown them into the vinegar, we boil it down to a third, and having pressed out the liquid we use it for the preparation of the drug. The drug is also effective for those suffering from podagra. In other copies it runs thus: ℞ litharge, wine-pitch, 160 drachmas each; deer marrow, terebinth resin, calf's suet, frankincense, comfrey root, juice of the sycamine, 80 drachmas each; dried oinanthe, centaury, one litra each; wax, 40 drachmas; verdigris, opopanax, storax, poppy juice, mandrake juice, myrrh, aloe, galbanum, chrysocolla, split alum, 12 drachmas each; vinegar, 3 xestai; castor oil, one litra. Prepare as has been described above, and pour it out into Italian wine, just as we did in the case of Moschion's fracture plaster.

[On the plasters properly called cephalic.] They are accustomed to call those plasters cephalic which they use for fractures in the head, as many as have occurred down as far as the diploe [542]. Their power is also to bring up scales of bones and to raise up fragments (θρέμματα), both in the head and in the other bones of the body. Some, by a common genus, call these too fracture plasters. But they are stronger than those properly called fracture plasters. For the plasters called fracture plasters by them possess the detergent and drying property; but these have in addition acquired a certain acridity, capable of drawing from the depth to the outer surface not only bones but, much more than these, some thick and viscous or altogether bad humour. Asclepiades mentioned plasters of this kind in the third book of the External Remedies, which have been written in the fourth

commentary of this treatise. But since he said that they are suitable also for the malignant ulcers and for certain of the Chironian ones among them — for the one which he himself entitles the cephalic plaster of Deileon, and after it the dark-green cephalic, and after these the cephalic of Philotas, then also the Isis, which he likewise names cephalic, and certain other such ones, [543] must be regarded as belonging to this genus — for this reason I have not now set them out again, but shall pass on to the fracture plasters and cephalic plasters written by the other physicians, having first stated the general power of each class. From what I said both earlier and in the course of this treatise, and in the books on the power of simple drugs, you, recalling these things, must recognize that those which they entitle cephalic are more vigorous than the fracture plasters. And for this reason they are naturally able to produce flesh when mixed with cerate, so that in another manner they are in a way of the same genus as the flesh-producing plasters as well. For when their power has been relaxed by the cerate, they become flesh-producing lint-dressings (emmota), with the addition, clearly, sometimes of oil, sometimes of rose-oil, sometimes of some other such thing. [On the fracture plasters and cephalic plasters which Heras wrote.] The first of such plasters that Heras wrote is the one named Isis, a drug that is quite a polychreston (of many uses). Next the one made from herbs, for which too, being a polychreston, he testifies that it is cephalic.

But the plaster made with squill, written next, has the same claim, [544] being among the quite widely useful drugs. And indeed, immediately after these, in writing another plaster, he says, word for word, as follows. Another cephalic, effective for fractures in the head; it brings up bones easily and detaches scales. And it does all the remaining things that the troche before it does. Take: scale of red copper, 25 drachms; alum, 20 drachms; aristolochia daktylitis, 20 drachms; ammoniac incense, 25 drachms; frankincense, 25 drachms; myrrh, 12 drachms; bull's suet, 4 litrai; wax, 4 litrai; terebinth, 4 litrai; dry pine resin, 4 litrai; oil, 1 kotyle; vinegar, a sufficient quantity. Grind the dry ingredients fine in the heat under the Dog-star for a sufficient number of days; having first soaked the ammoniac in vinegar, pour it on; last of all the meltable ingredients, scraped; and having united them, use. In some copies 'of old oil' has been added. But since he said that this very plaster does as much as the troche before it, it seemed good to me to append the composition of that one too, which runs as follows according to the wording of Heras himself.

A cephalic troche of three ingredients (trimigma), effective for fractures in the head and for [545] phymata and fistulas, podagra, calluses (poroi), and sciatica. Take: erythrias earth, 2 minae (others: 12); scale of red copper, 4 minae; Pontic fish-glue, 4 minae (but in the books of Heras 1 mina is found). Grind the erythrias and the scale fine separately, then pour sharp vinegar over them together, so that it has the thickness of honey, and triturate; and as they dry out pour on vinegar. Do this in the heats of the dog-days for 20 days. Then take the fish-glue, crush it, pour on 1 kotyle of vinegar and melt it over a gentle fire; then add the earth and the scale, and having poured it out into a vessel of red copper and set it in the sun for 8 days, stir it twice a day until it sets; then, taking it out little by little, grind it in a mortar, pouring on vinegar until it attains consistency; then form it into troches and collyria of unequal length and unequal thickness, and having dried them store them away. And at the time of use, to one part of the drug triturated with vinegar mix three parts of rose-oil cerate, and use it as a flat spread (platysma), then as a splenion for the fractures in the head, and on top mix in (μίσγε) greasy wool soaked in vinegar.

In the case of fistulas, once the collyrium [546] has been inserted, throw over it from above a compress (splenion) made from this together with cerate. Another, of many uses (polychreston). He also wrote another plaster of many uses, which he says is also suited to fractures. He speaks about it verbatim as follows. For fractures of the limbs, with a wound and without a wound, and for leipourgiai (defects) and sinuses. Of dry pitch 1 mina, of litharge 1 mina, of manna half a mina, of calf's fat 1 mina, of Tyrrhenian wax 4 minae, of opopanax 8 drachms, of scraped verdigris 16 (ιστ΄) minae, of Cyprian copper one sixteenth of a mina, of galbanum 1 drachm, of terebinth half a mina, of castor oil (kiki) or old oil 1 cotyle, of vinegar half a cotyle and a triobol. Boil the litharge and the oil and the fat on a gentle fire; then, when it changes colour, add the pitch, the resin, the galbanum, then [boil] until (ἕως ἕως) it sets, and then, having removed the fire and allowed it to cool a little, [add] the manna, then the opopanax and the verdigris ground with vinegar, pouring them into the pot, and having boiled briefly, when it is in good condition, take it off.

[547] We use the preparation by pouring cold water over it in summer, and in winter by removing the frost (πάγον). And whenever we wish to make the drug softer or to detach bone more quickly, we soften it with calf marrow. In this drug Heras is evidently intending the mina to be of sixteen ounces; for he would not have written 'one sixteenth of a mina' if he had not meant this. Another. And after this one, next in order, Heras wrote another plaster of similar profession, reading roughly as follows: one that prevents inflammation, for punctures and fractures. We have often used this, on the very same day, also for dislocations and fractures, and for sprains (λυγισμάτων) about the ankle or knee. It also disperses excellently the sluggish fluids that gather about the knees, and especially if the parts have been poulticed beforehand, two or three days earlier, with bitter-vetch meal kneaded with oxymel; and in general it is effective for every spasm (σπάσμα) and rupture, for it is marvellously inflammation-preventing. Take: litharge, 25 drachms; dry bitumen, 100 drachms; dry pitch, 50 drachms; wax, 50 drachms; pine resin, 25 drachms.

of ammoniac incense [548] 15 drachms, of split alum 15 drachms, of verdigris 15 drachms, of propolis 15 drachms, of old oil 3 litrai. Boil the litharge with the oil, and when it begins to thicken, add the asphalt and boil until it is well melted, for it melts with time; then the pitch, then the resin, the wax, the ammoniac, the propolis. Add each of them in turn, thickening the mixture and drawing the fire away from beneath. When they have become non-staining, add the verdigris and the split alum, and, having allowed one boiling-up, pour it out into a basin containing cold water. This we have used, after the rest of the fracture had formed callus, when a good many splinters were floating within, and in a few days it brought matters to such a point that the callus and the splinters were removed; it is exceedingly polychreston (of many uses). And after this Heras next wrote another plaster of the same kind as the aforementioned plasters, roughly as follows: a fracture-plaster, also for dropsical patients. Take dry pitch 1 mina, liquid pitch half a kotyle, sycomore juice 1 kotyle, litharge 1 mina, frankincense 1 mina, galbanum 8 drachms, terebinth half a mina, calf's suet 1 mina.

of wax one mina [549], of opopanax 8 drachms, of scraped verdigris 8 drachms, of unadulterated castor oil 4 cotylae, of acrid vinegar 1 cotyle. The litharge and the frankincense are boiled gently with the castor oil and the fat; then pitch is added, wax, resin, galbanum purified and diluted with a little vinegar. Of the remaining vinegar, one third part is mixed with the verdigris and two thirds with the opopanax, and these are added in. In another small dish [are placed] liquid pitch and the juice of the sycamore-fig and about an eighth part of the castor oil, so that the verdigris may not coagulate; then it is boiled moderately, just enough for it to be united. When it seems to have been well united, the drug is stored in wine. With this we have got the better of many dropsical patients, applying it and conducting the treatment without elaborate measures, taking thought only for good digestion. When, however, the sufferers perceive great progress, we pass over to the one written below it, the one made with salts. [Fracture-plaster of Andromachus.] Andromachus wrote the first of the fracture-plasters somewhat as follows. Fracture-plaster which I use continually. Of litharge 1 mina, of pitch 1 mina.

[550] of wax 1 mina; of bull's suet 1 mina; of frankincense 1 mina; of liquid pitch half a kotyle; of sycamine juice 1 kotyle; of terebinth 1 mina; of opopanax 8 drachms; of verdigris 8 drachms; of castor oil 1 kotyle. Some add also 1 mina of butter and 25 drachms of ammoniac incense, in astringent wine. After this one he writes another as follows. Another fracture-plaster. Of litharge 1 mina; of wax half a mina, though some say a quarter; of pitch 1 mina; of terebinth half a mina; of calf's suet 1 mina; of opopanax 8 drachms; of verdigris 8 drachms; of galbanum 8 drachms, though some say 6; of castor oil 1 kotyle; of vinegar an equal amount. Gallus used to add 12 drachms of split alum and 12 drachms of chrysocolla. In addition to those already mentioned, Andromachus wrote another fracture-plaster as follows. Black fracture-plaster. Take of litharge 200 drachms; of asphalt 200 drachms; of pitch 100 drachms; of wax 100 drachms; of split alum 30 drachms; of propolis 30 drachms; of terebinth 50 drachms; of ammoniac incense 24 drachms; of scraped verdigris 10 drachms; of oil 4 xestai, though some say 2 xestai; the ancients add also 60 drachms of pyrites stone. These, then, were written in sequence by Andromachus.

Apart from these, [551] among the green plasters a certain plaster is written last, as follows. Another green cephalic plaster, from the writings of Aphrodas: take of scale of copper 40 drachms, of Eretrian earth 20 drachms, of aristolochia 30 drachms, of fish-glue 16 drachms, of ammoniac salt 12 drachms, of misy 12 drachms, of myrrh 12 drachms, of frankincense 36 drachms, of burnt copper 16 drachms, of split alum 12 drachms and of round alum 16 drachms, of bryony 12 drachms, of black chamaeleon 12 drachms, of burnt resin 18 drachms, of ammoniac incense 18 drachms, of litharge 12 drachms; in another copy I found: of unburnt sulphur and of Illyrian iris 12 drachms each; of chalcanthum 12 drachms, of bull's gall half a cotyle, of vinegar one chous. At the rising of the Dog-star make pastilles of 4 drachms each; mix with 4 of wax, 6 cotylae of vinegar, 6 cotylae of oil. [On agglutinative plasters. Some call these both enhaemic and wound plasters. Their function is to make the divided flesh grow together and to glue it, so that the part is brought back to its original unity.
