And not only are bloody wounds glued together immediately upon the division, while the blood is still [552] flowing, as we sponge it away and then bring the parts together with sutures or fibulae, but we also unite and cause to grow together old sinuses, having first rendered them free of inflammation and clean by the application of drugs. It has been said in the books of the Therapeutic Method that a drug is called removing of filth primarily and in itself, but flesh-producing and agglutinative secondarily. For it received this designation not as itself producing flesh or causing to grow together, nor as though these were not the works of nature alone, but because, when such drugs are applied, the ulcers become fleshed and grow together. Their proper work is to render the affected part free of superfluity, so that its ichors may not hinder the production of flesh or the gluing-together. And it was shown that the drugs that cause union are more drying than the flesh-producing ones, and that the flesh-producing ones are of a cleansing power that is least biting, whereas the agglutinative ones are not in every case of a cleansing power, but it is necessary only that they be drying.

And since the drugs that produce the scar are much [553] more drying than these, together with being sufficiently astringent, let the agglutinative and uniting drugs be distinguished from these too by the fact that they dry more moderately. The defining mark of the agglutinative drugs is to allow no moisture to arise between the parts that are to be agglutinated; that of the cicatrizing drugs is not this alone, but also to consume the moisture present in the parts that are to be cicatrized, and in addition to make them callous and to harden them by astringency. The flesh-producing drugs, for their part, preserve the blood that is suitable for re-nourishment, both in quantity and in quality, as much and of such a kind as nature requires for the generation of flesh. And it keeps the ulcer clean—if it received it in such a clean state, being wholly non-biting; but if it received it having filth, it is necessary that it be detergent, in its own power, to the same degree as the thickness which the filth has reached, and it is necessary also that it bite and erode the newly-formed flesh.

It is clear, then, that, being of such a kind, it will not produce flesh in the ulcer nor fill up the hollow of the flesh, but will rather melt it away and diminish it; and for this reason the drugs that cleanse much [554] filth, about which I spoke earlier, are not always able to produce flesh, but only when, having been melted down either with a larger quantity of oil or with rose-oil, as in the case of the oily one and the one made with papyrus, the vehemence of their detergent action has been curbed, or when they become non-biting through admixture of cerate. Many of the polychrēsta (remedies of many uses) are of this kind, such as that of Machairion and the Isis. Now the aim of each of such remedies has been stated in the books of the Therapeutic Method; as for the material of the remedies, the simple material has been discussed earlier in another treatise, and the compound is discussed in the one now in hand. And in it one must first of all bear in mind the nature of the bodies being treated. Those that are moist and for this reason soft, such as those of women and children and eunuchs and those who live in a womanish manner, require weaker drugs; but those of men, and especially of all who through manly activities and the sun have acquired a hard habit of body, derive no benefit from the weak ones.

For this reason, then, not even the agglutinative drugs are common to both kinds of bodies; rather, those which are prepared from litharge and oil [555] and vinegar, which I went through in the first book, are agglutinative of weak and soft flesh, whereas those made from asphalt and verdigris and scale, and aloe and myrrh, are agglutinative of strong and hard flesh. Now asphalt in and of itself falls within the aim of these powers, but it is not possible to use it alone, melted with oil, for it is too crumbly to produce a plaster-like drug. In order, then, that a plaster may result, we mix wax and resin with it, and knowing that its power will in turn be slackened by these, we mix in, sometimes copper or scale of copper, often aloe or myrrh, or, to put it briefly, one of the drying drugs, in no mean quantity. [The barbaros plasters made with asphalt.] Here too I shall first set out those written by Andromachus, in his own very words. The barbaros which I use: take wax 200 drachms, pitch 200 drachms, resin 200 drachms, asphalt 200 drachms, frankincense 24 drachms, oil 1 cotyle. Another: take pitch 2 pounds, asphalt 1 pound, wax 1 pound, ammoniac incense 6 ounces, manna 6 ounces.

white lead [556] 3 ounces; oil, half a kotyle; vinegar, 4 kotylai. Aphrodas admired this one. Another black one. Take dry pitch, 1 litra; dry resin, 1 litra; asphalt, 1 litra; white lead, 6 ounces; manna, chalcanthos, scraped verdigris, 3 ounces of each; oil, half a kotyle; vinegar, half a kotyle. Another, from the writings of Gallus. Take goat suet, 30 drachms; verdigris, 8 drachms; wax, 50 drachms; aristolochia, 25 drachms; asphalt, 25 drachms; pitch, 25 drachms; ammoniac incense, 12 drachms; galbanum, 12½ drachms; silphium, 8 drachms—others, 20; manna, 12. Prepare. Another, the one called "invincible" (anikētos). Take wax, 100 drachms; bull suet, 30 drachms; asphalt, 25 drachms; pitch, 25 drachms; terebinth resin, 25 drachms; nitron, 22½ drachms; aristolochia, 12 drachms; galbanum, 8 drachms; myrrh, 18 drachms; frankincense, 12½ drachms; ammoniac, 8 drachms; amomum, 8 drachms; cardamom, 12 drachms; opopanax, 8 drachms; deer marrow, 15 drachms; verdigris, 12 drachms; aloe, 8 drachms; bdellium, 16 drachms; oil, 2 kotylai. I myself used to add propolis, 12 drachms.

[557] [Another blood-stanching one, of Julianus.] ♃ Of litharge 50 drachms, of bitumen 50 drachms, of wax 50 drachms, of Bruttian pitch 50 drachms, of roasted resin (phrykte) 15 drachms, of scale of copper 12 drachms, of frankincense 14 drachms, of galbanum 8 drachms, of chalcitis 4 drachms, of aloe 6 drachms, of oak-gall 4 drachms, of myrrh 4 drachms, of long aristolochia 6 drachms, of round aristolochia 4 drachms, of old oil 4 kotylai; but I use 3 kotylai of oil. [The Barbaros of Heras.] The one which Heras wrote as the Barbaros, thus. A black plaster for bleeding wounds, for considerable divisions of tissue and especially for those on the head, for fistulas, sinuses, fractures. It is suitable also for sufferers in the liver and in the spleen; it agglutinates without inflammation. It works also in the case of nerves and cartilages that have been cut through, and of bones, and it also checks, remarkably, blood that is flowing. Further, it works for undermining cavities (hypophorai) and sinuses, for it agglutinates greatly; and in the case of abscesses, after you have drawn off the fluid, apply this. It is also a most excellent blood-stanching remedy, especially in the case of those who bring up blood.

Having spread it onto two pieces of leather, apply one [558] to the chest and the sides, and the other to the back; it checks the blood remarkably. It is also effective for dog bites and human bites, being on the whole non-inflaming. This one, as experience has shown, has surpassed the wound plasters. Undo it in winter every seven days, in summer every five; but if there is urgency, every three. ♃ Of wax one pound, of pitch one pound, of bitumen one pound, of pine resin one pound, of manna six ounces, of white lead four ounces, of chalcanthum four ounces, of opopanax two ounces, of oil half an ounce (some say half a mina, others half a pound), of vinegar two cotylae. Put the wax, the bitumen, the oil and the vinegar—keeping back a little of it—into a new earthen pot and melt them; then add the pitch and the resin, having pounded them fine carefully. When it is half-boiled, take the pot off and, having cooled it somewhat, sprinkle in the chalcanthum, strained, triturated with vinegar from the two cotylae, little by little, so that it does not boil over. And when you have poured it in (ἐκχέῃς), heat it gently from beneath, stirring.

When it no longer stains, take it off the fire and pour in the opopanax, which has been soaked the day before in part of the remaining [559] vinegar so as to be dissolved; then sprinkle in the white lead and the manna, carefully triturated together, and, having warmed it a little so that it becomes united, taking care that the opopanax and the manna do not burn, pour it out into a mortar and, after letting it cool, knead it, store it away and use it. It is clear that the other barbaros plasters too, which Andromachus and the others wrote down, ought to be prepared in the same manner. Some do not put the opopanax into the cauldron, but, having triturated it with vinegar in a mortar, pour the fusible ingredients over it. And some, as I too have often done, triturate beforehand along with it also the manna and the white lead in the mortar with vinegar, and, having melted the fusible ingredients, pour them on. And often I have triturated the chalcanthum alone with the opopanax and put it into the cauldron, sprinkling in the manna and the white lead. Another barbaros, of Heras. Heras prefixed the title 'barbaros' to this one alone; but I have named the preceding one likewise, although it was called 'black' by him, since most of the more recent physicians are accustomed to call those made with asphalt 'barbaroi'.

Heras himself wrote about it as follows, [560] word for word. Barbaros for freshly inflicted wounds, sinuses, dog bites, human bites, inflamed condylomata, for all affections in the joints at their beginning, and for podagra. Take: wax, 1 mina; pitch, 1 mina; roasted resin, 1 mina; Judaean asphalt, 1 mina; litharge, 10 drachms; white lead, 5 drachms; verdigris, 50 drachms; opopanax, 4 drachms; oil, 1 kotyle; vinegar, 1 kyathos. Boil the wax, pitch, asphalt and resin until melted, then add the rest, triturated with the oil, and having lifted it off the fire and let it cool a little, drip in the vinegar little by little. Such, then, is the general type of the barbaros plasters. I, however, adding something as to how I myself use them, shall bring the discussion of them to a close. They are two: one for the greatest wounds, another for the smaller ones. Of the one employed for the greatest, the composition is as follows. [Barbaros of Galen.] Take: pitch, 8 litrai; wax, 6 litrai 8 ounces; pine resin, 5 litrai 4 ounces; asphalt, 4 litrai; oil, 1 litra, 210 ounces (σι΄).

of litharge [561] and white lead and verdigris, 24 drachms each; of frankincense, half a litra; of liquid alum, 12 drachms; of split alum, 4 ounces; of opopanax, scale of copper, galbanum, 12 drachms each; of aloe and opium and myrrh, 4 drachms each; of terebinth, 24 ounces; of mandrake juice, 6 drachms; of vinegar, 6 cotylae, which are 5 litrai. The proportion of the simpler barbaros in its composition is this: take pitch, wax, pine resin, roasted resin, asphalt — of these five, 1 litra each; of litharge, 10 drachms; of white lead, 5 drachms; of verdigris, 5 drachms; of opopanax, 3 drachms; of oil, in winter 9 ounces, in summer 6 ounces. The meltable ingredients are poured over the dry ones, which have been levigated in a mortar with acrid vinegar. And if you wish the drug to be more pain-relieving, you will mix in 1½ drachms of henbane juice and 1 drachm of opium.

[562] GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK III. These notes too I write for you, my companions, who have come to know through the very works of the art how great a power our treatment of those wounded in the nerves possesses, and that all were saved, neither maimed nor lamed—things which you have seen happening to those treated otherwise, just as also some of them were seized with spasm, or died with pains or putrefactions or fevers. And it is likely that these notes will fall also into the hands of

others [563] who are not able to make good use of what is written in these treatises, either because they have not learned the theory of the medical art from a teacher, but are altogether uninitiated and entirely untrained, or because they have learned badly, adhering to those who say that compound drugs have been discovered without reason, through experience alone. For these men manifestly err out of contentiousness. And in another way, no less than they, do those err who think that no drug ought to be compounded from simples that are opposite in their powers. But these latter have been refuted by the drugs recorded in the first treatise, which displayed their own great powers, derived from the very simples opposite to one another from which they had their composition. And not least also in what is to be written after this book, we shall display excellent drugs having their composition from things opposite in their powers.

But now, throughout this whole book, my discourse will be about our own method of treatment, which we devised for those wounded in the nerves, as I show how great a multitude of drugs possessing the same powers [564] I discovered, from having conceived the general manner of the treatment and from knowing the powers of the simple drugs. [What the general manner of the treatment of those wounded in the nerves is, and what the drugs are according to kind.] I observed all my teachers treating by the method of treatment now customarily called by the more recent physicians the one "for bleeding wounds" and "agglutinative". For at the beginning, applying some one of the drugs called "for bleeding wounds", they attempted to agglutinate the lips of the wound. And if it became inflamed, they fomented it with hot water in abundance, pouring oil in alongside, and they applied as a dressing (ἐπίπασμα) wheaten flour boiled in water-and-oil. And moreover I also saw the gladiators, those who had been wounded at the kneecap and above it, at the broad and thin tendon, being treated by them in the same way. But perhaps it would be better to say not being treated, but perishing; for very few of them survived, and these became lame.

And indeed, of the tendons in the extremity of the hand, through which the fingers are bent [565] and extended, I have seen a very great many, either bruised or pricked with the slightest puncture, putrefying in such a way as to resemble things boiled in water, and especially those boiled too long. For those treated by the aforementioned method are loosened and softened in their consistency just like these. I therefore condemned it, as putrefying the wounded part. And since I already knew that all things that putrefy suffer this from moisture and heat, I recognised that the treatment must be carried out by means of drying and cooling agents. But reflecting again that cold has truly been said by Hippocrates to be hostile to the nerves, I recognised that the best drug for those wounded in the nerves would be whatever dries and is intermediate between heating and cooling, or has not departed far from the mean in the direction of heating. The drug could nevertheless even be considerably hot, provided that the drying property belongs to it. For without moisture that which heats is not able to putrefy.

And further, in addition to these things, having also taken this into consideration, that it makes a great difference whether one applies the drug to the affected part when it is bare or through other bodies [566] lying in front of it, I recognised that it is fitting to use some drugs when the nerve has been laid bare, and others when it has been pricked while the bodies lying in front of it remain unaffected. For where one applies the drug to the bare nerve, there the aforesaid indication of the drugs that will be of benefit ought to be taken over in its pure form; but when the parts lying in front are unaffected, one must find a more fine-particled drug, so that its power is not exhausted beforehand by the bodies in between, but reaches into the depth. And such a drug, if it is by nature strongly drying, is able, even if moreover it should not be well-proportioned in respect of heat and cold, to do no harm either, since its activity in heating or cooling becomes weaker as it passes through the parts lying in front of the nervous body. Now that the aim of the drugs that will be of benefit had been found, in the fine-particled character of their substance, the next step was to recall the material.

And it had been established in the investigation of simple drugs that most of the heating ones are fine-particled, [567] while most of the cooling ones are thick-particled. For among them only one quality, the sour, sometimes occurs together with a fine-particled substance, and for this reason the sharpest vinegar is the most fine-particled of all cooling things, which has also been demonstrated to share in a slight heat. Of the heating ones, in turn, good juices (opoi) happen to be the most fine-particled, and it is already known to all men that the Cyrenaic one holds first place among them; but when this is not available we use also the Median one and those brought along with them from the eastern regions, such as the one called sagapenum. Of the same kind as these is also that of euphorbium, which is produced in the western parts of the inhabited world, whether one wishes to call it a juice or something else. For us it will suffice throughout the whole discourse to name this drug euphorbium, as is already the custom for everyone. But also, among those produced in our own country, both the juice of panax and those of the spurges are of fine-particled power. And indeed all the aforementioned juices heat vigorously.

But the juice of opobalsamum, being fine-particled [568] itself too, does not heat very much, yet has a fine-particled substance. And among the earthy substances, the froth of nitron and the aphronitron which is easily dissolved in water [are fine-particled], you understanding this, of course, as among earthy bodies. Next after these are the nitron called Berenician and the Asian stone; and the flower of the latter is the finest-particled of all the earthy substances. Among the mined substances, arsenic and sulphur are both fine-particled and hot. Next after these are misy and scale of copper and chalcitis, which also have something of astringency; for which reason we use chalcitis in its burnt state for the most part for the compositions of the finer-particled drugs. Fine-particled metallic drugs without manifest heating are spodion and pompholyx and what is called psorikon. Chrysocolla too is fairly fine-particled. Among the juices we learned that the laurel [oil] is fine-particled together with heating strongly, as regards sensation; for the cedar [oil], which heats no less than it in its potency, falls short in the heat perceived by sensation because of its fineness of parts.

For if he does not come thus prepared to the [572] benefit to be had from these commentaries, he will know the method only as far as discourse goes, but will accomplish no work worthy of it. For suppose that someone knows the very things I have said above about those wounded in the nerves, but through ignorance puts adulterated drugs into the compounds he makes, or does not even know their powers accurately in the first place: will it not be necessary that this man fail more often than he succeeds? To me, at any rate, it certainly seems so. Now, knowing the powers accurately differs very greatly from merely knowing them. For merely knowing is to recognize whether the drug is of such a nature as to dry or moisten or cool or heat us; but knowing accurately is, in addition to this, also to have come to know the quantity of the power. For some drugs have a power generative of lukewarm heat when they come into contact with our bodies, some of a moderate heat, just as others are a little stronger than this, and others still of a heat already so strongly boiling that it is able to burn. Accordingly the physician must aim not only at the quality of the condition, but also at what one might call the quantity in it.

[573] For 'quantity' in the case of quality is not said in an altogether proper sense. It is said nonetheless, just as a fever too is called great and small. And so extensive is the use of things said in this way that they already possess the force of a proper term, much as with 'box' (pyxis), 'coppersmith' (chalkeus), 'painter' (zōgraphos) and 'woodcutter' (dryotomos), and, to put it in a word, with those terms that began from what the grammarians call catachresis but later came to be accepted as being said in the proper sense. These things have been said by me on account of those who engage in dialectic at the wrong moment. What I left off saying is this: that what needs to be dried does not need simply that which dries, but with the appropriate measure; what has advanced into much moisture needs that which dries very much, what has advanced into little needs that which does this slightly, just as what has advanced into much needs that which dries greatly, though not extremely nor to the utmost. For the quantity of the dryness must always be proportionate to the quantity of the moisture.

I myself, then, when I first ventured to alter the common course of the treatment of those wounded in the nerves, aimed at estimating how great a degree of moisture and heat the [574] affected body had come to. And when a certain young man was shown to me who, at the first joint of the middle finger of the right hand, as a result of a contusion had the whole region around the nerve at that place so moist that it was already putrefying, the putrefying part itself I plastered with a poultice of dripped lye and raw lysis—know that it is barley meal that I call by this name—while the part that was not putrefying but was tense and painful I fomented by pouring over it plenty of warm oil, and then, having wiped it off with dry wool, I smeared around it a cerate as moist as we use in the case of fractures, having euphorbium mixed into it. This too had been prepared by me according to my own devising on an occasion of the following kind. Someone came to me in a severe winter and, showing his knee, said that it readily suffered when it had become chilled, but was immediately benefited by heating agents; and he asked to receive some such drug, for having travelled on foot in the cold he had been chilled and was in more violent pain than at other times. "Now then," he said, "I am going off to bathe, and I shall send for the drug from the bath."

Having said this, he went away; [575] and since I had no such drug ready, I ground euphorbium smooth with oil, and having melted wax I mixed it in, and a little later, when my friend sent asking for the drug, I gave it. And since he very quickly became free of pain, I was prompted from then on to use it on other parts similarly affected, about which I shall speak again. But now I return to the account of the one wounded in the nerves, on account of those who know nothing of these things which I am now expounding, but find fault over petty words; who, I prophesy, will find that I wrongly name as 'wounded in the nerves' all those who have been wounded in the tendons. For I suppose they call 'tendons' those stretched over the outside of the hand, both over the whole wrist and over the fingers. I for my part am not unaware that it would be clearer and more proper for them to be named 'wounded in the tendons'; but since all men customarily call them 'wounded in the nerves', in order that no one may say that I am innovating in the appellations, I preferred the customary term to the true one. And not even this term could have become customary, had not most physicians already, without reason, come to call the tendons too 'nerves'.

But whether you wish to call them [576] those wounded in the nerves or those wounded in the tendons, they will neither be saved on account of these words nor be convulsed, just as they will neither be maimed nor die. For an appellation has never saved a man nor killed one; rather, it is the power of the drugs that brings about each of these. And I, by changing these drugs, make those who are putrefying and being convulsed and maimed, and some of them even perishing, healthy and alive. For again, those who have had their nerves contused, as that man had been contused, they have already come to call those wounded in the nerves, not those contused in the nerves. But the treatment is common and the danger equal for both, those who have had something contused and those who have been wounded, whether in nerves or in tendons.

At any rate, that man, who was already putrefying in the parts around the first joint of the middle finger, and was suffering tension and pain in the parts lying above, became much better than he had been on the following day, on which, in place of the raw lysis (ὠμὴ λύσις), I mixed the flour of bitter vetch with dripped lye; and on the third day, while still being treated in the same way, he was already completely free of pain in the other parts, but at the contusion a certain sinewy body [577] resembling a thick membrane protruded, which, when I moved it moderately, easily fell out whole, being half-rotten. It seemed, then, to all those who saw it that this body was the whole nerve, rotted through, since they did not know how these tendons, clothed in sinewy membranes, both pass forward through the wrist and are stretched along the whole length of the fingers. But to me, when I had also drawn apart the rotted part of the contusion, the tendon appeared to be preserved. So, dissolving one of the trochisci, or cyclisci, or however one may wish to name them, of which one is also that of Polyeides, in boiled-down must (hepsema) or siraion—for this too you may be permitted to call as you yourself wish—and having first anointed the visible part of the nerve, I again used in the same way both the cataplasm and the unguent of euphorbium upon the same places, as before with each. And on the fourth day, seeing that everything around the first joint of the finger—previously contused, but at that time ulcerated—had subsided, I considered to what I should pass over from the cataplasm.

I considered, accordingly, that if the nerve were completely free of inflammation, [578] I should pass on to the cicatrizing drugs; but if some scirrhous remnant of its inflammation were left behind, I should apply one of the drugs that dry sufficiently. Since, then, something appeared to be left, I first used the drug made with the root of dracontium, which in other respects is the same as the Egyptian drug called Isis, but has taken in addition the root of dracontium. After this, having used the drug called Athena, from that I then came at last to the cicatrizing drugs. In another case, smearing the bared parts of the wound with the troche dissolved in siraion, I applied euphorbium on the outside, having mixed it with wax and resin in such a quantity that it became plaster-like and at the same time preserved the power of the euphorbium. How one might compound the drug with these aims in view, I shall say next. For indeed I also made another drug with vinegar, having as my aim in that case too its consistency and the fine-particled power of the vinegar, so that this might be preserved while the cooling power was dissipated.

Concerning these, however, how they were compounded [579] will be stated a little later; but now, since I devised the course of treatment of those wounded in the nerves through rational indication, without the silly chance encounter of the Empiricists, I wish to state it in its entirety, omitting no distinction, taking up the account again from the beginning. For whenever I take over someone who has just been wounded, sometimes I carry out the treatment by means of the liquid drugs, and sometimes by means of the plasters, applying on the outside wool as soft as possible, soaked in warm oil. But if I happen to be using the drug made with vinegar, I mix a little vinegar with the oil. And I undo the dressing twice or three times a day and foment with warm oil. And when the nights are long, I am accustomed to undo it during these as well. And I do this the more when the wound is being bitten by the drugs, inasmuch as whenever, when I am using such a drug from the beginning, the patient says he is neither bitten nor in pain, nor perceives any tension, I undo the dressing and foment twice a day, the first time around dawn, the second toward evening. Let the oil that is poured on be sufficiently warm, but only up to the point of not distressing the wounded part.

For just as the cold is most contrary [580] to such conditions, so the lukewarm is not completely beneficial. For we learned in the first book of On the Power of Simple Drugs that, just as water is of such a nature as to produce the most contrary effects according as it is hot or cold, so too is oil. For it in a way plasters over, or rather checks, the transpirations of the body when it is applied cold, whereas the hot disperses and thins. You can learn this also from meats boiled in it. For it makes them crumbly, just like those that have been kept beforehand until stale, even if you boil or fry them in it immediately upon the animal's being slaughtered. For this reason, then, I too have chosen the affusion with oil that is sufficiently hot, always avoiding the lukewarm, and still more the cold.

But I guard against the use of water throughout the whole treatment, to the point that it does not even touch the wound, so that, when right at the beginning it is necessary to wash the blood off the wounded part, one does this with oil; and when the patients, already in a moderate condition, take a bath, not even then does one permit them to put the affected place into the water—for in most cases those with wounded nerves receive the wound in the hands themselves. [581] And I remember one of those wounded in this way who, when he was on his fourth day and was completely free of pain and saw that the affected part was free of inflammation, went out of the house in great cold for some necessary business, and having spent a longer time at it, came home with the whole limb strained with tension as far as the neck and feeling great pain. When someone came to me and I arrived at his side and saw the state he was in, I ordered the oil on the part, which had become cold from his going out, to be wiped off, and having bathed the whole limb with hot oil, and then also the part of the neck directly in line with it, and having fomented it with oil-soaked wool and applied the liquid drug made with euphorbium together with castoreum, I soothed the man at once, and when sleep supervened, by evening all the symptoms had ceased. One must therefore make it a matter of the greatest importance that the wool remain warm, whether it happens to be soaked in oil alone or in oil-and-vinegar. This would come about if other dry wools are wrapped around on the outside and the patient remains indoors, when it is winter, until the fifth or the seventh day.

[582] day of the patient. For if up to this day no inflammation appears, and he is entirely free of pain and perceives no tension, he will thereafter be out of danger. And let it be a concern of yours that nothing wine-like shows itself in the vinegar, just as also in the case of the oil, so that it is free of all astringency. Let it therefore be neither the so-called omotribes or omphacine (for it is named in two ways), nor that from Iberia, which they call Spanish, nor indeed any other of those that contain olive shoots. The best oil, then, is the fine-parted one, such as in Italy the Sabine is, and elsewhere, among the nations under the Romans, all those oils that display no astringency.

What sort of thing rational indication is, and how much richer it is than bare experience without method, you will learn also from the following. Having come to many persons wounded in the nerves, often on journeys and on a voyage and in the country, or in a city but far from my own house, when neither the drug made with euphorbium was at hand nor the one made with vinegar, nor any other, but applying to the wound one of the drugs that happened to be available in that place, I always [583] hit the mark. For in the country I know that I myself applied to the wound fresh propolis, moist and oily, which the farmer had, and sometimes leaven alone, and sometimes having mixed both. The leaven should be as old as possible, while the propolis should be the opposite of it with respect to age; but if it should be rather old, let it be softened by the fire with oil, or in the sun. In the case of another countryman I mixed the juice of spurge with the leaven and applied it, having seen it growing near his farmyard; for I had judged the leaven deficient as being fresh. And once I melted propolis with oil and worked it into the leaven, having first kneaded the latter with the sharpest vinegar. It is better in such mixtures that the oil be old. [Also those] made with oxymel and the meal of beans or of bitter vetch or of darnel or of chickpeas or of bitter lupins or the fine dust of barley groats or barley meal, which I have used in the cities as cataplasms not only on parts already inflamed, but also straightaway at the beginning.

And in the country, having also found liquid pitch at a carpenter's, [584] I mixed it with leaven and applied it; and at another man's I applied bitter-vetch flour, having kneaded it up with the leaven. And if this is not available, one may mix in any whatever of the things mentioned before. And I have also applied immediately oxelaeum alone, hot, taken up in wool, when nothing else was available; for I had confidence in the vinegar, which was sufficiently sharp and old. In the case of another man who had already been chilled beforehand, because the nerve had been bruised an hour or even a still longer time earlier, I waited until one of the suitable things should be brought to me, having ordered that the part be bathed with oil; and then, having first mixed in vinegar, since the surrounding air was very hot, it being the season of summer, I kept bathing it with the mixture of both for as long as possible, until one of the other drugs was brought. And often, having mixed each of the flours mentioned with stacte, I applied it as a plaster both right at the beginning and afterwards, when the person had previously made bad use of one of the drugs for bleeding wounds. All these drugs, then, applied in whatever way, should be administered warm in their qualities.

And indeed once, from my own house as well, when none of the compound drugs was found ready to hand and I was in haste to go out, [585] I gave one of my people old euphorbium and ordered him to triturate it with old oil to the thickness of a liquid cerate and to apply it to the puncture of the tendon in the hand. When I returned and inquired of the wounded man whether he had a sensation of much heat in the place, he said that he perceived a moderate degree. So I asked again whether he was being bitten at the wound by the drug. When he said that he was not being bitten, but had a sensation as it were of some itching, I allowed the drug to remain on until night. And since, once the applications had been removed, the heat in the affected region appeared to me moderate and the puncture had not closed up, it seemed to me better to use the same drug. And indeed, since the man wounded in the nerve was faring faultlessly on the following day, and on the third and the fourth as well, I used the same drug through to the end; and someone who saw this, in the case of another man who had been wounded, used in the same way fresh euphorbium on the same place.

Of necessity, then, there followed for the wounded man much heat and bitingness and pain at the wound, so that the man was brought to me [586], as over an occurrence that was contrary to expectation. And I, understanding at once what had happened, threw off what had been applied, and having fomented him with oil I applied the drug made with vinegar. But if this had not been ready, I would have applied the one made with euphorbium, containing more wax. So one ought, as we were saying a little earlier, not to be ignorant of both the powers and the forms of the approved drugs, nor of which ones change their power quickly and which preserve it for a very long time. For euphorbium is among those whose heat quickly fades; and you will recognise it even without chewing it, by looking at the colour. For as it ages it becomes not ash-coloured, as at the beginning, but somewhat pale and somewhat yellowish. And at the same time it also appears then quite dry and dissolves only with difficulty when it is triturated with oil, whereas the fresh quickly turns to juice. But one must not mix it with the oil straightaway, but first triturate it gently in the mortar, so that it is not flattened out.

And what need is there to say that, when you taste it too, the fresh [587] appears most fiery, so as to burn the tongue, whereas the old produces little heat? Now it happens to many other drugs as well that their power becomes faded within a few years, but to none less than euphorbium, after thapsia at any rate. For the latter becomes quite weak after a year, and expires completely once it has become two years old. Euphorbium, however, when it is good from the beginning and is well stored, still preserves some power even in the third year, and sometimes even in the fourth; but it is already losing its strength in the fifth and sixth, and then, as time advances, it is completely extinguished. The one which I said I once used with oil, aged, without wax, was about five or six years old. Hence it is not even possible to comprehend its use within a fixed measure. For when it is new it is mixed with ten and twelve times as much oil together with three times as much wax; but as it grows old one must put in more of it; and when it has become three or four years old, either double the initial amount or an amount equal to the wax.

So whenever you wish the [588] drug to have a consistency similar to the unguents called akopa, which indeed is also that of the liquid cerate, the oil must be four times the wax. But when it is to become plaster-like, one must as a rule mix the wax in equal amount to the oil, especially if the wax is dry and old, since wax that is fresh and fatty requires less oil for making a plaster-like cerate, and still more so in the summer season. So someone wishing to make the cerate plaster-like, having melted the wax in oil according to the proportion I have stated, will mix into it a sixth part of fresh euphorbium, so that there is one drachm of the latter, six of wax, and six or five of oil. But since the glutinous and viscous quality does not belong to wax, as it does to resin and to pitch, for this reason I mix into the cerate resin or pitch or a portion of each. It is quite evident, then, that when these are mixed in, the oil is no longer to be put in equal to them. For wax requires a great deal of the fatty matter in order to become liquid, whereas among resins the dry ones need altogether little, while the liquid ones even want to take on some dry substance in order to reach a plaster-like consistency.

In [589] the waxes, then, there is no great difference in respect of moistness and dryness, whereas in the resins, conversely, as also in pitch, the difference between the dry ones and the moist is very great. The driest of the resins, then, is the one which some call roasted (phrykte), others colophony; second is the one from the jars (kerameia), impure and unroasted, but if one purifies it, it passes over into the roasted kind. Drier than both of these is what is called pine-blister (pityinon physema). This one, inasmuch as it is parched, I judged not suitable for the composition of the plaster under discussion and rejected, but I made use of the roasted one and the moist ones. And of these too some remain moist for a longer time, like the terebinth, while some dry quickly, like the strobilos (pine-cone) resin. Intermediate between both is the fir resin. And indeed in respect of their powers too the strobilos resin is hotter, the fir resin second, and the terebinth third after both. As for the cypress resin, I was wary of mixing it in, since it has something of astringency.

But someone will think that Dioscorides of Anazarbus disagrees with us in the account of resins, since he wrote the following statement in the [590] first book On Materials (περὶ ὕλης): "Of all the resins the terebinth takes first place, and after it the mastic (schinine), then the pine (pityine) and the fir (elatine), after which are counted the peuke-pine (peukine) and the strobilos (pine-cone) resin." For in these words Dioscorides appears to hold the strobilos resin to be the poorest and the terebinth the best. But I, of these three resins — strobilos, fir, terebinth — said that the strobilos is first and best in respect of heat, the fir second, and the terebinth last. Just as, then, one who says that of the austere wines in Italy the best is the Italian wine [speaks truly] — for the one makes the reference of his statement to a single quality, while the other pronounces simply about their whole substance, and (each) speaks truly — in the same way in the case of the resins too one might reasonably say that the terebinth is the best, as a drug of the most manifold uses (polychreston), yet not that it holds first place in heat.

As I was saying, then, it is possible for you, by mixing with the wax whichever of the resins you wish, to bring the simple cerate, which we compound from oil and wax [591] alone, to a more adhesive consistency. In this matter there is also need of trial, to judge our conjecture. For having mixed three times as much wax with the terebinth, you may determine whether the drug has already taken on a plaster-like consistency, or whether it is still rather dry and needs yet more resin; so that whenever, as you make trial in this way, it appears to you to be in due proportion, then you mix into the drug that is being made the twelfth part of euphorbium. But if you do not know whether the euphorbium is exactly hot, or falls somewhat short of being such, then after the preparation spread a little of what has been prepared on a linen cloth and apply it to your own shin or forearm for some hours; then, if it seems to you to heat moderately, suppose that what has been prepared is well-tempered. But if it either produces no perceptible heat or is more fiery than is fitting, it is possible either to relax the drug or to intensify it: to relax it by admixture of cerate, to intensify it by the addition of euphorbium.

If, however, you have oily propolis, know that it will be more suitable for you than all the resins, inasmuch as it is of a nature to attract [592] and draw out from the depth vaporous thicknesses of pneuma and superfluous moistures. For the resins, together with the wax, are taken up for the sake of the plaster-like consistency, not as falling under the aim of the treatment; but propolis pertains to the very aim of the cure. And once I used it alone, fresh, in a moist state, as I said, on a certain farmer who had a hard body, and it was wonderful how he benefited, using it alone until the end, so that he needed no drug at all; when another man had a deeper puncture, I mixed in a little of the juice of one of the spurges. To soft bodies, however, the drug appears rather hard to the touch, unless one softens it thoroughly by an admixture of oil. And indeed all the other drugs too, as many as are applied to those wounded in the nerves, ought to be moist and soft. Now the softness any oil is able to provide, but it is old oil that preserves the strength of the drug.

And just as I once, in the country, applied propolis, having selected it as the better drug among those then available, so too I applied leaven on another occasion [593] in the case of another patient, when no drug was at hand, since I knew that this too draws out what lies in the depth and disperses it. And the longer the time the leaven has been kept, the better it is. Not only are such things readily found in country districts, but also unburnt sulphur, which I myself also once used, mixing it with the tetrapharmakon. With this, then, I also often used, having mixed them in, aphronitron and Berenician nitron and aphrolitron—not the stony kind, but genuine aphrolitron, which has a foamy consistency—not only in the country for lack of the others, but also when the aforementioned drugs were available, for the sake of testing my devising by experience; and through such use alone the wounded man was cured, being, of course, fomented with the oil. For let this be a common rule for you in the case of all the drugs here said to be suitable for those wounded in the nerves. And also that which is called arsenikon by physicians, but arrhenikon by those who wish to Atticize everything, I mixed with the tetrapharmakos preparation, wishing to make trial of my devising.

And again, when this was not available, [594] [I mixed in] what is called sandarach, just as also lime, both slaked and unslaked, both unwashed and washed, putting in a little of the unslaked, more of the slaked, and still more of the washed. The exact quantity in each composition will be stated a little later, once I have first gone through all these simples and the distinctions governing their use. For in this discourse, on account of the Empiricists, who think that most of the compound drugs have been discovered by chance encounter, it seemed good to me to go through the treatment of those wounded in the nerves, which was discovered by me without chance encounter, from knowing the aim of their therapy and understanding the powers of the simple drugs. For by chance encounter some one of the simple drugs is discovered, whereas the rational method discovers many of the simples all at once, and very many compositions on the basis of them. At any rate, all those that are of such a nature as to draw outward from the depth and to disperse the moistures are suitable for those wounded in the nerves.

But since some of these have, coupled with them, heats that are rather immoderate, or strongly biting acridities or sharpnesses, it is reasonable to mix with them [595] other drugs capable of rendering the aforesaid excesses more moderate without harming the power. But it is not possible to do this correctly without knowing, for each of the drugs, not only the kind of its quality but also the quantity within it. For some, as we showed in the treatise On Simple Drugs, are of the first order of heating things, having departed a little from the well-tempered; others are in the second itself, standing further away; and some are of the third and fourth, certain others being already able to burn. Accordingly, in proportion to the vehemence of each drug in respect of its power, the power of the things mixed together is discovered, if one knows the temperaments of all the simple drugs. But the method of the Empiricists, which mixes only things of the same kind, comes about both through ignorance of the nature of each drug and, for those who do know this, through the quantity of the excess not being securely known.

I myself, then, composed the drug which I first prepared out of many homogeneous ingredients, because I did not yet know precisely the quantity [596] of the power of each. For I put in some arsenic and sulphur and misy and lime, both unwashed and washed, and pompholyx, and likewise spodion. In addition to these also flakes of copper and burnt chalcitis, both unwashed and washed, and furthermore the unburnt kind. These, then, I first ground fine in the sharpest vinegar over many days in the summer sun. The things to be poured over these were wax, of necessity, and a small amount of honey previously skimmed of its froth, and nearly all the resins, and propolis and pitch and ladanum. As liquids, henna-oil and lily-oil, opobalsam and marjoram-oil and must-oil and cedar-oil, and castor oil and old oil. And a little from each of the juices which I mentioned a little earlier. Later, removing now one, now another, for the sake of trial, I found that each of the simpler compounds, which I use up to the present day, fell short in nothing. Their proportions will be stated a little later. Such drugs, then, I used to prepare with vinegar and with the juices, mixing with them some wax and the resins mentioned and propolis and pitch, and likewise also with pigeon dung and the fine-particled herbs.

[597] The liquid drugs, then, are less distressing, both for other wounds and especially for those in the nerves. But we also use the plaster-like ones because of those who wish to bathe. For once the wool has been removed, having only such a drug itself lying upon them, they bathe with less disturbance. For it has been said before that not even then is it fitting to wet the wounded part with water, at least if it is in the hand. When, however, the wound has occurred in the foot, it is impossible not to wet the part, but one must at that time abstain from the bath for the first four days. But since in present-day life endurance has perished among all men, so that by now even those in the fields have become accustomed to bathe every day, we have those who are not very luxurious—and these would be the poor—obedient for the most part, but the rich, and especially those of them who have great power, either hard to persuade or entirely disobedient. The best course, then, would have been not even to treat them.

But since, I know not how, each for a different reason, some of us unwillingly and others willingly are compelled to put up with their softness, [598] I am accustomed to do something of this sort. Placing one of the plaster-like drugs upon the wounded part, I apply over it on the outside in turn several many-folded linen cloths soaked in oil, and over these again, on the outside, I apply a bandage of linen cloth; and after this, once more, in the bath itself I first pour the oil over the bandage, when the person wounded in the nerves is about to step into the tub; and obviously, when he has bathed, I remove everything that lies upon the part and employ the previously described regimen of the whole treatment. And it is quite evident that one who is going to take proper care of those wounded in the nerves must also be experienced in the nature of the parts. For it was said earlier that the tendons too, in which most of the muscles terminate, bring about no small sympathetic affections, first generating spasms, and later both putrefying themselves and destroying along with themselves all the neighbouring parts. Some of them are thin and broad like membranes, such as those which are stretched beneath at the ends of the thighs by the knees, on the inside of the hands, and on the underside of the feet.

For all these touch the skin, [599] those of them that are in the hands and the feet being quite firmly grown together with it, whereas those that run down to the kneecap are set free from the surrounding skin by flaying (κατὰ δάρσιν). And this too befell me by chance: for I devised the regimen of treatment for those wounded in the nerves while still young, when I first returned from Alexandria to my native city, being in my twenty-eighth year. And since I gave each of the drugs I had devised to my physician friends, not only to my fellow citizens but also to those of the neighbouring cities, in order that everything might be confirmed by experience; and since it seemed good, I know not how, to the high priest in our city to entrust the treatment of the gladiators to me alone, although I was young in age—for I was beginning my twenty-ninth year—at that time I treated those wounded in the front and lower part of the thigh by means of the regimen I had devised, myself cutting through the remainder of the tendon in those whose wound was transverse, so that the treatment was free of danger for me, while in those whose wound was small or straight I conducted the whole regimen with safety and at the same time with fear.

For whereas all the physicians before me [600] both fomented them for a very long time with hot water and applied poultices of wheaten flour moderately boiled in water-and-oil (hydrelaion), I did not apply the water at all, but, bathing them frequently with the oil together with the drugs mentioned, I quickly rendered them all healthy. And since by chance many had died in the preceding years, whereas under me not one of those wounded in the manner described died, nor anyone from any other wound, the second high priest after the one who had then entrusted the treatment to me likewise himself entrusted to me the care of the gladiators, after an interval of seven months. For the first held the high-priesthood around the autumnal equinox, the second at the height of spring. And when again under this one all were saved, the third and the fourth and the fifth likewise entrusted to me the treatment of the gladiators, so that I have had an extensive testing of the method of treatment. And indeed in this period something of the following kind was also devised by me, and those physicians who wish to handle the treatment of wounds correctly must pay particular attention to it.

For having observed [601] one of the gladiators called horsemen (hippeis) who had a transverse division, extending to a great depth, in the front and lower part of the thigh, and having seen the lip of the wound—the one drawn up above, the other drawn down below, as if toward the kneecap (mylē)—I ventured, departing from the treatment named 'according to breadth' (kata platos), to bring together with sutures the separated parts of the muscles toward one another. Taking care, then, not to sew the tendons together along with them, having first stripped those away, I thus employed the sutures through a great depth, knowing that it is free of danger into the fleshy part itself of the muscles, whereas the danger arises from the tendons—and this too I had not seen any of my teachers doing. For some of them, in wounds of this kind, used to sew together only the lips of the skin, while some, venturing to sew the muscles themselves in their fleshy parts, made the bringing-together of them at the surface, so that if ever the wound had come to extend to a considerable depth, not along the length of the limb, the surface of the muscle was agglutinated, while all the rest remained unagglutinated.

For in the case [602] of wounds running along the length of the limb, bandaging is sufficient to bring the parts of the wounded muscle together with one another; but in those in which the wound is transverse, since bandaging is able to help not at all, the whole thing is accomplished by the suture alone. If, then, one does not make these sutures through the depth, the parts of the muscle in this region remain unagglutinated. But after I had succeeded in this operation, certain persons among those inexperienced in the anatomy of all the muscles, imitating the same procedure (μιγνύμενοί τινες ταὐτὸ), flay away from beneath the underlying membranes, not knowing that these may be sutured together with the muscles without danger, whereas the tendons that have been flattened in a manner similar to them are sutured only with the greatest danger. But however much these may be flattened, nonetheless they are still both thicker and harder than the membranes. You will see quite thin tendons also in all the muscles of the epigastrium except the two straight ones, upon which the membranous aponeuroses of the oblique muscles are laid. But no other tendon besides those mentioned is flattened in a membranous fashion; for all those that are flattened preserve a considerable thickness, so as to escape no one's notice.

The sympathy, at any rate, of the parts lying above, as far as the very origin of the [603] nerves, occurs no less in the muscles at the end of the thigh, in those that insert into the elbow of the forearm, and in those that go into the heel. In both of these, then, the tendons are flattened, but while preserving a considerable thickness; and in the case of the heel still more so: the tendon descending from the calf appears both robust and thick, as being composed of three aponeuroses. This too had escaped the notice of the anatomists older than I, as had many other things concerning the muscles as a whole, and still much more concerning the veins, arteries and nerves. And many of my companions by now know all these things and demonstrate them to their pupils, when my anatomical books are read.

I mentioned the things that appear from dissection — which, as someone might suppose, have nothing in common with the treatise on the composition of drugs — because I feared that those who err through such ignorance might either regard the whole method of treatment with suspicion or strip off the membranes to no purpose, being wary of the harm that would arise from the things which they falsely suspect; just as certain others, not [604] knowing how to recognise the ligaments, regard them with the same suspicion as nerves and tendons when they are wounded, although they are free of danger whatever they may suffer, since they are insensible and have their origin from bones, not from muscles, as the tendons do, or from the brain and spinal marrow, as the nerves do. Very well, then, have many of the most esteemed physicians spoken, as on many other matters, so also on these: that the parts of medicine have need of one another — I mean the surgical, the pharmaceutical and the dietetic — and most of all the part concerned with surgery has need of both the others. If, therefore, you have often seen in apes the position and size of each tendon and nerve, you will remember accurately, should you ever have the opportunity of dissecting a human body, to find each one quickly just as you had observed it. But if you are wholly unpractised you would derive no benefit from such an opportunity, just as the physicians in the German war, although they had license to dissect the bodies of barbarians, did not learn anything more than what cooks know.

For the Empiricists' anatomy by chance encounter is a long piece of nonsense, like [605] goats being pricked with sharp rushes. And still more nonsensical than this is learning through the anatomical treatises, which resembles those called, according to the proverb, 'helmsmen from a book'. For when those who have clearly seen the nerves in the body and their tendons displayed by a teacher, unless they see them a second and a third time and many times in succession, do not remember accurately the place in which they lie, hardly could anyone be able to learn them by reading. At any rate, the best of the Empiricists of our time, who had read all the books of the anatomists, when a child at school had once made a stab with a stylus into the inner region of the upper arm, above its middle parts, applied one of the plaster drugs of which he had recently had experience as having cured a wound of a nerve, and seeing the child under it free of inflammation and free of pain, thought that it had been completely cured; but suddenly, on the seventh day, it died in convulsions.

So when he related to me what had happened as something hard to account for causally and perplexing, and I asked him to read out the written formula of the drug's [606] composition, he readily did this, and I at once said to him the following: 'When you were just now narrating to me what befell the freshly wounded boy, did you add anything more to your narration than that you had recently had experience of the drug having wonderfully cured a freshly wounded boy?' And when he admitted that he had added nothing else to his account, 'Then listen again,' I said, 'to me telling you what has happened. The wound of that which struck the nerve, which you say was cured by this drug, was a considerable one; and with confidence go on using it again on wounds of this kind. But punctures of nerves that have a narrow division of the skin cannot be treated by a drug of this sort, just as neither can the drug that treats the punctures be applied to the nerve itself when bare. For it is much hotter and more biting than that a bare nerve could endure the biting and burning inflammation caused by it.'

Where, however, skin and a membrane upon it, and perhaps flesh as well, lie in front, the biting drug, provided that it is also fine-parted, produces the same treatment with respect to the nerve as your drug does [607] when it touches only the bare affected nerve itself. But one must make it a matter of the highest priority that the orifice of the narrow punctures be kept open, so that the hot drug applied from outside, being attractive of what lies in the depth, may vaporise through it the moisture around the affected nerve; so that in such cases it is fitting also to enlarge by incision the mouth of the puncture, with two incisions through the skin cutting one another at right angles. These things, then, I said, and many others of what has been stated by us earlier, to the man who had erred so greatly in the treatment of the nerve-wounded child that, because of the faulty management, it was seized with spasm and died. It is clear, therefore, that the nature of the punctured part too will indicate that the puncture is at one time free of danger, at another suspect, when we see a nerve lying beneath, as in the case of the child punctured in the upper arm.

For it is not possible to explain in words the place at which the nerves that pass through the armpit and arrive at the whole arm mount upon the upper arm; and here too one may marvel at the contentiousness of the Empiricists, who in all other matters [608] assert that the person who has often seen any one of the works belonging to medicine imitates it better than if he happened to have seen it only a few times, and likewise that the person who does anything whatever performs it better if he has done it many times, yet that the things which come to knowledge through dissection, alone of all, can be known with certainty by someone who has merely read the account of the anatomical men—when in fact, even among those who have seen the parts of the body demonstrated by a teacher, there is no one who is able, having seen them once or twice, to remember them accurately, but one must see them many times. And not only are there large nerves travelling through the depth in many parts of the body, but there are also, as it were, certain roots of those nerves which are distributed to the skin alone; and those who have been punctured in these, if they are not properly treated, incur a sympathetic affection of the large underlying nerves from which these grow out—matters about which I wrote accurately in the Anatomical Procedures, since they had been omitted by all before me.

And if one has not seen these roots many times in apes, it is impossible for him, even should he at some time have a human body at his disposal for dissection, to discover them accurately [609] — just as, far more so, in the case of dissection by chance encounter, which they also call the 'viewing of wounds', it is not possible to find the place from reading alone. Nor indeed is it possible for anyone to become an eyewitness of a very great many wounds, apart from those which occur in wars; and even in the case of these no one, neglecting the task of treating the wounded man as quickly as possible, investigates where nerves underlie the wounded parts, and where arteries and veins. Accordingly, in the treatments of such affections those who are inexperienced in what appears from dissection are seen to resemble blind men walking with a staff, and for this reason to err most gravely. But whoever among them has combined into one both the experience of the parts, known from dissection, and the method for the composition and use of drugs, will always treat those wounded in the nerves, as we do, without any danger, so that neither does any of the more sovereign parts suffer in sympathy nor does the wounded or bruised nerve become inflamed; and where these do not happen, far more surely neither putrefaction nor crippling nor spasm nor death follows.

[610] [The compositions by means of metallic drugs for those wounded in the nerves.] Of the metallic drugs, the astringent ones are to be avoided, and most of all whenever the use of the compounded drug takes place upon a puncture; whereas those possessing a detergent power, like scale of copper, are useful. But since all the metallic drugs are coarse-particled—for they contain much of the earthy substance in themselves—they require some artifice in their preparation in order to become more fine-particled. This, then, I devised to accomplish by means of the most acrid vinegar, and above all one that has had its origin from a wine that is not harsh; but even if it has come from a wine not of this kind, yet is of considerable age, it is to be used. Pay close attention, however, in tasting it, lest it seem to you to display even the slightest trace of the quality of wine. For such a vinegar does not possess a strong power of eroding and cutting through what comes near it.

But one must triturate the metallic drugs in the most acrid vinegar, as old as possible and thinnest in consistency, avoiding thickness of consistency; and it is better that the trituration of the drugs take place [611] in the summer sun. Some of the metallic substances do not even need to be pounded or sifted, since they are easily dissolved by the vinegar, as chalcitis and misy; but some require both to be pounded and sifted, like the scale of copper. Now when I first prepared the drug, I also put arsenic (arrhenikon) into it, but afterwards it seemed to me superfluous; for it appeared to me that the drug would be sufficiently composed by means of the scale of copper, the misy and the chalcitis. In the first composition I also mixed in burnt verdigris (ios), for I suspected the unburnt of biting beyond what is appropriate. Afterwards, however, I also put in a little unburnt, small in relation to the proportion of the others; and so too with chalcitis: if I put it in raw, I mixed in a very small quantity, but if burnt, a quantity equal to the misy and the scale of copper. And of all the preparations I both expected and found by experience to be best the one in which the scale of copper was in the greatest quantity, burnt chalcitis second, and then misy.

So then, as I said, let whatever drugs you are going to mix be triturated in the sun in the summer season for many [612] successive days, in the most acrid vinegar. For the longer the time over which they are triturated, the more fine-particled they become and for this reason the more useful for narrow wounds, whereas in the case of exposed nerves at least one must guard against those that are excessively fine-particled and corrosive. For this reason the aforementioned trochisks are useful in all such cases, for they have taken on in addition some of the astringent substances as well. Renowned among them are that of Andron, that of Polyeides and that of Pasion. There is also another, a fourth and a fifth, which I habitually use, stronger than these. Their exact proportions will be stated as the discourse proceeds. For now, however, let only this much be said about their use: that one must, once they have been triturated dry, thereafter again add siraion and triturate them in this way, until the drug becomes glutinous and evenly smooth. Nowadays everyone among us also calls this siraion, the boiled-down must (hepsema) that is produced when the must is boiled. And let this too have nothing winy about it.

And it becomes such when the must is neither from austere grapes, [613] but from grapes as sweet as possible, nor from what flows first, but from what flows last. If, then, the must is of this kind, one must boil it until half of what was put in at the beginning is left; but if it is not of this kind, it must be boiled down until a third is left. With boiled-down must (hepsema) of this kind one must dissolve the troches, so that, having a honey-like consistency and taken up on lint plugs, they are applied to the exposed nerves—and especially the more moderate of them, such as that of Polyeides, and indeed much more so if the body is soft-fleshed, in which case it is also safer to withdraw entirely from the use of the troches, employing other drugs, about which something has already been said before and will be said again.

Once the laid-bare nerve has been covered with the lint-plugs, one must apply on the outside one of the drugs suited to narrow wounds, of which there are four kinds: this one, the drug made of metallic substances, about which it is proposed to speak; another, the drug made of juices, among which is also the one made with euphorbium; a third, the drug made of pigeons' dung; and a fourth, which I call the mild one, which I use also for the completely laid-bare nerves of [614] soft-fleshed bodies. One of these four must be placed around the whole affected part, taking in also a good deal of the healthy parts, and especially those lying above, on which one must also perform the affusion twice a day, or three times, if it is urgent. And indeed sometimes also at night, the lint-plugs remaining in place upon the laid-bare nerve, while the drug applied over them from outside is removed. But since there is a very great difference among human bodies both in respect of their original mixtures and the changes of the ages of life, and further, in addition to these, their pursuits, it is impossible for the compounded drug to be fitting for all. Therefore, on this account, let there be two prepared for you, the one stronger among those of the same kind, the other milder; mixing these with one another at the time of use, you will produce very many intermediate drugs according to the quantity of the mixture. For if you mix an equal amount of each, the mixture will be for you exactly the mean between both; but if more of one, it will have departed from the mean towards that one of the extremes to the degree that the mixture exceeded.

Let, then, the strongest [615] of the metallic ones be composed of these: let it have one part of raw chalcitis, two of misy, likewise raw, and three of scale of copper; and the weakest, likewise one of misy and of chalcitis, but both burnt, and four of the scale. And indeed let the one intermediate between both, which I have often used, be as follows: of misy and chalcitis and verdigris, all burnt, one part of each, and of scale of copper three parts. To these, then, ground fine as I have said before, let wax be mixed: in the case of the strongest, double; in the case of the weakest, two and a half parts; and in the case of the middle one, which lies between these, two parts and a quarter. For example, in the case of the first of the three written down, which I said was the strongest, the total parts assembled from misy and chalcitis and scale come to six in number. To these, then, you will add twelve parts of wax. And in the case of the weakest, if there are six parts of the metallic substances, you would put in twelve parts of wax, and in the case of the middle one the amount between. And again, between eighteen and twelve lies fifteen. So whether, then, you posit one drachm

you posit the one part to be one drachma—of all the ingredients, clearly—you put in as many [616] drachmas as there are parts; and if an ounce or a litra (for so it is customary among the Romans to name them), as many ounces or litras. There is among them a measure, with which they measure oil, incised with lines that divide the whole into twelve parts; and the whole measure is called by them a litra, and the twelfth part of it an ounce. The metallic substances and the wax, then, are weighed on a balance by means of a different ounce, whereas the oil is measured by the horn. Let the oil, therefore, be put into all the aforesaid drugs in proportion to the wax, exceeding it by half in all of them, so that if the wax is 8 ounces, the oil put in is 12 ounces, that is, the whole litra. And let the oil be like the Sabine, fine-particled and partaking least of astringency; and it is better if it is also old. But the oil called omotribes (of unripe olives) and that prepared with olive shoots are not suitable.

To all the drugs mentioned, when the metallic substances have been triturated in the mortar for several days with vinegar, let frankincense—the whitest and oily kind—be added in, [617] and then let it again be ground fine together with the metallic substances for some days, before the cerate is mixed in with them. Whatever quantity is gathered from all the metallic substances together, let the frankincense amount to half of that. But if you should wish to make the drug softer, put in more than the half, just as, if you wish it sharper, less than the half. Moreover, it is also possible to add some one of the aforementioned resins to the wax while it is being melted with the oil, you being aware that the drug becomes sharper when strobilos (pine-cone) resin is put in, softer when terebinth is, and intermediate between the two when fir resin is. Of the class of resins is also the so-called larix, which is on the whole moister than those previously mentioned, and similar in consistency to the liquid pine resin, which the dealers in sundries sell in place of terebinth to those who do not know how to distinguish them. Such a resin is sharper than terebinth in smell, in taste and in power. The so-called larix, then, has a power similar to this resin and to terebinth, but it is finer in parts than they and more discutient.

You will therefore mix with the wax, if you wish the drug to become plaster-like, a sixth part of the resins [618] mentioned, so that if you put in one pound of wax, you will put in two ounces of the resin; but if it should be very liquid, it will suffice to mix in even one alone. If, however, you are not concerned that the drug become plaster-like, there will be no great need to mix the resin into it. And mix in galbanum too, by all means: where, however, it is proposed to make the drug as mild as possible, in an amount equal to the weight of the frankincense; where stronger, half of it; and for the mean between both, the amount intermediate between the equal and the half, as for instance, if the drachms of frankincense were four, you will put in two of galbanum if you wish the drug to remain strong, four if mild, and three for the middle. For just as it has something soft and pain-relieving, so too it has something septic. And this belongs also to most of the emollients. Therefore, when you are applying the drug to a nerve that has been laid bare, the galbanum should not be mixed in to any great extent; but without denudation its admixture is of no small account, contributing to freedom from pain.

And so it is possible for you to have ready also a drug of this sort, for use on bodies that are highly sensitive, soft-fleshed and full of bad humours, in which there is more [619] galbanum. For all the metallic substances are roughening and painful, and, among liquids, vinegar. It is reasonable, then, that the drugs prepared from them appear rough and painful; and for this reason affusion with oil is suited to them, and likewise the admixture of galbanum. Fine-particled fat, moreover, is no less pain-relieving than galbanum. I think it right, therefore, that you also have another drug, prepared from these as well, which you will be able to mix with the one made from the metallic substances, both in the case of the bodies just mentioned and in whatever other cases there is ever a sensation of the drug being rough and painful. Of these fats too one should select those that are finer in parts; such are those of wild animals, and especially of the lion, the leopard, the hyena and the bear, and those of birds, and especially of geese. If this is not at hand, that of country cocks and hens. In the same way one should also prefer the fat of country geese; for the fat of animals reared in cities, inasmuch as they are shut up in idleness, is moister and coarser in parts.

But when the consistency of the drug is to be cerate-like, [620] let a third or a fourth part of wax be mixed in; or, if the fat should seem to you to be exceedingly moist, it is permissible to mix in even half as much wax, just as, if it should be dry, a fourth; and if it is in a middle state, a third. Since such a cerate is going to be useful to us for many purposes, let it be named the cerate of fats. [On the drug compounded with euphorbium.] It has been stated by me also earlier that old euphorbium falls very far short of the new. If, then, it is of the same year, it heats even more than the Cyrenaic juice, and especially more than that of the present day, ever since they have been making the plants grow by watering with water and preparing them for an abundant production of juice; for after one year it is sufficiently hot, but already falls considerably short of the fresh. When it has become two years old, it falls still further short of the new, just as at three or four it falls short still more. And if it should be of longer standing than these, its power is entirely dissolved. You will recognise, as I said, how it stands with respect to age and power by looking at its colour and its consistency.

For in colour the old appears yellower and paler [621] than the new, and in consistency hard and drier. If, however, you should wish to distinguish it by tasting, you will have a diagnosis of it that is not conjectural but certain. And the heating unguent which I said one should improvise from it will show you most precisely the power of the drug. It is composed according to the following proportion: one part is of euphorbium, three of wax, and of oil twelve. The wax must be three times the euphorbium, and the oil in turn four times the wax itself. When, then, you have compounded the drug in this way, by rubbing some part with it you will be able to know clearly how great a power it has. And it becomes most evident in the bath; for people are stung strongly, by the air indeed, but still more by the water, when the euphorbium is hot and new and strong. If, then, you have euphorbium of this kind and this very unguent that has been described, apply it confidently to punctures in which you are wary that the mouth may close.

But if it is weaker, add to the weight of the euphorbium in proportion to its weakness, sometimes putting in one and a half parts, [622] sometimes two, and at times an amount equal to the wax, and even more, if it is very old. The first application, at any rate, upon one who has been punctured in the nerve or the tendon will guide you toward the second. For if the wounded man himself says that he feels a biting, and to you yourself the parts around the puncture appear hot and the puncture itself raised more than it should be and somewhat inflamed at its lips, then either you will relax the power of the drug by the admixture of more oil, or, compounding another according to the former proportion or by means of older euphorbium, you will in this way make it well-proportioned. But if the opposites of what has been said are present, you will increase the power of the drug. And if everything appears to be in due measure, you will keep it as it is.
