The composition, then, which has the wax triple the euphorbium is the strongest of all, provided that, as has been said, the euphorbium is fresh; that which has it fivefold is the weakest, and intermediate between both is the one which has the wax fourfold the euphorbium.

As for the oil: if you wish to make such things as the unguents called by physicians akopa, you will put in four times the amount of the wax; but if such as the liquid cerate which we prepare for fractures, [623] double; and if the wax should be both dry and fat-free, even more than double. For the most part it will suffice to add half of one part to the double, so that the whole measure in relation to the wax comes to two and a half parts. But if you wish to make the drug plaster-like, you will mix with the wax an equal amount of oil, provided the surrounding air is moderate in respect of heat; but if the wax is old and parched and the surrounding air cold, a little more, just as also, if the wax is fatty and the surrounding air hot, a little less. And this "little" is a twelfth part on either side of the mean. For indeed I have at times mixed both eleven and thirteen ounces of oil with the pound of wax, according to the degree both of its consistency and of the heat and cold of the surrounding air.

And rarely a little more or less. But in order that the preparation may have binding quality (ἐπίδεσιν) and fattiness and viscosity, and not be crumbly, nor easily dissolved, nor easily falling off the skin, I mixed into it some resin, preferably, if it were available, genuine terebinth, and if not, at least the most readily procurable kind, which they call [624] 'roasted' (phrykte) and colophony. Let its weight be equal to the wax. For it preserves the pre-existing consistency of whatever drugs it is put into, provided that it too is in a well-proportioned condition. For it is evident that, just as in all other things, so too in resin there is the more and the less. If, then, it ever appears fattier and moister, one must recognise that the cerate which will result from the wax melted in oil will be moister than itself [would otherwise be]. In general, in those wounded in the nerves, whenever one ever misses the exact and middle consistency of the plaster-like drugs, it is better to incline towards the softer, even if the preparation is going to be smearing (μολῦνον). And likewise also that which is well-proportioned in consistency. And pitch preserves the consistency of the cerate. The best for such a mixture, as I said, is the fatty kind, just as indeed is also the [fatty] resin. But if you put in a liquid resin, such as terebinth is in its consistency, it is fitting that it be a third part of the wax; and of terebinth itself the fresh is much moister than the old.

Remember, then, to observe in all cases what you have heard concerning wax and resin, [625] For it is not of things that are dry and parched, whether through time or through their nature from the beginning, but of things of moderate consistency that one must mix, in the composition of the drugs, as much of each as is found written by me. Let, then, the form of the drug before us that is moderate in both power and consistency be one that has equal amounts of wax, roasted (phrykte) resin and oil, and a sixth part of euphorbium itself, so that there is a litra of each of those, but two ounces of euphorbium. If, however, we should wish to make it softer, it suffices to put in an eighth part of euphorbium, that is, one ounce and a half—this proportion being defined, as I said before, for euphorbium that is fresh and hottest; since if it is older, and on that account weaker, it has been said earlier that this ought to be more than the proportion of the others. And if we should wish to put in not resin alone but also pitch, we shall mix in half a litra of each, so that the weight is equal to the wax. But the drug is far better if, in place of the resin and pitch, one mixes in propolis equal to the wax.

But since it [626] does not have oiliness in the same way as the resins, if we wish the drug to be one that needs no bandaging (ἀνεπίδετον), we shall add some terebinth resin, or the resin called larch, or also the unrefined (συγκομιστή) pine resin. I call 'unrefined' that which they transport in cases (γλωσσοκόμεια) and earthenware vessels, which has in it many pieces of wood and stony bodies. But if you melt it and strain it, it then becomes pure, just like the Colophonian resin itself and the so-called roasted (phrykte) resin. It is also possible to mix in some of the so-called self-flowing (αὐτόρρυτοι) resins. In Lacedaemon and in certain other places they call these 'first-flowing' (πρωτόρρυτοι), while in Cilicia they name such a resin kapnelaion (smoke-oil); it is moister, hotter and of finer parts than all the liquid resins, so that this one will contribute to the power of the drug being compounded, and it is especially fitting to add it when the euphorbium is weak. It is also more fragrant than the other resins, as are the terebinth and the fir resin. And it has been said earlier that the fir resin is hotter than the terebinth, and the strobilos (pine-cone) resin hotter than this.

Different from the resins mentioned are the so-called physēma (φύσημα) of the stone-pine and that of the pitys-pine, each of which quickly becomes dry, free of fat and parched, so that it is pounded in a mortar and sifted through a sieve. For this reason, then, these are useless for the composition of the drug before us; but I have used [it] most frequently whenever the euphorbium is of the same year. For the composition, [I take] of oil and of wax and of roasted resin one litra of each, and half a litra of fatty pitch. And to these, once melted, I mix two ounces of euphorbium; if it should be weaker, three. If you should wish to mix terebinth alone with the wax, you will bring the drug to a well-proportioned consistency if the wax is threefold, the terebinth being moist and fresh. But if it has been dried out by time, you will mix in oil, half the weight of the terebinth. And this whole mixture made from the three—I mean the oil and the wax and the terebinth—when it amounts to one and a half litrai, will take in addition one ounce of euphorbium of the same year; if it is not such, one and a half. On the basis of what I have already said many times before, it is possible for us to increase the euphorbium in proportion to its age.

And [628] indeed, even if the drug, when applied to the wounded person at its first use, appears somewhat weaker, it is possible, after triturating the euphorbium with oil, to mix it with the plaster-like drug that has been previously softened in the hands; for when one does so, it readily unites. But in the very first compounding of the drug it is better to prepare the cerate separately beforehand, scraped, and thus to mix it with the euphorbium that has been triturated together with the oil. For when the melted ingredients are poured over it in the mortar, the so-called enkerides (lumps of wax) often form, and especially when the surrounding air is cold. And it is not necessary to add water to the wax as it is being melted together with the resin, as I used to do at the beginning, mixing in with it as much as was going to be consumed during the boiling itself. [The drug compounded from meltable substances.] I call meltable drugs both those that are melted through contact with fire and those melted by means of certain liquids, such as water, vinegar, wine.

Now by means of vinegar, without fire, there are dissolved ammoniac incense and the juice of sagapenum, and likewise that of panax, which they call in a compound [629] appellation opopanax. By means of fire: propolis, wax, resin, ladanum, fat, galbanum. It is better, however, to melt this last in a double vessel. We so name it when, in a cauldron holding hot water, another vessel is set, containing, together with the meltable substances, the galbanum too, while the cauldron is heated from beneath. Let you also have some such drug prepared, one in any case, but better two. Of these the stronger will be as follows. Having dissolved opopanax in vinegar, triturate it thoroughly; then, having melted over fire propolis and galbanum and terebinth resin, mix them with the opopanax. Of each of the others let there be one part, but of propolis six, provided it is fresh and oily. If it should happen to be dry and old, it is better not to use such at all; but if you are without the other kind, you will mix in two parts, not one. And if propolis is not available to you, put in its place oily pitch, such as the Bruttian is, and that brought from the regions about Pontus, which is at once oily and fragrant, and which they put into the black amaracine unguent, such as formerly all of it used to be prepared.

[630] For nowadays they compose a whitish amaracine even without it. But if you lack this kind too, use the other, while also doubling the terebinth, as has been said. I myself have on occasion also applied on its own the drug made with the oily pitch, which I also use for those bitten by rabid dogs. For this contains only the oily pitch, boiled in acrid vinegar, according to the following proportion: one Roman sextarius of the vinegar, one litra of the pitch, and of the opopanax a fourth part of a litra, which is three ounces. This drug does not allow the wound of those bitten by rabid dogs to cicatrize. It is also suitable for those who have been punctured in some sinewy part, since it does not allow the mouth of the puncture to close. But since it is hard, it is to be used only on hard bodies, such as those of diggers and reapers.

But if one of you should have only this at hand, and the person punctured is a child or a woman or someone of soft flesh, it is possible to melt it together with one of the discutient unguents—above all the amaracine (ἀμαρανίκου, presumably ἀμαρακίνου) and opobalsamum, secondarily the iris and the Commagene unguent, and when these are not available, [631] the white-violet, the lily, and henna oil. And if you lack these as well, melt it with old oil, or, if you happen to be in Alexandria, with castor oil and radish oil, for these are most abundant in that city, as indeed throughout the whole of Egypt. Mustard oil, too, is obtained without difficulty in those regions; and if at some point you mix in a portion of this as well, it is quite clear that you will produce a most pungent drug with respect to opening up punctures that have closed. And it is evident from what has been said that even if, having first triturated sagapenum instead of opopanax in a mortar with vinegar, you pour onto it melted resin and propolis and some fat of the more pungent sort, the drug will be of the same kind. There is another, softer kind of the meltable drugs, which does not contain vinegar, and which is prepared from resins and propolis and fats alone, with wax also added in for the sake of consistency, for from the admixture of it the drug becomes smoother to the touch. And let the fat be fine-particled and pungent, such as is that of the lion and the leopard, and after these that of the hyena and the bear.

And about goose [632] fat, what need is there even to speak, especially when the geese are from the countryside? But bull's fat too, when it has been aged, is suitable for these purposes, and so is the he-goat's. For being of a mixed nature and power, since they are both earthy and acrid, with time they incline toward the more acrid, evidently in much the same way as most things that are aged. For thus indeed even pig's fat itself, which is the softest of all, acquires acridity in the course of time. Wine, vinegar and honey have undergone this same thing; and in the kind of these drugs belong also the marrows. The best of them are the deer's and the calf's; rennets are more acrid than these, and are already close to the more vehement kind of drugs. I therefore require you to have also some drug of this sort, so that whenever the wounded part, having been bitten too immoderately by one of the strong drugs, becomes irritated, you may, having first fomented it with oil, cover it with one of such drugs.

For when it has been soothed in this way, it is possible to return again to the agonistic course of treatment. I, at any rate, when once a nerve-wounded part had been unbound, [633] seeing the wound irritated, and a liquid drug happening by chance to be at hand, the ear-remedy made with fats, warmed it in a double vessel and applied it to the affected part, and I saw a very swift benefit arising from it, by the very sensation of the patient; for he at once became free of pain, and afterwards, when we unbound it, it appeared to be in its natural condition. [On the drug compounded with pigeon dung.] The dung of the pigeons kept in the towers of country people is acrid, and I once used it in the country on a young man wounded in the nerves. And the farmer who had charge of this estate, having observed this — for he was not unintelligent — imitated it and always uses it and treats those who have been wounded in the nerves. Both the composition and the use are the same as those of the drug made with euphorbium, the other ingredients being the same, but the dung being put in instead of the euphorbium. This dung, however, falls short of euphorbium in fineness of parts, and for this reason it is useful in the countryside on hard bodies.

And I once also mixed it with the metallic drugs for the sake of trial, grinding it together with them in vinegar in the sun straight from the [634] beginning, just as I said a moment ago. And the drug became much more acrid, just as also when it receives unburnt verdigris. [On the drug compounded from herbs.] I also compounded, from fine-particled herbs, a drug for those wounded in the nerves, at the beginning from dittany and marjoram and aristolochia only, but later also from others, testing for myself whether I was aiming rightly at their composition; and all of them attained the end. Let the herbs suitable for this be bitter to the taste without astringency, or acrid, yet not immoderately so.

So then, since the rich man asked to receive some composition of a drug that was both sweet-smelling and costly, I gave [638] him several recipes, having made them according to the aforesaid method; and he, being eager to make trial of them, ordered both his freemen and his slaves to seek out for him persons with wounded nerves. When the drugs had worked beyond all expectation, he first praised me for having shared the recipes with him ungrudgingly, and then also honoured me with gifts; for indeed he was ready for such things too. The composition of the drugs given to him was as follows. Take of cinnamon, dittany and maron, forty drachms of each; for these are fragrant and fine-particled. As for amaracus, since it is not fragrant, I had intended not to mix it in at all; but then, since it was hard to procure in Rome, just as maron was too, and I saw that he delighted in things hard to procure just as in costly ones, I added to the recipe a small quantity of that as well, a fourth or a fifth, I think, of one part. These, having been pounded and sifted through a fine-meshed sieve, I ordered to be mixed into a cerate made with the best opobalsam and Tyrrhenian wax.

And I judged it to be well-proportioned to make eight parts of the wax, [639] and ten of the opobalsamum. And in order that the drug should not be crumbly, but somehow unified with itself, I also mixed in one part of terebinth resin, which is itself also fragrant when it is of the finest quality. But if, as I said, you should wish to make the drug more powerful, you should put in not one part of each of the aforementioned herbs, but more, so that it becomes one and a half. This drug, then, was attested by experience. And a second one after it, compounded from the same cerate and Cyrenaic juice, the mixture being made in the same proportion as with the euphorbium; and another, a third, compounded from the mixture of both; and the fourth, in addition to these, taking on stacte myrrh besides. But in cases where the nerve is bare, for these I compounded the cerate from the wax called perfumers' wax and from the perfumed oils named among the Romans spicatum and foliatum. And I mixed into it a twelfth part of pompholyx, whether you wish to say 'washed' in the masculine or 'washed' in the feminine; for whichever of the two ways you say it, you will neither benefit nor harm the drug at all.

It is also possible for you to prepare it with [640] Tyrrhenian wax. And it is possible, even without the aforementioned perfumed oils, to melt the Tyrrhenian wax in good nard, obviously in a double vessel, for this is common to all perfumed oils. And to the cerate, once scraped, you will mix in spike of nard, amomum, malabathrum leaf, and washed pompholyx, an equal amount of each. For in the case of punctures, as has been said, there is need of more acrid drugs, which always keep the wound open; but to those parts that have been laid bare one must apply those that possess a moderate astringency together with a non-biting discutient power. Amomum too has some share in astringency, but more than it the spike of nard and the malabathrum leaf. [On the drugs described by the other physicians for those wounded in the nerves.] The whole course of treatment of those wounded in the nerves, which I devised by a certain providence of the gods, none of the elders before me wrote down.

Drugs, however, that profess to treat certain persons with wounded nerves they did compose, but without distinction and without a varied mode of use, [641] indicating neither the treatment in the case of narrow punctures, of what sort it should be, nor that in the case of broader woundings, whether of a nerve or tendon laid bare or of one crushed; and much less, whether the affected part is already inflamed or has even come near to gangrene. I did, however, find one of the physicians of our own time using a drug similar to those prepared by me by means of the metallic substances, though he too used it without distinction. But since I learned that it was composed of a few of the naturally occurring substances, whereas the compound made from many I myself had at that time already prepared, I conceived the plan, by removing the greater number and composing another from a few, of examining afresh and testing through experience whether it appeared to fall short of the many-ingredient one by much or by little. I therefore made it a matter of the greatest importance also to obtain the recipe from the physician of our time, and having prepared it at once I found that it had a professed virtue and power similar to the varied one. The recipe for the composition of this, then, is as follows: wax, six ounces; oil, nine ounces; misy, six drachms.

of chalcitis [642] 1 drachm, of flakes of copper 2½ ounces, of frankincense 1½ ounces, of galbanum 1 ounce. Over the metallic substances, which have first been carefully levigated in acrid vinegar, pour the meltable ingredients once they have been melted, that is, the wax and the galbanum. I do not know who it is that composed this drug (συνθήκας). For I found the recipe neither in Asclepiades the Pharmakion, nor in Petronas, nor in Andromachus, although all these older physicians wrote down the best drugs. And it is quite evident that it is not in Heras the Cappadocian either, nor in Mantias, nor in Heraclides of Tarentum, men who had acquired great experience of drugs; but not even in the circle of Archigenes, Philippus, or any of his pupils. And having read everything written on drugs by Soranus and Menecrates and Crito and Damocrates and the others who hold a reputation for knowledge of drugs, in none of them did I find this drug that has just been written out.

What is written in the men whom I mentioned I shall set out in order, and I shall make my beginning from Asclepiades the Pharmakion, in the third book of the internal [643] remedies (τῶν ἐντὸς φαρμάκων), which he also entitles Marcellas, where he writes word for word as follows. Egyptian enhaimos wound-plaster of Andromachus, as Asclepiades records it. It is effective for severance of nerves and of muscles; it is effective for punctures, contusions, chafings, sprains; it is effective for abscesses. It is also a parakollēma (adhesive plaster) for those suffering from ophthalmia. It is effective for those with headache, and the drug is useful for many conditions. Take litharge, wax, 144 drachms each; ammoniac incense, 72 drachms; terebinth, 36 drachms; burnt greasy wool, 12 drachms; scale of copper, 8 drachms; scale of stomoma, 8 drachms; frankincense, 8 drachms; round aristolochia, 8 drachms; castor oil, 3 kotylai. Boil the litharge and the oil, and when it changes, add the wax and the resin. And when it becomes non-staining, add the ammoniac, having flattened it out, and then the greasy wool and the rest. This drug, to the degree that it became more polychreston (of many uses) by taking on the scale of stomoma, became to that same degree worse for wounded nerves. For if it is only a puncture, even the scale of copper is superfluous.

For unless it has first been ground fine for a considerable [644] time with acrid vinegar, none of the metallic substances is useful in these cases. For nerves and tendons that have been laid bare, however, it would be a good drug. And if they are already inflamed, it is proper to melt the drugs with rose-oil and so to use it as a lint-dressing (ἔμμοτον). But when there is no inflammation, right at the beginning the softer and moister of the drugs are better than the harder and drier ones. And it is better to use them melted in one of the discutient or soothing oils. By discutient I mean old oil, castor oil and Sicyonian oil; by soothing, rose-oil, chamomile oil and the oil made with marsh-mallow. Stronger than these, and for that reason suited to harder bodies, are the oil made with the root of the wild cucumber boiled down in the oil, and that made with iris, bryony and arum; and stronger than these is that made with dracontium, aristolochia and panax. I myself have often also used the oil made with the seed of the fir and that made with the flower of the black poplar, for I steep these in Sabine oil for a considerable time.

These things, then, which I have now said concerning the use of such [645] drugs, I ask you to keep in mind and to transfer to the other things that will be said. I, for my part, will do what I set out to do. For I shall add other drugs too of the same power, such as is the one written by Asclepiades next after the one previously mentioned, which runs word for word thus: "The Egyptian of Claudius Philoxenus the surgeon, for the aforementioned conditions. Take litharge, wax, 160 drachms each; ammoniac incense, 80 drachms; propolis, 40 drachms; dry resin, terebinth, flake of copper, frankincense, 16 drachms each; burnt greasy wool, flake of steel, 8 drachms each; opopanax, 4 drachms; castor oil, 3 kotylai." It is clear, then, that this drug too is similar to the one written before and will have the same manner of use as the one written by me a little earlier. And moreover, in the same place as these two plasters, Asclepiades wrote another, a third, speaking word for word thus: "The tawny [plaster] of Halieus. It works for bloody wounds and severings of nerves. It works also for old ulcers, those difficult to cicatrize, and rheumatic ones."

It is also a good emollient, [646] especially for the indurations that arise around the breasts. We use it also for dog-bites and human bites. It works excellently also for the strikes of sea stingrays and weevers and the other dangerous fishes. And in general its power is marvellous. ℞ litharge, wax, each 100 drachmas; terebinth, manna, frankincense, galbanum, Sinopic red earth, each 8 drachmas; oil, 1 sextarius. So not even Asclepiades himself professes that the drug is useful for punctures reaching tendons and nerves, but he says it is for severances of nerves, that is, obviously, when the wound has become larger and the nerve appears bare. For at that point drugs of moderate and soothing power are more suitable. And such is also the one he has just set out. These three plasters, then, Asclepiades wrote somewhere near the middle part of the book. But before them, higher up, he wrote another plaster too, a polychreston (of many uses), and one better than these three as regards severances and corruptions of nerves. The very wording in which Asclepiades wrote it is as follows. Moschion's fracture-plaster.

A successful drug [647] for freshly inflicted wounds and severings of the nerves and divisions accompanied by contusion. It also works for fractures accompanied by a wound; for it both helps the wounds and forms callus on the bones when applied with the requisite bandaging, and it helps incipient dropsical patients. It also works for contusions of the testicles. It also shrivels the protrusions around the seat. It also works for fissures when injected with butter. It also works for bronchoceles, dissolves every hardness, and works for chafings and sprains. It works for the callous excrescences on the feet and hands, which we call 'nails', so as to remove them even without ulceration; and in general the drug is most versatile. It also works for incipient dropsies. The details of the preparation are as follows. Take litharge, 1 mina (the mina contains 160 drachmas); dry pitch, 160 dr.; calf's fat, 160 dr.; terebinth resin, 80 dr.; manna of frankincense, 80 dr.; wax, 40 dr.; verdigris, 8 dr.; opopanax, 8 dr.; galbanum, 8 dr.; castor oil, 1 cotyle; vinegar, the same amount; juice of the sycamine, 1 cotyle; liquid pitch, half a cotyle.

Having put the litharge, very finely ground, and the castor oil [648] into an earthenware or bronze vessel and set it on the fire, boil it, and when it has come to the boil, add the fat and the manna, stirring continuously. And when it has thickened, add pitch, wax, resin, and boil. Up to the point of its being non-staining, sprinkle in galbanum, then verdigris and opopanax dissolved in vinegar. The juice of the mulberry and the liquid pitch we put into another vessel and boil. And when it has thickened, we add it to the first drug, and having set it again on the fire we boil it until it is non-staining, and having poured it out into wine we leave it for three days; then, having softened it, we use it, spreading it on a linen cloth. After the application of the drug one must soak a small bandage in wine, wring it out, and then put it around over the drug. As our teacher Lucius prepared it, it is as follows. We first melt the fat and the oil, and when it has dissolved, we strew over it the manna, very finely ground, and the litharge, and when it has thickened, we do what follows.

It is right to praise Asclepiades in this respect as well, that he writes the manner of preparation [649] of the drugs, and does not, like Andromachus, leave it out, without even adding what power it has. At any rate, the Egyptian plaster from Asclepiades, written by me as the first of the three, which he himself says is Andromachus’, — Andromachus wrote neither what power it has, nor how it is to be prepared, nor how it is to be used, but it has simply been thrown in, like some chance drug, written by him as the second in the book of external powers. For first of all he wrote the one which he himself names Pantagathion, and next this Egyptian one, adding, as I said, nothing else. For his wording runs in this manner: Egyptian. ℞ litharge, 144 drachms; castor-oil, 6 cotylae; wax, 144 drachms; ammoniac incense, 72 drachms; terebinth resin, 36 drachms; burnt wool, 18 drachms; scale of stomoma (steel), 8 drachms; scale of copper, 8 drachms; frankincense, 8 drachms; aristolochia, 8 drachms; some add: myrrh, 4 drachms; opopanax, 8 drachms, others 12. To these at the end there is written in addition: sea-water for the embrochē (soaking) of the wax, 8 cotylae.

What "for the steeping of the wax" (εἰς ἐμβροχὴν κηροῦ) means in his text [650] we do not clearly know, for it is possible to conceive of several meanings. It is a matter for wonder how Asclepiades, having written everything else in the same way as Andromachus, did not write an equal measure of the kiki-oil; for Andromachus wrote 6 kotylai, but Asclepiades wrote 3 kotylai. Nor did he add what is appended by Andromachus at the end of the recipe: "some (add) myrrh 4 drachms, opopanax 2 drachms." Again, he himself added, in the case of the burnt wool, "greasy with oesypum" (οἰσυπηρῶν), which is not appended in Andromachus' recipe. Next after the aforesaid Egyptian plaster Andromachus wrote five theriac plasters, and after these again another grey one, which he says is Eubulus'; and after this in turn another grey one, which he names Athena, and then next again two others simply called grey, and after these another, over which is written verbatim as follows: "Grey plaster for punctures (νυγματική). Of Andromachus. Take: ammoniac incense 8 drachms, fresh wax 8 drachms, terebinth 8 drachms, burnt copper 8 drachms, dry pitch 40 drachms—but according to Zeno, half and a quarter of a mina—litharge 4 drachms, Indian aloe 2 drachms, aristolochia 2 drachms."

[651] of galbanum, 2 drachms; of verdigris, 1 drachm (others say 2 drachms); of frankincense, 2 drachms; of oil, in winter 4 cotylai, in summer an eighth; of vinegar, half a cotyle, for the dissolving of the ammoniac. It is likely that he calls this one "nygmatic" (for punctures) because it is capable of being useful against punctures of the nerves.

[652] GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK 4. My preceding discourse ended with the compositions of the white plasters, both the others and all those that are suited to those ulcers that are hard to cicatrize, after we had distinguished those commonly called hard to cicatrize from those specifically named malignant, which are themselves, obviously, hard to cicatrize.

But since some ulcers become hard to cicatrize from the ichors and humours that flow in to the ulcerated parts, [653] while others do so because the affected part itself corrupts that which flows in, even if it be good, it is the ulcers of the second mode that they call, in the proper sense, hard to cicatrize and malignant; in these cases some are sometimes compelled to excise the whole affected part or to burn it, using either escharotic drugs or fire. And since in each of the two modes there is considerable latitude in respect of the more and the less, one ulcer being more hard to cicatrize and malignant than another, it is necessary that there be as great a number of the drugs that cure them as there is of the ulcers themselves. Reasonably, therefore, each of those who possess a single drug professing to cicatrize malignant ulcers often fails. For at least two must have been prepared by one whose aim is to treat all such ulcers, drugs of the same professed virtue and power, but differing from one another not simply in the more and the less, but, as one might put it most clearly, in the most and the least.

Just as, then, in the case of all affections we showed in the books of the Therapeutic Method that what is discovered first of all is the general power of the [654] remedies, and next the materials in which that power is contained, by the same reasoning now too, in the case of ulcers hard to cicatrize, the general power, whatever it is, of the drugs that will treat them must first be discovered. And this too was shown by me in that treatise: in those cases where there is no cachexia about the ulcerated parts, it has these two aims, one to repel that which flows in, the other to disperse what is lodged in the affected part. These things come about through opposite powers. For all drugs whose nature is to astringe drive back that which flows in, while those possessing an attractive power disperse what is contained in the affected part. For the most part, however, astringent things roughen, and in this respect they are distressing; while those that attract and disperse the moistures from the depth do not accomplish this without acridity. And upon acridity there necessarily follows a certain pain that bites the ulcerated part. And so it comes about that, because of the distress arising from the roughening and biting agents, the moisture flowing in to the ulcerated parts is provoked.

And when this happens, the ulcer both becomes inflamed [655] and at the same time is eaten away, so that, as far as depends on what has been said, the discovery of drugs that will help ulcers that are hard to cicatrize is without resource, and still much more so for malignant ones. One must therefore find, as far as possible, such a material of drugs by which the ulcer will be dried without pain—something which cannot be done precisely unless the one treating knows how the drug applied will act. For it is of necessity strong in both of the components that have been combined, the biting and the astringent. But the filth lying upon such ulcers and the abundance of moisture, becoming as it were screens for the ulcerated parts, dissolve the bitingness from the strong drugs. One must therefore attend to how much of the moisture in the ulcer the first application dried up, or, if it also has filth, how much of this too it cast off; and in this way to use it a second and a third time until it appears both clean and dry. And as soon as you see it in such a state, to pass over to another drug, of the same kind but weaker than the former.

For the stronger ones, [656] becoming painful by biting the ulcer, both set fluxes in motion and rouse inflammations. But if, on the other hand, you apply one much weaker than the first drug, the ulcer will be moist and foul. In this, then, the physician trained in the art is better than the one who treats an ulcer through experience alone, inasmuch as he knows that the ulcer is treated by drugs through no other power than that of rendering the part as dry as it was when it was in its natural state. This will be evident from the fact that neither does thin ichor flow off any longer nor is a generation of pus fostered. And they will arrive at this by being dried in the manner I have stated, that is, by being astringed and dispersed, and, when they are dry but still appear foul, by being cleansed through detergent drugs, concerning which, too, something has been said also in the commentaries on simple drugs. But the most complete method has been written in its entirety in the Therapeutic treatise, in which the one who is going to profit fully from what is now being said must have been previously trained in the art.

And that this has been settled for you, my companions, for whom these things are written, I know very clearly, [657] and in addition to this, further, that what is now being said by me is not merely a persuasive argument lacking the testing on actual practice. For you have often seen me cure completely many such ulcers by means of those very drugs with which certain physicians, using them unmethodically, accomplished nothing. Recall, then, the drugs whose nature it is to dry without biting; most of them are metallic substances. And indeed, when they have been burnt and washed, whatever bitingness there was before is lost—recall this too. So let it be permitted to you to use these in the present case: washed, in the case of children, eunuchs and women and all who by nature have white and soft flesh, and in addition to these in the case of those who are very sensitive and full of bad humours. But in the case of other bodies it is possible to use even the unwashed ones, making the first application of them in the morning, when those being treated have digested well. And if the whole body should also need some preliminary preparation, this too must have been carried out beforehand. The preparations have been described in the therapeutic treatise.

For in some cases it suffices merely to purge, [658] in some to remove blood, and in others to do both of these; in some, to cut out a varix lying above the ulcer, or to take care of the spleen or the liver; and in some also to scarify the parts around the ulcer, just as sometimes also to cut away the callus of the lips. But if we need none of these, one must examine the quantity of the moisture together with the filth, and so proceed to the appropriate drug, having recalled, among each of the simples, which ones dry but do not cleanse away the filth of the ulcer, which ones cleanse but do not dry vigorously, and which ones are of such a nature as to do both, considering in addition of what order each one is—a matter which is the most important of those that bear upon the treatment, yet has been neglected by those who wrote the books on materia medica. For these alone undertook to state the powers of the whole of it, as indeed did Dioscorides, whom one would say is second to none of those who have devoted their efforts to these matters. I, therefore, shall enumerate in order all the drugs that are able to dry ulcers without biting or roughening noticeably.

I shall begin [659] with the metallic substances, among which they also count the kinds of earth. Since there is much difference among them in respect of drying more and less, I shall begin from the intermediate ones and pass on to those which dry more strongly or more feebly. Moderately drying, then, are the Lemnian seal and cadmia, and more so than the latter the naturally occurring kind, which, without undergoing any transformation, is found in the winter torrents and streams and in the mountains of the Cyprians, and in other regions too, but especially in those where the mines are. I am accustomed to prepare it so as to be more drying, in the season of summer, by grinding it in the sun for several days in succession with vinegar or with wine that is tawny in colour and translucent in consistency, such as the Falernian is in Italy and the Tmolite in Asia; and such a wine is the most drying of wines. Of the same class are the Ariusian, produced in Chios, and the fragrant Lesbian at Eresos and Methymna.

Next after these come all the old wines, whenever they have been aged from among the white and astringent ones: in Italy the Signine, the Tiburtine and the Marsian; in Sicily the one called by them Aminaean; in Asia the Aphrodisian [660] and the Mysian (Μίσυος). For it suffices for me to have mentioned these as examples of the general powers. But I also prepare the cadmia in like manner with acrid vinegar, in the sun for many days in the summer season. And having dried it I store it away, so as to be able to sprinkle it on ulcers that are turning malignant. A stronger drug than this is burnt chalcitis, previously levigated in the same manner as the cadmia; after it the unburnt is so strong a drug as to produce eschars. It is better, therefore, to have it washed and then dried. For the washed dries more weakly than the burnt, but it is much milder and less biting. Burnt verdigris, too, is a drug similar to it; but the unburnt is a very strong drug, just as chalcitis is. But the latter has some share also of astringency, and much more than it has chalcanthum, which is the most drying of the metallic substances; whereas verdigris has no share at all of such a power. And of the same kind as chalcitis, as you have learned, are misy and sory.

For they are, as one might say, sprung from a single root, misy being finer in its parts [661] and less biting and caustic, while sory is thicker in its parts and less drying than both, just as stimmi too has a power more astringent and more drying than sory. A most suitable drug for ulcers that are hard to cicatrize because of moisture is also the one called diphryges, for it dries strongly, although it bites only moderately; and it too has, in addition to the acrid quality and power, the astringent one, both of which raw chalcitis and chalcanthum have in stronger measure—whether one wishes to name it in the masculine, or in the feminine, or in the neuter. For always remember not to quarrel over names where the task before us is to learn thoroughly a theory necessary for the works of the art. And all the kinds of alum too dry ulcers sufficiently, being vehemently astringent. Hence one would not use them on their own upon an ulcer, just as one would not use raw chalcitis and verdigris either. But when these and misy have been burnt they are useful, as indeed also when they have been washed: they become non-biting, but dry less.

It is safer, then, to use them washed, since most of the bodies which we are compelled to treat [662] have at least some one disposition that does not bear strong bitingness. You have heard these things often, but now too I shall remind you of them again, and I shall ask you to keep them in mind throughout the whole discourse that follows. Accordingly, all bodies that are plethoric and all that are full of bad humours, and in addition to these those that are soft-fleshed and considerably sensitive, are easily brought into inflammation when bitten. Included among the soft-fleshed are, evidently, the bodies of white women and those of children, eunuchs, and men white in complexion; and of those who inhabit a cold land, too, the bodies are moist and phlegmatic and for this reason both soft and white, just as those who inhabit a hot land, such as those in Egypt and Arabia, have a hard and dry habit of body. On the assumption, then, that you always keep these things in mind, I shall add also some other material of simple drugs capable of treating malignant ulcers. Sarcocolla, then, and ichthyocolla, and more than these chrysocolla, are of such a power.

But the best drug for such cases is also burnt lead, [663] and after it sory and stimmi, these too burnt. And the dross of lead dries well, as does also the scale of iron, and still more that of steel (stomōma). But that of copper, in addition to drying, also cleanses, wherefore it also makes the ulcers clean, the other scales not having this property. Sprinkling, then, all these drugs dry upon malignant ulcers, you will see them wonderfully dried without biting, as also the burnt shells of whelks, of purple-shells and of oysters, and all other such things. And the so-called transparent stone, which the Romans name specularium, is, when burnt, among the things that dry without biting, being useful for ulcers that are hard to cicatrize, though not for malignant ones; for it dries more moderately than is required for these. Of the same power as it are also burnt glass and the fiery deposit that forms in the copper heating-vessels.

Along with drying, the fruit of the Egyptian thorn (akantha) has in addition also an astringent power, as do the omphakitis gall-nut and rheon and pomegranate rinds, and not a few [664] roots and herbs. For indeed aristolochia and iris and akoron and artemisia and the root of panax and argemone, and the root of black chamaeleon and kyperon, and drakontion and xiphion dry sufficiently, and still more than these do kentaurion and polion. Slightly weaker than these is the earth called Eretrian, just as the ampelitis is stronger. Such, then, is one body of material of the simple drugs that treat malignant ulcers. From outside there are added to these certain things which are not applied by themselves, because of the vehemence of their power, but are mixed with others, such as unburnt verdigris (ios) and quicklime (asbestos) and unwashed lime (titanos) and soft aphronitron, which is in truth aphrolitron. For the more foamy it is, the better it is in both respects, both in biting less and in dispersing more. For you learned also in the books on simple drugs that the finer-parted substances possess such a power in comparison with the coarser-parted ones, among all things of the same kind.

But nothing is so much to be guarded against as the drugs called by Hippocrates 'softening' (malthakōdē), which belong to the [665] genus of oil. Of this kind are all the fats, and above all among them pig's fat, then next the resins, and after these wax. In another way, the emollients of hardened parts are also unsuitable: galbanum, bdellium, ammoniac incense, storax and the marrows. And in yet another way the acrid ones: pepper, ginger, mustard, kanchry and a great multitude of other such things. [How one should use the dry drugs just mentioned in the case of ulcers that are difficult to cicatrize and malignant.] It is necessary that such ulcers be full of bad moisture, and not a few of them also have abundant filth. Whenever, therefore, we are about to sprinkle on them one of the dry drugs, one must first wipe them out with a linen cloth that is soft, clean and dry, and, having filled the hollow of the ulcer with the drug, apply on the outside a flat piece (platysma) of a plaster that thins the lips, and over this again, on the outside, a linen cloth equal on every side, and over it a sponge from water or wine.

One must make it a matter of the utmost concern that the [666] sponge remain cold, which would easily come about if one continually poured cold water over it, without undoing the bandage. The bandage itself should be applied and wound round as Hippocrates taught in the books On Fractures, holding that the greatest harm would result from a bandaging that excels in fine appearance rather than in benefit. If, then, the bandage is a single one, it should proceed from below upwards, whether it be the shin, or the knee, or the ankle, or the elbow or the hand at its extremity, or any other part whatsoever (ἠέρος). But if you wish to use two, as in the case of fractures, let the first proceed from the affected part towards the region above only, and let the second go first from below, and then successively upwards, ending so as to arrive at the same place as the first. It is clear, then, that these bandages should be made of linen cloths, not of rag. One should undo them every third day, not every day, and having undone them not apply water to the ulcer, but, in the manner just described, wipe away the ichors with a linen cloth that is soft, clean and dry.

But if the parts around the ulcer also display something inflammatory, apply over the flat piece (platysma), from outside, extending over a wide area, [667] a liquid drug made from my phoinikine, not simply melted, but having taken up as much astringent wine as possible. Nor indeed is it proper to melt it in any oil whatever; rather, if some redness, or in general heat, prevails in the parts around the ulcer, in one of the astringent and cooling oils—such are myrtle oil and quince oil; and if these are not at hand, the oil called omphakine and omotribes (of unripe olives); but if hardness appears to prevail, the same phoinikine must be melted in old oil or in castor oil (kikinon). And it is safer, even if nothing bad appears in the region surrounding the ulcer, at any rate to apply the liquid drug to the region itself lying above it, so that it may repel whatever, from before (πρόσθεν), either bad or more than is proper, flows in, and especially when the ulcer, being on the leg, has a varicose vein lying above it. And if this is large and shows by its colour that it contains blood that is neither red nor good, but blacker and more melancholic, one must cut out the vein.

It once happened, when such a [668] vein had been excised, that the ulcer was immediately cicatrized, even though it was a year old, but that in its place, at the incision from which the vein was excised, a malignant ulcer arose, which could not be cicatrized. It is better, therefore, in such cases, having observed the strength of the patient under treatment, to begin with phlebotomy, and next to purge with a drug that evacuates the melancholic humour and, together with it, the phlegmatic as well, since this too sometimes flows in together with the melancholic in the generation of varices. Then, next, to scarify lengthwise the vein itself that lies above the ulcer and, having evacuated in abundance, first to heal this very incision that has been made in the vein; and when it already appears to be perfectly cicatrizing over, then to undertake the treatment of the malignant ulcer, as has been said before. And the spleen too, when it is in a bad condition, sometimes becomes the cause of such cacochymy (κεκοχυμίας, presumably for κακοχυμίας), just as the liver does also; having first made provision for these, one should in this way undertake the cure of the ulcer.

And by the same reasoning, even if the whole body is cacochymous or plethoric, one must first purge it and evacuate it beforehand, before applying to the ulcer [669] a drug. And in the very course of treating the ulcer by means of the dry drugs, at each unbinding one must attend to the action that has been produced by it upon the part, knowing and remembering that those which dry without cleansing — and such are those in which the astringent quality prevails — do not render the ulcer clean; whereas those which, in addition to drying, also possess the power of cleansing, render the whole ulcerated part not only dry but also clean. One must also know that clean ulcers are bitten by drugs by which they were previously not bitten at all, when they were foul. One must therefore pass from the drugs that cleanse more strongly to what is milder and less biting, at whatever moment the ulcer is found to be perfectly clean, just as, conversely, in the case of foul ulcers, one must return to the more cleansing drugs — unless it appeared foul because of having been bitten.

For this has sometimes deceived even physicians who are reputed to be good, so that they passed over to another drug, more detergent and more acrid, by which the ulcer, being eroded again, [670] appeared at the next undoing of the dressing equally foul or even more so, the flesh that had been melted down by the drug fouling it. For the flesh that is being melted down is dissolved into vicious ichors, and of these, whatever is more fine-particled in its consistency is dispersed by the drug, while the remainder, congealing there around the ulcers, becomes filth for them. One must therefore attend to whether the ulcer became foul because the underlying flesh was being eroded and melted down, or because it needed a drug that removes the filth, while the one applied was not of that kind. The distinction is made by the fact that the ulcer has at the same time become hollower and has its lips reddish and hotter, whenever it is being fouled by the acridity of the drug. Now perhaps it would be superfluous, in the present treatise, to add a description of the manner of using the compound drugs; for it has been stated in the Therapeutic Method. But things that are necessary and that bring great harm if overlooked, it is better to say even twice and three times for the sake of reminding.

Let this, then, also be added to the account: in the treatment of such ulcers, if it should be [671] possible, without harm to the whole body, for the patient to go without bathing, being rubbed down with linen cloths for a longer time, and next with oil, and then exercising with jumping-weights (halteres) if the affected part is a leg, or by running if it is in the parts above. But if it is impossible for the patient to go without bathing without harm to the whole body, one must not undo the bandaging, but, having bathed just as he has been bandaged, and having squeezed out the hot water of the sponge, one should at once pour on other, cold, water, so that no heat is left behind in the bandaging. And if the treatment should appear to be progressing, he may also be treated without the bandaging of a sponge, the moist phoinikine being applied externally, as has been said, and, without the application of a sponge, being secured with bandages wound around the part of the body being treated in the manner of a fracture. [Composition of plaster-like drugs.] Since the chief point of the treatment of malignant ulcers and those hard to cicatrize lies in the drug's drying without biting, and water and oil moisten most of all things.

[672] one must abstain from these, so as neither to apply them by themselves nor to mix them into the dry drugs that have been mentioned. One must therefore select a wax that is neither dry by nature nor has come to this condition through age, but fresh and oily by nature, which one will be able, by softening it in the sun, to make take up into itself some of the aforementioned dry drugs. If there is no sun, let it be softened by being warmed at a fire and by being let down into hot water. For the water is not mixed in throughout, but flows off quickly as the wax is softened, before it is applied to the ulcer. The proportion of the mixture is as follows. If one wishes the drug to be moderate, let him add to the wax a fourth part of the metallic substances; it will be stronger if a third is mixed in. And since the metallic substances themselves are to a lesser and a greater degree both non-biting and drying, the power will be intensified in the more drying ones and will be relaxed in those that dry less; just as, again, the use will be safer through the less biting ones and more hazardous through the more biting ones.

For it has often been said that some natures of bodies have both the skin and the flesh more sensitive, [673] while in some both of these are less sensitive. And in proportion to the greater and lesser degree of sensation, the affection of pain too follows to a greater and lesser degree, as indeed does that of inflammation; and there is no small difference also according to whether the body is soft-fleshed or harder, euchymous or cacochymous, or plethoric or empty or disposed in an intermediate manner among the conditions mentioned. It is not possible, then, to prepare one drug suitable for all human beings. But whichever of the drugs of the same kind has been prepared, it is fitting that one who has been trained according to the Method taught in this treatise should know how to use it; as, for instance, straightaway in the case of the material before us: if you mix an equal amount of each, of verdigris and of burnt copper, and half of one part of split alum, so that the whole made up from the three comes to either two and a half drachms or that many ounces, it will suffice to mix ten drachms of wax with the drachms, and ten ounces with the ounces, for the composition of a drug moderate and intermediate in power.

But it will be better and at the same time less biting if it takes diphryges instead of the split alum; and if a whole drachm of this is put in, just as of the [674] burnt copper and the verdigris, the drug will be finer. But if, suspecting the bitingness that comes from the verdigris, we should wish it to become completely non-biting, one must put in the verdigris burnt. And if we wish it also to remove filth, half a drachm of scale of copper must be added, so that the whole proportion becomes as follows. Take burnt copper and burnt verdigris and diphryges, an equal amount of each, that is one drachm apiece, and of scale of copper half a drachm; and let these be taken up in the fatty wax as it is being softened, as has been said before. But if it is drier than is needed for it to receive the things mentioned, one must, while softening it, mix in myrtle oil or quince oil or mastic oil or castor oil or henna oil or old oil of unripe olives (omotribes) or the fresh Spanish oil or the oil prepared among us with olive shoots. But if we should wish not to add anything oily at all to the drug, one must mix in some larch resin. And if we do not have this at hand, terebinth resin must be used in its place.

And those who read these things must always bear this too in mind: to resort first and foremost to what was mentioned first as best, [675] after that to the second and the third, and in succession to the others after the third, since we employ the order of the discourse in proportion to the excellence and power of the drugs. Someone, then, who has heard these things beforehand and knows the powers of the simple drugs will be competent to judge all the drugs that were written by those before us against malignant ulcers, as, for instance, straightaway Asclepiades, surnamed Pharmakion, wrote in the third book of his External Remedies as follows. [On the drugs written by Asclepiades.] A well-tested drug for chironian and hard-to-heal ulcers. Take: flake of copper, one ounce; scraped verdigris, one ounce; wax, half a litra; larch resin, one and a half ounces. Pour the melted ingredients over the dry ones, and, having taken it up, use it, softening it carefully and laying a flat plaster (platysmation) upon the affected part alone, so that it covers only the ulcer. The surrounding parts must be covered with a drug that keeps off inflammation.

In the treatment one should unbind the ulcer every third day, then foment it beforehand and, [676] washing off the same flat plaster, soften it and apply it again, until (ἔα; ἂν, apparently for ἕως ἂν) it begins cicatrization. This is the written prescription of the drug, and he rightly added to it "for Chironian ulcers"; for they call thus those ulcers that are not moderately malignant, but very extremely so. This drug is strong, inasmuch as it contains the metallic ingredients at a third part of the wax—the verdigris being the stronger drug, and the scale of copper much more moderate than the verdigris, yet strong too in itself. But if it were to have a proportioned mixture so as to treat also the moderately malignant ulcers, the wax would have been mixed with the other ingredients not threefold but fourfold; and it would be still more moderate if fivefold, so as to treat also those ulcers that are not yet malignant but are otherwise difficult to cicatrize. Just as, too, if one were to make the wax sixfold the metallic ingredients, so that there is one drachm of each, the verdigris and the scale, and twelve drachms of wax, and the proportionate amount of the larch resin. And it will be proportionate if there are three drachms of it.

But since the wax is fatty, even if less of the resin is put in, the drug will have sufficient consistency [677]. For in drugs of this kind the resin is put in for the sake of the consistency, just as indeed the myrtle oil or the mastic oil is too. I myself once also mixed in Attic oesypum while softening the wax, and in use the drug appeared to me to fall short either not at all or only very slightly of those prepared without these. It is quite evident that I say these things with regard to the vigour of the drug that will result; for the matter of benefit lies in relation to something, since the softer drug is able to suit the more moderate of the malignant ulcers more than the more vehement one. At any rate, where the ulcer itself is less malignant but its lips are callous and raised, the oesypum is better in these cases. A good drug for these is also the marrow of the deer and of the calf, which one must first triturate and mix with the wax beforehand, and then, once they have been united in this way, take up with them the metallic substances, previously triturated until they become fine as dust; for such things are biting. And let all the drugs that are dry and earthy in consistency be sufficiently triturated beforehand, such as oak-gall, the pomegranate flowers (kytinoi), the pomegranate rinds, and the fruit of the Egyptian thorn (akantha).

For indeed all such things are hard to triturate, [678] just as those made from dried juices or saps are easy to triturate — myrrh and aloe and acacia and all that are of the same genus as these. And Asclepiades rightly added, at the end of the written recipe of the aforesaid drug, in these very words: 'and undo these every third day and foment, and, having washed off the same small spread plaster, soften it and apply it again.' For unless the drug remains in contact with the skin for a longer time, it will accomplish nothing. This very point too has escaped most physicians, and they think that, if they wipe away the ichors of the ulcer three times a day, they are doing something better than those who wipe them away twice. And those who undo the dressing once a day the patients themselves often blame, as though they were being neglected. But it is fitting that you remember here too what has often been said by us in many of our treatises, that the qualities of all bodies that come into proximity act in some way upon one another, even if one of them is much the stronger. For indeed according to this principle they become in a way of the same kind with one another in the course of time, even if they differ very greatly.

And when the quality of the drug has become of like kind with the body being treated, the benefit [679] that follows is greater. For these reasons, then, the one who first thought of using the flat piece (platysma) that had been applied before would justly be praised, and it was fitting for us to follow him all the more, since we have also recognised that this idea is attested by experience. And reasonably he also orders that it be fomented every third day—that is, evidently, at each unbinding—for since the drug is strong, it naturally requires soothing. It is better, therefore, in cases that are not very malignant, that the wax be fourfold or fivefold of both the metallic substances taken together. Next after the drug written above Asclepiades has written another drug having the following composition: Take verdigris, 2 ounces; scale, 2 ounces; diphryges, 1 ounce; wax, 1 pound; larch resin, 3 ounces. This proportion of the simple drugs is again the same as the previous one, exceeding it only in the diphryges; at any rate all the other items are double those before. For in that recipe he put in 1 ounce each of verdigris and scale, and the wax threefold of both of them together, if indeed he required six ounces of it in all

he thought it right to put in of it; the resin, however, [680] at half an ounce beyond each of the metallic ingredients. In the second recipe, of this (the resin) he orders three ounces to be put in instead of one and a half, and of the metallic ingredients two instead of one ounce of each, and a litra of wax, whereas in the former recipe he put in half a litra. It is quite evident, then, that in the second he added only the diphryges, and since he orders an ounce of it to be put in in proportion to the doubled quantities of the others, if someone, mixing in single amounts all the ingredients of the former recipe, adds half an ounce of diphryges to them, he will make the composition of the drug as follows: take scale, 1 ounce; verdigris, 1 ounce; wax, half a litra; larch resin, one ounce and a half; diphryges, half an ounce. This too comes out the same as the former in every respect, except for the diphryges. Diphryges is a drug so moderate that even sprinkled on by itself it heals those ulcers that are hard to cicatrize; and burnt copper is similar to it. But verdigris is considerably stronger, so that it has fallen outside the range of treating even the very foul and moist ulcers, if one should sprinkle it on by itself; for it erodes and bites violently.

But in the case of Chironian ulcers, when it has been mixed with the other [681] drugs, it is itself so far released from the vehemence of its power, while it increases that of those others, that the drug compounded from all of them becomes a most excellent one. And by the same reasoning by which verdigris has been mixed with the drugs mentioned, unslaked lime too, small in proportion, has been added by some to many drugs. Slaked lime, on the other hand, is a moderate drug, and if it is also washed, it is altogether non-biting. This plaster, then, I have set down for the sake of an example, because I think it right that the young should exercise themselves on particulars and not be content with universals alone. But bringing the discourse back again to its beginning, I shall pass over to the plasters written by Andromachus. [On the plasters written by Andromachus for malignant ulcers.] I shall set out, then, for the sake of example, all those compound drugs which have been judged by experience to be suited to malignant ulcers, making my beginning from those written by Andromachus. One might, however, find fault with him for having written out the drugs without distinction.

For since this has been omitted, it comes about that most physicians use them [682] badly, and for this reason at times hit the mark wonderfully, while at other times they also fail, falling very far short. Although, then, he ought to have said that this particular one is strongest, and again another more moderate than this, and this one weakest, Andromachus wrote them all in sequence, adding no distinction. At any rate he begins these very ones having prefixed the heading 'cicatrizing (plasters)'; and after this heading he writes next: ♃ roasted cadmia 1 pound, burnt chalcitis 1 pound, wax 4 pounds, dry resin 3 pounds, myrtle oil 3 pounds; wine for the dry ingredients. After these he writes verbatim as follows: 'the one through ladanum'. And having added the proportions, he wrote again next: 'otherwise, as Alcimion (has it)'. Then here too, having written the proportions of the simple drugs, he adds, saying: 'the one through barley'. And after compounding this he again wrote thus: 'another cicatrizing (plaster). ♃ dry resin 18 drachms, diphryges 4 drachms, litharge 16 drachms, wax 10 drachms, oil 4 cotylae'; so that this drug is the sixth from the beginning in his list.

And after it again he writes six [683] others, prefixing to each the word "another," evidently bidding us to understand in addition the word "cicatrizing." Now five of them belong to the customary cicatrizing drugs, neither for ulcers that are hard to cicatrize nor for malignant ones, while the sixth belongs to those for ulcers hard to cicatrize, though not yet indeed to those for malignant ones. But the prescriptions of the remaining six drugs are suited to malignant ulcers, differing from one another in strength; and for these one of two things was required: either, making his teaching rational and methodical, to have written in addition the difference according to intensity, so that we would understand that on the more malignant ulcers the stronger drugs are to be used, and on the mildest the weaker; or, in the manner of the Empiricists, to write that for phagedaenic ulcers, and in general for those being eaten away and spreading, such-and-such of the drugs are suitable, for hollow ones such-and-such, and for the considerably sordid ones these, and for those accompanied by an inflammatory or scirrhous condition, or where the lips of the ulcer are hard or bank-like (ὀχθωδῶν) or black or have some other colour, the drugs proper to each.

Of these things he did none; instead he wrote, one after another, [684] six cicatrizing preparations, whose composition I shall state together with the appropriate distinctions. Now the first one written by him, the seventh from the beginning, is quite strong, inasmuch as it received an equal bulk of verdigris and of scale; but the admixture of wax has relaxed and diminished its strength, being eightfold of either and fourfold of both together. For he bids one mix an ounce of each of the verdigris and the scale, and eight ounces of wax, the composer of it having very properly guarded against mixing in any of the emollient things—I mean oil and fat, oesypum, butter and resin. But if the wax is not oily, it will hold the metallic substances hard to mix, and even if we force their mixture, doing it either beside a fire or in hot sun, a little later the drug will be hard, so that when it is applied to the ulcer the patient will think he is touching a hard hide of his own.

For all such drugs have the following manner of use: in which (ἢν) one, having also warmed one's hands, takes up from them a mass of such a size as, when softened and flattened out, will be laid over the whole of the ulcer, [685] so as to cover the lips as well. And when it is deep, the whole of its hollow is filled up in addition, the drug being inserted into it. And after this another flat piece (platysma) is laid on in turn, encompassing the lips too. And then upon this in turn a linen cloth soaked in cold water is laid over the whole, of such a size as to cover the drug; then, on the outside, a soft sponge, secured by a bandage of linen cloth wound once or twice in a circle around the affected part, of such a width that the whole ulcer is encompassed together with the lips, and also something of the parts lying above and below them; and let the bandaging be done 'from two heads'—they call it so when the whole middle of the band is laid upon the affected place, and each of the heads is drawn away toward the opposite side.

Then, if the linen bandage is strong enough to hold the sponge securely with a single turn, it will be sewn together there at its ends, the excess being cut away with scissors; but if it is weak, each of the heads will be brought once more over the affected part, drawn with equal tension—which is among the things most to be observed both in the first turn [686] and no less also in the second. Nor indeed should you forget that which Hippocrates, the first of those we know, discovered, a point in which error was formerly made by all before him and is now made by (ὑπὲρ) those who have not learned the art in the proper manner. For they think it better to keep the ulcerated part free from pressure and to wrap the bandage around on either side of it—and how harmful this is was shown by Hippocrates. So when these things have been done by you on the first day, on the second soak the sponge thoroughly, pouring cold water over it. If the surrounding air is hot and dry, this must be done even twice and three times a day, and the bandage must be undone every third day; but if it is winter, every fourth day. One must examine the alteration that has come about from the drug around the affected place, both in the cavity of the ulcer and at the lips, and indeed round about them. And let the examination be made by you on the basis of what you learned in the treatises On Temperaments; these ulcers have also been discussed in the Method of Healing.

For it has appeared either drier or moister or hotter [687] or colder than before, both the affected part as a whole and each of its parts. And in addition to these things it is fitting to examine whether some of the lips has been reduced, or has been somehow softened, or has been thinned, and concerning the change in colour and concerning the quantity of the sordes. For from these you will know whether it is fitting to apply a stronger or a milder drug, or the same as the first. And you will also be able easily to alter the first one itself: if you wish to make it milder, by mixing in, while kneading it, a little of one of the astringent oils, either myrtle oil or rose-oil or quince oil or lentisk oil or mastic oil or henna oil; but if stronger, either some of the scale or of the verdigris—for let a little of each of these be prepared for you, ground perfectly fine, so that you may add it while kneading. And I, as you know, also sprinkle in addition some one of the mild drugs upon the ulcer, and over it apply the first drug, the plaster-like one. It is quite evident that by mild drugs I mean diphryges, sarcocolla, burnt chalcitis, and likewise also copper and burnt verdigris and chalcanthum.

For all these are acrid when unburnt, but when burnt [688] they are moderate, and when washed after the burning they become non-biting. It is better also to remodel the plaster itself, as has been said, by admixture, and to apply one of the other drugs which Andromachus mentioned next in succession, looking not only at the powers of the ingredients being mixed but also at their quantities, as in the case of the very one just now mentioned. For the wax is mixed in fourfold quantity relative to both together, the verdigris and the scale of copper. So if it is mixed in threefold quantity it will make it stronger, just as, if fivefold, weaker. One must therefore proceed in this way in the case of the others too, for example in the case of the one written after the aforementioned drug, the eighth in the following order, which has this proportion: Take of chrysocolla 2 drachms, of scale 2 drachms, of wax 6 drachms, of diphryges 2 drachms, of litharge 8 drachms, of rose-oil or myrtle-oil a little. In this drug chrysocolla and diphryges, by themselves alone, when sprinkled on, are sufficient to treat malignant ulcers.

But the scale is a stronger, more roughening and more biting drug, and for this reason the man who composed the drug mixed in litharge, viewing with suspicion [689] the violent character of the scale and wishing to relax it by the admixture of the softer drug. And if someone were to mix the four without wax according to the stated proportion, he will have a dry drug for sprinkling on, not ignoble for the cure of malignant ulcers. But if you wish to make a plaster, it is necessary to mix in the wax as well. And on account of the quantity of the metallic substances Andromachus of necessity also made mention of the liquids in the formula before us, both rose oil and myrtle oil. For the wax is very small in amount relative to the quantity of the metallic substances. Where, then, he orders that chrysocolla, scale and diphryges be mixed in, two drachmas each of those mentioned, and eight of litharge, making fourteen in all, evidently, he needed either to mix in a very great deal of fatty wax or to add to the drug something of the oily substances. In the previously mentioned drug, however, the wax was four times the metallic substances. It is therefore possible for us, having removed the litharge, to compound the drug from the others, as I myself once did. For if someone does this, he will not need the myrtle oil, provided, as I said, that the wax is fatty.

But if it should be [690] hard, it will be necessary to add something of the liquids as well. For this reason, then, some seem to me to have added such specifications to the wax in drugs of this sort too, some writing "new" wax and others "fresh," not, by Zeus, because they require its age, as in the case of other drugs, but its moistness. For new wax is indeed really better, but not to such a degree that one should already avoid that of two or three years. It is now time to go on to the plaster written next after this one, which runs thus. Rx: diphryges, 84 drachms; litharge, 240 drachms; wax, 318 drachms; oil, 6 kotylai. This drug would be cicatrizing, for ulcers that are not yet malignant but already hard to cicatrize. For it dries, but not strongly, as does the one written after it; nor indeed is it fitting to prepare it in so large a proportion. For this is the same as it: Rx: diphryges, 14 drachms; litharge, 40 drachms; wax, 53 drachms; myrtle oil, 10 ounces. For the quantities written by Andromachus are six times these. This one, then, is truly cicatrizing, similar to the one made with cadmia and to the one called "sweet," about which an account will be given in the following book.

But the one written after [691] it is stronger, yet not close to the first of these six, which is seventh from the very beginning, into which he mixed both scale of copper and verdigris with a fourfold amount of wax. For, mixing in addition to these sixteen drachms of diphryges, he adds forty-eight drachms of litharge and sixty-six of wax; then, because of the quantity of these, he was compelled to mix with them one and a half cotylae of myrtle oil. Let this too, accordingly, be counted by us among the cicatrizing drugs. And the one after it is of the same kind, but quite mild and non-biting, composed of burnt and washed lead, spodion, cadmia, diphryges and terebinth. He says that Zeno also mixes galbanum into it, which to me appears superfluous for the purposes at hand. At any rate he writes its proportion as follows: Take of washed lead 2 drachms, of spodion 4 drachms, and likewise of cadmia 4 drachms, of diphryges 1, or 4; and he takes them up with 6 drachms of terebinth. And he says that Zeno mixes in half a drachm of galbanum, or, according to another reading, 4.

If [he mixed it in] with a view to softening the callous and hard lips, which for this reason are called [692] by some 'bank-like' (ὀχθώδη), he mixes it in rightly; but if with a view to the malignancy of the ulcer, not correctly. And even if it does not take galbanum in addition, even so it falls short of the strength [required] for malignant ulcers. It is therefore more plausible that he wrote these twelve drugs one after another as cicatrizing ones. For with the exception of two among them, the one that is seventh in order from the beginning and the one after it, all the rest are curative of ulcers that are difficult to cicatrize, but no longer of malignant ones. For indeed the twelfth after them is likewise cicatrizing, but too weak to treat malignant ulcers. The composition of this one too is of the following sort. ℞ molybdaena 100 dr., diphryges 16 dr., sory 10 dr., roasted Cyprian misy 8 dr., terebinth resin 8 dr., wax 40 dr., myrtle oil 40 dr. One should compound all drugs of this kind in a smaller proportion having the same ratio as this one, since you know that they quickly become hard and stony. It is therefore better to prepare only so much of each as there is need of.

and especially if winter follows upon the time of their use [693]. If you take a fourth part of each of the ingredients mentioned, there will be twenty-five drachms of molybdaena, four of diphryges, two and a half of sory, two of roasted misy, and of terebinth 9 drachms (otherwise 2), and of wax and myrtle oil an equal amount of each, 10 drachms, both together obviously making up the twenty. In the case of all such drugs, melt the meltable ingredients and cool them, then scrape them and mix them with the dry ingredients, which have been thoroughly triturated. For if you pour the melted ingredients over them, it often happens that enkerides (lumps of wax) are formed, and especially when it is cold. But if you make the mixture in a hot sun, it is also possible to pour them over while stirring vigorously, at first with the spathe, and a little later with the pestle. In all such cases it is better that the spathe be a branch of palm. These, then, are the twelve drugs which Andromachus wrote down, as I said, without distinction, having prefixed to them in common only this, that they are cicatrizing. But I have explained the difference between them clearly, as I think, in a way capable of guiding an intelligent man to their skilful use in particular cases.

Apart from [694] these, he also mentioned other polychrēsta (drugs of many uses), which, just as they are suitable for many other conditions, are so also for that of ulcers hard to cicatrize; these I too shall mention in the following book, where I go through the polychrēsta. But at present my account concerns those that are specifically suited to malignant ulcers and those hard to cicatrize—and rather indeed the malignant ones, which some also call Chironian, as does Andromachus himself.
