At any rate, next after the twelve drugs of which I have just now finished speaking, having written two for carbuncles (anthrakes) and one for herpetes, after these three he wrote another, a fourth, in these words: "Cicatrizing [plaster] for Chironian ulcers, of Dioscorides," having compounded a drug more varied (ποικιλώτερον; the text reads πσικιλώτερον), but not stronger, than the one written before, in which he mixed in the wax at four times the amount of both together, the scale (lepis) and the verdigris (ios). In the one now before us, having put in the wax in a smaller quantity than the proportion of the metallic ingredients, he orders it to be melted with a little myrtle oil or rose oil, without adding the quantity of these.

I shall now set down the whole of it according to the wording of Andromachus. [695] Cicatrizing remedy of Dioscorides for the chironian ulcers. Take chrysocolla, 2 drachms; scraped verdigris, 2 drachms; scale, 2 drachms; wax, 6 drachms; diphryges, 2 drachms; litharge, 8 drachms; a little rose-oil or myrtle-oil, enough for melting. This drug is exactly the same as the one written earlier, which, among the twelve cicatrizing drugs, comes in order after the one made from scale and verdigris, the eighth among them, as I said; it surpasses that one in a single thing only, the verdigris, and for this reason he wrote that one among the cicatrizing drugs, whereas for this one he made a greater promise, saying that it is suitable for the chironian ulcers. And indeed at this point too he mentions a most excellent drug, writing as follows. Cicatrizing remedy from the writings of Primion, for desperate cases. He intends the term 'desperate' to signify those ulcers which many, having striven to treat, did not attain their end, but abandoned as incurable. One should have confidence in this drug, which, among other things, has been tested by experience. He writes its composition thus: Take sory, 24 drachms.

of split alum [696] 16 drachms, of pomegranate rinds 16 drachms, of quicklime 16 drachms, of frankincense 32 drachms, of oak-gall 32 drachms, of wax 120 drachms, of calf's fat 160 drachms, of old oil 1 kotyle. This, then, is the proportion of the simple drugs that are mixed together for the preparation of the compound in question. But how one ought to prepare it he omitted, just as also in the case of many others that require an account of their preparation. For in the case of this one it is in fact quite easy, as will be stated a little later. But I want you to know before all else that if calf's fat should at some time not be at hand, one should mix in its place old pig's fat, which they call axoungion. This must be unsalted and not of very many years. Now old oil too is sufficiently discutient, and so too is the fat, both of them doing this without biting. Ox fat is similarly discutient, but not similarly non-biting. Calf's fat lies between both of them: by as much as it is more acrid than pig's fat, by so much is it milder than ox fat.

The drug, then, about which it is proposed to speak, has as its strongest ingredients sory and split alum and [697] pomegranate rinds and oak-gall, which however do not have a vigorous dispersive power, but the so-called astringent one. It is quite clear that one should always put in the oak-gall called omphakitis, and the alum that is Egyptian and split. If we should be without it, then the round kind, which is coarser in its parts than the split but no less astringent. That the rinds of the pomegranate are called sidia everyone knows. Yet the season of their prime is short-lived, if one wishes to pound and grind them dry. For together with their drying out, the pomegranate rinds also have a weaker power, which is lost along with their moisture as it is dispersed. It is safer, therefore, to take them while still full of juice and boil them beforehand in wine until they become easy to grind. The wine must by all means be austere, but neither too young—for austere wines are coarse in their parts before they have aged—nor too old, so that it has already become pungent. For the young wine does not penetrate into the depth of the body, while the old is pungent and biting. Better, therefore, is the one intermediate in age. This would be, for the most part, between the five-year-old and the ten-year-old.

[698] It is necessary now too to recall what has often been said to many people concerning austere and harsh wines, foods and drugs, and in general astringent ones, and, before that, concerning what is signified by the terms just mentioned. For by the word 'austere' is signified, among the Greeks, that which is moderately astringent, and by 'harsh' that which is violently and intensely so. The genus common to both is indicated by the name 'astringency', without its being further specified whether it is intense or faint. All astringent things, then, draw together and condense the pores, and bind and constrict the substance of the parts that come into contact with them. But they do this to a lesser or greater degree in proportion to the amount of astringency. And in the constricting and condensing of the surface of the body being astringed, the power of the astringents is shut out and prevented from proceeding to the depth. For this reason some physicians have rightly devised the mixing with such drugs of others that are fine-parted and possess a sharp power, in order that through these the powers of the astringents may be conducted, under their guidance, into the depth of the body.

Having understood this very point, then, the one who composed the [699] drug before us mixed unslaked lime into it. In the book of Andromachus, however, the designation 'lime' has been omitted, and only the word 'unslaked' is written, physicians expressing many other things too in this way for the sake of brevity of expression. Thus, to take an immediate example, in these very drugs which they have composed for ulcers hard to cicatrize and malignant ones, when 'scale' is written simply, without 'of copper' being added, and 'split' without 'alum', and 'terebinth' without 'resin' being added, we supply in thought for them the words omitted in the expression in this way, just as now too, in the case of 'unslaked', we supply 'lime'. For they call this alone, par excellence, both 'slaked' and 'unslaked', although the designation befits no less all the other things that are burned. So the one who composed this plaster, by mixing unslaked lime with the harshly astringent drugs, made the compound of all of them strong, so that its power reaches as far as the depth.

But since the composition had come to be made from the strongest drugs, and contained nothing assuaging or mitigating, nor [700] anything of the concocting material, he reasonably mixed into it a pus-producing drug, frankincense. Now if someone were going to use the compound dry, sprinkling it upon the ulcer, it would in that case be quite vehement and biting and roughening and corrosive. But since it was proposed to make it a plaster, it is clear that resin or wax had to be mixed in, or in addition to these fat or marrow, and, if it did not yet acquire a plaster-like consistency through these, to add some oil. And whenever I add the word 'some', you must understand, besides what is properly and simply called oil, also that which is named with an addition, rose-oil or myrtle oil or henna oil or something of that sort. For it has already often been distinguished in what respect saying 'rose unguent' differs from 'rose-oil', and 'henna unguent' from 'henna oil', and likewise for the others. Reasonably, then, the mixing of such drugs has not been the same for all who have composed such plasters. For that there are several causes of such a difference I have found not from speculation but from experience that has befallen me myself.

For sometimes I made haste to compound the drug from simples few in number, [701] sometimes from more, and there are times when I did so from very many or from all those of the same genus. And moreover, because I had some in abundance and others not at all or in very small quantity at that particular time, I turned to the composition of the drug from those I had, since the need was pressing; then, having found it approved by experience, I used it thus ever after. And often, deliberately setting out to make some of the compound drugs stronger and some weaker, so as to have drugs suited to a greater number of conditions, I made the compositions differ; and moreover also because the part that has the ulceration requires a greater number of powers, as when it is at once hollow and flabby and dirty, callous at its lips, and afflicted with flux from the parts lying above it. For if someone should wish to adapt himself to all the things that attend parts ulcerated in this way, it is necessary for him to mix materials of differing powers. But if he wishes to treat first some one thing, the one that is urgent, neglecting the others, it is not necessary to turn aside into a variety of drugs.

It is clear, then, that those before [702] me who composed such drugs also differed among themselves for the reasons stated above. For example, to take at once the drug now before us: the man who composed it chose calf's fat, since it is emollient of hardened lips. It was therefore going to furnish him a twofold use: the one, as something soft, for the uniting of the dry ingredients, which were the primarily beneficial ones; the other, so that it too might itself treat some one of the conditions that have befallen the affected part. Still more beneficially, however, would deer marrow be mixed in for hardened lips, or, if we did not have this, calf's. And if none of these were available, one of the liquid and non-acrid resins. For from the moistness, together with the viscosity, which all resins possess innately, there comes about a binding together of the dry drugs, while from their not being manifestly acrid comes the not irritating of the ulcer. Reasonably, then, some have mixed into such compositions of drugs either the terebinth resin or the resin called larch.

[705] Admirably, then, the one who composed it took on the one hand the astringent drugs, which possess a repelling power, so that nothing should flow to the affected part during the time of the cure, and on the other hand the discutient ones, for the sake of dispersing and evacuating the ichors contained in the affected part. As for their proportion, it stands thus. Of the split alum and the pomegranate rinds, since they are most vehemently astringent, he put in less, mixing sixteen drachms of each together into the same; but of sory half as much again as of each of these, that is twenty-four, since it is less astringent but no less drying; and an amount equal to both of them together, the split alum and the pomegranate rinds, he put in of oak-gall, adding two to the thirty drachms, so that the total from the drugs came to eighty-eight. Against these he set a strongly discutient and drying drug, quicklime, contenting himself with sixteen drachms, for these suffice to guide the power of the astringents.

At any rate, since one hundred and four drachmas had been gathered together from the metallic drugs, it would have been possible [706] to mix even more frankincense with them; and the drug would have become milder by just so much as more had been mixed in. But wishing to keep it strong, he mixed in less. You, however, may compound it in two ways. For after you have levigated the first five and mixed them all together, divide the resulting aggregate into two portions, and with the one portion mix sixteen drachmas of frankincense, with the other double that; then, having melted and cooled and scraped the cerate that results from the meltable drugs, and having divided this too in two, mix the one part with the one containing the greater amount of frankincense, and the other with the remaining one. And as regards the proportion of wax and fat, the first conjecture has sufficient latitude, since we do not know precisely what sort of thing the drug will be in its consistency. But after everything has been mixed it becomes clear whether it has turned out softer or harder than is proper, so that in the second composition we approach the conjecture more precisely, both of these very things and, along with them, of the oil.

For just as it is impossible to compound a drug without rational method, so without experience it is not [707] possible to know its power securely and accurately. Now this drug, Andromachus himself said, brings aid to those who have been despaired of. Next after it, having written something for paronychiae, after that he wrote again as follows, in these very words: "For malignant ulcers, in the case of Valeria Secunda." One must obviously supply in addition "I used." The material of the drug makes clear that it falls short of a treatment of the decisive (agonistic) sort, but that it is able to soothe the parts that have been exacerbated by the application of the decisive (agonistic) drugs. Its composition, then, is roughly as follows. Take of Tyrrhenian, 8 drachms — one must obviously understand "wax" — of bull's suet, 4 drachms; of terebinth, 4 drachms; of burnt lead, 4 drachms. Use it on a lint pledget (emmoton). This is what he wrote, in his very words. But he did badly in neither indicating for which malignant ulcers he says it is suitable, nor adding whether it is decisive (agonistic) or soothing. For soothing drugs are a different class: some of them also benefit the conditions a little, and some even harm them a little.

and some neither benefiting nor harming, but only soothing the pains; about these it will be spoken again [708], and many such remedies, put to the test through long experience, will be written down. And some indeed have been so marvellously well hit upon in their proportions as to benefit in every case, and sometimes even to cure, by themselves alone, the conditions of what one might call wild ulcers. But of the material of those remedies, the Tyrrhenian wax and the burnt lead do belong, though not the terebinth resin and the bull's suet; but, as I said, the account of such ulcers and drugs, being a separate one, awaits us later. For now, it is proposed to go through the hard-to-heal or Chironian ulcers, or however one may wish to name them, among which remedies are also these written in the fourth book of Criton, being five in all. [On those written by Criton: the remedy made with ladanum.] The remedy made with ladanum: a most excellent cicatrizing remedy, suitable for ulcers with raised, callous edges and for hollow ones. It must be kept unloosened for four days. Take: dry pitch, 100 drachms; scraped verdigris, 24 drachms; burnt copper, 15 drachms.

of red scale, 24 drachms; [709] of ladanum, 9 ounces; of litharge, 3 pounds; of oil, 1½ xestai; of good wine, 1½ xestai. This plaster I too have prepared, having approved its material, since it contains nothing of a soft nature (μαλθακῶδες). For this is how Hippocrates names the whole class of drugs that possess an innate moisture, such as fat is, and all the oily drugs, and obviously oil itself and water. Resin and wax too have something of the soft in them. In the middle between them—I mean between those that are dry in their mixture and the soft ones—stands pitch. And for this reason it is mixed with both classes without harm, just as litharge is too, and all the other drugs that lie about the middle mixture, even if at times they deviate slightly toward either one of the two excesses.

Pitch too is among such things, at least with respect to the opposition of drying and moistening, since it has already clearly departed from the intermediate drugs, but with respect to the other opposition, that of heating and cooling drugs, not yet; for it heats moderately, and for this reason it is also mixed with the drugs that bring things to suppuration, so that in the drug under discussion the dry [710] pitch is among the intermediate ones, and litharge still more so, and the others are among the drying drugs. But since a misunderstanding can arise here too, I shall discuss it, having first recalled a theorem useful for many purposes, which has been stated by me in other treatises as well, but has been sufficiently worked out in the treatise on simple drugs and in that of the therapeutic method. For we call a drug hot and cold, moist and dry, whichever is able to heat or cool or dry or moisten the human body, making our reference to the best temperament in a human being. And this is a kind of mean among the blameworthy temperaments, which for this very reason we call hot or cold or moist or dry, naming them derivatively from what predominates in them, whether you wish to call it quality or power or substance or temperament. And by the same reasoning, not even if you should wish to call the whole temperament by a name derived from the element that is in excess in the mixture will you impede the scientific knowledge of the matters.

For it has been shown in the therapeutic treatise that the discovery of remedies comes about through indication, [711] from the affections themselves, of the mixture contrary to them, and from the nature of each animal as a whole, and again in turn of each individual part, of the mixture that is proper and similar to it; so that even if someone has a simple hollow ulcer, the treatment will come about from drugs that are the same in kind, but which have no small difference in their particular species. And for this reason it was shown that, of ulcers that are indistinguishably alike, some are treated by drugs that dry sufficiently—root of panax, aristolochia, akoron and iris—while some are treated by frankincense alone, even though it does not produce flesh but rather brings to suppuration those natures in which aristolochia produces flesh. And just as in the bodies being treated the difference in particular cases is very great, so it is in the same way with ulcers. For a simple ulcer that is hollow and clean is treated by drugs that dry moderately, whereas one that is foul and malignant, raised like a bank at its lips but flabby in the flesh beneath the skin, requires drugs that dry most vehemently.

In the case of these ulcers, then, since the discussion concerns these as well, frankincense [712] is so weak a drug that it cannot even bring about suppuration. Litharge is stronger than this, but it too is still below the middle ones. Dry pitch is among the middle ones, just as burnt copper, chrysocolla and diphryges are above it in respect of drying. Burnt chalkitis, verdigris, misy, chalcanthum and scale of copper dry manifestly, and, in the other manner, all the astringent substances: oak-gall, omphakitis, pomegranate rinds, alum. Before being burnt, chalkitis, verdigris, misy and quicklime are corrosive. Now those which have the strongest powers seem to display the same activity upon all bodies, whereas the weak ones show the difference clearly; but if you pay attention there will appear no less, in the strong drugs too, a considerable difference in the activity which they produce upon soft and upon hard bodies; for they take hold of soft bodies more quickly, distress them more violently, and arouse greater inflammations.

Since, then, these things have been said by me usefully not only for the present matters but also for many others in this treatise, [713] I shall return again to the drug under discussion, in which I said that 100 drachms of dry pitch had been written by Criton, and 3 litrae of litharge—neither of them being able, from its own proper power, to heal a malignant ulcer, but having reasonably been mixed with the beneficial ingredients so that the drug being compounded might become a plaster. Their quantity, taken by a conjecture grounded in art, came out at the weight mentioned just now, the compounder taking care neither to mix so little of each with the strong drugs that the biting and corrosive ones became painful to those being treated, nor so much in both bulk and weight as to dissolve their power; for the scale of copper dries and cleanses strongly, and verdigris still more than it, and it does both these things and also eats through the flesh. Burnt copper, however, needs neither to be intensified by anything nor to be relaxed, being of moderate power for the present purposes. And it is evident that the measure of the oil was estimated both from the things mixed with it and from the quantity of the boiling.

For the metallic substances, when they are being prepared so as to dry without biting, require to be boiled for a longer time. [714] And for this reason Criton also added the boiling for them, writing somewhat as follows, in these very words: boil litharge and oil until it thickens to some degree, then the scale of copper and the verdigris until it thickens and becomes of good colour, then add the pitch, then, having cooled it, the ladanum made smooth with wine, taking care that it does not boil over when this is thrown in; then, having united them over a gentle fire, pour it out and knead it. This, then, is the written prescription for the boiling. But it is also possible, having added more oil, to boil for a longer time, first the litharge, and then the verdigris, the scale and the copper, thrown in upon it. For things boiled for a longer time acquire a twofold virtue, at least in the case of ulcers of this kind, becoming more drying and less biting. Concerning the other simple drugs, then, all those that are mentioned by Criton in the plaster before us, I have spoken in due measure.

But I have reserved the account of ladanum, namely that even on its own it suits ulcers hard to cicatrize when triturated with wine—not because it needs the power of wine, but because it is harder [715] than is suited to the plaster. But if one mixes oil with it and boils it, one blunts the power of the drug. And it is not so strong as to need to be blunted, as verdigris or chalcitis or scale or any such thing is, and for this reason it is softer. Such is the fresh ladanum, for it is most suitable for the cicatrization of ulcers hard to cicatrize. In Cyprus, at any rate, where it is produced in the greatest quantity, a certain physician, kneading it while it was still fresh and soft, applied it to such ulcers; and if it had hardened even a little, he carried out the softening with myrtle-oil, and when myrtle-oil was not available, with henna oil or rose-oil. Another drug, not long after this one, Criton wrote down in the fourth book in these very words, as follows. The plaster through chamaeleon, effective for the same things as the Tyrian. It is the most cicatrizing of ulcers hard to heal, callous and chronic. It also cures fissures in the anus and condylomata and indurations. Of litharge, 1 mina; of wax, half a mina; of verdigris, a quarter of a mina, and of chamaeleon an eighth; of oil, a mina.

Boil the oil and the litharge, stirring [716] with a spatula, until it thickens and takes on the colour of quince-yellow. When this has happened, sprinkle in the verdigris. Then add the wax, and having melted it carefully and taken it off the fire, sprinkle in the chamaeleon; when it has been united, pour it out into a mortar and, having kneaded it, take it up. This drug took chamaeleon, which is of the same power, in place of the ladanum; for both are cicatrizing for hard-to-heal ulcers. Their difference lies in the fact that that one contains burnt copper and contains no wax at all, whereas in this one there is wax, but no copper; and he did this reasonably. For in that one he made use of the ladanum, in place of wax, for the uniting of the moistureless drugs, whereas here, having nothing of that kind, he mixed in wax, which is a moderately emollient drug, but certainly not a cicatrizing one. It would have been possible here too for more oil to have been put in, as also old oil or castor oil. I myself, for such cases, also put in mastic oil, which partakes of several powers; for it has something emollient and discutient and astringent, all of which are needed by ulcers hard to cicatrize that are accompanied by hardness of the lips.

[717] [On what was written by Heraclides.] It is now time, then, to mention also what was written by Heraclides of Tarentum in his book addressed to Astydamas. For he is a trustworthy man if anyone is, writing only those things that have been judged by him through experience. This man, then, wrote word for word as follows: For old ulcers. Of scale, one part; of scraped verdigris, four parts. It is taken up with eightfold myrtle cerate. Now Heraclides, as one writing memoranda for physicians, added: take it up with myrtle cerate. But many of the physicians of today are so bold that, before acquiring from teachers any medical competence, they set out from such books to use good drugs unmethodically, and for this reason often fail. For example, it is possible, by mixing in less or more of the myrtle cerate, at one time to use the drug moister and softer, at another harder and drier—at the first application by a broad conjecture, as was said before, but in the second use arriving closer to the mark, as was shown.

[718] For, looking at the ulcer, if it has been insufficiently dried, we shall make the drug more vigorous, so that it dries more; but if it has been dried more than it should, we shall make it softer by mixing in more of the myrtle cerate. For the power of the metallic substances is relaxed not only by this one but by every cerate. Next after this, having added the word "another"—one must obviously understand "power" in addition—he appended the following: Having ground scale of copper fine, pour vinegar over it and triturate it under the Dog-star, making it the thickness of honey, or boil it. And when it has become dry, grind it further and mix in eight parts of cerate, and use it for fresh wounds and old ulcers and abrasions and chafings and chilblains that are not excessively ulcerous. You must know the following also concerning this drug: for the other conditions one may, with moderation, mix eightfold cerate with the scale; but for the very old ones, that is the hard-to-heal ones, even if you mix in sixfold or fivefold, you will do no harm, for they need stronger ones. Heracleides wrote the account of the drug thus: it is also possible to use the scale after having dried it out over a fire.

His statement [719] means that, even if we compound the drug at some other season, we may use fire in place of the heat of the sun. All such preparations, however, turn out better when triturated over many days in the summer sun, some with wine, others with vinegar. Those triturated with vinegar, then, become finer in their parts, and for this reason more reducing, more attenuating and more drying. For cicatrization, however, those triturated with wine are better, and need of these arises when ulcers hard to cicatrize have first been dried and then first been cleansed. They will be dried beforehand, then, by means of the strongly drying agents, cleansed by means of the detergent agents, and cicatrized (ἀπολωθήσεται) by means of the astringent ones. Another. Next Heraclides wrote another drug, made from the same material but not strong, because he mixed a large quantity of litharge with the diphryges. For he directs that thirty-five drachms of litharge be put into it, but eight of diphryges. And these he takes up with a cerate containing forty drachms of wax and three cotylae of oil.

I myself have often used diphryges alone with such a [720] cerate — not, however, even this for phagedaenic, Chironian and putrefactive ulcers, for it falls far short in power of the drugs that treat such conditions, but in cases of ulcers difficult to cicatrize that are without great malignancy; so that if one also mixes litharge with it, and that in large quantity, he will make the drug weak. After this there is written, next in order, a drug of the same profession, as follows. Take wax, 12 drachmas; terebinth resin, 3 drachmas; scale, 4 drachmas; ladanum, 4 drachmas; asphalt, 3 drachmas. Grind the ladanum separately, and the scale; then melt the others with myrtle oil and mix. But if the ladanum is soft, melt it. In this recipe Heracleides clearly indicated that, when the ladanum is hard, one should triturate it by itself in the mortar, but when it is moist and soft, one should melt it over a fire, either alone or with a little oil — which you have seen me always doing, not only with this, but also with ammoniac incense. The drug written after this by the Tarentine is also of the same profession, in the following proportion. Take chalcitis, 25 drachmas.

[721] of cadmia, 12½ drachmas. Having ground them separately and having mixed in unadulterated wine (ἀπαράχυτος) and boiled it, pour it over, so that the mass is moistened in due measure; then grind until it is dried, and having melted 50 drachmas of wax, 30 drachmas of terebinth resin, 8 cotylae of myrtle oil, mix 20 drachmas of the dry ingredients with the cerate. And this drug too contains none of the emollient ingredients. In its mixture with the cerate, however, the man trained rationally in the methods I have laid down would suitably work out the quantity of the mixture appropriate for each of the ulcers. And rightly, too, he pours the unadulterated wine—that is, one with which seawater has not been mixed—hot over the chalcitis and the cadmia, wishing to remove the acridity of the chalcitis by means of its heat. Another noteworthy drug is written continuously after this one, composed of simples of the following number and kind: of scale of stomoma (hardened iron), 4 drachmas; of scraped verdigris, 2 drachmas—in some of the copies 1 drachma is written; of chrysocolla, 25 or 15 drachmas; of wax, 25 drachmas. In some copies, however, we found neither the wax nor the verdigris.

Having ground the other ingredients fine, [722] melt the wax with a little resin, so that the drug is not excessively hard, and having mixed them, use it; and on top apply a sponge wrung out of vinegar. Demetrius the Bithynian said that he used the chrysocolla itself, taking it up in very hot wax. Heraclides indicated in the case of this drug too that the resin is mixed into such drugs not for a primary use, but in order to supply them with a certain viscosity toward a plaster-like consistency, and especially when the wax is neither oily by nature nor fresh, but hard and parched. The scale of steel (stomōma), however, dries strongly, in addition to having also an astringent power. And he said that Demetrius the Bithynian used it in this way, taking up the chrysocolla alone in the wax. And Demetrius did well to use it thus; just as I too often use, in such cases, not only chrysocolla but also each of the others by itself, softening it with soft wax.

It is clear that by 'each of the others' I meant those which I went through earlier as benefiting such ulcers, and that I have such drugs levigated, compounded with wax, for [723] each of the hard-to-heal ulcers that I may be treating. For sometimes I take up chrysocolla in wax, sometimes burnt copper or scale—and this either of stomoma or of iron or of copper—sometimes verdigris, unburnt or burnt, as also misy and chalcitis. And sometimes I also mix in one of the austere substances, about which I spoke earlier, whenever I wish to repel that which flows in; among these are alum, pomegranate rinds, oak-gall, the cytini and balaustion, and all other such things. Trusting me, then, that none of all the drugs mentioned up to this point is to be rejected, practise the method of their use, so that you may succeed just as I do. And since two other noteworthy drugs were written next in order by the Tarentine, it seemed reasonable to me to add those as well. The first of them he wrote roughly thus: Take scale, 4 drachms; manna, 4 drachms; split alum, 2 drachms; misy, 2 drachms; having triturated them with vinegar and made little pastilles weighing 2 drachms each, store away.

At the time of use, having melted wax [724] 4 drachms (others: 40), pine resin 2 drachms, bull's fat 4 drachms, and having let it congeal, mix it with the troche. Use it for wounds as an agglutinating and inflammation-preventing remedy. So much for the Tarentine. For my part, [I say that] one must use it, mixed in this way, for wounds, as he says (φησὶ); for the malignant ulcers, however, one should not mix in such a cerate, but the wax alone is sufficient, as we said in the case of the preceding ones. And if it should ever be necessary to mix with it some one of the emollient things, let it be a little myrtle-oil or henna oil or rose-oil. You will do no harm either, not even if you should mix in the resin called larch, nor the terebinth, which is less suitable for such ulcers, yet not to be rejected. The other resins, however, one should not mix in except in a great lack of the aforementioned. And so too concerning fat. For indeed this too should not be mixed in, unless you also wish to soften the lips. And that bull's fat is more drying than all the others that come from domesticated animals, you have heard many times.

For the fat of the lion, and that of leopards, [725] and obviously also that of the hyena, surpass it in fineness of parts. It is better, therefore, when fat must be mixed in, to put in goose fat, and preferably that of free-ranging geese; for it is sufficiently fine in its parts and soothing. And since there still remains one drug written down, continuous with the one written before, at which Heracleides made the beginning of his teaching, speaking thus: "the ipoterion (press-remedy), and especially for those of delicate skin" — since it belongs to the other material and power, which we said suits those who do not bear the application of strong drugs but are bitten, irritated and afflicted with flux, let the discussion concerning this be deferred, to be stated when I go through such drugs. But now I shall pass over to the drugs similar to those written before, adding only this much more about them: that Heracleides also, in another book entitled The Soldier (Stratiotes; printed στατιώτην), wrote the same drugs, disagreeing with himself only in the one that is third among them in order. For here it is written simply "of wax 40 drachms," whereas in The Soldier there is added "but some, 16 drachms"; and this is indeed better.

[726] is. For a large admixture of the wax diminishes the power of the drug. Heraclides mentions these same drugs also in the writings addressed by him to Antiochis, and first indeed the first of them, writing in those, just as in these, thus: "For those that are very old and callous you will use this: of scale, one part; of verdigris" — in some of the copies the δ΄ is written marked off with a point (ἀπεστιγμένον), but in some having a long line above it, so that it signifies either four parts or a fourth of one. And so too in the previously mentioned treatises I found it written differently, so that in this respect also there is need of the present treatise, in order that one may know how to distinguish the differences of the drugs. For such a person alone would use them properly. This very drug before us, at any rate, if it takes four times the amount of verdigris, will be quite pungent; but if someone puts in a fourth part of verdigris in relation to one part of the scale, he will have a moderate drug, as regards malignant [ulcers], and especially if he makes the mixture of them not with wax alone but with a cerate.

It has been said before that the wax must be both soft and fresh; [727] but if we are at a loss for such wax, then, heating the wax we have beside a fire or in the sun and softening it with a little myrtle oil, we shall in this way mix in both the scale of copper and the verdigris. It has also been said at the beginning of this book that a most excellent drug is one composed of scale of copper and verdigris, with four times the amount of wax added to it. And for this reason I use it continually, mixing in, for the most part, also an equal amount of burnt copper. The Tarentine, however, in the book written by him to Antiochis, has added to the use of this drug things which he did not add in those earlier treatises of his that I mentioned. I shall therefore write out his whole passage, which runs as follows: "For those that are extremely inveterate and callous you will use this one: of scale of copper one part, of verdigris a fourth; having ground them fine, take them up in a hard myrtle cerate of eight times the amount and use it, having first washed the ulcer with cold water." He added, then, also that one must first wash the ulcer with cold water. Now, therefore, I shall at once write out those of the things written by Andromachus for the same professed virtue that have been passed over by me.

For earlier I went through only the plasters. [728] But all the drugs which, prepared beforehand in the form of troches and mixed with cerates at the time of use, he says are cicatrizing for ulcers that are hard to heal, or all the dry powders for sprinkling, these I shall now add, beginning from what is written among the dry remedies near the end. [Dry remedies from the writings of Andromachus: a dry cicatrizing remedy.] ℞ Of bones (otherwise: of oyster-shells) burnt, 2 drachms; of manna, 1 drachm; of cadmia, 4 obols (in another copy, 4 drachms). Use them finely ground, also for spreading sores. Another dry cicatrizing remedy. ℞ Of pine bark, 6 drachms; of aristolochia, 6 drachms; of pumice, 4 drachms; of dry resin, 4 drachms; of manna, 6 drachms — it is quite clear that he means colophony —; of Illyrian iris, 2 drachms. Use them finely ground. Another, cicatrizing and for malignant ulcers as well. ℞ Of pine bark, 6 drachms; of burnt stag's horn, 4 drachms; of cadmia, 18 drachms; of manna (otherwise: of white lead), 4 drachms; of scraped verdigris, 2 drachms. Use them finely ground. Another. ℞ Of gall-nut, 4 drachms; of white lead, 8 drachms; of myrtle, 4 drachms; of litharge, 8 drachms; of dross of lead (μοβύβδου, read μολύβδου), 4 drachms. Use them finely ground.

Of these four drugs, the first is very simple, both non-biting and drying, [729] partaking of a faint astringency. The second, because bark of pine has been mixed into it, has a perceptible astringency, such as those drugs ought to have which are going to cicatrize well. The third, on account of containing not only the bark of pine but also verdigris, is suited to those ulcers accompanied by filth that is readily bred in the ulcerated parts; for it both removes their filth and does not hinder cicatrization. The one that follows has myrtle in place of the pine bark, and the other ingredients are drying without biting. After these, having written three other dry drugs, he added a fourth to them, in these very words: 'Another dry drug for ulcers with excess flesh, cicatrizing, non-biting, as Harpokras: of sandarach, chrysocolla, arsenic, an equal amount of each. This drug is effective also against malignant ulcers.' It resembles none of the preceding ones, but is suited to ulcers with excess flesh due to much moisture, being also reductive of them; for sandarach and arsenic are of such a power. And one of the things that wonderfully benefit malignant ulcers has been added to them, chrysocolla.

[On the things written by Archigenes.] [730] What Archigenes wrote about such ulcers in the second book of his work On Drugs is set down, in his own wording and in his very words, as follows. On uncicatrised and old ulcers. Of ulcers, cicatrise the old ones in this way: having thoroughly cleansed them with some common remedy, apply very old oil with lint-plugs. Or take up scraped verdigris in rose cerate containing a little resin, and apply. And taking up as much as possible of the scale of red copper in myrtle cerate, use it. Or washed starch, 3 parts; calf's fat, 3 parts; Tyrrhenian wax, 1 part: having melted the fusible ingredients, mix in the starch and use. Or diphryges and copper scale, 4 drachms each; manna, 8 drachms; having triturated them well with vinegar to the thickness of honey, melt wax, 32 drachms, with one and a half cotylae of oil, pour it over, and having united them use it as a lint-dressing; or make the oil less and make a compress. Or chalcitis and ceruse, an equal amount; of common salt, double; of litharge, double the salt; triturating alternately with wine and oil, use it as an oily salve.

Or litharge, white lead, diphryges in equal parts, quicklime [731] twice as much: use with myrtle cerate. Or diphryges, scale, oak-gall in equal parts, verdigris half as much, with myrtle cerate. Some also mix in pine resin. Or sprinkle on root of wild cucumber, and on top lint from cold water; it cleanses and cicatrizes. For ulcers in whatever place of the body that are hard to cicatrize: seed of hedge-mustard, finely ground, mixed and brought to a salve-like consistency, when applied in the manner of a splenium, very quickly cicatrizes even the malignant ones. A cicatrizing remedy for ulcers of the aged: for the ulcers of the aged use dross of lead with myrtle cerate; and if you wish to make it keep, mix in pig's fat as well. As for ulcers that are turning black, having first fomented them with barley loaves freshly baked, use butter and white lead in equal parts, carefully united.

[On putrefactive sores and spreading sores.] For putrefactive sores and spreading sores: bitter-vetch flour, liquid alum, the inside of a loaf of fine wheat flour, flesh of old pork or of other old salted meat, unwashed, liquid terebinth, [732] good honey, in equal parts by weight; beat them together and apply. Or: equal parts of aristolochia and of the juice of castor-plant leaves, half as much verdigris, in water, to the thickness of honey; smear it on, taking up a little of the liquid in addition. If the eschar does not come away, mix in an equal quantity of elaterium and verdigris. It works well in putrefactions: sory, finely ground, sprinkled on thickly, and dry lint on top. Or smear round aristolochia and oak-gall, in equal parts, with oil, around the sore. Or wrap the root of wild cucumber in leaves of cabbage or beet or dock and bury it in hot ashes; when it has softened, crush it and apply it: it cleanses vigorously. Or sprinkle on olive-shoots boiled in wine, with honey; or sprinkle on chalcitis, and put dry lint on top. Apply elaterium or linseed, finely ground, with chalcanthum; or sprinkle on thyme and wild staphis or the cultivated kind with boiled figs, or fig leaves finely ground with honey, or nitron with cumin and flour with honey, or the root of wild cucumber with honey, or boiled squill with honey, or hellebore with honey.

These also work against phagedaenae [733] and black discolorations and nomai (spreading sores); or: sory, 12 drachms, chalcitis, 10 drachms, misy, 4 drachms; triturate with half a kotyle of very sharp vinegar until it is dried, and take it up. Use it by dipping a probe and rolling it over the ulcer, and on top apply a single linen cloth soaked in wine-and-oil. If it is inflamed, apply henbane with barley-meal or cabbage with honey as a dusting. For those that have worms, smear on white lead and polion in equal parts with liquid pitch. [On cancerous ulcers.] For cancerous and malignant ulcers, sprinkle on burnt river-crab and cadmia, in equal parts, finely ground; or apply the ash of the crabs with cerate; or hedge-mustard seed, ground as fine as possible, made with honey to the consistency of lees, apply as a compress (plenion). It works excellently against Chironian ulcers and old ones and those hard to cicatrize and the malignant black ulcers (melantria) on the shins and the malignant ones in the breasts. It works excellently (ἄλρως, read ἄκρως) for drawing out scrofulous swellings and parotid swellings: beef suet, 3 litrai (as some say, 5), terebinth, 5 ounces,

of manna [734] half an ounce; of the earth called Sardian, which the fullers use, five ounces. Pour the melted ingredients over the dry ones, and having united them, use. Or apply boiled lentil with honey, or olive-shoots (θαλλία), or both, as a dusting. [On callous ulcers.] In the case of callous and bank-edged ulcers, the so-called "sweet" ulcers, the caustics proven by experience will also work; but specifically, smear around them roasted nitron and unslaked lime with the urine of an uncorrupted boy, or smear around them verdigris, frankincense, salt, honey. [On the plasters written by Asclepiades for such ulcers.] Asclepiades, surnamed Pharmakion, wrote most excellently concerning such ulcers.

For while there is one thing common to all of them, namely that they are hard to cicatrize, some of them fail to cicatrize because they are badly treated or because the person under treatment lives on a soft regimen, though they themselves have no malignancy of their own; others are hard to treat in themselves, either because bad humors flow into them [735] or because the ulcerated place has already acquired such a disposition that, even if the blood flowing in is good, it corrupts it. Asclepiades, then, having divided ulcers of this sort into three kinds, made his account of each separately, and these I too shall write out in order in his own words, adding an explanation or a judgment wherever some ambiguity may exist in the account. Concerning the first kind of such ulcers and drugs, then, Asclepiades writes word for word roughly as follows. When the bodies have become callused and are brought to a scar only with difficulty, the preparations written below are to be used. The plaster of Andreas, repressive of every excrescence. It is also a plaster for bleeding wounds, a wound-plaster, and prevents inflammation. It is good for spreading ulcers and glues together sinuses. It is good for the rheumatic ulcers and for those that are chronic and hard to cicatrize. Take litharge, 3 pounds; scale of copper, chalcitis, scraped verdigris, 3 ounces each; vinegar, 1 cotyle; old oil, 8 pounds. Prepare in the usual manner. The drug of Aster, well-suited for the aforesaid conditions. It is also a good discutient.

Take: [736] litharge, 1 litra; old oil, 2½ litrai; verdigris, 1 ounce; chalcitis, 1 ounce; red scale, 1 ounce; vinegar, 1 kotyle. Amphion's, for the same conditions. Take: litharge, 2 litrai; old oil, 4 litrai; chalcitis, 9 ounces; scale of copper, 4 drachms; vinegar, 1 kotyle. Prepare in the usual way. Turpilianus', the one called "of the philosophers". It is effective for the rheumatic ones among ulcers; it is effective for those that are chronic and hard to cicatrize; it brings up corrupted bones. Take: litharge, 3 litrai; old oil, 3 xestai; chalcitis, 2½ litrai; scale of copper, 25 drachms; vinegar, 1 kotyle. Boil the litharge and the oil until they reach consistency, then throw in the scale, very finely ground, and stir continuously; and when it is in good condition, add little by little the chalcitis, ground up with vinegar, the drug having been cooled somewhat; then, having set it on the fire, boil it again until it does not stain, and having emptied it out into a mortar, beaten it up and kneaded it, take it up and use it for the aforesaid conditions.

The Isis called tawny, a well-tried drug for the rheumatic [737] and chronic and malignant and hard-to-heal ones, and especially on the extremities. It must be prepared rather soft, for as it lies in store it contracts and becomes drier. It is as follows. ♃ Of litharge 100 drachms; of Sinopic red earth 8 drachms; of diphryges, of wax, of burnt chalcitis one ounce each (in another copy 4 drachms each); of raw chalcitis 2 drachms; of oil 2 kotylai. Boil the litharge and the oil until it has boiled up a second and a third time. When this has happened, sprinkle a little water on it with the fingers, then sprinkle on the diphryges and the roasted chalcitis, finely ground, little by little, sprinkling with the water until the drug no longer crackles as it is boiled. And when it has set, add the wax. Have lying ready the things ground with a little oil, the raw chalcitis and the Sinopic earth. And when the drug is in good condition, add these and stir continuously, and when it is in a good state, pour it out into a mortar, beat it up and knead it, take it up and use it. Another, of Scribonius Largus, a well-tried drug. ♃ Of wax 100 drachms (others: 50); of litharge 50 drachms; of myrtle oil 1 kotyle.

of burnt misy, of burnt chalcitis, of burnt split alum, [738] of white lead, of terebinth resin, two drachms each. Prepare in the usual manner. Another. It also represses the staphylomata in the eyes; it works for hard-to-heal conditions. Take Sinopic red earth 15 drachms, litharge 100 drachms, wax 40 drachms, pine resin 20 drachms, chalcitis 30 drachms, ammoniac salt 1 drachm, frankincense 1 drachm, oil 1 cotyle. Prepare in the usual manner. Another, as Aphrodas gives it. It works also for condylomata and hard-to-heal fissures. Take litharge 48 drachms, terebinth 28 drachms, roasted misy, roasted chalcitis 8 drachms each, Sinopic red earth, chalcanthum 4 drachms each, old oil 1 cotyle, water 1 cotyle, wax 40 drachms, castor oil 1 litra—others say half a cyathus. The dry ingredients are ground up with the water. And so much concerning these. [On the second kind of hard-to-treat ulcers, about which Asclepiades wrote word for word as follows.] For the rheumatic and hard-to-heal among ulcers one must use the preparations written below. The one through chamaeleon, which Philoxenus used for the rheumatic and hard-to-heal among ulcers.

♃ litharge [739] 1 litra, old oil 2 litrai, chamaeleon root 4 ounces, aristolochia 4 ounces, galbanum 2 ounces, gall-nut 2 ounces, frankincense 2 ounces. Prepare in the usual way. Another, the one called that of the Theban. ♃ litharge 1 litra, old oil 1 xestes, chalcanthum 24 drachms, chamaeleon 12 drachms, aristolochia 12 drachms, galbanum 8 drachms, frankincense 8 drachms. Prepare in the usual way. Another, the one with the reeds, for rheumatic and Chironian ulcers; it works also against the bite of every creeping creature. ♃ litharge one litra, old oil 2 litrai, of the root of black chamaeleon, aristolochia, unripe gall-nuts, of each 4 drachms, galbanum, ammoniac incense, frankincense, of each 2 ounces. Prepare, stirring with roots of green reeds. The so-called gangrenic (plaster) of Castus, a well-tested drug. ♃ litharge 120 drachms, oil 2 and a half xestai, root of black chamaeleon 16 drachms, vinegar 2 and a half xestai, verdigris 8 drachms, pine bark 8 drachms, myrrh 4 drachms.

Prepare in the usual way. The black plaster made with pyrites, [740] called that of Damonicus. It is effective against rheumatic, hard-to-heal and phagedaenic ulcers. It is also effective against fistulas when inserted, and it softens every hardness. ♃ Litharge, asphalt, 100 drachmas each, or 50; pitch, wax, 8 drachmas each; pyrites, terebinth, 25 drachmas each; propolis, split alum, 15 drachmas each; ammoniac incense, 12 drachmas; galbanum, aloe, 8 drachmas each; verdigris, manna, 5 drachmas each; old oil, 2 xestai. Boil the litharge with the oil until it thickens together, then add the asphalt, pitch, wax, resin, propolis, and when it has melted, let it cool and add the verdigris and the stone, then the ammoniac; then, having taken it off and cooled it a little, add the split alum, galbanum, manna, and after boiling briefly pour it out into cold water, and having left it for a day and a night, knead it and use. It is effective against hard-to-heal ulcers. Another. ♃ Pitch, wax, pyrites, 12 drachmas each; ammoniac incense, 10 drachmas; asphalt, 50 drachmas; litharge, 40 drachmas; propolis, 8 drachmas; split alum, 5 drachmas; verdigris, 2 drachmas; oil, 1 xestes. Another black plaster, the one made with willows, for the same conditions.

Take: of foreign [741] misy, of round alum, of chalcitis, of melanteria, of scraped verdigris, of split alum, of omphacine oak-galls, of white lead, half a litra of each; of wax, of dry resin, of Bruttian pitch, of asphalt, two litrai each; of acrid vinegar, half a xestes; of omphacine oil, two litrai; of the leaves of tender willow shoots, two litrai. Put the willow leaves into the vinegar and, setting it on the fire, boil, stirring continuously until a third of the liquid is left over. Pound the dry ingredients and sift them through the finest sieve, and having put them into a mortar, add to them the liquid after pressing it out, and triturate laboriously, as with the cephalic preparations. Boil the fusible ingredients until they no longer stain; then, having let them cool and scraped them up, add them to the finely ground ingredients, and having emptied the whole into a mortar, take it up and use it. The Indian plaster of Tharseus the surgeon, for the aforementioned conditions. Take: of wax, of roasted resin, of dry pitch, of liquid asphalt, Zacynthian, two litrai of each.

white lead, verdigris, chalcitis, foreign misy, melanteria, alum, both split and round, unripe oak-galls, pomegranate rinds, sumach, frankincense, of each (ἀκὰ, presumably for ἀνὰ) half a pound, vinegar as much as [742] suffices. Boil the meltable ingredients until non-staining; the dry ones, having pounded them and sifted them through the finest sieve and kneaded them with vinegar, take up with the meltable ingredients. Another, the Cyzicene. It works for chronic conditions and for severances of the sinews. ♃ Frankincense, of the finest, wax, myrrh, aristolochia, chalcitis, Illyrian (iris), galbanum, 4 drachms each; terebinth, litharge, 8 drachms each; oil, 1 cotyle. Put everything into a bronze vessel and boil over soft ashes, stirring, until a drop let fall into cold water has the thickness of honey. After this remove it while stirring; smear this onto a small piece of leather, apply it, and undo it in winter after the seventh day, in summer after the fifth. Another, from the writings of Philoxenus. ♃ Frankincense, myrrh, saffron, Illyrian (iris), bdellium, copper scale, chalcanthus, chalcitis, alum round and split, foreign misy, ammoniac incense, propolis, oak birdlime (ixos), opopanax, closed pomegranate rinds, 4 drachms each; aristolochia, 8 drachms; wax, 100 drachms, which he writes as a mina; bull's suet, 100 drachms; terebinth resin, 75 drachms, which he writes as three-quarters.

Having put the resin into a new [743] earthenware pot, boil it until it becomes odourless. Then, having cut up the fat and the wax, add them and melt them. Pound the dry ingredients and sift them through the finest sieve; then, having taken the meltable ingredients off the fire and allowed them to cool somewhat, sprinkle the dry ingredients onto them, stirring carefully. One must have ready, ground up with vinegar, myrrh, frankincense, bdellium and opopanax, and into these the contents of the pot are thrown and triturated, so that no enkerides (lumps of wax) form. When it is in good condition, take it up into a wooden box, having first smeared it with iris oil. [On the third kind of ulcers that are hard to treat, concerning which Asclepiades wrote the following word for word.] In the case of ulcers that do not close up at all, or that close up but break open again, either because the flesh is being corrupted or because the underlying bones too have become corrupted, one must use the preparations set out below. A successful drug for cheironian and hard-to-heal ulcers. Take scale of copper, scraped verdigris, one ounce each; wax, half a litra; larch resin, one ounce.

and a half. [744] [Pour] the meltable ingredients over the dry ones, and when you have taken it up, use it, kneading it carefully and laying a flat plaster over the affected part alone, so that it covers only the ulcer. The surrounding parts must be covered with a drug that does not provoke inflammation. During the treatment one must undo the ulcer every third day, then foment it beforehand, and, after washing off the same flat plaster, knead it and apply it again, until it begins to cicatrize. Another, well-tested. ℞ verdigris, scale of copper, 2 ounces each; diphryges, 1 ounce; wax, 1 pound; larch resin, 3 ounces. Prepare and use as has been said before. After these, concerning the so-called cephalic plasters, as Asclepiades wrote, word for word, thus. The cephalic of Deileon. For chronic and hard-to-heal ulcers; it brings up corrupted bones. ℞ scale of copper, manna, frankincense, dry resin, 100 drachmas each; vinegar, 12 cotylae. Grind the scale of copper with vinegar, and when it has been reduced to a smooth paste, add the most finely ground frankincense and the resin, and form into troches and dry in the shade.

In use, in cases where you wish to remove the callus, take one part of the drug and [745] an equal amount of cerate prepared with rose oil. In the other cases let there be one part of the drug and three or four parts of the cerate; for the mixture must be made suitable to the underlying conditions. A blackish-green cephalic, which Tryphon the elder used. It works for chronic and hard-to-heal (sores), and brings up corrupted bones. Take: scale of copper, 12; manna, frankincense, ammoniac incense, dry pine resin, treated calf's suet, terebinth resin, 16 drachms each; wax, oil, a quarter of a mina each; vinegar, 1 cotyle. Prepare in the usual manner. The cephalic of Philotas, for chronic and hard-to-heal (sores): it brings up corrupted bones and gradually melts away calluses. Take: Eretrian earth, 100 drachms; scale of copper, 50 drachms; fish-glue, 25 drachms; vinegar, 12 cotylae. The fish-glue must be cut up into thin pieces and put into a glass vessel, and, after pouring vinegar over it, one must let it soak, and when it has dissolved add it to the drug already prepared, and, having mixed them, form troches; the use has been indicated. The (cephalic) of Dionysius of Samos.

℞ Eretrian earth [746] 1 mina, scale of copper half a mina, fish-glue a quarter of a mina, frankincense an eighth of a mina, scraped verdigris an eighth of a mina, myrrh one sixteenth of a mina, vinegar 2 choes. Compound it during the heats under the Dog-star, triturating everything together with the vinegar in the sun. Cut the fish-glue into fine pieces and soak it with a little vinegar in a glass vessel; then, having mixed it with the ingredients in the mortar, form pastilles weighing four holkai each, and others eight, and dry them. For use, one part of the drug to three of cerate prepared with rose-oil; and over the splenia one applies greasy (oesypum-bearing) wool soaked in vinegar; for fistulas, to one part of the drug two parts of rose cerate; make collyria and insert them. The one made from herbs, as Leucius the Professor (ho Kathēgētēs) has it. ℞ anagallis, the kind with the blue flower, 56 drachmas; wild poppy 56 drachmas; leaves of green henbane and green leeks 56 drachmas each; scale of copper 25 drachmas; manna 20 drachmas; dry pine resin 16 drachmas; aloe 6 drachmas; cleft alum 4 drachmas and round alum 4 drachmas; ammoniac salt 4 drachmas; wax 1 mina.

of old oil [747] 2 cotylae, of vinegar a sufficient quantity. Having pounded the herbs carefully and dissolved them in vinegar, press out the liquid for the preparation of the drug. The Isis, a cephalic plaster, for Chironian and hard-to-heal ulcers; it is also good as a plaster for bleeding wounds. ♃ Of wax 100 drachms, of Colophonian resin 200 drachms, of ammoniac incense, of scale of copper, of burnt frankincense, of slender aristolochia, of verdigris, of ammoniac salt 8 drachms each, of galbanum, of manna, of myrrh, of aloe 12 drachms each, of round alum 6 drachms, of old oil 1 cotyle, of vinegar a sufficient quantity. Prepare it and use the drug sometimes undiluted, sometimes diluted. [On the plasters written down by Heras that are useful for the hard-to-treat kinds of ulcers.] He wrote down certain other plasters that are polychrēsta (of many uses), which he says are fitting also for ulcers hard to cicatrize and malignant ones. But of one that is outstanding in a special way for these alone he made mention, writing about it more or less as follows, in these very words: "The plaster of Hygieinos himself, of good colour (εὔχρους), for many conditions, effective on ulcers hard to cicatrize and on paronychias: there is no plaster finer than this one."

Take: of litharge [748] of the chrysitis kind, 1 mina; of wax, 1 mina; of the root of black chamaeleon, 36 drachms; of scraped verdigris, 18 drachms; of chrysocolla, 40 drachms; of oil, 3 cotylae. Boil the litharge and the oil over a gentle fire until it begins to boil up; then sprinkle in the verdigris, having taken it off the fire, and stir, boiling again, until it takes on its proper colour; then the wax; and when it is in good condition, the chrysocolla and the chamaeleon; and having poured it out into a mortar, sprinkle vinegar over it. For the conditions written above it is effective even with the chrysocolla mixed in. Without this, however, it is most soothing and works excellently for punctures of the nerves and wherever something needs to be brought up to the surface from muscles or nerves. Heras did well, at the end of his account of the plaster, in adding that with the chrysocolla it is not soothing; for this drug has something astringent, whereas the things being soothed require relaxing agents—on account of pain, evidently. For in this case only the symptom requires soothing, and indeed the soothing agents often harm the painful condition itself.

But, taking our stand against what is urgent, we first soothe the pain, and then in this way we proceed to those things that are able to cure the condition. [749] Chrysocolla, then, as has also been said before, is one of the drugs that are wonderfully of this kind for ulcers that are hard to cure, just as are many others of those that dry strongly while at the same time having something astringent; but none of such drugs is soothing. And since he mentioned both a mina and a cotyle, having ordered one mina of litharge to be put in and a cotyle of oil—for it has been said by me also in the preceding commentaries that some consider the mina to be of twenty ounces, others of sixteen, just as also some reckon the cotyle at nine ounces and some at twelve—one must make a distinction about these matters as well. And the distinction is made from the profession of the drug and from the quantity of the metallic ingredients. For on account of its profession it requires considerable boiling, and on this account also more oil; and on account of the admixture of the metallic ingredients, which are not few, the drug needs oily moisture.

Since, then, it takes neither fat nor marrow nor liquid resin, it is quite evident that the oil must be increased. [750] If, therefore, we reckon the mina at twenty ounces, we shall in any case put in three cotylae of oil, each of 12 ounces; but if at sixteen, it is possible to put in the cotyle of oil as nine ounces, though it is also possible to do so as 12, so that the boiling too, which is beneficial, may be carried further. For to drugs of this kind this is most beneficial, and also on account of the metallic ingredients, which are present in no small quantity. For if you add together the 36 drachms of chamaeleon with the 18 of verdigris and the 40 of chrysocolla, they would come to ninety-four drachms, and these too require the admixture of abundant oil, and especially because he thinks that 100 drachms of wax also should be put in; for assuredly in that case too it will need much oil. This plaster, then, Heras wrote down, attesting of it that it is suitable in the case of ulcers hard to cicatrize; and having written other polychrēsta (of many uses) in the same book, in addition to their many effects he also added that they help ulcers hard to cicatrize, or even malignant or Chironian ones.

For all have praised both the plaster called by him Aribarzaneios, as curing malignant, spreading [751] and hard-to-heal ulcers, and the Isis, as circumscribing gangrenes; and a third in addition to these, which he began with the following wording: "of good colour, for fresh wounds (enaimos), cicatrizing," saying that it also helps Chironian ulcers; and a fourth, which he himself names panacea; and a fifth, that of Hicesius. Concerning the plasters of many uses (polychrēsta), then, my account will come in the book after this one, in which I shall also write out these that have been praised by Heras. In this book I shall add the remedies for hard-to-treat ulcers, called Chironian by some, which have been put to the test through long experience both by our teachers and by ourselves. Some of them have also been attested by older men of repute, as indeed has the one written in the book entitled Mantias' "The Drug-seller at the Surgery" (pharmakopōlēs ho kat' iatreion). He wrote about them in these very words, thus: The verdigris plaster (iōdēs) of Mantias. ℞ of burnt copper 4 minae; of dry pine resin 8 drachms; of wax 8 drachms; of verdigris 10 drachms; of oil 1 kotyle; of Cimolian earth 4 drachms; of frankincense 4 drachms; of copper scale 4 drachms.

Having ground the dry ingredients fine, leave them in the mortar; and having melted the wax with the oil, pour it down [752] over the ground ingredients and let it soak in for a short time, and pour in one kotyle of vinegar, and work them smooth for three days, pouring in as much vinegar as it will take, so that it comes to have the consistency of a liquid cerate. Use it for every wound, and for old ulcers and those hard to cicatrize, and for all that are cancerous, with lint-pledgets. And over the compress one must bind on lightly greasy wool (wool with oesypum), moistened with wine and oil, undoing it in summer every two days and in winter every three, and wash the ulcers down with lukewarm water. As for deep wounds, pack the mouths themselves lightly with lint; for the preparation is one for use with lint and pus-producing. And in whatever case the ulcers have become clean and the eschar has fallen off, mix wax in equal quantity with verdigris and cicatrize. It also expels carbuncles painlessly, and arrests and completely cures every spreading malignant condition. Use it also for herpetes and for rotten nails. In like manner, for all cases one must use the wine and oil together with the wool; and fill eaten-away teeth with the drug. Plaster of Galen. Our own, a good one.

♃ Of wax, of pitch [753] and of bitumen, one litra each; of manna, of verdigris, of white lead, half of the aforesaid amount, that is, half a litra of each. Of pomegranate rind and oak-gall and Egyptian thorn (akantha) and Illyrian iris and round aristolochia and chalcanthum, of each of these a third of a litra, that is, four ounces. Of long aristolochia and burnt copper, a sixth of a litra of each, that is, two ounces each. Triturate the dry ingredients, then, with vinegar over several days, as has also been said before. When they have been well worked up, melt the meltable ingredients with oil, a kotyle, and pour it over them, sprinkling on the manna; and having cooled the meltable ingredients and scraped them, mix them in this way with the dry ingredients that have been triturated with vinegar, lest in the pouring you somehow produce enkerides (lumps of wax), and especially when the surrounding air is cold. Another of ours. ♃ Of bitumen and of liquid alum, one litra of each; of pitch and pine resin and wax, double of each, that is, two litrai each; of round aristolochia and oak-gall and Egyptian thorn (akantha), eight ounces each; and half of this weight

for each of these: of pomegranate rinds, burnt copper, manna and long aristolochia, that is, [754] four ounces each; of castor oil, or of old oil if you do not have the castor oil, two pounds, the pound having twelve ounces, so that the total is twenty-four ounces. And prepare this too in the same manner as the preceding one, levigating the metallic substances with vinegar and after this adding the dry ingredients and levigating again, then, when these have a mud-like consistency, mixing in the meltable ingredients as has been said before. Another. ♃ Of asphalt, terebinth resin and Bruttian pitch, one pound each; of oil, 24 drachms; of litharge, white lead, manna, verdigris, scale and opopanax, of each an amount equal to the twenty-four drachms of the oil; of ladanum two ounces, which is 16 drachms; and two cotylae of vinegar. This drug too is prepared in the same way as the two before it. Another. ♃ Of chrysocolla, scale and stomoma, 4 drachms each; of verdigris and chalcanthum, half of each, that is, 2 drachms each; of wax 25 drachms, that is, 3 ounces and one drachm; of terebinth resin 2 ounces, that is, 16 drachms.

Melt the wax together with the terebinth, then mix it with the other ingredients, preparing the [755] drug in two ways: sometimes, as in the preceding recipes, grinding the dry ingredients with vinegar, sometimes mixing them, thoroughly triturated without vinegar, with the meltable ingredients. Let the terebinth be rather liquid, as the resin called larch for the most part is. And in general, in all these drugs which are agreed to be suitable for cheironian ulcers, if you mix in larch resin in place of terebinth you will not go wrong. Another. Take wax 3 ounces, that is 24 drachms; burnt copper, scale and verdigris 2 drachms each, so that the three together make 6 drachms. Let the wax be rich, so that, when softened with a little rose-oil or myrtle-oil, it takes up the dry ingredients, well triturated—which is most necessary in the case of all the drugs compounded for cheironian ulcers. And indeed, even after mixing the dry ingredients with the wax, it is better to pound them further in a mortar. Another. Take wax 6 ounces; verdigris a sixth part of that, which is 1 ounce; burnt copper and larch resin 3 drachms of each, so that the two together make 6 drachms. Let the wax be rich.

and, having been thrown into hot water so as to become softer, let it be kneaded with the hands, the verdigris and [756] the burnt copper being taken up into it, and after this let them be pounded in a mortar, in which also the admixture of the resin will take place, it being dripped in little by little. Another. Take cadmia, 3 ounces; having mixed it with half the weight of chalcitis, which is 1½ ounces, and having triturated it well, pour on astringent wine and triturate again, and having made it honey-like in consistency, mix in the cerate made from wax and roasted (phrykte) resin. Let there be an equal amount of each, 1 ounce, so that both together are 2 ounces. And you will add to these a little myrtle oil while it is being melted. Another. Take old oil or castor oil, 1 kotyle; wax, pitch and bitumen, 1 litra each; manna, verdigris, white lead, at half of the aforesaid, which is half a litra of each; pomegranate rind, oak-gall, Egyptian thorn (akantha), iris, round aristolochia, chalkanthon, a third of a litra of each, which is 4 ounces; burnt copper, long aristolochia, a sixth of a litra, which is 2 ounces, of each. You will mix the meltable ingredients with the dry ones previously triturated in vinegar, as has been said before. Another. Take cadmia, chalcitis, 40 drachms each.

having triturated them with wine [757] over several days, you will mix in a cerate made from oil and wax. Let there be of the oil two litrai, and of the wax two hundred drachmas. But it is better to prepare this in a smaller proportion, putting in cadmia and chalcitis ten drachmas each, and wax and oil fifty drachmas each. Another. Take burnt cadmia and burnt chalcitis and terebinth and wax, an equal amount of each; you will grind the dry ingredients in wine. Another, with kiki (castor oil). Take verdigris one drachma, liquid alum one litra, of pomegranate rind and burnt copper and manna a third of a litra each, which is four ounces; of gall-nut twice as much, which is eight ounces; of pitch and pine resin two litrai each, and of bitumen half, that is a litra, which is also what you will have put in of the liquid alum; of round aristolochia, as of the gall-nut, eight ounces, and of the long aristolochia half, that is four ounces; of castor oil two litrai. You will grind the metallic ingredients with vinegar, as in the recipes written above. Another. Take wax three ounces, of burnt copper and scale and verdigris two litrai each.

Having first warmed the wax in hot water, [758] you will soften it in the hands, mixing in rose-oil; then, having taken up the dry ingredients, you will pound in a mortar for a considerable time, so that everything is truly unified by the third or fourth day. Undo this one too, and all the others of this kind, placing a sponge on the outside, [wetted] from water or oxykraton. Another. Take wax 6 ounces, larch resin half as much, that is 3 ounces, verdigris a third in relation to the larch, that is 1 ounce, Bruttian pitch 3 drachms, burnt chalkitis likewise 3 drachms. Prepare this one too in a manner similar to the preceding. Another. Take burnt copper, scale and verdigris, an equal amount of each; mix with one-and-a-half times as much wax, having softened the wax as has been said before, having first soaked it in hot water and having added, during the softening, either rose-oil or myrtle-oil, then having put it into a mortar. But it is better to mix in wax equal to the three weights, as fresh and as soft and as fatty as possible, so that you do not need much of the oily liquid. Another. Take verdigris and terebinth, an equal amount of each, of wax three times as much, and of split alum and cadmia and scale four times as much of each, so that there is of verdigris 1 part

[759] and of terebinth one part, of wax three parts, and of scale, cadmia and split alum four parts of each. Having pounded, sifted and triturated the dry ingredients thoroughly, put the wax and the terebinth into a mortar and pound them, sprinkling on the dry ingredients in addition, wetting the pestle with myrtle oil or rose oil, in warm air, for in this it will be pounded easily, and above all if it is pounded in the summer sun. The use is as with the others as well: the ulcer having first been scoured with aphronitron and washed down with melikraton and sponged well so that it is without moisture, and after this a flat piece (platysma) from the plaster having been laid upon the ulcer, then on the outside a double fold of linen cloth from cold water, then a new soft sponge; and you should undo it, obviously, every third or fourth day. Our wax-free plaster. ♃ litharge 3 pounds, old castor oil 4½ pounds, sharpest vinegar 2 pounds, black scale of copper and chalcitis and verdigris, of each of the three 2 ounces apiece.

One must boil the litharge beforehand with the oil until it reaches a viscous consistency, then add the metallic ingredients, which have been triturated [760] for several days with vinegar, and so you boil until it does not stain. It is also possible, right from the beginning, to mix the litharge thoroughly with the oil and the vinegar and boil it, and to add the scale, the chalcitis and the verdigris when it has become half-boiled. By a litra of oil and of vinegar I now mean the Roman one, which is twelve of its own ounces. And at times, putting in six litrae of oil to the three of litharge — and obviously, with this proportion, it is boiled for longer. When you prepare this drug too, it is better for the litharge to have been boiled beforehand with the oil alone, and then for the metallic ingredients to have been added with the vinegar. Since there are three of them, I said that two ounces of each are put in, to two litrae of vinegar, three of litharge, and the six litrae of old castor oil or, as I said before, the four and a half. This drug both agglutinates fistulas, and those that have already become callous it draws together and closes by drying, and, if one keeps to a good regimen, they do not break open again.

But when a considerable plethora has accumulated, there is danger, from a flux supervening, both that the part become inflamed again and that the fistula be opened up. And in the case of [761] inveterate ulcers that are hard to cicatrize, which are also called Chironian, we apply not only the drug itself undiluted, but also, melted in old oil or castor oil and applied on a pledget (ἔμμοτον), even if no pus, not even the least amount, had ever previously formed in the ulcer, it both concocts it and produces pus, and it renders the pus thick. You will loosen this too on the third day, if nothing prevents. And if the scale is of stomoma (steel), it is better; but if you have neither this nor the black, that of Cyprian copper will be put in. I once prepared this plaster also mixing in an ounce of Phrygian stone, and at another time an ounce of chrysocolla, just as also sometimes both; it glues together even great wounds. Another, for those of tender skin and ill-ulcerating (δυσελκεῖς), for the same ulcers. ℞ wax, 1 litra; rose-oil, 1 litra; white lead, 8 ounces; ammoniac salt, 4 ounces; Cyprian scale, 2 ounces; frankincense, 1 ounce; quicklime, 1 ounce; split alum, 1 ounce; verdigris, 1 ounce; pomegranate rinds, 1 ounce. The use is the same as for the foregoing. The drugs present compounded are nine, apart from the rose-oil, for that is the tenth.

Of the nine, five [762] are equal in weight: unslaked lime, pomegranate rinds, frankincense, split alum, and verdigris. The scale is of double weight, and the ammoniac salts are double this; and the white lead is double these. The wax, in turn, is half as much again as this, being brought to one pound, which is also the amount of the rose-oil.

[763] GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK V. Here the drugs of many uses (polychrēsta) will be discussed. They name polychrēsta (of many uses) those drugs which are suited to many conditions (diatheseis), and some of them to conditions that are not only of a different species but also of a different genus. All of them are composed of drugs of opposite nature, not only according to the primary qualities and powers but also according to the secondary ones.

It is quite evident that by 'primary' I mean heat and cold and dryness [764] and moisture, and those compounded from these according to any conjugation whatsoever; and by 'secondary' those that follow upon these, about which I went through at greater length in the fifth book of the treatise on simple drugs, showing that some drugs, not only of the compound ones but also of the naturally occurring ones, soften, while others harden, just as also some plug up and others unblock, and some breed filth upon the part while others cleanse away even the filth already lying upon it, and some thin, others thicken, and some condense, others rarefy, and some regenerate flesh, others cleanse it away, and some cicatrize, others ulcerate, and some draw, others repel, and other such differences among them. It has also been stated by me in the preceding commentaries what the necessary mixture of drugs opposite in their powers is, of which I shall remind you now too a little later. For it seems better to me to write out some two or three drugs among the renowned multi-purpose ones, and then to explain the rationale of their composition.

I shall begin from those known to all, which have been recorded both in the Narthex of Heras and among [765] others who have compiled books of drugs (pharmakitides).
