And since in the book before this one my discourse concerned the compound remedies (dynameis) that treat ulcers hard to cicatrize, it seemed good to me now too to expound first those of the plasters of many uses (polychrēsta) which were composed for the sake of malignant ulcers, which some call cheironeia; and as for the others that are called polychrēsta because they are suitable for many other affections, though not, however, also for the cheironeia, these I have resolved to go through afterwards, one after another. [On those written by Heras.] Since, then, a certain plaster that works excellently against such ulcers has been recorded in the book of drugs by Heras the Cappadocian, I shall begin from it, transcribing the man's wording, which runs roughly as follows. A good-coloured (euchrous) plaster for bloody wounds (enaimos), cicatrizing, agglutinating perfectly (akraiphnōs), and also filling up and cicatrizing, and, when dissolved with cerate, still more so with regard to cicatrization. It also works excellently, however, on the cheironeian ulcers and the others similar to them.

For it melts away the calluses and [766] after this generates genuine flesh. Very white. Take: wax, 2 litrai; roasted (phrykte) resin, 3 litrai; scraped verdigris, 6 ounces; manna, 3 ounces; oil, 5 kotylai; vinegar, 1 xestes. The melted ingredients are poured over the dry ones. Use the plaster for wounds; and when it is slackened with rose-oil it produces pus and cleanses; when dissolved with the cerate, for cicatrization. Some, however, put in, of the resin, 2 litrai of roasted (phrykte) and two litrai of terebinth, and having prepared it thus they took it up with scraped verdigris so that it had the firmness of a collyrium, and they inserted this wherever they wished to melt away calluses. For it does this readily, so as even to detach bones. And so Heras reasonably praises this plaster, as having its active power from the quantity of the verdigris and the vinegar, if we remember at all what was said in the book before this one. He also praises the one called by him panacea, which I write out next in his own words. The panacea of Heras, called by some 'Health' (hygieia). For every spreading sore (nome) and malignancy. It checks the spreading sores, neither producing eschars nor hardening the surrounding bodies.

but breaking up and withering away everything that has been corrupted, so that it differs in no way from a moist raisin. It also checks a flow of blood, both the other kinds and that through haemorrhoids, when dissolved in myrtle oil, and it withers and consumes the haemorrhoids themselves. In addition to these, it also heals fistulas and the so-called carbuncles (anthrakes) and the aegilopes and the so-called Chironian ulcers, and in general the whole class of hard-to-heal and chronic conditions—for the hidden places, such as the womb, being melted down in henna oil, while for the external ones it is better to apply it in the same way as each of the others. Applied to any ulcer, even if it is one of the wild (malignant) kind, it will at once make it milder and render the pains and the sleeplessness gentler. The formula is this: ground-pine (chamaepitys) 4 drachms; comfrey 4 drachms; chamaeleon 4 drachms; horehound 4 drachms (others say 6); polion 6 drachms; small centaury 6 drachms; elecampane 4 drachms; aristolochia 4 drachms; frankincense 12½ drachms; myrrh 3 drachms; aloe 6 drachms; galbanum 6 drachms and one and a half obols; oil 180 drachms; honey 30 drachms; propolis 2½ drachms; split alum 6 drachms and one and a half obols;

of terebinth [768] 6 drachms, one and a half obols; of chalcitis 6 drachms, one and a half obols; of asphalt 50 drachms; of ampelitis earth 50 drachms; of litharge 50 drachms; of oak-gall 3 drachms; of fine powder of iris 3 drachms. One must pound the herbs and the roots on the preceding day and put them into the oil. When they have remained in it through the whole night, in the morning one must add the litharge, the ampelitis and the asphalt and boil over a gentle fire. When the consistency thickens, take the pot off the fire. Let the honey, the resin, the galbanum and the propolis be melted together in another vessel. One must mix these in as well, pouring them into the pot, and after these the dry ingredients; and boil together with these until the drug no longer stains. Then, having again taken it off the fire, sprinkle in the myrrh and the frankincense finely ground. One must take care that it never boils over, and, as far as possible, boil it in an open space, for it becomes hard to extinguish if it catches hold of anything. This is what Heras says concerning the panacea.

But we must note that the material itself differs from that of the drugs described in the book before this one for the hard-to-treat [769] ulcers. For those were composed of mineral substances alone, some of few, some of more, with a few among them containing roots or herbs. But with this panacea the opposite is the case: it takes both chamaeleon and centaury, each of which is sufficient to benefit malignant ulcers. It takes also aristolochia and iris, weaker indeed than centaury and chamaeleon with respect to the cure of malignant ulcers, yet not to be rejected. And it takes strong herbs, which are often able even on their own to treat malignant ulcers: chamaepitys, polion and comfrey. Stronger than these are horehound and elecampane. Horehound, then, one might use even alone in cases where the flesh in the ulcer is quite moist and rather foul; but elecampane is not suitable, when sprinkled on alone, even in these cases, just as no other acrid substance is either.

For you learned, in the treatise on simple drugs, the difference between acrid and bitter drugs: the acrid ones being irritant and biting and hot and bringing fluxes upon the affected parts, [770] while the bitter ones are drying without biting and heating, and for this reason suitable for ulcerated parts. But since the man who compounded these herbs had set himself to make from them a plaster, not a dry dusting-powder, and for the composition of the plaster he was going to mix in either wax or resin, or at any rate litharge boiled for a longer time, by which the power of the herbs was being weakened, he mixed with them some of the drugs that are so strong that they cannot be applied to ulcers on their own. These strong drugs have a twofold general power and quality: some an austere and harsh one, others an acrid and harsh one. For this reason, then, of those having an acrid power he mixed in elecampane, and of those that are strongly styptic—for these we call austere and harsh—alum and the gall-nut, obviously the omphakitis. And chalkitis has both qualities in strong measure, just as also the powers that reside in them, being both acrid and astringent.

For it forms callus more quickly and more safely over all recent fistulas, old sinuses (ὑποφοραί), hollows (κόλποι), phymata, parotid swellings, and the abscesses in the breasts and [775] armpits, either so that they do not arise or, once they have arisen, are cured. And when we are in a state of defluxion (ὑπόρρυσις), it further removes scrofulous swellings together with their coats, bringing them to suppuration very quickly; it also stops a flux of the eyes when applied to the forehead. It also takes away livid patches, circumscribes gangrenes, cleanses putrefactions, and, in a word, it is good for everything. Take: wax, 100 drachmas; terebinth, 200 drachmas, though others say 100; scale of red copper, 8 drachmas; scraped verdigris, 8 drachmas; round aristolochia, 8 drachmas; frankincense, 8 drachmas; ammoniac salt, 8 drachmas; ammoniac incense, 8 drachmas; burnt alum or round alum, 6 drachmas; burnt copper, 8 drachmas; myrrh, 12 drachmas; aloe, 12 drachmas; galbanum, 12 drachmas; old oil, 1 kotyle; acrid vinegar, 2 kotylai. Pour the meltable ingredients into a mortar over the dry ones. Thus Heras wrote the Isis, without further adding to it the whole of its use in particular cases, as he was accustomed to do with others.

And indeed, also in calling it the plaster "of Epigonus" he differs from many, who I consider to have written more accurately about Epigonus, both on the other [776] matters and that, having been shut up in prison and having cured one of the very powerful men, he was released on that account. They say that he added the root of dracontium to the drug written above, and I myself have always used it in this way, since one of my teachers too used it, putting into the proportion written by Heras 8 drachmas of dracontium. Moreover, he put in half a cyathus of oil and 1 cotyle of vinegar, and he also put in colophony resin, not, as Heras did, terebinth; but also in the preparation of the plaster he disagreed with Heras, working up the galbanum with the vinegar together with the other ingredients in a mortar. And mixing them in this way, as Heras too says, with the meltable ingredients, he then kneaded the drug, for a very long time in his hands, applying very sharp vinegar; and after this he deposited it in a bronze vessel and, having poured [vinegar] over it, kept it for a longer time, and then, taking it up, used it. He called it, as some others also do, the plaster of Hermon the sacred scribe. In others you would find it written that this one too is from the inner sanctuaries at the Hephaesteum in Egypt, just like the one made with dittany.

[777] As for the proportion of the simple drugs that compose it, however, nearly all have written it the same, so that even if the heading differs, you should not suppose that the sacred plaster from the inner sanctuaries, that of Hermon the sacred scribe, and that of Epigonus are each a different one; for it is called by all these names. Melted together with a moist cerate it cleanses and cicatrises ulcers. And some have written that it is to be diluted with three times its quantity of cerate, others with twice, each party having fixed the proportion without making any distinction. For in those cases in which it renders the ulcer sufficiently clean if mixed with three parts of cerate, one must not mix in the double; but in those cases in which it cleanses less adequately, then the double quantity of cerate must be employed. For we know that every drug of this kind is more active when not mixed with much cerate, and weaker when mixed with more.

It is no worse, however, to say at least this much about dracontium too: that in summer, when the stem and the whole plant have dried up, one should take up the root, then, having placed it in a room that is dry but does not receive the sun, a little later, after six or seven days, cut the root into [778] small disks, and having threaded these on a linen thread hang them again in a room that is dry but sunless, and so, whenever you wish to prepare the drug, pound the root. This root, even by itself, when pounded and well triturated so as to become dust-fine, is curative of malignant ulcers. [The plaster made with dittany.] The plaster prepared with dittany too they call hiera, saying that this prescription also was found in the temple of Hephaestus at Memphis. And indeed all mention it with proportions of this kind or ones differing only slightly. Concerning this one too it will suffice to append the wording of Heras, which runs as follows: Hiera, the one from the temple of Hephaestus at Memphis.

It is effective for fresh bleeding wounds, for rheumatic ones, for severed sinews, old ulcers, undermining sores, contusions, putrefactions, carbuncles, blackenings, rheumatic ulcers, those hard to cicatrize, parotid swellings, chilblains, abscesses, scrofulous swellings, boils, indurations; it draws out missiles, splinters, bones from the head; wounds of wild beasts and bites of scorpions, of phalangia, [779] of the shrew-mouse, human bites. For every pain of the neck, shoulder and joints, in place of a malagma. It checks fluxes of the eyes, not only recent but also old ones, and it is effective for headache, smeared on when dissolved in rose oil; and also for pain of the womb, both anointed on and used as a fumigation from below. The plaster, when burnt as a fumigant, also drives away venomous creatures. It consists of: old oil, 2 cotylae; litharge, 100 drachms; scraped verdigris, 8 drachms; scale of copper, 6 drachms; liquid Colophonian resin, or according to some pine resin, 50 drachms; manna of frankincense, 12 drachms; ammoniac incense, 16 drachms; burnt copper, 8 drachms; diphryges, 6 drachms; gentian, 6 drachms; aloe, 8 drachms; galbanum, 12 drachms; propolis, 8 drachms; wax, 25 drachms; aristolochia, 10 drachms; Cretan dittany, 10 drachms.

Boil in a large pan over charcoals the litharge and the oil, until it is non-staining entirely or very nearly so; then, having lifted off the pot, mix in the verdigris and the scale and boil, and let it not stain at all; then, having removed it again, put in the resin and the ammoniac, sifted, stirring until it stops boiling; then, having set it on again and left it a little while, remove it and sprinkle in the copper and the diphryges, and having boiled it again until it does not stain — for sometimes, [780] when these have been put in, it is loosened again — then, having removed it, add the wax and boil again until it becomes non-staining, and this happens quickly; then, having lifted it off, you will add the propolis, and having set it on again and left it a little while, lift it off and add the aloe, manna, dittany, birthwort, gentian. When these have cooled sufficiently, you will sprinkle in each one separately, very finely ground, and having stirred, if it is non-staining, you will take it off; but if not, you will boil it over a light fire. These are the things Heras wrote about the plaster. We ourselves have sometimes compounded it also without the burnt copper and the diphryges, it becoming more attractive of what lies in the depth and more emollient and more discutient, though not, to be sure, suited to the ulcers hard to cicatrize. We have also made it without the dittany, again adding to the other ingredients, in its case, six drachms of chrysocolla, so that it becomes more therapeutic of malignant ulcers. [The black Hikesios.] The one named Hikesios — some have written it in the genitive case, "the one of Hikesios" — is a polychrēston (of many uses) drug. Heras, at any rate, writes the following about it.

The Hikesios [781] (plaster): for wounds and dog-bites, and dispersing indurations; for parotid swellings and condylomata and for malignant ulcers. It is also drawing (epispastic) and agglutinating, and it works also for dropsies. ♃ Litharge 100 dr.; Jewish asphalt 100 dr.; ampelitis earth 100 dr.; manna, propolis, 25 dr. each; galbanum 12 dr.; split alum 12½ dr.; terebinth resin 12½ dr.; iris 6 dr.; raw-pressed (omotribes) oil 6 kotylai; honey 1 kotyle; chalkitis 7½ dr.; omphakitis gall-nut 6 dr.; myrrh 6 dr. Boil the litharge and the asphalt and the ampelitis with the oil. When they are half-boiled, mix in the propolis and the resin and the galbanum, boiled separately in the honey. When it is setting, add the rest, and stir with a spatula of pine-wood. The weight of the ingredients of this plaster not all have written the same, as will be shown in what follows. [The black plaster from the two aristolochias.] A celebrated plaster, and a polychreston (of many uses), is also the one from the two aristolochias, which Heras himself too wrote in the following words.

[782] The black plaster made with the two aristolochias, effective for old, callous, hard-to-cicatrize and spreading sores. It is also a haemostatic, a cephalic plaster, it draws up bones, is agglutinating, effective for slackened joints, it cleanses parts afflicted with flux, and fills up when diluted. Pitch, one litra; wax, one litra; bitumen, one litra; terebinth resin, one litra; manna, half a litra or seven ounces; scraped verdigris, half a litra; white lead, half a litra; chalcanthum, four ounces; long aristolochia, four ounces; Illyrian iris, four ounces; pomegranate rind, two ounces; omphakitis gall-nut, two ounces; burnt copper, two ounces; akantha, four ounces; round aristolochia, four ounces; vinegar, one kotyle; castor oil or old olive oil, one kotyle. Having melted the meltable ingredients together, then drip in the white lead, the verdigris and the chalcanthum, finely triturated with the vinegar; then, having set it on the fire until it is unified, sprinkle in the dry ingredients after drawing away the fire; then pour it out and knead. These things, then, are what Heras and the others have written about it.

The reasoning of the one who composed it is not unclear to those [783] who remember what has been said by me on this very point both in the preceding books of this work. For it is composed of opposite powers, attractive and repellent, which have drying in common. What predominates in it is the element of the repellents, which belongs to the astringents: the chalkanthon, the pomegranate rinds, the oak-gall, the burnt copper and the thorn (akantha). For this reason he also said that it is suitable for joints that are paralysed (paralelymena), that is, slackened. The aristolochia and the iris he mixed with the astringents, these being of rarefying and discutient power; and so that the drug might become a plaster and not be a dry dusting-powder (epipaston), oil and wax were mixed in. Wax only as material, as also the oil—if this is the common oil and not castor oil or old oil; for we have learned that these heat and disperse. Terebinth resin, in addition to producing the plaster-like consistency for the drug, since wax alone cannot do this, also has something emollient and discutient and detergent. And while frankincense also has these properties, the manna has acquired in addition a wholly astringent power and quality.

For that is what they call [784] the shaken-off residue (aposeisma) of frankincense, which partakes also to some small degree of the bark. Sufficiently drying, too, is asphalt (hē asphaltos or ho asphaltos, whichever way you wish to call it), a drug suitable for the composition of a plaster. These, then, were sufficient for the composition of the plaster. But the one who composed this plaster, having set out to mix in drugs possessing a strong power, added to them verdigris and vinegar, which are capable of cutting and eroding, and both of being carried themselves to the depth of the bodies and of guiding the others there. These are mixed with the discutient drugs for the sake of thinning beforehand the thick moistures in the parts being treated. It remains, then, to say something also about the white lead, which, as is quite clear, he mixed in as suitable for plaster-making, not as something that would itself contribute anything. I, however, would rather have mixed in litharge, for it is both pore-blocking (emplastic) and cooling. White lead, on the other hand, though useful for certain other purposes, contributes nothing to the power of the plaster under discussion. [The plaster of Azanites.] The plaster of Azanites is of many uses (polychrēstos) and renowned. Heras writes about it as follows.

The [785] [plaster] of Azanites. Take: dry pitch, 1 ounce; wax, 3 ounces; pig's fat, 3 ounces; bull's fat, 3 ounces; oesypum, 3 ounces; pine resin, 5 ounces. It is effective for all malignant conditions, gangrenes, fistulas, fresh wounds, burns, chillings of the extremities (peripsygmoi), [used] as an acopon. It is also an emollient pessary. It is suited too for ulcers in the womb, phymata, parotid swellings. When the ulcers are hollow, use the drug in greater quantity; but when [it is used] for cicatrization, less. It is a peculiarity of the drug that it produces a filthy crust (epipagos). It is also effective in those suffering from ophthalmia, when applied to the eyelids. Oil is antipathetic to the drug, therefore be on your guard. When you prepare it, put in the pitch, the wax, the bull's fat; and when they have melted, the pig's fat, then the resin, and last the oesypum, after cooling. Melt the whole over fire and not over flame. It is especially effective in those in whom the blow is around the sinews or a muscle, and in malignant cases.

[The plaster of Halieus, by means of Sinopian earth.] The plaster of Halieus, famous and of many uses (polychrēston) no less than the preceding ones, written thus [786] by Heras. The plaster of Halieus, for old and hard-to-cicatrize ulcers. It is also discutient (diaphorētikē), and especially for indurations around the breasts. We use it as the best for most conditions. Of wax 1 mina; of litharge 1 mina; of manna 8 drachms; of terebinth 8 drachms; of galbanum 8 drachms; of Sinopian earth 8 drachms; of old oil 2 cotylae. Boil the oil and the litharge until it becomes non-staining, then the wax, the resin; and when these have melted, having taken it off the fire, mix in the Sinopian earth, the galbanum, then the manna. This also works extremely well for wounds inflicted by sea-creatures. Indeed, I once used it on someone who had been struck by a sea stingray and was suffering most dreadfully, and it worked marvellously; likewise also on those stung by scorpions. These things, then, Heras wrote. Next let us look at those of Criton. [On the things written by Criton.] Heras composed one book on the composition of drugs, entitled Narthex. But five such books of Criton survive, apart from the Cosmetics.

In the fourth [787] of these five he goes through the plasters of the same kind as those already written, some, just as Heras, being in every respect the same, others in addition, which Heras did not mention, and which I shall now write in order, together with not omitting it if he mentions any of those written by Heras in a different way, as he appears to have done in the case of the plaster of Hicesius. For Criton wrote other weights and measures of this plaster, as some others also did, not the same as Heras. I shall begin, accordingly, with the first, that of Hicesius, since it is itself disputed with regard to the weight of the simple drugs from which they compound the plaster. [The plaster of Hicesius.] Concerning the plaster of Hicesius Criton wrote verbatim as follows.

The (plaster) of Hicesius: for every wound, fresh or old; for contusions, sprains, fractures; for inflammations and every pain — for it makes (the part) painless at once; for abscesses, phymata, scrofulous swellings, carbuncles, parotid swellings, phygethla, condylomata, lichens, corns, black marks (melaniai), inflamed haemorrhoids, fistulas, burns, when it is loosened with myrtle oil or rose oil; [788] for ulcers, splinters, arrow-points, dog bites, human bites, wounds from wild beasts; use it also as a haemostatic (ischaimos) and in place of a malagma for everything — but do not apply oil — and as an anakollema on patients suffering from ophthalmia, on a piece of linen. Let the compresses (splenia) always be rather large. It is effective also in dropsical patients. Take: ampelitis earth, asphalt, litharge, 2 minae each; wax, frankincense, terebinth, propolis, 1/2 mina each; galbanum, split alum, 5 minae each; myrrh, gall-nut, iris, 12 drachmae each; chalcitis, 6 drachmae; honey, 2 cotylae; omphacine oil, 2 choes, but some say 2 cotylae. Boil the ampelitis, the asphalt and the litharge with the oil, having first worked them into a pulp (προχυλώσας), so that they become smooth. Boil over a gentle fire, stirring continuously with a spatula of pine-wood, so that it does not settle to the bottom, for it burns very quickly. Melt the meltable ingredients in another vessel, having first boiled the honey separately so that it thickens, and mix them with the ingredients in the kettle once these have been well thickened; for it dissolves again when these are added (προβληθέντων); then sprinkle in the dry ingredients when you have cooled it somewhat, last of all the frankincense, and, having united the whole, use it.

I received this recipe from [789] Herodotus. These are the things Criton wrote about the plaster of Hicesius. But he appears to differ from Heras concerning the proportion of the simple drugs from which the whole is composed. And of the disagreement, one part is clear, the other hard to adjudicate. For Heras, acting rightly, reduced the weight of all the drugs to drachmas, whereas Criton wrote the ampelitis earth and the asphalt and the litharge not according to the weight in drachmas, but required that two minae of each of them be put in. But there is disagreement among those who have written on weights and measures as to how great the weight of the mina is, some saying that the mina is sixteen ounces, some twenty, and some also making a distinction and asserting that the Alexandrian mina is twenty ounces and the other sixteen; and this is a still smaller matter. But among those who reduce the mina to drachmas there are some who say that the mina is a hundred drachmas, and some say more, since the ounce too most say is seven and a half drachmas, but some only seven, and others eight.

These things being so, then, it is difficult to find out how many drachmas [790] one ought to reckon the mina written down by Criton to be. He appears, however, in other passages too to be one who wants the mina to be 100 drachmas. And if this is so, one must understand that the composition of the plaster of Hicesius has been written by him at double, since Heras, writing about these first three drugs—ampelitis earth, asphalt and litharge—gave the weight of each as one hundred drachmas, whereas Criton raises it to 200. Let us see, then, whether what follows agrees with the double; for some items appear to, others do not. After the first three he mentions wax, frankincense, terebinth and propolis, requiring that half a mina of each be put in, that is, 50 drachmas. For we laid it down that the proportion has been written on the assumption that the mina is 100 drachmas. But if this is so, in the case of the frankincense—evidently written in place of manna—there will be agreement between Criton and Heras. Likewise too in the case of propolis, but certainly not in the case of terebinth. For twenty-five drachmas ought

ought to have been written by Criton, since at any rate [791] Heras wrote twelve and a half. But in the case of the wax the greatest disagreement arose between the men, since Heras did not put in wax at all. For we have learned that the power of wax is moderately emollient. Next, in Criton it is written: of galbanum, of split alum, a quarter of a mina each — the man agreeing in this with Heras. For the quarter of the mina, on the assumption that it is 100 drachms, would come to twenty-five drachms; and these are double the twelve and a half written by Heras. Departing in what follows from the name of the mina, Criton orders that of myrrh and oak-gall and iris, twelve drachms of each of the three, be mixed with the aforesaid, agreeing in this with Heras; for that man ordered six of each to be put in. Next again Criton has written six drachms of chalcitis, differing here in no small way from Heras; for since all the quantities are double, the chalcitis too ought to have been written not as six drachms but as fifteen, since Heras at any rate wrote seven and a half. In the honey, however, the men agree, Heras having written one cotyle,

while [792] Crito wrote two kotylai. There remains, concerning the oil, an inquiry of no small size that would arise for us, not only in respect of these two men but also in respect of others among those who have written the drug, as we shall say in what follows. These two, at any rate, differ from one another on this point. For Heras wrote six kotylai of omotribes oil (of unripe olives); for it is better to write thus than, as some have written, six kyathoi, since Heras directs that, in the boiling, one should bring the litharge, the asphalt and the ampelitis earth to a half-boiled state, and then at that point add each of the other ingredients. But they would not become half-boiled if six kyathoi were put in. For we know that for the 100 drachmai of litharge many of the men who compound drugs often direct that two kotylai be put in. And indeed I already said all this earlier, in the first of these commentaries: that it is admissible, in the case of the metallic substances too, for the kotyle to be nine ounces, as some have supposed; and it is admissible also for it to be twelve

to reckon it, as others direct, knowing well that, if the drug should be boiled for a longer time—and this will happen when more [793] oil has been put in—it will become more drying, whereas if it should be taken quickly from the fire, because of the small quantity of the oil it will become less drying, but more emollient and more soothing; so that the six kyathoi must be rejected altogether, and six kotylai, each one of nine ounces, must be put in. But if you should wish to boil the drug for a longer time, so that it becomes more drying, nothing prevents the kotylai of twelve ounces too from being put in. Since, then, six kotylai are written by Heras, it is clear that Criton ought to have put in twelve kotylai, so that in this respect too the measure might be double, as in the case of the other ingredients. But what is written in his text is 'of omphacine oil, two choes'. Here again one must condemn those who wrote 'two kotylai'. As for the chous (χρέα, presumably for χοέα), if we reckon it at six kotylai, the agreement between the two men remains; but if not six kotylai but six xestai, no small disagreement will arise. For the quantity will be large relative to the proportion of the other ingredients, if one should put in twelve xestai of oil.

So much, for the present, concerning, in the drug under consideration, [794] the disagreement between Heras and Criton. But when we come to Andromachus, something will also be said about his agreement with both of them in some respects and his disagreement in others. [The green Isis.] This man too wrote down the Isis, just as nearly all the others also have. But since both the whole of its use and its preparation have been written more carefully by him, together with the fact that he also disagrees in small points with Heras, it seemed good to me to subjoin also what has been written by him word for word.

The Isis, which some call Epigonus' drug, is effective: undiluted, against separations of scales and thick exfoliations of bones; applied on lint and as a splenium, both against splinters and the blows and bites of all wild creatures, and it heals all the punctures and wounds inflicted by iron, in wars and otherwise, and fistulas, when applied on top and inserted as a collyrium, removing the callus of these and gluing them together; and this same drug, diluted, for every wound, applied on lint and as a splenium, and for malignant and chronic wounds and those spoiled by others, in which cases scrape beforehand and use the [795] diluted drug. It works wonderfully also for the agglutination of sinuses, so long as they are large; for by drawing out the moisture and gluing these together it is well suited, both on lint and diluted and undiluted, in cases where we wish to melt away certain glands or membranes lying within. Use it also for fractures, with a wound and without a wound; for it forms callus very quickly and binds tight the affected parts. And in cases where another malagma does not work, this works exactly: nails loosened by a stumble it either fixes firm or casts off, and teeth loosened by a blow it fixes firm; and in general there are countless conditions for which it works when handled in different ways. The relaxed form of it is: of the undiluted one part, of cerate two parts; sometimes it is relaxed still further. For this, practice and exercise are required. For the cerate is also sometimes made with pine resin. The composition: of ammoniac incense, 8 drachms; of scraped verdigris, 8 drachms; of ammoniac salt, 8 drachms; of scale of copper, 8 drachms; of burnt copper, 8 drachms; of round alum, 6 drachms; of aristolochia, 8 drachms; of frankincense, 8 drachms.

of myrrh [796] 12 drachms, of aloe 12 drachms, of galbanum 12 drachms, of wax 8, of Colophonian resin 6 drachms (some, however, [use] the same amount of terebinth), of old oil 2 cotylae, of vinegar 2 cotylae. Epigonus also [adds] 12 drachms of juice of dracontium root, 12 drachms of juice of horehound, and 8 drachms of juice of seris (endive). Having pounded and sifted everything carefully, put it into a mortar and, little by little, in the sun, pour on the vinegar, until, by grinding it fine, it has used up the whole of the vinegar. And when it has become smooth, melt the meltable ingredients, cool them, scrape them carefully and add them to the things in the mortar, and having kneaded it, take it up. These things Criton wrote; but I, having prepared it without the juice of seris, and sometimes also removing the alums, used it on those wounded in the nerves in the same way as the drug made of metallic substances written up in the discourse on those wounded in the nerves. For it becomes stronger if it is laid aside washed all around on every side with the sharpest vinegar and kneaded over a period of about fifteen days.

[The plaster of Machairion.] It is at once renowned and of many uses (polychrēston); it is suited also to those conditions of ulcers about which [797] this whole treatise is being written. Criton wrote it thus, word for word. The plaster of Machairion, effective for all fresh wounds, agglutinating them and keeping them free of inflammation, and especially those accompanied by contusion. In cases of those bitten by rabid dogs it is excellent, applied over a wider area and changed very frequently, and taken as a pill about the size of a bean for 30 days. For every spreading sore (nomē), and especially the phagedaenic kind, and for ulcers in the ears and in the genitals; on denuded bones it makes flesh grow, and (it is good) for ulcers in the nostrils. It is also green. It is diluted with rose-oil or omphacine oil. ℞ round aristolochia 1 oz.; galbanum 1 oz.; opopanax 1 oz.; scraped verdigris 1 oz.; Illyrian iris 1 oz.; ammoniac incense 1 oz.; myrrh 1 oz.; terebinth 7½ oz.; wax 7½ oz.; omphacine oil 7½ oz. Triturate half of the oil with the verdigris; boil the rest with the wax and the terebinth.

[The Dysrachitis, word for word as Damocrates gives it.] This too [798] is one of the famous and widely useful drugs. Criton writes about it as follows. The dysrachitis, acting remarkably when applied upon callused sinuses and fistulas. If there is an opening capable of admitting a small piece of linen smeared with the drug, insert it, and it will act more quickly. Use the preparation on very moist, rheumatic and chronic conditions, changing it for the most part every third day. It also acts wonderfully on gouty patients when it is spread on as a plaster at the beginning of the paroxysm and applied around over a broad area; and let them be released to their customary walks and the business of daily life without the bath, until the third day, and let them continue for some days. For it does not give the matter passage toward an intensification of the affection. It is also suitable for every ulcer when mixed with cerate in the proportion of six parts. As the preparation ages it becomes stronger. ♃ round alum 8 drachmas; scale 12 drachmas; burnt copper 4 drachmas; aristolochia 9 drachmas; galbanum 10 drachmas; ammoniac incense 12 drachmas, others 10 drachmas; frankincense 9 drachmas; myrrh 9 drachmas; storax 1 drachma; misy 3 drachmas.

of chalcitis [799] 3 drachms; of the heart of squill 8 drachms; of liquid pitch 4 drachms; of Illyrian iris 9 drachms, others 4; of terebinth resin 10 drachms, others 7 drachms; of pine resin 10 drachms, others 6; of wax 75 drachms; of oil 1½ pounds. Some add also deer marrow, 8 drachms, others 20. Grind beforehand the scale, the copper, the misy, the chalcitis and the squill with very sharp vinegar in the sun, so that they are made smooth. When they have become very finely ground, add the aristolochia and the iris. Having first pounded these and sifted them through a fine-meshed sieve, and having again poured vinegar over them, grind them fine, and do this for as long as any roughness shows itself, not sparing in the consumption of vinegar. When they have become smooth, put in the alum, and do the same until this too has been ground smooth. Then the myrrh, after which the frankincense, then the ammoniac, and after these the storax, then the pitch. Let these be heated in the hot sun, so that the storax may be worked up.

When everything has become smooth and has acquired a thickness like sordes (ῥυπῶδες) and like gloios (γλοιῶδες), melt the wax, the resins and the oil, and, having poured a little of the [800] boiling liquid over the galbanum and united it, grind it in a mortar; and after cooling for a little while, add the melted ingredients, then, having put in the galbanum and dissolved it, strain into an earthenware vessel and, scraping it out, mix it with the things in the mortar. [The plaster made with willows.] The plaster made with willows, which is itself also renowned and a polychreston (of many uses), Crito writes, in the same way as the ones written above, thus: The plaster made with willows, suited for fresh (bleeding) wounds and loosened joints, and for fistulas when inserted into them, and for flabby flesh, especially that on the extremities. It works also for erysipelas and for very many other conditions, except burns. Take misy, chalcitis, verdigris, white lead, oak-galls, split alum and round alum, melanteria, 6 ounces of each; wax, pine resin, pitch, asphalt, willow leaves, 2 ounces of each; oil, 4 kotylai 4 ounces; chalcanthum, 6 ounces; pomegranate rinds, 6 ounces; vinegar, 6 xestai. Boil the willows with vinegar until 2 xestai are left.

boil; then add the leaves to the verdigris, previously ground fine, and to the white lead and the melanteria, and grind them together, [801] then the dry ingredients, finely ground, and again reduce to a juice, then pour the melted ingredients over. Asclepiades prepares this one without the chalkanthon and the pomegranate rinds, as has been written in the earlier book, the second. Next after this one Criton wrote another of willows, roughly as follows. The simple one of willows, as Herodotus gives it: ♃ melanteria, omphakitis oak-gall, split alum, round alum, 6 ounces each; wax, bitumen, dry pitch, willow leaves, pine resin, 2 pounds each; oil 1 pound; vinegar half a sextarius. [On the plasters of the same kind written by Asclepiades.] Among these, from those written above, are the one of the Fisherman, known to everyone, and the one of dittany. But since Asclepiades wrote clearly about them, for this reason I shall now also recall them. There is also another useful thing in what is written twice and three times: to come to know in respect of which of the ingredients put into them those who wrote them agreed with one another, and in which they disagreed; and likewise in the claims made about them.

[802] The plaster of Halieus. Tawny. It works for bloody wounds and for severings of nerves, and for ulcers that are old, hard to cicatrize, and rheumatic. It is also a good emollient, especially for the indurations that arise around the breasts. We use it also on those bitten by dogs and those bitten by human beings. It works supremely also for the strokes of sea stingrays and weevers and of the other dangerous fishes, and in general its power is marvellous. Take litharge, wax, 100 drachmas each; terebinth, manna of frankincense, galbanum, Sinopic red ochre, 8 drachmas each; oil, 1 xestes. Prepare in the usual manner. Galen's version of the plaster of Halieus. Take litharge, wax, 100 drachmas each; terebinth (the text's τερμινμινθίνης is a corruption of τερμινθίνης), myrrh, Sinopic ochre, scraped verdigris, scale of copper, 8 drachmas each; aristolochia, 8 drachmas; frankincense, 25 drachmas; diphryges, 6 drachmas; galbanum, 12 drachmas; ammoniac incense, 12 drachmas; oil, 2 kotylai. Prepare in the usual manner. The plaster of the hunters. A well-tried drug.

It works also against the wounds and bites of four-footed animals and the remaining [injuries] from venomous creatures. [803] Take litharge, 1 mina; old oil, scale of red copper, wax, roasted resin, 1 litra each; ammoniac incense, 4 ounces; galbanum, Sinopic red earth, 2 ounces each. Boil the litharge, the scale and the oil until they reach consistency, then add the wax and the resin. And when it has melted, having removed it from the fire, add the ammoniac, having flattened it out. And when it has cooled, add the galbanum and ammoniac, sprinkling on the Sinopic earth, and having poured it out into a mortar and kneaded it until soft, use it. The [plaster] of the Chalcidean. Agglutinative, non-inflammatory. It works also against divisions accompanied by contusion, and it glues together sinuses and dries them up and prevents abscessions; it brings up corrupted bones; and it works especially also on the extremities, and in general its power is wonderful. Litharge, copper scale, pine resin, wax, 100 drachmas each; ammoniac incense, galbanum, 16 drachmas each; diphryges, 12 drachmas; aristolochia, most finely ground, 40 drachmas; old oil, three xestai.

Boil the litharge and the scale with the oil, and when it changes colour, add the diphryges, then the wax and the pine resin [804] or the fir resin. And when it has melted and become non-staining, having taken it off the fire, add the ammoniac, having washed it. And when it has melted, sprinkle on the aristolochia once the drug has become cold, and stir continuously; then, having emptied it out into a mortar and kneaded it, take it up and use it. [The hiera through dittany, a marvellous preparation.] For severances and contusions of nerves and muscles. It is effective also for old and hard-to-heal conditions; it brings up corrupted bones and splinters and arrow-points, and it is also discutient. It is effective also for pains of the head and fluxes of the eyes; it is also a good malagma for pleuritics and hepatics. It is effective also for the wound of every venomous creature. Take: litharge, 100 drachms; Colophonian resin, 50 drachms; wax, 25 drachms; ammoniac incense, aristolochia, 16 drachms each; manna, galbanum, 12 drachms each; verdigris, dittany, burnt copper, aloe, propolis, 8 drachms each; diphryges, scale of copper, gentian root, 6 drachms each; old oil, in winter 2 cotylae, in summer 1½. Prepare in the usual manner.

The written version of this man differs [805] from that of Heras in respect of the weights in the following points: whereas this man orders that 8 drachms of dittany be put in, Heras ordered ten. And moreover, of aristolochia and of ammoniac incense this man puts 16 drachms of each, but Heras twenty-six of ammoniac incense and 10 of aristolochia. As for the oil, Heras wrote it without distinction, ordering simply 2 kotylai, whereas Asclepiades orders that much in winter, but one and a half in summer. [The plaster] of Diophantus the surgeon, which Phylacus used. Take litharge 150 drachms; white lead, pitch, scale of copper, wax, 18 drachms each; verdigris, dry pine resin, manna of frankincense, propolis, 12 drachms each; galbanum, aristolochia, cyperus, 6 drachms each; dittany, trefoil, ammoniac incense, 3 drachms each; Illyrian iris, artemisia, polion, horehound, 2 drachms each; old oil 2 kotylai. Prepare in the usual manner.

[On the plasters of the same kind written by Andromachus.] I set out, in this book, to go through plasters that are polychrēsta (of many uses) and at the same time effective against ulcers hard to cicatrize. [806] Among these, then, are also the ten finest of those written by Andromachus. The green (plaster) of Euangeus. Take: terebinth resin — others say dry (resin) — 50 drachms, others 100 drachms; wax 25 drachms; frankincense 3 drachms; scale 3 drachms; galbanum 3 drachms; aloe 3 drachms; myrrh 3 drachms; ammoniac salt 2 drachms; opopanax 2 drachms; scraped verdigris 2 drachms; burnt copper 2 drachms; aristolochia 2 drachms; ammoniac incense (gum ammoniac) 2 drachms; split (alum) — others say round — 2 drachms; fish-glue 3 drachms; vinegar 4 cotylae; oil a quarter of a cotyle, others an eighth. Use it without the insertion of a skōlēx (tent). The rhypōdēs (dirt-coloured) plaster, which I use. Take: fish-glue 3 ounces; sarcocolla 3 ounces; Asian stone 3 ounces; Eretrian (earth) half a pound; Samian earth 4 ounces; myrrh 4 ounces; frankincense 6 ounces; copper scale 8 ounces; ammoniac salt 3 ounces; scraped verdigris 6 ounces; split alum 2 ounces; Indian aloe 4 ounces; galbanum 4 ounces; wax 2 pounds; terebinth 2 pounds; oil 4 pounds; vinegar for soaking the fish-glue.

Sprinkle the dry ingredients, finely ground, [807] into the meltable ingredients. Another green plaster. Take: pine resin, 200 drachmas; ammoniac incense, 50 drachmas; opopanax, 8 drachmas; wax, 100 drachmas; propolis, 8 drachmas; galbanum, 8 drachmas; copper scale, 12 drachmas; verdigris, 12 drachmas; round alum, 8 drachmas; misy, 7 drachmas; ammoniac salt, 8 drachmas; chalcitis, 5 drachmas; unburnt sulphur, 8 drachmas; frankincense, 12 drachmas; bull's bile, dried, 6 drachmas, or liquid, 12; henna oil, 6 cotylae (others say 4); vinegar, a sufficient quantity. Green plaster of Epicurus, holding out much promise. Take: wax, 200 drachmas; Colophonian resin, 300 drachmas; scale, 16 drachmas; burnt copper, 16 drachmas; verdigris, 16 drachmas; slender aristolochia, 16 drachmas; aloe, 24 drachmas; round alum, 12 drachmas; myrrh, 24 drachmas; galbanum, 24 drachmas; ammoniac salt, 16 drachmas; vinegar, 4 cotylae; oil, 2 cotylae, and sometimes less. Green plaster, holding out much promise, of Alcimion or Nicomachus. For fistulas and for parts that are turning black, or spreading sores; it glues bones together, and brings up and disperses scrofulous swellings. Take: galbanum, 16 drachmas; burnt copper, 8 drachmas; scale, 24 drachmas; wax, 50 drachmas; goat's or calf's suet, 30 drachmas; frankincense, 25 drachmas.

[808] of dry resin 25 drachms, of ammoniac incense 25 drachms, of terebinth resin 25 drachms, of nitre 25 drachms, of aristolochia 25 drachms, of bryony 12 drachms, of the herb orchis 12 drachms, of dry iris 4 drachms, of Indian aloe 12 drachms, of split alum 8 drachms, of bull's gall 8 drachms, of vinegar one cotyle, of oil 1 cotyle; and when it is smeared on, with rose-oil. A green plaster for herpetes, according to Andromachus, and for Chironian ulcers and those hard to cicatrize. Take of burnt barley 10 drachms, of verdigris 8 drachms, of wax 80 drachms, of henna oil 1 cotyle. This drug contains a great deal of verdigris in relation to the proportion of the wax and the henna oil. For the burnt barley, sprinkled on by itself, benefits the Chironian ulcers, neither intensifying the power of the wax and the henna oil nor weakening that of the verdigris. And if it is removed, the drug becomes similar to many of those written down in the book before this one, in the section on the cure of such ulcers. It will not, however, take a generous amount of henna oil, especially if the wax is oily, but only as much as is necessary for softening the wax that has been mixed with the verdigris.

All the plasters written above have become of many uses (polychrēsta) [809] for this reason, that they have taken on drugs that are emollient, attractive, discutient, concoctive, and further those that dry without biting; and most of them also drugs that are strongly astringent, whose power is repellent of the humours flowing in upon the affected part. The materials of the aforesaid power of drugs you have written by name in the treatise on simple drugs, in the sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth and eleventh books. And I have mentioned many of them by name in the present treatise and shall mention them again; and indeed I have added this drug here too, wishing to remind you of these very things which I have just said, since in fact it too is of the same kind as those written before in the book preceding this one, and it would have been more appropriate for it to have been written together with those. [The black Hicesian plaster of Andromachus.] This plaster Andromachus wrote not in the place where he wrote the green ones, but higher up, near the beginning, and in a proportion differing greatly from that in which, as I showed earlier, both Crito and Heras wrote it.

The [810] recipe runs thus. ♃ Of bitumen, 300 drachmai; of ampelitis earth, 200 drachmai; of litharge, 60 drachmai; of galbanum, 36 drachmai; of terebinth, 36 drachmai; of split alum, 36 drachmai; of propolis, 72 drachmai; of manna, 50 drachmai; of myrrh, 12 drachmai; of iris, 12 drachmai; of chalkitis, 6 drachmai; of oak-gall, 10 drachmai; of oil, one chous and a half; of honey, half a kotyle. He did well in removing the ambiguity concerning the mina and writing everything in drachmai, so that we have to inquire only about the chous; for on this point those who wrote six kotylai did better. They began the recipe with a triple quantity of bitumen, as compared with the recipe written by Heras; for Heras wrote 100 drachmai, whereas this man wrote 300, and in some copies, which are not trustworthy, I found 200. The ampelitis earth, however, is clearly written as double that in Heras. But the litharge, which itself too ought to have been equal in weight to the ampelitis, has been put in by him in a much smaller amount; for he mixes in sixty drachmai of it, while of galbanum thirty-six

having put in [thirty-six] drachmai, he does not preserve the proportion relative to Heras and Criton, just as also in the case of the split alum; for in this [811] he departs slightly from the exact proportion, which comes out to thirty-seven and a half. In the terebinth he differs slightly from Heras, by as much, evidently, as in the galbanum and the split alum; but from Criton very greatly, since the latter orders a mina and a half to be put in, which, relative to the proportion of his other ingredients, comes out to fifty drachmai. In the case of the propolis, however, he deviated slightly relative to double the proportion. And in the manna too he differs from both Heras and Criton; for he ought to have put in 100 drachmai relative to their proportion; and in the chalkitis he subtracted very much indeed from the proportion. In the other ingredients the disagreement is slight, except as regards the honey; for he ought to have put in 3 kotylai relative to their proportion, but he has put in half a kotyle (κοτύλας ἥμισυ). And so too in the oil: relative to Criton he ought to have put in three choes, and relative to Heras eighteen kotylai; but he in fact wrote one chous and a half.

[How Heracleides of Tarentum wrote the [812] black plaster of Hicesius.] For every wound, and especially those on the extremities, rendering them painless and agglutinating them; also for dog-bites and boils, and dispersing indurations, especially those around the breasts, and the condylomata in the anus. Take: litharge, 100 drachmas; asphalt, an equal amount; ampelitis earth, an equal amount; manna, 25 drachmas; propolis, an equal amount; galbanum, 12½ drachmas; split alum, terebinth resin, an equal amount; iris, 6 drachmas; chalcitis, 7½ drachmas; oak-gall, 8 drachmas; myrrh, an equal amount; honey, 1 cotyle; oil of unripe olives (omotribes), 6 cotylai. Boil the litharge and the asphalt and the earth with the oil, stirring with a spatula of pine-wood. When it has set, add the propolis and the resin and the galbanum; let these have been previously boiled in the honey; and once these have been mixed in, immediately lifting the pot from the fire, sprinkle in the dry ingredients. Since Heracleides wrote these things in his books addressed to Antiochis, I wonder how some of those after him did not preserve his text. Heras, then, appears to have followed Heracleides in every respect, except in the myrrh and the oak-gall.

For whereas Heraclides puts in eight [813] drachms of each of these, Heras took six of each of these. And in Asclepiades, in the second book of the External Remedies, everything has been written in fourfold proportion relative to Heras, together with the fact that twelve kotylai of omphacine oil have also been written, Criton having written two choes. And yet his composition had everything at the double amount, which is why some seem to me to have written in addition two kotylai; but this very thing in turn is at odds to a greater degree both with the truth and with the writing of the Tarentine and of Heras. For Heras wrote 180 drachms, reducing the oil to weight and not to measure, on the basis that the kotyle weighs sixty drachms; for the Attic one at any rate does weigh that, being of nine Italian ounces. For the nine Italian ounces, those marked on the graduated horns, weigh seven and a half weight-ounces, which come to sixty drachms, the single ounce containing eight drachms; so that in this respect too Heras agrees with Heraclides in putting in three kotylai, Asclepiades having written twelve, since everything in his composition has been written at four times the amount.

But Heras, since [814] the bulk of the drug became large according to the Tarentine's prescription, seems to me for this reason to have written a quarter of all [the quantities]. For one must, as I said, make a slight alteration in the myrrh and the oak-gall. And although others too have written this plaster of Hicesius, those who prepared it more accurately, in accordance both with the Tarentine and with the [prescription] judged by us through boiling to be the true one, have turned out in agreement; but those who [did so] more carelessly, whether in one only or two of the ingredients mixed in or even more, are seen to disagree with Heracleides. Therefore it seemed to me superfluous to mention them. For the drug is to be prepared as Heracleides directed or as Heras [did], for the difference between them is very slight. Heracleides says that the following is the plain [plaster] of Hicesius: Take asphalt 50 drachms, litharge 50 drachms, oil 10 kotylai; boil, and when it sets, add wax 5 drachms, galbanum 5 drachms, myrrh 5 drachms.

[The Cyzicene of Heras.] This too is one of the celebrated plasters, written down by nearly everyone, these authors having for the most part written things that agree as regards the proportion of the simple drugs, but having also disagreed in some, [815] as will be evident when we have set down below how each of them thinks it ought to be compounded. Heras, then, writes as follows, word for word, about the plaster before us. Cyzicene, effective for fresh wounds and for old ones that are undermining (ὑπόνομα). It especially disperses the hardnesses in the breasts, draws, cleanses, fills up, agglutinates, cicatrizes. It is effective also for cancerous hardnesses, lipourga (λιποῦργα), and in cases where it is not possible to use the scalpel, as on the neck, use it in the form of a collyrium. It also soothes abscesses that are threatening, disperses phymata and ganglia, and brings collections to a head and breaks them. It also brings up missiles and bones and splinters. And it painlessly shakes off eschars as well. In the case of the undermining ulcers one must use the large compresses (splenia). It also disperses scrofulous swellings (choirades) and checks haemorrhoids and is supremely effective in affections about the bladder. It contains: frankincense 4 drachms, myrrh 4 dr., saffron 4 dr., Illyrian iris 4 dr., bdellium 4 dr., scale (of copper) 12 drachms, chalcanthum 4 dr., split alum 4 dr., round (alum) 4 dr., ammoniac incense 4 dr., misy 4 dr., rind of sweet pomegranate 4 dr.

of aristolochia, of unripe oak-gall (omphakitis) [816] 8 drachms each—otherwise 16; of chalkitis 4 drachms; of ammoniac incense 4 drachms; of oak birdlime (ixos) 8 drachms; of opopanax 8 drachms; of scraped verdigris 8 drachms; of acacia 8 drachms; of rose-flower 8 drachms; of terebinth resin 1 mina—others 50 drachms; of poppy juice 6 drachms; of wax 2 minae—others 4 drachms; of treated calf's suet 1 mina—others 150; of common vinegar 2 kotylai; wine for the dry ingredients. Since both Heras and Andromachus have written these things about the Kyzikene, it will seem to some that there is a very great disagreement, inasmuch as Heras puts in 4 drachms of frankincense and saffron and myrrh and of what is written by him next in order, whereas Andromachus puts in 8. But what I was already saying before too, that we must keep in view, this I shall say now as well: if, in the case of all the simple drugs, someone were to put in even double the quantities written by others, the same proportion results, just as also if all were triple. And so now too Andromachus has put in nearly everything doubled, Heras having put them in single.

But he differs in adding aloe, Heras not having added [817] it, and indeed also the root of panax. For Heras wrote opopanax only; Andromachus, however, not this only but also panax. And they customarily call thus the root of the herb which they name panax. Andromachus has in addition also added the juice of poppy for the sake of freedom from pain, and acacia and flower of roses as astringents. The boiling Heras wrote, as is his custom, but Andromachus omits it, as it is again this man's custom too, since he rarely writes the boiling. Nevertheless, from his adding at the end "two kotylai of common vinegar; wine for the dry ingredients", it is clear that he wishes the dry ingredients to be ground fine with the wine or the vinegar, and then the meltable ingredients, once melted, to be poured over these. Heras, however, made no mention at all of vinegar or wine, and at the end of the boiling he added the following: "Finally, throw the dry ingredients and the opopanax into the cauldron, and having united them, pour out and knead, smearing your hands with iris oil."

But I myself prepare it according to Andromachus' method, triturating the opopanax in the mortar together with the dry ingredients: if I should wish to make the drug stronger [818] and more discutient, mixing in the vinegar during the trituration; but if more astringent and more repellent, the wine. Just as, again, of the wine itself too, I sometimes choose the harsh kind, sometimes the tawny, and sometimes the old, sometimes that of middle age. For the harsh and not old wine is more astringent, while the old and not harsh is more discutient. [The Cyzicene, according to Asclepiades.] This plaster has already been written also in the fourth book, when I wrote in that book, all in sequence, the drugs which he advised one to have against malignancy. And now, since he too disagrees with both Heras and Andromachus, it seems to me better to write out verbatim what he wrote in the third book of the external drugs, in these very words. Cyzicene. It is effective for chronic conditions and for severances of the nerves. Take frankincense of the finest quality, wax, myrrh, aristolochia, chalcitis, Illyrian (iris), galbanum, 4 drachmas each; terebinth resin, litharge, 8 drachmas each; oil, 1 cotyle.

Having put everything into [819] a bronze vessel, boil over soft ash, stirring until, when a drop of it is let fall into cold water, it has the thickness of honey. After this take it off while stirring; having smeared this onto a small piece of leather, apply it, and loosen it in winter after the seventh day, in summer after the fifth. [Another, from the writings of Philoxenus.] Take frankincense, myrrh, saffron, Illyrian (iris), bdellium, scale of copper, chalkanthon, chalkitis, round and split alum, foreign misy, ammoniac incense, propolis, oak birdlime (ixos), opopanax, closed pomegranate rinds (σιδίων μεμυκότων), four drachms of each; aristolochia, eight drachms; wax, bull's suet, one hundred drachms of each, which he writes as a mina; terebinth resin, fifteen drachms, which he writes as three quarters. Having put the resin into an earthenware pan, boil until it becomes odourless; then, having grated the suet and the wax, add them and melt. Pound the dry ingredients and sift them through the finest sieve; then, having taken the meltable ingredients off the fire and allowed them to cool somewhat, sprinkle the dry ingredients over these and stir carefully.

One must also have ready, ground with vinegar, myrrh, frankincense, [820] bdellium, opopanax. To these add the contents of the pan and rub, so that no wax-lumps (enkerides) form. When it is in good condition, take it up into a wooden box, having smeared it over with iris ointment. [The one through the two aristolochias, as Andromachus.] Concerning this Andromachus writes, word for word, as follows: the one through the two aristolochias. Take roasted (phrykte) resin one litra, wax one litra, pitch one litra, castor oil or old oil one kotyle and two kyathoi, white lead six ounces, verdigris six ounces, chalcanthum four ounces, manna six ounces, long aristolochia four ounces and round four ounces, Eretrian earth six ounces, Illyrian iris four ounces, oak-gall two ounces, vinegar one kotyle—I use more—pomegranate rinds two ounces. Grind the dry ingredients with vinegar, then the meltable ingredients. [The one through dittany, as Damocrates.] It has often been said by me that metrical writings are more useful than those written in prose, not only for memory but also for the accuracy of the proportion of the ingredients that are mixed.

For this reason, [821] then, I have now also appended the plaster through dittany, which preserves an exact proportion in the writing of Damocrates. It is one of the celebrated plasters, and the only one containing the Cretan herb called dittany; it heals the strokes of venomous creeping things and the bites of all quadrupeds, even if one of them has gone rabid, and callused ulcers, and the corruptions of the nerves and of muscles and of the cartilages lying upon the bones, when they already have corruption in depth. It also treats the ulcers about the breasts and neck and spine, even if the condition be of long standing; and all those things which I said, a little earlier, that the plaster called Egyptian does. This plaster, being exceedingly good, some think to be even the only one better than all the good ones, not having experience of many drugs.

It contains litharge, twice one hundred drachmas, [822] and of old oil a quarter of a litra (though some say rather a quarter of a kotyle); twice twenty-five drachmas of Pontic wax; of good Colophonian resin, double the wax—but some rather [use] the same amount of terebinth resin; of verdigris of copper and of Indian aloe, of burnt copper and of good diphryges, sixteen and a half [drachmas] from each ingredient; twenty-four drachmas of galbanum; of manna and of frankincense equal amounts, twice twelve; of ammoniac twice five and twice twenty; sixteen drachmas of Attic propolis; of long aristolochia twice ten drachmas; twice six drachmas of scale of Cyprian copper, and of the driest gentian root an equal amount. To all these add in addition twenty holkai of dittany herb, dried, bearing its flower, finely ground.

and having put the litharge with the oil [823] into a new, wide-mouthed earthenware pan, boil over a light and gentle fire, stirring with a spatula, until it acquires the thickness of Attic honey. And having added also an equal amount of the scale, boil again more vigorously; then, when the drug has become tawny, add the copper and the diphryges, and, making the drug non-staining and set, add the wax together with the resin. When these have melted together, when you see the plaster blended, you lift the pot from the fire, and, having added propolis and galbanum, ammoniac, manna and aloe, then, having cooled the fiery and boiling heat of the drug, you will sprinkle in aristolochia, very finely ground, and gentian and the herb dittany; and having beaten the drug up further with the spatula and with the hands, and making it into cakes, keep it, using it for the circumstances I mentioned before.

[824] [On the troches of Asclepiades.] Just as some of the physicians named plasters from their colour, and not from the profession of their power, as quince-yellow, white, grey and tawny, so too they name troches from the shape given them in moulding, though they differ not with respect to one affection but with respect to very many. Following them, therefore, we too shall write out all of them in order—those at least that are approved—whether one calls them cyclisci (small disks) or trochisci (troches), for they name them in both ways. They did well in prefixing to each its profession, and especially Asclepiades, whose drugs written in the third book of those for external conditions I shall set out first. Troches of Asclepiades. Troches of many uses (polychrēsta) of Aristarchus of Tarsus.

It works for recent and old ulcers; it works also for teredones [worm-eaten bone], honeycomb sores (keria); it works for fistulas, ears discharging pus, corrupted bones; it works for spreading sores (nomai), reduces every excrescence, removes pterygia; it works for the conditions about the womb, for ozaenae, phagedaenae, condylomata; it works for chronic and hard-to-heal conditions; it works [825] for incipient phthisics, splenetics, coeliacs, dysenterics, being given in the weight of three obols with the appropriate drink. It also benefits synanchic patients and spreading sores of the gums, and in general it is well suited to conditions both external and internal. Take: myrrh 6 drachms, saffron 3 drachms, crocomagma 3 drachms, pomegranate blossoms (kytinoi) 6 drachms, chalcanthum 6 drachms, split alum 6 drachms, aloe 6 drachms; take up in Falernian wine and make troches and dry in the shade. At the time of use, dissolve in a liquid suited to the underlying conditions. The troche of Neapolites: take myrrh 6 dr., frankincense 6 dr., oak-galls 8 dr., lycium 8 dr., alum 8 dr., crocomagma 8 dr., aloe 8 dr., pomegranate blossoms 12 dr., copper 8 dr., in Falernian wine. The one inscribed 'Andronios': take pomegranate blossoms 10 dr., split [alum] 4 dr., chalcanthum 12 dr., myrrh 4 dr., frankincense 8 dr., aristolochia 8 dr., oak-galls (kykidōn, read kēkidōn) 8 dr., sweet wine 2 cotylae. In Heracleides it reads thus: take pomegranate rinds 10 dr., aristolochia 8 dr., oak-galls 8 dr., ammoniac salt 4 dr., frankincense 4 dr., split [alum] 4 dr., chalcanthum 2 dr., myrrh 4 dr.

[826] take up with sweet wine. The seal (sphragis) of Polyeides: ♃ pomegranate rinds 6 dr., myrrh 8 dr., split alum 5 dr., frankincense 4 dr., aloe 8 dr., chalcanthum 3 dr., bull's gall 6 dr.; take up with sweet wine. The "raven" seal (korakine sphragis). It works for inflammations of the tonsils and relaxed uvulas, and for gums that are rotting (mydonta); it works for spreading sores (nomai). It works for the conditions around the seat and removes the callus from fistulas. ♃ round Cretan aristolochia, cytini (pomegranate flower-cups), roasted chalcitis, frankincense, myrrh, chalcanthum, crocomagma, Indian aloe, bull's gall, 8 dr. of each; of sweet wine a sufficient quantity. A troche for spreading sores. ♃ savin 50 dr., myrrh 3 dr., sory 2 dr., cyperus 2 dr., chalcanthum 2 dr., frankincense 2 dr.; take up with wine. In other copies: olive leaves 2 dr., dried myrtle 4 dr., the plant orchis 4 dr., arsenic 1 dr., myrrh 4 dr. From the writings of Heracleides. ♃ orchis 2 dr., arsenic 4 dr., oak-galls 8 dr., scale (lepis) 8 dr., scale 6 dr., sory 8 dr., myrrh 2 dr., frankincense 2 dr., acacia juice 2 dr.; take up with wine.

The one entitled "through [827] the plants" (dia tōn phytōn). ℞ pomegranate rinds 8 dr., myrtle leaves 8 dr., dry walnut shells 8 dr., fruit of thorn (akantha) 8 dr., oak-galls 4 dr., mined salt 8 dr. All are crushed, then kneaded with vinegar and put into an earthenware vessel, then roasted and ground fine with vinegar. And when it is in good condition, add myrrh 4 dr., frankincense 2 dr., and form into troches; the use is with vinegar. In Terentius it is entitled "astringent" (styptikē). It works against every spreading ulcer (nomē) and the conditions around the anus (daktylios). ℞ sandarach, misy, chalkanthon, split alum, two drachmas each; myrrh, flakes of copper, aloe, chalkitis, 3 dr. each; pomegranate flowers (kytinoi), rose blossom, oak-galls, 4 dr. each; juice of acacia 8 dr.; pomegranate rinds 8 dr. Take up with a decoction of myrtle berries boiled down to half. Troche for herpetic conditions. Of Areios, for herpetes. ℞ Cimolian earth 8 dr., roasted misy 16 dr., Sinopic red ochre (miltos) 3 dr. Grind each separately with water, then, having mixed them together, form into troches. The use is with vinegar. Another, the one with origanum. ℞ origanum 2 dr., olive leaves 2 dr., acacia 2 dr.

of chalcanthum [828] 2 drachms, of Spanish salt 2 drachms; take up with vinegar. From the writings of Largus, a successful drug. ♃ Of litharge or white lead 38 drachms, of split alum 12 drachms, of acacia 8 drachms, of saffron, frankincense, diphryges, opium, 2 drachms each. Triturate with water and form into pastilles. The use is with water. Another, very excellent. ♃ Of round alum, of chalcitis, of melanteria or sory, 2 drachms each; of misy, of pomegranate rinds, 4 drachms each; of quicklime 16 drachms; of vinegar 1 xestes. Boil the pomegranate rinds with the vinegar, and when they have dissolved, triturate with the acacia and add to the rest, and when it is in good condition, form into pastilles. The use is with water. As Threptus (prepared it), for creeping affections and wherever one must check a spreading sore. It is effective also for the affections in the mouth, for ears discharging pus, for eruptions, excrescences of flesh and the ulcers in the nostrils, for the affections about the seat. ♃ Of pomegranate rinds 10 drachms, of omphakitis gall 8 drachms, of aristolochia 8 drachms, of aloe 4 drachms, of myrrh 8 drachms, of split (alum) 2 drachms, of frankincense 4 drachms, of chalcanthum 4 drachms; take up with sweet wine.

[829] [Tawny troches of Hierax of Thebes, the one made with halicacabum.] It works for psydrakes, epinyctides, and the ulcers in the nostrils. It works for fissures (rhagades) and for whatever you wish to cicatrize without pain. ♃ Of white lead (psimythion) one litra, of litharge ten litrai, of split alum, of bark of halicacabum, of chalkanthon, of Sinopic earth, half a litra each; take up with vinegar. Of Lucius the Teacher (Kathegetes), a well-tried drug. ♃ Of alum, of Corinthian verdigris, of Sinopic red ochre, an equal amount by the measure of a kotyle; take up with vinegar. From the writings of Areius. For spreading psorai, herpetic sores, excrescences of flesh, pterygia, ears running with pus, ulcers hard to heal. It works for fissures and condylomata. ♃ Of split alum, of Sinopic red ochre, of scraped verdigris, of gum, of oak-galls, of kytinoi (pomegranate-flower cups), an equal amount of each; take up with vinegar. As Magnus of Philadelphia used it for the aforesaid conditions. ♃ Of split alum, of Corinthian verdigris, of chalkitis, of Sinopic red ochre, of gum, an equal amount by measure; take up with vinegar. A troche for erysipelas. ♃ Of saffron one drachm, of opium one drachm,

white lead [830] 2 drachms; take up with sweet wine. In other copies it has 8 drachms of glaucium. The saffron-coloured (remedy) of Andromachus, a well-tested drug. Take litharge 4 drachms, that is, half an ounce; white lead 4 ounces; unburnt sulphur 1 ounce; saffron, opium, 1 ounce each; take up with juice of strychnos. At the time of use dilute with sweet wine. (The remedy) of Gaius of Neapolis. Take white lead, acacia, glaucium, opium, an equal amount of each; take up with sweet wine, and anoint continually. Another. Take white lead 8 drachms, acacia 8 drachms, ammoniac incense 4 drachms, saffron 2 drachms, opium 2 drachms, juice of knotgrass or of seris or of strychnos or of hound's-tongue. From the (writings) of Agathinus. Take white lead 6 drachms; manna, frankincense, 1 drachm each; crocomagma 2 drachms; unburnt sulphur 2 drachms; yolks of boiled eggs 6 drachms; take up with sweet wine. For fissures and condylomata. (The remedy) of Menestheus for fissures in the anus; it is effective against spreading sores. Take aloe 6 ounces, saffron 3 ounces, split alum 3 ounces; take up with wine and make troches.

At the time of use, let the [831] liquid be suited to the condition. Of Apollophanes, for fissures and condylomata. Take stibium 8 drachmas, acacia 6 drachmas, verdigris 1 drachma, opium 2 drachmas, frankincense 1½ drachmas, myrrh 2 drachmas, gum 4 drachmas; form into troches with wine free of sea-water. But as Nicolaus gives it: Take stibium 8 drachmas, acacia 8 drachmas, verdigris one drachma, opium 3 drachmas, myrrh 4 drachmas, gum 4 drachmas; form with wine. From the writings of Magnus, for fissures and condylomata; it checks spreading ulcers. Take aloe 8 drachmas, acacia 4 drachmas, oak-gall 2 drachmas, saffron 2 drachmas, frankincense 1 drachma, myrrh 1 drachma; take up with wine. The one entitled "that of the juices", for spreading ulcers and scabby conditions. Take Indian lycium, Indian aloe, myrrh, copper, split alum, chalcanthum, pomegranate-flower cups (kytinoi), frankincense, 4 drachmas each; juice of myrtle-berries, half a kotyle; compound and form into troches. The "Virtue" of Petronius, a well-tried drug for fissures and condylomata; even in the greatest intense pains it brings relief, and quickly.

♃ Of stibium, acacia, lead burnt and washed, [832] 16 drachmas each; of Cyprian spodos, fruit of heath (ereikē), split alum, frankincense, chalkanthon, myrrh, opium, 8 drachmas each. Take up with wine and make pastilles. At the time of use, dilute with sweet (wine). [The pastilles written by Andromachus are in the (book) of external remedies.] Pastille of Darius, good for the seat. ♃ Of stibium 16 drachmas, of acacia 16 drachmas, others 8; of verdigris 40 drachmas; of poppy juice 3 drachmas, others 2 drachmas; of gum 4 drachmas; of myrrh 1 drachma; of frankincense 3 drachmas, others 2 drachmas; wine, others water. A polychrēston (of many uses), both pus-forming and relaxing. ♃ Of frankincense bark 2 drachmas, of copper scale 4 drachmas; form (the pastilles) with wine, dilute with honey. The remedy (iatreion) of Musa. ♃ Of split (alum), aloe, myrrh, chalkanthon, 6 drachmas each; of saffron 3 drachmas, of krokomagma 3 drachmas, of kytinoi (pomegranate flower-cups) 4 drachmas; take up with honeyed wine made from Falernian wine. For erysipelata, from Agathocles. ♃ Of white lead 8 drachmas, of round alum 2 drachmas, of krokomagma 2 drachmas, of unburnt sulphur 2 drachmas.

to the ingredients, finely ground, the juice of strychnos is poured over, and form [833] troches; at the time of use, with dry wine. Isidorus' remedy for nomai. ♃ greasy wool 40 drachms, lead filings 10 drachms, scale 10 drachms, bitumen 10 drachms, split alum 5 drachms and round [alum] 5, pomegranate rinds 5 drachms, oak-galls 5 drachms, misy 5 drachms, chalcitis 5 drachms, frankincense 5 drachms, myrrh 2 drachms, amurca 8 cotylae, or of dry [amurca] 5. The black troche which I use. ♃ pomegranate rinds 10 drachms, aristolochia 8 drachms, oak-gall 8 drachms, split [alum] 4 drachms, aloe 4 drachms, myrrh 2 drachms, chalcanthum 2 drachms, frankincense 4 drachms; take up with wine. Its use is with sweet wine. Troche of halicacabon. ♃ litharge 24 drachms, white lead 12 drachms or 24, root of halicacabon 8 drachms, chalcanthum 4 drachms, split [alum] 4 drachms, ruddle enough to colour it; take up with water. Troche of origanum. ♃ green olive leaves 8 drachms, pomegranate rinds 6 drachms, origanum 4 drachms, acacia 12 drachms, chalcitis 4 drachms, split [alum] 4 drachms, misy 4 drachms, of dry wine. The troche with sumach. ♃ oak-gall 3 drachms, acacia 4 drachms, chalcanthum 5 drachms,

of chalcitis half a drachma, of split alum [834] 8 drachmas, of round alum 4 drachmas, of misy 3 drachmas, of pomegranate rinds 5 drachmas, of scale (of copper) 4 drachmas, of myrrh 2 drachmas, of aloe 2 drachmas, of aristolochia 2 drachmas, of frankincense bark 4 drachmas, of bull-glue 3 drachmas, of tanners' sumach a quarter of a choenix — others say half a choenix — of vinegar 1½ cotylae, for soaking and grinding the sumach. The seal of Polyeides. Of split alum 3 drachmas, of frankincense 4 drachmas, of myrrh 4 drachmas, or of myrrh 8 drachmas, of chalcanthum 2 drachmas, of pomegranate flower-cups (kytinoi) 12 drachmas, of bull's gall 6 drachmas, of aloe 8 drachmas. Take up in dry wine. The Andronian troche. ♃ Of pomegranate flower-cups (kytinoi) 10 drachmas, of oak-gall 8 drachmas, of myrrh 4 drachmas — others say 18 drachmas, others 28 — of aristolochia 4 drachmas, of chalcanthum 2 drachmas, of split alum 2 drachmas — others say 4 drachmas — of Cyprian misy 2 drachmas. Take up in sweet wine. Use it for many purposes, as a drug of many uses. The troche of Achillas. ♃ Of scale (of copper), of misy, of aloe, 2 drachmas each, of aristolochia 8 drachmas, of split alum 4 drachmas, of myrrh 2 drachmas, of frankincense 4 drachmas, of oak-gall 8 drachmas, of chalcanthum 2 drachmas, of pomegranate rinds 8 drachmas, of bull's gall 2 drachmas. Take up in vinegar. A troche against spreading sores (nomai), of Isidorus the acquaintance. ♃ Of manna, of frankincense, 30 drachmas each,

of pomegranate flowers (kytinoi) [835] 8 drachms, of split alum 8 drachms, of oak-galls 8 drachms, of chalcanthum, aristolochia, myrrh, Cyprian misy, quicklime, 10 drachms each, of acacia 8 drachms. Take up in wine or vinegar and, having ground fine, use. Another troche, of many uses (polychrēstos). ♃ of oak-gall 8 drachms, of pomegranate flowers 12 drachms, of burnt copper 8 drachms, of verdigris 6 drachms, of split alum 8 drachms, of chalcanthum, acacia, bull's gall, frankincense, aloe, lycium, myrrh — in another copy also misy — 8 drachms each. Grind fine, during the heats under the Dog-star, with much vinegar. Troche of Apollonius Archistrator, the smilinos, as Alcimion gives it, of many uses. ♃ of white lead 10 drachms, of litharge 5 drachms, of aloe 50 drachms, of split alum 4 drachms, of frankincense 4 drachms, of myrrh 1 drachm — others 2 drachms — of Cimolian earth 25 drachms. Take up in wine; use sometimes with wine and rose oil. For erysipelas, the one which I use. ♃ of litharge 7 pounds, of white lead 1 drachm, of opium 3 ounces, of unburnt sulphur 3 ounces, of saffron 3 ounces. Take up with sweet wine; use with sweet wine. Glaucias' troche, of many uses. ♃ of liquid alum 100 drachms, of myrrh 8 drachms, of saffron 8 drachms. Take up with sweet wine. Good for erysipelas.

℞ Acacia [836] 8 dr., misy 4 dr., opium 2 dr., frankincense 4 dr.; take up with vinegar. It is effective also against herpetes. Another, effective for the same conditions. ℞ Opium 4 dr., acacia 4 dr., diphryges 4 dr., split alum 4 dr.; take up with water, use with vinegar. Another, for erysipelas. ℞ White lead 8 dr., unburnt sulphur 4 dr., meconium 2 dr., rue leaves 2 dr., split alum 4 dr., Cimolian earth 2 dr., starch 2 dr.; honey and vinegar. For herpetes, the one of Tiberius Caesar. ℞ Diphryges, meconium, split alum, acacia, 3 ounces each; taking up with vinegar or water, use. The keranitos (κερανίτος), a polychreston (of many uses). ℞ Orpiment 32 dr., aristolochia 32 dr. (others 8), iris 32 dr., oak-gall 16 dr. (others 8 dr.), round alum 6 dr., chalcitis 6 dr., scale of copper 16 dr., chalcanthum 8 dr., dry resin 8 dr., vinegar 4 choes. Grind, during the heat under the Dog-star, in a bronze mortar and with a pestle. But if you do not have a bronze mortar, put in 1 mina of scale, which is 100 dr.
