The trochiskos called Bithynian, prepared in Sicily.

For spreading sores (nomai), fistulas, pterygia; with double cerate [837] for herpetes, erysipelas and other conditions. ℞ pomegranate rinds 6 dr., oak-gall 6 dr., Illyrian iris 4 dr., aristolochia 6 dr., chalcanthum 3 dr., schistos alum 6 dr., chalcitis 6 dr., misy 3 dr., nitron 2 dr., frankincense 2 dr., cadmia 6 dr., scale of copper 4 dr., chrysocolla 2 dr., vinegar; prepare it during the days of the Dog-star. A troche for condylomata and the inflammations in the finger and pterygia. ℞ frankincense, acacia, stimmi, 2 dr. of each; verdigris, myrrh, opium, poppy, gum, Celtic nard, 2 dr. of each; triturating with astringent wine, smear it around. [A dry remedy of many kinds, shown through the things written above as to what each is suited for. The ones written by Andromachus at the end of the external remedies.] A dry septic remedy, non-biting. ℞ sandarach 2 dr., arsenic (arrhenikon) 2 dr., quicklime 4 dr., manna 4 dr.; use them finely ground. A haemostatic, which I use. ℞ chalcitis, misy, manna, 4 dr. each; others say 2; use them finely ground. A yellow one which I use. ℞ chalcitis 100 dr., chalcanthum 50 dr.

of roasted misy, [838] 25 drachms; of burnt copper, 12½ drachms. Use finely ground. Great haemostatic (ischaimos). ♃ Of Cyprian misy, 7 drachms; of chalcanthum, 7 drachms; of pine bark, 4 drachms; of manna of frankincense, 4 drachms; of copper scale, 4 drachms; of burnt copper, 15 drachms; of chalcitis, 15 drachms; of quicklime, 8 drachms, but others 40 drachms; of roasted gypsum, 4 drachms, but others 5. Use finely ground. Haemostatic of Aphrodas. ♃ Of chalcitis, 6 drachms; of manna of frankincense, 2 drachms; of roasted terebinth resin, 4 drachms each. Use finely ground for haemorrhoids. Another, as Harpocras. ♃ Of sandarach, 2 drachms; of arsenic, 4 drachms; of quicklime, 8 drachms. Make troches, grinding with water for 40 days, and so smear it around. For haemorrhoids, the one I use. ♃ Of arsenic, 8 drachms; of sandarach, 8 drachms; of elaterium, 4 drachms; of thapsia, 2 drachms; of chrysocolla, 4 drachms; of quicklime, 4 drachms. Use finely ground. A dry (powder) from those of Gallus, a polychreston (of many uses), for pterygia. ♃ Of litharge, 8 drachms; of verdigris, 10 drachms. Use finely ground; it is praised. A good one for pterygia. ♃ Of chalcitis, of burnt dried figs, of pomegranate rind, of copper scale, an equal amount of each. At the time of use mix in (μίς γε, read μίσγε) boiled honey, and making it plaster-like, apply. Every other day undo it, wiping around, and neither fomenting nor sprinkling powder on it.

[839] Anthera which I use. ℞ sandarach 32 dr. (others say 16); schist alum, myrrh, saffron magma, 16 dr. each; iris 16 drachmas; cyperus 66 dr. Anthera from Magnus. ℞ cassia 24 dr.; schist alum 4 dr.; gall-nut 4 dr.; sory 4 dr.; misy 4 dr.; sandarach 8 drachmas; pomegranate rind 1 drachma; myrrh 4 obols; cinnamon 4 obols; saffron 2 dr.; tamarisk fruit 2 dr. Use finely ground. Cephalic dry powder. ℞ iris 4 dr.; frankincense 2 dr.; panax 2 dr.; aristolochia 2 dr. Use finely ground, also for spreading sores (nomai). Cicatrizing dry powder. ℞ burnt oyster-shells 2 dr.; manna 1 drachma; cadmia 3 obols. Use finely ground, also for spreading sores. Another cicatrizing dry powder. ℞ pine bark 6 dr.; manna 6 dr.; aristolochia 6 dr.; pumice 4 dr.; resin 4 dr.; Illyrian iris 12 dr. Use finely ground. Another cicatrizing one, also for malignant ulcers. ℞ pine bark 6 dr.; burnt stag's horn 4 dr.; cadmia 22 dr.; white lead 4 dr.; manna 4 dr.; scraped verdigris 2 dr. Use finely ground.

of the External Remedies, which he entitles Marcellas.] Andromachus [844] mixed together the dry remedies that are suited according to the affection with those according to the affected parts. But by Asclepiades, in the fifth book, they have been written out separately, those according to the affection being indicated by headings of their own, and those involving an affected place likewise by headings of their own. For without a place there have been written by him the cicatrizing remedies and the escharotic ones and those suited for spreading sores (nomai) and carbuncles and the so-called haemostatic remedies (ischaima). With an affected place, however, all those for polyp and ozaenae and haemorrhages from the nostrils and spreading sores in the mouth and sodden gums and the mound-like excrescences on the chin, and for paronychiae and pterygia and for fissures in the anus and for haemorrhoids. Some, moreover, have even received their name from the affected part, yet are suited also to the other parts, such as are the remedies called 'cephalic' by physicians, which are suited pre-eminently in the case of the bones but are also able to make flesh grow in the ulcerations that arise in the whole body. For on the head it is not qua head that they are naturally best suited.

Indeed, when the bone has not been laid bare, we have no need of them at all; but in cases where it has been laid bare, [845] since we are wary of the use of drugs that make greasy, we use the dry ones alone, avoiding what are called by physicians emmota (lint-dressings), which are applied by means of lint-pledgets that have been smeared. And just as in the head, when the bones have been laid bare, their use is especially suitable, so in the same respect also in all the other bones that have been laid bare, whether it happens to be the upper arm or the forearm bone (ulna) or the radius or the thigh or the shin. Therefore I too, being about to write out in sequence the dry remedies recorded by Asclepiades, having found that he wrote the cephalic remedies first of all, will myself also write them first, because they are useful not only for the bones laid bare in the head, but also for all the others that are similarly affected. Second after them I shall write the cicatrizing remedies, passing over all those in between which pertain to an affected part. And after the cicatrizing remedies, all the rest in sequence according to the order I have just stated. Some of these dry drugs, however, have a twofold use, so that one can use them both dry by themselves and mixed with certain other things, as Asclepiades himself also indicates.

[846] [Dry cephalic remedies.] A dry cephalic remedy which Lucius the teacher used. It detaches scales of bone, brings up corrupted bones, and fills hollows with flesh. The drug is fat-free. Rx: Illyrian iris, 4 drachms; panax, 4 drachms; aristolochia, 2 drachms; manna, 2 drachms. Others (prepare it) without aristolochia. Pound and sift everything; use it on its own and with honey. The remedy with silphium. It melts away callused parts, cleanses foul parts, fills up the hollows of ulcers, and melts away the little tunics that remain. Rx: dry pine resin, 12 drachms; pumice, or roasted sory quenched in wine, 8 drachms; Illyrian iris, 8 drachms; aristolochia, 8 drachms; silphium, 50 drachms; scale of copper, 2 drachms; frankincense, 4 drachms. (Use it) dry and with honey. In other versions it does not contain silphium. The remedy with bitter vetch, of Xenocrates. Rx: flour of tawny bitter vetch, 8 drachms; Illyrian (iris), 10 drachms; manna, 5 drachms; aristolochia, 5 drachms; scale, 5 drachms. Use them finely ground, also with honey. In other versions: bryony root, 8 drachms; manna, 12 drachms; scale, 12 drachms; iris, 12 drachms; bitter vetch, 10 drachms;

of long aristolochia, [847] 15 drachms. The one inscribed "the [remedy] of serapias" separates scales and produces flesh; it is among the strongly desiccating ones. Of serapias, the orchis, 8 drachms; of Illyrian iris 8 drachms; of dry horehound 8 drachms; of bitter-vetch flour 10 drachms; of aristolochia 50 drachms. Use dry and with honey. Cephalic remedy of Tryphon. It separates scales. ♃ Of pine bark 6 drachms; of scale of copper 6 drachms; of burnt pumice 6 drachms; of manna of frankincense, aristolochia, Illyrian iris, pine resin, 4 drachms each; of myrrh, aloe, 2 drachms each. Use dry and with honey. But in the recipes of Athenaeus the drug is without pine bark; it also contains an equal amount of oak-gall, in the manna [preparation] (μαννίνῳ). [Dry cicatrizing remedies.] Concerning all ulcers—recent, old, easily treated, hard to treat—it has been stated both in the books of the Therapeutic Method, in the third, fourth and fifth,

[and] a reminder also in this treatise in what precedes, where I showed that for hollow wounds without any complicating circumstance the flesh-producing drugs are of a [848] detergent, non-biting faculty, whereas the cicatrizing ones are more drying, together with astringency that does not bite, and those that reduce overgrowing flesh are hot and acrid. And indeed which of the cicatrizing ones I consider the best has been stated by me earlier in the Therapeutic Method, in which the methods of cure of all affections have been set out, and, of those pertaining to wounds, earlier in this treatise now before us. But Asclepiades wrote down cicatrizing drugs, just as Andromachus also did, without further specifying whether they are for uncomplicated wounds or for those properly called hard-to-cicatrize, which were shown to differ from one another by several differences, each having its own particular aim of treatment. In some cases, however, they have added that it is also for malignant [ulcers], or again, that it is for condylomata and fissures. But Asclepiades, although more accustomed than Andromachus to add the qualifications, omitted them in the case of the cicatrizing remedies. Yet from what I have gone through, both in the therapeutic treatise and in the one now at hand, it will be clear to those who apply their mind how each of the drugs written down is to be used. Dry cicatrizing [remedy].

[849] [Asclepiades' ash-coloured remedy, from the writings of Magnus.] ℞ Quicklime 6 dr., manna of frankincense 4 dr., scale 4 dr. Otherwise: quicklime 12 dr., scale 4 dr., manna 4 dr. As Archibius has it: ℞ scale 8 dr. and manna 8 dr., or 4 dr.; in other copies, 8 dr. of quicklime. As Heliodorus has it: quicklime 8 dr., manna of frankincense 8 dr., scale 4 dr. A tawny cicatrizing remedy. ℞ roasted misy 8 dr., scale of copper 10 dr., manna 6 dr. Use finely ground. [Cicatrizing remedy of Magnus.] ℞ Diphryges 4 dr., scale 4 dr., Illyrian iris 2 drachms, manna 2 drachms. Use finely ground. The remedy with pumice. ℞ roasted pumice quenched in wine 8 drachms, scale 4 dr., manna 4 dr., iris 4 drachms, dry pine-resin 4 dr. Use finely ground. Another, of Ptolemy the disciple; it is effective also for ulcers that are hard to heal. ℞ pine bark 6 dr., roasted cadmia 8 drachms, scale 4 drachms, burnt stag's horn 4 dr., manna 4 drachms. Use finely ground.

In other copies it has: of burnt and washed lead [850] four drachmas, of molybdaena eight drachmas. Dry escharotic. It has been said concerning these too that they are of an acrid and caustic power, so that their use occurs both in the case of those (conditions) arising through excessive moisture and dyscrasia of the affected part, and on account of the putrefactions that arise in some parts. Escharotics of Asclepiades. The quince-yellow (remedy) of Lucius the teacher, escharotic and excising calluses, sprinkled on and pressed in with the olive-tip of a probe. It is also repressive and cicatrizing of hard-to-heal (sores), if one uses the drug in thin cases, employing what is called the fine dust. ♃ Of raw chalcitis eight drachmas, of cadmia four drachmas; fasting, take it up with saliva to such an extent that the drug is only just moistened, then gather it together and, having covered it, let it become quince-yellow, and having dried it in the shade, moving the pestle around lightly, take it up as has been stated before. Among others the drug is called grey. It is taken up with the most acrid vinegar and dried and ground fine.

In other copies, as Eunomus the Asclepiadean used it, [851] it runs as follows. ℞ chalcitis 12 drachms, cadmia 6 drachms, sandarach 6 drachms; it is taken up in vinegar. Another. ℞ roasted chalcitis, roasted chalcanthum, roasted cadmia, an equal amount of each, and take it up with saliva while fasting. The one inscribed "vigorous" (eutonon). ℞ roasted chalcitis 8 drachms, chalcanthum 8 drachms, sandarach 8 drachms, cadmia 8 drachms; sprinkle on dry. The one made of the four. ℞ roasted chalcitis 4 drachms, roasted misy 4 drachms, diphryges 4 drachms, roasted chalcanthum 4 drachms; use. An exceedingly excellent escharotic. ℞ split alum 16 drachms, chalcanthum 16 drachms, oak-galls 16 drachms, Cyprian misy 16 drachms, sory 4 drachms; use them finely ground. [A successful one, as Eunomus used it.] ℞ foreign misy 16 drachms, sory 12 drachms, burnt copper 2 drachms, burnt split stone 8 drachms, chalcanthum 4 drachms, sandarach 4 drachms, split alum 4 drachms; use them finely ground, sprinkling on and pressing in with the knob of the probe. For nomai (spreading ulcers).

The putrefactive ulcers, when they spread over the surrounding places, they call specifically nomai (spreading sores), and it is clear that such [852] conditions require the most vigorous drugs; indeed we often even use cauteries upon them. Remedies of Asclepiades for nomai. Of Lucius the teacher, for nomai: ♃ unburnt sulphur 2 dr., arsenic 2 dr., scale 2 dr., burnt copper, enough to give colour; (apply) dry and with honey. [Of Publius the teacher.] ♃ Arsenic 4 dr., scale 2 dr., elaterium 1 dr., papyrus enough to give colour. As Eunomus used it: ♃ arsenic 4 dr., scale 4 dr., unburnt sulphur 2 dr., elaterium 2 dr., burnt papyrus enough to give colour. In other copies: sandarach 4 dr., scale 6 dr., arsenic 4 dr., elaterium 2 dr., burnt papyrus 4 dr. From the writings of Areius, for nomai, which also cleanses foul ulcers without biting when dissolved in rose-oil. It works also for erosions in the womb. Theotropus gave it. ♃ arsenic 4 dr., burnt papyrus 4 dr., burnt and washed lead 4 dr., copper scale 4 dr. Triturate each separately, then, having mixed them together, use for the aforesaid conditions.

As [853] Ptolemaeus used it: ℞ burnt lead, arsenic, scale, burnt papyrus, 4 drachmas each; native sulphur, 2 drachmas; use them finely ground. As Apelles [used it]: a successful drug, entitled "the one made with papyrus", for spreading sores (nomai). It not only arrests [the spreading] but also prevents it when it is beginning. It is also effective for dysenteric patients when infused by way of rose-oil. And whenever, he says, on being infused into dysenteric patients it causes a biting sensation, the spreading sore is to be suspected. The particulars of the composition are as follows: ℞ burnt papyrus, burnt lead and burnt and washed copper, arsenic, scale of steel (stomoma), an equal amount of each; native sulphur, half the amount; use them finely ground, either with honey or with rose-oil. Moschion's [remedy] for spreading sores: ℞ elaterium, 2 drachmas; burnt papyrus, 2 drachmas; scale of copper, two drachmas; arsenic, 4 drachmas; worm-verdigris, 1 drachma; salt ammoniac, one drachma; use them finely ground with rose-oil. [Fragrant remedy of Lucius the teacher.] ℞ scale, 4 drachmas; gall-nut, 4 drachmas; sandarach, 2 drachmas; arsenic, 2 drachmas; myrrh, 1 drachma; chalcanthum, 1 drachma;

of frankincense [854] 2 drachmas, of elaterium 1 drachma, of burnt papyrus enough to give colour. As we use it: take scale 8 drachmas, oak-gall 8 drachmas, myrrh 8 drachmas, sandarach 4 drachmas, arsenic 4 drachmas, elaterium 4 drachmas, frankincense 3 drachmas, chalcanthum 3 drachmas, papyrus enough to give colour. As Prasion used it: take arsenic 2 drachmas, scale 2 drachmas, chalcanthum 1 drachma, sandarach 2 drachmas, myrrh 1 drachma, frankincense 1 drachma, oak-galls 1 drachma, papyrus 4 drachmas; use them very finely ground and with rose-oil. Heracleides, however, had this formula: take oak-galls 6 drachmas, arsenic 4 drachmas, sandarach 4 drachmas, scale 4 drachmas, frankincense 3 drachmas, chalcanthum 3 drachmas, Minaean myrrh 2 drachmas, papyrus 8 drachmas. As Cleobulus used it: take scale 2 drachmas, sandarach 2 drachmas, arsenic 2 drachmas, myrrh 1 drachma, frankincense 1 drachma, chalcanthum 1 drachma, oak-gall 1 drachma, papyrus enough to give colour.

[For anthrakes.] The anthrax is an ulcer that quickly produces an eschar, with strong phlegmone of the whole surrounding part, so that violent fevers too are brought on [855] and extreme dangers; hence one must place upon the eschar itself a strong drug, and indeed such of these as have been said to be suitable for nomai, while the surrounding parts one must plaster with cataplasms that have an even power, so as both to repel and to cool moderately and to disperse. But concerning the cataplasms it has been spoken in the treatise on these; now we shall make mention of what has been written by Asclepiades. For anthrakes, the remedies recorded by Asclepiades. The remedy of the Massaliote. He set this forth publicly for the city in view of its power, because anthrakes were prevalent and were carrying off many. ♃ chrysocolla 4 dr., roasted nitron 4 dr., Asian stone 4 dr., arsenikon 4 dr., sandarach 4 dr., roasted misy 4 dr., chalkitis 4 dr., split alum 4 dr., diphryges 4 dr. Having ground them each separately and then together, we store them in a Cyprian bronze vessel. At the time of use we apply it, pressing it on with the flat of the probe, until the anthrax turns black; then we place on top the green remedy written below. It is this: ♃ frankincense 1 dr., scraped verdigris 1 dr.

of copper scale one [856] drachm, of split alum four obols, of ammoniac salt four obols, of wax seven drachms three obols, of dry pine resin fifteen drachms, of old oil one kotyle. Grind the dry ingredients in the sun with vinegar; melt the meltable ones and pour them over, and having beaten the mixture up and taken it up, use it. In Demosthenes the Massaliote, the one who also composed the drug, it has two kotylai of oil. [Of Apion, for carbuncles.] ♃ Of red nitron, arsenic, sandarach, chalcitis, chalcanthum, diphryges, an equal amount of each; grinding fine with vinegar, drying and grinding again, use. Of Apollonius Organicus. ♃ Of chrysocolla one drachm, of split alum one drachm and of round [alum] one drachm, of sandarach one drachm, of ochre one drachm, of raw misy one drachm, of chalcanthum one drachm; use finely ground. The anthizousa ("blooming") remedy of Magnus for putrefactions, spreading sores, carbuncles, pterygia, ears flowing with pus; it also works for spreading sores in the mouth. ♃ Of split alum 8 drachms, of chalcitis 6 drachms, of sandarach 3 drachms, of dry pomegranate rinds 2 drachms, of chalcanthum 1 drachm.

[857] of misy 2 drachms, of nitron 2 drachms, of dried omphacium 2 drachms. Use it dry and also with honey. Another, of Diodorus. ♃ Of omphacine oak-gall 4 drachms, of misy 2 drachms, of chalcitis 2 drachms, of arsenic 2 drachms, of sandarach 2 drachms, of split alum, chalcanthum, Asian stone, diphryges, red nitron, 1 drachm each. Sprinkle on with the ingredients finely ground, applying it with the knob of a probe. Haemostatic of Asclepiades. A well-tested drug of Lucius the teacher. ♃ Of chalcitis 16 drachms, of manna 12 drachms, of terebinth kneaded with vinegar; with these dry, sprinkle the places that are haemorrhaging. In two other copies we have rather found: ♃ of chalcitis 8 drachms, of manna 16 drachms, of roasted terebinth 16 drachms. And as Dioscorides of Tarsus gave it to Areius the Asclepiadean, checking haemorrhages marvellously: ♃ of chalcitis 8 drachms, of manna 16 drachms, of dry resin 8 drachms, of gypsum 8 drachms. The other ingredients are pounded and sifted and mixed and stored away in a bronze box; and at the time of use an equal amount of the drug is mixed with the gypsum. From the writings of Heraclides, for haemorrhoids.

He used this for [858] haemorrhages of the nostrils, dipping wool in it and twisting it like a lamp-wick. Take pomegranate rinds of the sour pomegranate, 3 ounces; Egyptian alum, 4 ounces; chalcitis, 1 ounce; use them finely ground. In the case of the nostrils, fill a piece of wool with the drug and insert it. The so-called Heracles, for haemorrhages. He used this in place of a cautery; it is escharotic. It is also effective against pterygia, it reduces every excrescence, brings up bones, and detaches scales. Take sory, 4 dr.; chalcanthum, 4 dr.; burnt chalcitis, 4 dr.; tanners' sumach, 4 dr.; use them finely ground. A successful haemostatic. Take foreign misy, 6 dr.; chalcanthum, 6 dr.; pine bark, 4 dr.; chalcitis, 4 dr.; manna, 4 dr. (others: 20); gypsum, 4 dr.; use them finely ground. Another. Take frankincense, 1 ounce; foreign misy, 4 dr.; unripe oak-galls, 4 dr.; chalcitis, 4 dr.; burnt corks, 8 dr.; tanners' sumach, 4 dr.; use them finely ground.

[859] GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK 6. Having divided up the plasters called polychrēsta (of many uses), since they are suited to many conditions, in the book before this one I gathered together those that are able, along with the other things they profess to do, also to heal the hard-to-treat among ulcers.

But now I shall pass to another kind of the plasters of many uses (polychrēsta), each of which acts upon many other things and indeed also upon the putrefying parts, [860] these being of a different condition from the ulcers that are properly called hard-to-treat. For in the former the putrefaction spreads, and for this reason most physicians call these conditions nomai (spreading sores); whereas in the latter it is circumscribed in a single place without putrefaction, so that even the so-called phagedainai eat away the adjoining parts, yet without putrefying them and bringing on fevers, which is what usually follows upon the spreading sores accompanied by putrefaction. The chief point of the cure was, in the case of the previously mentioned kind of hard-to-treat ulcers, which they also call Chironian, to find drugs that, as far as possible, do not bite, but dry strongly. But these which are now to be written down are all biting, if one were to use them unmixed, without their being mixed with cerate. When mixed with cerate they are able to cleanse a foul ulcer and to produce flesh, and also to disperse a certain hardness and tension, yet not to cure the hard-to-treat ones.

Their power is shown by the affections for which they are trusted to be employed with good effect; and what was said in the preceding discussion I shall say now as well: one must remember [861] what has been written in the treatise on simple drugs, where in the first books I set out the method by which the powers of drugs are discovered, together with exercising oneself in it on a good many examples, and in the following books I made mention of each one by name. For one who remembers those things will easily follow the reasoning of those who composed these drugs now set before us, and will obviously himself also compose others at whatever time he is at a loss for those already tried beforehand. For many such things happen to many people on journeys abroad, both other journeys and especially those by sea, seeing that even while remaining in their own place some have lost the stock of drugs by which they used to treat those in need, so that they wasted away from grief and died. It is best, then, to use drugs that have already given proof of themselves, in accordance with the method described.

But if, as I said, we should ever be at a loss for these, [it is best] that they themselves possess such a habit as to be able to compose drugs resembling those that have already given sufficient proof, just as you often see me too doing, [862] both on journeys abroad and otherwise. At any rate, some of the ones improvised in such circumstances, when tested by experience, appeared in no way inferior to the most renowned. For we make their first composition from technical conjecture, and after this, on the basis of experience—some having appeared most approved, others falling short of the aim—a second correction in turn comes about, and sometimes also a third, bringing them to the perfection of what they promise. But without the method described both in the preceding commentaries and in the therapeutic treatise, it is impossible to use correctly the drugs mentioned before, and still more impossible to compose oneself drugs resembling those. Now then I shall begin with plasters of this sort. The plaster made of herbs has been written up by almost all who have collected the renowned plasters in the writings of one book or of several, not differing much in the proportion of the simple drugs that are mixed. Here too, then, I shall begin with those written by Crito, first mentioning the plasters which Crito wrote in the fourth book On Simple Drugs, in his very words.

[863] [The plaster through herbs, of Crito.] The plaster through herbs, which I use, works against carcinomata and putrefactions; it brings scrofulous swellings (choirades) to suppuration and, pressing them out, removes leprai and dissolves boils (dothienes); it is suited to gouty patients and dissolves calluses (poroi); the same is a cephalic plaster, which without trepanation detaches scales of bone, brings up bones, and scrapes the bones to some extent; the same, for freshly inflicted wounds and for spreading sores (nomai), applied on lint, cleanses thoroughly and fills up, together with rose cerate, one part being mixed to two parts of cerate, and sometimes three or four; and with myrtle cerate, in two or three parts, it cicatrizes. Take of herbs from waterless places near the sea: of the pimpernel which has the blue flower 56 drachms, of horned poppy 56 drachms, of horehound 56 drachms, of tender leaves of henbane 56 drachms; put these into a mortar and pound them until they are crushed and broken down, only do not waste their juice; then put them into a mortar-basin and grind. And in another mortar-basin have of scale of red copper 25 drachms, of manna 8 drachms, of dry pine resin 16 drachms, of aloe 16 drachms, of fissile (alum, schiste) 4 drachms,

[864] of round (alum), 4 drachmas. Grind these in the sun with vinegar so that they have the thickness of strigil-grease (gloios); then, having mixed in the herbs, triturate until it is well united; next make a cerate from 100 drachmas of Chian wax—others say one mina—and two kotylai of old oil; boil and mix. Thus Heras. But some put in the two kinds of anagallis, and some also chrysocolla and Eretrian earth and ammoniac salt and arsenic, split (schiston), four drachmas of each. What Asclepiades has written about this plaster has also been set out in the book before this one, being in some way similar to these things; for which reason it seemed to me superfluous to write them again, since I am now about to go through the common account concerning them. For indeed the one who first compounded this drug used acrid herbs for the purpose of vigorously dispersing the bad humours in the affected parts—for this reason, at any rate, he also orders that they be from waterless and seaside places—and, opposed to these, other herbs of cold faculty, for the sake of soothing the vehemence of the acrid ones, such as henbane and poppy are.

For they also have something that mitigates pains, since they impart a numbing coldness [865] to the parts they come near. And moderate numbness relieves pain, says Hippocrates. He also added, from the metallic substances, both flake of copper and fissile alum, about which I spoke earlier, each of which drugs is suited to malignant ulcers. Aloe he mixed in from among the drugs that are astringent and dry without biting, and manna from among those that concoct, soothe and promote suppuration. The pine resin he added as material for the formation of a plaster, just as he did the wax and the oil, while at the same time it also comes about through these that the vehemence of the acrid drugs is mitigated. Pine resin, however, also has the property of drying, and the drier it is, the more so—of the kind he thinks fit to put in. He says that some have also mixed into the drug chrysocolla and Eretrian earth, both of which heal the hard-to-treat ulcers. Contrary to these, ammoniac salt and what is called arsenic are of such a nature as to irritate ulcers by their acridity, yet they are also suited to putrefying ones.

And for this reason, against the Cheironian ulcers the drug set before us [866] in the discussion is not very useful. But in cases where some putrefaction is present, it is suitable for putting a stop to this, since it disperses the ichors that produce it. The same power of the drug also cures the scrofulous swellings (choirades). And since some of the ingredients thrown into it are detergent, for this reason it also cleanses leprai. For the aim in the case of this affection is, as it were, to scale off the hardened part of the skin; and this is accomplished by things that over-dry together with cleansing. For if the condition of the skin were able to return to the state according to nature, no one would over-dry what has already been dried out. But since it is not possible for what is already leprous to be healed, the second aim would be, the one that is common in the case of all incurable things, to cut out the incurable part of the body. And it is cut out sometimes by iron, sometimes by fire, sometimes by a drug, either caustics or those that are at once discutient and detergent, such as the one now set before us. Just as, then, this account is common to every lepra, so too is the one concerning the production of flesh (sarkosis).

For since, as has been shown in the third book of the Therapeutic Method, the drugs called flesh-producing are of a non-biting [867] cleansing power, while all the materials that enter into this drug now before us in our discussion have the cleansing quality but do not have the non-biting quality, for this reason we mix with them a liquid cerate composed of wax and resin (pine-resin) melted in oil. For wax and oil, just as they are blunters of acridities, so too are they pore-blocking (emplastic) and for this reason generative of filth. Resin, on the other hand, while it has the non-biting quality, does not have the pore-blocking one, being of a cleansing power that is already biting for ulcers but non-biting for unulcerated parts. The due proportion in the mixture we shall find conjecturally before experience, but scientifically after experience, together with the recognition that the clean ulcer requires a cleansing power that is precisely non-biting, whereas the filthy one requires a stronger one. For in the latter the filth is a screen set before it, while the clean one, being bare, comes into contact with whatever touches it. And moreover, of the bodies themselves, some have a more sensitive substance, others a less sensitive one, and some a softer, others a harder.

For this reason, then, Criton too, in the case of the drug under discussion, orders that to one part [868] of it there be mixed sometimes two parts of the cerate, sometimes three or four; he did not, however, define when one ought to mix the two parts and when the more, on the assumption that the person who is going to use the drug already has some practice in the art and is able to reason out what is now being said by me. It is better, to be sure, for the cerate to have been prepared with rose-oil, though the superiority is not great in such ulcers as these, even if it were melted with olive oil. For rose-oil is indeed better than olive oil in cases that have something inflammatory about them, but the ulcers that are going to be filled with flesh are in every case free of inflammation. And Criton rightly added the note that in the case of ulcers requiring cicatrization the cerate ought to have been prepared with myrtle-oil, for those have need of astringency. This much suffices to have been said, for the present at least, about the flesh-producing and the cicatrizing drugs. For the method of their use and composition has been stated in the books of the Therapeutic Method; while the exercise upon the particular materials, which belongs to the present treatise, will be stated in the book after this one.

[869] [Plaster with squill.] Next after this one Crito wrote another plaster of the same faculty by kind, in these very words, as follows. ♃ of chalcitis, of round aristolochia, 30 drachms each; others, 15 drachms; of iris 30 drachms; others, 15 drachms; of dry pine resin 30 drachms; others, 15 drachms; of ammoniac 15 drachms; of myrrh 15 drachms; of storax 15 drachms; of scale of red copper 15 drachms; of roasted squill 108 drachms; sharpest vinegar: triturate for 40 days in the heat of the dog days. First the scale and the storax, a little at a time from each of them; then, having added the ammoniac and the copper and the squill, so that it may be worked up; then the resin little by little; after these the myrrh; then, when these are smooth, the remaining dry ingredients. When the days have been completed, make a cerate of the following sort: of wax 5 litrai; others, 240 drachms; of terebinth resin 1 litra; others, 30 drachms; of oil 2½ xestai; others, 6 kotylai; of galbanum 30 drachms; of liquid pitch 30 drachms. Add the galbanum last, then, having cooled it, take it up carefully. This, then, is the composition of the drug.

Concerning its use, Criton [870] writes the following, in these very words: "In use, employ the drug undiluted for fractures in the head, for fistulas, for spreading sores (nomai), for excrescences of flesh, for the widening of orifices, and for undermining (hypophora). But if you wish to make it milder, so that it becomes flesh-producing and cicatrizing, to one part of the drug add twelve parts of rose cerate. In the case of burns, add eight to one part." These things Criton wrote well concerning the use of the drug, inasmuch as he used it, being pungent and opening and dispersing and on this account also drying, for fistulas and excrescences of flesh and for putrefactions, that is spreading sores, and for the widening of orifices, as is the case with sinuses that have narrow mouths; and for fractures in the head, whenever we attempt to treat them without trepanation—such being those that have not extended as far as the meninges; and for the sake of producing flesh, mixing in fourteen parts of rose cerate, until cicatrization. But it is better to say: until the filling up of the hollow in the ulcers.

For of necessity, in the case of the spreading (eating) ulcers—which I said are the same thing as the putrefactive kind—when they are being treated by the strong [871] drugs, such as the one before us, first the drug cleans away the putrefying parts, and on this account they become hollow. Then, after the putrefaction has ceased, the ulcer requires both cleansing and filling up, and when it has been filled up, at that point also the cicatrizing agents. But the drug itself, when it has not yet been mixed with cerate, being acrid, is not only unable to produce flesh but also clears away the excrescent flesh, just as Criton himself said. And it is especially fitting to bear in mind this point, which was also stated in connection with the plaster before this one, which he named the plaster through herbs: that all compounds composed of heating and detergent substances, even if they are strongly acrid, become flesh-producing when mixed with cerate. Some, however, despair of them when, having mixed in the cerate in double quantity, they see it still biting to such a degree that it is unable to produce flesh, as is the case with this plaster. For being much more acrid and more biting than the plaster through herbs, it is useless for the production of flesh even if it is mixed with four times as much cerate.

There is need, therefore, of an intelligent man and one practised in the use of [872] such drugs, who at the very outset considers how many times over it needs to be mixed with the cerate, and who, after the first use, if the drug still appears sharper than to be able to produce flesh, conjectures how much more of the cerate must still be added, as Criton did in the case of the present one. For do not suppose that he discovered straightaway, at the first conjecture, that the cerate must be mixed in twelvefold; rather, he recognised that it must be more than what is mixed with the plaster made of herbs, but how much more he found out after the first conjecture. For if, when eightfold had been mixed in, it still appeared biting, he mixed it in tenfold; and just so, if it was still biting at tenfold, he went on to the twelvefold.

But since, as I said, in accordance with the amount of filth and the moistness of the ulcer, and the sensitivity or insensitivity of the parts that share in the affection, and further the softness and hardness of the bodily habit, the quantity of the cerate that is mixed in must be varied—which has been said many times—we must understand, keeping this in mind, that the quantity for use in such cases is written down with the road from there toward the other cases becoming easy for everyone in either direction [873] as far as the extremes. By extremes I mean the complete states formed from all the indications of the same kind; concerning which, once I have now stated a single example, you must keep it in mind throughout and no longer expect to hear about it repeatedly. I say, then, that the indications of the same kind for mixing in the greatest amount of cerate are the ulcer's being clean and dry, and the body of the person being treated being sensitive and soft; those for the least are much moisture and filth in the ulcer, and the body of the patient being hard and insensitive. Rightly, moreover, scale of copper was mixed with all the ingredients from which it is composed, these being discutient, since it is a drying drug and has in it no small amount of astringency. And it is not only in the case of this plaster that you must know that, through the admixture of much cerate, the plaster becomes flesh-producing and cicatrizing for ulcers that are not malignant, but also in the case of all the others that are of the same power; and next after them Criton wrote the one "with whetstone" (δι’ ἀκόνης), which he says he himself uses, and he directed that it be compounded thus.

[874] [The plaster with whetstone.] The plaster with whetstone (ἀκόνη), which is in use among us, is effective against all chronic conditions, and specifically against headache when applied to the forehead, and against chronic pains of the side; for those with gout, those with sciatica, pains of the shoulders, toothaches, when it is put onto the worn parts (τετριμμένοις). It also draws down the menses when applied above the pubes. It helps also those who have pain in the stomach-mouth and those who suffer from flux and those who do not retain food; and it is useful for everything, apart from a burn and from those who do not tolerate an acrid drug. It is suited also to hardness of the liver and of the spleen, and to scrofulous swellings, and to those with sciatica. In their case, specifically, let the use be for seven days; but if they are delicate, five; let the part not touch water or oil until it has raised pustules and drawn out thick ichors; then, having removed it, use the white cerate made with water; but if you want something more active, the whetstone-plaster with pepper. Take: wax, galbanum, terebinth, roasted pine resin, laurel oil, old oil, one litra of each; copper scale, one and a half litrae.

[875] of verdigris, 6 ounces; of ammoniac incense, 1 ounce; of mustard, adarkē, sulphur, 1 ounce each; of southernwood, centaury, chalcanthum, salt ammoniac, frankincense, common salt, round alum, litharge, propolis, Cnidian berry, 3 ounces each. Having pounded and sifted them all together, take them up in the astringents (στυπτικοῖς) together with the oils. This, then, is the composition of the plaster before us, which differs not a little from the one written out before in heat. At any rate it contains mustard and adarkē, sulphur and Cnidian berry, which reach such a degree of heat as to ulcerate whatever they remain in contact with for too long. And laurel oil too is among the things that heat considerably, and after these chalcanthum and the salts. You have learned, moreover, that these also partake of astringency, the salts of a slight one, chalcanthum of a great deal. But concerning the mixing of astringent drugs with the discutient ones it has been stated previously, in the case of the plasters of many uses (polychrēsta). For in general nothing can become a polychreston (of many uses) unless it also partakes of the opposite faculty.

For if the power is simply dispersive alone, it will suit one single kind of affections, that which ought to be dispersed; and if [876] it is of an astringent kind, one other, in which it is fitting to drive back that which flows in. Hence the astringent drugs suit those affections which are beginning to be generated from an influx of humours, whereas the dispersive drugs, without the admixture of astringents, suit those bodies into which nothing can flow because they have been previously evacuated; since, if there is some superfluity of humours, not only is the fluid contained in the affected parts dispersed, but fluid also arrives at them, because the dispersive drugs are naturally such as to draw under themselves, just as they draw the fluids contained in the parts they touch, so also those lying in the depth of the body. Reasonably, then, there are mixed with the dispersive drugs those called checking and repellent, the man who arrived at their composition having used this reasoning, and experience bearing witness to the reasoning.

Reasonably, then, in the case of the drug before us, although it has as its aim to heat and to dry, and for this reason also to produce psydrakes (pustules), something of the astringents too was mixed in — though not ones sufficient in relation to the many strongly heating drugs, these two, chalcanthum and salts; but scale of copper too was mixed in according to the same [877] reasoning, and alum, which has received this very name on account of its astringing strongly. Another. Crito wrote another most renowned plaster, which he calls the Mesiane, having a different kind of material from the one written above and from the one about to be written by me now next in order, which Crito himself calls 'Invincible', being composed of drugs most of which are acrid, whereas the Mesiane is not of this sort, as will be shown after this at its own proper occasion. And indeed, also naming others 'cephalic', whose general power will be stated a little later, having written them next after the one called Mesiane, after these he writes the one called 'Invincible' by himself, which is of a power similar to the one written above, which he called the 'by means of the whetstone'. Crito's text concerning it runs roughly as follows, in these very words: The Invincible, which is in use with us. It is useful for everything: it draws, it breaks open, it cleanses, it glues together, it presses out (ἐξιποῖ), by means of a compress and the placing-alongside of channels (σωλήνων), and also when dissolved, always having a clay-paste (πηλὸν) made with vinegar-and-oil.

It also disperses indurations and helps contractions of the sinews, being applied without [878] fomentation, so that they are not chilled all round. And when loosened it serves in the role of an unguent, like an acopon; for it also stops the fatigues that occur at the beginnings of diseases and those arising from an unclear cause. It is also a malagma for the extremities, applied in large compresses. It is also agglutinative of fresh bleeding wounds, once they have been sutured or fastened with clasps, a folded pad of vinegar alone being applied in addition over the compress, cold in summer, warm in winter. It is effective also against the affections in the soles of the feet and against cuts, putrefactions, conditions around the fingers and toes, and fractures accompanied by wounds. It is possible to use neither any other flesh-producing nor cicatrizing remedy, but to trust in it alone. It is effective also against human bites, dog bites, and bites of wild beasts. Its greatest profession is that it does not allow concealed abscesses to form in the colon and the peritoneum, provided at least that suppuration has not already taken place, or, when they have formed, it thins them and makes them burst into the intestines. One must apply a compress to the place, and on top of it a felt pad of warm oxelaion (oil and vinegar), and foment twice a day.

But do not undo it except after three or four days; then, after fomenting [879] with vapour, apply it again. It was called "invincible" on account of its marvellous and numerous works. Take: scale of copper, 58 drachmas; pyrethrum, stavesacre, Cnidian berry, mustard seed, cachrys, pigeon's dung, slender aristolochia, verdigris, cyperus, rocket seed, cumin, 16 drachmas each; nitron, 32 drachmas; salt ammoniac, 32 drachmas; bay-berries, 120 drachmas; manna, 120 drachmas; iris, 120 drachmas; acrid vinegar, 16 xestai; decoction of dried figs, 4½ kyathoi. Having pounded and sifted all of them together, triturate them with the vinegar during the heats of the dog-days. When it has become dry and green, add some of the decoction of figs, and having softened it together take it up and store it in a copper pot of red copper. The decoction of dried figs is as follows: take fat dried figs, 5 litrai; water, 6 xestai; boil until 2 xestai are left. The use is: one part of the drug, diluted with vinegar so as to become glutinous, to six parts of the resin-wax.

The unmixed resin-wax is one part wax, three parts roasted resin, melted together with a little oil; the medium one [880] is one part wax, two parts resin; the relaxed and well-tempered one is one part wax, one part resin; the slackened one is two parts wax, one part resin; the over-relaxed one is three parts wax, one part resin. It is also recorded that, in the case of wild lichen, it has proved suitable when applied unmixed. These things Crito wrote in these very words. I, for my part, shall make the beginning of my discussion from the last of the things said by him. They call lichens 'wild' when they see them receiving no benefit from the weakly drying drugs, but being irritated by the strong ones. In their case, therefore, there is need of a drug that is sufficiently active, yet not violently biting, which, as I said, having been composed on the basis of skilled conjecture, is put to the test by experience. The drug before us is composed of many acrid, fine-particled and discutient substances. It also contains some of those that cleanse without biting and some of those that are slightly astringent.

The acrid ingredients among those in it, then, are pyrethrum and mustard and Cnidian berry and pigeon's dung, verdigris and bay-berry and nitron, then the so-called ammoniac salts [881] and, in addition to these, the acrid vinegar; for that is the kind he requires to be put in. Of the detergent ingredients, those that are entirely non-biting are iris and aristolochia, and still more so than these—so as to belong already to the class of the concocting drugs—manna; more vigorous are kanchry (κάγχρυ) and wild raisin (stavesacre); and still more vigorous than these are cumin and the seed of rocket. Cyperus is drying without biting, but it also has something astringent, as does the scale of copper too, which is a strong drug. For it was necessary, as was shown before, that this drug should also partake somewhat of the astringent faculty, and for this very reason scale was mixed in abundantly. And if the manna really is manna and not frankincense, it too would have something astringent. And it too has been put in much more abundantly than the scale, reasonably, so that it may soothe the vehemence of the acrid drugs, along with concocting the humours in the affected part. Most soothing and most concocting, together with dispersing in some degree, is the decoction of dried figs. All these, then, mixed together have reasonably made the drug a polychreston (of many uses).

And to their active efficacy the vinegar contributes [882] most of all, in which he orders the drugs to be ground fine under the summer sun. For all things prepared in this way become fine-particled, and for this reason their power sinks down to the depth of the bodies. [On the plasters of the same kind written by Heras.] The one made with the herbs, which I wrote out above as Criton prepares it, Heras himself also prepares in the same way, inasmuch as Criton too made mention of him. But he differs in the preparation of the one made with squill. For of the ammoniac and the myrrh and the pine resin and the storax and the scale and the squill Criton mixes with the other ingredients as much as Heras does; but in the case of the aristolochia and the iris he differs. For whereas Heras wrote: of round aristolochia 30 drachms, of dry iris 30 drachms (others, 10), and after these things Criton in turn wrote thus: Take aristolochia 30 drachms, iris 30 drachms (others, 40). At the end of the preparation Heras having written: when the days have been completed, make a cerate as follows: Take wax 5 pounds (others, 40 drachms), terebinth 1 pound (others, 30 drachms),

of old oil [883] 2½ xestai, others say 6 kotylai. For my part, I do not approve of mixing into the drug 240 drachms in place of the 5 litrai of wax. For sometimes they themselves write 100 drachms for the litra, and sometimes for the mina, but no one has ever written a litra so small as to be 48 drachms; yet this is what results when 240 drachms are put in instead of the 5 litrai. And likewise neither 30 drachms in place of the litra of terebinth. [The plaster of Serapion.] Crito wrote this one too, in his book of drugs (the Pharmakitis), in the following words: the plaster of Serapion, which some call Egyptian, others Aphrodite. It is effective for every wound, and one must persist with it without despairing. It is effective for punctures and splinters and parotid swellings, and for perforation (κατατίτρησις) and phymata, and, having pressed out the matter (ἐξιποῦσα), it glues the parts together; it is effective also for every hardness and for epinyctides and for a flux upon the joints and for contusions of the ears; it is effective also for ulcers of the aged, Chironian ulcers and thick-lipped ulcers. ♃ old oil 3 kotylai, litharge 200 drachms,

of ammoniac [884] incense 168 drachms, of Colophonian pine resin 68 drachms, of wax 168 drachms, of galbanum 20 drachms, of verdigris 50 drachms (others, 20 drachms), of myrrh 4 drachms (others, 8 drachms). Boil the litharge and the oil until it seems to have thickened moderately; then, lifting off the pan, add the ammoniac, then the resin, then the wax. Having melted each one of them attentively, so that it does not burn on, lift it off again and add the galbanum and the verdigris; then, setting it on the fire, boil until it becomes quince-yellow and of good consistency. Last of all, lifting it off, add the myrrh, and having stirred it, pour it out, and taking it up in a skin, store it away. [How Andromachus wrote the aforesaid plasters.] Andromachus wrote three compositions of this plaster, the first differing slightly from the one of Crito written above, and after it two others having greater disagreement. The promise of the drug and its preparation have been well written before by Crito; Andromachus, at any rate, wrote about it as follows. The plaster of the herbs.

[885] Take: anagallis, the one with the blue flower, 56 drachmas; horehound, 56 drachmas; wild poppy, 56 drachmas; green henbane, 56 drachmas; scale (of copper), 25 drachmas; frankincense, 8 drachmas; dry resin, 16 drachmas; aloe, 16 drachmas; split (alum), 4 drachmas; wax, 1 mina; old oil, 2 cotylae; vinegar. Many used to put both of the two anagallides into the plaster made from herbs, but Theocritus also Eretrian earth and chrysocolla and salt ammoniac and arsenic, 4 drachmas of each. [Other plasters of the same kind, about which Andromachus wrote.] For gangrenes and putrefactions and old and malignant spreading sores (nomai), the plaster of Isidorus of Antioch. Take: litharge, 4 drachmas; scraped verdigris, 8 drachmas; oil, 6 cyathi; Talius Aelius (uses) 12 cyathi, and worm-verdigris (ios skolex).

Having put the litharge and the verdigris, finely ground, into a pot and poured on three cyathi of oil, boil over a gentle fire, stirring with a wooden spatula, until it becomes green; then, having taken it off the fire and poured it into a mortar, grind it for a considerable time while it is hot. [886] Then again, having poured into the pot three cyathi of the oil, boil it, stirring so that it does not burn on, until it becomes quince-yellow, and again, having emptied it out, grind it as one does collyria. And again, having taken it up into the pot, boil it, stirring, until it becomes red, and having emptied it into a mortar again, for the third time, grind it for a considerable time; and again, for the fourth time, boil it in the pot so that it thickens together, and again, while it is hot, having poured it out and ground it, take it up and store it in a red box, and use it for the conditions mentioned. Next after the one written above, Andromachus wrote word for word as follows concerning another plaster. A moist plaster for spreading sores (nomai), which I use, and for many other things. Take: wax 8 drachms, terebinth resin 8 drachms, prepared bull's suet 4 drachms, chalcitis 2 drachms, scale of copper 3 drachms, manna of frankincense 2 drachms, omphacine (unripe) oak-gall 4 drachms, myrtle oil 5 cotylae. The dry ingredients are worked up with vinegar and honey; then, in this way, the melted ingredients are poured over. [Grey plasters of many uses (polychrēsta).

for the works of the art there is need both of method and of practice] That of remedies [887] some are discovered by reason alone, some by experience, and this too without requiring reason, while certain ones require both working together with one another, has often been demonstrated to you; and in addition to this, that the things discovered through reason and experience make use of a conjectural road for the discovery of what is sought, and, having been hoped for by reason, are confirmed by experience; and moreover, that in conjectural hope there is no small difference in respect of the more and the less, just as also throughout the whole of life. For we do not hope alike that there will be rain at the winter solstice and at the rising of the Dog-star. For at the winter solstice it rarely fails to occur, whereas at the rising of the Dog-star it rarely occurs. But since all the works of the arts are brought to exactness by continuous practice, it is not sufficient to learn only the universal in them, but one must also act many times in the particular cases. For practice through imperfect activities is the road to the acquisition of perfect ones.

For this reason, then, I too, in all the treatises which I composed for you, my companions, at your request, did not content myself with the general theorems alone, but also added many exercises, [888] by means of which I hoped that your knowledge of them would become clearer and more secure. Just as, then, in the case of all the other parts of medicine, so too in the case of the treatment of those wounded in the nerves I wrote, first showing you the rational path to the discovery of remedies, and next after this the materials, in which you learned that the powers discovered by reason are contained. For in the commentaries on the power of simple drugs, which are eleven in number, I wrote up the powers in the particular materials, all of them, or at any rate the greatest number of the most useful ones.

For indeed this was shown to be necessary for a ready supply of remedies, and not only so that you yourselves too may be able, without prepared drugs, in situations of want to be well supplied with remedies—as Erasistratus once found a supply of the juice of herbs when he did not have a stomatic drug with him in that place on his journey—but also so that, even if you lose the written recipes of those who compounded them, you yourselves may nevertheless be able [889] to compound ones closely similar to those that were lost. And moreover, the training acquired through the present treatise is also useful for employing well the drugs discovered by others. What need is there to say that it is useful also for being able to distinguish both the things superfluously thrown into compound drugs and, conversely, all that has been omitted by those who first compounded them? As I showed when making my argument about the drugs in the third book, those suited to those wounded in the nerves, so likewise I shall now show, exercising you on the drugs discovered by physicians older than myself. For the general method was written by none of my predecessors, neither accurately with distinctions nor deficiently without distinctions; but neither did anyone write down a drug professing to cure those who have been pricked in a nerve by some sharp object—such as needles and children's styluses are—a drug able to do this one thing alone excellently, whereas I went through a not easily counted multitude of them in the aforementioned book.

Some of them, however, who wrote down notable drugs of many uses (polychrēsta) — those at least who were more careful — added, in addition to the other things they profess these drugs [890] to do, sometimes that they are beneficial also for those wounded in the nerves, at other times for severings of nerves and muscles, and there are times when they said that they also help punctures or contusions of them. But you, from what you have learned, are able to recognise before trial whether someone professes things possible or impossible concerning what he has written. And it is also possible for you, in the case of drugs that have been written down without a statement of what they are naturally able to do, to recognise the conditions on which they are to be used. So then, in order that I may begin, by way of example, with a certain plaster drug of many uses (polychrēston), written second in order in the pharmacological book of Andromachus which he composed on the drugs applied externally to the body, without his indicating for what it is especially to be used, it is possible for you once again to exercise yourselves in how one must recognise, from the simple drugs written down, the power of the compound. [The grey Egyptian of Andromachus.] For Andromachus wrote as follows, word for word: The grey Egyptian. Take litharge, 44 drachms; castor oil, 6 cotylae; wax, 144 drachms; ammoniac incense, 72 drachms; terebinth resin, 36 drachms.

of burnt wool [891] 18 drachms; of scale of steel (stomoma) 8 drachms; of scale of copper 8 drachms; of aristolochia 8 drachms; of frankincense 8 drachms; some add myrrh 4 drachms; of opopanax 2 drachms; of sea-water 50 drachms, for the soaking of the wax. This, then, is the recipe of the drug, which is in truth a good one and of many uses; but he himself omitted to say in which cases it is to be used. Now if, having first stated the power of each of the simple drugs, as we did in eleven books, and having also written some general method of the composition of drugs, as I did in the book preceding this one, he had proposed such recipes to the others then living for the sake of exercise, so that they might answer for which affections it can be useful, we would truly have praised his teaching. But since he did none of these things, one might find fault with him in every way. For this reason, then, his books on drugs, although they contain the compositions of a very great many excellent drugs, have with good reason been neglected by physicians.

For among a thousand, some one person seems to possess the perfection of the art, while the rest, [892] just like laymen, are content if they are able to use correctly the drugs that have been clearly written up. And why need one speak of such physicians, when even some of those called Empiricists, although they have shown themselves noteworthy through the works of the art, nevertheless say that they do not know by what reasoning each of the compound drugs was discovered—and why do I say 'by what reasoning'? For they say that none of such things was discovered by reasoning at all. Useless to them, therefore, is the prescription of this grey plaster, which in its heading teaches only the colour, without the professed virtue in respect of its power, which it would have been better to have written before the colour. Since, then, Andromachus omitted to state its power, let us attempt to discover it from the kind and the power of the drugs that are mixed in it. Now you have learned that litharge, being of the middle mixture with respect to heating and cooling, has departed slightly towards drying.

And indeed you also know that its use in plasters is twofold: if it remains unmelted, as material only; but if it is melted, also as something able to dry, [893] and the more so if it is boiled for longer. Now, however, there is a question as to how far it will be boiled, since Andromachus has written that six cotylae of kiki, which is castor oil, must be mixed in. For he did not make clear of how many ounces, reckoned from the Roman litra, he wants the cotyle to be; and yet it would have been better for one who had lived in Rome to speak of litrai and xestai and ounces, and to leave aside the name of the cotyle, which is in use in the Greek cities outside Italy. Now if the name of the cotyle were the same in all of them, there would be no question. But as it is, since there is a very great difference in quantity among them, he ought to have said either 'I mean the Attic cotyle' or the Alexandrian or the Ephesian or some other. Now the majority of those who have written on measures and weights say that the cotyle written of by physicians in the pharmacological books is of nine ounces, of those reckoned from the Roman litra. But others say that the one of twelve ounces is meant by them, just as in Rome they customarily name the litra of oil.

But I have already heard someone saying that the kotyle written by the physicians in the pharmacological books [894] has sixteen Roman ounces; and it is no small difference with respect to the power of the drug whether one puts in large kotylai or small ones. I, at any rate, in Rome once weighed the so-called litra of oil, which they measure by means of the graduated horns, wishing to learn how much weight it has by the balance. And I found that the twelve measure-ounces of oil are equal to ten weight-ounces. Therefore the physicians ought to write more carefully in the pharmacological books what sort of ounces or litrai of the liquid drugs they order to be put in, whether the measure-ones or the weight-ones. For it is evident that of these liquid bodies, just as of the solid ones, some are heavier and others lighter. And the weight of each of the liquids put into drugs has been stated by me in another treatise; but now let us resume the matter before us. For as to the three kotylai, if one sets each at nine measure-ounces, he will make the three come to twenty-seven ounces.

and when each of these is divided [895] into 8 drachmas, they will have two hundred and sixteen drachmas. But if one were to suppose that each kotyle consists of 12 ounces, there will be thirty-six ounces, and 288 drachmas, each ounce being divided into 8 drachmas. I myself have found by experience, having often boiled litharge in oil, that the well-proportioned mixture of it comes about when the weight-litra of litharge is set equal to the measure-litra of oil; and that if one puts in more oil, it being of course boiled for a longer time, it becomes more drying. In the case of the white plasters, on account of the colour, we mix white lead too with the litharge, for the most part equal to equal by weight. And the kotyle of 9 ounces is put in, in relation to the weight-litra of litharge, by those who wish to preserve the colour, because the longer boiling makes the litharge blacker; but the drug becomes less adhesive when only a little oil has been put in.

For this reason some have mixed in either terebinth resin or the transparent kind called colophony, trying, as far as possible, to harm neither the colour nor the power of the drug, [896] and to add to it, by the admixture of the resin, the property of not easily falling off, because the drug becomes crumbly if so much of the litharge and of the white lead is boiled in so much oil. Others, on the same principle, added white wax to the drug once it had been boiled. To litharge that has double the quantity of oil, however, even if you add nothing resinous or waxy, the adhesive quality will belong as a result of the boiling, and much more so if you mix in triple the oil to the litharge, that is, if you mix three measure-litrai of oil with three weight-litrai of litharge. It is likely, then, that Andromachus wants the castor oil to be put in at nine metric ounces [per kotyle], so that the six kotylai come to fifty-four metric ounces, which is the same as four and a half Roman metric litrai. And it is quite clear that, if at some time castor oil is not available to us, we shall take old oil in its place.

And I myself have often put Sicyonian oil into the discutient plasters, and when that too was not available, I improvised another oil and made it similar to those, by boiling down in it roots of wild cucumber and bryony [897] and marshmallow. That Andromachus wants the drug before us to be both discutient and emollient is quite evident from his putting castor oil into it, and a very large amount of ammoniac incense. For he wants the wax to be equal to the litharge in weight, and the ammoniac a half; and yet in many of the renowned plasters this drug is put in not at a half, but at a fourth part or a fifth, and often a seventh and an eighth, and sometimes a tenth, by weight, in relation to the litharge. Concerning wax we have learned that it holds the rank of material in the compositions of such drugs, not the contribution of an active power. It too possesses some slight emollient power, but it has not been taken up into the drug before us on account of this, just as the terebinth resin has not either, although it is far more plastic (πλαστικωτέρα) in power than wax. For indeed it softens more than wax does, and in addition it heats and disperses, whereas wax has neither of these. But the ammoniac incense, if put in alone, will make the drug dry and crumbly (αὐχμηρόν).

But for [898] plaster-making—for it is no worse to name it thus—both the wax and the resin are useful. For in fact softening and dispersing belong to the drug even from the ammoniac alone, which holds the first place among emollients and is a rival also to the discutients. And if you recall what was said in the fifth book of On the Powers of Simple Drugs, as to what sort of mixture such drugs must have, you will have no further need of fresh instruction. For the primary active powers of drugs lie in heat and cold and moisture and dryness; the secondary are the emollient, the discutient, the repellent, the attractive, the concocting, the detergent and the septic, just as the tertiary are those agglutinative of wounds, the cicatrizing and the flesh-producing. And so the drug compounded from castor oil and ammoniac incense is sufficient to disperse and to soften and, evidently, also to dry, having taken on as suitable material the wax and the resin and the litharge that has been boiled for a longer time.

And he orders that there be added to it [899] also some burnt wool and aristolochia, drugs that are most discutient and most desiccative; after these he mentions a concocting and soothing drug, frankincense. And if we should also put in some myrrh and opopanax—for he says that some people mix some of these too into the drug—we know that myrrh heats and dries in no ignoble fashion, while opopanax does both of these even more vigorously and is moreover of an attenuating and discutient faculty. But of this only a very little is put in, since, I think, the one who added it feared the acridity of the drug and wished to make the plaster not only discutient and emollient but also suitable for wounds. For this reason, then, he also mixed into it the scale of copper and of steel (στομώματος), drugs that have an astringent faculty together with drying strongly. At any rate, on account of the admixture of these, the Egyptian plaster under discussion becomes a good drug for bleeding wounds and for not a few other ulcers.

And indeed also for abscesses and for all [900] such things as need to be dispersed, you have often heard that those remedies which, together with the discutient drugs, contain also something of the astringents become safer, whereas those without the astringent ingredients are more effective, but not safe. For often such a remedy draws fluxes, when the body being treated is plethoric or full of bad humours. But if the body is empty and free of superfluity, the more discutient drugs, taken by themselves without the astringents, reach their goal more readily. Since, however, the drugs are applied to such bodies only in few cases, for this reason it has seemed safer to mix in also something of the repellents. Thus indeed some have added a little chalcanthum to the discutient plaster made with salts, although the salts themselves also have something astringent.

The drug under discussion, then, has been found to be strongly discutient, so that it is able to disperse even pus already present—at least when it is not very abundant—without perforating the skin; emollient for parts that are becoming scirrhous or hardened in any way whatever; agglutinative of large wounds, just as it is also cicatrizing of ulcers that are already becoming malignant, [901] and of all the other affections that are apportioned (μετρεῖται) a power at once discutient and repellent, among which are also the things applied to the forehead for eyes affected by flux, which are called by physicians anakollēmata. This same drug will also be suitable for nerves that have been laid bare, even if they happen to have been cut in some part of them. For those that have been cut through, no longer having the danger that arises from sympathy, also take away the sensation of the bodies lying beneath it (ἑαυτῷ), into which it is held down (κατίσχεται). Yet these too require such a drug. For moistening agents easily putrefy them; for this reason the drying small disks too, although they are considerably astringent, are nevertheless suitable for nerves that have been laid bare—those, at least, which have not yet already arrived at the peak of inflammation. For these are irritated and exacerbated by such drugs. But these matters will be spoken of as the discussion proceeds; concerning the plaster under discussion, let us add what is lacking to the account.

But since most physicians, out of ignorance, apply such plasters in a hard state, it is better to make them into lint-dressings (ἐμμότους) by melting them, [902] or to work them soft straightaway in the course of preparation. Then, when they have made trial of them on large divisions in which nerves have been laid bare, they expect that they will be much more beneficial in the case of punctures, being ignorant here too of a most important theorem, concerning which I have already discoursed when teaching you — things which I first discovered by reasoning and then recognised as confirmed by experience; for this reason I remind you of it now as well. For punctures of nerves require drugs that are much hotter and more discutient than when a whole nerve has been laid bare, a considerable wound having occurred. For those that have been laid bare do not tolerate the application of acrid and very hot drugs, because of the bitingness, but they need relaxing and discutient ones mixed in due proportion with the astringent drugs. But also that it is better to take hold of the parts around the wound with drugs that are acrid, fine-particled and sufficiently discutient, such as the one made with euphorbium. I, then, inferred that the plaster under discussion was capable of doing what I have said before, and having prepared it I found experience bearing witness.

But later [903] at some point, when I also came upon the pharmacological books of Asclepiades and Criton, I learned that they had written, not indefinitely as Andromachus too had done, but with distinctions, clearly, what power it has. Both for this reason, then, and because they disagree in certain points with Andromachus regarding the preparation, it seemed better to me to append the very words of those authors as well, and then in this way to say something also about their disagreement regarding the composition of the drug. [On what has been written by Asclepiades and Criton about the plaster under discussion.] Concerning the Egyptian plaster written down by Andromachus, Asclepiades wrote as follows. Andromachus' Egyptian, bloodless, wound-plaster. It is effective for severings of nerves and muscles; it is effective for punctures, contusions, chafings, sprains. It is also an adhesive application for those suffering from ophthalmia. It works for those suffering from headache, and the drug is useful for many conditions. ♃ Of litharge, of wax, 144 drachms each; of ammoniac incense, 72 drachms; of terebinth resin, 36 drachms.

of greasy, oesypum-laden wool, burnt, [904] 18 drachmas; of scale of copper, 8 drachmas; of scale of steel (stomōma), 8 drachmas; of frankincense, 8 drachmas; of round aristolochia, 8 drachmas; of castor-oil (kiki), 3 cotylae. Having first stated these things, Asclepiades next writes the manner of the boiling—Andromachus not having preserved even this part of the composition in the case of the plasters, for it has been omitted in almost all of them. But concerning the boilings not a little has been said in the fourth book, and it will also be spoken of now, a little further on. It is worth examining the matter of the disagreement which Asclepiades made with Andromachus in the quantity of the simple drugs. For he thinks it right to put in not six cotylae of the castor-oil, as Andromachus does, but three; and in the case of the aristolochia, Andromachus having made no prior specification, he himself added 'round', just as also in the case of the burnt greasy wool. The weight, however, he puts in equal to that of Andromachus. At any rate he writes thus: ♃ of greasy wool, burnt, 18 drachmas; of round aristolochia, 8 drachmas.

But what Andromachus added at the end Asclepiades did not write at all, saying nothing either about the [905] myrrh or about the opopanax, and much less about the sea-water, although Andromachus had clearly written beforehand: 'sea-water for the soaking (ἐμβροχή) of the wax, 50 drachmas'; for neither Asclepiades nor Criton added this. The round aristolochia, however, Criton puts in in the same way as Asclepiades, just as also the 18 drachmas of greasy (oesypum-bearing) wool and of castor oil—for he wrote literally thus—6 kotylai. The boiling of the plaster is written by Asclepiades in the following manner: boil litharge and castor oil until it thickens together, then the scales, and when it becomes of good colour, add the rest. In Criton, in the following manner: boil litharge with castor oil until it has the thickness of honey. When this has happened, sprinkle on the scales and boil together for a sufficient time, until it becomes non-staining; then terebinth and wax, and, once these have been united, ammoniac previously softened by the fire with the fingers. And when already lifting it from the fire, sprinkle in the ash of the greasy wool, afterwards at the end the frankincense, and then take it up thus.

And concerning [906] what the drug professes, Criton wrote more carefully, verbatim thus: "The Egyptian, which keeps every division and every contusion free of inflammation. It is also well suited to every bite of wild beasts, and it benefits also the inflammations that arise without ulcers. It is good also for pains of the nerves and muscles that arise without a manifest cause." [Another grey plaster of Andromachus.] Andromachus also wrote other grey plasters, somewhat of the same kind as the one written above. He calls the one Athena, the other nygmatic (for punctures). The Athena is suited to more conditions than the nygmatic, and especially to those accompanied by ulcers, since it is both more varied in composition and partakes still more of astringent drugs; whereas the nygmatic is more relaxing and more pain-relieving than this one. Concerning the former of the drugs mentioned, then, he wrote verbatim thus: Grey Athena. Take: litharge, 100 drachmas; terebinth resin, 36 drachmas; wax, 25 drachmas; Sinopic red earth, 24 drachmas; ammoniac incense, 36 drachmas; galbanum, 12 drachmas; aloe, 8 drachmas; diphryges, 8 drachmas.

of burnt copper [907] 6 drachms, of mastic 6 drachms, of aristolochia 5 drachms, of propolis 5 drachms, of manna 6 drachms, of copper scale 6 drachms, of Asian stone 3 drachms, of trefoil seed 2 drachms, of comfrey root 1 drachm and four obols, of oil 4 cotylae. Concerning the other grey plaster Andromachus wrote, in his very words, as follows. Grey plaster for punctures (nygmatic). Take: of ammoniac 8 drachms, of fresh wax 8 drachms, of terebinth resin 3 drachms, of burnt copper 8 drachms, of dry pitch 40 drachms—but according to Zeno a half and a quarter of a mina—of litharge 4 drachms, of Indian aloe 2 drachms, of aristolochia 2 drachms, of galbanum 2 drachms, of verdigris 1 drachm (others say 2 drachms), of frankincense 2 drachms, of oil in winter 4 cotylae, in summer an eighth, of vinegar half a cotyle, for the dissolving of the ammoniac.

And Andromachus wrote many other plasters together with these, adding nothing to them beyond the name of their colour, composed of drugs opposite in their powers; but some of them have the relaxing and anodyne [quality] predominating, others the discutient and detersive, and others astringency. So that we too must, having confidence in all [908] of them, use each suitably: for ulcers hard to cicatrize and malignant, those that contain more of the astringent; where it is proposed to soothe and relax, those [containing] the relaxing; and where to draw out and disperse, those [containing] the heating [drugs] and those which draw to themselves the vicious humours of conditions lying in the depth. To some of them this too has been added in writing: "Simple grey plaster, which I use." For he wrote three such in succession, not composed of many ingredients, and of these too I thought it better to append the composition in his own words: "Simple grey plaster, which I use. Take litharge 24 drachms, kiki (castor) oil 1 cotyle, burnt copper 4 drachms, manna 4 drachms, resin 4 drachms, Colophonian 8 drachms. Another, anodyne, of Isidorus. Take litharge 36 drachms, wax 36 drachms, oil 1½ cotylae, Colophonian resin 15 drachms, copper scale 9 drachms, manna 50 drachms. Boil. Another, which I use. Take litharge 144 drachms, dry resin 144 drachms, scale 24 drachms, oil 3 cotylae."

He calls [913] one of them that of Phtheirographos, which he says is compounded of these: ♃ litharge 100 dr., resin 50 dr., ammoniac incense 30 dr., wax 50 dr., scraped verdigris 12 dr., copper scale 2 dr., aristolochia 8 dr., centaury root 8 dr., oil 2 cotylae.
