And that of Irion he says is compounded thus: ♃ litharge 144 dr., dry pitch 144 dr., terebinth 72 dr., ammoniac incense 72 dr., manna and frankincense 102 dr. each, calf's fat 144 dr., wax 36 dr., aristolochia 9 dr., burnt copper 9 dr., scraped verdigris 9 dr., galbanum 9 dr., opopanax 9 dr., vinegar half a cotyle, oil 1½ cotylae, castor oil an equal amount. It is quite clear that he wants the litharge and the pitch and the calf's fat to be double in weight the terebinth and the ammoniac incense and the frankincense, fourfold the wax, and sixteenfold the aristolochia and the burnt copper and the verdigris and the galbanum and the opopanax.

And this drug too is sufficiently of many uses (polychrēston), just like the others [914] written above, and one must use all of them with confidence. Hellespontia, according to Andromachus. This plaster too, being renowned, Andromachus recorded among the grey plasters, in this proportion: ♃ litharge 100 dr., pitch 50 dr., ladanum 25 dr., scraped verdigris 8 dr., burnt copper 8 dr., scale 2 dr., old oil 200 dr. [Hellespontia of Heras.] But since Andromachus differs from Heras in the composition of the drug, it seemed good to me to add also what has been written by Heras, which runs word for word as follows. Hellespontia, diapnoic (promoting transpiration), non-inflammatory. For scrofulous swellings (choirades), phygethla (glandular swellings), parotid swellings, the splenion, once applied, draws, produces pus, breaks (them), agglutinates, and in general it acts on all burns, and it also soothes gouty patients. ♃ old oil 100 dr., dry pitch 50 dr., ladanum 25 dr., litharge 100 dr., scraped verdigris 8 dr., galbanum 4 dr. Having ground the litharge finely with the oil, boil it.

And when it thickens together, add the pitch [915] and the verdigris, then ladanum and the galbanum, and having thus poured it out into a mortar, soften it and use it. Some, in order that it may become of good colour and grey, mix in also 8 drachms of scale (lepis); for otherwise it becomes very black. I have often used this also in cases of gout, and it worked excellently. One must use pine-torchwood (daidia) instead of ordinary wood. It is evident that the two men disagree in the other items only slightly, but in the proportion of oil very greatly; for Andromachus puts in double what Heras does. It can also be prepared in the other way, provided we know that if more oil is put in, it indicates (dēloi) that the boiling becomes longer and that the drug itself will turn out more drying; but if less, that the boiling that is to be done will hold back (antechein) and the drug will be less drying. [The plasters of many uses (polychrēsta) written by Damocrates. The Tyrian, needing no bandage.] Following on these, I should like to describe the uses and the compositions of plasters that need no bandage.

They are effective for divisions that are not great, [916] and for the larger wounds of the flesh itself, and the superficial bites of four-footed animals; they also disperse recent boils (dothienes). They open those that already contain pus too, and, carrying off the eschars upon them, they will very quickly bring on cicatrisation without surgery. And when applied to the forehead they alone most easily check the fluxes of those suffering from ophthalmia. Of this kind I shall first describe the better plaster, easily procured, of good colour, effective; I call it the Tyrian, for it takes on the colour of Tyrian purple, if it is made in the way it ought. Prepare it thus: of good litharge put in five pounds, and of wax one, and of pine resin three, the oily kind and free of wood.

And of good verdigris of copper and of galbanum, and of burnt copper and of good scale, [917] put in four ounces of each ingredient; and of rich oil, fifteen pounds and one. And boil the plaster carefully in this way: having put the very finely ground litharge together with the oil into a rather large and new earthenware pot, rub it up with the hands, then stir it also with a spatula, and boil it over a fierce and continuous flame. And when it takes on the consistency of honey, add the verdigris and the scale, and let it boil for a sufficient time; then add the copper. And having again let it boil for a short time, pour off a little of the drug from the pot; cool it and rub it up with the hands and the fingers, and when you see it well-coloured and hard, then add the pine resin and the wax. Then, when all have been carefully united, again drip off a little.

And if you see it well-coloured and well-blended, lift the pot at once from the fire, [918] and add galbanum that has been softened beforehand. But if the drug is far too hard, add oil to it for a good temperament, straining it thus; then, into another cold vessel, knead it with the hands and so store it away. I shall write out another, of the same kind as the one before it. It works for the affections I mentioned before: this one cicatrises, better than all drugs, ulcers hard-to-heal and callous and chronic. The exanthemata that arise on the face this one treats without any harmful biting; and in seats that have fissures, it casts off the knotty indurations and the calluses. Prepare it thus: a mina of good litharge. A mina is a litra and a third part of a litra. Of good Pontic wax, half a mina; of verdigris, good scraped, a fourth part of a mina; of black chamaeleon, an eighth part.

[919] And the good root is the Cretan, the first; then the Cilician. And of old oil a mina, with a slight tipping of the scale beyond; but if it is not at hand, use fresh. Boil, having put the litharge, ground smooth, and all the oil into a pot, stirring with a spatula. And when it sets and becomes quince-yellow, sprinkle in the verdigris, then add the wax, and having melted this, and having lifted it from the fire, sprinkle in a little of the chamaeleon. And when all have been united and have cooled somewhat, pour it out into a mortar, and so store it away. The Egyptian. The Egyptian, which keeps free of inflammation every division and all contusions, and the bites of all four-footed creatures and of reptiles, and all inflammations that have arisen without ulcers, and pains of nerves and muscles without a cause.

[920] Andromachus, praising this one, since he had the greatest expertise in drugs, used to give it to his friends. He said that there were of litharge three times forty drachmas and another twice twelve; of white Pontic wax an amount equal to these; of pure ammoniac three times twenty and twelve more; of frankincense twice four; of scale of copper and of scale of steel (stomōma), again twice four of each ingredient; of pure terebinth three times twelve; and eighteen kotylai of castor oil by measure; of foul wool, burnt, eighteen.

And he said to burn them in this manner: putting into a new dish or a wide-mouthed pot an abundance of greasy wool, having first smeared the body (of the vessel) with gypsum or with ash, or with potter's earth mixed with water, burning it in a fierce fire, and when it is easy (to do so), [921] pounding it and sifting it—at least as far as it seems to be well; and to burn them likewise also in baking-ovens, and in furnaces that have been very strongly fired, and grinding them fine in this way, take the weight that is required. And he bids one boil the very finely ground litharge together with all the castor oil, having mixed them in a new pot, and when the drug has reached the thickness of honey, to sprinkle on the scale and boil it together for a sufficient time, until it becomes non-staining; then to throw in the terebinth and the wax, and then, when these have been united, the ammoniac softened by the fingers. And when about to lift the pot from the fire, to sprinkle in the finely ground frankincense, and to throw in also the ash of the greasy (wool) at the very end, but before the frankincense, a little later (than the rest).

But some, wishing this drug to be called their own, remove the one [922] of the one scale and put in the sixteen; and they use scale of copper, not of steel (stomōma). Another. In no way inferior to the former Egyptian, doing the same things, and sometimes even better, if one prepares the drug carefully so as to be thick and uses it not carelessly for the same purposes. It contains five pounds of oil, an equal amount of castor oil, four of litharge of the chrysitis kind, forty-eight drachms of scale of copper, of good terebinth resin three times twelve, of manna of frankincense the same as the terebinth, of pure ammoniac two pounds, and of white Pontic wax two and a half pounds.

Boil the oil, the scale, and the litharge until it comes together and becomes very good in colour and a sufficiently hard plaster; then, in this way, throw in the terebinth and the wax, then [923] the ammoniac softened with the fingers; then, having lifted the pot from the fire while it is boiling, you will then throw in the manna, when the drug is already cooling. I have often made this without litharge, throwing in an equal quantity of good molybdaena, and have used it with the greatest satisfaction for the purposes we mentioned before, and made of a better colour. [On the diaphoretic and epispastic plasters.] Those who have written on the powers of compound drugs called some of the plasters epispastic, just as they called others diaphoretic. And to some of them they attested both, that they both draw and disperse. For indeed the powers are close to one another, the attractive power that draws things from the depth, and the diaphoretic power that disperses what has been drawn. For those that draw also disperse something in any case, and those that disperse also draw. But in the diaphoretic drugs the diaphoretic power prevails, and in the attractive ones the attractive.

The attractive ones, then, are composed by means of those simple drugs which [924] have the power to draw the surpluses of the humours from the depth to the skin, while the discutient ones are composed from those which are of a nature to disperse what has been drawn. But in order that a plaster may result, as was said in what precedes, with one of them litharge is mixed, with another resin, with another wax, with another oil, with another pitch—such things having neither a noteworthy discutient power nor an attractive one, as do propolis or lime or marrow or galbanum or the flower of the Asian stone or foam of nitron or aphronitron or vinegar or dripped lye, pepper and mustard and soapwort, and both the edible kinds of salts and the ammoniac ones, and in addition to these many others, concerning whose power it has been stated in the treatise on simple drugs. But now I shall state the plasters that have already given sufficient proof by experience, saying only this much more about them: that some have also mixed some of the astringent drugs with the epispastic ones, guarding against what happens in those cases in which there will be a surplus of humours.

For they sometimes draw more than is fitting, so that they produce the attraction not only from what lies in the depth at the part under treatment, but also from all the [925] surrounding parts. And I have said before, in the discussion of the flesh-producing powers, that the attractive and the discutient ones, just as also all those that cleanse more than they should, become flesh-producing by admixture of cerate—of more cerate in those whose power is strong, of less in those whose power is weak. But if the compound attractive or discutient drug happens to contain also something astringent, one must not use such a drug as a flesh-producing one, because the astringent powers are useful for the agglutination of wounds and of sinuses and for the cicatrization of ulcers, but useless for the production of flesh. For enough has already been said by us on this matter. [The discutient and attractive plasters written by Andromachus. A salt plaster for many purposes.] Take: common salt, 4 litrae; scale of copper, 4 ounces; magma, half a litra; manna, 1 litra; wax, 14 litrae; henna oil, 16 litrae; vinegar. Another, of Theudas, a flesh-eating plaster, for malignant ulcers, fistulas, teredones, scrofulous swellings. Take: terebinth resin, 4 ounces;

[926] of frankincense 4 ounces, of wax 4 ounces, of litharge 1 ounce (others use an equal amount of arsenic in place of the litharge), of red scale 4 ounces, of scraped verdigris 8 ounces, of salt ammoniac 6 ounces, of vinegar 1 kotylē; I add in addition 1 kotylē of oil, 1 kotylē of wine, a kotylē of squill vinegar. Another discutient, of Candidus, which I use: take of terebinth resin 3 pounds, of wax 50 pounds (?), of galbanum 2 ounces, of nitron 2 ounces, of Asian stone 2 ounces, of frankincense 4 pounds, of deer's marrow 4 ounces, of ammoniac incense half a pound, of propolis 3 ounces, of bay oil 6 ounces, of bull's suet half a pound; the dry ingredients over the melted ones. Another for scrofulous swellings, from Nymphodotus: take of Asian stone 8 drachms, of aphronitron 8 drachms, of quicklime 16 drachms, of calf's suet 16 drachms, of wax 24 drachms, of terebinth resin 32 drachms. Another discutient for bronchoceles, with which Clemens Sertorius was cured, and for indurations: take of litharge 50 drachms, of pine resin 40 drachms, of old oil 10 kotylai, of galbanum 4 drachms (in another copy, 1 ounce), of burnt copper 20 drachms,

of ammoniac [927] incense 40 drachms; of split (alum) 4 drachms; of manna of frankincense 4 drachms; of wax 50 drachms. Add the galbanum and the manna last. Another, the one made with asps, dispersive of scrofulous swellings and for gout. Rx: of terebinth, of Asian stone, of asphalt, 360 drachms each; of aphronitron, of calf's (fat), of wax, of bay-berries, of ammoniac incense, 340 drachms each; of pyrite stone 80 drachms; of quicklime 108 drachms, otherwise 1 mina; of ash of asps 140 drachms; of old oil 2 cotylae. Add the ash last, when the drug has cooled; otherwise it is ruined. Another, drawing, the one of Sarkeuthites. Rx: of terebinth 1 mina; of wax 1 mina; of nitre 2 minae; of bdellium 32 drachms; of ammoniac incense 32 drachms; of oil 2 cotylae; of sea-water or brine 2 cotylae; of red ochre 32 drachms. Another, that of Ctesiphon, dissolving some things, but drawing together and cleansing others. Rx: of aphronitron 1 pound; of manna of frankincense 1 pound; of dripped lye 1 pound; some add also vinegar, 1 pound. Another, drawing, made with salts. Rx: of common salt 80 drachms; of white lead 80 drachms; of old oil 40 cotylae, otherwise 3.

of chalcanthum, [928] 24 drachms; of vinegar, half a kotyle. Another, the one with salts, in another version. ℞ of white lead, 8 drachms; of common salt, 50 drachms; of old oil, 8 kotylai (otherwise 2); of aristolochia, 8 drachms; of propolis, 10 drachms. This one Silon commended. Another, the one with pelagian earth, discutient. ℞ of litharge, 4 minae; of pelagian earth, a quarter; of ammoniac salt, a quarter; of white lead, a quarter; of wax, a quarter; of vinegar, 1 kotyle; of oil, 4 kotylai. Another, that of Kyrtos, epispastic. ℞ of Illyrian iris, 50 drachms; of manna, 50 drachms; of terebinth resin, 50 drachms; of aphronitron, 50 drachms; of pumice, 50 drachms; of ammoniac incense, 25 drachms; of galbanum, 16 drachms (otherwise 6); of cachrys, 12½ drachms; of wax, 100 drachms, but some say 8; of oil, 1 kotyle. Another, the one with bay-berries. ℞ of resin, of red nitron, of new wax, of bay-berries, of Colophonian resin, of calf's fat, of ammoniac incense, 70 drachms each; of henna oil, one sixteenth of a kotyle; and some add mistletoe, 50 drachms. Another epispastic, of Harpalos. ℞ of ammoniac incense, 8 drachms; of wax, 4 drachms; of iris, 4 drachms; of manna, 4 drachms; of pepper, 4 drachms; of unburnt sulphur, 4 drachms; of pumice, 4 drachms.

[929] of terebinth, 8 drachmas; a little oil. Another drawing plaster of Harpalus. Take of terebinth, 8 minae; of pumice, 15 drachmas; of nitron, 16 drachmas; of ammoniac incense, 16 drachmas; of wax, 4 drachmas; a small quantity of oil; of red ochre (miltos), enough to colour the dry ingredients, together with vinegar. Another. Take of mustard, 4 drachmas; of nitron, 4 drachmas; of wax, 8 drachmas; of terebinth, 30 drachmas; of bay-berries, 4 drachmas; of quicklime, 4 drachmas; of oil, one sixteenth of a kotyle; of henna oil, 8 drachmas. Another, which disperses pus. Take of wax, terebinth resin, dry pitch, calf's suet, red nitron, bay-berries, quicklime, pumice, ammoniac incense, an equal amount of each. Another, of Codamus, or of King Nicodemus. Take of wax, 100 drachmas; of red nitron, 100 drachmas; of roasted resin, 100 drachmas; of ammoniac incense, 25 drachmas; of propolis, 25 drachmas; of oak mistletoe, 12½ drachmas; of oil, 1 sextarius; of dripped lye, 1 sextarius. Another, dispersive, for melikerides. Take of old oil, 100 drachmas; of litharge, ??1 drachmas; of ammoniac incense and of galbanum, 19 drachmas each. Another. Take of litharge, 100 drachmas; of common salt, 60 drachmas; of old oil, 6 kotylai (according to another reading, 1).

Another drawing [930] and dispersing plaster, of many uses (polychrēston). ♃ Litharge 1 litra, white lead (psimythion) 1 litra, galbanum 1 litra, mined salt half a litra, scraped verdigris half a litra, oil 3 xestai, chalcanthum 2 ounces. Another dispersing plaster, the one with soapwort. ♃ Litharge 2 litrai, oil 3 litrai, white lead 4 ounces, pitch 4 ounces, terebinth resin 4 ounces, wax 2 ounces, manna (of frankincense) 3 ounces, aristolochia 2 ounces, soapwort 2 ounces, oak-galls 3 ounces, good wine 3 kotylai. Sprinkle the wine in last. Another dispersing plaster, according to Scribonius. ♃ Litharge 5 litrai, oil 5 litrai, dry pine resin 5 litrai, propolis 8 litrai, of the oak (mistletoe) 3 ounces. Another drawing and dispersing plaster. ♃ New wax 100 drachmai, dry pine resin 100 drachmai, nitron 100 drachmai, oil 3 kotylai; some add frankincense 100 drachmai, dripped lye 3 kotylai. For hardnesses there is mixed in ammoniac incense 12 drachmai, galbanum the same amount, scraped verdigris, propolis, oak (mistletoe) the same amount. Another, for scrofulous swellings (choirades), of Minucianus, which I use in the case of girls (kata koras). ♃ Terebinth resin 1 litra, wax 8 litrai, propolis 1 litra, galbanum 8 litrai, oak mistletoe 8 litrai.

Having melted these, [931] sprinkle in 2 ounces of burnt wine-lees, 8 pounds of aphronitron; then, setting it off the coals, add 3 cotylae of oil; then, having taken it down, sprinkle in 1 ounce of root of wild cucumber, 4 ounces of root of xiphion, 4 ounces of flower of Asian stone. Another, of Antipater. Take nitron 1 pound, terebinth 1 pound, old oil 1 pound, water 1 sextarius and more; when, while being boiled, it no longer bubbles, add ammoniac incense 2 ounces, galbanum 1 ounce, bdellium 1 ounce, frankincense 2 ounces, sandarach 2 ounces, Asian stone 2 ounces. The Asian stone and the sandarach are ground smooth with a little oil; the meltable ingredients are scraped up and mixed with the dry ones. Another discutient, of Antipater. Take molybdaena 300 drachmas, wax 150 drachmas, terebinth 30 drachmas, chalcitis 6 drachmas, galbanum 8 drachmas, myrrh 8 drachmas, manna 8 drachmas, oil in winter 4 cotylae, in summer 3 cotylae. Another, of Xenocrates, anodyne, discutient, according to Castus, the one of Polystomus for podagra. Take white lead 150 drachmas, wax 3 pounds, terebinth 30 drachmas, aphronitron 30 drachmas, old oil 3 cotylae. Another discutient for melicerides, of Alexander. Take Spanish salt 1 pound, litharge 1 pound.

[932] of white lead 1 pound; of wax 1 ounce; of terebinth resin 1 ounce; of galbanum, or alternatively of opopanax, 2 ounces; of mustard 6 ounces; of old oil 3 pounds; of vinegar 8 xestai. Another, the Hygieia, discutient and drawing, for the breasts, made with birdlime (ixos). ℞ of litharge 2 pounds; of oil 2 pounds; of oak birdlime 4 ounces; of oak-galls 4 ounces. Another, evacuative of pus without rupture, according to Asclepiades. ℞ of resin 2 pounds; of wax 2 pounds; of nitre 8 pounds; of butter 1 pound; of lion's fat 6 pounds; of old oil 1 pound. Melt together; use daily, spreading on some of the drug as a plaster. Another, which presses out humours and abscesses, especially in the knees and joints, drawing without incision, non-inflammatory and a wound-plaster. ℞ of dross of lead 100 drachms; of terebinth resin 100 drachms; of old oil 2 kotylai; the resin last. Another, discutient and rupturing and cicatrizing, provocative, which I use. ℞ of oak birdlime 60 drachms; of pitch 50 drachms; of ammoniac incense 100 drachms; of wax 50 drachms.

of roasted (phrykte) resin [933] 15 drachms, of pyrites stone 10 drachms, of galbanum 8 drachms, of manna 4 drachms, of Illyrian iris 4 drachms, of cachrys 4 drachms, of pigeon dung 4 drachms; in some copies also 4 kotylai of honey, in some also 20 drachms of propolis. Having melted the meltable ingredients, sprinkle in the dry ones. [The epispastic plasters written by Asclepiades.] A white epispastic. It works for scrofulous swellings (choirades) and parotid swellings and the local abscesses; it works for fistulas and aegilopes, so as to deliver from them without incision; it works for the rheumatic and hard-to-heal conditions; it works for dropsical patients. Take: of litharge 80 drachms, of white lead 80 drachms, of salt 80 drachms, of old oil 1 sextarius. Grind the salt, white lead and litharge, pouring the oil over them; then, having mixed them carefully and put them into an earthenware vessel, boil, stirring continuously, until it no longer stains; and having poured it out into a mortar and beaten it up, take it up and use. Another. Take: of litharge 100 drachms, of white lead 10 drachms, of salt 50 drachms, of oil 3 kotylai, of wax 50 drachms, of terebinth 12 drachms.

prepare in the [934] usual manner. Another. ♃ Of manna 16 drachmas, of split alum 8 drachmas, of old oil 2 kotylai. Another. ♃ Of litharge 1 litra, of white lead 1 litra, of mined salt 1 litra, of wax 50 drachmas, of terebinth 25 drachmas, of manna 16 drachmas, of split alum 8 drachmas, of old oil 1½ kotylai. Another, of Leucius, for the aforesaid conditions, a successful drug. It works for the rheumatic ulcers and the chronic ones and those hard to heal. ♃ Of litharge 100 drachmas, of white lead 100 drachmas, of salt ammoniac 100 drachmas, of chalcanthon 100 drachmas, of pine resin 100 drachmas, of old oil 3 xestai, of vinegar 1 xestes, of wax 50 drachmas. Prepare in the usual manner. Another, the Hygieine, a successful drug for the aforesaid conditions. ♃ Of litharge 100 drachmas, of white lead 100 drachmas, of salt 100 drachmas, of liquid alum 100 drachmas, of old oil 10 xestai, of vinegar 1 xestes, of wax ½ litra, of terebinth resin ½ litra. Prepare in the usual manner. Another black drawing plaster; it works for scrofulous swellings, parotid swellings and the local abscesses; it dissolves every hardness.

It is also a good emollient (malagma), [935] as Antonius the root-cutter used it. It is effective for the affections about the joints. Take mined salt, one pound; litharge, one pound; the purest strigil-scrapings (gloios), four pounds; and galbanum, fifty drachmas. Grind the salt and the litharge, then, adding the strigil-scrapings, beat them up diligently, and having put the mixture into an earthenware vessel and set it on the fire, boil it, stirring continuously; and when it has become non-staining, take it off the fire and add the galbanum, pounded with a wooden pestle, and when it has dissolved, pour it out into a mortar, beat it up, and use. Another, which Andromachus used: it is effective for scrofulous swellings (choirades), parotid swellings, indurations on the breasts, and local abscesses; it draws out the surrounding fluid and glues together sinuses. It is effective for fistulas and aegilopes; it is effective for rheumatic ulcers that are chronic and hard to heal. Take white lead, eighty drachmas; mined salt, eighty drachmas; chalcanthum, twelve drachmas; old oil, three kotylai; vinegar, four kotylai.

Boil the salt and white lead, ground very fine, with the oil, and stir until it does not stain; and when it is in good condition, having taken it off the [936] fire, add the chalcanthum, which has been ground fine with vinegar, sprinkling it on little by little and continuously, and taking care that it does not boil up; then, having poured it out into a mortar and beaten it up, take it up and use it. [The discutient (plasters) written down by Asclepiades, in his own wording.] When the swellings have been dissolved and have resolved into fluid, the preparations written below are to be used. Cerate of Ctesiphon, for scrofulous swellings, ganglia, parotid swellings and the abscesses on the breasts; like no other of the drugs it both dissolves the swellings and draws off all the fluid lying nearby through the rarefied passages, and it glues together sinuses. It works for fistulas and aegilopes, so as to deliver (the patient) without incision. It is also a good malagma for sciatic, gouty and arthritic patients, when applied after the paroxysms, so as to free them from the whole condition. The matters of its preparation are as follows. Take wax, 1 litra; terebinth, 1 litra; nitron, 1 litra; old oil, 1 litra; water, 1 kotyle.

Grind nitron and water, so that it is completely dissolved, and having put it into an earthenware vessel and set it [937] on the fire, boil it, having covered the vessel with a lid and stirring at intervals. When the loud noise has ceased, add the meltable ingredients, stirring continuously until it no longer stains; having emptied it into a mortar and beaten it up, take it up and use it. Or prepare it in this manner: the meltable ingredients are melted, and when they have dissolved, we add to them the nitron ground fine with the water, adding it little by little and stirring continuously and taking care that it does not boil over. Another, which Menecrates used, specifically for scrofulous swellings and for the hardnesses on the breasts; for it perforates them and discharges the surrounding fluid, and glues together the sinuses and brings them to a scar. ℞ wax, 1 litra; terebinth resin, 1 litra; woody resin, 1 litra; galbanum, 1 litra; old oil, 1 litra; aphronitron, 1 litra; ash of myrrh, 1 xestes, which comes to (ἄγγει) 3 ounces.

Put the resins into a bronze or earthenware vessel, set it on the fire and melt them, and having dissolved out of these as much as suffices to dissolve the galbanum, then, having mixed the meltable ingredients together, boil until it no longer stains; then, taking it off the fire, let it cool, and add to these [938] aphronitron, and stirring continuously and having beaten it up, add it to the ashes, ground as fine as possible, and having mixed them together and taken it up, use it, undoing the dressing every fifth day, then every third day, until the parts around the swellings have been perforated, then undoing it daily, carry on the treatment. Another, the one with aphronitron, called by some Dionysia, a well-proven drug for the aforesaid conditions, which Largus used. Take wax 1 litra, terebinth 1 litra, manna 1 litra, aphronitron 1 litra, oil 1 xestes, potter's water (pēlopoiikon) 1 xestes, raw misy 2 ounces. Compound it in the manner (described) (συντίθει καὶ τρόπον). Another, the one with Asian stone, a well-proven drug for the aforesaid conditions. Take wax 1 litra, terebinth 1 litra, nitron 1 litra, frankincense half a litra, flower of Asian stone half a litra, henna oil half a litra, potter's water as much as suffices. The dry ingredients are dissolved in potter's water so as to have the thickness of strigil-grease (gloios), and are ground thoroughly. The meltable ingredients are melted and cooled and added to the ground ingredients; having beaten it up and taken it up, we use it. Another, the Asian one, of the Neapolitan; it is effective for the aforesaid conditions.

Take: of wax [939] 1½ litrai, of red nitron 1 litra, of flower of Asian stone 1½ litrai, of manna half a litra, of myrrh 3 ounces, of old oil 1 litra, of clay-making water 1 kotyle. Prepare in the usual manner. Another, effective for the aforementioned conditions. Take: of wax 100 drachmas, of terebinth 100 drachmas, of foam of nitron 1 litra, of old oil 1 litra, of manna of frankincense 1 litra, of flower of Asian stone half a litra, of galbanum 12 drachmas, of propolis 12 drachmas, of ammoniac incense 12 drachmas, of clay-making water a sufficient quantity. Another, a tawny one, from the writings of Damocrates, effective for the aforementioned conditions. Take: of litharge 1 litra, of white lead 1 litra, of rock salt 1 litra, of Sinopic red earth half a litra, of wax 2 ounces, of galbanum 2 ounces, of terebinth 2 ounces, of old oil 3 kotylai, of vinegar enough to dissolve the Sinopic earth; prepare in the usual manner. Another, effective for the aforementioned conditions. Take: of litharge 1 litra, of white lead 1 litra, of rock salt 1 litra, of Sinopic red earth half a litra, of wax 4 ounces, of galbanum 2 ounces, of terebinth resin 2 ounces, of old oil 3 kotylai.

of vinegar, enough to dissolve the Sinopic earth; prepare in the [940] usual manner. Another, the one made with mastic; it works for the aforementioned conditions. ♃ Of wax 1 litra; of mastic, manna of frankincense, Sinopic earth, aphronitron, half a litra each; of myrtle oil 3 ounces; of sea-water 3 kotylai. Another, that of the Neapolitan; it works for the aforementioned conditions. ♃ Of litharge 1 litra; of white lead 1 litra; of mined salt 1 litra; of Sinopic red ochre half a litra; of wax half a litra; of pine resin half a litra; of galbanum 2 ounces; of oil 3 kotylai; of vinegar a sufficient quantity. [The discutient plasters written by Damocrates.] A good discutient plaster, quince-yellow, for the scrofulous swellings of children that are not old, the indurations around the muscles and the skin, and the inflammations that persist for a longer time; it both fills up with flesh and leads to cicatrization.

It is prepared thus: of good litharge, at most a litra; of white lead, half a litra. To these one adds a litra of fresh [941] rich oil. Having put in the litharge, boil it with the oil, and when you have made it like a salve in thickness, then add the white lead, finely ground. But when you see that it does not stain and is very well-tempered, and a little harder, add wax and pine-resin; and when these have melted, lift the pot, still boiling, from the fire, and then put in the ammoniac, flattened out with the hands and fingers, as wax customarily is beside the fire; then, stirring the drug with the spatula and kneading it again with the hands, store it away thus. Another. Another for all these conditions; it disperses scrofulous swellings more effectively, and benefits those who suffer, having apprehension of an abscess of the hypochondrium together with some swelling and fear. Being black, it has this preparation: of liquid pitch and of dry, two litrai each.

[942] and of dense, glassy asphalt add 2; of roasted (phrykte) pine resin 4; of wax 3; of frankincense 1 pound and a third part; of scale of copper twice 4 ounces; of common fresh oil 5 ounces. Grind the frankincense and the scale, pouring in a moderate amount of vinegar, and, having ground them carefully and brought them to the thickness of honey, then boil the wax and the rest with new oil, and so pour them hot over the ground ingredients, and having mixed everything carefully and vigorously with the hands, store it away, keeping it covered with a skin; for it forms a crust (ἐπίπαγος) and becomes rough. The discutient (plasters) with salts, of Damocrates. Prepare this too, as a most excellent drug: of good white lead and of good litharge, a pound of each, and of salts ten ounces.

Every white salt is sufficiently serviceable for the drug, [943] but much better are the ammoniac and pure sea-salt; and three times the weight of a litra of oil many years old. Boil the oil and the rest, likewise finely ground, until they become harder than a malagma; for when stored away they become softer. Another. Another, better, for it disperses indurations, better than all [the others] those that have become exceedingly chronic, and bronchoceles and large meliceris, the scrofulous swellings that are hard to change, and the ankyloses. Prepare it thus: of very finely ground salt a litra, two of plain white lead, and of galbanum two ounces, the same of pure propolis, of aristolochia an equal part to the galbanum, and of good oil many years old two litrai; and if it is very thick, add another one. Boil it likewise, and when it is well blended,

[944] Lift it from the fire, and then sprinkle in the finely ground aristolochia, having added the softened propolis and the galbanum. Another discutient of Damocrates, with quicklime. Exceedingly good, dispersing scrofulous swellings, reducing every oedema and healing the watery conditions of the liver or of the spleen, bringing on abundant excretions of urine, and it resolves chronic sciatic affections. Ulpianus, a naturally gifted young man, by using this benefited very many. It contains one pound of Pontic wax, one of roasted (phrykte) resin and one of pine resin, of fresh quicklime one ounce, of split alum one ounce, and of Pontic orpiment an amount equal to one of these.

Pouring fragrant vinegar over these, a little, grind them for a sufficient time in a larger mortar, [945] and adding a little oil to the wax and the resin, melting them over a fire of fierce flame, and mixing everything carefully and making a malagma of the thickness of a non-staining plaster, keep it stored away, using it, in the cases where it is needed, with a fresh compress (splenion). And the most excellent man and father of the drug used to say that the drug is serviceable and good also for deliverance from long diseases, and that in those cases where a chronic inflammation of some viscus has made the hypochondrium hard or large it helps greatly; for it brings on sweats and dissolves the hardnesses of the hypochondria, and quickly effects deliverance from the diseases, and it also brings down retentions of the natural menses when applied for a few days. But I, removing the lime, put in double alum, and I found the drug acting better, not producing the small pustules (psydrakia).

[946] GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK 8. Physicians call malagmata those things that are emollient of bodies that have been hardened contrary to nature, all of them being of a moderately hot mixture, yet not drying, just as they do not clearly moisten either. For those that are precisely emollient, being somehow intermediate between things that moisten and things that dry, produce, as it were, a certain diffusion of the substance of the parts that are being hardened.

They are called emollient, however, even if in other cases they deviate slightly [947] toward drying and moistening, provided only that they possess the capacity to melt the underlying substance of the parts they touch—which happens, evidently, because their heat is moderate. And that after the hardness has been melted there is need of discutient drugs has been stated both in the fifth book of On the Power of Simple Drugs and in the fourteenth of the Therapeutic Method. The best treatment, then, of parts that are hardening—which indeed become scirrhous if they are not treated by medicine according to method—comes about when the one treating considers how far by nature the substance of the body under treatment departs from the commensurate moisture and dryness, as also the constitution of the affection itself, to what degree it has increased, and in addition to these the more and the less in the softening drugs themselves; for if you look to these things, the first use of the emollient drug will be conjectural, yet with art. And after one or two

days, you will understand whether it is fitting to intensify or to relax the power of the drug, as has been said both in the preceding books and [948] in the Therapeutic Method. Now the physicians have compounded emollient and discutient drugs as looking to both aims at once, that of the liquefaction of the hardened and scirrhous part and that of discussion, not using each of the two alternately, as you often see me doing, but always effecting the two things through the compound drug. It is quite evident that in the mixture either the softening ingredients are more than the discutient ones, or the reverse, and the degree of more and less among them is no small matter. It is quite evident too that often they are mixed in equal proportions as regards their powers; and it is necessary, just as in the case of the other drugs, so also in the case of these, for one who wishes to practise medicine well to prepare for himself several drugs of the same kind, or at any rate to have two to mix, the strongest in the kind and the most moderate, in order that from their varied mixture, made in a manner suited to the occasion, he may produce the very many drugs that lie between the extremes.

For fat does not have the same power as bdellium and storax and ammoniac incense, just as, among the fats themselves, neither do the goose [949] and the hen's, or leopard's or lion's or hyena's, or that of some other animal. For the fat too is in accordance with the temperament of the animal: that of the hotter animals is more heating, that of the drier more drying; and most physicians know that the strongest in both respects, I mean in heating and in dispersing, is the fat of the lion. Close to it is that of leopards, so that it has little of the emollient. Goose fat has a lesser power in heating and dispersing, but it has something more in softening. And that of hens stands at a proportionate distance from this one. To all of these, moreover, belongs also being finer-parted than those in four-footed animals. But again among those there is a very great difference, pig's fat being the softest and moistest and for this reason the weakest of the others, so that it suits tender bodies, such as those of women and children and eunuchs and of delicately-living men, bodies made effeminate by rearing in the shade, by lack of exercise, and by rather frequent baths of fresh waters.

But that of goats and of cattle, to the extent that it is stronger than that of swine, to that same extent is suited to bodies [950] that are harder, both by nature, and to the more scirrhous among the harder ones. That of bulls and he-goats is suited to the stronger bodies and affections. And the same difference relative to one another, according to the more and the less, holds also for the others. I shall begin from the weaker ones, having first spoken beforehand about the affection that consists in hardness and scirrhosis. For since the resistance under the pressing of the fingers is an accident common to parts that are inflamed and to those that are being hardened, the affections are distinguished by the painful and the painless, for this is no longer common to both.

Just as in all other things that are naturally such as to change into one another there is a borderland partaking slightly of both, so too between the inflammatory swellings and the scirrhi without inflammation, such as those of indurated parts are, there exists a certain intermediate condition, painless, unless you press the fingers upon it, but painful when one does this; which, for the sake of clear and concise teaching, must be called either scirrhous inflammation or inflammatory scirrhus, not attending here to the [951] magnitude of the swelling. For 'inflammation' and 'scirrhus' are names of the form of the affections, not of the quantity in either of them, an inflammation being large either on account of the size of the inflamed part or on account of that of the swelling contrary to nature, and small when it has either occupied a small place or has a slight swelling. I shall now speak of the treatment of a small inflammation and of a small scirrhus, just as also of a large inflammation and a large scirrhus, according to the forms of the affections. For from these the treatment of those called large and small in the other sense will also be understood. The cure of a large inflammation, then, comes about through cataplasms and certain liquid drugs. That of a small one, when it is mixed with a scirrhous hardness, comes about sometimes through cataplasms, and also through drugs that are cerate-like and liquid, and further through the emollient plasters. Through such means the cure of a small hardness also comes about; but in the case of this the aim is simple, just as also when inflammation alone is present. In the case of a hardness that has something inflammatory, however, the aim too becomes composite.

[On the parhygros.] And for this reason [952] the drug too is in a way composite, such as this one which is known to everyone and greatly praised by certain others and especially by Heras, the one called parhygron (moist). For this cures a part that still has a slight inflammation when it is applied not a long time after its preparation but immediately. But when the affected part has acquired in addition a painless hardness, even if the drug is still a little longer standing than the fresh one, it is useful; just as, if the affected part has been altogether freed from the inflammatory condition, the drug of longer standing is better for it. And clearly the age of the drug ought to be increased in proportion to the intensity of the hardness; however, a part that has become excessively hardened not even the aged drug will soften. For this drug called parhygron has a mixed profession and a mixed power, because its material too is mixed: since pig's fat and wax are the weakest of emollients, while litharge and white lead have nothing emollient, as we have learned.

Heras, who praised this drug most of all, compounds [953] it from the following ingredients, in these very words: Take fresh pig's fat with the fibres removed, 44 ounces; wax, 24 ounces; white lead, 6 ounces; litharge, 6 ounces. The meltable ingredients are poured over the dry ones, and it sets with time. Just as I said that wax and pig's fat are of a weak emollient power, so too, if you mix a little wax into oil, you will make what is called by physicians cerelaeum (wax-oil). The oil, evidently, must be neither that called omphacine and omotribes (of unripe olives), nor that which has had olive shoots added to it in its preparation. [The differences and powers of the emollient drugs by kind.] Now the emollients that are thus weak also treat small inflammations; those weaker than these (ἀτονώτερα), the slight hardnesses without inflammation.

Those still stronger than these [treat] the greater [hardnesses], just as those that are curative of a hardness that has come near to scirrhus are the most effective, of which sort is the kind of the marrows, differing from one another in more and less, as I shall distinguish next, [954] and that of both bdelliums, the Arabian and the Scythian, and that of the storaxes. For of these too the most effective is the one pale yellow in colour, which indeed is produced at its finest in Pamphylia. The one that has departed from this toward the greyer is produced in many places and falls far short in power of the pale yellow one. And indeed this one itself, too, inclines in the course of time toward a golden colour. This one, then, we use for the antidotes, because it is scarce, so that when preparing anything with storax for the emperor at any rate you will always use this one. And if any of those near at hand is liberal with regard to expenditure on drugs, for him too you will compound the drug from such storax. In the case of the others, you will select the best of the greyer sort, judging chiefly by the smell and by the colour, for the blacker is inferior. Among those that strongly soften parts that are becoming scirrhous is the so-called ammoniac incense, and more so the oily and fresh sort of it. Less than these, but nevertheless themselves active, are goat and ox [fat].

Among these themselves, the fat of he-goats and bulls is stronger, while that of cows and she-goats is weaker than these, yet not ineffective [955] either. That of kids and calves is weaker still even than these, but is nevertheless more active than that of the young pig. A power more discutient than these, though not more emollient, is possessed by lion's and leopard's fat, and that of the hyena and of the goose, inasmuch as they also have a substance of finer parts than goat's and ox's fat. That of hens is ranked in between goose fat and pig's fat. Just as also, among the marrows, the best is that of calves. And resins, all those which do not have a pungent smell, when mixed with any of the aforementioned substances, provide the adhesive quality to the compounded drugs and do not destroy their emollient quality; most suitable are the so-called Chian and the larch resin. After these comes the peuke-pine resin, and after that the fir resin. The strobilos (pine-cone) resin is strongly pungent, while the pine resin (pityine) is non-oily and greatly drying; they call it specifically physema. These, then, are to be avoided. The Chian and the fir resin are to be used not by themselves alone, but together with wax and some one of the other substances, whatever seems to suit the condition. And Bruttian pitch too has the same power, as having something adhesive and oily in it.

But the [956] other kind of pitch is not to be mixed in, just as asphalt is not either, for they have reached a greater degree of dryness; and we have learned that drying agents are contrary to softening ones. And since people are accustomed to call the pine resin, when roasted, also Colophonian, one should know that there is also another Colophonian resin, closely resembling Chian mastic, which has something emollient in it, just as that one does, and frankincense too. There is also something emollient in the Egyptian mastic, but the greater part of its power is concoctive and discutient. And frankincense too has some such emollient quality, but this is useful when it is boiled, just as is the seed of fenugreek; for this too softens when it has been well boiled, and still more if it should be mixed with fat. But those things which, without boiling, on account of the dryness of their consistency, need to be slackened and melted and steeped and loosened require some one of the oily substances. Such are olive oil itself, when it has no astringency at all, and the scrapings (gloios) from the baths, and further the so-called lily-oil (sousinon), and in addition to it, to a far greater degree still, the Commagenian.

And further, butter too is of the same order, [957] as are the decoction of marsh-mallow and that of fenugreek. Between things that are soft in this way and the strongest, such as bdellium and storax, ammoniac incense has the same power which propolis also has. Concerning bdellium, moreover, this too must be distinguished: that the Scythian is far better for these purposes than the other, the Arabian, and especially when it is fresh and soft, which they also call "fatty" (λιπαρόν). For this too is a custom among the more recent physicians, in the case of such drugs, to call the more emollient one also "moister"; and this one is evidently also moister. Galbanum too and the so-called opopanax, in addition to dispersing, have something emollient as well; opopanax excels in dispersing, galbanum in softening and concocting. Such, then, is the power of emollient drugs. And you, whenever you either examine and judge one of the drugs recorded in the pharmacological books or compound one yourself, having just now heard the differences among drugs according to the more and the less, and having heard also those of bodies and of affections, will apply the strong ones to the strong and the weak ones to the weak.

[958] And in the interval, when one applies another after the one previously applied, it is fitting to pour simple, oily oil over the affected part. Of the drugs called adhesive (echekolla), none should be removed before it comes away of its own accord; rather, even if one bathes, it should be allowed to remain in place. One should also avoid baths in medicinal waters, and especially those that are vitriolic (chalcanthous), aluminous and sulphurous. These things are sufficient for intelligent men who have also acquired some practice in the works of the art.

[The differences and powers of emollient drugs according to kinds.] But since not all are such men, and since it is proposed in this treatise not, as in that of the Therapeutic Method, to state the method alone, but together with one or two examples of the particular cases, there must also be added the drugs that are established by experience, which are set down by those before us who are esteemed in the pharmaceutical part of the art; I shall therefore proceed to the differences according to kinds among the emollient drugs, making my beginning from the softest [959] of them, which cure even small inflammations. Of the compound emollients some are, as one might say, weaker, in the first order; some not much stronger than these, in the second; and certain others in the third; and in addition to these, others in the fourth. It is fitting to use, as has been said before, against slight hardnesses and soft bodies those of the first order; against bodies and affections stronger than these, those of the second, just as also those of the third and the fourth proportionately. And they also describe those falling under each of these separately. [Emollient drugs of the first order.] Butter or Colophonian resin and white wax, not old, the three equal in weight, melted together with one another, are emollients of the first order. So too the moist (parhygros) [cerate], when it is fresh; but one that has aged becomes more discutient. The weakest of the emollients is wax melted with butter, or by means of lily-oil (sousinon) or Commagene [ointment].

And weaker than these is the so-called cerate-oil (kerelaion), when into a litra of relaxing oil having no [960] astringency twelve or sixteen ounces of wax are put. And the cerates made with eggs, too, have some slight relaxing quality. Stronger than these, but still weak themselves, are the cerates made of oesypum, resin and wax, melted together in equal weight. But if they are somewhat older, they will need an admixture of one of the relaxing oils, either susinon or Commagene oil, or of pig's or hen's or goose fat. Emollient drugs of the second order. As in the case of the simple drugs, we made four orders of those of the same kind, defining the more and the less among them, and of some I said that the power is ambiguous, whether their power is to be placed at the end of the first order or at the beginning of the second, and likewise concerning the second and the third and those following upon these. In the case of some, having ventured to make a pronouncement, I said that certain ones are at the beginning of this order and certain ones at the end of this order, just as I said that some are, without any addition, of the first or the second or the third or the fourth order.

But such pronouncements require much particular experience, on many bodies and [961] affections; and so, if after me anyone should arise who is, like me, industrious and zealous for truth, let him not make pronouncements rashly on the basis of two or three uses. For it will often appear to him through long experience, as it appeared to me also, that the things stated as belonging to the second rank must be transferred into the third as it begins, or simply at the beginning of the third. For since the difference of the bodies to which the drugs are applied, and of the affections themselves, has no small excess in the more and the less, it is most difficult to make a single pronouncement upon all of them, and in addition the simple drugs themselves have no small difference. And since I have pronounced on the power in the case of the best of each species and kind, if someone makes this examination by experience on the worst, he will make it falsely, and he has not defined the ranks of their power.

It is therefore safest to write accurately of the difference of the drugs themselves in relation to one another in respect of more and less, [962] just as I have done in the other cases and shall do now. [That different differences in respect of more and less arise in the emollient plaster of Mnaseas according to the differing quantity, age and boiling of the simples.] For indeed in the second rank of the emollients one would not least place the plaster composed by Mnaseas, since all who have mentioned it agree with one another that it is made from old oil, litharge and pig's fat, but differ both in the quantity of each of these and in that some compose it from fresh fat, others from old fat, which is now customarily called by everyone axoungion. For on these grounds the weakest would be that made from litharge, pig's fat and oil, neither of the latter being old; the stronger, when of these the oil is old but the other is put in new; and the one stronger than this, when both are old. Accordingly, with respect to the oil and the fat being put in new or old, the differences will be four:

[963] will be: sometimes with both fresh, sometimes with both old, sometimes with the oil old but the fat fresh, or the reverse, with fresh oil but old fat put in. And according to the proportion of these three simple drugs themselves to one another there are several further differences. For either the three are mixed in equal amounts by weight and measure—and many say that the one compounded by Mnaseas himself is composed of three equal parts—or two are equal and the third not equal but less or more, or the three are mixed in unequal amounts. It is quite evident, then, that many differences will arise. For when more litharge is put in, the drug will become milder in its power, and when less, stronger. And it will be more emollient if we put in more of the fat, but more discutient if more of the oil. For indeed something else also comes in when more oil is put in, which has great power to make the drug more discutient; and this is, as I said in the first book, if you boil it for longer. At any rate, if you boil the litharge alone in a greater quantity of oil, the drug will be more drying.

and [964] you will boil it for longer when you have put in more oil, if indeed it is going to have the consistency of a plaster. For if someone were not to attend to this, but were to boil for an equal time both that which has less oil and that which has more (κατὰ τὸ πλέον), it is obvious that the one with which more oil has been mixed will be more emollient in its power, just as if someone, having mixed raw litharge with oil, should wish to use it as an akopon. Wherefore I bid you always keep in mind what has already often been said by me: that we should not, as some make their pronouncements about drugs without qualification, act in the same way ourselves, saying without qualification that this composition of a drug is better than that one. For each of the two can be well composed for affections differing in kind, and sometimes for the same affection at different occasions. Accordingly, anyone who has first heard all these things now said by me, being not only industrious or retentive in memory but also intelligent by nature, will read with profit what has been written and what will be written by me with distinctions.

And I shall also tell you the distinctions in the case of the drugs under consideration, which come about through the addition of three or four syllables, [965] an addition of just the kind that Andromachus appears to have made in the case of the drug of Mnaseas that is under consideration in the present discussion. For in his catalogue of the quince-yellow plasters, having written it eleventh in order, he was not content to state it simply, as with those mentioned before it, where he heads each of them with 'another' and 'another', but he added the word 'soft' (ἁπαλή). This, then, is what I would have expected him to have done for all of them, and, in the case of the quince-yellow plasters themselves, to have begun from the softest one, and, passing from it to the one that is a little stronger, to have made this clear by adding in writing that the second is stronger than this by some small degree, and that the third in turn is stronger than that, and then the fourth than that one.

just as, again, if he thought that some had an equal power, he should have added this very thing; or, if he were wary of running a risk in such pronouncements, he should at least have taught beforehand the simple emollient drugs, distinguishing the more and the less among them, so that the reader of the many emollient plasters written by him in sequence might recognise that the one composed of storax, ammoniac, bdellium, propolis and galbanum, of bull's [966] and goat's fat and of the marrows is stronger, while the one that has none of these is weak—but either all its ingredients are weak in power, or they are stronger than these themselves yet intermediate in their mixtures and powers, or one or two of the strong ones have been mixed in with the weak ones. For it is clear that in all drugs the intermediate latitude in respect of the more and the less is not small, on the basis of a common power of all of them conceived generically, according to which drugs are said to be of the same genus and of the same species, just as others differ by generic or specific differentiae. Since, then, these matters have been defined by me, and someone setting out from them will be able without difficulty to distinguish those that have a stronger power and those that have a softer one, I shall now give the account of them, writing in sequence those that have been written down by the men most experienced in drugs, whether you wish to call them plasters or malagmata. I shall begin with those written by Asclepiades in the fourth book of the External Remedies, which he entitles Marcellas.

[967] [The malagmata of Asclepiades.] The malagma of Amythaon for distensions of the hypochondria: it dissolves every hardness, and it works also for joints that are difficult to move. Take: ammoniac incense, 36 ounces; wax, 36 ounces; terebinth, 8 ounces; bdellium, 8 ounces; frankincense, 4 ounces; myrrh, 4 ounces; galbanum, 8 ounces; henna oil, 4 kotylai. The myrrh, frankincense and bdellium are soaked in wine, while the ammoniac is dissolved in vinegar. All are pounded, the pestle being smeared with the henna oil, until complete dissolution. This drug is one of the ancient and celebrated ones, as is also the one written after it by Asclepiades, in the following manner. The diasmyrnon apolophonion (?), a successful drug. For distensions of the hypochondria it dissolves every hardness; it works for hepatic, splenic and nephritic patients; it works for every nervous sympathy; it works for pains and fixations of the joints. Take: wax, 16 ounces; terebinth, 16 ounces; ammoniac incense, 16 ounces; bdellium, 16 ounces; myrrh, 16 ounces; propolis, 16 ounces.

[968] iris 16 ounces, storax 16 ounces, of the sediment of iris perfume as much as suffices, of fragrant wine a sufficient quantity; prepare as stated above. And the drug written by Asclepiades after this one is indeed more noteworthy than those written below, but less effective than they are for the dissolution of hardened parts. Another, of Dioscorides, a well-tested drug for limbs that move with difficulty and for ankyloses; it dissolves every hardness, and it is effective also for the conditions of the inner parts and for abscesses in depth. Take wax 1 mina, roasted (phrykte) resin half a mina, galbanum half a mina, Illyrian iris half a mina, of the sediment of iris oil a sufficient quantity, of wine as much as suffices; the drug is a pounded one; prepare as stated above. The drug written next by Asclepiades after the aforementioned one is the same as the one written by Heras at the end of his book on drugs, but it has some slight difference in the proportion of the four simple drugs, as will be evident when both have been written out.

But first I shall mention the one written by Asclepiades, [969] which runs word for word as follows. The drug of Lucius the teacher, inscribed 'for ankylai'. It works for abscesses deep down; it works also for contractions of the sinews and for the fixations of the joints, which we call ankylai. It works for those with opisthotonos and for every sympathetic affection of the nerves. It is also a good acopon, when dissolved in iris-oil or cyprus-oil or laurel-oil. It works for chronic and hard-to-heal indurations. Take of bdellos 16 drachms, of calf suet 16 drachms, of ammoniac incense 16 drachms, of Illyrian iris 16 drachms, of opopanax 8 drachms, of galbanum 8 drachms, of cachrys 8 drachms, of storax 8 drachms, of frankincense 8 drachms, of pepper 160 grains, of the dregs of iris-unguent as much as suffices, of wax and of terebinth half a litra each, of wine a sufficient amount; the drug is a pounded one; prepare as has been stated before. Where, then, Heras differed from Asclepiades in the proportion of the simples, I shall now show, as I promised. First of all, Asclepiades wrote as a drug 16 holkai of bdellos; but Heras not bdellos, but 80 holkai of bdellium.

And these are fivefold [970], obviously, of the sixteen. Next, whereas Asclepiades wrote sixteen drachms of calf's fat, Heras wrote five times as many, as also in the case of the bdellium; for the eighty drachms are, obviously, fivefold of the sixteen. As a third drug after those already written Asclepiades wrote ammoniac incense, deeming that sixteen drachms of this too be put in. According to the proportion of the preceding ones, therefore, Heras too ought to have written eighty drachms; but he wrote not so many, but a hundred, so that he put in twenty more. Another drug after the drugs written before Asclepiades wrote, speaking thus: of Illyrian iris, sixteen drachms; and Heras preserved the proportion of this, writing eighty. After the drugs written before, Asclepiades wrote opopanax, eight drachms; and Heras preserved the proportion with respect to this too, writing forty. Of a sixth drug, galbanum, Asclepiades made mention, putting in eight drachms; Heras preserved the proportion with respect to it as well, deeming that five times as much be put in; for forty is fivefold of eight. The seventh drug Asclepiades wrote thus:

of cachrys [971] 8 drachmas. So Heras too, if he were preserving the proportion, ought to have put in 40; but as it is, not so, but twice as many, for he himself has written 16. As the eighth, Asclepiades mentions storax, putting in 8 drachmas; Heras preserved the proportion of this, putting in fivefold. As the ninth drug Asclepiades wrote frankincense, putting in 8 drachmas of it, but Heras requires not fivefold but double. As the tenth Asclepiades mentioned pepper, putting in 160 grains, and in agreement with him again Heras put in 500. In some of the copies, I know not how, 20 are written, just as in others 108. As the eleventh Asclepiades wrote wax, as also, as the twelfth, the terebinth resin, requiring that half a litra of each be put in. So Heras too, if he were preserving the proportion, ought to have put in fivefold of each, which was two litrai of each with a further half of a litra added. But he does not do so; rather, he requires that three litrai and 4 ounces of each be put in.

It is quite evident, then, that of the cachrys Heras puts in [972] double the proportion, just as also of the frankincense. But of the ammoniac incense he exceeded by a fourth part, just as indeed also of the terebinth resin together with the wax by a third; for in the case of these too he exceeded by a third part, and in this respect he made the whole composition of the drug similar to that of Asclepiades. For having exceeded in the proportion of the cachrys, which has nothing soft in it but is only dispersive, he increased along with it the emollients as well, the frankincense and the wax and the terebinth. This drug, then, Asclepiades names as that of Lucius the teacher; and in what respects it differs from Heras I have gone through. It is of the highest rank among the emollients, for you would not find anything more emollient than it for parts becoming scirrhous. And the one who composed it aimed also at dispersing what is contained in the parts becoming scirrhous. The other drugs before it have a slight advantage over those written earlier. And among them are included also the incisive agents for thickened and viscous humours, which often become useful for tumours that are becoming scirrhous, whenever their scirrhosis is brought about by viscous humours.

Opopanax, then, attenuates [973] moderately. They call by this name the root of the panax, whose stalk they tap for juice to make opopanax; for it is of a cleansing, not of an incisive power. But vinegar together with goat's dung cuts and cleanses and disperses powerfully not only thickened and viscous humours but also the solid bodies themselves; these are added in the drug written next after the one before us, which he says is inscribed as Alcimion's. He writes, then, about the former in the following manner. Another malagma of Marcus Telentius Asclepiades, exceedingly noble against the aforesaid conditions. It works especially against inflations of the womb; the drug is inscribed 'Asclepiadeion' because it is referred back to Asclepiades the Bithynian. Take myrrh, 3 drachms, or otherwise 3 ounces; opopanax, half a litra; wax, one litra and a half; galbanum, 3 ounces; manna, half a litra; ammoniac incense, half a litra; roasted resin, one litra and a half; vinegar, one kotyle. It is to be used also for every nervous sympathy. Another, inscribed as Alcimion's. Take wax, one litra

[974] and a half, of Colophonian resin one pound and a half, of ammoniac incense one pound and a half, of galbanum three ounces, of myrrh three ounces, of frankincense three ounces, of opopanax one pound and a half, of propolis three ounces, of vinegar two xestai, of goat's dung three ounces. Grind the ammoniac, adding one xestes of vinegar; then add to these the myrrh, the frankincense, the opopanax, and triturate again. Pound the propolis together with the galbanum. Boil the wax and the resin, adding two kotylai of oil, and when it has thickened together, add the propolis and the galbanum, stirring continuously; and when it has dissolved, take it from the fire and let it cool, and having scraped it off, add it to the triturated ingredients and, having mixed them, take it up and use it. After the malagma written above there is written in the book of Asclepiades another, having a little emollient power, but for the most part heating. For it contains not only the juice of gentian, but also the saps, both that of peucedanum and that of sagapenum, drugs which heat vehemently.

There is mixed into it also aphronitron and flower of Asian stone, drugs of attenuating [975] and cutting power. And that unburnt sulphur heats, everyone knows, just as indeed also pitch-wine (pissites). I shall append this drug too in Asclepiades' own wording. A malagma inscribed 'Pharmianon', for the aforesaid conditions. It is especially effective for pleuritics, for it relieves the pains at once when applied during the paroxysms themselves. After the application of the drug, when redness has arisen around the places, one must lift off the splenion and, after allowing an interval, apply it again; it relieves also the conditions that have become chronic. Take wax, 5 litrai, or 1 litra; ammoniac incense, 3 litrai; roasted (phrykte) resin, 3 unciae, or 1 litra; terebinth, 1 litra; frankincense, 1½ litrai; myrrh, 6 unciae; aloe, 6 unciae; oesypum, 3 unciae; juice of gentian, 3 unciae; juice of peucedanum, 3 unciae, or opopanax, 6 unciae; sagapenum, 4 unciae; aphronitron, 6 unciae; flower of Asian stone, 6 unciae; propolis, 3 unciae; unburnt sulphur, 4 unciae; pitch-wine, 5 xestai. Boil the pitch-wine and the juice of the gentian, and having melted the meltable ingredients, let them cool.

Having pounded together the ammoniac and the frankincense [976] and the myrrh and the aloe and put them into a mortar, pour the liquid onto these. And when it has dissolved, triturate diligently. Having pounded and sifted the dry ingredients, add them to those that have been ground fine, and having beaten them up carefully, add to these the meltable ingredients, boiled up again, free of lumps of wax (ἐγκηρίδων). And having mixed, take it up and use it. After the aforesaid, Asclepiades next wrote another malagma similar to it, in the following words. Another, that of Neapolites; it was prepared for Aquilia Secundilla. ℞ pitched wine, 6 xestai; wax, 6 litrai; ammoniac incense, 3 litrai; roasted (phrykte) resin, 3 litrai; terebinth resin, 1½ litra; frankincense, 1½ litra; myrrh, 6 ounces; aloe, 6 ounces; aphronitron, 6 ounces; flower of Asian stone, 6 ounces; juice of the root of gentian, 6 ounces; sagapenum, 4 ounces; unburnt sulphur, 4 ounces; propolis, 4 ounces; root of panax, 3 ounces; sampsychon (marjoram), 3 ounces; white pepper, 3 ounces. Prepare and use as has been said before. [The malagmata written by Andromachus.] A hard and dry malagma. ℞ pitch, 3 litrai.

of wax [977] 2 litrai, of resin 1 litra, of galbanum 2 ounces, of ammoniac incense 2 ounces, of manna 4 ounces, of vinegar 3 xestai, of the juice of the root of peucedanum 6 ounces, of oesypum 4 ounces. Otherwise: Take pitch 4 litrai, wax 2 litrai, resin 1 litra, ammoniac incense 1 litra, manna 1 litra, galbanum 6 ounces (others, 1 litra), vinegar 3 xestai. Another, of Aristocles. Take pitch 4 litrai, wax 8 litrai, roasted resin 4 litrai, terebinth resin 4 litrai, ammoniac incense 2 litrai 8 ounces, galbanum 1 litra 4 ounces. Another, the one for ankylai (contractures). Take bdellium 16 drachmas, frankincense 16 drachmas, ammoniac incense 8 drachmas, opopanax 8 drachmas, galbanum 8 drachmas, calf's suet 16 drachmas, of pepper 160 grains, storax 8 drachmas, cachrys 16 drachmas, Illyrian iris 16 drachmas, of terebinth resin half a mina, of wax half a mina, of kyprinon oil 4 kotylai, of wine a sufficient quantity. The one with melilot. Take Celtic nard 10 drachmas, cyperus 8 drachmas, cardamom 8 drachmas, Illyrian iris 8 drachmas, myrrh 8 drachmas, saffron 4 drachmas, melilot 25 drachmas,

of ammoniac incense [978] 8 drachmas, of terebinth 50 drachmas, of fresh wax 100 drachmas, of henna oil half a kotyle, of vinegar a sufficient quantity. Some give of ammoniac incense 100 drachmas. For all internal conditions. The one made with seeds. ♃ Of ammoniac incense 50 drachmas, of wax 50 drachmas, of terebinth 50 drachmas, of fenugreek 25 drachmas, of prepared bull's suet 25 drachmas, of Illyrian iris 25 drachmas, of nitron 25 drachmas, of honey 6 kotylai, of vinegar 1 kotyle, of panax 25 drachmas, of henna oil a little. But as Philonides gives it: ♃ Of fenugreek seed, of anise seed, of storax, of unwashed bdellium, of manna, of frankincense, of cardamom, of fresh cyperus, of panax root, of Illyrian iris, of aphronitron, of each 25 drachmas apiece; of ammoniac incense, of terebinth, 50 drachmas each; of bull's suet 60 drachmas, of melilot 60 drachmas, of wax 2 drachmas, otherwise 100; of honey half a kotyle, of wine 1 kotyle. Another, as Harpocras gives it: ♃ Of fenugreek, of nitron, of panax, of iris, 8 drachmas each; of terebinth, of ammoniac incense, of wax, 100 drachmas each; of bull's suet 100 drachmas, otherwise 50; of honey 1 litra, of vinegar 2 xestai.

celery seed, cumin, fennel or anise, [979] 50 drachms each; melilot 50 drachms, though some say 25; marjoram 50 drachms; cardamom, ammi, 50 drachms each; take up in cyprine oil. The one through marjoram, for many conditions. ℞ new wax, bay-berries, ground fenugreek, marjoram, 100 drachms of each; terebinth 150 drachms; nitron 32 drachms; pepper 32 drachms, though some say sixteen; cyperus 16 drachms; cyprine oil 2 kotylai, or storax oil. The one through bay-berries. ℞ wax 75 drachms; Bruttian pitch 75 drachms; bay-berries 75 drachms; nitron 75 drachms; roasted resin 75 drachms; galbanum 12 drachms; ammoniac incense 12 drachms; cachrys 12 drachms; ammi 12 drachms; white pepper 16 drachms; cyprine oil 6 drachms, or 6 kotylai. Another malagma, of good colour, of many uses. ℞ wax 1 pound; roasted resin 1 pound; ammoniac incense 6 ounces; liquid alum 6 ounces; flower of salt 6 ounces; some add mistletoe 6 ounces. The one of Apollophanes. ℞ wax 80 drachms; ammoniac incense 80 drachms; bdellium 80 drachms; Illyrian iris 80 drachms; terebinth resin 40 drachms; manna of frankincense 40 drachms; it is pounded together with iris oil.

The plaster with alum, [980] another version. Take: wax, 100 dr.; pitch, 50 dr.; liquid alum, 25 dr. (but I [use] 50 dr.); mistletoe-glue (ixos), 50 dr. A good one for sciatic patients. Take: seed of wild rue, silphium, bay-berries, aphronitron, southernwood, colocynth, cardamom, ammi, 4 dr. each; green rue, pitch, terebinth resin, ammoniac incense, wax, fat, 8 dr. each; galbanum, 6 dr.; opopanax, 4 dr.; unburnt sulphur, 4 dr. For splenetics. Take: wax, 1 mina; resin, 1 mina; ammoniac incense, half a mina; liquid alum, 50 dr.; strigil-grease (gloios), 1 cotyle; caper root, 50 dr.; calamint root, 50 dr.; myrobalan dregs (magma), 50 dr. Use vinegar for the dry ingredients, oil for the meltable ones. A malagma of many uses. Take: mustard, 4 dr.; manna, 2 dr.; rue, 4 dr.; aphronitron, 4 dr.; caper root, 6 dr.; ammoniac incense, 4 dr.; myrobalan, 25 dr.; the fine centaury, 4 dr. or 7; flower of Asian stone, 4 dr.; fenugreek, 4 dr.; cardamom, 4 dr.; wax, 75 dr.; resin, 100 dr.; honey, 6 cotylai; sediment of iris-oil, 1 cotyle.

of vinegar, for the ammoniac, [981] 2 kotylai. The Polyarchion, from the letter. ℞ cyperus 1 mina, cardamom an equal amount, manna an equal amount, wax an equal amount, roasted (phrykte) terebinth 1½ minas, liquid (terebinth) 3 minas, henna oil a sufficient quantity. I (add) bdellium 1 mina. The second recipe. ℞ cyperus 1 mina, cardamom the equal amount, bdellium an equal amount, frankincense an equal amount, balsam an equal amount, wax 1½ minas, roasted (phrykte) resin a quarter of a mina, henna oil 6 kotylai, fragrant wine 1½ kotylai. As I myself use it. ℞ cyperus 1 mina, cardamom an equal amount, amomum an equal amount, bdellium an equal amount, wax 1½ minas, roasted (phrykte) resin, terebinth a quarter of a mina, henna oil 1 kotyle, cassia, cinnamon, ammoniac incense, Indian nard, saffron, myrrh a quarter of a mina each, fragrant wine as much as suffices. A malagma of Apollonius effective for many conditions. ℞ wax, pitch, roasted (phrykte) resin 125 drachms each, nitron, frankincense 50 drachms each, calf's and bull's suet, butter 75 drachms each, oesypum 15 drachms, water 6 kyathoi. A malagma good for hepatic patients. ℞ ammoniac incense 144 drachms (others: 102 drachms), bdellium 144 drachms, saffron 12 drachms, myrrh 12 drachms, wax 144 drachms.

[982] others, 100; of vinegar a fourth of a kotyle; of henna oil 1 kotyle, but I use 10 kotylai. An emollient plaster (malagma) for rheumatic flux of the stomach and intestines. Take: of oinanthe 1 ounce; of the flesh of dates 2 ounces; of acacia 1 ounce; of roses one ounce; of omphakion 4 ounces; of aloe 4 ounces; of oak-gall 4 ounces; of round alum 4 ounces; of pitch 4 ounces; of wax 3 ounces — others [read] of frankincense; of myrtle oil 3 ounces. Wine [is added] to the dry ingredients. For dropsical patients and those troubled by flatulence. Take: of liquid pitch 1 pound; of wax 1 pound; of nitron 6 ounces; of unburnt sulphur 6 ounces; of split alum 6 ounces. Another emollient plaster for sciatic patients and many other conditions. Take: of wax 72 drachms; of terebinth 48 drachms; of ammoniac incense 32 drachms; of propolis 43 drachms; of galbanum 36 drachms; of bdellium 25 drachms; of saffron 5 drachms; of opopanax 12 drachms; of foam of nitron 30 drachms. Pound up with iris unguent and use. Another emollient plaster, of Andreas, of many uses (polychrēston). Take: of pyrethrum 8 drachms; of Cnidian berry 8 drachms; of salt ammoniac 8 drachms; of root of wild cucumber 8 drachms; of pine resin 8 drachms; of terebinth 8 drachms; of wax 30; of juice of sycamine 12 drachms, others 10 drachms.

of rose-oil [986] 4 cotylae, of fenugreek unguent 1 cotyle, of good olive oil 1 cotyle. Melt these over a gentle fire, stirring lightly. And let there be ready at hand, pounded fine: of Illyrian iris 2 choenices, of aristolochia 1 choenix, of finely pounded hypocistis half a choenix, of finely pounded oak-gall 2 choenices, of manna 1 choenix, of bdellium 1 choenix; of cinnamon, Cilician saffron, myrrh, cassia, Indian nard, flower of rush (schoinos), aromatic reed, amomum, pepper, juice of sumach, blood of sea-tortoise, the herb androsaemon, pyrethrum, of each 35 drachms; of old vinegar 1 cotyle. Having mixed all the ingredients together into the same vessel, soften and pound them together until it becomes ductile and thoroughly worked, and store it away. It is effective also for fluxes (rheumatismoi) of the chest and lung, and for those with pain in the bregma of the head; it renders them painless at once. The preparation is called Asclepius. A sciatic plaster, very good for sciatics, from Heras the Cappadocian. ♃ of liquid pitch 3 or 2 cotylae, of wax 1 litra, of pine-resin 1 litra.

unburnt sulphur, [987] 1 litra; nitron, 1½ litrai; wild raisin (stavesacre), 1 xestes; pyrethrum, 1 litra; burnt wine-lees, 2 litrai; cardamom, 1 xestes; galbanum, half a litra. The meltable ingredients over the dry ones. Another malagma, of Bacchius, which Caesar used. ♃ pig's fat, 2 minae; wax, 2 minae; elecampane, aromatic reed, root of panax, rock salt or ammoniac salt, 10 drachmas each; transparent bdellium, ammoniac incense, 2 minae each; flower of schoinos, iris, 1 mina each; frankincense, pepper, galbanum, 25 drachmas each. The boiling, as for the kardameleion. Another malagma, the golden one, for arthritics. ♃ strobilos (pine-cone) resin, 2 litrai; axungia, galbanum, 12 drachmas each; wax, 24 drachmas; laurel oil, 12 drachmas. Boil as you know. Another malagma, for pain of the sides. ♃ cyperus, cardamom, manna, ammoniac incense, terebinth resin, wax, iris oil, 1 litra each. Boil the ammoniac separately; work the meltable ingredients smooth, and having melted them with a cyathus of iris oil, sprinkle on the ammoniac, then mix in the dry ingredients, dipping your hands in iris oil. Another malagma, of Cloniacus, of good colour.

♃ [988] Of orpiment 3 ounces, of split alum an equal amount, of quicklime the same, of roasted resin 3 pounds, of wax an equal amount, vinegar for the dry ingredients, oil for the meltable ingredients 8 ounces. Use it also in cases of splenetics. [Malagma of Damocrates.] Since things written in metre are also useful for memory and preserve the proportions of the drugs accurately, for this reason I am accustomed to append also the recipes of Damocrates, among which this one too is appended. There will certainly often be need of a good malagma too for those who are very fond of medicine, for great strains of muscles and for ruptures of joints, and further also for sprains, thickenings of sinews and hardnesses of muscles accompanied by inflammation, and indeed also for bites; for these this is most effective. It also removes lichens and leprai, applied for at most ten days, being changed every other day or every two days.
