[989] Of translucent pitch, the driest, two litrai; one of pine resin (pityine) and one of good wax; of ammoniac and of liquid alum, again, make one each; having measured out two xestai of most acrid vinegar, have it ready prepared. Rarely, some have added two ounces of galbanum as well, wishing to soften more quickly those hardnesses that have also lasted some time. Prepare it thus: having taken off a third of the vinegar, pour it over the ammoniac and the alum, and, making them smooth in a rather large mortar, bring them to the thickness of fresh liquid honey. The pitch and the remainder boil in a new pot, so that it is all but the very least roasted off (ἐκφρυγῇ); then pour it over what has been well ground in the mortar, and beat it up until it takes on a yellow colour resembling the melinon (quince-coloured plaster). But if you wish by all means to mix in galbanum too,

[990] You will add this together with the wax and the pine resin, after removing the pot from the fire a little later. Some, however, add an equal weight of manna, removing the alum from the drug; and, using it for such cases, they glue together fresh divisions with this preparation. Use this also from the first day in the cases I mentioned before, when they are in a condition calling for caution, for scarifications and what follows upon them. On top of the splenion apply a sponge soaked in vinegar and bind it on with pressure; in this way you will also apply it to those with affections of the spleen. And in those in whom you suspect that a scirrhus will form in some viscus, use the malagma without fear. After this drug Damocrates wrote the one made with salts, beginning it thus: If it persists in any of these for longer periods of time, prepare this too, as a most excellent drug.

[991] Then after this he writes another one too, made with salts, and after both of these again another, one that professes to disperse scrofulous swellings (choirades) and dropsical conditions of the liver and of the spleen. But it seemed better to me to write these drugs among the discutient plasters. [On relaxing drugs.] Certain drugs are customarily called "relaxing" (chalastic) by almost all the more recent physicians, drugs in the case of which, as the name itself shows, they relax the parts that are tensed. For "to be relaxed" is said as the contrary of "to be tensed." At any rate it has been written somewhere by Hippocrates too as follows: "of hard skin, softening; of tensed skin, relaxation." If, then, one were to use the names in their proper sense, one will say that certain drugs are emollients of hardened bodies, namely those that dissolve their hardness, just as the relaxing ones are curative of tension.

Now it happens in inflammations that the skin is stretched, sometimes receiving this symptom from the underlying swelling, and sometimes also itself being inflamed along with it; yet the essence of the inflammation is not [992] the hardness of the inflamed part but, entirely to the contrary, as we show in our discussions concerning it, moistness. In parts that are becoming scirrhous, however, it is not moistness that prevails in the affected part, but hardness. Of both affections the genesis and the cure are in a certain way of the same kind: for they are generated from an influx, and they are cured when these [humours] have been evacuated. Yet the manner of the evacuation is not the same in both; rather, as has been shown in the treatise on the Therapeutic Method, in which the method of cure of all the other affections too has been stated, in the case of inflamed parts the repellent quality of the drugs is beneficial during the first periods, and the discutient quality throughout; whereas in scirrhi the discutient quality alone is beneficial, without the repellent. Now those parts that have become completely scirrhous are completely incurable; and one must diagnose them by the fact that no sensation at all remains in the affected parts.

Those, however, in which there is sensation, but faint, are treated by means of drugs which do indeed disperse the thickened humour, yet do not do this strongly and all at once, [993] as the discutient drugs do. Such drugs they call epispastic (drawing) and expressive (squeezing-out). One should not wonder at the change into hardness that comes about from inflamed parts, when at the same time the humour that has flowed in is both thicker and viscous, and the cure is effected through drugs that dry violently. For just as, in the case of external things, many bodies when they come into contact with fire itself are parched, but by water are softened again, in the same way, in inflamed parts, the moisture in the affected place, under the action of drugs that heat and dry more strongly, retains something viscous and thick left behind, once the thin part has been dispersed. And it is in this way that in arthritic affections the tophi (poroi) come about, and in nephritic affections the stones. But if ever the flux that is going to produce an inflammation is thin in consistency, and its cure is effected through drying and heating drugs, nothing scirrhous is left behind. And not least, drugs that cool and astringe violently are also accustomed to produce scirrhi.

And we see many people who, from erysipelas that have suffered these things immoderately, have scirrhous [994] tumours, through the ignorance of the physicians who treated them. The first difference, then, between the drugs that treat inflammations and those that treat scirrhi is the one stated. A second is that which arises because of the pain conjoined with inflamed parts, which does not allow a strong drug to be applied to the affected part. For these drugs act with pain, while the inflamed parts are already in pain because of the affection and for this reason require the softest drugs. The more vehement ones, besides not resolving or soothing the pains, even exacerbate them and make the inflammations greater. The first use, then, in the case of painful inflammations is that by means of drugs that are sufficiently moist, together with heating moderately; next, that by means of those that are slightly thicker and more drying; and the third, by means of those called relaxing (chalastic), which some write down among the malagmata. Of these the most emollient are those that are cerate-like in their consistency, when they are compounded from butter and wax and fats and a relaxing oil.

And there is mixed with these a little oesypum and resin and [995] pitch, as also frankincense and galbanum and some of the Illyrian iris. And the drug called 'dia chylōn' (through juices), a curative drug for inflammations that are no longer strongly painful, was discovered by Menecrates, as he himself says and as certain others testify on his behalf. The book in which the drug is written up is entitled 'Autokrator hologrammatos' (The Emperor, in Whole Letters): 'Autokrator' because it has been dedicated to him, and 'hologrammatos' because, without numeral signs, two and three and four and five and each of the other numbers, whether of resin or of pitch or of some other drug, are written out in whole syllables. Menecrates did this because it often happens that errors are made in the written texts not only unintentionally, but also deliberately on the part of some out of envy, who make the letter omicron a theta by drawing another, transverse, line through the middle of the round stroke, and the letter iota, likewise, by adding another transverse line, just as also, when one stroke is scraped away from the letter gamma (γράμμα in the text) and from rho, it happens that the shape of iota is left behind.

In the same way, in the case of many letters, by addition in some, by combination in others, by subtraction in others, [996] it comes about that the characters signifying them undergo alteration. But Menecrates accomplished nothing more for the time that followed, since those who copied out his book did not write the names of the numbers in full letters, but by means of the characters signifying them. Reasonably, then, the books of Damocrates on drugs, written in metre, have won approval, and if all had been written in this manner, it would have been best. But since not a few of the approved drugs have been left out, for this reason we also need the other pharmaceutical books, in which some have written compositions of varied drugs. But the drug through juices discovered by Menecrates has been written by Damocrates in the following trimeter verses, together with certain others as well, two of them, similar to it, having been written before it.

[The remedy through juices, of Damocrates, by Menecrates.] Having said, then, before this how wounds that remain without inflammation will be glued together, we shall next say how those that are greatly inflamed [997] it will be possible to treat well with drugs. When, a muscle having been wounded, or some nerves, or even a membrane near a bone having been pricked, after the fourth day there comes an addition of frequent pains and inflammations and fevers with symptoms — much sleeplessness, derangement of mind, violent thirst, dryness of the tongue — inclining day by day towards the worse; a lees-like, thin ichor, red wounds, and all the bodies near them having turgors, distensions, inflammations, oedemata: then do not plaster them with variegated cataplasms. For it is the custom of the young to do this, so that, having escaped the peaks of the inflammations, they may not furnish the slanderers with a cause of accusation. But he who has confidence in his own practice must also go down together with the sick into their fears, not waiting upon fortune and nature.

[998] Prepare, then, for the affections mentioned above, the drug that is suited also to those with podagra, to be applied to the sick at every season; for in the intervals it provides ready ease of movement, and the not being readily troubled quickly by tophi (πῶροι) and by frequent attacks; at the onsets it does not allow them to take on magnitude, and at the heights it brings about the declines quickly, provided one does not readily shift over to other remedies. Prepare the drug in this manner: having put in two pounds of litharge, very finely ground, of the chrysitis kind, four of very old axungia (lard), and one pound and a third of a pound of oil, many years old and very thick, and not foul-smelling, not black, not rough; for thus the drug will be effective.

Having carefully melted the axunge in a dish, take off from it the membranes and the salts, [999] straining it through a strainer into another, larger pot; and, having added oil, bring it to the boil again—yet not all the oil, but two parts of it; leaving the third aside, keep it lying in readiness, so that, should you be pressed to add it, it may be at hand for you. And there will certainly be need of it in winter, at any rate, when the oil that is put into the drug has become thick through the long time. And sprinkle the litharge over the boiling contents; boil on a gentle and continuous fire, stirring with a spatula—better if it be one of pine.

And when the drug, having been boiled for a moderate time, has taken on the thickness of a plaster and has likewise taken on the foul smell of a drug, quickly lift the pot from the fire, making it slightly harder in summer and soft in winter, yet nonetheless such that it does not stain; and stir it likewise until it has cooled down moderately, [1000] then again with firmer hands work (πρόσπασσε) the whole of it, once it has been softened, and so transfer it out of the pot. And when there is need, knead it again vigorously, and having carefully spread it upon soft leather, thus apply the compresses, of good size. But if you ever wish to make this plaster more effective for thick sinews and muscles, and hard breasts, and swollen joints, take a pound of the roots of wild mallow, clean and fresh, and cutting them into pieces of the length and thickness of a finger, throw the pieces into what is boiling in the pot. And when, having been charred (ἀνθρακωθέντ’), they have given up all their moisture and their power to the drug, remove the little roots of the mallow with a strainer, and having sprinkled on the litharge finely ground, then boil, as I said before, and again store it away likewise and use it in the same way.

[1001] This drug, says Menecrates, the man who first discovered it—a most excellent man, steadfastly devoted to the art—possesses the virtues of both. For it keeps freshly inflicted wounds free of inflammation, and he has persuaded us that it glues together divided parts and treats ulcers that are excessively inflamed, as well as wounded muscles, without any other of the things able to give help—poultices, sponges and fomentations. It does everything that I said earlier the plaster made of litharge and axoungion does. He says that it is also the best pessary in long-standing and in fresh inflammations of the womb, and that it fills up hollow ulcers and, when diluted with rose-oil or at least with good myrtle-oil, brings them to a scar. And in general he says that every poultice and drug applied from outside upon these is superfluous for those who use this one.

[1002] The drug is worthy of being recorded; and by now it is trusted even by the envious. He says to make it in this manner: seven litrai by weight of oil in summer. In another copy I found: half of the oil, of rich and fresh axoungion. But in winter, as he says, you will put in nine, and only six of most finely ground litharge. Of fenugreek he said a half part of a xestes, and the same of burnt linseed. And of wild mallow he said three litrai by weight, of the root still having its fresh juice, to boil in water, eight xestai by measure, in a new, wide-mouthed earthenware pan, throwing in the root of the mallow cleaned, cut up, fine and bruised, the fenugreek washed, and the linseed likewise well.

And when it has been reduced to juice and taken on thickness, [1003] press out the juice through a linen cloth and keep it; and having weighed out the four pounds by weight and mixing in the oil, boil the whole upon charcoals. And when fine bubbles, after larger ones, rise up densely upon the contents in the pot, then sprinkle on the litharge, finely ground, and boil with a gentle and continuous fire, until the juice, having been dried up together with the fat, the drug becomes a quince-yellow plaster, of good colour, not staining, but not very hard. Having added this discovery to the ancient drugs, he reasonably called the drug "the one through juices". Another. And this drug too is of the same kind, even though it is prepared through other ingredients.

For it works, to be sure, for the conditions I mentioned before, quite simply all of them: the crude ones, those difficult of concoction and resistant to change, [1004] the great wounds in muscles and membranes. For it readily resolves their scars; and applied to all arthritic sufferers, it will soothe the places that have become chronic. It contains: of the driest pitch, two pounds; of pure Pontic wax, two pounds; again, of terebinth, the very moist kind, two pounds; of manna of unadulterated frankincense, one pound; and half a pound, or something a little less, of white, above all fatty, fresh butter. Melt the other ingredients for a long time and over a fierce fire, continuously, watching whether the drug turns out such that it does not stain when rubbed by the fingers. When this happens, lift it off the fire and then sprinkle the manna over the melted ingredients, stirring the drug for a long time with the spatula.

When it has thus cooled and been softened, store it away. [1005] And when you have mixed into this preparation a large quantity of fresh rose-oil, you will use it also for ulcers that are excessively hollow and fleshless, and for inflammations of tendons, and for those conditions which are hard to bring over into white pus. [On akopa.] The professed virtue of the akopa drugs is indicated by their very name. For people call kopoi (fatigues) the conditions that arise in bodies from many or vehement movements, either in the whole body or in those parts that have laboured more. These conditions are painful, most of all to those who are moving, but already also to those who are at rest, in the case of those that are more vehement.

Later it became customary also for physicians, even if the drug compounded by them is not for fatigues (kopoi) but rather for a pain lingering in the depth of the body, or for difficulty of movement, or impaired sensation, or hardness of a part, or tension, or a scirrhous swelling, to call all such drugs likewise akopa, provided only that they have a consistency, in respect of fluidity, similar to that of the akopa, which is close to [1006] the moist cerates, such as we use also for dislocations and fractures. For of this kind of consistency the most fluid is what is called by the more recent physicians kerelaion (wax-oil); next after it come the akopa unguents, and after these, having a thicker consistency, the cerate of the moist kind, then that of the ones termed tender and soft. Last is that of the non-staining ones (amolynta), similar to that of what are properly called epithemata; and next after these is the consistency of the plasters, these too having among themselves no small difference in the more and the less, so that some physicians have given the name kerotomalagmata to certain of them, naming them thus from the consistency alone, namely those of the drugs applied externally which are no longer fluid, yet not yet hard to such a degree as the plasters. Since, then, all the differences mentioned are indicative not of the power of the drugs but of their form in respect of consistency, the appellation of akopa formerly signified the power of the drugs, but later their consistency.

And for this reason they were compelled to name them together with distinctions, [1007] calling this one an akopon that is relaxing, that one emollient or heating or anodyne or metasyncritic, just as also (they said it) suits such-and-such an affection, for example sciatica, paralysis, pain of the sides, or in common all pains. Now there is a naturally occurring simple drug that is a help for all fatigues, oil, which we also name without any addition, since in the ancient times it was in fact the only one; but later castor oil was added to it, among you at any rate. For in Egypt this too was ancient, and after castor oil again others, radish oil and mustard oil and sesame oil, and other such ones, just as among us too lily oil and mastic oil and lentisk oil, and those more elaborate than these, extending even to the perfumed unguents.

It is quite clear, then, that the drugs called akopa among the ancients must all be liquid in their consistency, since oil alone treats the superficial fatigues (kopoi), while those that are both deep-seated and more violent it treats together with one of the relaxing drugs thrown into it, which are of a nature to heat moderately, such as galbanum and terebinth resin [1008] and, in addition to it, a certain resin called colophonian and the roasted (phrykte). Hotter than these are fir resin and strobilos (pine-cone) resin, while larch resin is slightly hotter than terebinth. All such things are mixed with relaxing oils, of the kind that Sabine oil is, wax also sometimes being added. An akopon unguent for those already in pain deep down is also the one made from the seed of the fir, chamomile, dill and black-poplar flower, concerning which we shall say in what follows how it is prepared. The sousinon (lily unguent), the gleukinon (must unguent) and the Commagene unguent are also among the akopon unguents, as are all those compounded with soft fat (pimele) and hard fat (stear), pig's fat relaxing most moderately, hens' fat more than these, and goose fat still more than this. A stronger fat, so as now to heat more violently and for this reason also to disperse considerably, is lion's and leopard's fat. In the middle between these and ox and goat fat is that of foxes and of the hyena.

All these, then, belong by kind to the acopa properly so called, differing from one another in heating more or less, so that some will even seem to have fallen out of the whole kind [1009] of acopic unguents when they are examined on soft bodies, although they appear most beneficial to harder ones, such as those of country people are. For it has also been said many times that hard bodies tolerate the stronger drugs, whereas those that are soft and moist, like those of children and women and eunuchs, do not bear the power of such drugs. And it is quite evident that the so-called myracopa too come about from acopa being mixed with perfumed oils, being in no way better than the others except in respect of fragrance. As I am accustomed, then, to write down what has been tested by the older physicians through long experience, so too I shall do now, making my beginning from what was written by Asclepiades. [The acopa and myracopa written by Asclepiades in the fourth book of the External remedies.] Acopa. It is effective against the discomforts arising from fatigues, and for nervous sympathetic affections. Themison used it. The drug is exceedingly good. Take: of marjoram 1 xestes, of libanotis 1 xestes, of fenugreek 1 xestes.

of cardamom [1010] half a xestes, of savin half a xestes, of sweetish wine three xestai, of Venafran oil three litrai, of wax two litrai. Having put the dry ingredients into the wine, leave them to steep for three days; on the following day, having added the oil and stirred carefully and set it on charcoals, boil, stirring. And when it has boiled up continuously, press out the liquid, and having grated the wax and added it to this and set it again on the fire, boil. And when the wax has melted, having taken it off the fire, let it cool, and having cooled it, store it in a glass or tin vessel and use it, sometimes undiluted, sometimes also diluted with one of the perfumed oils. Another. Take of marjoram one xestes, of libanotis (rosemary) one xestes, of fenugreek one xestes, of bay twigs six litrai, of flower of schoinos (rush) three ounces, of old wine three xestai, of sweet oil three xestai, of the root of wild cucumber and of Celtic nard half a litra each, of wax three litrai. Prepare and use as has been stated before. Another drug, a well-proven one. It is effective also for the paretic, for the tremulous, and for every nervous sympathetic affection. Menius Rufus indeed used it.

It works for sufferers from podagra, from arthritis and from sciatica, [1011] so as to deliver them from the whole condition. Its use is in the intervals; during the paroxysms we use the drug diluted. ♃ Of marjoram 2 xestai, of fenugreek 1 xestes, of libanotis 1½ xestai, of melilot 1 xestes, of Illyrian (iris) 1 litra, of cyperus 1 litra, of savin 1 litra, of cachrys 1 litra, of cardamom half a litra, of flower of schoinos half a litra, of cassia half a litra, of southernwood half a litra, of myrtle fruit half a litra, of bay fruit half a litra. Having bruised all of these and put them into a double perfumer's vessel, add 8 xestai of Tmolite wine; let them steep for 3 days; then add 16 litrai of Sabine oil, 1 litra of iris-unguent, 1 litra of mastic-unguent, 1 litra of Syrian, 1 litra of gleukinon, 1 litra of myrtle-unguent, 1 litra of bay-unguent, and setting it on the fire boil it; then, having pressed out the liquid from the boiled ingredients, pour it off into another vessel and boil again, apart from the boiled-out materials, adding half a litra of wax, 1 litra of larch resin, of myrrh (and) of stacte 1 litra each; and when these have melted, use as has been said before. Another. ♃ Of marjoram 2 litrai, of fenugreek 2 xestai, of libanotis 2 xestai.

of savin [1012] two litrai, two xestai; of melilot two litrai; of cyperus one litra; of Macedonian iris one litra; of cachrys one litra; of cardamom one litra; of aromatic reed half a litra; of flower of schoinos half a litra; of tubular cassia, of costus, of sage, half a litra of each; of bay-berries half a litra; of the root of wild cucumber half a litra; of myrtle twigs half a litra; of fragrant Tmolite wine eight xestai; of Sabine oil twenty-four litrai; of iris-oil one litra, of kyprinon one litra; of mastic-oil one litra; of gleukinon one (the unit, written κι., is uncertain, presumably litra); of myrtle-oil one litra; of ammoniac or of amaracine one litra; of hedychroun one litra; of malabathrine oil one litra; of stacte of myrrh one litra; of opobalsamum one litra; of wax fifteen litrai. The dry ingredients are steeped, as has been said before, for three days, and to these are added the oil and most of the perfumed oils. But the malabathrine oil and the amaracine and the hedychroun and the stacte and the opobalsamum are kept for last, so that in the preparation of the drug, when the wax has already been melted, these are added. How one must prepare it, and in what manner the drug is to be used, has already been shown.

The acopon inscribed as 'the one through honey' [1013]. It is effective for fatigue-like discomforts and for contractions of the nerves. It is effective for those suffering opisthotonus and for those convulsed in the canine manner; it is called tetramyron (the four-unguent). ♃ Honey, 3 ounces; iris oil, 3 ounces; rose-oil, 3 ounces; henna oil, 3 ounces; must-oil, 3 ounces; wax, 3 ounces; terebinth, 3 ounces. Boil the honey separately. Melt the meltable ingredients and, having put them into a mortar, beat them all up together, and having ground fine, take it up and use. Another. ♃ Henna oil, iris oil, rose-oil, must-oil, 6 kotylai of each; wax, 24 drachms; terebinth, 8 drachms; honey, 6 drachms. Prepare and use as has been stated before. Another, which is called lexopyreton (fever-ceasing). ♃ Rose-oil, 4 kotylai; iris oil, 4; must-oil, 4; henna oil, 4 kotylai; wax, 12 drachms; terebinth, 14 drachms; stacte myrrh, 4 drachms; boiled honey, 16 drachms. Prepare as has been stated before. Another, from the writings of Aphrodiseus. ♃ Rose-oil, 4 kotylai; iris oil, 4 kotylai; henna oil, 4 kotylai; wax, 12 drachms; must-oil, 4 kotylai; goose fat, 12 drachms; terebinth, 4 drachms; stacte, 4 drachms; opobalsam, 2 drachms; boiled honey, 8 drachms. Prepare in the customary manner.

Another akopon, called "foul-smelling," for [1014] the aforesaid conditions. Take wax 8 dr., terebinth 8 dr., galbanum 6 dr., ammoniac incense 6 dr., old oil 2 cotylae, deer marrow 8 dr. Prepare in the usual manner and use it both undiluted and diluted. Another, for every sympathetic affection of the nerves. Take terebinth resin 56 dr., wax 28 dr., ammoniac incense 32 dr., galbanum 32 dr., deer marrow 24 dr., boiled honey 24 dr., old oil 2 cotylae. The ammoniac is dissolved in vinegar. Another. Take wax 24 dr., terebinth 24 dr., galbanum 6 dr., ammoniac incense 6 dr., old oil 2 cotylae, deer marrow 8 dr., storax 16 dr. Prepare in the usual manner. Another. Take wax 24 or 28 dr., terebinth 16 dr., galbanum 6 dr., storax 8 dr., old oil 2 cotylae, honey 1½ cotyle, deer marrow 8 dr., flower of salt as much as suffices; dissolve the ammoniac in vinegar. Another, for those suffering from sciatica, for those suffering from opisthotonos, and for every sympathetic affection of the nerves. Take wax 6 oz., terebinth 1 litra, ammoniac incense 1 oz.

of opopanax [1015] 2 ounces, of galbanum 2 ounces, of deer marrow 2 ounces, of bull's marrow 2 ounces, of oesypum 2 ounces, of iris oil 1 kotyle, of honey 3 ounces. Prepare in the usual manner. Another, for conditions of excessive fatigue and for contractions of the sinews. ℞ wax 50 drachms, terebinth 25 drachms, aphronitron 6 drachms, oesypum 6 drachms, boiled honey 6 drachms, ammoniac incense 6 drachms, deer marrow 6 drachms, galbanum 6 drachms, bull's suet 6 drachms, dried bay-berries 6 drachms, oil 1 kotyle, wine without sea-water 1 kotyle. Prepare in the usual manner. Another, inscribed 'Acuntianum'. ℞ wax 2 ounces, galbanum 3 ounces, nitron 3 ounces, liquid terebinth 3 ounces, oesypum 2 ounces, bull's suet 2 ounces, henna oil 4 ounces, quince oil 4 ounces, iris oil 4 ounces, honey 4 ounces, common oil 6 ounces, old oil 4 ounces, ammoniac incense 1 ounce, frankincense 1 ounce. Prepare in the usual manner. Another. ℞ old oil 1½ xestai, terebinth 1 litra, ammoniac incense 2 ounces, wax half a litra, galbanum 3 ounces.

[1016] oesypum 2 oz., frankincense 1 oz., verdigris 2 oz., honey 2 kotylai (otherwise, 4 oz.), deer marrow 3 oz., goose fat 2 oz., wine 2 kotylai, aphronitron 2 oz. Prepare in the usual way. Another, a green akopon (chlorakopon). It is effective for those suffering from opisthotonos, for sciatics, for the paralysed, for those with tremors. ♃ myrrh 4 dr., ammoniac incense 4 dr., frankincense 4 dr., nitron 4 dr., verdigris 4 dr., opopanax 10 oz., galbanum 4 oz., terebinth resin 2 lb., wax 2 lb., malabathron unguent half a xestes, henna oil half a xestes, vinegar as much as suffices. Dissolve the ammoniac, the myrrh and the nitron, and when they have been dissolved, add to them the opopanax and the galbanum. When these have been triturated, add the meltable ingredients, and having mixed and taken up the preparation, use it. Another. ♃ myrrh 4 dr., terebinth resin 2 lb., wax 2 dr., ammoniac incense, frankincense, nitron, verdigris, 4 dr. of each, quince unguent half a xestes, henna oil 3 oz., iris oil 3 oz., old oil 3 xestai, opopanax 3 oz., galbanum 4 oz., vinegar a sufficient quantity. Prepare as has been described above.

Another, for chronic conditions, [1017] exceedingly noble. Take: wax, 1 mina; old oil, 4 xestai; terebinth resin, 1 litra; myrrh, 4 ounces; frankincense, opopanax, root of wild cucumber, verdigris, nitron, 4 ounces each; white pepper, 2 ounces; galbanum, 4 ounces; deer marrow, 4 ounces; henna oil, 4 ounces; iris oil, 4 ounces; quince oil, 4 ounces; of the shoots of green rue, 3 ounces; vinegar, a sufficient quantity. Boil the roots of the wild cucumber and the rue with the vinegar, then press out the liquid and add it to the dry ingredients, and having triturated carefully, take it up with the meltable ingredients, and use the drug sometimes undiluted, and at times also diluted. This is done in proportion to the underlying conditions. Another, a successful drug of Bassus. He himself, having used this, after having previously been paralysed, was saved. Take: myrtle oil, 4 ounces; henna oil, 4 ounces; old oil, 1½ litrai; chalkanthos, 1½ litrai; wax, 1 litra; terebinth resin, 1½ litrai; galbanum, 3 ounces; manna, 4 ounces; opopanax, 2 ounces; bryony root, 4 ounces; verdigris, 4 ounces; aphronitron, 4 ounces.

of pepper [1018] 2 ounces, of pyrethrum 4 ounces, of kid's fat 6 ounces, of euphorbium 4 ounces, of vinegar a sufficient quantity. Boil the bryony and the pyrethrum with the vinegar; then, having pressed out the liquid and added it to the dry ingredients and triturated carefully, take up with the meltable ingredients. The use has been indicated. Another, the one made with castoreum, for paralytics and for chronic conditions. ♃ of oesypum 3 ounces, of deer marrow 4 ounces, of turpentine resin 3 ounces, of ammoniac incense 2 ounces, of galbanum 2 ounces, of castoreum 2 ounces, of white pepper 2 ounces, of euphorbium 2 ounces, of adarkē 2 ounces, of foam of nitron 2 ounces, of opopanax 2 ounces, of storax oil 1 ounce, of iris oil 2 ounces, of old oil 1 kotyle, of wax 1½ pounds. Compound in the usual manner. Another, which Bassus used, who had been paralysed for a long time and was freed from a disease of this kind. ♃ of myrtle oil 4 ounces, of quince oil 4 ounces, of cyprine oil 4 ounces, of old oil half a pound, of wax one pound, of turpentine resin half a pound, of galbanum 5 ounces, of frankincense 4 ounces, of opopanax 2 ounces, of verdigris 2 ounces, of bryony root 4 ounces, of aphronitron 4 ounces,

of pepper [1019] 2 ounces, of pellitory 2 ounces, of kid's fat 6 ounces, of euphorbium 1 ounce, of vinegar a sufficient quantity. The composition is the one common to such drugs. Another anointing-salve (synchrisma) for gouty and arthritic patients, the one made with salts; it frees the patient from the whole condition. The use is daily. ♃ Of dirty salts, that is, of the earth itself, 1 litra; of split alum 1 litra; of lees of Italian wine 1 xestes; of the flower of Asian stone 4 ounces. Pound the dry ingredients diligently, and having added the lees and ground them fine carefully, add to the ground ingredients 1 xestes of old oil; and having beaten it up, take it up and use it. In other recipes it is taken up with Attic honey. Another. ♃ Of dirty salts 3 ounces, of split alum 3 ounces, of the flower of Asian stone 3 ounces, of frankincense half an ounce or 6 ounces, of myrrh half an ounce or 6 ounces, of lees of Italian wine half a xestes; prepare as has been said before. Another anointing-salve, the one compounded for Patroclus, freedman of Caesar; it frees the patient from the whole condition. The use is daily, both in the morning before the bath and after the bath and towards evening.

One must take as much of the drug as suffices, dissolve it, and anoint [1020] the feet and rub them without bruising. ♃ Frankincense 10 drachms; white pepper 10 drachms; aphronitron 8 drachms; myrrh 4 drachms; ammoniac incense 6 drachms; vinegar, a sufficient quantity; henna oil 1½ kotylai. The dry ingredients are pounded and sifted through a very fine sieve, the rest are dissolved in vinegar and triturated; then all are mixed together, and the henna oil is added to the triturated ingredients; and having taken it up we use it. Another. ♃ Frankincense 8 drachms; myrrh 8 drachms; ammoniac incense 8 drachms; split alum, white pepper, 8 drachms each; nitron 8 drachms; vinegar, a sufficient quantity; henna oil 2 kotylai; wax half a litra. The meltable ingredients are melted and added to the triturated ones. Another, that of Neapolites, a drug successful for sufferers from sciatica, arthritics and gout-sufferers; it frees them from the whole condition. ♃ Frankincense 2 ounces; white pepper 2 ounces; ammoniac incense 2 ounces; myrrh 2 ounces; flower of Asian stone 2 ounces; split alum 2 ounces; nitron 2 ounces; juice of centaury 2 ounces; lees of Italian wine 1 xestes.

of oil of henna (cyprinum), laurel oil, myrtle oil, storax oil, and wax, [1021] one litra each; of terebinth resin half a litra, of galbanum one ounce, of opopanax half an ounce; the meltable ingredients are poured over the ingredients that have been triturated. Another. It was compounded for Domitius Nigrinus; it frees the patient from the whole condition. Take of stacte of myrrh two ounces, of frankincense two ounces, of ammoniac incense one ounce, of red nitron or of unrefined salt two ounces, of split alum two ounces, of flower of Asian stone two ounces, of colocynth pulp two ounces, of mandrake juice two ounces, of honey two ounces, of euphorbium two ounces, of saffron unguent six ounces, of quince oil six ounces, of storax oil six ounces, of malabathrum oil six ounces, of laurel oil six ounces, of must oil (gleucinum) six ounces, of hedychroum unguent six ounces, of marjoram oil six ounces, of seal fat six ounces—if this is not available, one must use very old deer marrow—of wax one litra, of galbanum one ounce, of terebinth resin half a litra, of opopanax half an ounce, of lees of Italian wine one xestes. Prepare as stated above.

This preparation is to be used following upon the Podarces prepared for Sabernius Valens, which is entitled [1022] 'Pompey's sumptuous'. The one made with black poplar: for sciatics, arthritics, paralytics, the tremulous; it is effective also for daily use. Take: of shoots of black poplar, 1 mina; of root of wild cucumber, 4 litrai; of tube-cassia, 2 litrai; of crocine unguent, 2 litrai; of saffron, 3 ounces; of fragrant wine, 12 xestai; of Sabine oil, 300 xestai; of marjoram, 4 litrai; of wax, 4 litrai. Having chopped the shoots of the poplar carefully, keep them in a double perfumer's vessel, and add to these the marjoram and the cucumber root, chopped coarsely, and to these add the wine, and leave everything to steep for 9 days. On the following day, having added the oil and beaten it up thoroughly, boil, using a gentle fire. Then, having pressed out the liquid and added to it grated wax and triturated marrow, and having set it upon the fire, boil; and when it has melted, taking it off the fire, add the crocine, stirring continuously. The crocine, having triturated it, take up with the blood of a land tortoise, so that it has the thickness of old oil. The tortoise is slaughtered at the collar-bone with a reed sharpened on both sides.

Having added the melted ingredients to the [1023] saffron and beaten them up together, take it up and use it. The drug delivers one from the whole condition. It becomes still better if it receives in addition a generous quantity of the tortoise's blood. Another, effective for the discomforts arising from thorough chilling and the contusions resulting from blows. Take: of black-poplar shoots 1 mina; of wild cucumber root 4 litrai; of pipe-cassia 2 litrai; of deer marrow 2 litrai; of saffron 3 litrai; of fragrant wine 12 xestai; of oil 10 litrai; of marjoram 4 litrai; of wax 4 litrai; of the blood of a land tortoise, however much you throw in, you will benefit the drug; prepare as has been described before. Another akopon, the one made with toads. A man of the xystos (an athlete) used this both as an akopon and as a malagma, and was delivered from the whole condition. The details of the preparation are as follows. Take: of old Sabine oil 3 litrai; of wild cucumber root 3 litrai; of wax 3 litrai; of apochyma 3 litrai; of old pig's fat 3 litrai; of toad-frogs (βατράχων φρυνίχων), the large ones, 3 in number, or, failing that, 5 of the small ones; of deer marrow 3 ounces; of aphronitron 3 ounces; of unburnt sulphur 3 ounces; of bay-laurel oil 3 ounces; of iris oil 3 ounces.

of malabathrum unguent [1024] one pound; of marjoram one pound. Cutting the roots into thick pieces and throwing them together with the marjoram into the oil, and setting it over charcoals, boil; and when the roots have dried out, press out the liquid, and throw away the roots and the marjoram. Then having put the frogs into a small woven basket and sewn up its lips, and having placed it in the oil that was pressed out, and having again set the vessel upon the fire, covered with a lid. When a sufficient interval has passed, so that the frogs have melted away, lift out the small basket and, having pressed out the liquid, throw the basket away. To the oil that is left over add the fusible ingredients, stirring continuously. Last of all add the marrow and the galbanum, and when it has dissolved, taking it off the fire and allowing it to cool somewhat, sprinkle on the dry ingredients, pounded and sifted through the finest sieve, stirring continuously; and having poured it out into a mortar and beaten it up, add one pound and a half of malabathrum unguent, and having beaten it up, take it up into a leaden vessel and keep it so that it cannot evaporate. The drug is to be used at one time as a malagma, when the decline (of the affection) has set in; and there are times when it is also used as a liniment.

[1025] For taking as much of the drug as suffices, dissolving it in perfume and bringing it to the consistency of a liquid cerate, we use it. Another, that of Halieus, a successful drug, in which Halieus, passing his time and being gripped by the affection to such a degree that his body was distorted, used the drug and was freed from the whole condition. The preparation was given to Valerius Paulinus. It is as follows. Take of Sabine oil three litrai; of young shoots of black poplar one litra; if the shoots are not available, one must use marjoram, so that the marjoram is double. It contains also of marjoram one litra; of henna oil one litra; of iris oil one litra; of mastic one litra; of stacte of myrrh half a litra; of wax three litrai; of apochyma three litrai; of fatty pig's lard three litrai; of unburnt sulphur three ounces; of foam of nitron three ounces; of galbanum three litrai; of deer marrow four ounces; of land tortoises, ten: the blood must be put in when the drug has been prepared and is already being triturated. One must prepare it as has been stated. In the use of the drug, one must take up one litra and add to it, for the sake of fragrance, three ounces of opobalsam

[1026] and one ounce of malabathrum unguent. This is prepared thus for daily uses. Another, that of Halieus, altered by Valerius Paulinus. ♃ wax 3 litrai; root of wild cucumber 3 litrai; apochyma 3 litrai; fatty pig's fat 3 litrai; Sabine oil 3 litrai; henna oil 1 litra; lily oil 1 litra; saffron oil 1 litra; mastic 1 litra; stacte half a litra; deer marrow 1½ litrai; galbanum 1½ litrai; toads, 5; marjoram or black-poplar shoots 3 litrai; unburnt sulphur 3 ounces; aphronitron 3 ounces; the blood of several tortoises. Prepare as stated before. Another, of Flavius Clemens, a successful drug. We know of men contorted in the whole body by podagra and cheiragra who, having used this, were saved to such an extent that they walked about unmaimed. ♃ Sabine oil 12 litrai; root of wild cucumber 12 litrai; wax 1 litra; terebinth 1 litra; deer marrow 1 litra; galbanum 1 litra; frogs, 6 in number.

We divide the oil, and in one part we boil the frogs, in the other the roots; then, having strained the [1027] liquid, we use it for the preparation of the drug, and we use the drug as an akopon. This drug [we prepared] for Valerius Paulinus in this manner, adding to the recipe: of marjoram one litra and a half, of saffron unguent one litra, of malabathron unguent one litra, of opobalsam three ounces, the blood of ten tortoises, of deer marrow two litrai, of galbanum two litrai, of old pig's fat three litrai, of apochyma one litra, of wax three litrai and a half, of unburnt sulphur one ounce, of aphronitron four ounces, three toads, the blood of fifteen tortoises, and in place of the saffron unguent, of Syrian unguent one litra, of marjoram one litra and a half. Prepare in the usual manner. Another, of Pompeius Sabinus; it is entitled "costly." It was prepared for Aburnius Valens; it is effective for those suffering from sciatica, for arthritics, for those with podagra, for those with tremor, and for every nervous affection. The details of the preparation are as follows: ♃ of marjoram two litrai, of fenugreek two litrai, of melilot one litra, of libanotis one litra, of savin one litra and a half, of cachrys one litra, of henna (kyprinon) one litra, of southernwood one litra, of cardamom half a litra, of bay-berries half a litra, of fragrant wine twenty-four xestai.

of iris perfume, [1028] 15 pounds; of henna oil, 2 pounds; of bay oil, must-oil (gleukinon) and malabathron oil, 2 pounds each; of Syrian unguent, 2 pounds; of wax, 2 pounds; of terebinth resin, 1 pound; of galbanum, 2 ounces; of opopanax, 3 ounces; of purified ammoniac incense, 4 ounces; of long pepper, red nitron, flower of Asian stone, pith of colocynth, split alum, 4 ounces each; of frankincense, 4 ounces; of centaury, 4 ounces; of mandrake juice, stacte of myrrh, boiled honey, 4 ounces each; large toads (phrynoi), six in number; the blood of 10 land tortoises. The drug is prepared in several stages. Having pounded the aromatic and dry ingredients coarsely and put them into a double perfumer's vessel, and having poured wine over them, we let them steep for three days; and on the fourth,

having taken off as much of the wine as suffices, with this we soak ammoniac incense, frankincense, galbanum, opopanax and the remaining juices; once these have dissolved we triturate them, and to these, once triturated, we add, pounded and sifted, alum, red nitron, colocynth, flower of Asian stone, pepper, and we triturate the rest of the dry ingredients; to these we add [1029] stacte of myrrh and the honey. When these have been prepared in this way, we add all the liquids to the ingredients soaking in the wine and, setting them on the fire, we boil, stirring continuously. And when the greater part of the wine has been consumed, we press out the liquid and, putting the frogs into it, as has been stated above, we boil, and then we add the meltable ingredients; and when these have melted, lifting it from the fire, we add it to the triturated ingredients and, having beaten it up and taken it up, we use it. Another metasyncritic acopon: for sciatics, arthritics, the paralysed, those with tremors. Julius Secundus used it. It removes (ἀνασκεύαζε) chronic conditions; it is good also for those with headache. Take adarkē 2 oz., stacte of myrrh 2 oz., aphronitron 2 oz., euphorbium, opobalsamum 2 ounces each, storax unguent 1 pound. Pound and sift the dry ingredients, and add to these stacte of myrrh and opobalsamum, and having beaten it up, take it up with the storax unguent and use the drug, sometimes undiluted, sometimes slackened; and it assists concoction. Another, composed for Orfitus.

Using this he was relieved of the affection about the thorax, which had become troublesome and [1030] of long duration. ℞ Adarkē, 2 oz.; stacte of myrrh, 2 oz.; aphronitron, 3 oz.; euphorbium, ½ oz., otherwise 6 oz.; malabathrine perfume, 1 pound; of what is called in Latin foliatum, half a pound; wax, 2 oz.; opobalsam, 2 oz. Prepare in the usual manner. Another, that of the Neapolitan; it was compounded for Agrippa. ℞ Adarkē, with the reeds removed, 3 ounces; euphorbium, 3 oz., otherwise 6; aphronitron, 3 oz.; stacte, 3 ounces; opobalsam, 3 ounces; malabathrine perfume of the first (grade), 1 pound; foliatum of the first (grade), half a pound; hedychroun, half a pound; crocinum, half a pound; Asian nard of Thyateira, of the first (grade), half a pound; wax, 3 oz. Prepare in the usual manner. Another, a royal myrakopon (perfumed akopon), for long-standing affections; it also assists concoction. ℞ Aromatic reed, 3 oz.; carpobalsam, 3 oz.; amomum, 3 ounces; cardamom, 3 oz.; flower of rush, 3 oz.; rose-coloured cassia, 3 ounces; melilot, 3 oz.; marjoram, 3 oz.; savin, 3 ounces; fenugreek, 3 oz.; cyperus, 3 oz.; nard, 3 oz.; white pepper, 3 ounces.

of Troglodytic myrrh half a litra, [1031] of euphorbium, adarkē, nitre, half a litra each, of Falernian wine 16 xestai, of malabathrine unguent of the first preparation 2 litrai, of nard of the first composition 1 litra, of foliatum of the first grade 1 litra, of opobalsam 1 litra, of crocinum 1 litra, of styracinum of the first grade 1 litra, of amygdalinum 1 litra, of Commagenian 1 litra, of gleucinum 1 litra, of irinum 1 litra, of hedychrous 2 litrai, of amaracinum of the first grade 2 litrai. Boil in the manner of perfumers. The drug is exceedingly good; it was prepared for Celer the primipilarius. It is effective for sciatics, arthritics, paralytics, those with tremors, for sprains, ruptures, and for the scirrhous conditions of the viscera, and it assists concoction when smeared on the mouth of the stomach and on the back. Another, composed for Aquilia Secundilla. Take euphorbium, opobalsam, stacte of myrrh, 2 unciae each, of foam of nitre 3 unciae, of wax 1 uncia, of malabathrine unguent 1 litra, of foliatum half a litra, of crocinum half a litra, of nard unguent half a litra, of hedychrous half a litra, of amaracinum half a litra; prepare in the usual way. The recipes written above would indeed have sufficed.

For Asclepiades wrote carefully both their preparations [1032] and their uses, whereas Andromachus did so more carelessly, as is his habit, not even indicating what each of them is naturally fitted to do, but leaving that to us; for he has always composed his writings as if for practitioners of the art. But since some of the acopa, though similar to one another, differ in their proportions, for this reason I have written these too in advance, since readers are able, on the basis of what Asclepiades taught, to reason about these as well — which of the acopa will best suit which affections. And I too shall speak, after going through some general accounts concerning them, from which those who attend to what will be said will arrive more methodically at their uses. [The acopa written by Andromachus.] The green acopon of Halieus. Take: wax, terebinth resin, old oil, one and a half pounds each; aphronitron, four ounces; galbanum, three ounces; scraped verdigris, three ounces; opopanax, six ounces; ammoniac incense, three ounces; manna, three ounces; vinegar, two ounces; quince oil, two ounces; henna oil, two ounces; iris oil, two ounces; goat's fat, one ounce. Another good acopon. Take: wax, sixteen pounds; aphronitron, eight drachms;

[1033] bay-berries, 8 in number; white pepper, 1 drachm; crocomagma, a sufficient quantity; deer marrow, 2 drachms; myrrh, 1 drachm; wax, 1 drachm; Rhodian wine, 1; a little vinegar for the dry ingredients. Another, that of Bassus the Stoic. Take: root of wild cucumber, 1 litra; castoreum, 2 ounces; deer marrow, 6 ounces; old oil, 2 litrai; wax, 1 litra; aphronitron, 3 ounces; bay-berries, 2 xestai; green rue, a bundle the size of a handful; rosemary (libanotis), an equal amount; old Sabine oil, 10 litrai. The roots and the herbs are boiled down in the oil, then they are pressed out, then the meltable ingredients are poured over. Another. Take: opopanax, 1 ounce; resin, 1 ounce; pine resin, 2 litrai; wax, 1 litra; ammoniac incense, 6 ounces; oesypum, 2 ounces; old oil, 1½ xestai; flower of salt, 2 ounces. Another. Take: wax, 1 litra; deer marrow, 2 ounces; Babylonian unguent, 1 litra; hedychroon, 1 litra; stacte, 1 litra; malabathrum, 1 ounce; nard, 1 ounce; opobalsamum, 6 ounces. Melt the marrow in sea-water or in brine, having worked up the meltable ingredients together, and last of all the opobalsamum. But if the akopon is liquid, add more wax.

Another acopon [1034] of Quadratus. Take iris unguent 1 ounce, wax 1 ounce, cyprinum 1 ounce, laurel oil 1 ounce, old oil 3 ounces, terebinth resin 1 ounce, deer marrow 1 ounce, oesypum 1 ounce, pepper 1 ounce, nitron 4 drachms, unburnt sulphur 4 drachms, pyrethrum 4 drachms, honey 1 ounce. The meltable ingredients are poured over the dry ones. Another, the foul-smelling acopon. Take terebinth resin 56 drachms, wax 28 drachms, oesypum 6 drachms, honey 6 drachms, deer marrow 6 drachms, ammoniac incense 6 drachms, galbanum 6 drachms, aphronitron 6 drachms, sometimes opopanax 6 drachms, bay berries 6 drachms, old oil 1 sextarius, wine 2 cotylae; some add castoreum 3 drachms. Another, the one with marjoram. Take wax 1 pound, omphacine oil 3 sextarii, marjoram 1 sextarius, fenugreek 1 sextarius, old wine 4 sextarii, a bundle of mallow, a bundle of linozostis (mercury-plant), roots of wild cucumber. Another, as Antimachus gives it. Take fresh marjoram, libanotis (rosemary), aspalathus, savin — which is herba Sabina — and fenugreek, 2 sextarii of each, wax 1 pound, old wine 3 sextarii, gleucine oil 3 sextarii. Another, from Philocles.

Take: of oil [1035] boiled down for a long time with roots of wild cucumber, 3 xestai; of wax, one mina; of terebinth resin, 1 mina; of deer marrow, 25 drachms; of goose fat, 25 drachms; of galbanum, 12½ drachms; of marjoram, 1 xestes; of rosemary (libanotis), 1 xestes. These last are ground fine with fragrant wine and mixed in; and it becomes a malagma if more wax is mixed in. Another successful akopon, according to Aphrodas. Take: of aphronitron, 3 drachms; of pepper, 40 grains, and the same amount of long pepper; of frankincense, 16 drachms. Having pounded these, pour on 1 kotyle of fragrant Chian or Rhodian wine, 9 drachms of honey; then melt in a dish 12 drachms of Tyrrhenian wax, 42 drachms of bull's fat. Another, which was Asphalartesios'. Take: of krokomagma, 4 drachms; of deer marrow, 12 drachms; of oesypum, 6 drachms; of goose or pig fat, 12 drachms; of terebinth resin, 12 drachms; of iris oil, 18 drachms; of henna oil and of gleukinon oil, 18 drachms each. Melt the honey, then mix it with the dry ingredients, and having ground it together with the things in the mortar, use it. Another akopon, the barbarian one, made with euphorbium, for sufferers from sciatica and for many other things. Take: of opopanax, 1 ounce; of Tyrrhenian wax, 1 ounce; of terebinth resin, 2 ounces.

of galbanum [1036] 1 ounce, of ammoniac incense 2 ounces, of euphorbium 2 ounces, of castoreum 2 ounces, of white pepper 2 ounces, of deer marrow 4 ounces, of oesypum 4 ounces, of limnestris half an ounce, of storax oil, laurel oil, marjoram oil, 3 ounces of each, of old oil 2 sextarii, of hedychroum 6 ounces. Prepare and use. It works for desperate conditions of the sinews, and particularly also for those with sciatica. Another acopon, with which Arruntius Aquila was cured; effective for sciatica and for every tension of the sinews. ♃ of opopanax 2 ounces, of galbanum 1 ounce, of turpentine-resin 2 ounces, of white pepper and castoreum 2 ounces of each, of oesypum 4 ounces, of cassia 4 ounces, of deer marrow 4 ounces, of wax 1 pound, of storax oil 6 ounces, of iris oil 6 ounces, of laurel oil 6 ounces, of old oil 1 pound, of euphorbium 2 ounces, of ammoniac incense 2 ounces. Mix in the euphorbium with a little honey. Another acopon, that of Glytus, as Philoxenus the grammarian (gives it). ♃ of wax 2 pounds, of ammoniac incense 1 pound, of galbanum 1½ pounds, of storax 1 pound, of bdellium 1 pound, of myrrh 2 ounces, of frankincense 9 ounces, of Attic oesypum 1 pound.

[1037] propolis, 1 litra; terebinth resin, 1 litra; old oil, 2 litrae; henna oil, iris perfume, almond oil, 2 litrae each; Syrian perfume, 3 litrae; opopanax, 1 litra. Prepare. Another green akopon, according to Clemens Sertorius, which I use. ♃ scraped verdigris, 6 ounces; roasted (phrykte) resin, 4 ounces; myrtle oil, 1 litra; mastic oil, 1 litra; old oil, 1 litra; laurel oil, 2 litrae; Syrian perfume, 1 litra; gleukinon (must-oil), 3 litrae; lamb's fat, 3 ounces; Pontic wax, 3 litrae; galbanum, 1 litra; tender myrtle leaves, green rue leaves, green libanotis, tender laurel leaves, 6 ounces each; the herb sage, half a litra. Pound the green ingredients and steep them in the oils for a night and a day, then boil them down together with the meltable ingredients. When you take it off the fire, add the verdigris, and having strained it, store it. It works for every pain of the sinews. Another heating akopon, according to Castus, for chronic conditions and spasms. ♃ pitch-oil, 1 xestes; Syrian perfume, the same amount; Illyrian iris, the same amount; terebinth, 1 litra; axungia, 1 litra; ship-scrapings, 1 ounce.

[1038] boil, stirring with fresh rue. Another akopon, that of Orion the hair-dresser, a good one. ♃ Of wax 6 litrai; of propolis 5 litrai; of Illyrian iris 4 litrai; of terebinth resin 4 litrai; of opopanax 3 litrai; of old oil 4 litrai; of galbanum 2 litrai; of mastic oil 3 litrai; of myrtle oil 3 litrai; of ammoniac incense 1 litra; of deer marrow 3 litrai; of oesypum 6 litrai; of bay-berries 1 litra; of storax oil 3 litrai; of almond oil 3 litrai; of calf's fat 3 litrai, and of lion's fat 1½ litrai; of opobalsamum 1½ litrai. Prepare carefully. Another good myrakopon (perfumed akopon). ♃ Of malabathron, of hedychroon, of Babylonian saffron nard, half a litra each; of stacte 6 ounces; of opobalsamum 6 ounces; of wax 6 ounces; of Commagene unguent 6 ounces; of aloe 2 ounces; of honey 3 ounces. Prepare. Another myrakopon, which I use. Of white wax 2 ounces; of aromatised goose fat 1 ounce; of aromatised bull's fat 1 ounce; of aromatised lion's fat 2 ounces; of aromatised crocodile fat 1 ounce; of deer marrow 1 ounce; of ammoniac salt 2 ounces; of white pepper 2 ounces; of frankincense 1 ounce; of cinnamon 3 ounces.

[1039] of aphronitron 1 ounce, of Illyrian iris 2 xestai, of nard perfume 1 xestes, of Alexandrian malabathrum 2 xestai, of stacte 2 pounds, of Syrian saffron-perfume 2 pounds, of honey 4 pounds, of opobalsam 1 xestes, of Commagene (goose-fat) 2 pounds. Prepare, as you know how. Another myrakopon (perfumed akopon). ℞ of Tyrrhenian wax 6 ounces, of ammoniac 4 ounces, of euphorbium 4 pounds, of white pepper 4 ounces, of limnestris 4 ounces, of the magma (sediment) of malabathrum 6 ounces, of opobalsam 1 pound, of malabathrum 1 pound, of stacte 6 ounces, of foliatum 6 ounces, of nard 3 pounds. [Preparations of gleukinon.] Preparation of gleukinon, as Andromachus gives it. Following the akopa written above, Andromachus wrote a preparation of gleukinon, not badly joining it to the akopon ointments; for it is most anodyne and most effective against fatigue (akopōtaton). It is written by him word for word as follows. Preparation of gleukinon, which I use. ℞ of myrrh 2 pounds, of Indian nard 2 pounds, of costus 3 pounds, of storax 1 pound,

of bdellium, of sampsychon (sweet marjoram), of xylobalsamum (balsam-wood), of lentisk (schinos), of cardamom, of spathe (of the date-palm), [1040] of Illyrian iris, of misy, of asarum, two litrae of each; of melilot, one litra; of Celtic nard, one litra; of aspalathus and of calamus, half a litra of each; of long aristolochia, one and a half litrae; of seed of libanotis (rosemary), two xestai; of frankincense, three litrae; of cassia, three litrae; of fenugreek, two xestai; of sphagnos, two litrae; of amomum, two litrae; of frankincense bark, one litra; of dried roses, two litrae; of savin, six unciae; of fennel, two litrae; of balsam fruit, two litrae; of saffron, three unciae; of bay-berries, one litra; of white pepper, one litra; of opobalsamum, three unciae; of malabathrum leaves, two litrae; two green pine-cones; of green rue, two unciae; of ammoniac salt, four drachms; of nitron, four drachms; of old wine, twelve xestai; of good must (gleukos), two and a half keramia; of old oil, five litrae. Prepare for forty days. Having written these things, Andromachus no longer gave the manner of the preparation, as Criton did. Moreover, he also did not make clear how many Italian litrae or xestai he wants the keramion to be. Preparation of gleukinon, as Criton gives it in the second book of the Cosmetics. Criton wrote the preparation of the gleukinon at the end of the book, in the following words.

[1041] Gleucine has a heating, relaxing power. It is effective against the conditions in the uterus and against every nervous sympathy; and of this there are many preparations. The one called simple is as follows. Take a metretes of fresh must of Maronean grapes, put it into a tin vessel and boil over charcoals, and when it has boiled up three or four times, pour it out into an earthenware metretes-vessel, set it in the sun and add 6 choes of white omphacine oil, 6 minae of lentisk (others: half a mina), of nard the same, of calamus the same, of aspalathus the same, 1 mina of elate, 1 mina of cyperus, 8 minae of cardamom, of amomum the same, 5 ounces of melilot. Let all be finely ground; then, having stirred them together for 8 days and cleared off the must, use it. Preparation of gleucine, as Dioscorides in book 1 of On Materia Medica. Dioscorides wrote thus.

Gleukinon in its simple form is prepared from omphakine oil, mastic (schinos), Celtic nard, calamus, spathe, aspalathos, melilot, kostos and must, the grape-pressings (stemphyla) being rubbed together in the middle (?) in the vessel that holds the aromatics, the wine and [1042] the oil; it is stirred for 30 days, twice a day, then it is pressed out and stored away. It has a warming, emollient, relaxing power, acting against shivering-fits and all nervous conditions and those in the womb. It is more beneficial than any akopon, being emollient. Preparation of gleukinon, according to Heras. But since Heras wrote the preparation of gleukinon more clearly than they did, at the end of his book on drugs, I shall set out his text too, word for word, as follows. Composition of gleukinon oil, which acts against chillings and especially nervous conditions; it benefits those suffering from opisthotonos and those suffering from emprosthotonos, applied warm by means of clean wool soaked in the oil and laid upon the places. ♃ Venafran oil, 208 litrai, otherwise 250; old, fragrant Falernian wine, 3 xestai; Aminaean must, 108 xestai; elecampane (helenion), 12 litrai; spathe, 5 litrai; aspalathos, 5 litrai; hedysaron, 2½ litrai; mother(?) artemisia, 2½ litrai; kyperos, 2 litrai; myrrh, 3 litrai, others 1 litra; white pepper, 2½ litrai; splanchnon, 2½ litrai; xylobalsamon (balsam wood), 2½ litrai.

of long aristolochia [1043] 1 pound 3 ounces; of dry myrtle leaves 1 ounce; of dry libanotis 5 ounces; of dry bay leaves 12 ounces; of bdellium 2½ pounds; of Illyrian iris 2½ pounds; of storax 1 pound 3 ounces; of dry cassia 1 pound 3 ounces; of ladanum 1 pound 3 ounces; of cardamom 1 pound 3 ounces; of saffron 1 pound 3½ ounces; of balsam fruit 2½ pounds; of frankincense 5 pounds; of crocomagma 5 pounds; of panax 1 pound 3 ounces; of aromatic reed 5 pounds; of asarum 2½ pounds; of black cassia 2½ pounds; of amomum cluster 1 pound 3 ounces; of flower of schoinos 5 pounds; of costus 5 pounds 3 ounces; of Celtic nard 5 pounds; of melilot 1 pound 3 ounces; of marjoram 1 pound 3 ounces; of dry roses 1 pound 3 ounces; of fenugreek ½ pound, or 2½ pounds; of opobalsamum 5 small vessels; of malabathrum unguent 1 pound. Having pounded the dry ingredients and sifted them through a rather coarse sieve, steep them in wine. As for the bdellium, even if it is not dry, pound it too; but if it is oily, dissolve it in the wine, pounding it in a mortar.

Having put it into a small tin perfumer's vessel, and having stoppered it [1044] carefully, leave it for twelve days and twelve nights. And let the must coincide in time, from grapes cleanly pressed out, so that it may have no dew in it. Having put the must into a large copper vessel, so that there is room also for the boiling-up of the must, add all the things that have been soaked in the wine, both the oil and the wine; and twice a day let it be stirred with a perfumer's spathe for an hour. And let the spathe be wiped off carefully, so that what has remained on it, having turned sour (ὀξῦσαν), may not harm the drug when the spathe is put in again. Let the vessel be fitted with a lid, and on top with several patchwork cloths (κεντρῶσι), and let it be bound round carefully. And let a coiled pad be placed under the vessel. When fifteen days have passed, let the ammoniac and the amomum itself be added, pounded rather coarsely. And for thirty days, in a double vessel over charcoals, one must give it two or three boilings, adding to the unguent also the opobalsamum. Then, having taken down the vessel and cooled it to a certain degree, pour off the unguent.

The remainder is to be squeezed out in small baskets while they are still warm, first by hand, then by means of a press; having done something on account of the unguent (the text here is corrupt), one is to throw into [1045] the unguent itself the malabathrum, provided we have put the unguent, poured out, over hot water, and to stir it with the spatula so that it may be mixed; then, after leaving it for one day, store it away in glass vessels, [or] earthenware ones smeared with gum. [The acopa written by Heras.] An acopon for paralytics, and in general for every pain. Take: of fresh rue one pound, of dry pennyroyal one pound, of cyperus one pound, of nitre fifty drachmas, of fenugreek one pound, of dry mercury-herb one pound, of horehound one pound, of libanotis one pound, of aristolochia one pound, of bitter almonds, peeled, half a modius, of iris two pounds, of terebinth resin two pounds, of bay-berries two pounds, of root of wild cucumber two pounds, of ammoniac incense two pounds, of savin two pounds, of white hellebore six pounds, of fresh myrtle three pounds, of dry bay leaves three pounds, of wax four pounds, of bdellium four pounds, of wine two kotylai; in another copy, of wine twelve choes, of oil four choes.

Having pounded coarsely those ingredients that need to be pounded, pour on water and, in turn, the pounded ingredients; pour on in addition also the wine and the oil [1046] and let it stand overnight, and on the following day boil it until these ingredients, floating in it, have been thoroughly boiled down and the oil has taken on the quality from the boiled ingredients. All this comes about with time. Then, having removed and pressed out the dregs, add the wax and the resin and the bdellium. Another, a green acopon, for sciatica and paralyses. I used this in the case of Phortes. Take: terebinth resin, 1 pound; manna, 4 ounces; galbanum, 4 ounces; aphronitron, 4 ounces; ammoniac incense, 4 ounces; opopanax, 4 ounces; goat suet, 6 ounces; verdigris, 5 ounces; henna oil, 1 cotyle; iris oil, 1½ cotylai; quince oil, 4 ounces; Syrian [oil], 3 ounces; pepper, 3 ounces (some say 4 ounces); old oil, 1½ sextarii; adarkē, 1 ounce; vinegar, as much as is fully sufficient. Triturate the verdigris and the opopanax and the aphronitron with the vinegar, and melt the rest and pour it over. Another acopon for chronic sciatica, for ankyloses and paralyses; it is very effective. Take: old oil and iris oil, 6 pounds; and laurel oil, 6 pounds; pyrakinon [oil], 6 pounds; wax, 6 pounds; terebinth, 2 ounces.

euphorbium [1047] 2 ounces; ammoniac incense 3 ounces; castoreum 2 ounces; opopanax 2 ounces; galbanum 2 ounces; deer's marrow 2 ounces; pepper 2 ounces. Having melted the meltable ingredients, pour them over the dry ones, and having united them, use. Another akopon for sciatic affections and in general for everything. Take myrrh one part, pellitory half a part. To the finely ground ingredients pour in gleucine oil, so that the drug becomes of a glutinous consistency; and at the time of use, mixing in rose-oil, use it. [Damocrates' preparations of akopa.] Since there is much talk among lovers of medicine about the use of all the akopa and the myrakopa, I shall state what these are and how they benefit, and how one must prepare each one of them as a drug. Now they all act against pains of the nerves, and of all flesh and of the muscles, such pains as fatigue has taken hold of, or chilling, or as have arisen without any evident cause.

And these must often be applied for similar pains and conditions of ill-affection, [1048] to those who are easily overcome by chills and fatigues, if a person, having used them beforehand, goes out in that state to the services imposed by the necessity of life. And it also puts flesh on certain parts of the body that are wasting, if one anoints the affected parts after food; and it will suit those who recover with difficulty, and old men who use them in winter toward evening. But what each of the akopa does we shall state in other verses, appending the useful information to their recipes, or even placing it before the recipe. Now, however, I shall say how one must make the first. Of ammoniac, then, ten (οὐγγίαι), whether one prefers ounces or another weight; the same of frankincense; of galbanum four; of deer marrow four; and four, the same amount, of the oesypum which they send from Attica; of transparent terebinth four; and of good fresh honey again ten.

[1049] and an equal weight to this of Pontic wax, and of fresh, soft goose fat ten; of Falernian wine five kotylai, or a little fewer or even a little more generous, and of old good oil twice twenty. But try to add this not foul-smelling, for thus it will be agreeable to those who use it. Prepare it as follows.

In a larger mortar, having crushed the frankincense into quite small lumps, and the ammoniac too, pouring on wine at once, and having allowed these to be soaked through in due measure, grind with the pestle and, bringing it to the thickness of honey, add the honey and the oesypum and the deer marrow; then, uniting these in the mortar, melt the wax in a pot together with all the oil and the fat and the galbanum and the terebinth, and having let them all melt, pour them over the things in the mortar, [1050] and having stirred a little with the pestle, so that it may cool somewhat, then rub all these together with the hands until everything is united and takes on the thickness of good liquid honey; and so store it away in a vessel of tin or even of boxwood, using it carefully as a most excellent drug. It is also most beneficial for women in whom there has arisen an inflammation of the womb bringing hardnesses and fear of scirrhus; in their case order that the drug, smeared on a pessary, be thus applied to the womb. This also works for pains of the ears, those without ulceration, the violent ones unaccompanied by a flux: mix a fourth or a third part of Sergetic (Σεργητικοῦ) iris unguent with the drug, and having soaked wool in it while warm, insert it into the passage. Another.

This too is a green akopon, very effective, [1051] which is why it acts better at the onsets of the pains; and it is beneficial to arthritics and to gout-sufferers who, before the baths, are rubbed with the drug on the feet and the sinews that have become thickened. For in this way I have known some to become healthy. It contains: of good frankincense, 1 litra; of ammoniac incense, 2 litrai; of the whitest aphronitron, 1 litra, and this same, having cleansed it; of Attic oesypum, of good myrrh, of galbanum without wood, of pure opopanax—of each one of these, weighing carefully, twice 4 ounces; of fresh euphorbium, 4 ounces, and equal to these of rough limnēsion—those who sell the ingredients in Italy, and those who buy them, call this adarkē; of very good Pontic wax, 2 litrai; of pure terebinth resin, 2½ litrai;

[1052] of laurel oil and henna oil and gleucine oil, one pound of each; of Sergetic iris oil, of old oil and of fresh mastic oil, of each of these again two pounds by weight; of vinegar, a moderate amount. With this, having triturated the dry ingredients for a sufficient time, grind carefully, and you will add, having melted them, the perfumed oils, the wax and the galbanum and the terebinth, and the juice of panax, and the other moist ingredients, pouring them out hot and still boiling onto the mortar. Rub down the ingredients in it with the pestle and vigorously with the hand, and having united them all, store the drug away in a box of the kind I mentioned a little earlier. Use it with confidence in all conditions that have become chronic. Another. This too is an acopon easily procured and good, and especially in winter, on journeys at any rate, able to help those who are easily affected.

[1053] It contains three ounces of pure galbanum, one ounce of fresh opopanax, three of flower of salt, four of oesypum, eight pounds of good ammoniac incense, one pound of wax, of roasted pine resin, the kind that is not foul-smelling, twice four ounces, and a pound of Sabine oil, twice four; and more of it in winter: throw in about a pound; of dark Falernian wine ten ounces. Prepare it thus.

In a mortar crush the ammoniac; then, having poured in wine, soak it a little and, having ground it carefully, then add the flower of salt and the oesypum; then, while grinding it thoroughly and bringing it to the thickness of honey, having melted the meltable ingredients, afterwards add the galbanum and the opopanax and melt again, and pour it over the things that have previously been made smooth in the mortar and well united, [1054] and having thus mixed the drug with the hands while it is still warm, store it away in a glass vessel. Another myrakopon (perfumed akopon). And this myrakopon too is among the exceedingly fine ones. For it is pleasant and helps effectively against the pains which I mentioned a little before. It contains three ounces of the fine stacte, three of opobalsam and three of Attic honey, and three of pure Pontic wax; of krokinon (saffron unguent), the Syrian perfume, four ounces; of the whitest ammoniac and of fine salt, two ounces; and one and one part of white and purified terebinth; and of cinnamon and malabathron add in addition one litra and a third part of a litra. But if by chance malabathron is not available to you, add the same amount of Gangitic nard.

This perfume is among those that are moderately good, [1055] but sufficiently medicinal, as no other is. Or the same amount likewise of Sergetic iris-unguent, or of Cyzicene, and this of amaracine (marjoram unguent). You will use these when the malabathrum is not at hand, as I said; for I think it a moderate myrakopon (perfumed akopon), benefiting those who use it no less. Prepare it thus: having ground up carefully, add the honey, and having ground fine in due measure, and having mixed in the stacte and the opobalsam, again grind carefully the clean terebinth; and having put the wax and the crocine into a double vessel, melt the aforesaid in water, towards evening, in another pot.

And having melted these, pour in the malabathron, and having united everything in due measure, so that it does not boil, lift the double vessel out of the pot; and having cooled the drug carefully and scraped it off, and having added it to the things mentioned before, grind it again in the mortar until [1056] the whole is well united and becomes a single drug. But if you wish to make it more effective for the sinews and for chronic conditions and affections and for tensions of the muscles, mix into the whole weight two ounces of good and still fresh euphorbium, having first ground it together with the salts and the honey and the opobalsamum for a sufficient time. And having thus united all the aforementioned things, store it away in a box or in a glass vessel, using it preferably after baths. But when making a myrakopon (perfumed akopon) for a king and Augustus, prepare this most easily and without fire, containing a measure of opobalsamum of about three ounces, and of the strongest malabathron fifteen ounces, of good cinnamon the same, and of odourless, whitest wax ten drachms.

[1057] Prepare it thus: put a third part of the malabathrum, together with the wax cut up into the smallest pieces, into a thin silver bowl. Having melted it over very hot water, cool and scrape it, and adding it, ground smooth, in the opobalsamum and the cinnamon, grind again, uniting the whole; then finally, pouring the malabathrum into them, unite it by rubbing with the hands, and so store it in a silver vessel or a thick glass one; for in this way you will keep the drug safely. And by adding a third of a pound of Gangitic nard you will make the drug sweeter, and a better unguent for fresh conditions. But if cinnamon is not at hand, by not putting it in you will have it very slightly inferior, yet truly good, and far better than any other myrakopon.

But if you wish to make it more effective [1058] for the conditions I mentioned before, add four drachms of Atlantic euphorbium. For thus it will be pleasant and active, even though it is composed of few ingredients. But I have come to know some who use many fats, and much marrow, and certain aromatics, and juices and unguents and certain oils; and having in turn, of course, made use of these, I recognised that such things belong to men without taste, who have not judged the ingredients and the simple natures of these.

B.translation: For verdigris eats away the [367] ulcerated flesh, being a hot and acrid drug, whereas cerate is mild and non-biting, but instead of new flesh it breeds filth upon the ulcers. How this too is mixed together, and the other things that are compounded in the same way out of opposites, I have already stated in the third book of the therapeutic treatise; but the exercise in particulars will now also be set out, with an example for each affection. [What one who is to compound drugs well must know in addition.] Concerning the power of simple drugs, it has been stated in another treatise that one must know the power of each, not only by kind, as some have written, saying that it either heats or cools or dries or moistens, but in a determinate and articulated manner, namely of which order it is, as we have shown. For some drugs produce each of the effects mentioned altogether faintly, some perceptibly, some strongly, just as others completely.

It is therefore not sufficient to know that this [368] drug heats or cools; one must further determine to what extent it heats and cools. For all the resins heat, and this is common to them, but they possess no small degree of more and less in their heat. Many juices also heat, differing from one another by no small difference in the more and less. For if you were to compare the juice of panax with the Cyrenaic and the Median, the former will seem to you to be nothing in comparison with those. And why need one carry the argument far afield, when we are able to recall the difference from the very things we take every day? Dill, at any rate, and rue and onion, though all of them heat, differ greatly from one another, so that in treatments too we shall apply to a part that has been considerably chilled the drug that heats considerably, and to one that has departed slightly from its natural state the one that heats moderately, just as, indeed, to one that is thoroughly chilled the one that heats most vehemently.

It was therefore reasonable that we established four orders among the heating drugs, distinguishing from those that heat to a slight degree those that do this clearly, those that heat very much, and those that heat intensely together with [369] burning. Within each of the four differences, some drugs are, as it were, at the beginning of the difference, some at its end and close to the one after it, and some in between. Thus among those that ulcerate through heat, as also among those called septic, some display their own power as soon as they are applied to the body, while others need two or three or four hours; some need a whole day, or the following night as well, or even more days and nights in succession. Whoever is going to compound any drug must know these things, in the case of cooling drugs just as in the case of heating ones; and likewise in the case of moistening and drying drugs. Of the materials of drugs, some come from plants, some from minerals, and some from animals. You have learned all of them, distinguished, in the treatise on simple drugs.

For this discourse of mine is addressed chiefly to my companions, who have asked me now to write these things a second time, after those that were lost. And just as it is fitting that you know precisely the powers [370] of all the simple drugs, so that in every place you may easily compose, from what is at hand, the things that are of benefit to bodies in need of treatment, so too [it is fitting that you know] the differences of all the dispositions contrary to nature … treatise (ὑπόμνημα) [the text appears defective here: probably a first treatise, on the differences of diseases, has dropped out]; second, the one on the [difference] of symptoms, and third after these, the one in which I go through the causes that produce diseases. And besides these, three others on the causes in symptoms. You also have my writing on plethos and the one on the difference of fevers; and after these the books of the Therapeutic Method, through which you learned both the dispositions by which a function is damaged, and that the treatment is of these first, just as, in turn, prevention is of the causes that produce them.

Heras, on the other hand, deserves praise for having written down both the indications of the drugs [431] and the modes of their use, which Andromachus omitted altogether in the case of the white plasters, only rarely adding the indication by itself; nor indeed did he write how the drug ought to be boiled.
