But perhaps no one would blame him on this point, since he was writing for those already trained in the medical art, not for laymen. To fail to add the indications, however, or the general powers, is no small error. For what will anyone say in his defence? Perhaps that these things were written for those who know the powers of the simple drugs. And yet none of those needs Andromachus, since he is himself able to compound drugs in like manner. [White plaster of Heras for hydrophobics.] So we come once more to Heras, who after the Attalic plaster writes another white one, in these very words: 'White, for those bitten by a rabid animal. It is also strictly effective for hydrophobics. For, applied to the wound, it at once rescues from the danger.'

To those, however, who are very severely gripped [by the affection], one should also make from it a pill the size of a Pontic nut and give it, and [432] do this for forty days. It does, however, change its colour on the compresses and becomes black. It is effective also for human bites, dog bites, abrasions, and wounds hard to cicatrise; it also removes hypopia (bruises beneath the eye), 1 keration, and conglutinates wounds. It is effective also for phymata and fissures. It is also an emollient pessary. One must, however, undo it every other day and sponge off the blackness that forms on the ulcers, and do this until the blackness no longer appears. The same is also cicatrising and good for everything. Having said this by way of preface, Heras next wrote the proportions of the plaster in the following words: White. ℞ White Pontic wax, 2 pounds; golden litharge, 1 pound; white lead, 1 pound; myrrh, 2 ounces; deer marrow, 2 ounces; uncut frankincense, 1 ounce; old oil, 1 sextarius. These, then, are the proportions of the ingredients composing the plaster. Next he wrote the boiling as follows: Boil the litharge with the oil, and when it appears to become viscid in consistency, [add] the wax, then sprinkle in the white lead and stir.

When it has become unified and no longer soils, take away the [433] live coals and add the marrow. After cooling it, add the myrrh and the frankincense, and use it after softening it. In this respect too, then, Heras deserves praise: he did not leave it to us to boil the plaster however we might wish, but added the directions himself. For the obvious course would have been to boil the white lead together with the litharge right from the beginning, as with the other white plasters. We ourselves are generally accustomed to do this, and indeed he himself wrote so in the case of others. But in the case of this one, at least, he bids that it be thrown in later. He does not add the reason why it is better to do this, yet he shows that no single manner of boiling is equally useful in all cases, but that with some it is possible to employ two or even three, altering not only the colour but also the potency of the drugs. Thus in the case of the one now before us he did not want the white lead to be boiled with the litharge, knowing that in being boiled down it does not preserve its exact whiteness, and that it loses the astringency which it has together with its cooling.

It is quite clear that, in the case of inflamed parts, one must also [499] heal the inflammation, and in the case of parts that have their flesh badly tempered, one must make it well tempered. Since the flesh becomes badly tempered in four simple ways and in four other, compound, ways, the cure will be by means of the opposite qualities. But these matters will be discussed again later; next I shall speak about the strongly cleansing drugs. [On the strongly cleansing drugs.] It has been said earlier that these belong to the same genus as those mentioned before, which, because they cleanse moderately, were applied to hollow, clean, uncomplicated ulcers without biting at all. Those that remove a great deal of filth have an intensified cleansing power, so that some of the green drugs already mentioned differ from the simply flesh-producing ones in one thing alone, the quantity of verdigris. Some differ also by the admixture of other drugs that cleanse vigorously, such as the one called Isis and that of Machairion, which we habitually use, the one called 'oily' on account of the way it is used.

For where our task is to fill a sinus with flesh, we melt it in a large quantity of oil and pour it in through a straight-bored horn joined, in the manner of a clyster, [500] to a pig's bladder; we also use for this the so-called pus-drawers (pyulci). Of these too, those with a wider bore are serviceable for such a purpose. It is evident that we make a foul sinus clean by using the drug less diluted, that is, mixing it with less oil, and a clean one by using it more moistened through the admixture of more plentiful oil. If, then, there should be some suspicion of a slight inflammation still mixed in with the sinus, let the drug by all means be melted in rose oil. But if the sinus is free of inflammation, let it be melted in oil; and if it tolerates the admixture of old oil without being bitten, let the drug be dissolved in that. Suitable for such use is not only this drug but also that of Machairion and the isis, and all the others which my predecessors have written become flesh-producing for hollow ulcers when mixed with cerate.

For all these, without being mixed with cerate, are melted with olive oil and rose oil and injected into the sinuses, because the so-called consistency suited to lint-tents (emmotos) cannot be injected into sinuses. In just this way, too, we take the dry drug made with burnt papyrus [501], mix it with a large quantity of rose oil, and pour it into them. Just as sinuses need the more liquid drugs, since the thicker ones cannot be injected, so those hollow ulcers that are superficial require a thicker drug, because the liquids quickly run off them and the lint-tents are left dry. Reasonably, then, in such cases we mix cerate with the strongly detergent drugs, but in the case of sinuses we mix in a very large quantity of olive oil or rose oil. These drugs that are detergent in this way are certainly also discutient, and for this reason also strongly desiccant, and there arises a certain common class of them which they call polychrest. Beyond this class lies that of the very acrid plasters, such as also those called 'with salts', which one must not apply where we wish to promote the growth of flesh. For, besides their other properties, salts also have this peculiarity: they are astringent rather than detergent.

Of this same kind as cedar oil [569] is also the so-called percolated lye. And of this lye itself, the one that is made from a fine-particled material when it has been burnt surpasses cedar oil in potency. We prepare such lye, then, from the apple tree and the fig, and still more from the wild fig, which they call caprifig (erineos), and from spurges when they are burnt. The best of the spurges is the one called characias. Among the seeds called cereal seeds, bitter vetch is the most fine-particled, without heating perceptibly; darnel (aira) is fine-particled while clearly heating; barley does not heat at all. Of intermediate substance among them are those that are bitter in their qualities: they fall short of the very fine-particled ones, but have nothing thick-particled. Some of them have departed a little from the intermediate ones, some in the direction of heating, others in the direction of cooling. I went through the materials of all these in the treatise on simple drugs, as I did also for the tree-fruits, among which are bitter almonds and pistachios.

Of the material derived from plants I make no mention for the present, for I wish to go back to the beginning and relate when and [570] how I made use of each of the things I devised. For from this, I think, the naturally gifted among the young will be urged on to come to know the material of drugs by becoming eyewitnesses of it, not once or twice, but many times. For the discrimination of perceptible things is made exact by continual observation, and the greatest proof of this is the case of twins who seem to us indistinguishable, but who are not indistinguishable to those familiar with them, so that these do not mistake them (μὴ παραδραμεῖν). Now the material from herbs, shrubs and trees it is best to examine before it is taken out of the earth, through the stages of its fruiting: when the fruiting is about to begin, when it is beginning, when it is advancing, and when it is at its peak. For this continual observation of them will teach you at what time one would do best to take them and to keep them, placing them in dry rooms, so that they are neither baked by the rays of the sun nor moistened by damp from the ceiling or the walls. This would come about if the rooms are neither underground nor at ground level (?), nor under roof-tiles, while having their windows turned toward the south. But the drugs at any rate should not be stored near them.

I urge my companions [571] to imitate me in this respect too, if indeed they wish to perform the works of the art well. For you know how the finest drugs are conveyed to me every year from each of the nations, because the damnable dealers in petty wares corrupt them in every way. But perhaps it is better to blame not these alone, but much more than them the merchants who bring the drugs, and still more than those the very men who are called root-cutters, but who, no less than roots, bring down saps and juices and fruits, flowers and shoots from the mountains into the cities; for these are the first of all to practise villainy upon them. Whoever, then, wishes to have an abundant supply of remedies from every source, let him become experienced in all the material from plants, and all that from animals and minerals, and in those earthy bodies that we bring into medical use without mining, so as to distinguish the genuine and the spurious among them; and after this let him train himself in my treatise in which I wrote on the power of simple drugs.

Such, besides those already mentioned, are maron, amarakon (marjoram), polion, argemone, chamaepitys (ground-pine) and centaury, and all the others that I went through in the teaching on simple drugs. Such too are the roots of all the aristolochias, and of dracontium, wild cucumber, bryony, althaea (marsh-mallow) and iris, and of acorus, meum, asarum, phu and gentian [635] and panax; for you have the material of all such things in the treatises on simple drugs. One must know not only that one should pound the roots and the whole herbs and sift them carefully through fine-meshed sieves, but also that one should grind them again with care, as one does the dry collyria, until they become downy. For what is coarse-particled is of no benefit to the nerve-wounded, who need, as has been said, fine-particled drugs. Let what has been sifted (?) and ground be taken up in something cerate-like, in a measure that keeps the proportion stated earlier for the euphorbium drug. For as much two-year-old euphorbium as went into that drug, so much dittany, meum and acorus must be put into these, together with whatever else is similarly hot to the taste. And as much of the three-year-old as went into those, so much aristolochia, iris, dracontium and gentian must go into these, together with whatever else is bitter in like manner to these. [On the costly preparations of drugs for the nerve-wounded.] It would not be useless to know drugs of this kind too.

For there is sometimes need of them, [636] more rarely, just as there is often need of the cheap ones. For where a certain man possessing no more than five hundred myriads, a lover of drugs and a lover of medicine, thought fit to use none of the cheap ones, much more will some rich man, or even a monarch, wish to have a drug of this kind, one that is at once fragrant and prepared at great cost in money. The rich man I recounted in the first book of On Prognosis from the Pulses I mentioned without his name, just as I do now too; what sort of man he was you will learn from the following two actions of his. He himself was attempting to treat a malignant ulcer of a household slave. When he accomplished nothing, he put the man into my hands, and on seeing him cured he asked for the recipe of the drug. He did not know that there are many differences among malignant ulcers, and many among drugs, but supposed that one drug can cure them all, at any rate even when the person applying it does not use it with art. When he heard what it was composed of, and all the ingredients were cheap, he said: 'Keep this for the beggars, but teach me one of the more costly ones.'

Moreover, when a young slave-boy had a chronic affection in the ears [637], and he himself had done no good with the many drugs he had used without method, he ordered that this boy too be brought to me to be treated. And when he later learned that it had been cured by means of one of the commonplace [drugs], he did not deign to take the prescription of the drug. This same man, then, having seen many of the nerve-wounded, with fingers cut off and putrefied, and some even dying or crippled, and having then learned that none of those treated by me had been in danger, but that all had quickly become healthy, asked to receive from me some drug at once fragrant and costly, with which he would be able to treat the nerve-wounded. I, for my part, had already often given many improvised prescriptions to companions and to physician friends, according to the method written above, so that the rationale of their composition might be confirmed by the outcomes. But a costly one, such as he wanted, I would not have given to poor people, since I thought it better that cures be effected through readily procurable [drugs].

You must also remember the following in compounding, a point neglected by most physicians and by some even [703] got wrong through ignorance. For they trust the petty-ware dealers who profess to supply old oil, not knowing how they produce what they hand over: they take old pig's fat, once they have thoroughly stripped it of its fibres, melt it, and mix it with common oil. Made in this way it looks thick to those who see it and smells foul to those who smell it, like the old oil. The foul smell is indeed similar, but to someone who accurately remembers each of the two the difference is clear. For the peculiar quality of the smell of fat is one thing, and that of old oil another. Moreover, the thickness of the adulterated product itself is not continuous, nor homoeomerous, as is that of the unadulterated oil; rather, it becomes thicker at the bottom of the vessel, while the part on the surface is thinner. That is why those who have counterfeited it stir it up when they hand it to the buyers. But even if the oil is truly natural, without such knavery, it bears this very name 'old', yet its potency is not close: the three-year-old is not near the thirty-year-old, nor the four-year-old the fifty-year-old. For both the oil and the fat acquire a certain biting quality over time, when they have grown old.

But this is very great, and very great too is the alteration in potency. For both oil and fat become most strongly discutient when they have been aged. Having put this to the test, since by some chance I had very old oil and fat, my father having kept them for a long time, I myself in turn, while still quite young, laid up both in abundance, so that I might be able to use them aged after I had used up my father's. And after this too I again stored away both, not infrequently, to be aged. And now I have so great a quantity of them that it would suffice even if I were to live a hundred years. And so the drug under discussion, having always received with me oil and fat forty years old, benefited the most malignant of chronic ulcers beyond expectation. Such ulcers are those in which the affected part itself has come into so great a cachexia that, even if the blood arriving at it for the sake of nourishment is well concocted, it alters and corrupts it; and if what flows in is cacochymous to such a degree that, even if the part had suffered nothing at all, it would be eaten through by that alone.

It has been said in what precedes that the austere quality is necessary for malignant ulcers, and especially [771] when they are fluxional. With all these, then, that I have mentioned were mixed litharge, resin and frankincense, so that the drug might become plaster-like. But litharge belongs to the intermediate material, while frankincense is concoctive and pus-producing, if we look to the well-tempered nature. For it was shown that in moister bodies it is flesh-producing. It was also shown that none of the concoctive drugs, which indeed also possess the power called suppurative, is strongly discutient, just as none is acrid either. For such drugs heat moderately, and moreover soften rather than dry. It was therefore well that some frankincense too was mixed in the composition of the plaster under discussion, so that it might also have something soothing and mild. Clearly the oil too is of the same power. In the first instance it was mixed in for the sake of boiling the plaster, but it brings with it two powers in itself: the soothing power, and the power that blunts strong drugs, whether these are of acrid or of austere power.

Ampelitis earth dries and disperses [772] without having anything clearly pungent. For this reason it is suitable for malignant ulcers, even if you were to grind it by itself and sprinkle it on. Galbanum too was mixed into the present composition because it is concoctive and emollient, and soothing and anodyne. Frankincense also has the same powers, but weaker than in galbanum, since galbanum is the stronger in both respects. Terebinth resin too, together with its detergent and dispersive property, has something concoctive of such conditions. Bitumen, we know, is of a drying power together with a heat that is not very violent. To all these, then, the man who composed the plaster added a drug of drawing power, propolis, since he wanted the plaster to be a polychrest. Everything that is polychrest must have the most varied powers, so as to treat a larger number of conditions. In the same way he also added no small amount of honey, knowing that it dries and disperses and is most appropriate to putrefying parts.

For it, in turn, is also one of the things that do not putrefy, and it preserves the things mixed with it as such, [773] except those that are extremely prone to putrefaction, which are moist and hot. And indeed the composer of the drug put in more honey than of the other ingredients. For apart from the three that need to be boiled, asphalt, litharge and ampelitis earth, it is more than the others; and to these very ingredients, the asphalt, the litharge and the ampelitis, he added as much oil as will be suitable for the boiling, making allowance also for the other dry ingredients that are put into the drug. Moreover, he directed that, once everything has been thoroughly boiled, the myrrh and the aloes be added on top, both of them drying without biting, but differing in that the aloes is astringent, whereas the myrrh is finer-particled and more drying. I do not know what Heras had in mind in writing this panacea with smaller proportions, when it has been written by others with larger ones. For some wrote it as having all its ingredients doubled, and others quadrupled.

Of galbanum, at any rate, Heras wrote six drachms and one and a half obols, whereas others wrote ten drachms and a half, just as, again, [774] others wrote twenty-five, increasing the rest too in proportion, so that nowhere in the proportions is an obol or a half-obol mentioned. You must therefore pay attention, when you compare the panaceas written down by the others with this one, to whether they have all the ingredients double or quadruple, and, if all have been increased in proportion, not consider those to be different from this one. [The isis, called by some 'of Epigonus'.] A polychrest drug is the one they call isis, praised by everyone. I shall now set out what Heras wrote about it, which runs word for word as follows: 'The drug called by some "of Epigonus", by others isis, effective against every wound and against wounds on the head with cuttings-through of the bones. It heals without breakdown, and is effective also against punctures, splinters, human bites and dog bites, and it draws out the venoms of the viper, of scorpions, of sea-dragons and of the sting-ray, and it is effective against fractures of the limbs accompanied by a wound.'

[362] GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK 1. A treatise on this subject had already been written by me before as well. The first two books of it were published, but they were left behind, together with the rest, in the storehouse on the Sacred Way, at the time when the whole precinct of Peace was burned, and with it the great libraries on the Palatine.

For at that time the books of many others perished, and also those of mine that were lying in that storehouse, and none of my friends in Rome [363] acknowledged having copies of the first two. Since, then, my companions were pressing me to write the same treatise again, it seemed necessary to me to make clear the facts about the books previously published, so that no one who had come across them earlier might ever seek the reason why I have treated the same subjects twice. In those books, then, from the beginning of the first book, I directed my argument against those who sophistically do away, so far as they can, with the claim of compound drugs, and who also abusively attack some of the simple ones as well, at the same time mocking those who have written about them, to the effect that some benefit the liver, others the spleen, others the kidneys or bladder or head or lung. For, they say, does someone stand over them and give them orders, as in the tragedy: 'You, go to the streams of Inachus; and you, march about Cadmean Thebes'?

so here: 'You, go to the gates at the liver; you, to the bladder, or else to the two kidneys'? Or is what has been swallowed into the stomach distributed to the liver, and from there carried to every part [364] of the body? But this very jibe shows that those who say these things are so inexperienced in the power of drugs as not to know that the lung alone, of all the parts in the body, is ulcerated by the sea hare, and again the bladder alone by cantharides; that by others the stones in the kidneys are broken up, and by others expectorations from the lung and chest are made easy, just as by others other effects are brought about specifically in some one part. This argument I worked out in many forms in the first of the books I had written earlier, as I said, just as in the second I worked out another, since some think that in compounding the mutually opposed powers of the simple drugs are entirely destroyed. For if, they say, you mix the most boiling-hot water with the coldest, neither of the things mixed will remain as it was before, but some one third thing will come into being, different from both.

But here too they were shown to be talking idle nonsense, because they do not know that some of the things applied to the body act according to their innate powers, and some according to their acquired [365] qualities. For who does not know that hemlock or poppy juice cools? And yet, if you heat them strongly and apply them to the body of an animal, you will produce an ulcer much as a cautery does. So too, conversely, if you grind mustard in cold air, with very cold water in the winter season, and apply it suddenly to a rare and weak body, the body will shiver no less than if snow or ice had touched it. But if it stays in contact with the body of an animal for a longer time, it will first produce a sensation of slight heat, then of more, and then of so much that the body seems to be burned by fire. Conversely, hemlock and poppy juice applied hot, if they stay in contact with the body for a longer time, will produce so great a cooling that the bodies become insensible, even if they were previously most sensitive.

Since, then, all such matters have been determined by us in the commentaries On the Power of Simple Drugs, which are eleven in number, I shall now turn to the useful instruction itself. Whoever has trained himself in it, even if he does not carry with him at all the written formulas of the many-ingredient preparations, will not be at a loss for the remedies suitable to each [366] affection, provided that he, as I said, is experienced in the material of simple drugs. As a by-product, this account also exposes the contentiousness of the Empirical physicians, who trace back nearly all compound drugs, except for a very few, to dreams, chance and accidental encounter (periptōsis). These few they say they discovered by the reasoning common to all human beings, which they themselves call epilogismos. For instance, they say, when we mix together drugs that have shown the same action through experience, but one acted better or worse on one body and another on another, it seemed reasonable to us (so say some of the Empiricists, though certainly not all) to combine several such drugs, so that at least one of them might be found appropriate to the nature of the body under treatment. This, they say, is what happened in the case of this most novel drug called the 'cephalic', in which were mixed all the drugs known even singly to make flesh grow in ulcers. But by what reasoning verdigris mixed with simple cerate produces a flesh-producing drug, when neither of the ingredients mixed produces flesh, this they do not go on to say.

You have learned, too, that the first goal of treatment is found from the diseased dispositions, and when the nature of the affected part co-indicates along with these. Together with the krasis of the air that surrounds us, many of the best physicians also take into consideration the state [of the weather], the age, the season and the region, as well as pursuits and habits, [371] about which some things will be said now too, wherever there is need of them. All these things, then, you must have thus ready at hand in memory, if you wish to be well supplied in every place with drugs both simple and compound. Further, in addition to these, you must bear in mind that sometimes a single natural, simple drug is sufficient to cure the disposition contrary to nature, while sometimes there is need of a compound one; and why indeed we do this must be stated next. [What the use of compound drugs is.] If it were possible to cure all the dispositions contrary to nature by means of simple drugs alone, we should never have needed a compound drug; but as it is, this is not so. For often, when we wish the body to be heated through to such and such a degree, we have no simple drug of that kind. For the drug that treats must be proportionate to the disposition being treated. If, then, the disposition is cold, standing four numbers away from the natural state, it is evident to everyone that the drug which is to treat it must be hotter than the moderate by an equal quantity.

[372] But since sometimes no such simple is at hand, if we have a supply of two, of which the one is hotter by five degrees and the other by three, by mixing them we shall produce the mean, exceeding the moderate by four degrees. Some of the simples, moreover, cannot even be brought into use without a further admixture, as when we wish to apply a plaster drug to someone. For none of the simples is suitable for such a use: neither bitumen nor wax nor resin, just as neither pitch, propolis and ladanum, and still more verdigris and white lead or litharge or molybdaena or any other of the metallic drugs. Likewise herbs alone cannot make a plaster drug either. Reasonably, therefore, those who first compounded plaster drugs devised, through the admixture of oil, to boil the metallic substances and to melt the meltable ones, and to throw in with them also dry herbs, pounded and sifted.

In other conditions, again, there is need of a single drug only, one of the natural ones, but we mix something in with it, sometimes [373] intending to blunt the vehemence of its power, sometimes to mitigate its unpleasantness, as Hippocrates said in On Regimen in Acute Diseases in the following passage: 'If the pain is below the diaphragm and gives no sign towards the collarbone, one must soften the belly either with black hellebore or with peplion; with the black, mixing in daukos or seseli or cumin or anise or some other of the fragrant things, and with the peplion, juice of silphium.' In this passage Hippocrates clearly indicated that there is need of the purging drug, but that only its unpleasantness, in the drinking and in the belly, requires a seasoning. For indeed many of the drugs that are drunk are so unpleasant to those who take them that the stomach is upset and they are vomited at once; and some, even if they are able to remain in the belly for a little while, are at any rate vomited afterwards, having provoked noxious belchings.

Just as such drugs as Hippocrates mentioned are, as it were, seasonings of the purgatives, so for the drugs called anodyne there are other things that mitigate their violence, as when we give poppy juice [374] or henbane seed or the bark of mandrake root; so this too is a use for the compounding of drugs. The greatest use, however, is in the case of affections that require opposite powers at the same time, for instance repellent and discutient, or detergent and smoothing, or at once thickening and thinning the humours; and accordingly the most versatile and finest drugs contain the opposite powers within themselves, as we shall show. But this too is a use for the compounding of drugs, when we wish to have a single drug suitable against many venomous beasts or deadly poisons; it is this use that produced the antidote called theriac, and besides it the Mithridatic and many others. There are also certain other uses, smaller than those mentioned, which nevertheless often compel us to resort to the compounding of drugs; all of these you will learn in this treatise. For now I shall at once begin on the matters before us, first mentioning a plaster drug of very wide use compounded by me.

[375] [On the plaster drug made with chalcitis.] By what reasoning did I compound the plaster made with chalcitis, which I call the palm plaster (phoinikinē), an agglutinative and cicatrizing remedy for wounds (helkē), and curative of inflammations whenever, once melted, it has the consistency of a liquid cerate? You, leaving the Empiricists to confess their own ignorance, and standing apart also from the followers of Thessalus, who are ignorant of the finest of the drugs discovered by physicians, which are composed of contrary powers, must train your reasoning so that you are able to compound drugs using the same methods as I do. Then you yourselves may be persuaded by the work itself that everything discovered by our predecessors was also compounded by reasoning, the accidental encounter (periptōsis) of the Empiricists being a trifling thing. I must now, then, set out the reasoning behind the composition of the drug before us. Old olive oil and fat have a discutient power, while chalcitis and the juice of the palm have a repellent and astringent power.

From these, then, I compounded a drug which you know very many people are already [376] using, because it has been judged better than all others of the same kind, having been tested by the results themselves. For reason discovers the composition, but experience judges the excellence of what has been discovered, so that even those inexperienced in logical methods come to trust what has been compounded according to the art. To the drugs just mentioned I added litharge, which cannot contribute anything of great consequence either to those that check what flows in or to those that disperse what is already fixed in the inflamed parts; for it is of a drying faculty, though not a strong one. Rather, I mixed it in as a drug suited to the composition of a plaster, for it is boiled together with the aforementioned until it reaches a non-soiling consistency. The fat should be unsalted and as old as possible, and the oil likewise old. For you have learned, I think, that oil and swine's fat are of a faculty close to one another, the fat being slightly more emollient and hotter in faculty.

You have also learned that as they grow old they become finer in their parts and more discutient, and that for this reason the new ones are more soothing for painful inflammations [377], while for those that are not of this kind the old ones are more beneficial. And the more chronic and hard to resolve the inflammation is, the more useful the old ones are, and they alone are sufficient to treat it, provided that nothing is still flowing into the affected part. But if something does flow in, the power of the drug too must be mixed, such as is the power of the one compounded by me. It was for this reason, then, that I mixed the chalcitis and the palm with the discutient ingredients, knowing that altogether few inflammations become chronic in which nothing flows in; for it is on account of the humours flowing into them that they are wont to become chronic. When inflammations are beginning and increasing, the power of astringent and cooling drugs ought to predominate; and for this reason this plaster drug, melted down to the consistency of a liquid cerate, becomes sufficiently polychrest, sometimes taking in addition wine or vinegar or water, and at other times being melted with omotribes oil, or with one of those oils that have astringency, such as the Spanish and the Istrian, or with one of the sweet oils without astringency, or with old oil.

And [378] I have often also melted the drug down with myrtle oil and quince oil, in cases where there is need of a stronger astringency. This, then, is the composition of the drug, made up in the following proportion. Of old fat, which the sellers call axungia (axoungion), let there be 2 litrai; of old oil, 3 litrai; of litharge, 3 litrai; and of chalcitis, 4 ounces. They must be boiled in the following manner. Take out the membranes of the fat and crush the rest, so that it becomes easily melted. After this, melt it over a fire. Then take a strainer and strain it, so that it becomes clean, with nothing of membrane in it, and weighing the aforesaid two litrai. Then you will mix the 4 ounces of chalcitis, ground smooth, together with the three litrai of oil, into the fat, adding also the 3 litrai of litharge. When you have united everything in a mortar, put it into the cooking-pot (kakkabē), stirring with a stick of palm wood. One of the large branches will suffice you, so that you use the thick part of the wood for stirring, serving the purpose of the so-called spatha. For that is the name they give to the implement with which they stir the things being prepared, and we too, holding to what is clear, shall call it the same as they do.

[379] The part continuous with the thick part of the branch you should clean all round, rub off the thin outgrowths on either side, and cut it up, having first scraped off the bark, so that the pieces, when thrown in, may impart to the drug the juice they contain. The spatula, then, should be used right from the beginning, but the thin pieces of the palm should be thrown in when the drug comes to a consistency like that of a cerate. For if you throw them in from the beginning, the juice of what has been thrown in, which we want to remain, will be used up in the boiling. And as for the spatula itself, with which you stir the drug from the beginning, when the part being soaked in the pot becomes dry, so as no longer to have its own juice, cut that part off, throw it away, and use the rest. And again likewise, if the part being soaked in the drug happens to have dried, cut it off again. It is evident that the palm branch must not have been cut from the tree many days beforehand, for it dries out in time and becomes juiceless. So if it is winter, let it be removed on the day before; but in summer the branch must be removed from the tree on that very day on which you boil the drug.

When the drug, boiled [380] in this way, has become non-staining, you will use it by itself as a plaster on ulcers that are hard to cicatrise and on bloody ones; dissolved in oil, on inflamed parts, in podagra, in arthritis, in buboes, in phymata, in burns, in chilblains, in fractures, in contusions, and in all the so-called fluxional conditions. Indeed, many of those who cut hernias apply it immediately after the operation, carrying on the treatment with embrocations and cataplasms. If, however, you add six ounces of chalcitis, which is half a litra, the drug will be more agglutinative of large wounds and more cicatrising of ulcers that are hard to cicatrise. In this respect, however, there are other drugs of the same power too. But when it has been melted with oil, one should rely on it more than on all the others in fluxional conditions. At any rate, in Rome, where very many such cases occur, nothing has been so highly esteemed.

It is suitable, as I said, both for podagra and for arthritis at every stage [381] in which there are no violent pains requiring soothing affusions and poultices. So while such conditions (διαθέσεως, apparently for διαθέσεων) are beginning and still increasing, once you have melted the drug, let it cool. Then scrape it with a spatula-probe, put the scrapings into a mortar, pour in wine, and work it with the hands at the mortar so that it takes up the wine. Let this wine be one of the more austere kinds, of middling age, not thick in consistency but as translucent as possible. For such a wine, being finer in its parts, penetrates into the depth of bodies. Pour it onto the melted drug only so far, working it with the hands, as it is taken up and mixed in, and the liquid does not float alongside, unmixed with the drug that is being worked and softened. One can also mix in the wine without first cooling and scraping, by pouring it into the melted drug while it is still warm. At the beginnings of inflammations, then, the repellent faculty ought to predominate. In the stages of increase one should take away something of it and add something of the discutient faculty.

When the swelling of the inflammation has reached its proper peak [382], the powers, both the repellent and the discutient, must be similar to one another, unless some violent pain requires a soothing drug. But when the inflammation is declining, the discutient power should predominate, so that at that time none of the wine at all is mixed in. Moreover, in the melting itself as well, where we want the astringent quality to predominate sufficiently, one should put in Spanish oil or Istrian oil or the oil called omphacine and omotribes. Where we want it to have both powers similar, melt it with sweet oil that is neither fresh nor old. When we wish to make it discutient, old oil or castor oil is suitable. Let the proportion of the plaster drug in the melting be as follows. Let the oil be a little more than the drug, and evidently more so in summer, so that, the drug being ten ounces, one would add one pound (litra) of oil, and that would be sufficient.

It is quite clear that it becomes more active when it contains more of the drug, but more soothing [383] and more anodyne the more liquid it becomes when melted with rose-oil. It takes on the consistency of a cerate for anointing when one litra of the drug is melted in half a litra of oil. Such a preparation is useful in the declines of inflammations. And for the inflammatory swellings that arise spontaneously in the seat and along the straight intestine, nothing benefits so much. On those occasions, however, it must have been melted with a larger quantity of oil, so that it can be injected through a straight-bored horn with a pig's bladder tied to it, as we are accustomed to use in such cases. In these cases I have also often melted it with rose-oil, a pot [kakkabē] being placed beneath the vessel in which it is melted, the pot containing hot water and set over glowing coals or over a smokeless flame. Melted, however, according to the proportion stated above, so as to have the consistency of a liquid cerate, it benefits both ulcers on the genitals and those at the seat. And not least all the other ulcers as well, even including ulcerated chilblains and burns. For it quickly renders all of them free of inflammation and clean, and fills them in with firm flesh, especially when it contains more chalcitis.

It is quite clear [384] that wine too must be mixed into the drug that is to do this. If it also takes up vinegar, it is excellent for burns, applied both immediately and afterwards at every stage, whether the burn already has blisters or not. It is plain that even if someone is burnt by boiling water, this affection too is called a burn (pyrikauton). And if one applies the drug before inflammation has set in, nothing so prevents the generation of inflammation; so that, as I said, some of those who operate on hernias use it straight away, without even first moistening the wound. For contusions too, and fractures, and parts that have been struck in any way whatever, it is most suitable when applied in liquid form. And when enclosed with bandages in the manner of a fracture bandaging, it is wonderfully beneficial for all oedemas and emphysemata. But if the body is cacochymic, or else very sensitive, one must, when applying it at the beginning to the contused and struck parts, mix fresh henbane into it.

If you lack fresh [henbane], on account of the season of the year [385] or the locality, you will have no less [benefit] by adding instead that which has been stored through the summer, such as is also brought to us to Rome from Crete every year. And still more than this, by mixing in the juice of mandrake you will make the drug anodyne. You know that this too is brought from Crete, of the finest quality, in earthenware cups. It suffices to mix one ounce of the juice with a litra of the oil of the plaster being melted. Sometimes, too, you may put in more, and sometimes less, according to the requirement of the condition. In such bodies it also helps that the drug be melted with rose oil. Parts of the body that have been bruised by a fall, or struck with wood or stone, even if some ecchymosis occurs, should have the melted drug applied immediately at the beginning, as has been said, with wine mixed in. On the third day, or at any rate the fourth, if the part is free of inflammation, one should remove the wine and melt the plaster in old oil. For if the ecchymoses are astringed further, they become hard to disperse.

This drug I also use for erysipelases, and especially [386] for phlegmonous ones, and still much more for erysipelatous inflammations. At the beginning, then, I apply it melted in rose oil prepared from omotribes oil (oil of unripe olives) without salt; for such an oil is the finest for erysipelases. With it, once melted in this way, let there be mixed in the mortar the juice of strychnos (nightshade), being kneaded in and moistened precisely, wholly through the whole; or, if this is not at hand, that of psyllion (fleawort). When it is summer, also the juice of the unripe grape together with that of purslane or of aeizoon (houseleek). For the juice of the unripe grape on its own is more astringent than it should be, and so great an astringency harms erysipelases, since by condensing the skin it shuts in their heat. Purslane juice, on the other hand, cannot even be pressed out on its own because of its viscosity. Best, therefore, is to press out the juice of the unripe grape and pour it onto purslane that has been pounded in a pounding-mortar, and so pound it again; then, when the mixture of both has been precisely united, press out the juice. In the same way you will also press out the juice of the aeizoon; for neither from this is it possible to press out an abundant quantity on its own, just as it is not from kotyledon (navelwort) either.

And if you also press out fresh juice from the apples of the mandrake [387] when they are ripe, you will make the drug more suitable. If it is not the season, one should at any rate mix in some of the juice that is brought from Crete or from some other such place. I am also accustomed to mix in juice of henbane, and sometimes poppy juice (mēkōneion) as well; for this is the name given to the sap of the poppy. It is better also to add some glaucium together with this. Much weaker than these, but easy to procure, is the juice of thridakinē, both of the wild and of the cultivated kind, which all the Greeks of today call not thridakinē but thridax, naming only the wild kind thridakinē. Weaker than these for cooling are the juices of seris, of knotgrass, of trefoil and of mouse-ear; still, these too do cool. And more than these does the lentil that grows on stagnant pools. If none of these is to hand, mix in vinegar and water. Let all such drugs have their acquired qualities cold, the vessels being set in very cold water or in snow.

And let the drug made with the palm plaster (phoinikinē) itself likewise be thoroughly chilled when it is applied [388] to cases of erysipelas, until their intensely fiery character ceases. It is quite clear that the remedies which benefit erysipelatous conditions through an acquired cold quality must be changed continually, and especially when the erysipelas is pure, without any admixture of inflammation (phlegmonē). When, however, the intensely fiery character has ceased, or when from the beginning there was no pure erysipelas but either an erysipelatous inflammation or an inflammatory (phlegmonous) erysipelas, we no longer need the acquired cooling. Rather, we also abstain from the strongly cooling juices, and mix the moderately cold ones into the melted drug. After these let us then mix in juice of linseed and of chamomile as well. After that we shall use the melted drug by itself alone, mixing nothing else into it.

If ever the erysipelas has already become livid through the power of the cooling agents, one ought no longer even to call such a thing erysipelas. At that point it is fitting to abstain not only from the admixture of wine but also from rose-oil and the astringent oils, for the palm plaster (phoinikinē) alone, melted in old oil, is sufficient to disperse what has become livid [389]; and at that point the affected parts are douched with hot water and scarified. And if you should ever decide to do this, you must immediately apply the liquid drug of the melted phoinikinē containing wine, and after one day remove the wine. But if we take over an erysipelas that has already been chilled further by physicians who cool immoderately, so that it is already even turning black, we shall make greater use of the douching and of the scarification. Apart from these measures, we shall also mix some unslaked lime into the liquid drug; and if those affected are soft-fleshed, we shall mix it in washed. At that point the juice of coriander is also good when mixed into the drug. This juice is indeed of great benefit also together with rose-oil cerate. For these conditions and conditions of this kind, many other drugs too will be described in the following account, some having a power similar to that of the phoinikinē, others even more active.

For fluxional conditions this is the best drug of all, and it has often accomplished something greater than was hoped for. [390] Thus, on one occasion, when a thigh had suppurated near the groin while the inflammation throughout the whole of it was unconcocted, the leg was positioned by us so that the ichors would flow out towards the groin. Through the ulcer that had formed, since this went on for a fairly long time, the flux that had descended into the thigh was evacuated; but a fistulous condition arose under the skin throughout the whole thigh, so that I wished to incise it near the kneecap, so that on both sides there would be an outflow for the ichors, and the liquid drugs injected would have free passage to pass through further. But when the thigh was unbandaged on the following day, on which I had decided to cut it, everything was found to have fallen together and to be dry and without moisture. It was plain, then, that it was reasonable to use the drug both on that day and likewise on the next, and on the days following, since on each of them the part became of better colour and, as a whole, healthier.

So, the youth having been treated in this way, afterwards I treated with the drug many fluxional conditions which had a single opening, [391] but whose interior was unagglutinated and fistulous. One must not give up using it, even if it appears to give no perceptible benefit for many days. For later, at some point, within a single day it displays a very great benefit all at once. So use it with confidence throughout in fluxional conditions: when the sufferer is a soft-fleshed person, or some child or woman, putting in 4 ounces of the chalcitis in accordance with the proportion stated before. But when the affected body is strong and hard, add proportionately either one ounce or two, so that there are 5 or 6 ounces of the chalcitis, three litrae of each, both of the old oil and of the litharge, and two of the old fat, which, as I said, the sellers call axungia. In fluxional conditions let it be thinned with sweet oil, neither fresh nor old, and let it take in addition the austere wine, being of middle age.

This drug exposed the nonsense of Thessalus: it displays a most efficacious benefit, yet it is compounded of ingredients opposite in their powers, and if you take away [392] one of the two, it will accomplish none of the things described. For from the astringent ingredients alone, without the relaxing ones, it will achieve nothing excellent in fluxional conditions, or generally in inflammations that are beginning and increasing. For it will not have the soothing quality. Nor, from the relaxing ingredients alone, will it have the discutient quality, which arises without astringency; to these relaxing ingredients belongs the power of softening what has become hardened. It would be precisely relaxant and moderately emollient if it did not contain the oil and the fat very old. At any rate, the drug that Mnasaeus compounded contains the oil, the litharge and the fat in equal amounts to one another, and it is most contrary to inflammations that are beginning and increasing. Clearly this drug of ours also contains the same ingredients as that of Mnasaeus: the litharge, the fat and the oil. But what if it takes up none of the astringent ingredients?

it enervates the parts and dissolves their tone, and for this reason they also become fluxional. For you have learned that it is not always through much heat, as some suppose, that the parts of the body suffer flux; rather, this happens to them [393] rarely. It is the weakness of the parts that produces fluxional conditions, and this weakness is for the most part brought about by a cold dyscrasia. If, then, one moistens and heats them with relaxing drugs, they become completely slack and feeble. Conversely, if one strongly astringes the swellings in fluxional conditions, one will seem at the beginning to accomplish something, but will render the residue itself hard to resolve and scirrhous. For the most part, moreover, such conditions do not even tolerate the application of strongly astringent agents, being pained and drawn tight by them. And every pain exacerbates inflamed parts and becomes a cause of fluxes, even if the sufferer does not have a fluxional dyscrasia.

But it is no wonder that Thessalus, being inexperienced in the works of the medical art and unable to discover the conditions by reason, is ignorant of everything concerning the cures of inflammations. You, however, who have often observed the most evident benefit, in many conditions, both of this phoinikinē and of other drugs compounded from opposite powers, must yourselves also attempt, whenever at some time you lack [394] those already compounded, to compound drugs according to the same method from what is readily available in that place. When an inflammation is expected to occur, or has already begun, they should have more of the astringency; in the stages of increase themselves, less; and in the peaks and declines they should have more of the relaxing and discutient power. Always, however, let both be mixed, the repellent and the discutient, except if at some time, when the inflowing matters have already completely ceased and the body is empty, one may proceed without danger to the discutient powers, just as in the first onsets one may proceed to the repellent ones. [On plasters prepared with litharge.] Since, in the composition of my phoinikinē plaster, I said that there is a discutient power in the old fat and the oil, and a contractive and repellent one in the chalcitis and the palm, and since these cannot make a plaster drug without the litharge, it therefore seemed good to me to discuss next the use of litharge.

For as regards the power of the phoenicine plaster [395] one must consider that it neither counteracts anything nor contributes anything; it has only the status of a material suitable for the making of a plaster drug. It therefore seemed reasonable to me to go through the account of such drugs using litharge as an example. There are not a few substances that contribute either no power at all or a very small one to the preparation, but furnish the service of material for the production of a plaster or cerate-like drug. For litharge does not perceptibly warm, just as it does not cool or moisten either. It has a slight drying power at the first remove from the exact mean, that is, from the mean between moistening and drying. Nor indeed is it of an emplastic power, just as it is not of a deobstruent one. Likewise it is not detergent, just as it is not perceptibly soiling either. It has, however, departed somewhat gently from the mean toward the thicker-particled. But in more prolonged boiling it lays aside even this, as it melts and is altered through the power of the fire. Alone by itself and raw, it benefits chafings of the thighs from walking journeys, from which it is also clear that it dries slightly.

That [396] it has neither an acrid nor a sweet quality, nor a sour, bitter, austere, acerbic, or in general astringent one, the taste is a sufficient witness, as are also ulcers, which are neither bitten by it, nor heated, nor cooled, nor cleansed, nor filled with flesh, nor, when they have produced excess flesh, cleaned down. It is therefore open to us to use litharge for many purposes, sometimes carrying out its boiling with oil and water until it reaches a plaster-like consistency, at other times in oil and vinegar, and sometimes in oil and wine. In whichever of these it is boiled, the drug turns out better when it has been boiled for a longer time. This will be achieved through the quantity of the liquids mixed in. For litharge too belongs among the meltable drugs, becoming wholly fluid, just as resin and wax do, but not immediately upon touching the fire; hence this escapes the notice of many, and they think that it does not become fluid at all.

When boiled with oxelaeum (vinegar and oil), then, it melts more quickly, just as it does also with verdigris, since verdigris itself is evidently of a nature to liquefy, as are chalcitis [397] and misy. Of these, chalcitis undergoes this most quickly and litharge most slowly; verdigris and misy lie between them. Sory also liquefies, but over a longer time, for it is more earthy and more stony than chalcitis and misy. But these things will be discussed again later. Litharge you will melt more quickly if you boil it with oxelaeum, and more slowly with hydrelaeum (water and oil); yet it liquefies in this way too, if each of the two liquids is double its amount. I myself have often mixed in even more than double, as will be said a little later. It is better to mix the three together in a mortar right from the beginning: the litharge, the water and the oil. If you are concerned that the drug should turn out white, put in oil that is purer and more translucent, and water that is likewise pure and white, and let it be boiled in an open-air place exposed to the sun. For murky air blackens the drug, whereas clear air contributes greatly to its whiteness, as does also the water sprinkled onto it in such air.

Guard also against carrying out the boiling over wood, or over coals that are only beginning to burn through, [398] for the smoke readily blackens it. Having therefore burnt the coals through beforehand, when they are thoroughly glowing, then begin to boil. And if these should not hold out long enough to complete the boiling, prepare coals in the same way on another hearth and set them in place under that pot. As regards the drug's becoming white, then, what must be watched for has been sufficiently stated. It becomes more adhesive to the degree that it has more liquid, as has been said. So that if you put in one litra of each of the three, it will be hard to detach. And moreover the litharge also remains unmelted, and this is itself the chief cause of its readily falling off, just as also of its staying on for longer, if the litharge on being boiled has been dissolved and altered. It will be whiter and will boil more quickly if two litrae of water are put in to three of each, of litharge and of oil. And I customarily use this on small wounds. The power of the drug boiled with water is evident to us if we remember what was said in the treatise on simple drugs.

[399] [On the plaster prepared with litharge and hydrelaeum (water and oil).] Water always moistens and cools by its own proper substance; but when it has taken on an acquired heat, it heats for as long as it retains that heat, and when it has become cold, it cools. Oil, however, if it is fresh, does not work against the drug, for it remains moist and moderately cold, which is the kind of thing that soft-fleshed bodies and cacochymic bodies most need. Women, then, and children, and those among adults who have a soft habit of body (these are also white in colour), need drugs of this kind. Boiled, as has been said, with a larger quantity of oil and water, it becomes so hard to dislodge that it does not run off even when the patients bathe. Moreover, it is also beneficial for ulcers that are cicatrizing that the drug remain on for several days in succession, for in this way they cicatrize both better and more quickly.

It is obvious that such a drug suits scratches and abrasions and, to put it briefly, small ulcers; in these cases the cerate called 'moist' and certain other similar ones are more useful [400] than drugs having a strong power, of the kind we apply to large wounds. Concerning the general power of all of these I have written in the third book of the Therapeutic Method, in which I went through the generic and common accounts, which they call universal, for each differentia of ulcer, showing of what kind the powers of the drugs that are to heal them ought to be; here, however, I go through the particular materials, defining the proportions of the ingredients that are mixed, and showing the ways in which, when prepared, they will turn out best. Litharge, then, prepared with hydrelaeum (water and oil), as has been said, makes the plaster at once most pleasant to the touch and hard to fall off, and moreover white to look at, having a moderate cooling power. Employing this power, it both prevents anything from flowing into the ulcerated parts and drives back again toward the surrounding places what has already flowed in. The effect is thus like what happens when we make a sponge soaked through with cold water and apply it to some part of the body.

For the sponge makes the whole place shrivelled and contracted, not [401] only repelling what flows in, but also squeezing out what is contained in it towards the neighbouring parts. And the plaster just described in the account might be said to dry not by primary power but incidentally. For properly and primarily, those things that disperse, and those that change the temperaments towards the drier, are called drying; but incidentally also those that, through cooling, check what flows in and squeeze out what is contained. In general, nothing that moistens, whether primarily or incidentally, is beneficial for ulcers, as has been shown in the third book of the Therapeutic Method. [On the plaster prepared with litharge and oxelaeum.] Concerning the litharge prepared with hydrelaeum, then, this too is sufficient. It is now time to pass on to the one compounded with oxelaeum (vinegar and oil). The drug, then, becomes moderately drying if the oil and the vinegar are each double the litharge. And if the oil is also old, it dries still more.

[402] But if more than double of each of them is put in, it makes the drug stronger, so that it even heals fistulae, those that do not yet have a hard callus. One part of litharge is put in, and two and a half of each of the other two. And indeed I have sometimes mixed in triple of each and boiled the drug through a whole day. It became black, but glistening like good bitumen. This has a most drying power, and it treats ulcers that are hard to heal and fistulae of the kind I described, and it is agglutinative of bloody wounds. In a word, it is drying without biting. For this reason, then, it also treats all the other ulcers, both the larger and the smaller, up to cicatrisation. It is worth going through some other of its effects as well, which one would perhaps not even expect, considering how contemptible its materials are. For when someone had reached a crisis in a fever by way of a parotis that suppurated, a small fistula was left behind, which was shown to me in the country six months after its beginning.

For the patient was a boy, the son of a farmer, about fifteen years of age. Having given him as much of this plaster [403] as I had with me, to be applied, I myself returned to the city and, being taken up with a great many medical engagements, forgot about the one who had received the drug. But after two months he came back healthy, although I had not at all expected this to happen. For when we let a pig's bristle down through the little fistula, it appeared to go in as far as the articulation. By chance, a few days later, another little boy was shown to me, of the same age as the previous one and having a similar condition; I applied the plaster, and it happened that this one too was completely healed. After this I cured with this drug not a few from the same condition, children, women and young men alike. If, then, you too wish to use it for such cases, put in the oldest oil and the sharpest vinegar, made, that is, from wine alone, not as some prepare it, mixing in water. Let the vinegar be as pure and transparent as possible.

For thus it would be finer-particled and better for [404] the purposes we need it for. With this drug I have also often cured hardened muscles. [On the plaster prepared with litharge and oinelaion (wine-and-oil).] It remains for me, then, to treat of the litharge prepared with oinelaion (wine-and-oil). In the proportions it holds the same as those already described, and its excesses of potency correspond to the quantity of the liquids. For I have prepared it by putting in the three in equal amounts. I have also made it with each of the liquids double the litharge, and with half as much again added on top of the double, and sometimes even triple. I once prepared it also in this way: in the summer season, in hot sun, the litharge was ground each day with Falernian wine, and this was done for 15 days, I pouring on more wine whenever the previous wine had been dissipated. After the said days the drug, when boiled, became sufficiently drying. I also used it against fluxional conditions in the same way as the palm plaster (phoinikinē), dissolving it in oil, just as was said before in the case of that plaster.

With it I also cured a thigh that had become chronically hardened, and I applied it to [405] bloody wounds, and it proved excellent for everything. Accordingly, for this preparation, if one does not have Falernian at hand, let there be another wine, tawny in colour and thin in consistency, so as to be translucent. Of this kind is the Ariusian, grown on Chios, and the very fragrant Lesbian, of which little is produced at Mytilene, but more, and at the same time better, at Eresus and Methymna, and the Tmolite, which resembles the Falernian. This too is very thin and translucent, tawny in colour, moderately sweet and very fragrant. When it has been aged, it can be used for all the purposes for which Falernian is used. There is also another Tmolite wine, similar to it in colour and consistency, but neither sweet nor fragrant. It has a certain astringency, and falls far short of the sweet one. These, then, are the drugs that are made when the litharge is boiled. [On the use of raw litharge.] Without boiling, on its own, as I said, it is useful for chafings.

But if it is prepared beforehand by being ground with vinegar or wine and then dried, it becomes a remedy for ulcers that are hard to cicatrise [406] on account of moisture. And if you should wish it to be non-biting, you will use it washed. [How one must wash litharge and the other metallic substances.] It is washed easily because, owing to its natural weight, it quickly settles to the bottom in the liquids in which it is levigated. It becomes most completely non-biting when it has been washed with water. But to sensitive bodies it brings a slight sensation of biting when it has been washed with vinegar or wine. One must levigate it thoroughly with the liquid through the whole day and then let it settle during the night. Then, early on the following day, one pours off the liquid and pours on fresh liquid, grinds it again in the same way, and pours it off again on the following day. One does this until there appears, together with the liquid, something like a fine scum of the litharge. When nothing any longer collects on the surface, there is no further need to pour off. To go on grinding it for more days, however, even if nothing collects on the surface, is better. And do this in hot sun, for in this way the drug becomes more drying.

It is quite clear that it is better to do this in the summer season, not only in the case of litharge but also of the [407] other substances that are prepared in this manner. For cadmia, the flake of copper, burnt copper, and besides these what is called diphryges, white lead, misy, sory, stimmi, all the stones, and in addition to these titanos (lime), are both washed and ground smooth in the same way as litharge, with one of the liquids mentioned. Sometimes I also carry out their preparation with sea water; about these matters more will be said later as the discourse proceeds. For at present my task is to go through the plasters (emplastroi), which the more recent physicians both write and pronounce with the rho in the last syllable, just as everyone is accustomed to do in the case of the kentrion and the mēlōtris (ear-probe). For in these cases too the original imposition of the names seems to have been without the rho: the kentrion was named from kentein ('to prick'), whose last syllable does not have the rho, and the mēlōtris is compounded of mēlē (probe) and ous, ōtos (ear). Now, however, since almost everyone pronounces them with the rho, one would not err in uttering them as they do, and especially the kentrion.

For I have shown [408] in my work Against Those Who Censure People Who Commit Solecisms that even the Attic men themselves followed the prevailing usage. Indeed, it has also been shown by others before me that the Attic dialect itself has undergone a manifold change, and that all those who have the greatest reputation among the Greeks for skill in speech follow the custom of their own time. We too, then, since we find that all the pharmaceutical books now have the name of the plaster (emplastros) written with the rho, shall ourselves also follow the prevailing usage. [On the drugs prepared with molybdaena.] I have also said before that the use of molybdaena is closely similar to that of litharge. For all the drugs that are compounded with litharge can also be prepared with molybdaena. In potency they differ from one another only to this extent: the substance of molybdaena is thicker-particled and colder, while that of litharge is finer-particled and intermediate between hot and cold.

With respect to the colours of the drugs prepared with them, there is a certain difference [409] in it, inasmuch as molybdaena brings the colours toward the duskier. For this reason, of the white plasters which contain not only white lead but also litharge, none is prepared with molybdaena. For when it is mixed in, the white colour becomes ash-coloured. But what pertains to the potency is not only not lost, at least in the white plaster prepared with hydrelaeum (water and oil), but actually becomes better, and especially in the case of soft-fleshed persons. When, however, we wish to disperse something, litharge is better than molybdaena. So too, in all the other drugs that are recorded as compounded with litharge, if one puts in molybdaena, both the colour of the drug and its potency undergo alteration to the extent that I have just set out.

[On the white plasters prepared with litharge and white lead.] Physicians mix white lead with litharge in preparing the white plasters either for the sake of the colour, or in order to add some astringency and cooling to the drug. But they see that such a preparation also turns black [410] when it is boiled for longer, and especially when it is boiled over wood, perhaps not smokeless wood either, and not in clean air. They are therefore compelled to take it off the fire quickly, and for this very reason to mix in neither abundant water nor oil. So they reasonably thought of adding resin to it, so that it might be ductile and coherent by taking on a certain viscosity, especially when the liquid resin is mixed in. But the drug becomes worse with such a mixture, since resin has something biting about it, while its drying property is not at all strong, and you have learned that this property is what ulcers most need. Which resins are very biting will be stated again when all of them are discussed. The mildest among them are two: first the terebinth, second the one called larch. It is therefore better to mix these in whenever anyone wishes to prepare such a plaster. All things become much softer to the touch, both those prepared with resin when they take on some wax, and those prepared with wax when resin is mixed with them. One must therefore add wax as well to the resin.

And in order that the colour of the plaster [411] may be kept white, the wax ought to be white. White by nature is the Pontic wax; for it is now customarily called so even if it comes from some other place, because white wax is produced in the greatest quantity in Pontus and in the smallest quantity in other places. White, but not by nature, is the wax called Tyrrhenian. This one, then, has no evident acridity; but of the naturally white kinds some are acrid, and these must be washed first. Their washing is done as follows: they are melted over a fire, then thrown into clean spring water, and there stirred about and thoroughly cleansed. In this way pitch, resin and the so-called physema are also to be washed; about these a more exact account will be given later. But now, since I am writing out the composition of the white plaster, I shall next relate the remainder of what I was saying.

For when the wax has been added together with the resin to the white lead and the litharge, which have been boiled beforehand, until the drug becomes completely non-soiling, you would then have a white plaster, if you wish, sometimes adding water to it, sometimes oil alone, and of this oil sometimes [412] new, sometimes old. For you have already heard what power water and old oil have. You also know that both omphacine oil and the oil cultivated in Iberia, which they now call Hispania, impart something of astringency to the drug. The Istrian oil has not only a slight astringency but also bitterness. So the preparations made with the astringent oils will differ from those made with the sweet oil, inasmuch as at the beginning and at the end of ulcers all things having something of astringency are better, but in the middle stages the sweet ones. For at the beginnings ulcers need repellent drugs, so that they do not even begin to become inflamed; and after that they need the more relaxing ones: if inflammation does not occur, for the sake of transpiration, but if it has already occurred, on account of it too, so that it may be resolved more quickly. It is quite clear that the discussion concerns a small inflammation. For in small ulcers, on which we use these white plasters, a large inflammation cannot supervene unless some error has been committed.

That the astringent quality is also beneficial when the ulcers are already cicatrizing, [413] no one is unaware. It is time, then, to state the proportion of the drugs that are compounded into the most useful white plaster. [The weighing-out of the plaster.] Let there be an equal part of each of the metallic substances, the white lead and the litharge, and, if you wish, let this be a weight of one litra of each. Of oil let there be a measure equal to both together, or, as the Romans call it, two litrae; of the wax let there be a half-litra, and of the terebinth half of that, that is, a weight of three ounces. If you also mix in frankincense, you will make the drug more anodyne and more concoctive of inflamed small ulcers, but weaker as regards cicatrization. For you will produce excess flesh, since frankincense is among the flesh-producing drugs, as you have also learned in the third book of the Therapeutic Method. It is better, then, to put in a little alum as well, both for the sake of cicatrization and for another reason: relaxing drugs, when applied to plethoric and cacochymic bodies, prompt the affected parts to suffer flux.

The drug compounded from all of these will be able to disperse unnatural swellings [414] in those with soft flesh, such as are neither very large nor painful, and especially when it receives an abundant quantity of frankincense. And the frankincense would be abundant, given the quantities stated above, if it is equal in weight to the terebinth. But if the frankincense is half of the resin, the drug will be less dispersive, but more cicatrizing than the one that has double the frankincense. And if you should wish to make it somewhat more dispersive, then add also a little of the white pepper, which can do no harm at all to the cicatrization of the ulcers. So then let the weight of the alum be γο. [an abbreviated weight, apparently corrupt], and half that of the pepper. It is reasonable, then, that three drachms of the latter be added, and six of the alum. And since, among the alums, the one called split, which is also white in colour, is better than the others, it is fitting to add this one.

[The white (plaster) made with white pepper, as Attalus and Heras (prepare it).] It benefits the ulcers of old people and of those with soft skin, and it heals every ulcer, those that are rather moist and hard to cicatrise, and excoriations, such that the skin hangs loose, sometimes [415] blackening, on the point of the elbow, the shin and the knee, where there is not even flesh beneath, but only the periosteal membrane. Accordingly, for one listing everything in order, the drug turns out to be composed of the following: of litharge and of white lead, a litra of each by weight, and of oil two litrai by measure. For among the Romans the litra-weight of solid bodies is called by the same name as the litra-measure of liquids, which is found in great numbers throughout the whole city, being made of horn. In addition to these, of wax a half-litra by weight, of terebinth resin three ounces, of frankincense either half as much as this or an equal amount, and of alum six drachmas, and of the pepper three. The boiling is evident: first the metallic ingredients are boiled in the sun until the mixture becomes completely non-staining, or even a little harder; then at that point the wax and the resin are put in, and then, when everything has been united, first the frankincense, and after it the alum and the pepper.

One should put in the so-called Rhodian white lead if one wishes the [416] plaster to turn out quite white. But in the city formerly called Dicaearchia and now Puteoli, too, some of those who prepare white lead are accustomed to make it white, like the Rhodian. That one should prepare the plaster in the sun, and mix in water, so that it becomes at once whiter and more cooling, has been said before. If one wishes to make it more cicatrizing, no water at all is to be mixed in; it is to be prepared with old oil only, putting in two and a half [γο β΄ ἥμισυ: unit uncertain, presumably pounds], or even three. This drug is not among those first composed by me. It was composed many years ago by Attalus, who was king of us Pergamenes, a man who took pains over drugs of every kind; it is compounded in the proportion stated above, and we should be surprised if anything of the same kind could be compounded better than it. Heras too mentions it in his book of drugs, which some entitle Narthex and others Tonos dynameōn [the Strength of Powers]; he requires that the oil be old, and that an equal amount of water, or half as much, be mixed with it.

The rest of the proportion [417] is as I have written it, except that he wrote kotylai, not litrai, for both the water and the oil, without making clear of how many ounces he means the kotylē to be, whether ounces by weight or ounces by measure. For those by weight judge the heaviness of bodies, those by measure their bulk. Now when he says that this drug treats the ulcers of old men and of the soft-skinned, he speaks the truth; but he is more generous than he ought to be when he claims that it heals every ulcer. For it treats those that are moister and for this reason hard to cicatrise, but none of the malignant ones, just as it treats none of the bloody wounds either; yet he says it treats all of these too. When, however, he says that it treats abrasions, he speaks the truth. For often, when in some patient the skin had been stripped off so far that it hung down together with the underlying flesh, I applied the drug and saw the stripped-off part united to it again; and, what is greater than this, sometimes when it was already turning black.

And again another thing still greater than this: on the olecranon, the shin and the knee, where there is not even flesh, but only the periosteal membrane or a broad tendon lies beneath. So for abrasions [418] you would have this drug as the best, but for sinuses and abscesses it is neither the best of all nor second in excellence to the best. In these affections when they are of moderate size, however, in those with soft skin, and in women, children and old men, it is a good drug. So here too Heras has borne more witness to the drug than he ought. And he did so much more when he praised it for bites, saying that it suits all of them.
