For what does the 'all' added to the statement mean? Does he mean even if the creature that bit is a wild beast, or does he speak only of the bites of all human beings? Yet each is false. In the case of wild beasts it is plainly so: no one would say that wounds which are cured with difficulty by drastic drugs can be successfully treated by this one. And if he is speaking about human beings, even so the statement is so lacking in distinctions as to harm rather than benefit those who hear it. Someone, at any rate, persuaded one of the physicians to apply this plaster to a young man bitten on the index finger in the pankration. He fared so badly that the whole bitten part was in danger of rotting away, since putrefaction had supervened in it.

Only with difficulty, [419] after being treated over a longer time, did it close up. Since this bite had been made not into a nerve but into flesh, it would have been nothing surprising for it to be healed by such a drug. For the bites of human beings are much like other wounds, unless the biter is very cacochymic, or has fasted for rather longer, or is enraged, so that both the whole body and the parts about the teeth have become bilious. Yet not even in these cases will the drug be seen to do anything worth mention of that kind; rather, it will be enough for one who uses it at once to suffer no harm, before one of the drugs specifically suited to such cases is applied to the bitten part, about which it will be said later. For now it will suffice to say only this much: that in cases where the biter is either a human being of the kind we have described, or an ape, or a dog, or some other such animal,

[Explanation and composition of the Attalic white of Andromachus, and that it harms those bitten by rabid animals and the nerve-wounded less.] The white plasters prepared with new oil and water, without taking in the pepper and the [420] frankincense, do great harm to the bitten parts, even if the saliva of the animal that bit has only the very slightest venomous quality. Less than all of these the Attalic is by nature apt to do harm, because terebinth, the old oil, the frankincense and the pepper are put into it. In the same way, in the case of the nerve-wounded too, the other whites are more harmful, but the harm from this one is much smaller, since it has old oil and has no water. It is less harmful still if it contains the whole three ounces of frankincense and not half. For I have said before as well that, even if we prepare it in this way, in such whites the alum works to the detriment of the drug. For the drug needs not astringent things, but things that draw outward sufficiently what is troubling in the depth, both the punctured nerves and the venomous saliva of the animals. Heras also says that this plaster heals burns when diluted with rose-oil or myrtle-oil or myrrh-oil. But here too it falls far short of the drugs that treat burns well, about which too it will be spoken later.

For in these cases the other white [plasters] [421] that contain neither frankincense nor resin are better. But these too fall very far short of those that specifically heal burns, just as I said that the one compounded by me cures them completely when vinegar has been added to it. For that one is useful at every stage, whereas the white [plaster] made with pepper is useful for burns that have been flayed. When, then, [the burn] is being brought to a scar, it is useful; before that, on its own it is useless, but when dissolved in myrtle oil it is useful, though certainly not with a strength equal to the drugs specifically suited to burns. Heras says that it is also suitable for those who have been bitten. But here too there is need of a distinction. For in hard [lesions] that are difficult to concoct the drug is rather weak, but in the more moderate ones it is adequate, especially in old people, children and women, and, to speak summarily, in the soft-fleshed. The drug is also useful for ionthoi, as Heras also wrote, and truthfully, but he made his pronouncement about eruptions without a distinction.

For of these too it cures those that are moderately somewhat hard, but those that have reached a greater degree of heat or have something phlegmonous about them it exacerbates, [422] and especially at the beginning. Next after what has been said, Heras wrote word for word as follows: 'It was effective also on a three-month-old hardness which had formed after childbirth, and it dispersed it.' In this he says nothing impossible. But he ought to have added of what part the hardness was: whether of the whole uterus itself, or only in the neck or the mouth, or in the horns, or in one of the bodies lying upon it from outside. Heras also praises this same plaster for fistulas more highly than its nature warrants, both all the other kinds and especially those that occur in the ring; for this is the name he himself used, declaring that it cures them. In the same way Heras also praises the present plaster for podagra and anthrakes, epinyctides and condylomata, lepras and lichens and bruises under the eyes. If, then, he supposes that someone who used it because better remedies were not at hand would derive moderate benefit, his supposition is true; but if he praises it as the best drug for these conditions, he is plainly speaking falsely, since there are many others better. At any rate, at the end of his praises of it he wrote as follows, in these very words.

[423] "Use it especially when an ulcer is broken down again by acrid drugs and drugs for bleeding wounds and becomes inflamed again, and in abscesses about the knee." Here too he ought to have added: in the account of the abscesses, the soft-fleshed, namely children, women and old men; and in the case of the ulcers, their kinds, as we shall do in the account of malignant ulcers. For the plaster set out in the present account is cicatrizing for none of the ulcers that are malignant in this way. A distinction is needed between those hard to cicatrise and the malignant ones, for not all malignant ulcers are hard to cicatrise. Both their difference and the drugs that are by nature able to benefit each of the two will, of course, be discussed as the account proceeds. A white plaster can also be prepared from the metallic substances alone, as I was saying a little earlier about litharge boiled by itself.

For if white lead is added to the litharge, and then twice as much of each of oil and water is mixed in, and one carries out the boiling, as I said just now, over coals that have been burned through beforehand, in clear air, [424] the drug will be adhesive and white in colour, and more cooling than the one prepared from litharge alone. For just as molybdaena is of a more cooling and coarser-particled nature, even if one sets it beside litharge, so too is white lead, or even more so than molybdaena. And if the oil put in is also old, this drug too will have no small viscidity, so as not to fall away easily from the body to which it happens to have been applied. If you wish the plaster to turn out white, put in oil as pure and as clear as possible, for many oils are not such. The drug will be soothing and anodyne if one also adds fat to it, as I myself am accustomed to do. Let the fat be goose fat, or, if this is not available, fowl's fat; and if we do not have even this, let us put in pig's fat, knowing that goose fat has no small superiority over the others, yet using the inferior ones too whenever we are without the finest; for indeed, when cinnamon is not available, we turn to the best cassia.

With the proportion stated above it is sufficient [425] to mix in, of the fat, half a part of the weight of each of the metallic ingredients, so that there is one part each of litharge and of white lead, double of oil and double of water, or even a little more, and half a part of the fat. In what sense I call the things measured double, half and equal to the things set on the balance, I made clear a little earlier, when I explained the homonymy between the Roman litra by weight and the litra by measure. I have prepared this drug in many forms. For I have mixed the four in equal amounts and put half a part of the fat into them, and sometimes also one and a half parts of each of the liquids. By way of example, the proportion will be as follows: of litharge, 1 litra; of white lead, 1 litra; of the oil and of the water, of each, half a litra; and of the remaining ingredient, the fat, a half-litra. But sometimes I also put in a third of a litra, just as also one litra of the water.

But what laymen, and those physicians who resemble such people, are often in the habit of saying, beware of ever saying it yourselves: that, as they put it, this or that drug becomes better if it takes in addition this or that ingredient, [426] whatever it is they may name. Some of them, for their part, confess that they do not know, but ask us which of the compositions and preparations is the finest. They do not recognise that one is more useful for one condition and another for another, and that simply and without qualification none is best. For this reason, then, I require you to know precisely the powers of the simple drugs, for it is not possible to use the compound well while these are unknown. For instance, in the case of the white plaster set out in this present account, fresh fat mixed in will make the drug more anodyne, so that it benefits the wound even if the wound is slightly inflamed, but it will make it worse for cicatrization. The drug without the fat is more cicatrizing, but not equally anodyne. It has also been said before that with the addition of water it becomes more cooling, and with old oil more discutient. He, therefore, who is able to recognise what the wound needs more will himself compose drugs best and will also use best those already compounded.

And you have often watched me, using the drugs of the physicians who had called me in for consultation, [427] cure many of the cases over which they were at a loss. A drug, then, is called best not absolutely, but among those that profess to do some particular thing, just as I said that the palm plaster (phoinikinē) is best for fluxional conditions, when it is used in accordance with the distinctions stated earlier. [On the other white plasters.] The white plasters mentioned above were prepared in the manner I have described from of old. But many other kinds were compounded after them, as later physicians took away some ingredients, added others and substituted others; about these too it is better to speak, for the sake of exercising you in a varied way in the compounding of drugs. Andromachus, then, in the book which he entitles Remedies for External Conditions (dynameis pros ta ektos), has written roughly as follows, in these very words: 'White plaster which I use. Litharge, 1 mina; white lead, 1 mina; wax, a quarter; resin, a quarter; oil, 3 kotylai; water, 2 kotylai.' This is what Andromachus wrote, without adding for which cases it is suitable or going through its boiling.

Some, then, [428] say that the mina contains twenty ounces, others sixteen. The drug could be prepared either way. Yet it does not seem right to me to put in an equal amount of resin and of wax, for the Attalic is better composed, taking twice as much wax as resin. It is plain that if the resin is put in in an amount equal to the wax, the plaster would be more adhesive, but not similarly pleasant to the ulcers; rather it would have something acrid. Moreover, he also did not act rightly in failing to make clear what kind of resin he wants to be put in. But we, knowing that the terebinth is better in every respect than both the Colophonian and the so-called roasted, will put that one in. And if we are also well supplied with larch, nothing prevents us from using it, for they are somewhat similar. As for the three kotylai of oil, I think he is writing of the Attic ones, or else he would certainly have written litrai. And yet one might wonder how, while living in Rome, he named kotylai instead of litrai. For these are the local names there: that of the litra, that of the xestes, and that of the ounce.

From many drugs written down long ago, before the affairs of the Romans had grown to so great [429] a power, I have conjectured that what those writers call a kotyle is equal to nine ounces of the litra now in use at Rome. Is it not, then, that Andromachus too thinks fit to put in the three kotylai on the understanding that each of them is of 9 ounces, and by the same reasoning the two of water as well? Knowing beforehand, then, as we do, the power of each of the simples, however you prepare it you will be able to use it for whatever purposes the mode of composition promises, leaving it to others to inquire which of the compositions is the best. For all of them are both best and not best, as has been shown by me earlier. And indeed, next after this one, Andromachus in turn writes another, the following. [Another white one.] ℞ Litharge, 160 dr.; white lead, 200 dr.; wax, 50 dr.; terebinth resin, 24 dr.; oil, half a kotyle; water, 6 cyathi. This plaster, then, having more white lead than litharge, would be whiter than the former one, and more cooling, at least in this respect.

but it would fall off easily, even if we suppose the kotyle to hold sixteen and two-thirds ounces [430], as some say. The admixture of terebinth, however, helps it in this respect, so that the drug does not become brittle, since otherwise it would be entirely without fat and dry, having little oil and water. In this case too Andromachus did not add either the boiling or the indication. [Another white.] Next after this he writes another, a third, which has all the other ingredients the same as the Attalic plaster made with white pepper. But these two are added to it: of the plant orchis 8 dr., of struthion two ounces; and he puts no water at all into this drug. Of frankincense too he thinks fit to put in the five and twenty drachms, without writing it out, as Heras is accustomed to do. Some, however, put in ten, two and twenty. Here too, however, he mixes in two kotylai of oil, leaving us the same lack of clarity that I mentioned earlier. One might greatly blame him for not having added the indications of the drugs. For surely the one written second does not have the same power as the first and the third.

Perhaps, then, someone will also ask why the person who first composed the drug, whoever he was, wishing the drug to be discutient [434], nevertheless tried to keep the white lead raw in it. It seems to me that he arrived at this kind of preparation for this reason: so that the drug might also have something of the repellent faculty. For drugs that have none of this faculty are not safe for plethoric bodies. So that it might suit these too, it is likely that the white lead was mixed in raw. It is quite clear that the drug before us makes great promises, from its having taken in both the myrrh and the deer marrow, since in all other respects it has the same ingredients as these common plasters. We have learned that myrrh is a strongly drying drug and sufficiently fine-particled, and that marrow is inferior to none of the so-called emollients. This faculty, like all the other secondary ones, has been discussed in the fifth book of the treatise On Simple Drugs.

It seems, however, that the composer of the drug relied not on these alone but also on the white Pontic wax, which has a drug-like power, and for this reason put in a very large amount of it [435]. I think that Heras means the Roman sextarius. For among the Athenians neither this measure nor this name existed. But now, since the Romans have held power, the name of the sextarius is current among all the peoples who use the Greek language, though the measure itself is not equal to the Roman one, for different people use different sextarius-measures. Among the Romans (Ῥωμαϊκοῖς), at any rate, the sextarius contains one litra and a half and a sixth, so that the ounces amount in all to 20. These they mostly measure with horns incised on the outside with certain circular lines. Some have falsely supposed that the Roman sextarius holds eighteen ounces by measure. It seems, then, that Heras too, when he writes 'cotyle', means half of the sextarius; but whether they (δηλοῦσιν) indicate the 9 ounces from the litra-horn, or the ten, is unclear. And whether the drug is also suitable for those bitten by a rabid animal, whether swallowed or applied externally, it is not possible to know from reasoning.

For it has been shown by us that such drugs have their activity by the whole peculiarity of their substance, and for [436] this reason are judged by experience. But I never dared to make trial of this drug, to see what power it displays in those bitten by a rabid animal, because I have a drug that cures reliably, the one made with crabs, and, when this is not at hand, certain others that have never failed. To abandon what is reliable in so dangerous an affection and, for the sake of a meddlesome experiment, to betray the safety of the person who has been bitten seemed to me terrible and unjust. Concerning those bitten by a rabid animal, then, let this much suffice to have been said. As for the other things written by Heras about this plaster, I say, just as in the case of the Attalic one, that some of them are true, while some are exaggerated. For it is a most excellent drug, as plasters go, for the so-called hypōpia (bruises under the eyes), but as an agglutinative for bloody wounds it is not among the first and best. And in general, concerning this class of plasters, I find that very many physicians, not only those of the present day but also those who have written treatises, have bestowed praises greater than the truth warrants; about these it will be said in the following discussion.

But now, coming to the one before us, [437] we shall again examine what Heras has said. For he says that it heals phymata, without adding any of the distinctions that I wrote down concerning the palm plaster (phoinikinē). For some phymata are very hot and burst out violently, while others are cold and dry. A great many others lie between these: some exactly in the middle between those mentioned, some departing a little from the middle state to either side, and some departing further in the same way to either side, and some near the extremes, or somehow equally between the middle ones and the extremes. It is impossible to fit this plaster to all of these, unless indeed he should wish to melt it with certain liquids, so that there come to be many modes of its use, which he ought to have stated, as he did in other cases. For this reason I say that it is just to praise him for what he wrote in that way, but to blame Andromachus.

As for this plaster's being suitable for human bites and dog bites, consider that you are hearing from me the same arguments that I stated concerning the Attalic plaster as well, and likewise concerning the other things that he attests of the [438] drug. Just as in the case of that one, so in the case of this one too, I say that the drug is a good one, but that it falls far short of those that act best for each of those conditions, so that one may use it with confidence when none of the best ones is at hand. Nor is this a small thing in drugs, just as in regimens and in everything pertaining to the art. At first I despised it, so that I did not think it even worthy of Hippocrates when he exhorts us to do everything in the art so as to help or not to harm. Later, however, I recognised that it has very great force, when I saw some of the physicians who, with the very drugs by which they had earlier succeeded so as to be admired, later failed in other cases so as to be laughed at. And for this reason I have always tried to use such remedies in which the hope of benefit sometimes involves uncertainty, while the fact that no harm will result is a matter of exact knowledge. The things, then, for which Heras praised the Attalic plaster and this one are, as I said, not great.

But when the drugs that accomplish these things to a great degree [439] are not at hand, no one using these would cause manifest harm, even if he should do no good. Anyone, however, who wishes to use this drug on phymata will himself find out how, from what I said in the case of the palm plaster (phoinikinē), by melting it down now in one way, now in another. The whole treatment of phymata will also be discussed at greater length in what follows, and through it I hope you will possess an exact and complete method for the drugs that are able to benefit phymata. Let this plaster be called by you 'the white plaster for those bitten by a rabid animal', just as the Attalic one is called 'the one made with white pepper'. Next after this one Heras also writes down another plaster, in these words: 'The white Ariobarzanean plaster, with which Xenocrates dispersed the abscess about the tarsus when it had already undergone change.' Then, having stated the proportion of the ingredients put into it, and after that the boiling, at the end he added, word for word, as follows: 'It is effective above all for malignant, spreading and hard-to-heal ulcers, and in general for every ulcer.'

But the proportion itself of the ingredients that make up the drug he wrote, I do not know why, as a third part of the one written out in full by others [440] in the following manner. (X) Litharge 200 dr., wax 50 dr., old oil 3 kotylai, white lead 80 dr., terebinth 32 dr., burnt trumpet-shells 10 dr., frankincense 19 dr., water 12 cyathi. All these ingredients that I have just stated Heras wrote at a third part: ♃ litharge 66 dr. 4 obols, wax 16 dr. 4 obols, old oil 1 kotyle, and white lead 26 dr. and four obols; of terebinth resin 10 dr. and four obols, burnt trumpet-shells 3 dr. and two obols, and frankincense 6 dr. and two obols, water 4 cyathi. Then, next, he writes the boiling as follows: Grind the litharge and the white lead with the water and the oil, then boil in a new pot over a gentle fire, stirring carefully with an iron spatula so that it does not burn. When it is half-boiled, add the wax, and when it has melted, the resin and the frankincense, and boil until it becomes to some degree non-soiling; then, when it seems to be close to being right, add the trumpet-shells and boil them together for the remaining time.

When it has completely thickened, pour it out into a mortar in which a little water has been placed beforehand [441], and use it after kneading it soft. This drug has been prepared for dispersing without biting, since it contains little white lead relative to the proportion of litharge, and the white lead is boiled together with the litharge from the beginning; and it is a strongly drying drug on account of the burnt trumpet-shells. Burnt purple-shells and oysters have more or less the same power. It is quite clear that the shells of these animals are burnt without their flesh. Heras wrote one book of compound remedies (δυνάμεις). Asclepiades, surnamed Pharmakion, wrote ten, apart from those on theriac remedies and on women's remedies. He too added the indication of each drug, in many cases also the boiling, and in some cases also the manner of use. Andromachus collected many compound remedies, hardly fewer than those in the ten books of Asclepiades Pharmakion. He arranged them in three books: one in which he describes the drugs applied externally, a second in which he describes those taken into the inside of the body, and a third on the eyes.

One might, as I said, find fault with him for not adding the preparations, [442] nor the modes of their use, nor their powers, nor their indications. [The white plasters written by Asclepiades.] Passing now, then, to Asclepiades, I shall set out the white plasters written by him at the end of the third book of the external remedies. He himself entitles these books First Marcella, and Second, Third, Fourth and Fifth, just as he entitles the other five, on internal remedies, First Mason, and Second, Third, Fourth and Fifth. In the third Marcella, towards the end, he wrote down white plasters. The first is one whose indication, he says, is for burns, abrasions and tender skin, and which he says is called Akesis ('Remedy'). He says to boil the four ingredients together, litharge, white lead, oil and water, all in equal amounts. It is plain that this drug turns out friable and without greasiness, so that it cannot even stay on the skin without bandaging. For unless, as I said earlier, the metallic ingredients are boiled for a longer time, the plaster necessarily turns out like this.

[443] And they are boiled longer when they have a larger share of the liquids in the mixture. Next after this one Asclepiades wrote another white plaster, which has the same stated use but not the same composition. For he does not put in an equal weight of the metallic ingredients; instead the white lead is one and a half times the litharge, and he also adds calf's suet, making the whole proportion as follows. Take: white lead, 120 dr.; litharge, 80 dr.; calf's suet, 30 dr.; wax, 25 dr.; oil, 2 kotylai. This drug has little oil in relation to the proportion of the metallic ingredients, if one assumes that the kotylē holds 9 ounces, Roman ones, those marked on the customary litra-horns. And since the white lead has been increased in it, and for this reason it became more astringent than the one written before, its composer mixed in the suet. And knowing that the suet of oxen is both hotter and more discutient than that of pigs, he took care not to put in the suet of a full-grown ox. For indeed in every kind of animal the young have a moister and less hot suet than the full-grown.

This composition too, then, would be more elaborate [444] than the simple white plaster he wrote up earlier, while having nothing more to offer by way of benefit. He wrote a third, another white plaster, a cicatrizing one, made from white lead equal to the litharge, wax a fourth part, and, on the same lines (?), terebinth in turn at a half part of the wax. The oil has been put in nearly equal to both metallic ingredients together, and the water in turn equal to this oil itself. For the man who composed the drug intended that 100 drachms of each of the white lead and the litharge be put in, 25 drachms of wax, and 12 of terebinth, and two kotylai each of the oil and the water. So if you recall the Attalic plaster, which has the metallic ingredients in the same way as this one, as it also has the oil together with the water, but the wax double that in this one, and the terebinth likewise, you will know clearly what difference these drugs have from one another. For in those there were also added frankincense, alum and pepper. And indeed Asclepiades too mentions that Attalic plaster, though without naming it Attalic, and without putting in the pepper either.

But all the rest [445] he wrote in the same way, word for word, as follows. 'The white [plaster] called that of Mnasaeus; it is effective also for chronic and hard-to-heal [conditions]. Take: of litharge and of white lead, 100 drachms each; of wax, 8 drachms; of terebinth and of frankincense, 25 drachms each; of split alum, 12 drachms; of oil, 2 kotylai.' Do not suppose that it makes any difference if you find somewhere 100 drachms written in place of one litra. Rather, consider this: whether the one who wrote the 100 drachms mixes with them half that amount of wax, and of the wax in turn half as terebinth, so that there are 50 [drachms] of wax and 25 drachms of terebinth, or whether he makes some other proportion. For if he makes the one stated, he will not differ from the one who says a litra, a half-litra and three ounces. For the litra holds 6 drachms in addition to ninety, and the half-litra, evidently, forty-eight, just as, again, half of this is twenty-four. So the same proportion is preserved, and it makes no great difference whether the two kotylai of oil are mixed with the 100 drachms of the metallic ingredients or with the ninety-six. In this respect, then, the drugs will not differ, whether a litra is named or 100 drachms.

But in the following respect the drug written up by Asclepiades [446] differs from the Attalic plaster: the Attalic has six drachms of split alum and three of white pepper, whereas the one written up by Asclepiades does not contain the white pepper, but has double the weight of split alum. It is clear that the drug of Asclepiades will be somewhat more astringent and on that account more cicatrizing, and the Attalic more dispersive, so that, as I said before as well, those who ask which of the two is better do not know how to use drugs. For cicatrization the drug of Asclepiades is better, but for dispersion the Attalic. In a word, one must remember what was written by Hippocrates in the work On Nutriment, that the bad and the not bad are spoken of in relation to something, and clearly so too the harmful and the beneficial.

For on another reckoning you might say that the Attalic is better than this plaster, in that it is of more numerous uses. Indeed, Asclepiades himself, writing next after the one now described that very plaster, the one made with white pepper, does not call it Attalic but Pamphilian, being ignorant, as I [447] think, of the man who first discovered it, and attaching to it the name of the man who used it and gave it to him. At any rate he wrote its promise word for word as follows: 'Another, called the Pamphilian, a successful drug. It works for old and hard-to-heal [ulcers], carbuncles, epinyctides, achores, psoric conditions; it glues down sinuses; it works for abscesses, condylomata, and the drug is of more numerous uses than nearly any.' He says that it is composed of white lead, litharge, wax, terebinth and the two kotylai of oil, in the same way as in Heras, and in addition to these, split alum and white pepper; but he makes no mention of water in the preparation, nor indeed of the frankincense either. Some, however, put in not twenty-five but half that, and the same holds also regarding the water: for, having written that two kotylai of old oil are to be put in, he afterwards added in writing two kotylai of water, or one kotyle.

I, however, have very often prepared the drug even without water, and it appears to turn out better for all other purposes, except in those with soft skin. For in these the one that has taken up water is better, and especially when [448] the ulcers are slightly inflamed. Along with the white plasters already mentioned, Asclepiades also describes another, which promises to treat those bitten by a rabid animal, just as the one recorded by Heras also carried this promise. This one too takes, in addition to the simple white plaster composed of litharge, white lead, frankincense and wax, the further external additions of deer marrow and myrrh. He puts into it 40 drachms of litharge, 30 drachms of white lead, 10 drachms of frankincense and an equal amount of myrrh, of deer marrow two short of ten, 50 drachms of white wax, and 1 sextarius of old oil. First of all those he spoke of, Asclepiades wrote the one he calls the Rhodian, as discutient and treating hardnesses in the breasts, composed of the following: of litharge and Pontic wax he directs one to put in 1 pound each; of white lead and of prepared pig's fat half of a pound, that is six ounces of each; of myrrh 4 ounces; of roasted eggs 2 yolks; and 1 and a half kotylai of oil.

He says that this one is also good as an anal remedy, [449] without having first written down with what he wants the drug to be melted, but leaving it to us, perhaps, to conjecture that it must be melted sometimes with rose oil, sometimes with myrtle oil, and sometimes with one of the oils. [How one should compose white plasters for ulcers that are hard to cicatrise and malignant.] Which ulcers I call hard to cicatrise and which malignant, it is the right moment to distinguish, not only for what is being said at present but also for what is going to be said, since the distinction will prove useful. Those, then, that arise from an influx of fluids that are either copious or acrid, without the affected place having already acquired such a condition that, even if what flows in is wholesome, it nevertheless corrupts it, I call hard to cicatrise; those that already have the said condition I name, in a special sense, malignant.

Now, therefore, since my predecessors have written up certain of the white plasters as cicatrising well the ulcers that are hard to cicatrise, for this reason I too am writing out white plasters which I composed both for all the ulcers that are hard to cicatrise and for some of the malignant ones, [450] those that do not have an altogether bad constitution; for in the case of the latter the suitable drugs will be stated later. First, here too, I shall state the method by which you will learn to compose many such plasters. Its aim is twofold: the one common to all drugs that are compounded by method, the other particular, which distinguishes these with respect to their colour. Recall, then, all those things which you came to know in the treatise on simple drugs as drying without biting, yet very strongly. Besides not biting or being evidently astringent, they must in every case also be able to cleanse. For most ulcers of this sort appear hollow, since they have arisen from erosion by malignant humours, and for this reason they need to be filled with flesh. And it has been shown in the third book of the Therapeutic Method that all flesh-producing drugs have a cleansing faculty. Now, many other drugs too have a drying faculty capable of treating such ulcers.

But now let us call to mind those substances that are able either to preserve the whiteness of the compounded [451] plaster or at any rate not to harm it much. Such are cadmia and pompholyx and titanos (quicklime), and burnt oyster-shells and purple-shells and whelks, and the bony part of the cuttlefish. Nor would flake of copper much spoil the colour, nor that part of burnt chalcitis which is not tawny-red but ash-coloured or whitish. How such a substance must be prepared will be stated later, in the account of the theriac antidote. Each of the substances mentioned, if it is washed, becomes entirely free of biting, as do also the wax, which must be mixed into the drug while it is being prepared, and the resin. It has been said that the wax called Tyrrhenian or Pontic is suitable for the preparation of the white plaster. Of the resins, the one called larch and the terebinth are more profitable for the more malignant of the ulcers. It is fitting also to put in some portion of frankincense, so that the condition of the malignant ulcers may be concocted and brought to suppuration.

Not only must each of the drugs mentioned be washed, but the metallic ones at least must also be ground smooth for as long as possible in a sunny place with water [452] or vinegar or sea water or wine. And let each of these be pure, white and perfectly transparent, so that it may contribute something to the whiteness of the drug. Concerning white lead, too, it has been stated earlier, as also concerning the oil, the manner of boiling, the surrounding air and the fire, how each of them may contribute something to the whiteness. As in the other cases, so in these too one must know the powers of water, vinegar, sea water and the whitest wine, and mix in the compounding whatever is most useful for the condition being treated. For in raised ulcers, whose lips are thick and hard and in need of much thinning, the substances ground with vinegar and sea water are more useful than those ground with water; but in those where the moisture carried in the ulcers is acrid and biting, each of the metallic substances should rather be ground in water, just as, again, it should rather be ground in wine in those where the fluid flowing in upon the ulcers appears abundant.

Each, then, of the things I have mentioned, ground for a good many days in each of the liquids named, I added on each occasion to the drugs made with white lead and litharge, [453] and I found by trial that all of them cicatrise excellently. Some of the recipes I also gave to friends who needed such drugs, and when these were put to the test by them as well, they were seen to make good their promise. So when, as has been said, the litharge has first been boiled with the white lead and the drug has come close to the non-soiling consistency, one must add the larch resin or the terebinth resin together with the white wax, and when these have been well united, one must add in turn the metallic ingredients, in the following proportion. Of the litharge and the white lead, as usual, let a litra of each be boiled with two litrae of oil, you often adding also a half-litra of water. For in this way the litharge melts more quickly, and the boiling uses up the water, so that it contributes nothing appreciable to the moistness of the drug. Of resin three ounces, and of wax double these, are sufficient. Nevertheless, even if you sometimes put in two of the resin and four of the wax, you will find that the compositions differ in no great way even so.

One and a half ounces of frankincense [454], added after the wax and the resin, is also sufficient. And after these, three ounces of the others, which are 24 drachms. You will put in two, three, more, or all of those I mentioned, according to whichever of each you happen to have a supply of. For example, if you have all of them, you will put in an equal amount of each: I mean the cadmia and the pompholyx, the burnt whelks (kērykes) or oysters, and the flake of copper. There will be 6 drachms of each, which makes up the three ounces. If you also mix in washed lime (titanos), 5 drachms of each will be put in. If you also add burnt chalcitis, 4 drachms of each, so that all six together make up the three ounces. Let the burnt chalcitis be washed and, of course, ash-coloured in hue, not as most of those who burn it make it, pale yellow (ōchroxanthos), as one might call it. And if someone has only two of these, let him put in three ounces from both together, that is, one and a half of each. For the present it is enough for you to know these things for the composition of white plasters for ulcers that are hard to cicatrise.

White and moist cerates are also prepared from the same ingredients. They differ from the plasters in that the litharge and the white lead are not boiled, and in that fat is added, either of goose or of hen or of pig, or calf's fat. If you ever have a supply of wine or vinegar, of the whitest and most translucent kind, you will add these instead of water. [Damocrates on the white plaster.] Since the preparations (dynameis) of drugs written down in metre are easy to remember and also preserve their exact proportion, it seemed better to me to record these as well. Damocrates has written of other white plasters, and indeed also of a white one which he commends; I shall therefore set out the recipe in the very verses written by him, in the metre called trimeter. 'Along with these, the friends of medicine must have / A fine white plaster for abrasions, / And for burns, and for the sores that arise / On the surface without evident cause. / It is prepared thus.'

of white lead a litra; [456] of litharge, preferably now the soft kind, one litra and a third part of a litra; of clean Pontic wax five ounces; of terebinth, the purest, an ounce; of frankincense powder (manna) or of frankincense five ounces; of white oil, good and fresh, two and a half litrai, and of water 1 sextarius. Boil the oil, white lead, litharge and water on a gentle fire, stirring constantly with the spatula. When all of it has been thoroughly dried out by the heat, and the water properly so, and you see the drug smooth and white, soft and non-soiling, then you put in the terebinth, next the wax, and after that, last, the frankincense. Lift the pot from the fire and stir, and when the drug has cooled moderately, pour it out into the mortar and work it up. It is for women or delicate children, and for old people or for young people in a bad habit of body.

[457] Into this mix a third part of the alum plaster, which we set out a little earlier, and use it for everything, even freshly inflicted wounds. Mix into it, once melted, rose-oil and a little wax, and you will have a fine liparan (greasy salve), after pouring in a little white, austere wine. The compounding of the alum plaster that he mentioned is in the fifth book of this treatise.

[458] GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK II. Since the present treatise has, among its other aims, this one as well, that if we should ever lose the book in which we keep the compounding of the drugs we use written down, we ourselves should be able to compound drugs closely resembling those that are lost, it is necessary, first, that we have learned in general some outline of a way by which we shall find what we have set before ourselves.

secondly, to have been trained in this [459] way on many particular cases, knowing that without having gone through such training none of the tasks is carried out correctly. Terrible, too, is what has already befallen certain people, two physicians whom I know. For the one, wasting away from grief at the loss of such writings, died, and the other withdrew from medical practice. Those who have been trained in the way I describe have, besides being able to compound useful drugs, also the capacity to be critical judges of what was written by the physicians before us, and to make suitable use both of everything written by them and of whatever one discovers oneself according to the method that is going to be taught. It is better, then, to use those already tested through experience, once one has learned the method of their use; but, as I said, necessity often overtakes us, so that we also use untried ones, improvising. In the book before this one, then, it has been stated how one might prepare plasters from litharge alone, mixing in sometimes oil alone, and sometimes vinegar or wine or some of these, and from what proportion of them a white plaster can be produced when properly boiled.

We said [460] that from these plasters there come some that are cicatrising, some also that are agglutinative of bloody wounds, some that are curative of small inflammations, some of them that also treat sores hard to cicatrise, as many as are not malignant, and some of them that disperse swellings contrary to nature, as many as are neither large nor scirrhous. And not long after its beginning there was also written in it the plaster composed by me, which I call the palm plaster (phoinikinē). In this book, the one now before us, there will be discussion of the green plasters, and of the quince-yellow, the tawny, the dusky and the flame-red ones, among which are also the so-called two-coloured plasters, and, in between these, certain others: some that have names, such as the whitish quince-yellow, the dark green, the dirty-coloured, and those tending to the colour of the air and to dark blue, and some that are altogether nameless. Now, to write down next to one another those that are similar in power is useful, so that the one who comes upon several of them, or who reads the book, may choose the plaster most suitable to the body under treatment and to the affection.

But recording together those that are similar in colour is not the practice of people who look to a technical similarity [461]. However, some men of great power sometimes order us to make them a quince-yellow plaster that is agglutinative of wounds, or cicatrizing, or emollient of parts that are becoming hardened, or able to accomplish something else of that kind. For that reason some of the more recent physicians were compelled to write those similar in colour one after another and to add to each its proper claims. I shall therefore try to make my teaching a kind of mixture, beginning from the more technical arrangement. For first I write the flesh-producing plasters for hollow wounds, most of which are green in colour, noting which of them are also agglutinative, which are curative of wounds turning malignant, and which can accomplish something else of that kind. Second, I write the agglutinative ones, not only of fresh wounds but also of sinuses, among which there are also many that carry the healing through to cicatrisation. And of all these I shall make one row of the quince-yellow ones, another of those called 'barbarian', another of the grey ones, and likewise for the other colours.

I shall also speak, in one further book [462], without regard to similarities of colour, of those that treat ulcers which are difficult to cicatrise, which they also call Chironian. And after this, in another book, of those that treat both these and certain other conditions, which are called polychrest and are so in fact. And after all these I shall attempt to go through by method whatever remains to be known of the plasters classified according to their faculties. These things, then, have been said beforehand as a kind of common preface to all the plasters that are to be recorded; but I shall now pass on to those written in this book, placing before them a common account, as if nothing had already been said by me beforehand. The first, of those I know, to write down the compositions of very many drugs worthy of praise was Mantias the Herophilean; Heracleides of Tarentum, who became his pupil, is seen to imitate him not only in the use of drugs but also in the dietetic part of the art. After them certain others wrote in several books, just as both Mantias and Heracleides had done.

There are also those who set down their account of them in one or two books only, as Heras of Cappadocia did, who neither recorded any untested drug nor [463] left out their preparations, and went through all their particular uses. Many drugs have been written up carefully, in several books, by Musa, by Asclepiades and by Crito. Andromachus wrote the curative drugs for the parts outside the body in one book, and those for the parts inside in another single book, and there is also a third, smaller than these, on eye remedies. For a very few of them the preparation and the use are not appended. But neither any of these nor anyone else wrote out the reasoning behind the composition of each of the drugs, and for this reason those from experience [the Empiricists] make their pronouncements more boldly, although what they say is unintelligible, for they refer the discovery of compound drugs to accidental encounter (periptōsis). They took courage from the fact that none of the Dogmatic physicians had written out in an articulated way the method of their composition.

For when the dogmatists, asked for the reasoning by which each of the drugs they use is compounded, have nothing to say, and, having lost their written formulas, are unable to improvise other compoundings, they are themselves rightly despised, and they make the Empiricists [464] bolder in contradiction. But if they understood the nature of each affection that they treat, and knew a method such that from it they could discover both the aim of the treatment and the power of each of the simple drugs, they would not be ignorant of the reasoning of compounding. For instance, let it be proposed to consider how one would cure a hollow ulcer that is uncomplicated (for there is no harm in our also naming it so, as some call it, for the sake of concise teaching), as though no drug suitable for it had yet been found. For, having been taught by reason that the healing of hollow ulcers comes about when other flesh is generated in place of that which has been destroyed, sprouting evidently from the underlying flesh itself, we have realised that this cannot come about while there is filth in the ulcer or much moisture present. But the detergent drugs remove the filth, and the drying ones disperse the moisture.

It is necessary, then, to know the materials of such drugs, not simply by kind, as Dioscorides wrote in another way, but as we did in our works on simple drugs, [465] where we wrote not only that this particular drug heats or cools or produces some other such effect, but also that it is a drug of that kind in the first remove from the mean, or the second, or the third, or the fourth. And often, too, we wrote that it is so at the middle of each of these, or at its beginning, or at its end, so that there are twelve ranks of the drugs named according to any predominance whatever. For sometimes we need a drug that heats or dries moderately, and sometimes one able to do either of these most intensely. But the man who knows only, in a general way, that the part needs to be heated will choose pepper and mustard no more readily than frankincense. These things have been said by us before, and they have also been said in the third book of the Therapeutic Method. But since my readers already know them, together with the appropriate demonstration, I shall carry the present discussion forward to the remaining matters, beginning from this point.

Since it was shown that ulcers which are to be filled with flesh need a drug that dries and cleanses moderately without biting, we must recall what the material of such drugs [466] is. It has been set out in the treatise On the Power of Simple Drugs, together with a statement of the rank appropriate to each. For this, as I said, is the most useful thing: that if ever one needs a stronger drug, one knows what to pass on to; and when none of the simples is at hand, we come to the compound. First, then, let it be supposed that we have wax and verdigris, but nothing else of the things directly suited to a hollow ulcer, by which I mean frankincense, iris and birthwort, meal of bitter vetch, root of panax, and all other such things. We know, then, that if wax alone is applied the ulcer will be found foul, since wax can neither cleanse nor dry, whereas if verdigris is applied the ulcer will be bitten and eroded and will become inflamed. We shall therefore decline each of these and make from both together another drug, intermediate between them, weaker than verdigris but stronger than wax. But since wax falls a little short of what could usefully be applied, while verdigris exceeds it by much, we shall mix a little verdigris with much wax. How much, then, to how much?

[467] For this is what must be stated next: that it is not possible to find out exactly the quantity of each before trial, but it is possible to make a conjecture, to judge, and to compose at the first attempt a drug that will have no failure worth mentioning. I once did just this in a certain village, where I myself had no drug accompanying me, nor was any other of the people there supplied with one, and I found, of the things suitable for a composition, only verdigris and wax. Taking both, and melting the wax over a fire together with rose-oil so that a liquid cerate was produced, I mixed with the pound of cerate one ounce of verdigris, that is, the twelfth part. For I had considered mixing either the tenth or the twelfth part, suspecting that the larger would be more acrid than the wax, and the smaller weaker. When we came to the trial of the compound, both the tenth and the twelfth appeared to be correctly mixed, according to the differences of bodies. For it was indicated to us, as is also attested through experience, that strong bodies tolerate stronger drugs, whereas the weaker ones do not bear the application of such drugs.

By stronger bodies I mean [468] those that are drier in their mixtures, such as are the bodies of farmers, sailors and hunters; by weaker, those that are softer by nature or by habit, such as are the bodies of women, eunuchs and children, and of all who are moist by nature in their mixtures, having a white and soft body. Hard bodies, then, fill with flesh when more verdigris is mixed into the cerate, soft bodies when less. Hence, as has often been said, it is impossible for one drug to suit all bodies. Rather, the drug must be intermediate, as being adapted to the intermediate mixture, and must be brought towards either side, being judged by its use from day to day. For if it appears to have done what is required, one should persist with it; but if it has acted rather deficiently, one should increase its potency, just as one should also reduce it whenever it has acted beyond what is fitting.

For example, in the case of the very drug under discussion, the one made of cerate and verdigris, one must consider whether the ulcer has been filled with flesh; or whether flesh has not been generated, but the ulcer has been found dirty and full of moisture; or whether, besides not having been filled with flesh, [469] the patient has had some sensation of biting, and the ulcerated part has appeared hotter or at any rate redder. If, then, the drug appears too weak, you will increase its potency by an admixture of honey or of verdigris; but if too strong, you will mix in oil or rose-oil, softening the drug that is to be taken up on the lint-plugs. On the occasion itself, cerate and verdigris are mixed in this way, just as I said they were once mixed by me. But let those who practise medicine have in readiness a plaster already made, which they name 'the green' from its colour. It is sufficient to treat fresh wounds, those that are not large, and it can also be melted down with rose-oil to the consistency of a drug applied on lint. It will need to contain some resin as well, either the kind called Colophonian and roasted, or the terebinth. It has been said that the so-called larch resin is in some way similar to the terebinth. Here too the quantity of their admixture is a matter of conjecture.

For if we mix in more of the resin than is fitting, it appears soft while it is being softened by the hands, but when spread on linen cloth it will a little later become like hard skin, [470] readily falling off the body. But if less of the resin than the proportionate amount is mixed with the wax, it will not have the very quality that is called 'echekollon' (adhesive tenacity), such that when pulled it stretches out further; and it is evident that, even if it is applied over some part, it will adhere poorly and quickly fall off it. What, then, is the proportionate mixture for a plaster-like consistency? If you would trust me, an equal amount of each. But let neither the wax be dry and old, nor the resin. For the consistency of what is mixed from them turns out finest in this way, if both are taken unctuous and soft. But if one of the two should exceed, it is always better for the resin to predominate, so that some even mix a double quantity with the dripping (?) wax. [Preparation of the simple green plaster of Andromachus, and an exposition concerning its power.] And indeed the green plaster, for so they themselves call it, some have made with a double quantity of the resin, putting in two litrai of it, one of wax, and two cyathi of oil.

Of the verdigris, some add two ounces and others three to such a mixture [471] of the wax and the resin. Moreover, in the preparation some knead the verdigris into the meltable ingredients once these have melted, while others first let them cool, then scrape them off and make the mixture in the mortar. Those who wish to make the drug more agglutinative of bloody wounds first grind the verdigris with vinegar in the mortar and then add the cerate, scraping it in. So if any of you is asked which of these green plasters is best, remember what I have often said, and answer that all are best for one who knows the conditions to which each is suited, just as all are bad for one who does not know them. For my part I say that the one that takes vinegar in addition dries more vigorously. And it is quite clear that the one containing more verdigris is strong, more drying, and more cleansing of foul wounds. Its limit is that it accomplish these things without biting.

For a drug so strong that it already actually bites when applied to clean ulcers will never make them fill with flesh, and in another way it will make them moist and foul, much like those that dry and cleanse insufficiently; but with the more acrid ones the ulcer becomes hollower, and redder [472] and hotter. And sometimes the patient himself perceives its biting. Do not, therefore, praise any drug simply, without adding the condition for which it is praised, neither in the case of any other drug nor in the case of those now before us. Those, then, who wrote out the green [plasters] one after another and did not shrink from distinguishing the conditions for which they are suited err less than those who did not do even this. But those who have written without distinctions, prescribing at the transitions between them 'another green', produce the very worst teaching, if indeed one ought to call such writing teaching at all. Andromachus, at any rate, in the book which he entitles 'Of the external [remedies]', a little after the beginning wrote first the grey ones, then the tawny ones, and after these the black ones; then, turning to the green ones, he made the beginning of the teaching as follows: having written 'Green ones' as a heading, he wrote as the first of all this one, word for word: Green of Gallus. ♃ Of pine resin, 300 drachms; of wax, 100 drachms; of scraped verdigris, 50 drachms.

of frankincense [473] 25 drachms; of vinegar, a sufficient quantity. Now perhaps he ought to have said something about the preparation as well: whether he wants the frankincense too to be ground smooth together with the verdigris while the vinegar is poured in, or only the verdigris. For either way is possible, and in many compositions some have written it this way, others that way. In this case, however, it is possible to divine his intention, that he wants both, the frankincense and the verdigris, to be triturated with vinegar. But for which affections the drug is to be used ought by all means to have been made clear. Is it, then, that because before this one he had written two plasters, over the first of which he wrote as a heading 'For gangrenes and putrefactions and chronic and malignant spreading ulcers', and over the second 'For spreading ulcers, which I use, and many other things', he therefore wrote this green one next without any addition, indicating that it suits the same conditions? But again, writing another one next, he said simply 'Green of Potamon', then another, a third green, and a fourth, 'Green, which I use', and a fifth, 'Another', and after these a sixth, a seventh, an eighth, a ninth, a tenth and an eleventh

[474] and a twelfth, and a 13th, 14th, 15th and 16th, prefixing to each of them only this one word, "another". He wrote them all as differing from one another in potency, yet not all of them as suitable for putrefactions, spreading ulcers and gangrenes, as one can recognise from their material. From this it is also clear that he wrote them alongside one another according to the similarity of their colour, not of their potency. We, then, shall state the potency of each of them, starting from the nature of the simple drugs. For this will be most useful to those who wish not only to understand in general the method of the composition and use of such drugs, but also, through being able to improvise, to discern of what potency are the remedies written by the older authors without specification. So we shall examine the one which Andromachus wrote first, taking up and considering each of the simples of which it is composed. First, then, he mentions in it pine-cone resin.

This kind is, as was said in the books On the Power of Simple Drugs, the most heating [475] of the resins, just as the terebinth is the most moderate of them all in both respects. For all resins heat and dry, but some of them do this more, others less. The strongest, then, is the strobiline, and the most moderate, as I said, the terebinth. And indeed the quickest to dry are the strobiline and what is called by a name of its own the pine 'physema' (pityinon physēma). This too is a resin by kind, and it dries and heats: in drying it does not fall short of the strobiline, but in heating it falls short by no small amount. These, then, become free of fat (?) when dried, which is why they cannot be used to make plasters that are pleasant to the touch, as the sticky and moist resins can. Between the pine physema and the strobiline resin, at least as regards heating, stands the fir resin. It is moist, however, and itself remains so for a longer time, just as does the Colophonian resin that smells of frankincense; some indeed call only this one Colophonian. It has something sweet in its smell, like the fir resin, and it heats moderately, as that one does. It is produced in very small quantity, and for this reason it is costly.

Most liquid of all, however, is the second variety of the resin called [476] larch resin. For this too is in a way twofold: one kind is closely similar to terebinth in every respect, while the other is more pungent than it, hotter, more liquid, more unpleasant in smell, and more bitter and hotter in taste. The liquid resin that settles at the bottom of the earthenware vessels holding pine resin resembles terebinth exactly in consistency and colour, but differs from it in smell and taste: it is more unpleasant in smell, and also more pungent, and more biting in taste. For this reason it is better to mix terebinth into all drugs that are meant to heal ulcers well, since the first and foremost aim in these is that what is applied should be non-biting. Let us go back, then, to the plaster under discussion. Into it Andromachus directs one to put 300 drachms of strobiline resin mixed with the hundred drachms of wax. In this neither he himself nor, at any rate, the man who composed it aimed precisely at either the consistency or the potency.

For it will not be adhesive, and it will turn out acrid. He did well to provide a remedy for it against both by mixing in frankincense, but [477] relative to the quantity of those ingredients he mixed in little, and especially since he adds 50 dr. of verdigris, and these are an eighth part of the four hundred made up from the wax and the resin. But no one would fault this in one whose aim is to make a sufficiently drying drug; whereas for one who wished to render it flesh-producing and agglutinative of moderate wounds, the 50 dr. would properly be mixed in. And in this way it would become milder and more flesh-producing, more adhesive and of more manifold use. One must praise the admixture of the frankincense, since it helps towards a plaster-like consistency; for it is both anodyne and concoctive. If, then, he had mixed in an equal weight of it to the verdigris, that is, the 50 dr., he would, as I said, have made the drug more adhesive and milder. But since he mixed in twenty-five, wishing to preserve the drying strength of the verdigris, he has made the plaster suitable both for the agglutination of larger wounds and for the healing of ulcers that are hard to treat. That he intended it to be of this kind is shown also by the admixture of the vinegar.

It is therefore in our power to make it either more vigorous or milder [478], by mixing in either more or less vinegar, and likewise sharper or less biting vinegar. For from the admixture of sharper vinegar, as also from that of a larger quantity, the drug will be more drying, and more agglutinative of bloody wounds, when a winy vinegar has been mixed in. In the composition it is better to grind the verdigris with sharp vinegar for several days in hot sun. For its biting quality will be softened, while its power will be diminished not at all. The frankincense need not be mixed in from the beginning; one day is enough for it. For I think you remember this too, since it has often been said: when strong drugs, such as verdigris, misy, chalcitis, sory, lepis and chalcanthum, are ground in vinegar for several days, their biting is blunted and their virtue is increased. For all mineral substances, being by nature rather coarse-particled, do not extend their powers into the depth of the bodies under treatment.

So, in order that they may become finer-particled, one must apply to them the processing by means of trituration and vinegar; for when they have been thoroughly refined by this, [479] they sink down to the depth. And there accrues also another benefit in such preparations of drugs: for, when thoroughly processed, they pass through the pores throughout the body, being held back nowhere on their passage, and for this reason, even if they are hotter by nature, they act without biting. So too, of the humours themselves that are generated in the body, the thin ones are readily dispersed by transpiration without biting, whereas the thicker ones, being retained and wedged in, cause distress whenever they are biting. The same argument applies also to burnt metallic drugs; but these retain something biting from their contact with the fire, and when they have laid this aside in the washings they become altogether non-biting. Those, however, which instead of fire undergo something similar to burning through trituration with vinegar in the sun do not even acquire the heat that comes from fire. Yet the burnt ones too become much better when ground fine in vinegar. These things, then, being common to many drugs, are necessary to know, and likewise the matter of their use, one thing in some affections, another in others.

But in the case of hollow [ulcers], [the drugs are used] when, taken up [480] on pledgets of lint, they are inserted into them. So the plaster under discussion, if you melt it with rose-oil and use it, will be useful for foul and moist ulcers, but biting on those that are uncomplicated; and for this reason it will be necessary to mix with it a liquid cerate made of wax and resin, melted either with rose-oil or with olive oil. There may sometimes also be need of myrtle-oil, and one must also know some method for mixing these. Of olive oil, at any rate, the name is one, but its quality and power are not. For the omphacine [oil, made from unripe olives] is colder, while that from ripe olives is hotter. And if it grows old, it will increase its power of heating. So too the oil that contains salt, in proportion to how much of it it has taken up, is more heating and more drying than the oil that has not taken any in. And that which [contains] tender shoots of the olive, which they call thalloi, is more astringent.

What is more useful is dictated to you both by the form of the ulcer and by the nature of the body under treatment: the ulcer is treated by contraries, the ulcerated body by similars. So you will melt with myrtle oil the drug that is to be applied on lint when the flesh being generated seems to you flabbier than is proper [481], and all the more when the ulcer is close to cicatrising; whereas when some slight inflammation still remains in the surrounding parts, it is best to melt the drug with rose oil. You have learned that the best rose oil is the one made solely from many roses steeped for a long time in oil prepared without salt. If, then, someone keeps these things always ready in memory, and remembers, as I said, the powers of all the simple drugs, he will himself compose green plasters of many kinds, and will make the best use of each of those already compounded. The plaster set out in the discussion up to this point, for instance, which Andromachus wrote down as the first of the green ones, can be reworked in many ways: on the one hand by putting in some other resin instead of the strobiline resin; on the other by increasing the frankincense, or by putting in along with it one of the dry flesh-producing drugs, such as iris, birthwort, bitter-vetch meal and others of this kind. Moreover, one can also vary the composition by mixing in an emollient for the hardened lips of the ulcer.

From this line of thought some mixed in ammoniac incense [482] and galbanum, others deer's or calf's marrow or fat, just as, again, others mixed in one of the repellent drugs, wishing to check the influxes. Accordingly some put in split alum, others round alum, others the omphacine gall. Others again mixed in ladanum, which has both properties, emollient and repellent, so that the lips might be softened and nothing might flow in from the parts lying above. And indeed all those who wished to treat the hard-to-heal ulcers, so that the drug might be a polychrest, mixed into the aforementioned ingredients chrysocolla or diphryges or burnt copper or scale, some of copper, some of steel or of iron. And nearly all the things now mentioned preserve the colour of the green plasters, whereas others, though of the same properties, spoil it if they are mixed in. For this reason I too have not mentioned all the substances of each property, but only those that will preserve the colour of the plaster being compounded.

For the proposal was not simply to speak about agglutinative or flesh-producing plasters, but about these with the further condition that they be green. Consequently both the things just mentioned, and chalcanthum [483] and raw chalcitis, when mixed in in a small measure, preserve the colour of the drugs under discussion. Concerning the composition of such drugs, then, enough has been said. Concerning their use, this too ought to have been added in writing by Andromachus. But since he has omitted it, we shall add it ourselves, having first stated one general account concerning the use of such drugs. And this account is a necessary one; then (εἶτα), having stated the universal method, it is fitting to leave the particular [uses] to those who have learned it. Such a procedure is the work of men trained in dialectic; [the other is] to write out for them the particular [uses] in the case of all [the drugs], as Heras and Crito and Asclepiades and many others besides have done. And indeed there is also a third kind of teaching, which we ourselves practise: we neither write out the use for all the particular drugs, nor yet entrust the whole to the universal, common teaching of the method alone. Rather, we teach this first, and after it we write out one, or a second, or even a third example, for the sake of clarity and of the exercise of those who are learning.

[484] This is, of course, just what we are now showing in practice, having already done it in the preceding sections as well. For once we have found, from the power of the ingredients that make it up, to what degree the drug attains in drying and cleansing, from this we shall also find the condition for which it will be useful. For where there is much moisture and filth in abundance, there one must apply a drug that dries and cleanses to a considerable degree; but where there is the so-called uncomplicated ulcer, requiring fleshing, there one must apply the most moderate of the drying and cleansing drugs. The less and the more within this one must find from the nature of the person being treated. For to harder bodies, whether hard through natural krasis, or through age, or through region, or through their occupations, one must apply more strongly drying drugs, and to moister bodies those that dry less. So the first use of each of the drugs called emmota (drugs applied on lint) is taken conjecturally from the indications just stated; the second, as I also said before, is taken from the signs that appear in the body being treated.

For if the hollow ulcer is found to be free of inflammation and [485] clean, one should make no change; but if it is moister or dirtier, one must intensify the drying and cleansing drug. If it is more hollow than before, one must weaken the drug. It is intensified by the admixture of honey, and mitigated by the admixture of oil and cerate or of one of the oily preparations, such as rose-oil, myrtle-oil and oil of cypros prepared simply, without the astringent bases which they add either for the sake of fragrance or so that the preparations remain unspoiled for a longer time. But if some fault-finder should accuse us of leading the discussion, contrary to what was proposed from the beginning, to the uses of the drugs, when we had promised to speak about their compounding, let him reflect that a certain compounding also takes place in the use, and keep quiet. For the first compounding in the use is that of the drugs mixed with the cerate, and the second consists in adding rose-oil, myrtle-oil, oil of cypros, oil of schoenus or honey. Enough about these matters; we shall now come to the written account of the plasters that have already given sufficient proof by trial.

These, then, are the drugs that Andromachus wrote down, [486] noteworthy drugs for those who know how to use them. But since they are of this kind, one must select from them those composed of fewer or more readily obtainable simples, those that are more polychrest, and those that keep most closely to the aim proposed. What I mean would become clearer with an example. Let the example, then, be a hollow ulcer, uncomplicated, in a healthy body. Such an ulcer will be treated by the so-called simple green plaster, melted together with rose-oil. They call 'simple' the one made of verdigris, wax and resin. I, as I said, mix an equal amount of each of the two, and of verdigris a tenth, or a twelfth, or an eighth. Clearly it is a twelfth if we mix a pound of wax and a pound of resin with two ounces of verdigris; and a tenth if with the two ounces of verdigris we mix twenty of both together, the resin and the wax, that is, ten of each. And indeed, even if we mix an eighth part of verdigris into the cerate made of wax and resin, that too will be well. For such a drug will be more acrid and more detergent, yet certainly not useless; for it will be suitably applied to hard bodies.

[487] A finer composition will result if one mixes an eighth part of verdigris into the composition made with wax and resin, having first ground the verdigris for several days with the most acrid vinegar. It would be finer still if we were also to mix in frankincense, a half part relative to the verdigris. Of oil you will mix in, when you prepare the drug without vinegar and frankincense, as many cyathi as there are ounces of verdigris. But when you mix in frankincense and vinegar, if the roasted [resin] is somewhat fattier and softer and you are preparing it in summer, you will mix in none; but when it is hard, and in winter, one cyathus. It is also possible for you, if you mix one of the liquid resins with the wax, to need no oil at all. Of the most liquid you will mix in a third of the weight of the wax, and of the less liquid one a half. Such a composition, clearly, will come about as follows: having melted and cooled the wax and the resin, mix them with a part of verdigris, sometimes an eighth, sometimes a tenth, sometimes a twelfth, recognising that for hard bodies the first proportion is suitable, for soft ones the third, and for intermediate ones the intermediate.

[488] You will grind the verdigris with vinegar. If you should wish to make the drug milder, put in a weight of frankincense half of that which you used of the verdigris. And if someone [wants it] milder than this, you will mix the verdigris with an equal amount of frankincense. And even without scraping [it], having cooled the resin together with the wax, we melt them and pour them over the verdigris and the frankincense that have been ground in a mortar with vinegar. These, then, are the first compositions of the green plaster: agglutinative of bloody wounds, such as are not large, and able to heal the other [lesions] up to cicatrisation, and fleshing, if it is melted with some oily liquid. By 'oily' I mean rose-oil, which it is most fitting to use, prepared in the way I have described, and after this myrtle-oil, cyprus-oil and mastic-oil. As for olive oil itself: in cases where you wish to add some heat to the drug being melted, you will mix in this common [oil]; where [you wish to add] cooling, the so-called omotribes (oil of unripe olives); and where astringency, myrtle-oil.

But where you want a mixed power, one that has something concoctive and also something repellent, mix in rose-oil; and where you want slight astringency together with greater heat, henna-oil [489] and mastic-oil. Many other compositions too, as I said, will be made with the simple drugs just mentioned, when there are mixed in either flesh-producing or emollient or astringent drugs, or those that heal the hard-to-heal ulcers. Some have also mixed in some of the discutient drugs, just as also some of the cicatrizing ones. Certain others, mixing in everything, have either made a useless karykē [a rich mixed sauce] or had the good fortune to produce a polychrest drug. Knowing the materials of these, you will yourselves be able both to use those already discovered and to compound similar ones. I too shall write out some of the reputed ones, beginning again from those that Andromachus wrote. There are, then, about thirty following the one written above. I shall set out only those praised by him. The fourth from the first is written thus. Green plaster which I use. ♃ scraped verdigris, 9 drachms; chrysocolla, 9 drachms; terebinth resin, one mina of 16 ounces; wax, half a mina; a little vinegar.

As I said before as well, Andromachus did not add to each of the plasters its declared indication (ἐπαγγελία). Yet from the material of the simple drugs from which he compounds the one before us, [490] it is not unclear that it is able, on its own and before being melted, to treat ulcers, and that when melted it becomes an emmoton, that is, a drug applied on lint. The mina one should put in at sixteen ounces, for the mina of twenty is large in relation to the equal measure of chrysocolla and verdigris. After this one he wrote three others in succession, and then he writes another, word for word as follows. 'Another, which I use. ℞ Scraped verdigris, one pound; manna, 10 ounces.' (I use 1 pound.) 'Wax, 5 pounds; roasted resin, 5 pounds; liquid resin, 5 pounds; oil, 1 cyathus; vinegar, as much as suffices.' I also add 10 ounces of ammoniac incense. With these Andromachus stopped. It is quite plain, if we remember anything of what was said earlier, that this very plaster also has a power similar to the one written before. Next after the one written before, Andromachus, writing another, began thus: 'Another, mallow-coloured.' After this he wrote out beneath it the proportion of the simple drugs from which he compounds it, as follows: '℞ Scraped verdigris, 1 pound; pitch, 2 pounds; manna, 1 pound; wax, 2 pounds; resin, 2 pounds; oil, 1 pound; vinegar, as much as suffices.'

This [491] one, then, is similar to the preceding ones. It is clear that the verdigris and the manna, a pound of each, must each be triturated with the vinegar. Of the wax, the pitch and the resin, twice as much as of each of those, that is, two pounds of each, must be melted with the pound of oil and so mixed with the ingredients triturated with the vinegar. As we have often said, this should be done by cooling and scraping them rather than by pouring them on (?), so that, should the surrounding air be cold, the so-called wax-lumps do not happen to form. Next after this one he wrote another approved plaster as follows. Green plaster of a hundred drachmas. ♃ Ammoniac incense, 8 dr.; flake, 12 dr.; manna, 8 dr.; dry resin, 12 dr.; verdigris, 8 dr.; calf's suet, 14 dr.; terebinth resin, 8 dr.; wax, 30 dr.; oil, a quarter of a cyathus; vinegar, as much as suffices.
