This one can both conglutinate large wounds and cleanse the foul among ulcers. When cerate is added to it as it melts, it can make flesh grow. Before being melted it can also heal the thick-lipped among ulcers, press down sinuses, and in general disperse and repel.

[492] For it is compounded from opposite powers. And the green plaster written next after it is of similar power and use, having this proportion: ℞ terebinth, 1 mina; the herb serapias, 25 dr.; scraped verdigris, 10 dr.; calf's suet, 25 dr.; wax, 25 dr.; frankincense, 12 dr.; oil of cypros for the dry ingredients. And the plaster called Isis by the others he himself wrote without this name, thus: Green plaster of Epigonus. Although everyone records it, I shall nonetheless write here too the proportion of its simple drugs according to this man, since some disagree about them. For he directs one to put in burnt copper, ammoniac salt, flakes of copper, verdigris, ammoniac incense, birthwort and frankincense, an equal amount of each, 8 dr., that is 1 oz.; and of aloes, myrrh and galbanum one and a half times these, of each, that is 1½ oz., which is the same as saying 12 [dr.?] and a half; of round alum, 6 dr. He also mixes in 200 dr. of Colophonian resin, and of wax half that, that is 100.

[493] and half a kotylē of oil. But he says that some mix in a quarter, and a sufficient amount of vinegar, and of dracontium root half an ounce, which is 4 drachms. This he wrote in at the end, since it is not found in the recipe of the isis. For Epigonus added it, and in this the isis of Epigonus differed. Next after those written above Andromachus wrote the green (plaster) of Pasion in the following proportion. ℞ Colophonian resin 300 dr., wax 150 dr., verdigris 8 dr., round alum 8 dr., copper scale 12 dr., frankincense 16 dr., burnt copper 8 dr., ammoniac salt 8 dr., oil half a kyathos, vinegar a sufficient amount. This drug, because it has taken in the ammoniac salts beforehand, became more drawing, more discutient and more detergent than the preceding ones; in all other respects it is similar. After one intervening recipe Andromachus wrote one stronger and of more manifold use than the one written above, which he calls the green (plaster) of Alcimion, in the following proportion. ℞ turpentine 200 dr., wax 150 dr., copper scale 18 dr., scraped verdigris 16 dr., round alum 16 dr., galbanum 16.

[494] of frankincense 10; of sal ammoniac 12 dr.; of burnt copper 16 dr.; of birthwort 10 dr.; of Indian aloe 12 dr.; of myrrh 16 dr.; of ammoniac incense 18 dr.; of galbanum 12 dr., but others 8; of oil half a kotyle, of vinegar half a kotyle. Next after this one he writes another, called Athena, as he himself added at the end. The proportion of the simple drugs of which it is composed is as follows. ℞ Of wax 250 dr.; of terebinth 200 dr.; of roasted [resin] 100 dr.; of calf's suet 50 dr.; of galbanum 24 dr.; of manna 24 dr.; of sal ammoniac 12 dr.; of burnt copper 12 dr.; of aloe 12 dr.; of copper flake 24 dr.; of round alum 12 dr., and of split [alum] 8 dr.; of chalcanthum 8 dr.; of misy 8 dr.; of opopanax 8 dr.; of scraped verdigris 6 dr.; of ammoniac incense 6 dr.; of Sinopic ruddle 3 dr.; of vinegar 3 kotylai; of oil 2 kotylai. Put in the ruddle at the beginning. This drug too, which is called Athena, is polychrest, as I said; how one must use the polychrest drugs will be made clear in the discussion of them. Next after this one he wrote another green [plaster], word for word thus: Green [plaster] with oil of cypros, of Aphrodas.

[495] ♃ Wax, 24 dr.; dry resin, 12 dr.; scraped verdigris, 8 dr.; Aphrodas, 12 dr.; manna, 8 dr.; oil of cypros, one eighth of a kotyle. It is pounded together with it, and it can be suitable for the hard-to-treat ulcers; and for this reason he wrote it down, since it is compounded of few ingredients and is capable of being quite useful. Next, since Andromachus writes many other green plasters, compounded of many ingredients and polychrest, it seemed best to me to leave them aside and to mention only the simple ones, as they themselves call them. He writes, then, word for word as follows: 'Another simple green plaster, which I use. ♃ Resin, twelve litrai; wax, 8 litrai; scraped verdigris, two litrai; calf's fat, two litrai; vinegar, one litra; and I put in one litra of manna.' It is quite clear, then, that he wants the vinegar to be ground smooth with the two litrai of verdigris and the litra of frankincense, just as I said before, and then the meltable ingredients to be mixed with these. I mean the eight litrai of the fat, together with the eight of the wax and the twelve of the resin.

This plaster would be strictly plain if it had taken neither the fat nor the [496] manna. For in that case the verdigris would be a tenth part of the two together, the resin and the wax. And if the resin were hard, some oil too would certainly have been mixed in, as was said before. But since it has taken calf fat, it is no longer strictly plain, having taken in addition an emollient and concocting drug. And much more so if it should also take the manna, for this is concocting and suppurative and has something flesh-producing about it. [A general account concerning plasters of the same colour.] That drugs should be grouped together in writing them up not according to similarity of colour but according to similarity of power is surely quite clear. At any rate, as Andromachus does, so too some others write up, one after another, not only the green plasters but also the quince-yellow, the grey and the white ones. Now how the white ones are made I stated in the first of these commentaries; how the green ones are made has been said before as well, and I shall now recall it.

[How green plasters are made.] Verdigris is put into them, and not a little of it: enough to overpower the colour of the other [497] ingredients and to make the whole like itself. Whoever compounds such a plaster must attend, besides the quantity of the verdigris, to the colour of the ingredients mixed with it and to the manner of the boiling. In the ingredients mixed in, he must guard against the colours that are hard to change, such as those of yellow, russet and black drugs. By yellow and russet I mean such colours as that of mēlitis (?) and of burnt chalcitis, and of arsenikon and sandarachē. By black I mean such as those of pitch, asphalt, ampelitis earth and gagates stone. As for the boiling, the verdigris should not be added to the ingredients while they are being united over the fire; it should be mixed with them in the mortar once they have been united, if you want the drug to stay green in colour. But if you wish to make the plaster quince-yellow, you must know that in the boiling the verdigris changes first into this colour, and later into tawny, so that the plaster called two-coloured results. For in the time after the boiling, after a few days, the duskier part forms on its surface, while the tawny part gathers into the depth of the drug.

Since what is fitting has been said about their colour, [498] I shall pass again to the account of the powers, recalling from where I first set out in this book. I set out, if we remember at all, to speak about the flesh-producing drugs, the aim of whose power lies in cleansing and drying moderately and without biting. Their compoundings by species, however, are various, varying according to the materials of the simple drugs. It is evident that the drugs properly and primarily called flesh-producing are flesh-producing for uncomplicated wounds, that is, those which are hollow but do not have filth or inflammation present with them, and still more, have no influx of bad fluids, nor badly tempered flesh in the hollow wound. For if any of the things mentioned is combined with the hollowness, that must be treated first. The aims of their treatment are, in the case of filthy wounds, the drugs that are able to cleanse; in the case of those arising from an influx of fluid, to dry and to repel what flows in. And if this be copious and hard to overcome, first to cut off the cause of the influx.

In respect of drying, at least, they are in no way inferior to aphronitre and nitre. But those have no share in the astringent power, just as neither has [502] the flower of the Asian stone, and for this reason they are able both to disperse and, mixed with cerates, to cleanse foul ulcers. Salts do not have this capacity, because of their astringency. For you, then, who remember these things and have heard the method both of the composition and of the use of all such drugs, I shall write down in what follows the drugs that have been tested by experience at the hands of the reputable physicians, with a view to knowledge of the best drugs. First came Mantias and his pupil Heraclides of Tarentum, who wrote down many drugs; these, having come down to their successors, were sifted by experience. The best among them these successors themselves wrote down again, while those that seemed less effective than the others they left aside. Fittingly, then, I too make more mention of those who came after them. Among these, the ones who are thought to have succeeded best in the experience of drugs are Petronius Musa, Heras and Andromachus, and Asclepiades and Criton. Not a few drugs have also been written down by Archigenes and Philippus.

There is also a single book by Menecrates, entitled [503] 'Autokrator: written out in full words, of noteworthy drugs.' So whatever finest drugs have been written down by these men and are praised by them, and those of which we have experience, both from among these written ones themselves and from those our teachers used, and anything further that we too have discovered, this I shall write in what follows, explaining to which kind each of them belongs. Now, since I have gone through the green plasters, I shall write next after them the quince-yellow ones. [Quince-yellow plasters.] Most green plasters, and especially the brighter-coloured among them, become such because verdigris predominates in them; the quince-yellow ones come about in the same way. But the green ones have the verdigris unboiled, while the quince-yellow have it boiled, though moderately. For if you boil it further, you will produce the plasters which some call 'two-coloured' and others 'tawny'. Physicians are accustomed to call simply 'green', 'quince-yellow' and 'tawny' those plasters that glue together wounds that are not very large, bring to a scar the ulcers which physicians are accustomed to call 'uncomplicated', and fill hollow ulcers with flesh when melted with rose oil.

Those of them, however, for which the claim is greater are polychrest. [504] Some do not have many claims, but one noteworthy one: either to be suitable for the malignant among ulcers, or to disperse pus or melicerides, or to soften indurations, or some other such thing among the conditions that are neither to be despised nor easily treated. Andromachus, then, wrote down fourteen quince-yellow plasters, of which five contain verdigris, while the others have been made without verdigris. Of those containing verdigris, one is the first written of the fourteen, another the fourth, and after it a certain sixth, and after that the seventh and the tenth. All those, then, to which he has added nothing special in writing both agglutinate ulcers and cicatrise them. And, if one wishes, when melted with rose oil they also fill hollows with flesh. They also treat moderate inflammations, just as they also soften moderate indurations. Those that contain ammoniac incense do this more, and among these themselves those do it more that contain more of it in proportion to the other ingredients. In some he himself has added 'soft', that is, plainly, suited to soft skins.

And the one to which 'drawing and squeezing-out' is added, [505] showing that it is suitable for intense pain, synanche and pain of the side, or that it disperses internal abscesses: he testifies to something more in these than in those written down without qualification. I shall therefore set them all down in order below. [Quince-yellow plasters of Andromachus.] The quince-yellow plaster that I use. Take: litharge, 104 dr.; oil, in summer 1 kotyle, in winter half a kotyle; wax, 48 dr.; Colophonian, 48 dr.; ammoniac incense, 24 dr.; scraped verdigris, 8 dr.; galbanum, 8 dr.; myrrh, 8 dr. Another. Take: litharge, 100 dr.; oil, 3 kyathoi or half a kotyle; Colophonian resin, 64 dr.; ammoniac incense, 40 dr.; white lead, 24 dr. Another. Take: litharge, 40 or 50 dr.; white lead, 6 dr.; Tyrrhenian wax, 16 dr.; dry pine resin, 16 dr.; ammoniac incense, 2 dr.; oil, 1 kotyle. Another. Take: litharge, 100 dr.; Colophonian, 64 dr. (others, 48); wax, 84 dr.; galbanum, 8 dr.; myrrh, 8 dr.; verdigris, 8 dr.; opopanax, 6 dr.

of oil, in summer 1 kotyle, [506] in winter ½ kotyle or 3 kyathoi. Another. ℞ litharge 100 dr., pine resin 100 dr., wax 12 dr., oil ½ kotyle or 3 kyathoi, Falernian wine ½ kotyle. The litharge is ground fine with the wine until it has dried, then it is boiled. Another. ℞ litharge 100 dr., old oil 70 [? text 'ο΄'] or 2 kotylai, wax 100 dr., worm-verdigris 25 dr., black chamaeleon 12½ dr., chrysocolla 40 dr. Another. ℞ litharge 200 dr., old oil 3 kotylai, wax 168 dr., ammoniac incense 100 dr., myrrh 4 dr., verdigris 8 or 20 dr., Colophonian resin 128 dr., galbanum 20 dr., black chamaeleon 8 dr.; but some use propolis, 8 or 20 dr., in place of the chamaeleon. Another. ℞ old oil in which as much chamaeleon as possible has been boiled down, 1 xestes; litharge 1 litra. Having brought the oil to the boil, sprinkle in the litharge and boil. Another, for spreading ulcers (nomai). ℞ sandarach 3 dr., split alum 4 dr., frankincense 4 dr., myrrh 4 dr., ammoniac incense 18 dr., wax 18 dr., terebinth resin 6 dr., pig's fat 2 dr., honey one-sixteenth of a kotyle.

[507] Another. Take: of litharge 108 or 120 dr.; of wax 108 or 120 dr. (in another [copy] 100); of ammoniac incense 50 dr.; of terebinth 40 dr.; of birthwort 25 dr.; of root of zeia 8 or 20 dr.; of worm verdigris 16 dr.; of split alum 16 dr.; of old oil 2 cotylae. Another, simple. Take: of litharge 100 dr.; of axunge 75 dr.; of old oil 75 dr. For those with tender skin; it also disperses. Another, called aphra, an emollient quince-yellow [plaster] of Diophantus, attractive and expressive, by which joints were treated. Take: of prepared birdlime 1 litra; of wax 1 litra; of terebinth resin 1 litra; of galbanum 3 ounces. Melt and use. Another, the Salome, for every violent pain and for synanche, together with a cupping-vessel, and for pain of the side. Take: of litharge 2 litrae; of old oil 8 ounces. Boil together. [Another quince-yellow [plaster], from Heracleides, which disperses internal abscesses without pain.] Take: of litharge 100 dr.; of white lead 100 dr.; of wax 80 dr.; of dry resin 60 dr.; of ammoniac incense 50 dr.; of galbanum 16 dr.; of old oil 2 cotylae. As Rusticus, the pupil of Isidorus, [has it]: take: of litharge 50 dr.

[508] of white lead 50 dr.; of ammoniac incense 50 or 40 dr.; of wax 25 dr.; of dry resin 30 dr.; of elm, the kind in little sacs, 15 dr.; of galbanum 8 dr.; of old oil half a kotylē or 1½ kotylai. Andromachus wrote down the boiling of none of these plasters. I, however, stated earlier what is essential to their colour: the verdigris must be neither raw, as in the green ones, nor boiled for a very long time, as in those called two-coloured and tawny. Rather, the verdigris should be thrown in when the pot is already about to be taken off the fire. Then, when it changes and becomes quince-yellow, one should lift it from the fire, provided the drug is by now non-staining. If not, give it a little further time over a very gentle fire, and then take it off. For on a very fierce fire it readily changes to tawny. For this reason I shall also set down two other famous quince-yellow plasters, the one called that of Menoetes, the other that of Serapion. Many have also written down how these are boiled, and you will have a model for the preparation of the plasters written by Andromachus.

[509] [Menoetes' quince-yellow plaster.] ℞ Litharge, 4 pounds; oil, 3 pounds; translucent terebinth, 2 pounds; wax, 1 pound; verdigris, frankincense, galbanum, 4 ounces each; ammoniac incense, 6 ounces. Boil the litharge and the oil until it has thickened considerably, then add the resin and the wax. And when these have melted well, set the pot down and let it cool well, then add the verdigris, and after stirring it down below, boil it again over a gentle fire until it becomes quince-coloured. Then, having ground the galbanum and the frankincense, pour it off into a mortar in which the ammoniac has previously been ground in vinegar so as to be viscous, and after kneading, take it up at once; pour on a little vinegar and leave it until the following day, and then knead it again and store it. [Serapion's quince-yellow, for wounds and dispersive, for boxers (?), all-purpose.] ℞ Litharge, 100 drachms; ammoniac incense, 28 drachms; wax, 56 drachms; Cyprian verdigris, 9 drachms; myrrh, 1 drachm; Colophonian resin, 56 drachms; galbanum, 9 drachms.

of oil [510] half a kotylē, in summer one kotylē and a quarter. Boil the litharge and the oil; when it changes, [add] the ammoniac, then the wax, and after taking it off [the fire] put in the galbanum, the verdigris and the rest, and boil gently. Many of those before me wrote down such boilings for the quince-yellow plasters they recorded, and from these you will be able to boil the other quince-yellow ones as well, by analogy. One must put in the litharge first, then the resins and the ammoniac, then the galbanum and the verdigris. Then, if it takes either frankincense or myrrh or aloe: for these must be added afterwards, when the drug is lifted off the fire, since they do not tolerate boilings. It has been said before that it must also be boiled gently, especially once the verdigris has been put in; and moreover that one must add this after setting the pot down on the ground and letting it cool a little, and all the more so if the vessel in which the boiling takes place is small. For when verdigris is added to the previously boiled mass while it is still seething, it has often made the drug overflow the vessel.

In the first quince-yellow of Menoitas, the one called 'the boxers'' (pyktikē) because boxers in particular use the drug, we have also learned before [511] that the ammoniac can be ground smooth with vinegar in the mortar, all the other ingredients having been mixed in the pot, and then it being poured down over it. [Quince-yellow plasters of Heras.] For scrofulous swellings (choirades), of Heras. Those written by Heras run word for word thus. A quince-yellow for old sinuses, even if they have perforated into the empty spaces. The same also disperses scrofulous swellings that have recently formed in children; it is effective also for torn joints. ♃ Golden litharge, 100 drachms; dry pine resin, 100 drachms; Pontic wax, 12 drachms and four obols; oil, half a kotylē; Falernian wine, half a kotylē. The litharge is ground smooth with the wine until it has dried; then it is boiled thus with the oil until it changes, and then the resin and the wax are mixed in and it is boiled until it no longer soils. The gold-coloured plaster of Menoitios, effective for those with tender skin, and especially eunuchs. It is suited to abrasions, to every ulcer, old and fresh, and to burns.

It is an emollient (malagma); it disperses phymata, parotid swellings, scrofulous swellings (choirades), and all indurations [512], and it also works for fissures and condylomata; it is very good. Rx: litharge, 100 dr.; old oil, 100 dr.; dry pine resin, 50 or 100 dr.; wax, 50 dr. Boil the litharge and the oil until the mixture begins to draw together, and add the resin ground smooth, and when this has melted, the wax. When it is right, pour it out into a mortar previously smeared with oil, and having worked it up by rubbing, take it up. It is adhesive and does not soil. That of Hygieinus (?), of good colour, for many purposes, working on sores that are hard to cicatrize and on paronychias. There is no finer plaster than this. Golden litharge, 1 mina; wax, 1 mina; root of black chamaeleon, 36 dr.; scraped verdigris, 18 dr.; chrysocolla, 40 dr.; old oil, 3 kotylai. Boil the litharge and the oil on a gentle fire until it begins to boil up; then, having lifted it off the fire, sprinkle in the verdigris, and stir, boiling it again, until it recovers its proper colour; then add the wax. When it is right, add the chrysocolla and the chamaeleon; and having poured it out into a mortar, sprinkle it with vinegar.

[513] For the conditions mentioned above, then, it is effective even with the chrysocolla mixed in. Without this, however, it is most soothing and acts supremely against punctures of the nerves, and wherever something must be brought up to the surface from muscles or nerves. Of these three plasters that Heras recorded, the first is both prepared with wine and named after wine. Many of our teachers and friends use it, prepared, of course, without verdigris; it has also been recorded by Andromachus and by nearly all who have compounded plasters of various kinds. Most people, preparing it carelessly, make the drug a contemptible one. But it is excellent if it is prepared, as has been written, with Falernian wine. If this is not to hand, one should put in an old tawny wine, thin in consistency; and as a general rule this may well be tawny, for transparency is a property peculiar to the white wines.

There are, among us in Asia, very fine tawny wines: the one called Tmolite, the Lesbian, and the Ariusian produced in Chios, the most renowned among the ancients, which everyone used for the finest of drugs and especially [514] for the antidotes, just as they now use the Falernian. If, then, we put such a wine onto the litharge in the heats of the dog-days, or otherwise in a hot sun, and then triturate it, or even triturate it without sun for a long time, so that the liquid is dried up and the litharge itself is left either completely without moisture and dry or something close to this, the drug turns out excellent. One of my teachers prepared it, after the litharge had first been made ready dry, triturated in Falernian wine, in roughly this way. Warming the oil in one vessel and the wine in another, he poured them little by little over the litharge: sometimes he began with the wine and, having ground and mixed it well, added some of the oil; at other times, beginning from the oil, he passed over to the wine. Doing this alternately many times, he used up each of them; and then, having poured it out of the mortar into a cooking-pot, he added the pine resin, which they specifically call physema, ground fine, then the wax, and boiled it gradually until it was non-soiling.

He also used it for sinuses, first smearing them with the blood of a pigeon: not of the domestic kind, [515] but of those that some call 'foraging' (pigeons), which go into the towers that people among us build in the fields. Some call these pigeons wild. Likewise, in large fresh wounds, he would smear them all over with the blood of such a pigeon and then apply the drug, having great confidence in it. Of the wine he put in one and a half cotylae, not, as Heras and Andromachus did, only half a cotyle; and in this respect the drug turned out much better. If you wish to make it fragrant, you will mix in half an ounce of opopanax, that is, 4 drachms. For the sake of a good colour, put in the white Pontic wax. This drug also brings ulcers well through to cicatrisation. [Crito's quince-yellow drugs.] On the quince-yellow drugs about which Crito wrote, which he himself calls boxwood-yellow. Boxwood-yellow plaster for freshly inflicted wounds. The same also cicatrises and draws. Rx litharge 4 pounds; wax 4 pounds; terebinth 8 ounces; verdigris 8 ounces; old oil 2 sextarii.

of vinegar, half a sextarius. Boil the litharge, oil, verdigris and vinegar together over a gentle [516] fire. When it is about to thicken, add the resin and the wax, and, having united them, use it especially on fresh wounds. Criton also wrote, before this one, another which he calls 'box-coloured' (pyxinē). It is simple as regards the number of the ingredients mixed in, but great in what it promises. At any rate, he writes on it word for word as follows: 'The one with chamaeleon, which does the same things as the Tyrian. It is most cicatrizing of hard-to-heal, callous and chronic ulcers, and it also heals fissures in the anus, condylomata and indurations. ♃ Litharge, 1 mina; wax, 6 minae; verdigris, 4 minae; chamaeleon, 8 minae; oil, 1 mina. Boil the oil and litharge, stirring with a spatula, until it sets and becomes quince-yellow. When this has happened, sprinkle on the verdigris, then add the wax; and having melted it carefully and lifted it from the fire, sprinkle on the chamaeleon. When it has become united, pour it off into a mortar, knead it and take it up.'

Criton has also written up certain other plasters in the fourth book of his Drugs: boxwood-coloured, as he himself names them, but quince-yellow according to the [517] others. Some of them, however, are compounded without verdigris, while others do take verdigris but will be described under another kind of drugs, according to the similarities of their power: the cicatrizing ones among the cicatrizing, those made with juices among those made with juices, and among the emollients those that by nature soften, as also the plaster of Mnasaeus, which he prepares in many forms in the book under discussion. Now, then, it is time to pass on to the agglutinative plasters that differ in colour both from one another and from the quince-yellow ones. [On the tawny plasters, which they call two-coloured.] Some are compounded from the same material as the quince-yellow plasters that contain verdigris, as I also said before, differing in one thing only, in having been boiled for longer. For all of them are green on account of the raw verdigris; they become quince-yellow when it has been boiled moderately, and tawny when it has been boiled more. It is therefore quite clear that the quince-yellow and the tawny plasters must contain more oil than the green ones, even if they should have all the other ingredients the same.

And for this reason one should put into the pot first [518] the litharge, which is to be boiled until it reaches a glutinous consistency; next the verdigris; and after it, if any of the metallic substances is being added, such as burnt copper and copper flake, these; and when the mixture has thickened, then the wax and resin, if the drug also takes these; and at the end frankincense, myrrh, aloe and all other such things. This is how one prepares the most celebrated of the tawny plasters, which they call 'the one with dittany'. It is itself also one of those named 'sacred', like the Isis, since they say that these were brought from the temples in Egypt. This one, then, is polychrest, and for this reason it will be written up in the following discussion together with the polychrest plasters. For now I shall discuss the other tawny plasters, both those that are strictly simple and those that lie between these and the polychrest ones. Just as the simple green plasters were composed of wax, resin, oil and verdigris, according to the proportion stated in that place, so the tawny ones have their composition with litharge added and with more oil than the green ones.

If, then, you wish the plaster to be boiled for a longer time, [519] you will increase the oil, and you will have the drug more drying, and for this reason more agglutinative of bloody wounds; but if you wish it boiled moderately, it suffices for the measure of the oil to be as much as the weight of the litharge. For having measured out a Roman litra of oil we shall put it in to a litra of litharge by weight. But if we wish the drug to be boiled for a longer time, we shall put in not only one and a half litrai of oil, but even two and more. More drying than the tawny plasters prepared in this way are those which contain no resin and wax at all, but are compounded only of the so-called metallics, such as some others of our predecessors wrote down, and such as the one which I use constantly, compounded by me and boiled in the following manner. Having first boiled the litharge with the oil, I add the metallics ground smooth with vinegar, and so boil it until it no longer stains. I put in 4 litrai of oil; the older it is, the better it will be, and more so if it is Sabine. Of litharge, 3 litrai.

and of the most acrid vinegar [520] 2 litrai. The metallic substances are these three: scale of black copper, verdigris and chalcitis, an equal weight of each, 2 ounces apiece, which is sixteen drachmas. When the oil is old and thick because of its age, you should put in four and a half litrai; I have once put in even 5, and I put that amount in for this reason, that it was winter. For we know that more oil is put in in winter than in summer. You will, of course, first boil the litharge to a viscid consistency. If you also have castor oil, put it in instead of the old oil. This drug readily agglutinates bloody wounds, and more so in hard bodies than in soft and womanish ones and those of children, of which kind are also the bodies of eunuchs. When it is diluted with castor oil or old oil and applied as an emmoton, that is, on lint, it is wonderful how it concocts the most intractable of ulcers, those that produce no pus at all. It also agglutinates sinuses, and it makes fistulas adhere, dries them and closes them completely.

And whenever you wish it to accomplish these things well, grind the metallic ingredients in the most acrid vinegar for several days, and preferably [521] in the sun. Likewise grind and dry the litharge, then mix it with the oil and boil it in the manner stated. For sores hard to cicatrise, however, it is not necessary for the metallic ingredients and the litharge to have been worked up so thoroughly in the grinding, for even without this the drug becomes more cicatrising. At that point add to it also an ounce of diphryges and an ounce of chrysocolla. These are not put in together with the scale and the verdigris, nor yet when the drug is already completely boiled, but at the time in between. For such ingredients of drugs need enough boiling to be precisely united with the ingredients already present, and this comes about over a moderate time, neither very long before the lifting of the pot from the fire nor close to it. This plaster by itself is capable of agglutinating fistulas, sinuses and large wounds. A new sponge, not hard, soaked in old wine, also assists it. In the case of sinuses let the bandaging be done from the base, with the bandage proceeding towards the opening, as will be shown more clearly in the discussion of fistulas.

[522] [On cicatrizing drugs.] Whether you wish to call the plasters that produce a scar 'epulotic' (cicatrizing) or 'synulotic', and likewise also the other drugs, both the dusting-powders and those applied by means of lint plugs, it makes no difference at all for the cures they effect, provided you remember the faculty that such drugs ought to have, which was stated together with all the others in the books of the Therapeutic Method. For by as much as the agglutinative plasters were shown to be more drying than the flesh-producing ones, by so much are the cicatrizing ones more drying than the agglutinative. For our aim in them is to make skin out of the flesh that has been generated in hollow ulcers. Hence this kind of drug must also be astringent, whether it is to be smeared on or sprinkled on. Our purpose here is to mention only those plasters. For the drugs applied by means of lint plugs are made from these melted in rose-oil or myrtle-oil. And myrtle-oil is indeed more useful than rose-oil, inasmuch as it is also more astringent.

If you have neither of these, they are to be melted in oil of cypros, mastic-oil and [523] quince oil; and if you have none of these, in omotribes oil (oil of unripe olives), or in the oil from Iberia, which they call Spanish. When you do not have even this, crush tender shoots of olive and put them into some other oil, whichever comes to hand. And if you are at a loss for these too, it is better to melt them in old oil. At any rate, from this you would get the drug made more drying. Now the majority of physicians abandon the drugs that have for a long time given sufficient proof by experience to all the best physicians, and have for this reason become renowned. They do so in order that they themselves may seem to have something better than their predecessors. But one must know that among the renowned drugs, those praised by everyone, the drug with cadmia and the one with ladanum are the best for cicatrization. Yet the proportion of the simple drugs mixed into them is not agreed upon among all physicians. For this reason, then, it seemed good to me to write down the proportions approved by each of those who have written them up. I begin from those written by Asclepiades, in the third book of the External Remedies, which he entitles Marcellas.

[524] [Asclepiades writes thus about cicatrizing plasters.] For particular ulcers which, without any other affection, are already tending towards a scar, one should use the preparations written below. The cicatrizing (plaster) with cadmia. Lucius the Preceptor used this. ℞ cadmia, burnt and prepared with wine, and roasted chalcitis, 16 dr. each; wax, 80 dr.; Colophonian pitch, 8 oz.; Italian wine, as much as suffices. Grind the chalcitis and the cadmia with the wine so as to have the thickness of a liquid cerate. Break up the wax and the resin, put them into an earthenware vessel, and add to them 1 lb. of myrtle oil. Set it on coals, stirring continually. When it has melted, take it off the fire and let it cool. Scrape it out, add it to the ground ingredients, mix, take it up and use it, diluting it with myrtle oil. Let the blend be suited to the condition. Another with cadmia. ℞ roasted cadmia, roasted chalcitis, diphryges, 16 dr. each.

of wax, of roasted resin, of myrtle oil, a half-litra each; of Italian wine as much as suffices. Prepare as stated before, and use the drug sometimes [525] diluted, sometimes undiluted. Another. ℞ Of litharge, of white lead, of cadmia, of diphryges, of resin, 8 drachms each; of chalcitis 2 drachms; of wax 8 drachms; of myrtle oil a sufficient amount; of Aminaean wine as much as suffices. Another, of Euphranor. ℞ Of diphryges, of roasted misy, 8 drachms each; of roasted chalcitis, of molybdaena, 2 drachms each; of cadmia 1 drachm; of wax 6 drachms; of Colophonian resin 3 ounces; of myrtle oil 6 litrae; of Italian wine a sufficient amount. Another, the one made with ladanum, a successful drug, which not only cicatrises but also cuts away callosities and corrects deficiencies. ℞ Of chalcitis, of litharge, of ladanum, 24 drachms each; of bitumen 8 drachms; of wax 72 drachms; of myrtle oil one cotyle (some say 18 drachms); of wine one cotyle. Prepare in the proper way. In use, employ it both on a compress and diluted. Another. ℞ Of litharge 100 drachms; of pitch 50 drachms; of ladanum 25 drachms; of scraped verdigris, of burnt copper, 8 drachms each; of myrtle oil 2 litrae; of copper flake 4 drachms. Prepare and use. Another, the one called 'pyrikaustos' ('fire-burnt'), from the Attalic remedies, a successful drug.

[526] ℞ Oil, 1 kotylē; split alum, manna, frankincense, litharge, galbanum, 1 dr. each; wax, 24 dr.; alkanet, 8 dr.; deer's marrow, pig's fat, verdigris, white lead, 2 dr. each; the yellow [i.e. the yolk] of three eggs. [Pour] the meltable [ingredients] over the dry ones, and use the drug sometimes diluted, sometimes undiluted. Another, a successful drug; it is effective for old and hard-to-heal [lesions]. White lead, litharge, split alum, manna, galbanum, frankincense, deer's and calf's marrow, 4 dr. each; wax, alkanet, egg yolks, 8 dr. each; oil, 4 kotylai. Pound the marrows carefully and melt them together with the meltable [ingredients], stirring with the alkanet so that it becomes coloured; then take it off the fire, strain it into another vessel and let it cool; scrape it up, add it to the dry [ingredients], take it up and use it. The white [plaster] called Magnē (?), a successful drug. It is effective also for chronic wounds and those that cicatrise with difficulty, and it is effective also for psoric conditions. It is also a good anal remedy when diluted with rose-oil or myrtle-oil. ℞ Litharge, 100 dr.

[527] of wax 50 dr., of white lead 100 dr., of terebinth 25 dr., of frankincense 25 dr., of split alum 12 dr., of oil 2 kotylai. Compound them in the proper way and use it, sometimes as a plaster, sometimes with the drug thinned. Another, called the Pamphilian, for the aforementioned conditions; it glues sinuses together and removes the callus from fistulas. It acts on the fluxional among ulcers and on those that are chronic and hard to cicatrise; it both treats psōrai and takes away bruises under the eyes. It also acts for those suffering from headache, and for the fluxions of the eyes, when applied on the forehead. It is also a good anal remedy when thinned with rose oil or myrtle oil. The particulars of the preparation are as follows. ℞ of litharge 100 dr., of wax 50 dr., of terebinth 25 dr., of frankincense 25 dr., of white lead 100 dr., of split alum 16 dr., of white pepper 3 dr., of old oil 2 kotylai. Melt them together in the proper way, using it sometimes with the drug thinned, sometimes spreading it as a plaster.

For in the case of achores on the head, or roughnesses about the eyes (ὄψιν), or the so-called epinyctides, or affections about the seat, [528] it is smeared on, the drug being diluted with myrtle oil or mastic-oil. Another, of Telamon, a successful drug: it works also against carbuncles, dries up sinuses when inserted and infused, and is also a good cicatrizing drug. ♃ Pine resin, wax, quicklime, litharge, 50 dr. each; white lead 25 dr.; oil half a kotyle. Boil the litharge and the oil until it thickens, then the wax, then the resin. Grind the quicklime and the white lead fine, and pour the melted ingredients onto them. In use, put oil on hot ashes and add some of the drug, having crushed it; and when it has been heated, put it into a mortar and beat it diligently until it becomes like gloios, and storing it away use it as a very great drug, sometimes smearing it on with feathers, sometimes infusing it. In the case of the so-called carbuncles, spread it on a piece of linen and apply it. Another, the well-known one of Moschion, for whatever you wish to clear of callus and to cicatrize; it is also a good anal remedy. ♃ Litharge, white lead, quicklime, 8 dr. each; deer marrow, wax, 16 dr. each; myrtle oil, as much as suffices.

[pour] the meltable ingredients over the dry ones [529] and, having worked them carefully until soft, make pastilles. In use, it is first dissolved in water or milk, as much as you wish, so as to have the consistency of gloios (strigil-scrapings). Then a sufficient quantity of rose-oil or of myrtle oil is added, and having beaten it up carefully and taken it up into a lead box, use it as has been stated before. [Cicatrizing plasters of Andromachus.] Rx: cadmia, 1 litra; burnt chalcitis, one litra; wax, 1 litra; dry resin, 3 litrae; myrtle oil, 3 litrae; wine for the dry ingredients. Another, the one made with ladanum. Rx: litharge, 40 dr.; ladanum, 32 dr.; chalcanthum, 8 dr.; split [alum], 12 dr.; wax, 100 dr.; flake, 8 dr.; bitumen, 32 dr.; myrtle oil, a quarter of one kotyle; Falernian wine for the dry ingredients. Otherwise, after Alcimion, which I prepared myself. Rx: ladanum, 8 dr.; hyssop, 4 dr.; propolis, 8 dr.; bitumen, 8 dr.; litharge, 4 dr.; copper flake, 4 dr.; raw misy, 4 dr.; wax, 24 dr.; myrtle oil, 8 minae. The one made with barley. Rx: white lead, 50 dr.; litharge, 50 dr.; burnt barley, unground, 1 xestes; wax, 50 dr.; oil, 1 xestes.

[530] the last; the barley. Another cicatrizing (plaster). ℞ Cadmia, 2 ounces; chalcitis, wax, terebinth resin, of each 4 ounces; hyssop, 1 ounce; myrtle oil, 4 ounces; chalcanthum, 4 ounces; wine for the dry (ingredients). Another cicatrizing (plaster). ℞ Dry resin, 18 drachms; diphryges, 4 drachms; litharge, 16 drachms; wax, 10 drachms; oil, 4 cotylae. Next after these Andromachus wrote six other plasters curative of ulcers that are hard to cicatrize, which it did not seem good to me to add here now; for they will be stated together with those that treat the ulcers that are hard to heal, in the fourth (book) of these treatises. But since Andromachus, in the same place of his book, before the cicatrizing (plasters) just written down, also wrote certain others, without first stating of them that they are cicatrizing for uncomplicated ulcers, and especially in children, women and eunuchs, and in general in those who have soft flesh, it seemed good to me to add these too here; in Andromachus they bear the title taken from their colour. For he wrote about them thus, word for word: "White cicatrizing (plasters) of Andromachus. The white one which I use."

Take of litharge [531] 1 mina; of white lead 1 mina; of wax 4; of resin 4; of oil 3 kotylai; of water 1 kotyle. Another. Take of litharge 160 dr.; of white lead 200 dr.; of wax 50 dr.; of terebinth 24 dr.; of old oil half a kotyle; of water 6 kyathoi. Another. Take of litharge 100 dr.; of white lead and of wax, 50 dr. each; of terebinth 25 dr.; of split alum 6 dr.; of white pepper 3 dr.; of the herb orchis 8 dr.; of struthion 2 dr.; of manna 25 dr. Another. Take of litharge 70 dr.; of white lead 100 dr.; of wax 50 dr.; of old oil 2 kyathoi, otherwise 2 dr.; of water 2 kotylai. Another. Take of litharge 25 dr.; of wax 57 dr.; of pig's fat 37 dr.; of myrrh 2 dr.; the yolks of 4 boiled eggs (some say raw). The 'Virtue'. Take of clean gloios 12 kotylai; of litharge 3 minas; of scale 6 dr., but others 16 dr.; of Colophonian resin 6 minas, but others 50 dr.; of wax 1 mina, but others 45 minas; of sea-water 3 kotylai. [Panacea of Andromachus.] Take of litharge 150 dr.; of wax 40 dr.; of terebinth 53 dr.

of old sea-water, or rather [532] of old wine, 2 kotylai; of oil-dregs (gloios) 6 kotylai; of scale 16 dr.; of castor oil 2 kotylai; of white lead 80 dr.; of ammoniac incense 24 dr.; of calf's fat 80 dr.; of quicklime 24 dr.; of birthwort 25 dr. Boil as you know how. [The white plaster of Telephanes.] ♃ Of litharge 80 dr.; of white lead 120 dr.; of myrrh 3 dr. 2 obols; of sagapenum 5 dr.; of frankincense 6 dr. and a four-obol weight; of oil 2½ kotylai. Boil all together. Another. ♃ Of white wax 1 litra; of myrrh 1 ounce; of frankincense 1 ounce; of deer's marrow 2 ounces; of hyena's fat 2 ounces; of deer's rennet 2 ounces, or kid's; of natron 2 ounces; of galbanum 1 ounce; of ammoniac incense 4 ounces; of litharge 1½ litrai; of white lead 6 dr.; of old oil 1½ kotylai; of sea-water half a kotylē. It is called the Kaunian. Another. ♃ Of litharge 200 dr.; of wax 52 dr.; of oil 3 kotylai; of white lead 80 dr.; of terebinth resin 32 dr.; of burnt whelks 10 dr.; of frankincense 19 dr.; of water 1 xestēs. Another. ♃ Of fresh pig's fat 88 dr.

of white [533] wax, 48 dr.; of white lead, 12 dr.; of litharge, 12 dr. Another, for herpētes, carbuncles, condylomata and fissures; exceedingly free from inflammation, as Heras the Cappadocian [makes it]. In this one, then, he did rightly in not writing simply "of wax" but adding "white" as well, for in this way it would turn out white in colour, as he intends. But after this, when he writes another, he did not add "white" either to the wax or to the wine; we, however, must add it, if indeed we wish to make the plaster white. Its composition is written by Andromachus himself, word for word, as follows. [White plaster with wine, of Publius.] Rx: of cadmia, 1 pound 9 ounces; of litharge, 2 pounds; of white lead, 2 pounds; of Greek wine, 2 sextarii; of rose oil, 5 pounds; of wax, 3 pounds; raw eggs, 12 in number; of frankincense, 3 ounces. Boil. I went through the boilings of white plasters in the first book, at the same time setting out the method not only of their boiling but also of their composition. And perhaps nothing further remained to be added to the teaching about such plasters. But since this

[534] book not only taught the account of the flesh-producing plasters, which for the most part are green, but also of all the agglutinative and cicatrizing ones, those, that is, which cicatrize ulcers free of malignancy; and I also went through the quince-yellow and the tawny ones. For this reason it seemed good to me to write in addition, in this book, the white plasters too, of which I made no mention at all in that book. And so that nothing may be lacking to the present book, I shall also add the plasters named by them 'cephalic' and 'fracture' plasters, which are agglutinative of large wounds and of sinuses, and which, when they are relaxed so as to become suitable for use with lint, are also flesh-producing. [On the fracture and cephalic plasters.] Those who wrote down the most numerous and finest drugs, whom I went through by name earlier, called a certain kind of plasters 'cephalic' and 'fracture' plasters, assigning them the name chiefly from fractures in the head.

Such plasters are of a cleansing, dispersing and drying [535] power. Most authors mixed into them a little of the astringent drugs, for two uses, as has been said: both to repel what flows in to the affected parts and to guide the power of the cleansing drugs down into the depth. It was stated by us earlier that, unless the astringents are worked up by trituration until they become fine as down, they will furnish harm rather than benefit in those plasters that have the drawing power. And I said that the best processing of them comes about when they are ground fine in sharp vinegar. I shall therefore now begin the record of such drugs with those written by Asclepiades. [On the fracture plasters of Asclepiades.] The first he wrote in the third book of the External Remedies, word for word as follows: 'Black plaster, the best, for fractures. I used this drug on fractures with many bones floating loose, and when everyone was advising that the floating bones be lifted out, the best plaster accomplished something akin to the incredible.'

For the floating fragments, which had become separated from the other bones, it held together so firmly [536] that it made them unite by callus with the others. It is as follows. ℞ Litharge, asphalt, 200 drachms of each; dry pitch, wax, 100 drachms of each; terebinth resin 50 drachms; split alum, propolis, 30 drachms of each; ammoniac incense 24 drachms; verdigris 10 drachms; oil 4 sextarii. Prepare as stated before. Other plasters of the same kind as the one written above were written by Asclepiades in the same book, verbatim as follows. Another fracture plaster, of Pythion. Helenus used this one. It is effective also for wounds from a blow; at the removal one must loosen the compress with a sponge soaked in hot water, for the drug is strongly adhesive. The same drug is effective also for scrofulous swellings (choirades) and fistulas. And over fistulas and sinuses one must cut out the compress, that is, over the opening, so that the fluid being discharged has room. One must also bathe with the drug on. The preparation is in this manner. ℞ Judaean asphalt 5 pounds 4 ounces; dry Bruttian pitch, the same amount; roasted resin 8 pounds; wax 4 pounds; frankincense 4 pounds.

of red scale one litra [537] 4 ounces; of oil, in summer one litra, in winter 1½ litrae; of vinegar 1 kotyle. Melt the meltable ingredients; grind the frankincense and the scale with the vinegar and add them to the rest, taking care that it does not boil up. When you have stirred it, pour it out into a mortar, and when you have pounded and softened it, take it up and use it. In another copy I found: of red scale 1½ litrae. It is quite clear that the one which takes more of the scale becomes more active. Moschion's fracture plaster, a successful drug for freshly inflicted wounds, for severances of the nerves, and for divisions accompanied by contusion; it works also for fractures accompanied by a wound. For it both helps the wounds and forms callus on the bones when applied with the proper bandaging; it helps also those who are beginning to be dropsical. It works also for contusions of the testicles; it also shrivels the protrusions about the seat. It works also for fissures when thinned with butter; it works also for bronchoceles; it dissolves every hardness. It works also for chafings and sprains.

It also acts on the callus-like outgrowths on the feet and hands, which we call 'nails' (hēloi), so as to remove them without ulceration [538]; and in general it is a most polychrest drug. It also acts on incipient dropsies. The particulars of its preparation are as follows. Litharge, 1 mina; in this drug the mina contains 160 holkai. Liquid pitch, 160 dr. Calf's suet, 160 dr. Terebinth resin, 80 dr. Manna of frankincense, 80 dr. Wax, 40 dr. Verdigris, 8 dr. Opopanax, 8 dr. Galbanum, 8 dr. Castor oil, 1 kotylē. Vinegar, the same amount. Juice of the mulberry (sykaminos), 1 kotylē. Liquid pitch, half a kotylē. Put the litharge, ground very fine, and the castor oil into a vessel of earthenware and of bronze, set it on the fire and boil. When it boils up, add the suet and the manna, stirring continuously. When it has thickened, add pitch, wax and resin, and when you have boiled it until it no longer soils, sprinkle in galbanum, then verdigris and opopanax dissolved in vinegar.

The juice of the sycomore and the liquid pitch we put into another vessel and boil, and when it thickens we add it to the first drug, and setting it on the fire again we boil it until it no longer soils; [539] and pouring it out into wine we leave it for three days; then, softening it, we use it, spreading it on linen. At the application of the drug one must soak a small strip in wine, squeeze it out, and then put it around the drug. As our teacher Lucius prepared it, it is as follows. We first melt the suet and the oil, and when it has dissolved we sprinkle on the manna, very finely ground, and the litharge. And when it thickens, we do what follows. Both in this drug and in the one written next after it, he says the mina contains 160 drachms. It is quite clear, then, that he means the Alexandrian mina, which contains 20 ounces, so that each of the ounces contains 8 drachms; for in this way the mina will turn out to contain the 160 drachms. Another, of Claudius Philoxenus, entitled 'of Apelles' (ἀπελοῦς), for fresh wounds (ἔναιμος), for fractures. It also works for the conditions mentioned before. ♃ (Take): litharge, 1 mina, that is, 160 drachms; calf suet, 160 drachms; frankincense, 80 drachms; opopanax and terebinth resin, 80 drachms of each; wax, 40 drachms.

of verdigris, split alum, [540] chrysocolla, galbanum, 12 dr. each; of castor oil 1 kotyle; of vinegar as much as suffices. Add the frankincense, the verdigris, the opopanax, the alum, the chrysocolla and the like last, first dissolving them in vinegar and grinding them carefully. In another copy it reads thus. ♃ Of litharge 160 dr.; of pitch 160 dr.; of calf suet 160 dr.; of terebinth resin 80 dr.; of manna of frankincense 80 dr.; of wax 40 dr.; of opopanax and scraped verdigris 16 dr. each; of chrysocolla and split alum 12 dr. each; of ammoniac incense 6 dr.; of castor oil 1 kotyle; of vinegar the same. Compound it in the same way as the fracture plasters. The oenanthe fracture plaster, a successful drug. It works for the aforementioned conditions. ♃ Of litharge 160 dr.; of wine-pitch 160 dr. (this we take as it runs off from the Italian jars); of terebinth resin 80 dr.; of frankincense 80 dr.; of prepared calf suet 80 dr.; of prepared deer marrow 80 dr.; of wax 40 dr.; of dry oenanthe, of symphytum root and of the foliage of centaury 1 litra each; of scraped verdigris and opopanax 8 dr. each; of poppy juice, myrrh, aloe and galbanum 8 dr. each.

[541] of vinegar, 3 cotylae; of castor oil, 1 cotyle. Having chopped the comfrey, the oenanthe and the centaury into coarse pieces and thrown them into the vinegar, we boil it down to a third, and, squeezing out the liquid, we use it for the preparation of the drug. The drug is effective also for gouty patients. In other copies it reads thus: ℞ litharge, wine-pitch, 160 drachmas each; deer marrow, terebinth resin, calf suet, frankincense, comfrey root, juice of the mulberry, 80 drachmas each; dry oenanthe, centaury, one litra each; wax, 40 drachmas; verdigris, opopanax, storax, poppy juice, juice of mandrake, myrrh, aloe, galbanum, chrysocolla, split alum, 12 drachmas each; vinegar, 3 sextarii; castor oil, one litra. Prepare as stated before and turn it out into Italian wine, just as we have done in the case of Moschion's fracture plaster.

[On the plasters specifically named 'cephalic'.] They are accustomed to give the name 'cephalic plasters' to those which they employ for fractures in the head that have reached as far as the diploe [542]. Their power is both to bring up scales of bone and to draw up fragments, both in the head and in the other bones of the body. Some, using the common genus, call these too 'fracture' plasters. But they are stronger than those specifically named 'fracture' plasters. For the so-called fracture plasters have, on their part, the cleansing and drying quality; these, however, have in addition taken on a certain pungency, able to draw out from the depth to the outer surface not only bones but, much more than these, some fluid that is thick and viscous, or altogether bad. Asclepiades made mention of such plasters in the third book of his External Drugs, which have been written out in the fourth

book of this treatise; but since he said that they are also suitable for malignant ulcers and for certain Chironian ones among them – for both the one which he himself entitles the 'cephalic of Deïleon', and after it the 'black-green cephalic', and after these the 'cephalic of Philotas', then also the isis, which he likewise calls cephalic, and certain others of this sort, must be considered to be of this kind [543]; for this reason I have not now set them out again, but I shall pass on to the fracture plasters and cephalic plasters written by the other physicians, having first stated the general potency of each of the two. From what I said both earlier in this very treatise and in the books On the Potency of Simple Drugs, you must call to mind and recognize that those which they entitle cephalic are more powerful than the fracture plasters. And for this reason, with cerate, they are by nature apt to produce flesh, so that in another respect they are in some way of the same kind as the flesh-producing ones as well. For when their potency has been relaxed by the cerate, they become flesh-producing drugs for use on lint, with the addition, evidently, sometimes of oil, sometimes of rose oil, sometimes of some other such thing. [On the fracture and cephalic plasters which Heras wrote.] The first of such plasters that Heras wrote is the one called isis, a quite polychrest drug. Next the one made from herbs, to which, itself being polychrest, he attests that it is cephalic.

But the one made with squill, written next, also carries the same claim, [544] being one of the quite widely useful drugs. And indeed, writing directly after these another plaster, he speaks word for word as follows: Another cephalic, effective for fractures in the head; it brings up bones easily and detaches scales. It also does all the other things that the pastille before this one does. ℞ Flake of red copper, 25 dr.; alum, 20 dr.; finger-shaped birthwort, 20 dr.; ammoniac incense, 25 dr.; frankincense, 25 dr.; myrrh, 12 dr.; bull's suet, 4 lb.; wax, 4 lb.; terebinth, 4 lb.; dry pine resin, 4 lb.; oil, 1 kotyle; vinegar, as much as suffices. Grind the dry ingredients smooth in the heat of the dog days; having first soaked the ammoniac in vinegar for a good number of days, pour it on; last, add the meltable ingredients, scraped, and when you have made everything into one, use it. In some copies 'of old oil' is added. Since he said that this very plaster does everything that the pastille before it does, it seemed right to me to write out that pastille's composition as well, in Heras' own wording, which runs as follows.

A cephalic troche of the triple mixture (trimigma), effective in fractures of the head and for [545] phymata and fistulas, podagra, callosities (pōroi), ischiadic affections. Take: of red earth 2 minas (other [copies]: 12); of scale of red copper 4 minas; of Pontic isinglass 4 minas; but in the books of Heras 1 mina is found. Grind fine the red earth and the scale separately, then, together, pour in sharp vinegar so that it has the thickness of honey, and triturate; and as they dry out, pour in vinegar. Do this in the heats under the Dog-star for 20 days. Then take the isinglass and crush it, pouring over it 1 kotyle of vinegar. Melt it over a gentle fire, then add the earth and the scale, and having emptied it into a vessel of red copper and set it in the sun for 8 days, stir it twice a day until it sets; then, taking it out little by little, triturate it in a mortar, pouring in vinegar until it thickens; then shape troches and collyria of unequal length and unequal thickness, and having cooled them, store them away. And at the time of use, to one part of the drug triturated with vinegar mix three parts of rose-oil cerate, and use it on a platysma (a broad spreading), then with a compress in cases in the head, and on top mix (?) greasy wool [soaked] in vinegar.

In the case of fistulas, once the collyrium [546] has been inserted, lay over it on top a pad spread with this together with cerate. Another polychrest. He also wrote down another polychrest plaster, which he says is suitable for fractures as well. He speaks about it, word for word, as follows: For fractures of the limbs with a wound and without a wound, and for impaired functions (λειπουργίας) and sinuses. Dry pitch, 1 mina; litharge, 1 mina; manna, half a mina; calf's suet, 1 mina; Tyrrhenian wax, a quarter of a mina (μνᾶς δ΄); opopanax, 8 drachms; scraped verdigris, a sixteenth of a mina; Cyprian copper, one-sixteenth of a mina; galbanum, 1 drachm; terebinth, half a mina; castor oil or old olive oil, 1 kotyle; vinegar, half a kotyle and three obols. Boil the litharge, the oil and the suet over a gentle fire; then, when it changes colour, add (ἀπόδος) pitch, resin and galbanum; then [boil] until (ἕως ἕως) it thickens. Then take it off the fire and let it cool a little, and pour into the pot the manna, then the opopanax and the verdigris ground with vinegar; boil it briefly, and when it is right, lift it off.

[547] We use the preparation by pouring cold water over it in summer, and in winter by taking off its chill. When we wish to make the drug softer, or to make a bone come away more quickly, we thin it with calf's marrow. In this drug Heras clearly means the mina to be sixteen ounces, for he would not have written one-sixteenth of a mina unless that was what he meant. Another. And after this one, next in order, Heras wrote another plaster with a similar claim, running roughly as follows: Non-inflaming, for punctures and fractures. We have often used this one on the very same day also for dislocations and fractures, and for sprains about the ankle or knee. It also disperses exceedingly well the sluggish fluids that collect about the knees, especially if the parts are first poulticed for two or three days beforehand with bitter-vetch meal kneaded with oxymel. And in general it is effective for every strain and rupture, for it is marvellously non-inflaming. Take: litharge, 25 dr.; dry bitumen, 100 dr.; dry pitch, 50 dr.; wax, 50 dr.; pine resin, 25 dr.

of ammoniac incense [548] 15 dr.; split alum 15 dr.; verdigris 15 dr.; propolis 15 dr.; old oil 3 litrai. Boil the litharge in the oil, and when it begins to thicken, add the asphalt and boil until it has melted thoroughly, for it melts only with time; then the pitch, then the resin, wax, ammoniac, propolis. Put in each of them while thickening the mixture and drawing off the fire. When they no longer soil the fingers, add the verdigris and the split alum, let it boil up once, and pour it out into a basin containing cold water. We used this after the fracture had otherwise formed a callus, when a good many splinters were lodged in it, and within a few days it brought things round to the point that we removed the callus and the splinters. It is very polychrest. And after this, next in order, Heras wrote another of the same kind as the plasters mentioned above, roughly as follows. Plaster for fractures, and also for dropsical patients. Take dry pitch 1 mina; liquid pitch half a kotyle; juice of the sycamore-fig 1 kotyle; litharge 1 mina; frankincense 1 mina; galbanum 8 dr.; terebinth half a mina; calf suet 1 mina.

of wax one mina [549], of opopanax 8 drachms, of scraped verdigris 8 drachms, of unadulterated castor oil 4 kotylai, of acrid vinegar 1 kotyle. The litharge and the frankincense are boiled gently with the castor oil and the fat; then the pitch is added, the wax, the resin, and the galbanum, cleaned and softened with a little vinegar. Of the remaining vinegar, one third is mixed with the verdigris and two thirds with the opopanax, and these too are added. In another small dish go the liquid pitch, the juice of the sycomore, and about an eighth part of the castor oil, so that the verdigris may indeed be drawn together; then it is boiled moderately, just until it has become united. When it seems to be well united, the drug is put away into wine. With this plaster we got the better of many dropsical patients, laying it on and conducting the treatment without elaboration, taking forethought only for good digestion. When, however, the sufferers perceive much progress, we pass over to the plaster with salts written below it. [Fracture plaster of Andromachus.] Andromachus wrote the first of the fracture plasters roughly as follows: ‘Fracture plaster which I use continually. Of litharge 1 mina, of pitch 1 mina.

[550] of wax, 1 mina; of bull's suet, 1 mina; of frankincense, 1 mina; of liquid pitch, half a kotyle; of the juice of the mulberry (sykaminos), 1 kotyle; of terebinth, 1 mina; of opopanax, 8 drachms; of galbanum, 8 drachms; of verdigris, 8 drachms; of kiki oil, 1 kotyle; some add also butter, 1 mina; of ammoniac incense, 25 drachms; in austere wine. After this one he writes another thus: Another fracture plaster. Of litharge, 1 mina; of wax, half a mina, others a quarter; of pitch, 1 mina; of terebinth, half a mina; of calf's suet, 1 mina; of opopanax, 8 drachms; of verdigris, 8 drachms; of galbanum, 8 drachms, others 6; of kiki oil, 1 kotyle; of vinegar, an equal amount. Gallus added split [alum], 12 drachms; chrysocolla, 12 drachms. Another fracture plaster, besides those previously mentioned, Andromachus wrote thus: Black fracture plaster. ℞ of litharge, 200 drachms; of asphalt, 200 drachms; of pitch, 100 drachms; of wax, 100 drachms; of split [alum], 30 drachms; of propolis, 30 drachms; of terebinth, 50 drachms; of ammoniac incense, 24 drachms; of scraped verdigris, 10 drachms; of oil, 4 xestai, others 2 xestai; the ancients also [add] of pyrites stone, 60 drachms. These, then, were written in sequence by Andromachus.

Apart from these, [551] among the green plasters a certain plaster is written last, as follows. Another green cephalic, from the [prescriptions] of Aphrodas. ℞ Scale [of copper], 40 dr.; Eretrian earth, 20 dr.; birthwort, 30 dr.; isinglass, 16 dr.; ammoniac salt, 12 dr.; misy, 12 dr.; myrrh, 12 dr.; frankincense, 36 dr.; burnt copper, 16 dr.; split alum, 12 dr., and round [alum], 16 dr.; bryony, 12 dr.; black chamaeleon, 12 dr.; burnt resin, 18 dr.; ammoniac incense, 18 dr.; litharge, 12 dr. In another [copy] I found: unfired sulphur and Illyrian [iris], 12 dr. each; chalcanthum, 12 dr.; bull's bile, half a kotyle; vinegar, 1 chous. Under the Dog [Star] make pastilles of 4 dr. each. Mix with wax 4 [units]; vinegar, 6 kotylai; oil, 6 kotylai. [On agglutinative plasters. Some call these 'for bleeding wounds' and 'for wounds'. Their function is to make the divided flesh grow together and to agglutinate it, so that the part is brought back to its original unity.

Not only are fresh bloody wounds agglutinated immediately after the division, while the blood is still [552] flowing, as we sponge it off and then bring the parts together with sutures or clasps; but old sinuses too, once we have first made them free of inflammation and clean by the application of drugs, we unite and make grow together. It has been said in the books of the Therapeutic Method that a drug is called 'removing filth' primarily and in its own right, but 'flesh-producing' and 'agglutinative' secondarily. For it has received this name not because it itself produces flesh or makes the parts grow together, nor as though these were not the works of nature alone, but because, when such drugs are applied, ulcers fill with flesh and grow together. Their proper work is to render the affected part free of superfluities, so that its ichors may not hinder the production of flesh or the agglutination. It was shown that the drugs that make parts grow together are more drying than the flesh-producing ones, and that the flesh-producing ones are of a detergent faculty that is least biting, whereas the agglutinative ones are not necessarily detergent at all, but need only be drying.

And since the drugs that produce the scar are also much [553] more drying than these, together with being sufficiently astringent, let the agglutinative and conglutinative drugs be distinguished from these too, by their drying more moderately. The defining mark of the agglutinative drugs is that they allow no moisture to arise between the parts that are to be agglutinated. The cicatrizing drugs do not do this alone: they also consume the moisture already present in the parts that are to be cicatrized, and in addition make them callous and harden them by their astringency. The flesh-producing ones preserve the blood suitable for renourishment, in quantity and in quality, as much and of such a kind as nature requires for the generation of flesh. And the drug keeps the wound clean. If it took over the wound already in that state, it is itself most non-biting. If the wound has filth, the drug must be detergent in its own power to the same degree as the thickness the filth has reached; but then it must also bite and eat away the newly formed flesh.

It is clear, then, that being of this kind it will not incarnate the ulcer nor fill up the hollow of the flesh, but will both melt it down and diminish it; and for this reason the drugs that cleanse much filth [554], about which I spoke earlier, are not always able to incarnate, but only when, having been melted either with a larger quantity of oil or with rose oil, as are both the 'oily' drug and the one made with papyrus, the vehemence of their detergent action is curbed, or when through the admixture of cerate they become non-biting. Many of the polychrest remedies are of this kind, such as that of Machairion and the Isis. Now the aim of each of these has been stated in the books of the Therapeutic Method; and as for the material of the remedies, the simple material was stated earlier in another treatise, and the compound is stated in the present one. And first of all in it one must bear in mind the nature of the bodies being treated. Those that are moist, and for this reason soft, such as those of women and small children, and of eunuchs and of those who live in a womanish manner, require weaker drugs; but those of men, and especially of all who through manly activities and the sun have acquired a hard habit of body, are not benefited at all by the weak ones.

For this reason, then, the agglutinatives are not common to both kinds of bodies either. Those that are prepared from litharge and oil [555] and vinegar, which I went through in the first book, are agglutinative of weak and soft flesh; those made with asphalt and verdigris and scale, and with aloe and myrrh, are agglutinative of strong and hard flesh. Asphalt itself, on its own, falls within the aim of these powers, but it cannot be used alone, melted with oil, for it is too friable to make a plaster-like drug. So that it may become a plaster, we mix wax and resin with it. Knowing that its power will in turn be weakened by these, we sometimes mix in copper or scale of copper, and often aloe or myrrh, or, in short, one of the drying drugs, and not ineffectively. [The barbarian plasters made with asphalt.] Here too I shall set out first those written by Andromachus, in his own wording. The barbarian, which I use. ℞ Wax, 200 dr.; pitch, 200 dr.; resin, 200 dr.; asphalt, 200 dr.; frankincense, 24 dr.; oil, 1 kotyle. Another. ℞ Pitch, 2 lb.; asphalt, 1 lb.; wax, 1 lb.; ammoniac incense, 6 oz.; manna, 6 oz.

white lead [556] 3 oz.; olive oil, ½ kotyle; vinegar, 4 kotylai. Aphrodas admired this one. Another, black. ℞ Dry pitch, 1 litra; dry resin, 1 litra; bitumen, 1 litra; white lead, 6 oz.; manna, copper vitriol, scraped verdigris, 3 ounces of each; olive oil, half a kotyle; vinegar, half a kotyle. Another, from the drugs of Gallus. ℞ Goat suet, 30 dr.; verdigris, 8 dr.; wax, 50 dr.; birthwort, 25 dr.; bitumen, 25 dr.; pitch, 25 dr.; ammoniac incense, 12 dr.; galbanum, 12½ dr.; silphium, 8 dr. (others: 20); manna, 12. Prepare. Another, the one called 'Invincible'. ℞ Wax, 100 dr.; bull suet, 30 dr.; bitumen, 25 dr.; pitch, 25 dr.; terebinth resin, 25 dr.; nitron, 22½ dr.; birthwort, 12 dr.; galbanum, 8 dr.; myrrh, 18 drachmas; frankincense, 12½ dr.; ammoniac, 8 drachmas; amomum, 8 drachmas; cardamom, 12 dr.; opopanax, 8 drachmas; deer marrow, 15 dr.; verdigris, 12 dr.; aloe, 8 drachmas; bdellium, 16 dr.; olive oil, 2 kotylai. I, however, used to put in 12 drachmas of propolis.

[557] [Another enhaemon plaster of Julian.] ℞ Litharge 50 dr., bitumen 50 dr., wax 50 dr., Bruttian pitch 50 dr., roasted resin 15 dr., flakes of copper 12 dr., frankincense 14 dr., galbanum 8 dr., chalcitis 4 dr., aloe 6 dr., oak-gall 4 dr., myrrh 4 dr., long birthwort 6 dr., round birthwort 4 dr., old oil 4 kotylai. But I used 3 kotylai of oil. [The 'barbaros' of Heras.] The one which Heras recorded as 'barbaros', as follows. A black enhaemon plaster for considerable divisions, and especially for those in the head; for fistulae, sinuses, fractures. It is suitable also for those with liver complaints and those with spleen complaints; it agglutinates without inflammation. It works also on severed nerves and cartilages, and on bones, and it remarkably checks even blood that is flowing. Further, it works for hypophorai and sinuses, for it agglutinates powerfully; and in the case of abscesses, after drawing off the fluid, apply this. It is also a most excellent haemostatic, especially for those who bring up blood.

Spread it on two pieces of skin; apply one [558] to the chest and the sides and the other to the upper back, and it stops the blood remarkably. It is effective also for dog bites and human bites, being wholly free from inflammation. This plaster, as experience has shown, has surpassed the plasters for wounds. Remove it in winter after seven days, in summer after 5; if there is urgency, after three. ♃ Wax one litra, pitch one litra, asphalt one litra, pine resin one litra, manna 6 ounces, white lead 4 ounces, chalcanthum 4 ounces, opopanax 2 ounces, oil half an ounce (some say half a mina, others half a litra), vinegar 2 kotylai. Put the wax, the asphalt, the oil and the vinegar, keeping back a little of it, into a new pot and melt them; then add the pitch and the resin, having carefully chopped them small. When it is half-boiled, lift the pot off, let it cool somewhat, and sprinkle in the chalcanthum, ground with vinegar and strained, taking from the two kotylai little by little, so that it does not boil over. When you have poured it in, heat it gently from below, stirring.

When it no longer soils, lift it from the fire and pour in the opopanax, which has been steeped one day beforehand in part of the remaining [559] vinegar so that it dissolves. Then sprinkle in the white lead and the manna together, both carefully ground, and warm it a little so that it unites, taking care that the opopanax and the manna do not burn on. Pour it out into a mortar, let it cool, knead it again, store it away and use it. It is clear that the other barbarian plasters too, which Andromachus and the others recorded, should be prepared in the same way. Some do not put the opopanax into the pot; instead they grind it with vinegar in a mortar and pour the melted ingredients over it. Together with it some also first grind the manna and the white lead in the mortar with vinegar, as I too have often done, and then pour on the meltable ingredients after melting them. Often, however, I have ground only the chalcanthum with the opopanax and put it into the pot, sprinkling in the manna and the white lead. Another barbarian plaster, of Heras. Heras prefixed the title 'barbarian' to this one alone. But I named the preceding one in the same way, although he had called it 'black', since most of the more recent physicians are accustomed to call the plasters made with bitumen 'barbarian'.

Heras himself wrote about it [560] word for word as follows: 'The barbaros, for freshly inflicted wounds, sinuses, dog bites, human bites, inflamed condylomata, for all affections in the joints at their onset, and for podagra. ℞ Wax, 1 mina; pitch, 1 mina; roasted resin, 1 mina; Judaean asphalt, 1 mina; litharge, 10 dr.; white lead, 5 dr.; verdigris, 50 dr.; opopanax, 4 dr.; oil, 1 kotyle; vinegar, 1 kyathos. Boil the wax, pitch, asphalt and resin until melted, then put in the rest, triturated with the oil; and, having lifted it off and cooled it a little, drip in the vinegar little by little.' Such, then, is roughly the pattern of the barbaros plasters. But I shall add something, namely how I myself use them, and so bring my account of them to a close. There are two: one for the largest wounds, the other for smaller ones. The composition of the one employed for the largest is as follows. [Galen's barbaros.] ℞ Pitch, 8 litrai; wax, 6 litrai, 8 ounces; pine resin, 5 litrai, 4 ounces; asphalt, 4 litrai; oil, 1 litra, 210 (?) ounces.

of litharge, [561] of white lead and of verdigris, 24 drachms each; of frankincense, half a pound; of liquid alum, 12 drachms; of split [alum], 4 ounces; of opopanax, of scale, of galbanum, 12 drachms each; of aloe, of opium and of myrrh, 4 drachms each; of terebinth, 24 ounces; of the juice of mandrake, 6 drachms; of vinegar, 6 cotylae, which are 5 pounds. The proportion in the composition of the simpler barbaros is as follows. ℞ Of pitch, wax, pine resin, roasted resin, bitumen, these five, 1 pound of each; of litharge, 10 drachms; of white lead, 5 drachms; of verdigris, 5 drachms; of opopanax, 3 drachms; of oil, in winter 9 ounces, in summer 6 ounces. The meltable ingredients are poured over the dry ones, which have been ground smooth in a mortar with acrid vinegar. If you wish the drug to be more anodyne, you will mix in 1½ drachms of the juice of henbane and 1 drachm of opium.

[562] GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK III. These notes too I write for you, my companions, who have come to know through the very works of the art how great a power our treatment of the nerve-wounded has, and how all were saved, being neither maimed nor lamed. These are things you saw happening to those treated otherwise, just as you also saw some seized by spasm, or dying with pains, putrefactions or fevers. It is likely, however, that these notes will also fall into the hands of

others [563], these notes, that is, falling into the hands of people who are unable to make good use of what is written in them. This may be either because they have not learned the theory of the medical art from a teacher, but are wholly uninstructed and altogether untrained, or because they have learned badly, keeping to those who say that compound drugs have been discovered without reasoning, through experience alone. For these plainly go wrong out of love of contention. In another way, and no less than they, so do those who think that no drug ought to be compounded from simples that are contrary in their powers. But these were refuted by the drugs written down in the first book of notes. Those drugs displayed their great powers, and they were made from simples whose composition was from contraries. And not least in the books that are to be written after this one, we shall show excellent drugs whose composition is from things contrary in their powers.

Now, however, my account throughout this whole book will concern our own method, which we devised for the nerve-wounded, as I show how great a number of drugs having the same powers [564] I found, from having devised the general manner of the treatment and from knowing the powers of the simple drugs. [What the general manner of treatment of the nerve-wounded is, and what the drugs are according to species.] I observed all my teachers treating by the method which is now customarily called by the more recent physicians the 'bloody' (enaimos) and agglutinative method. For at the beginning they applied one of the drugs called 'bloody' (enaima) and tried to glue together the lips of the wound. And if it became inflamed, they bathed it with hot water in abundance, pouring oil in alongside, and applied as a sprinkled application (epipasma) wheaten flour boiled in hydrelaeum (water-and-oil). Moreover, I also saw the gladiators, those who had been wounded at the kneecap and above it at the broad and thin tendon, being treated by them in the same way. But perhaps it would be better to say not 'being treated' but 'perishing'; for very few of them came through, and these were left lame.

And indeed, of the tendons at the extremity of the hand, through which the fingers are flexed [565] and extended, I saw very many, whether contused or pricked by the slightest puncture, putrefying in such a way as to resemble things boiled in water, and especially things boiled for a longer time. For in the same way as these, the parts treated by the aforementioned method become slack and soft in their consistency. I therefore condemned that method, as one that putrefies the wounded part. And since I further recognised that all putrefying things undergo this through moisture and heat, I judged that the treatment ought to be carried out by means of things that dry and cool. But then, reflecting that cold has truly been said by Hippocrates to be hostile to the nerves, I judged that the best drug for the nerve-wounded would be one that both dries and holds a middle position between heating and cooling, or that has not departed far from the mean in the direction of heating. Indeed, the drug can even be quite hot, provided that it has the property of drying. For without moisture it is not possible for what heats to cause putrefaction.
