Further, in addition to these, having also considered this further point, that it makes a great difference whether one applies the drug to the affected part when it is bare or through other bodies [566] lying in front of it, I recognised that it was proper to use some drugs when the nerve has been laid bare, and other drugs when it has been punctured while the bodies lying in front of it remain unaffected. For where one applies the drug to the bare nerve, there it was proper to adopt the indication already stated for the drugs that had been of benefit in its unmixed form. But when the parts lying in front are unaffected, one must find a finer-particled drug, so that its power is not dissipated beforehand in passing through the intervening bodies, but reaches the depth. And such a drug, if it is by nature strongly drying, is able to do no harm even if it should not be well-proportioned in respect of heat and cold, since its activity in heating or cooling becomes weaker while it passes through the parts lying in front of the nervous body. The aim of the drugs that had been of benefit having been found to lie in the fine-particled character of their substance, the next step was to recall the material.

It had been established in the investigation of simple drugs that most of the heating drugs are fine-particled, and [567] most of the cooling ones thick-particled. For among these [the cooling ones] only one quality, the sour, is sometimes found together with a fine-particled substance; and for this reason the sharpest vinegar is finer-particled than all the cooling things, and it has also been shown to partake of a slight heat. Among the heating drugs, in turn, the saps are the finest-particled, and the foremost of them, as all men already know, is the Cyrenaic; but when this is not to hand we also use the Median, and those brought along with them from the eastern regions, such as the one called sagapenum. Of the same kind as these is also the sap of euphorbium produced in the western parts of the inhabited world, whether one wishes to call it a sap or something else. For our part it will suffice throughout the whole discussion to call this drug euphorbium, as is now the custom with everyone. But also among those produced in our own country, the sap of panax and the saps of the spurges are of fine-particled power. And indeed all the saps mentioned heat vigorously.

The [juice] of opobalsam, although it too is fine-particled, does not heat very much; but it has a fine-particled substance. Among earthy things, the foam of nitre and the aphronitre that is readily dissolved by water [are fine-particled], you understanding of course [that they are so] as among earthy bodies. Next after them comes the nitre called Berenician, and the Asian stone. The flower of this [stone] is the most fine-particled of all earthy things. Among mined substances, arsenikon and sulphur are both fine-particled and hot. Next after these come misy, copper flake and chalcitis, which also have something of astringency; for this reason we mostly use chalcitis burnt for the compositions of the more fine-particled drugs. Mineral drugs that are fine-particled without heating perceptibly are spodium, pompholyx and the so-called psoricum. Chrysocolla too is quite fine-particled. Among the juices we have learnt that laurel [oil] is fine-particled and at the same time heats strongly, so far as perception is concerned. For cedar [oil], although it heats no less than it in potency, falls short in heat as perceived because of its fineness of parts.

For if he does not come thus prepared to the [572] benefit to be had from these treatises, he will know the method as far as words go, but will accomplish no work worthy of it. For suppose that someone knows the very things I have said before about the nerve-wounded, but through ignorance puts adulterated drugs into the compounds, or does not even know their faculties precisely in the first place: will it not necessarily follow that this man fails more often than he succeeds? To me, at least, it very much seems so. Knowing the faculties precisely differs very greatly from merely knowing them. For merely to know is to recognise whether the drug is of a nature to dry or to moisten or to cool or to heat us. But to know precisely is, in addition to this, to have recognised also the quantity of the faculty. For some drugs have a faculty productive of lukewarm heat when they come into contact with our bodies, some of moderate heat, just as others have a faculty of heat a little stronger than this, and others again of heat already seething so strongly that it is able to burn. The physician must therefore aim at not only the quality of the condition but also its quantity, as one might call it.

[573] For 'quantity' is not said at all properly in the case of quality. Nevertheless it is said, just as a fever too is called great and small. And so widespread is the use of expressions said in this way that they now have the force of a proper term, much like pyxis (box), chalkeus (smith), zōgraphos (painter) and drytomos (woodcutter), and, in a word, like those terms which began from what the grammarians name catachresis, but later came to be believed to be spoken properly. I have said these things on account of those who practise dialectic out of season. What I left off saying is this: that what needs to be dried does not simply need what dries, but needs it with the appropriate measure. What has advanced into much moisture needs what dries very strongly; what has advanced into little moisture needs what does this slightly; just as what has advanced into much moisture needs what dries greatly, yet not extremely nor to the utmost. For the quantity of dryness must always be proportional to the quantity of moisture.

I, then, when I first ventured to alter the common method of treating the nerve-wounded, made a conjecture as to the degree of moisture and heat that the [574] affected body had reached. And when a certain young man was shown to me who, at the first joint of the middle finger of the right hand, had as a result of a contusion the whole region at it, around the nerve, so moist that it was already putrefying, I poulticed the putrefying part itself with percolated lye and raw lysis (know that this is what I call barley meal); and having bathed with plenty of warm oil the part that was not putrefying but was tense and painful, and then wiped it with dry wool, I smeared around it a cerate as moist as the one we use for fractures, having euphorbium mixed into it. This cerate too had been prepared by me according to my own devising, on an occasion of the following kind. Someone came to me in a severe winter and, showing me his knee, said that it was readily affected when chilled, but was immediately helped by warming things. He asked to receive some such drug, for, having travelled on foot in the frost, he had been chilled through and was in pain more severely than at other times. 'Now then,' he said, 'I am going off to bathe, and I shall send for the drug from the bath-house.'

Having said this, he went away. [575] Having no such drug ready, I ground euphorbium fine with oil, and having melted wax I mixed it in; and a little later, when my friend sent asking for the drug, I gave it. When he very quickly became free of pain, I was prompted by this to use it on other parts similarly affected, about which I shall speak again later. But now I return to the account of the nerve-wounded, because of those who know nothing of the things I am now expounding, yet find fault with petty words. These, I divine, will find that it is wrong to call 'nerve-wounded' those who have been wounded in the tendons. For I think they call 'tendons' the structures stretched along the outer side of the hand, over the whole wrist and the fingers. For my part, I am not unaware that it would be clearer and more proper for them to be named 'tendon-wounded'. But since all men customarily call them 'nerve-wounded', I preferred the customary name to the true one, so that no one might say that I am innovating in names. Yet not even this name could itself have become customary had not most physicians already, without reason, taken to calling the tendons 'nerves' as well.

But whether you wish [576] to call them 'nerve-wounded' or 'tendon-wounded', they will neither be saved by these words nor be seized by spasm because of them, just as they will not be crippled or die because of them either. For a name has never yet saved a man, nor killed one; it is the power of the drugs that brings about each of these outcomes. And I, by changing these, make those who are putrefying and in spasm and crippled, and some who are even perishing, healthy and alive. For moreover physicians have long been accustomed to call those whose nerves have been crushed, as that man's had been crushed, 'nerve-wounded', not 'nerve-crushed'. But the treatment is common to both, and the danger equal, those who have had some part crushed and those who have been wounded, whether in nerves or in tendons.

That man, at any rate, who was already putrefying in the region of the first joint of the middle finger, and was suffering tension and pain in the parts lying above, became much better than he had been on the following day, on which, instead of the raw solution, I mixed the meal of bitter vetch with strained lye; and on the third day, while still being treated in the same way, he was by now entirely free of pain in other respects, but at the contusion a nerve-like body [577] resembling a thick membrane protruded, which, when I moved it moderately, came away easily and whole, being half-putrefied. It seemed, then, to all who saw this body that it was the whole nerve, putrefied through, since they did not know how these tendons, clothed in nerve-like membranes, pass forward through the wrist and are extended along the whole length of the fingers. But when I opened up the putrefied part of the contusion, the tendon appeared to me to be preserved. So, dissolving one of the troches, or 'little discs', or whatever one may wish to call them (of which the one of Polyeidus is also one), in boiled-down must or siraeum (for you too may call this whatever you yourself wish), and first anointing the exposed part of the nerve, I again used the poultice in the same way, and the ointment with euphorbium on the same places, as before for each. And having seen on the fourth day that everything had subsided around the first joint of the finger, which had previously been contused but was then ulcerated, I considered to what I should pass on from the poultice.

I therefore resolved that, if the nerve were entirely free of inflammation, [578] I would pass on to the cicatrizing remedies; but if some scirrhous remnant of its inflammation were left behind, I would apply one of the strongly drying remedies. Since, then, something did appear to remain, I first used the drug made with the root of dracontium, which has all its other ingredients the same as the Egyptian drug called Isis but has the root of dracontium added. After this I used the one called Athena, and from that I then went on to the cicatrizing remedies. In another case, smearing the exposed parts of the wound with the pastille dissolved in siraeum (boiled-down must), I laid euphorbium over it on the outside, having mixed it with wax and resin in such quantity that it would at once become plaster-like and preserve the potency of the euphorbium. How one might compound the drug while looking to these aims I shall state next. For I also made another drug with vinegar, and in that one too I had as my aim both its consistency and that the fine-particled potency of the vinegar should be preserved while its cooling potency was dissipated.

How these were compounded, however, [579] will be stated a little later. For now, since I devised the course of treatment of the 'nerve-wounded' by rational indication, without the nonsensical accidental encounter (periptōsis) of the Empiricists, I wish to set it out in its entirety, omitting no distinction and taking up the account again from the beginning. Whenever I take on someone who has just been wounded, I sometimes carry out the treatment with the liquid drugs and sometimes with the plasters, laying over them on the outside wool as soft as possible, soaked in warm oil. If I am using the drug made with vinegar, I mix a little vinegar into the oil. I unbind the dressing two or three times a day and pour warm oil over the part. When the nights are long, I am accustomed to unbind it during the night as well. I do this all the more when the wound is being bitten by the drugs. For when I have used such a drug from the beginning and the patient says he feels neither biting nor pain, and perceives no tension, I unbind and pour oil over the part twice a day, the first time around dawn and the second towards evening. Let the oil that is poured over be quite hot, but only so far as not to distress the wounded part.

For just as cold is most contrary [580] to such dispositions, so the lukewarm is not entirely beneficial. For we learned in the first book of On the Power of Simple Drugs that, just as water by nature produces most contrary effects according as it is hot or cold, so too does oil. For when it is applied cold it in a way plasters up, or rather it holds back, the transpirations of the body, whereas hot oil disperses and thins. You can learn this also from meats boiled in it. For it makes them friable in the same way as meats that have been kept overnight beforehand, even if you boil or fry them in it immediately upon the slaughter of the animal. For this reason, then, I too chose the affusion with oil that is sufficiently hot, always avoiding the lukewarm, and still more the cold.

The use of water I avoid throughout the whole treatment, to the point of not even letting it touch the wound. So when, right at the beginning, the blood has to be washed off the wounded part, I do this with oil. And when the patients, already in a moderate condition, take a bath, not even then do I allow them to put the affected place into the water. For the most part those with wounded nerves are wounded in the hands themselves [581]. I remember one of those wounded in this way who, since on the fourth day he was entirely free of pain and saw that the affected part was free of inflammation, went out of his house in severe cold on some necessary business. Having spent rather a long time over it, he came home with the whole limb tense right up to the neck and feeling great pain. When someone came to fetch me and I went to him and saw the state he was in, I ordered the oil on the part, which had grown cold from his going out, to be removed. I poured hot oil over the whole limb, and then also over the part of the neck in line with it, fomented with wool soaked in oil, and applied the liquid drug made with euphorbium together with castoreum. With that I soothed the man at once, and when sleep came on, all the symptoms had ceased by evening. One must therefore take the greatest care that the wool remains warm, whether it happens to be soaked in oil alone or in oxelaeon (oil with vinegar). This can be achieved if other, dry wool is wrapped around it on the outside, and if the patient stays indoors, when it is winter, until the fifth or the seventh

[582] day of the patient. For if up to this day no inflammation appears, and he is entirely free of pain and perceives no tension, he will thereafter be out of danger. Let it be your concern that nothing winy shows itself in the vinegar, just as also in the case of the oil, so that it is free of all astringency. Let it therefore be neither the so-called omotribes (oil of unripe olives) or omphacine (for it is named in two ways), nor the oil from Iberia, which they call Spanish, nor indeed any other of those that contain shoots of the olive. The best oil, then, is the fine-particled kind, such as the Sabine is in Italy, and elsewhere, among the nations under the Romans, those that show no astringency.

What sort of thing rational indication is, and how much richer it is than bare experience without method, you will learn from these cases too. Often, when I came upon many nerve-wounded people on roads, on voyages, in the countryside, or in the city but far from my house, and neither the drug made with euphorbium nor the one made with vinegar was at hand, I applied to the wound some other of the drugs that chanced to be available in that place (the text reads 'nor any other'), and I always [583] attained my aim. In the countryside, I know that I applied to the wound fresh propolis, moist and fatty, which the farmer had; sometimes leaven alone; and sometimes both mixed together. The leaven should be as old as possible, whereas the propolis should be the opposite of it in respect of age. If the propolis is rather old, let it be softened with oil by the fire or in the sun. In the case of another rustic, I mixed the juice of the spurge with the leaven and applied it, having seen the plant growing near his farmyard. I had judged the leaven deficient because it was fresh. And sometimes I melted propolis with oil and worked it into the leaven, having first kneaded the leaven with the sharpest vinegar. In such mixtures it is better for the oil to be old. Then there are the poultices made with oxymel and flour of beans, or of bitter vetch, or of darnel, or of chickpeas, or of bitter lupins, or with fine meal of barley-groats, or with barley flour. These are the poultices I have used in the cities, not only on parts already inflamed but also immediately at the outset.

In the country, too, having found liquid pitch at a carpenter's, [584] I mixed it with the leaven and applied it; and with another patient I kneaded the meal of bitter vetch into it. If this is not at hand, it is possible to mix in any one whatever of the aforementioned as well. I have also taken up oxelaeum (vinegar-and-oil) alone in wool and applied it warm at once, when nothing else was at hand; for I had confidence in the vinegar, since it was both sufficiently sharp and old. In another case, where the part had already been chilled beforehand because the nerve had been bruised an hour or even still longer before, I waited until something of the suitable remedies should be brought to me, having ordered the part to be bathed with oil poured over it. And then, having first mixed in vinegar, since the ambient air was very hot, it being the summer season, I kept pouring the mixture of both over it for a very long time, until some one of the other drugs was brought. Having often mixed each of the aforesaid meals with the percolated lye, I applied it as a poultice, both right at the beginning and afterwards, when the person had already made improper use of one of the 'bloody' (enaimos) drugs. At any rate, let all these drugs, in whatever way they are applied, be administered hot in their qualities.

Moreover, once also, from my own house, when none of the compound drugs was found ready to hand and I was hurrying to go out, [585] I gave one of my people some old euphorbium, and ordered him to grind it with old oil to the consistency of a liquid cerate and apply it to the puncture of the tendon in the hand. When I returned and asked the wounded man whether he had a sensation of much heat in the place, he said he felt a moderate one. So I asked him again whether he was being bitten at the wound by the drug. When he said that he was not bitten, but had the sensation as it were of some itching, I allowed the drug to remain applied until night. And when, after what had been applied was removed, the heat in the affected region appeared to me moderate and the puncture had not closed, it seemed to me better to use the same drug. And indeed, since on the following day the man with the wounded nerve was in an irreproachable condition, on the third and fourth days too, right to the end, I used the same drug; and someone who had seen this used fresh euphorbium in the same way on another man wounded in the same place.

Of necessity, then, great heat, biting and pain in the wound ensued in the wounded man, so that the man was brought to me [586], as though for something unexpected that had befallen him. And I, understanding at once what had happened, threw off what had been applied, and after pouring oil over him I applied the drug made with vinegar. Had this not been at hand, I would have applied the drug made with euphorbium that contains more wax. So then, just as we were saying a little earlier that one must not be ignorant of the potencies and the forms of approved drugs, so too one must not be ignorant of which of them change their potency quickly and which preserve it for a very long time. For euphorbium is one of those whose hotness quickly fades. You will recognise this even without chewing it, by looking at its colour. For as it grows old it becomes not ash-coloured, as it is at first, but somewhat pale and somewhat yellow. At the same time it then also appears quite dry, and it dissolves only with difficulty when it is ground with oil, whereas the fresh is quickly reduced to juice. One must not mix it with the oil straight away, but first grind it gently in the mortar, so that it is not flattened out.

And why need I say that, when you taste it as well, the fresh [587] appears most fiery, so as to burn the tongue, whereas the old produces little heat? It happens, then, with many other drugs too that within a few years they have their power fading away, but with none less than euphorbium, after thapsia at least. For thapsia becomes quite weak after a year, and when it has become two years old it breathes out its strength entirely. Euphorbium, however, when it is both good from the beginning and well stored, still preserves some power even in the third year, and sometimes also in the fourth; but it is already slackening in the fifth and sixth, and then, as time advances, it becomes completely dimmed. The aged euphorbium which I said I once used with oil without wax was about five or six years old. Hence it is not possible to define its use in a fixed measure. For when it is new it is mixed with ten and twelve times as much oil, together with three times as much wax; but as it grows old one must put in more of it; and when it has become three and four years old, either double the original amount or an amount equal to the wax.

Now, whenever you wish the drug to have a consistency similar to the ointments called acopa, [588] which is indeed also the consistency of the liquid cerate, the oil must be four times the wax. But whenever it is to become plaster-like, one must mix the wax in, on the whole, equal to the oil, especially if the wax is dry and old; for fresh wax, being also fatty, needs less oil to make a plaster-like cerate, and still more so in the summer season. So someone wishing to make the cerate plaster-like will melt the wax in oil in the proportion I have stated and will mix into it a sixth part of fresh euphorbium, so that there is 1 drachm of that, six of the wax, and six or five of oil. But since the gluey and viscous quality does not belong to wax, as it does to resin and to pitch, for this reason I mix into the cerate resin or pitch, or a portion of each. It is quite clear, then, that when these are mixed in, the oil is no longer to be put in equal to them. For wax needs much fat for moistness, whereas of the resins the dry ones need altogether little, and the moist ones even want to take on some dry substance besides for a plaster-like consistency.

[589] Among waxes, then, there is no great difference with respect to moistness and dryness; with resins, by contrast, as also with pitch, the difference between the dry ones and the moist ones is very great. The driest of the resins is the one which some call 'roasted' and others 'Colophonian'. Second is the one from the potteries, unpurified and unroasted; but if one purifies it, it passes over into the roasted kind. Drier than both of these is the so-called pine physēma (blister-resin). This, as being parched, I rejected, considering it unsuitable for the composition of the plaster under discussion; instead I used both the roasted resin and the moist ones. Of these too, some remain moist for a longer time, such as terebinth, while others dry quickly, such as strobiline. Intermediate between the two is fir resin. Moreover, in their powers as well, strobiline is hotter, fir resin second, and terebinth third after both. Cypress resin I was wary of mixing in, as having something of astringency.

Someone will think that we disagree, in our account of resins, with Dioscorides of Anazarbus, who wrote the following statement in the [590] first book On Materials: 'The terebinth takes precedence over all the resins, and after it the mastic resin, then the pine resin and the fir resin, after which are counted the peuce resin and the strobiline.' For in these words Dioscorides evidently regards the strobiline as the worst and the terebinth as the best. But I, of these three resins, strobiline, fir and terebinth, said that the strobiline is first and best in respect of heat, the fir resin second, and the terebinth last. Just as, then, the one who says that of the austere wines in Italy the Italian wine is best speaks the truth (for the one refers his statement to a single quality, while the other pronounces simply about their whole substance), in the same way also with the resins one might reasonably say that the terebinth is the best, as being a most polychrest drug, but not that it ranks first in heat.

As I was saying, then, by mixing with the wax whichever of the resins you wish, you can bring the simple cerate, which we compound from oil and wax [591] alone, to a more adhesive consistency. In this, however, there is also need of experience, to judge our conjecture. For you can mix a threefold quantity of the wax with the terebinth and learn whether the drug has already taken on a plaster-like consistency, or whether it is still rather too dry and needs still more resin. Then, whenever it appears to you, as you test it in this way, to be in due proportion, mix into the drug being made a twelfth part of euphorbium. If you do not know whether the euphorbium is properly hot, or falls somewhat short of this after the preparation, spread a little of what has been prepared on a linen cloth and lay it on your own shin or forearm for some hours. Then, if it seems to you to heat moderately, take the preparation to be well tempered. But if it either produces no perceptible heating or is more fiery than is fitting, you can either weaken the drug or intensify it: weaken it by mixing in cerate, intensify it by adding euphorbium.

If, however, you have greasy propolis, know that it will be more suitable for you than all the resins, since it is by nature apt both to draw in [592] and to pull out from the depth vaporous thicknesses of pneuma and superfluous moistures. For the resins are taken together with the wax for the sake of the plaster-like consistency, not as falling under the aim of the treatment; but propolis pertains to the very aim of the cure. And once, as I said, I used it alone, fresh, in liquid form, in the case of a certain farmer who had a hard body, and it was wonderful how he benefited, using it alone to the end, so that he needed no other drug; in the case of another, who had the puncture deeper, I mixed in a little of the juice of one of the spurges. To soft bodies, however, the drug appears rather hard to the touch, unless one softens it thoroughly by mixture of oil. And indeed all the other drugs that are applied to the nerve-wounded ought to be liquid and soft. Softness, then, any oil can provide, but old oil can preserve the strength of the drug.

Just as I once, in the country, applied propolis, having selected it as the better drug among those then at hand, so too on another occasion [593] I applied leaven to another patient, when no drug was at hand, since I knew that this too both draws out and disperses what lies in the depth. And the longer the leaven has been kept, the better it is. Not only are such things easily found in country places, but also unfired sulphur, which I myself once used as well, mixing it with the tetrapharmacum. With this, then, I often mixed and used aphronitre, and Berenician litron, and aphrolitre (not the stony kind, but true aphrolitre, which has a frothy consistency), not only in the country for want of other things, but even when the aforementioned drugs were at hand, in order to test my devising by experience; and through this use alone the wounded man was cured, being of course bathed with the oil. For let you take this as common to all the drugs here said to be suited to the nerve-wounded. And what physicians call arsenikon, and those who wish to Atticize everything call arrhenikon, I mixed with the tetrapharmacum preparation, wishing to test my devising.

And again, when this was not at hand, [594] [I mixed in] the so-called realgar (sandarachē), just as I also did with lime (titanos), both slaked and unslaked, both unwashed and washed, putting in a little of the unslaked, but more of the slaked, and still more of the washed. The exact quantity for each composition will be stated a little later, once I have first gone through all these simples and the distinctions (diorismoi) governing their use. For in this discourse it seemed good to me to set out the treatment (agōgē) of the nerve-wounded because of the Empiricists, who hold that most compound drugs have been discovered by accidental encounter (periptōsis). This treatment was discovered by me without accidental encounter, from knowing the aim (skopos) of their therapy and from understanding the powers (dynameis) of the simple drugs. For by accidental encounter a single one of the simple drugs is found, whereas the rational (logikē) method finds many of the simples all together, and a great many compositions based on them. At any rate, all things whose nature is to draw outward from the depth and to disperse (diaphorein) the moistures are suitable for the nerve-wounded.

But since some of these have joined to them heats that are rather immoderate, or strongly biting pungencies or acidities, it is reasonable to mix with them [595] other drugs that are able to make the said excesses more moderate without harming the potency. It is not possible to do this correctly without knowing, for each of the drugs, not only the kind of its quality but also the amount within it. For some, as we showed in the treatise on simple drugs, belong to the first order of heating drugs, having departed only a little from the well-tempered; others lie in the second order itself, standing further off; and some belong to the third and the fourth, certain others being already able to burn. Thus, in proportion to the intensity in the potency of each drug, the potency of the drugs mixed together is found, provided one knows the temperaments of all the simple drugs. But the [composition] of the Empiricists, which mixes only drugs of the same kind, comes about through ignorance of the nature of each drug; and, among those who do know this nature, because the amount of the excess is not securely known.

I myself, then, compounded the first drug I ever prepared from many ingredients of the same kind, because I did not yet know precisely the quantity [596] of the potency of each. For I put in some arsenikon, sulphur, misy, and quicklime both unwashed and washed, and pompholyx, and likewise spodium. In addition to these, also copper flakes and burnt chalcitis, both unwashed and washed, and moreover the unburnt kind. These, then, I first ground fine in the sharpest vinegar for many days in the summer sun. The things to be poured over them were, of necessity, wax, a little honey skimmed beforehand, nearly all the resins, propolis, pitch and ladanum. As liquids there were henna-oil and lily-oil, balsam juice, marjoram-oil, must-oil and cedar-oil, and both castor oil and old olive oil. Of each of the juices I mentioned a little earlier there was also a small amount. Later, removing one ingredient at one time and another at another for the sake of trial, I found that each of the simpler compounds, which I use to this day, fell short in nothing. Their proportions will be stated a little later. I prepared such drugs with vinegar and with the juices, mixing into them some wax, the resins already mentioned, propolis and pitch; and likewise also with pigeon dung and the fine-particled herbs.

[597] Liquid drugs, then, cause less distress, both for other wounds and especially for those in the nerves. But we also use the plaster-like ones, on account of those who wish to bathe. For once the wool has been removed, having only such a drug lying on [the part], they bathe with less discomfort. For it has been said before that not even then is it proper to wet the wounded part with water, at least if it is on the hand. When, however, the wound has occurred in the foot, it is impossible not to wet the part, but in that case one must abstain from the bath for the first four days. But since in present-day life the endurance of all men has perished, now reaching even to those in the countryside, accustomed as they are to bathe every day, we find those who are not very given to luxury (and these would be the poor) for the most part compliant, but the rich, and above all those of them who wield great power, either hard to persuade or wholly disobedient. It would therefore be best not to treat them at all.

But since, I know not how, each for a different reason, some of us unwillingly and others willingly are compelled to put up with their softness, [598] I am accustomed to do something of this kind. Placing one of the plaster-like drugs on the wounded part, I again lay over it on the outside several many-folded linen cloths soaked through with oil, and over these in turn, on the outside, I put a bandage of linen cloth. After this, again in the bath itself, I first pour the oil over the bandage when the nerve-wounded patient is about to step into the tub [reading πύελον for πτύελον]; and when he has, of course, bathed, I take off everything that was laid on and follow the previously described course of the whole treatment. It is quite clear that whoever is going to take proper care of the nerve-wounded must also be experienced in the nature of the parts. For it was said earlier that the tendons too, in which most of the muscles terminate, bring on no small sympathetic affections, first producing spasms, and later both putrefying themselves and destroying along with themselves everything that lies near. Some of them are like membranes, thin and broad, such as are stretched underneath at the ends of the thighs next to the knees, on the inner side of the hands, and on the underside of the feet.

For all these touch the skin, [599] those of them that are in the hands and the feet being quite firmly grown together with it, whereas those that reach down to the kneecap come away from the surrounding skin by flaying. This too befell me by chance. For I devised the treatment of the nerve-wounded while I was still young, when I first returned from Alexandria to my native city, having reached my twenty-eighth year. And since I gave each of the drugs I had devised to physicians who were my friends, not only to my fellow citizens but also to those of the neighbouring cities, so that everything might be confirmed by experience; and it seemed good, I know not how, to the high priest of our city to entrust the treatment of the gladiators to me alone, although I was young in age. For I was beginning my twenty-ninth year. At that time I treated those wounded in the front and lower part of the thigh by means of the treatment I had devised: in those who had the wound transverse, I myself cut through what remained of the tendon, so that the treatment might be without danger for me; and in those who had the wound small or longitudinal, I carried out the whole treatment with both safety and apprehension at once.

For whereas all the physicians before me [600] bathed them very extensively with hot water and applied a poultice of wheaten flour boiled to a moderate degree in hydrelaeum (water and oil), I did not apply water at all. Instead, by frequently pouring oil over them together with the drugs already mentioned, I quickly made them all healthy. By chance many had died in the preceding years, but under my care no one died, either among those wounded in the way described or from any other wound. So the second high priest, the one who followed the man who had then entrusted the treatment to me, likewise himself entrusted me with the care of the gladiators, after an interval of seven months. For the first held the high priesthood from about the autumnal equinox, the second from the height of spring. And again, since under him all were saved, the third, the fourth and the fifth in the same way entrusted me with the treatment of the gladiators, so that I had extensive testing of the method of treatment. During this time something of the following kind also occurred to me, and those physicians who wish to undertake the treatment of wounds correctly must above all pay attention to it.

For having observed [601] one of the gladiators called 'horsemen' with a transverse division, reaching to a great depth at the front and lower part of the thigh, and having seen the lips of the wound, the one drawn up above and the other drawn down below, as if towards the kneecap, I ventured, departing from what is named the 'broad' method, to bring the separated parts of the muscles together to one another with sutures. Taking care, then, not to stitch the tendons together with them, I first stripped those away, and in this way I used the sutures through a great depth, knowing that there is no danger as regards the fleshy part itself of the muscles, but that the danger arises from the tendons; and I had not seen any of my teachers doing even this. For some of them, in such woundings, sutured only the lips of the skin, while others, venturing to suture the muscles themselves at their fleshy parts, made the bringing-together superficially, so that if ever the wound had come about penetrating to a considerable depth, not along the length of the limb, the superficial part of the muscle would become agglutinated, but all the rest would remain unagglutinated.

For in the case of [602] wounds along the length of the limb, bandaging is sufficient to bring the parts of the wounded muscle together with one another; but in those where the wound is transverse, since bandaging can be of no help, the whole thing is accomplished by suture alone. If, then, one does not make these [sutures] through the depth, the parts of the muscle in this region remain unagglutinated. When I had succeeded in this operation, certain people inexperienced in anatomy, imitating the same thing, flay off from beneath all muscles the underlying membranes, not knowing that these may be sutured together with the muscles without danger, whereas the tendons that are flattened out like them are sutured with the greatest danger. Yet however much these may be flattened, they are nevertheless still thicker and harder than the membranes. You will see quite thin tendons also in all the muscles of the epigastrium except the two straight ones, upon which the membranous aponeuroses of the oblique ones are laid. No other tendon besides those mentioned is flattened in a membranous manner; for all those that are flattened retain a considerable thickness, so that they escape no one's notice.

The sympathetic affection (sympatheia) of the overlying parts, however, up to the origin of its [603] nerves, occurs no less in the muscles at the end of the thigh and in those that insert into the elbow of the forearm, and in those that insert into the heel. In each of these the tendons do become broadened, but while preserving a considerable thickness; and at the heel even more so: the tendon that descends from the calf (gastroknēmia) appears both robust and thick, as being composed of three aponeuroses. This too had escaped the notice of the anatomists older than me, as had many other things concerning the muscles as wholes, and still far more concerning veins, arteries and nerves. But many of my companions already know all these things and demonstrate them to their students when my anatomical books are read.

I have mentioned these things that become evident from dissection, though, as one might suppose, they have nothing in common with a treatise on the composition of drugs, because I feared that people, going wrong through ignorance of this kind, would either regard the whole method of treatment with suspicion or needlessly strip off the membranes, guarding against a harm which they falsely suppose will come from them. In the same way certain others, who do not [604] know how to recognise the ligaments, regard them with the same suspicion as wounded nerves and tendons, although the ligaments are free of danger whatever they suffer, since they are insensible and take their origin from bones, not from muscles as the tendons do, nor from the brain and spinal marrow as the nerves do. Many of the most esteemed physicians have therefore spoken very well on this matter, as on many others, in saying that the parts of medicine need one another (I mean the surgical, the pharmaceutical and the dietetic), and that the surgical part above all needs both of the others. So if you look often in apes at the position and size of each tendon and nerve, you will remember them precisely, and should you ever have the opportunity of dissecting a human body, you will quickly find each one as you had observed it. But if you are wholly unpractised, you would gain no benefit from such an opportunity, just as the physicians in the German war, who had licence to dissect the bodies of barbarians, learned nothing more than cooks know.

For the dissection of the Empiricists by accidental encounter is a long piece of nonsense, like [605] the goats pricked by sharp rushes. Still more nonsensical than this is learning through anatomical treatises, which resembles those called, in the proverb, 'helmsmen from a book'. For when those who have clearly seen the nerves of the body and their tendons demonstrated by a teacher do not remember accurately the place in which they lie unless they see them a second and a third time and many times in succession, hardly could anyone learn them by reading. At any rate the best of the Empiricists of our time, who had read all the books of the anatomists, once, when a child at a school had been pricked with a writing-stylus in the inner region of the arm, above its middle parts, applied one of the plaster drugs of which he had recently had experience, when it had treated a man wounded in a nerve. Seeing the child free of inflammation and free of pain under it, he thought it had been completely cured; but suddenly, on the seventh day, it was seized with spasm and died.

When, then, he related to me what had happened as something whose cause was hard to assign and baffling, I asked him to read me the written recipe of the drug's [606] composition. He readily did so, and I at once said this to him: "In relating to me just now what befell the freshly wounded boy, surely you added nothing else to your account than that you had recently had experience of the drug wonderfully curing a freshly wounded boy?" When he agreed that he had added nothing else to the account, "Then listen again," I said, "while I tell you what actually happened. The wound of the one who had struck the nerve, which you say was cured by this drug, was a considerable one; and you may confidently use the drug again for wounds of that kind. But punctures of nerves that have a narrow division of the skin cannot be cured by such a drug, just as the drug that cures punctures cannot cure them either when it is applied to the bare nerve itself. For that drug is much hotter and more biting than a bare nerve could endure, given the biting and inflaming it produces."

Where, however, skin and a membrane over it, and in some places flesh as well, lie in front of it, the biting drug, provided it is also fine-particled, effects the same treatment for the nerve as your drug does [607] when it touches the affected nerve alone, laid bare. One must make it of the utmost importance that the opening of narrow punctures be kept open, so that through it the hot drug applied from outside, which is drawing of what lies in the depth, may evaporate the moisture around the affected nerve; so that in such cases it is even fitting to enlarge the mouth of the puncture by further incision, with two incisions in the skin intersecting each other at right angles. These things, then, I said, and many others of those stated by us earlier, to the man who had erred so greatly in the treatment of the nerve-wounded boy that through the faulty management the boy was seized with spasm and died. It is quite clear, then, that the nature of the punctured part too will indicate that the puncture is sometimes without danger and sometimes suspect, namely when we see a nerve lying beneath it, as in the case of the boy punctured in the arm.

For it is not possible to explain in words the place at which the structures that pass through the armpit and reach the whole arm come upon the upper arm. And in this too one may well marvel at the contentiousness of the Empiricists, who say that in all other matters [608] the man who has often seen any one whatever of the operations of medicine imitates it better than if he happened to have seen it only a few times; and likewise that the man doing anything whatever performs it better if he has done it often; but that the things that come to knowledge through anatomy alone can be known securely by someone who has read the historia of anatomical men. Yet even of those who have seen the parts of the body demonstrated by a teacher, no one who has seen them once or twice is able to remember them accurately; one must see them often. And not only are there large nerves travelling through the depth in many parts of the body, but there are also certain roots, as it were, of the nerves distributed to the skin alone. Those who are pricked in these roots, if they are not well treated, incur a sympathetic affection of the large underlying nerves from which these branch off. I wrote about these accurately in the Anatomical Procedures, since they had been passed over by all who came before me.

And unless one has seen these roots many times in apes, it is impossible for him, even if he should at some time have a human body available for dissection, to find them out precisely; [609] just as, much more so, in anatomy by accidental encounter, which they also call 'wound-viewing', it is not possible to find the place from reading alone. Nor indeed is it possible for anyone to become an eyewitness of very many wounds, apart from those that occur in wars; and even in these no one, neglecting to treat the wounded man as quickly as possible, examines where nerves lie beneath the wounded parts, and where arteries and veins. Accordingly, in the treatments of such affections those inexperienced in what is made evident by anatomy are seen to resemble blind men who walk with a staff, and for this reason they err very greatly. But whoever, from these, puts together into one both the experience of the parts known from anatomy and the method concerning the composition and use of drugs will always treat the nerve-wounded, as we do, without any danger, so that neither is any of the more principal parts affected in sympathy, nor does the wounded or bruised nerve become inflamed. And where this is so, much more will neither putrefaction nor crippling nor spasm nor death follow.

[610] [Compositions by means of metallic drugs. Compositions for the nerve-wounded.] Of the metallic drugs, the astringent ones are to be avoided, and especially when the compounded drug is used on a puncture; but those that have a detergent power, such as copper scale, are useful. Since all metallic substances are thick-particled (for they contain within themselves much of the earthy substance), they require some artifice in their preparation in order to become finer-particled. This, then, I devised to accomplish by means of the most acrid vinegar, especially vinegar that has had its origin from a wine that is not harsh; but even if it has come from a wine not of that kind, provided it is of considerable age, it is to be used. Pay careful attention in tasting it that it does not seem to you to show even the slightest quality of wine. For such vinegar does not have a strong power of corroding and cutting whatever comes near it.

In the most acrid vinegar, one as old as possible and as thin as possible in consistency, one must triturate the metallic drugs, avoiding thickness of consistency; and it is better that the trituration [611] of the drugs take place in the summer sun. Some of the metallic drugs need neither to be pounded nor to be sifted, since they are readily dissolved by the vinegar, such as chalcitis and misy; but some need both to be pounded and to be sifted, as does the scale of copper. When, then, I first prepared the drug, I also put some arsenic into it; afterwards, however, this seemed to me superfluous. For it appeared to me that the drug would be compounded sufficiently from the scale of copper, the misy and the chalcitis. In the first composition I also mixed in the burnt verdigris, for I suspected that the unburnt bites more than is fitting. Afterwards, however, I also put in a little unburnt, in proportion to the others. And so too with the chalcitis: if I put it in raw, I mixed in a very small amount, but if burnt, an amount equal to the misy and to the scale of copper. The best of all those prepared, both as I had expected and as I found through experience, was that in which the scale of copper was in the greatest quantity, second the burnt chalcitis, and then misy.

Let whatever drugs you mix, then, as I said, be ground smooth in the sun in the summer season for many [612] successive days with the most acrid vinegar. For the longer the time over which they are ground, the finer-particled they become, and for this reason the more useful for narrow wounds; though in the case of laid-bare nerves, at least, one must guard against things that are excessively fine-particled and erosive. For this reason the troches mentioned are useful for all such cases, for they have taken in some of the astringent substances as well. Renowned among them are that of Andron, that of Polyides and that of Pasion. There is also a certain other, a fourth and a fifth, which I customarily use, stronger than these. Their exact proportions will be stated as the account proceeds. For now, however, let this much be said about their use: one must grind them dry and after that add siraeum and grind them again in this way, until the drug becomes glutinous and uniformly smooth. Everyone among us now also calls this siraeum, the boiled-down must produced when must is boiled. Let this too have nothing winy about it.

Such boiled must results when the must comes not from austere grapes but from grapes as sweet as possible, and not from the first running but from the last. [613] If, then, the must is of this kind, it should be boiled until half of what was put in at the beginning remains; if it is not of this kind, it must be boiled down until a third is left. With boiled-down must of this sort one should dissolve the troches, so that, having a honey-like consistency and taken up on lint pledgets, they may be applied to the exposed nerves. This holds especially for the more moderate of them, such as that of Polyeides, and all the more so if the body is soft-fleshed. In that case it is safer still to give up the use of the troches altogether and employ other drugs, about which I have already spoken and shall speak again.

When the exposed nerve has been covered with the pledgets, one must lay on from outside one of the remedies suited to narrow wounds. Of these there are four kinds: one is this one, the one made with metallic substances, about which it is proposed to speak; another is the one made with juices, among which is also the one with euphorbium; a third is the one made with pigeons' dung; and a fourth, which I call the mild one, which I also use for completely exposed nerves of [614] soft-fleshed bodies. One of these four must be put round the whole affected part, taking in along with it a large portion of the healthy parts as well, and especially of those lying above, on which one must also make the affusion twice a day, or three times if the case is pressing. And indeed sometimes at night as well, the pledgets remaining in place over the exposed nerve while the remedy laid on over them from outside is lifted off. Since there is a very great difference among human bodies, both in their original temperaments and in the changes of the ages, and further, in addition to these, in their habits of life, it is impossible for a compounded drug to suit everyone. For this reason, then, have two prepared, the one stronger among those of the same kind, the other milder. By mixing these with one another at the time of need, you will produce a great many intermediates according to the quantity in the mixture. For if you mix an equal amount of each, the mixture will be exactly the mean between both. But if you mix more of the one, the mixture will have departed from the mean towards that extreme by as much as that one exceeded in the mixture.

Let, then, the strongest [615] of the metallic substances be composed of the following: let it have one part of raw chalcitis, two of misy, likewise raw, and three of flake of copper. The weakest: likewise one part each of misy and of chalcitis, but with both burnt, and four of the flake. And indeed let there also be one intermediate between both, which I have often used, of this kind: of misy, chalcitis and verdigris, all burnt, one part of each, and of flake of copper three parts. To these, then, ground fine as I said before, let wax be mixed: in the strongest, double the amount; in the weakest, two and a half parts; and in the middle one, which lies between these, two and a quarter parts. For instance, in the first written of the three, which I said was the strongest, all the parts, summed from misy, chalcitis and flake, come in number to six. To these, then, you will add twelve parts of wax. In the weakest, if there are six parts of the metallic substances, you are to add twelve parts of wax, and the intermediate amount in the middle one. And intermediate between eighteen and twelve is fifteen. If, then, one drachm

…you suppose the one part, obviously of all of them, to be [one drachm], you will put in [616] as many drachms as there are parts; and if [you suppose it to be] an ounce or a litra (for this is how they are customarily named among the Romans), as many ounces or litrai. Among them there is a measure with which they measure oil, incised with lines dividing the whole into twelve parts; and the whole measure is called by them a litra, and the twelfth part of it an ounce. Now the metallic substances and the wax are weighed on a balance by a different ounce, whereas the oil is measured with the horn. Let the oil, then, be put into all the aforementioned drugs in proportion to the wax, exceeding it by half in all of them, so that if the wax is 8 ounces, the oil put in is 12 ounces, that is, the whole litra. Let the oil be like the Sabine, fine-particled and having very little share of astringency; and it is better if it is also old. But the oil called omotribes (oil of unripe olives), and that prepared with shoots of the olive, are not suitable.

To all the aforesaid drugs, once the metallic ingredients have been ground in the mortar with vinegar for several days, let frankincense be added, the whitest and fatty kind; [617] then let it again be levigated together with the metallic ingredients for some days, before the cerate is mixed in with them. Whatever quantity is collected from all the metallic ingredients together, let the frankincense amount to half of it. If you wish to make the drug softer, add more than half; just as, if you wish it more acrid, less than half. Moreover, to the wax as it is being melted with the oil you may also add one of the aforementioned resins, knowing that the drug becomes more acrid when the strobiline is added, softer with the terebinth, and between the two with the fir resin. Of the kind of the resins is also the so-called larch, which is on the whole more liquid than those mentioned before, but close in consistency to the liquid pine resin, which the petty dealers sell in place of the terebinth to those who do not know how to tell them apart. Such a resin is more acrid than the terebinth in smell, in taste and in potency. With this resin, then, and with the terebinth the so-called larch has a similar potency, but it is finer-particled than they are and more discutient.

If you wish the drug to become plaster-like, you will therefore mix [618] a sixth part of the aforementioned resins with the wax, so that if you put in 1 litra of wax, you will add 2 ounces of the resin. If the resin is very liquid, it will suffice to mix in only one. If, however, you are not concerned that the drug should become plaster-like, there will be no great need to mix the resin into it. Mix in galbanum too, by all means. Where the aim is to make the drug as mild as possible, add an amount equal to the weight of the frankincense; where the aim is a stronger drug, half. For the mean between the two, add the amount between the equal and the half. For example, if the drachms of frankincense are four, you will add two of galbanum if you wish the drug to remain strong, four if you wish it mild, and three if you wish it middling. For just as galbanum has something softening and anodyne, so it also has something putrefactive. This belongs also to most of the emollients. Therefore, when you apply the drug to a nerve that has been laid bare, the galbanum ought hardly to be mixed in at all. Without such laying bare, however, its admixture contributes not a little to freedom from pain.

And so it is possible for you also to keep ready a drug of this kind, in which there is more [619] of the galbanum, for those who are sensitive, soft-fleshed and cacochymic. For all metallic substances are roughening and painful, and among the liquids, vinegar. Reasonably, then, the drugs prepared from them appear rough and painful. And for this reason both the affusion of oil and, likewise, the admixture of galbanum are suitable for them. Fine-particled fat is no less anodyne than galbanum. I therefore think it right that you should also have some other drug prepared from these, which you will be able to mix with the one made from the metallic substances, both in the bodies mentioned and in any others that at any time perceive the drug as rough and painful. Of these too, select those that are finer-particled. Such are the fats of wild animals, especially of the lion, the leopard, the hyena and the bear, and those of birds, especially of geese. If this is not available, use the fat of country cocks and hens. In the same way, prefer also the fat of country geese. For in animals reared in the cities, being shut up idle, the fat is moister and thicker-particled.

When the consistency of the drug is to be something cerate-like, [620] let a third or a fourth part of wax be mixed in; or, if the fat should appear to you very moist, it is permissible to mix in even a half of wax, just as, if it should be dry, a fourth. If it is intermediate, a third. Let such a cerate, which is going to be useful to us for many purposes, be called 'the cerate from fats'. [On the drug compounded from euphorbium.] I have said before as well that old euphorbium falls very far short of new. If, then, it is of the same year, it heats even more than the Cyrenaic juice, and especially more than that of the present day, ever since they have been making the plants grow by irrigation with water and preparing them for the production of a large quantity of juice. For after one year it is sufficiently hot, but already falls considerably short of the fresh. When it has become two years old, it falls still further short of the new, just as at three or four years it does so still more. If it should be any older than these, its potency is entirely dissolved. You will recognise, as I said, how it stands in respect of age and potency by looking at both its colour and its consistency.

For in colour the old appears yellower and paler [621] than the new, and in consistency hard and drier. If, however, you wish to distinguish it by tasting, you will have a diagnosis of it that is not conjectural but certain. The warming ointment, which I said one may improvise with it, will show you most precisely the potency of the drug. It is compounded in the following proportion: one part of euphorbium, three of wax, and twelve of oil. The wax must be three times the euphorbium, and the oil in turn four times the wax itself. So when you have compounded the drug in this way, by rubbing some part of the body with it you will be able to know clearly how much potency it has. It becomes most evident in the bath. For people are bitten by the air as well, but still more strongly by the water, when the euphorbium is hot, fresh and strong. If, then, you have such euphorbium and this very ointment that has been described, apply it confidently to punctures in which you are wary lest the opening close.

But if it is weaker, add to the weight of the euphorbium in proportion to its weakness, sometimes putting in one and a half parts [622], at other times two, and occasionally an amount equal to the wax or even more, if it is very old. The first application, however, in the case of someone who has had a nerve or a tendon punctured, will guide you to the second. For if the wounded man himself says that he has felt a biting, and to you yourself the parts around the puncture appear hot and the puncture itself more raised than it should be, and becoming somewhat inflamed at its lips, you will either weaken the power of the drug by mixing in more oil, or, compounding another according to the earlier proportion, or with older euphorbium, you will in this way make it moderate. But if the opposite of what has been described is present, you will increase the power of the drug. And if everything appears to be in due measure, you will keep it as it is. Now the composition that has the wax triple the euphorbium is the strongest of them, at least when, as has been said, the euphorbium is fresh; the one with fivefold wax is the weakest; and midway between both is the one that has the wax fourfold the euphorbium.

As for the oil, if you wish to make the kind of ointments that physicians call akopa (anti-fatigue ointments), you will put in four times the amount of the wax; if you wish to make the sort of moist cerate that we prepare for fractures, [623] double; and if the wax should be both dry and without fat, even more than double. In general it will suffice to add half of one part to the double amount, so that the whole measure, relative to the wax, comes to two and a half parts. If you wish to make the drug plaster-like, you will mix an equal amount of oil with the wax. If the ambient air is moderate in heat, [an equal amount]; but if the wax is old and parched and the ambient air cold, a little more; just as, if the wax is fatty and the ambient air hot, a little less. This 'little' is a twelfth part on either side of the mean. For indeed I have sometimes mixed both eleven and thirteen ounces of oil with the pound of wax, according to the degree of its consistency and of the heat and cold of the ambient air.

But rarely a little more or less than that. And so that the preparation should have adhesion, oiliness and viscosity, and should not be friable, nor easily dissolved, nor apt to fall away from the skin, I mixed resin into it: preferably genuine terebinth, if it was to hand, and if not, at least the most readily obtainable kind, which they call [624] roasted and Colophonian. Let its weight be equal to that of the wax. For it preserves, in whatever drugs it is put into, the consistency they already had, provided that it too is of moderate consistency. For it is evident that, as in all other things, so too in resin there is the more and the less. If, then, it ever appears oilier and moister, one must recognise that the cerate that will be made from wax melted in oil will be moister than it would otherwise be. In general, in the case of the nerve-wounded, whenever one misses the exact and middle consistency of plaster-like drugs, it is better to lean toward the softer, even if the preparation is going to be one that smears. And likewise also the one that is moderate in consistency. Pitch preserves the consistency of the cerate. As I said, the best for such a mixture is the oily kind, just as with resin too. If you put in a liquid resin, such as terebinth is in consistency, its amount should properly be a third part of the wax; and of terebinth itself, the fresh is much moister than the old.

Remember, then, to observe in all cases what you heard regarding wax and resin. [625] For it is not of those that are dry and parched, whether through age or through their original nature, but of those that are moderate in consistency, that one must mix as much of each in the composition of drugs as is found written by me. Let, then, what is moderate in both potency and consistency for the drug under discussion be this: to have equal amounts of wax, of roasted resin and of oil, and of the euphorbium itself one sixth, so that there is one litra of each of those, and of the euphorbium two ounces. But if we should wish to make it softer, it suffices to put in an eighth part of the euphorbium, that is, one and a half ounces. This proportion, as I said before, has been determined for euphorbium that is fresh and hottest, since, if it is older and for that reason weaker, it has been stated earlier that it ought to be more than its proportion to the other ingredients. And if we should wish to put in not resin alone but pitch as well, we shall mix a half-litra of each, so that their weight is equal to that of the wax. But the drug is much finer if, instead of the resin and the pitch, one mixes in propolis equal to the wax.

Since it does not have the oiliness [626] in the same way as the resins, if we wish the drug to be one that needs no bandage, we shall put in some of the terebinth resin, or of the so-called larch resin, or even of the 'collected' pine resin. I call 'collected' the resin that they transport in boxes and in earthenware jars, which has many pieces of wood and stony bodies in it. But if you melt it and strain it, it then becomes clean, like the Colophonian itself and the so-called roasted resin. One may also mix in some of the so-called self-flowing resins. In Lacedaemon and in some other places they call them 'first-flowing', while in Cilicia they name such a resin kapnelaion. It is moister, hotter and finer in its parts than all the moist resins, so that it will add to the potency of the drug being compounded, and it is especially fitting to put it in when the euphorbium is weak. It is also more fragrant than the other resins, just as the terebinth and the fir resin are. It was stated earlier that the fir resin is hotter than the terebinth, and the strobiline hotter than the fir resin.

Different from the resins mentioned [627] are both the so-called strobiline *physema* (exudation) and the pityine one. Each of them quickly becomes dry, fatless and parched, so that it can be pounded in a mortar and sifted through a sieve. For this reason these are useless for the composition of the drug under discussion. But I have used the following very often, when the euphorbium is of the current year. For the composition: of oil, of wax and of the roasted resin, one litra of each, and a half-litra of the fatty pitch. With these, once they have melted, I mix two ounces of euphorbium; if it should be rather weak, three. If you wish to mix terebinth with the wax, terebinth alone: you will bring the drug up to a moderate consistency if the wax is threefold, provided the terebinth is liquid and fresh. If it has been dried out by time, you will mix in oil to half the weight of the terebinth. This whole mixture made from the three, I mean the oil, the wax and the terebinth, when it amounts to one and a half litrae, will take in addition one ounce of current-year euphorbium; if the euphorbium is not of that kind, one and a half. From what I have already said many times before, it is open to us to increase the euphorbium in proportion to its age.

And [628] indeed, even if the drug, when applied to the wounded part, appears in its first use to be somewhat weaker, one may grind the euphorbium with oil and mix it into the plaster-like drug once this has first been softened in the hands; for when it is done this way, it readily unites. But in the very first composition of the drug it is better to prepare the cerate beforehand separately, scraped (?), and then mix it in this way with the euphorbium that has been ground with the oil. For when the melted ingredients are poured over it in the mortar, the so-called wax-lumps (enkerides) often form, and especially when the surrounding air is cold. It is not necessary to put water into the wax while it is melting with the resin, as I did at first, mixing in as much water as was going to be consumed during the boiling itself. [The drug composed of meltable substances.] I call 'meltable' drugs both those that are melted through contact with fire and those melted through certain liquids, such as water, vinegar, wine.

Now ammoniac incense and sagapenum juice are melted by vinegar without fire, and likewise the juice of panax, which they call by a compound [629] name opopanax. By fire, on the other hand, are melted propolis, wax, resin, ladanum, suet and galbanum. It is better to melt this last in a double vessel. We give this name when, in a pot containing hot water, another vessel is set which contains the galbanum along with the meltables, while the pot is heated from beneath. Have a drug of this kind prepared as well: one at the very least, but better two. The stronger of them will be as follows. Dissolve opopanax in vinegar and grind it thoroughly; then melt propolis, galbanum and terebinth resin over the fire and mix them with the opopanax. Of each of the others let there be one part, but of the propolis six, provided it is fresh and oily. If it happens to be dry and old, it is better not to use such propolis at all; but if you lack the other kind, you will mix in two parts, not one. If you have no propolis, put in oily pitch in its place, such as the Bruttian, and the pitch brought from the districts about Pontus, which is at once oily and fragrant, and which they put into the black amaracine, the kind that was all prepared in former times.

[630] for nowadays they compound a whitish amarakinon even without it. And if you are without pitch of this kind as well, use the other kind, while also doubling the terebinth, as has been said. I myself have sometimes applied, on its own, the drug made with fatty pitch, which I also use for those bitten by a rabid animal. For this drug contains only fatty pitch, boiled in acrid vinegar in the following proportion: one Roman xestes of the vinegar, one litra of the pitch, and of the opopanax the fourth part of the litra, that is, 3 ounces. This drug does not allow the wound of those bitten by a rabid animal to scar over. It is also suitable for those who have been punctured in some nervous part, since it does not allow the mouth of the puncture to close. But since it is hard, it is to be used only on hard bodies, such as those of diggers and reapers.

But if this alone should be available to one of you, and the person who has been punctured is a child or a woman or someone soft-fleshed, it is possible to melt it with one of the discutient unguents: above all amaracine [ἀμαρανίκου, presumably for ἀμαρακίνου] and opobalsam, and in second place iris unguent and the Commagenian, and, if these are not [631] available, white-violet unguent, lily unguent and oil of cypros. And if you are short of these too, melt it with old olive oil, or, if you happen to be in Alexandria, with castor oil and radish oil, for these are very plentiful in that city, as indeed throughout the whole of Egypt. Mustard oil is also not hard to come by in those places. If you sometimes mix in a portion of it as well, it is plain that you will make a most acrid drug for opening up punctures that have closed. It is evident from what has been said that, if you first triturate sagapenum in place of opopanax in a mortar with vinegar and pour over it melted resin, propolis and one of the more acrid fats, the drug will be of the same kind. There is another, softer kind of the melted drugs, which does not contain vinegar. It is prepared only from resins, propolis and fats, with wax also added on account of the consistency, for through its admixture the drug becomes pleasanter to the touch. Let the fat be fine-particled and acrid, such as that of the lion and the leopard, and after these that of the hyena and the bear.

And as for [632] goose fat, what need is there even to speak of it, especially when the geese come from the countryside? But bull's fat too, when aged, is suitable for these purposes, and so is that of the he-goat. For since these are of a mixed nature and power, being both earthy and acrid, with time they incline towards the more acrid, evidently in the same way as most things that are aged. Thus indeed even pig's fat itself, though it is the mildest of all, acquires acridity with time. Wine, vinegar and honey undergo this same thing. To the kind of these drugs belong also the marrows. The best of them are deer's marrow and calf's; rennets are more acrid than these, and they are already close to the more vehement kind of drugs. I therefore think it right that you should also keep some drug of this sort at hand, so that, whenever the wounded part has been bitten too immoderately by one of the strong drugs and becomes irritated, you may first bathe it by pouring oil over it and then cover it with one of these.

For once it has been soothed in this way, it is possible to return again to the combative course of treatment. I at any rate, when on one occasion a nerve-wounded part had been unbandaged, [633] seeing the wound irritated, and there happening to be at hand a liquid drug, the ear-remedy made with fats, warmed it in a double vessel and applied it over the affected part, and I saw a very rapid benefit arise from it, by the very perception of the patient; for he at once became free of pain, and afterwards, when we unbandaged it, it appeared to be in its natural state. [On the drug composed with pigeons' dung.] The dung of pigeons in country towers is pungent, and I once used it in the countryside for a young man with a nerve wound. And the farmer in charge of that estate, having seen this, for he was not unintelligent, imitated it and always uses it and treats those wounded in the nerves. Both the composition and the use are the same as for the drug made with euphorbium, everything else being the same, except that the dung is put in instead of the euphorbium. This dung falls short of euphorbium in fineness of parts, and for this reason it is useful in the countryside on hard bodies.

I once also mixed it with the metallic ingredients, for the sake of trial, grinding it together with them right [634] from the beginning with vinegar in the sun, just as I said a moment ago. And the drug became much more acrid, just as it also does when it receives unburnt verdigris. [On the drug composed of herbs.] I also composed a drug for the nerve-wounded from the fine-particled herbs: at first from dittany, marjoram and birthwort alone, but later also from others, testing myself as to whether I was conjecturing rightly about their composition, and in every case I attained my aim. Let the herbs suitable for this purpose be bitter to the taste, without astringency, or else acrid, though not immoderately so.

So when the rich man asked to receive some composition of a drug both fragrant and costly, I gave him several [638] prescriptions, which I had made according to the method stated above. Eager to test them, he ordered his free men and slaves to seek out for him persons with wounded nerves. When the drugs worked beyond all hope, he first praised me for having shared the prescriptions with him ungrudgingly, and then also honoured me with gifts, for he was ready for such things too. The composition of the drugs given to him was as follows. ℞ Of cinnamon, dittany and maron, 40 drachmas of each. For these are fragrant and of fine parts. Amaracus, since it is not fragrant, I had in mind not to mix in at all. Then, since it was hard to obtain in Rome, as is maron too, and I saw that he delighted in things hard to obtain just as in costly ones, I added to the prescription a small portion of it as well, of one part, I think a fourth or a fifth. I ordered these, pounded and sifted through a fine-meshed sieve, to be mixed with a cerate made with the best opobalsamum and Tyrrhenian wax.

I judged it a suitable proportion to make eight parts of the wax, [639] and ten of the opobalsam. So that the drug should not be crumbly but should in some way hold together with itself, I also mixed in one part of terebinth resin, which is itself fragrant when it is of the finest quality. If, as I said, you wish to make the drug more potent, put in not one part of each of the herbs mentioned but more, so that it comes to one and a half. This drug, then, was attested by experience. So was another, a second one after it, compounded with the same cerate and Cyrenaic juice, the mixing being done in the same proportion as for the euphorbium; and another, a third, compounded from the mixture of both; and the fourth after these, which took percolated myrrh in addition. In cases where the nerve is laid bare, for these I compounded the cerate from the wax called perfumers' wax and from the unguents named among the Romans spicatum and foliatum. Into it I mixed a twelfth part of washed pompholyx, whether you wish to say 'washed' in the masculine (peplymenou) or in the feminine (peplymenēs); for whichever way you say it, you will neither help nor harm the drug.

You may also prepare it with [640] Tyrrhenian wax. It is possible too, leaving out the unguents mentioned, to melt the Tyrrhenian wax with good nard, in a double vessel, of course, for this is common to all the unguents. To the cerate, once it has been scraped, you will mix spikenard, amomum, malabathrum leaf and washed pompholyx, an equal amount of each. For in punctures, as has been said, there is need of more acrid drugs, which always keep the wound open. To those with exposed [nerves], however, one must apply drugs that have a moderate astringency together with a non-biting discutient power. Amomum too has some share of astringency, but spikenard and malabathrum leaf have more than it. [On the drugs stated by the other physicians for the nerve-wounded.] The whole method of the treatment of the nerve-wounded, which I devised through a certain providence of the gods, none of the elders before me wrote down.
