They did, however, compose drugs professing to cure certain patients wounded in a nerve, but without distinction and without a varied manner of use. [641] They made clear neither what the procedure should be for narrow punctures, nor what it should be for wider wounds, or for a nerve or tendon that has been laid bare or crushed. Still less did they say what to do if the affected part should already be inflamed, or has even come close to gangrene. I did find one particular physician of our own time using a drug similar to those I prepare from metallic substances, though he too used it without distinction. I learned that it was composed of a few natural substances, whereas I had at that time prepared the compound made from many. So I had in mind to remove most of the ingredients, compose another drug from a few, and then examine it again and test it by experience, to see whether it appeared to fall short of the many-ingredient drug by a great deal or by a little. I therefore made it a matter of the utmost importance to obtain the recipe from the physician of our time. Having prepared it at once, I found that it had a claim and a potency similar to those of the elaborate drug. The recipe for its composition is as follows. ℞ Wax, 6 ounces; oil, 9 ounces; misy, 6 drachms.

of chalcitis [642] 1 drachm; of copper flakes 2½ ounces; of frankincense 1½ ounces; of galbanum 1 ounce. Once the metallic substances have first been ground smooth in acrid vinegar, carefully melt the meltable ingredients, that is the wax and the galbanum, and pour them over. I do not know who composed this drug. I did not find the recipe in Asclepiades Pharmakion, nor in Petronas, nor in Andromachus, although these wrote down the best drugs of all the older physicians. It is quite clear that it is not in Heras the Cappadocian either, nor in Mantias, nor in Heraclides of Tarentum, men who had acquired much experience of drugs. Nor is it in Archigenes and his circle, Philippus or any of his pupils. I also read all that Soranus, Menecrates, Crito, Damocrates and the others who have a reputation for knowledge of drugs wrote on drugs, and I found the drug just written down here in none of them.

What is written by the men I have named I shall set out in order, and I shall make my beginning from Asclepiades the Pharmakion, in the third book of the internal [643] drugs, which he also entitles 'Marcellas'; he wrote word for word as follows. Andromachus' Egyptian wound plaster for bleeding wounds, as Asclepiades records it. It acts against severance of nerves and of muscles; it acts against punctures, contusions, chafings, sprains; it acts against abscesses. It is also an application to be stuck on for those suffering from ophthalmia. It acts for sufferers from headache, and the drug is useful against many conditions. ℞ Litharge, wax, of each 144 dr.; ammoniac incense 72 dr.; terebinth 36 dr.; greasy wool, burnt, 12 dr.; flake of copper 8 dr.; flake of steel 8 dr.; frankincense 8 dr.; round birthwort 8 dr.; castor oil 3 cotylae. Boil the litharge and the oil, and when it changes, add the wax and the resin. And when it no longer stains, add the ammoniac, having spread it flat, and then the greasy wool and the rest. The more polychrest this drug became through taking in addition the flake of steel, the poorer it became for those wounded in a nerve. For if there should be only a puncture, even the flake of copper is superfluous.

For unless they have first been ground smooth for a considerable time [644] with acrid vinegar, none of the metallic substances is of use in these cases. In the case of exposed nerves and tendons, however, it would be a good drug. But if the part is already inflamed as well, one should melt them down with rose-oil and use it in this way as a lint-dressing. Even without inflammation, right at the very beginning the softer and moister drugs are better than the harder and drier ones. And it is better to use them melted down in one of the discutient or soothing oils. By discutient I mean old olive oil, castor oil and Sicyonian oil; by soothing, rose-oil, chamomile oil and the oil made with marsh-mallow. Stronger than these, and for that reason suited to harder bodies, are the oil made with wild cucumber, its root having been boiled down in the oil, and the oil made with iris, bryony and arum; and stronger than these is the oil made with dragonwort, birthwort and panax. I myself have often used both the oil made with the seed of the silver fir and the oil made with the flower of black poplars; for I steep these in Sabine oil for a considerable time.

Now as for all that I have just said about the use of such [645] drugs, I ask you to keep it in mind and to carry it over to the others that are going to be mentioned. I for my part shall do what I set out to do: I shall add other drugs as well of the same potency, such as is also the one written by Asclepiades next after the one mentioned before, which runs word for word as follows. The Egyptian [plaster] of Claudius Philoxenus the surgeon, for the conditions mentioned above. Take: litharge, wax, of each 160 drachms; ammoniac incense, 80 drachms; propolis, 40 drachms; dry resin, terebinth, flake of copper, frankincense, of each 16 drachms; burnt greasy wool, flake of steel, of each 8 drachms; opopanax, 4 drachms; castor oil, 3 kotylai. It is quite clear, then, that this drug too is similar to the one written before, and will have the same manner of use as the one written by me a little earlier. And indeed, along with these two plasters, Asclepiades wrote another, a third, speaking word for word as follows. The tawny [plaster] of Halieus. It is effective for wounds that are still bloody and for severances of nerves. It is effective also for old, hard-to-cicatrize and fluxional ulcers.

It is also a good emollient, [646] especially for the indurations that arise about the breasts. We also use it for dog-bites and human bites. It is supremely effective too against the stings of sea stingrays and of weevers (drakontes) and of the other noxious fishes. And in general its power is marvellous. ℞ Litharge, wax, 100 drachms each; terebinth, manna, frankincense, galbanum, Sinopic red earth (miltos), 8 drachms each; oil, 1 sextarius. So Asclepiades himself does not profess that the drug is useful for punctures into tendons and nerves. Rather he says it is for severances of the nerves, evidently when the wound has become larger and the nerve is seen laid bare. For at that point drugs of a moderate and soothing power are more suitable, and the one he has just described is of that kind. These three plasters, then, Asclepiades recorded somewhere near the middle part of his book. Before them, higher up, he recorded another polychrest plaster as well, better than these three as regards severances and destructions of the nerves. The very wording in which Asclepiades recorded it is as follows: Moschion's fracture plaster.

A successful drug [647] for freshly inflicted wounds, severings of the sinews, and divisions accompanied by contusion. It is also effective for fractures accompanied by a wound; for it both helps the wounds and forms callus on the bones when it is applied with the proper bandaging, and it helps incipient dropsical patients. It is also effective for contusions of the testicles. It also shrivels like a raisin the protrusions about the seat. It is also effective for fissures when mixed in with butter. It is also effective for bronchoceles; it dissolves every hardness; it is effective for chafings and sprains. It is effective for the callous risings on the feet and hands which we call hēloi ('nails'), so as even to remove them without ulceration; and in general the drug is of the most manifold use. It is also effective for incipient dropsies. The particulars of the preparation are as follows. ℞ Litharge, 1 mina (the mina contains 160 drachmas); dry pitch, 160 dr.; calf's suet, 160 dr.; terebinth resin, 80 dr.; manna of frankincense, 80 dr.; wax, 40 dr.; verdigris, 8 dr.; opopanax, 8 dr.; galbanum, 8 dr.; castor oil, 1 cotyle; vinegar, the same amount; juice of the mulberry (sykaminos), 1 cotyle; liquid pitch, half a cotyle.

Put the litharge, ground very fine, and the castor oil [648] into an earthenware or bronze vessel, set it on the fire and boil; and when it boils up, add the suet and the manna, stirring continuously. And when it thickens, add the pitch, wax and resin, and boil until it no longer stains; sprinkle on the galbanum, then the verdigris and the opopanax dissolved in vinegar. The juice of the mulberry and the liquid pitch we put into another vessel and boil. And when it thickens, we add it to the first drug, and setting it on the fire again we boil it until it no longer stains, and pouring it out into wine we leave it for three days; then, having softened it, we use it, spreading it on a linen cloth. After the application of the drug one must soak a small bandage in wine, squeeze it out, and then put it around the drug. The way our teacher Lucius prepared it is as follows. We first melt the suet and the oil, and when it has dissolved, we sprinkle in the very finely ground manna and the litharge, and when it thickens, we do what follows.

It is just to praise Asclepiades on this account too, that he writes out the manner of preparation [649] of the drugs, and does not, as Andromachus does, leave it out without even adding what power the drug has. Certainly the Egyptian plaster from Asclepiades, the first of the three written out by me, which he himself says belongs to Andromachus: Andromachus wrote neither of what power it is, nor how it is to be prepared, nor how it is to be used. It has simply been thrown in, like some chance drug, in the book of external remedies he wrote, as the second. For first of all he wrote the one which he himself names Pantagathion, and next this Egyptian one, adding nothing else, as I said. For his wording runs as follows: Egyptian. ℞ Litharge 144 dr., castor oil 6 kotylai, wax 144 dr., ammoniac incense 72 dr., terebinth resin 36 dr., burnt wool 18 dr., flake of steel 8 dr., flake of copper 8 dr., frankincense 8 dr., birthwort 8 dr. Some add myrrh 4 dr., opopanax 8 dr.; others 12. At the end of these is written: sea water for the soaking of the wax, 8 kotylai.

What he means by 'for the soaking (embrochē) of the wax' [650] we do not clearly know, for several meanings can be conceived. It is surprising that Asclepiades, having written everything else in the same way as Andromachus, did not write the same measure of the kiki: Andromachus wrote 6 cotylae, but Asclepiades wrote 3 cotylae. Nor did he add what Andromachus appended at the end of the text: 'some: myrrh 4 dr., opopanax 2 dr.' On the other hand, he himself added 'greasy' to the burnt wool, which is not appended in Andromachus' text. After the Egyptian plaster just mentioned, Andromachus wrote five theriac plasters, and after these another, a grey one, which he says is Eubulus'. After this again another grey one, which he names Athena, and then next again two other grey ones, simply so called, and after these another, over which is written, word for word, as follows: 'Grey plaster for punctures. Andromachus'. ℞ Ammoniac incense 8 dr., new wax 8 dr., terebinth 8 dr., burnt copper 8 dr., dry pitch 40 dr., or, according to Zeno, a half and a quarter of a mina; litharge 4 dr., Indian aloe 2 dr., birthwort 2 dr.'

[651] of galbanum 2 dr., of verdigris 1 dr. (some write 2 dr.), of frankincense 2 dr., of oil in winter 4 cotylae, in summer an eighth, of vinegar half a cotyla for dissolving the ammoniac. It is likely that he calls this plaster 'for punctures' (nygmatikē) because it can be useful against punctures of the nerves.

[652] GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK IV. My first book ended with the compoundings of the white plasters, both the others and those that are suited to sores hard to cicatrise, after we had distinguished those commonly called hard to cicatrise from those specifically named malignant, which are themselves, of course, hard to cicatrise.

Since some ulcers become hard to cicatrise from the ichors and humours flowing in upon the ulcerated parts, [653] and others because the affected part itself corrupts what flows in, even if it should be wholesome, the ulcers of the second kind they call specifically 'hard to cicatrise and malignant'. In these some people are sometimes compelled to excise the whole affected part or to burn it, using either escharotic drugs or fire. And since there is considerable latitude in each of the two kinds, in that one ulcer is more or less hard to cicatrise and malignant than another, the number of drugs that heal them must necessarily be as great as that of the ulcers themselves. Reasonably, then, each of those who possess a single drug that professes to cicatrise malignant ulcers often fails. For whoever proposes to treat all such ulcers must have prepared at least two drugs, of the same claim and power, but differing from one another not simply by more and less but, as one might put it most clearly, by most and least.

Just as, then, in the books of the Therapeutic Method we showed that in the case of all affections what must be found first of all is the general power of the [654] remedies, and next the materials in which that power is contained, so by the same reasoning now too, in the case of sores hard to cicatrise, the general power, whatever it may be, of the drugs that are to cure them must be found first. This too was shown by me in that treatise: in cases where there is no bad condition about the ulcerated parts, it has these two aims, one to repel what flows in, the other to disperse what has become lodged in the affected part. These are accomplished through opposite powers. For drugs that are by nature astringent check what flows in, while those that have a drawing power disperse what is contained in the affected part. In general, however, astringent drugs roughen, and in this respect they are distressing. Those that draw and disperse the moistures from the depth do not accomplish this without acridity. And acridity is of necessity followed by a certain pain that bites the ulcerated part. So it comes about that, through the distress caused by the roughening and biting drugs, the moisture flowing in upon the ulcerated parts is provoked.

When this happens, the ulcer becomes inflamed [655] and at the same time is eaten through, so that, as far as what has been said goes, the discovery of drugs that will help ulcers hard to cicatrise is a matter without a ready way, and much more still for malignant ones. One must therefore find, so far as is possible, a material of drugs of such a kind that by it the ulcer will be dried without pain; and this cannot be done precisely unless the one treating knows how the drug applied will act. For it is of necessity strong in both of the things combined in it, the biting and the astringent. But the filth that lies upon such ulcers and the quantity of moisture, becoming as it were a kind of protective covering for the ulcerated parts, weaken the biting that comes from the strong drugs. One must therefore attend to how much of the moisture in the ulcer the first application has dried, or, if it also has filth, how much of this too it has thrown off. And in this way one should use it a second and a third time, until the ulcer appears clean and dry. And as soon as you first see it in such a state, pass over to another drug of the same kind, but weaker than the former.

For the stronger ones [656], becoming painful by biting the ulcer, both set fluxes in motion and rouse inflammations. But if, on the other hand, you apply one much weaker than the first drug, the ulcer will be moist and foul. In this respect, then, the physician trained in the art is better than the one who treats an ulcer through experience alone, inasmuch as he knows that the ulcer is healed by drugs through no other power than their making the part dry in the way it was when it was in its natural state. This will be evident from thin ichor no longer flowing off, and the generation of pus being fostered. And they will arrive at this when they are dried in the manner I have described, that is, when they are astringed and dispersed, and, once they are dry but still appear foul, when they are cleansed by means of detergent drugs. Something has also been said about these in the commentaries on simple drugs. But the most complete method has been written out in its entirety in the therapeutic treatise, in which anyone who is to be fully benefited by what is now being said must have been trained beforehand.

That this is already known to you, my companions, for whom these things are written, I know very clearly, [657] and, in addition to this, that what I am now saying is not an argument that is merely plausible apart from the testing in actual practice. For you have often watched me heal completely many ulcers of this kind by means of those very drugs with which certain physicians, using them without method, accomplished nothing. Recall, then, the drugs whose nature is to dry without biting; most of them are metallic substances. And moreover, when they have been burnt and washed, whatever biting they had before is lost; recall this too. Let it be open to you, then, to use these for the present: washed, in the case of children, eunuchs and women, and all who by nature have white and soft flesh, and in addition to these in the case of those who are very sensitive and cacochymic. In other bodies one may also use the unwashed ones, making the first application of them early in the morning, when the patients under treatment have digested well. And if some preparation of the whole body beforehand is needed, this too must have been carried out first. The preparations have been described in the therapeutic treatise.

For in some cases it suffices only to purge, [658] in some to take away blood, and in others to do both of these. In certain cases one must cut out an overlying varix, or take care of the spleen or the liver; in certain cases also scarify the parts around the ulcer, just as indeed one must sometimes cut away the callus of the lips. But if we need none of these, the quantity of the moisture must be examined together with the filth, and so one must proceed to the appropriate drug. One must recall, of each of the simples, which ones dry but do not cleanse away the filth of the ulcer, and which ones cleanse but do not dry vigorously. As for those that are by nature able to do both, one must further consider of what order each one is. This is the most important of the things that matter for the treatment, but it has been neglected by those who wrote the books on materia medica. For these alone undertook to state the powers of the whole of it, as indeed did Dioscorides, whom one would call second to none of those who have taken pains over these matters. I shall therefore next list all the drugs able to dry ulcers without biting or roughening noticeably.

I shall begin [659] with the metallic substances, among which they also count the kinds of earth. Since there is great difference among them in drying more and less, I shall begin with those in the middle and pass on to those that dry more vehemently or more feebly. Now, Lemnian seal dries moderately, and so does cadmia; and more than this the natural [cadmia], which has not undergone transformation and is found in torrents and streams, in the mountains of the Cypriots, and in other places, but especially in those where there are mines. I am accustomed to make it more drying by grinding it in summertime in the sun for many days in succession with vinegar or with wine that is tawny in colour but clear in consistency, such as Falernian in Italy and Tmolite in Asia; wine of this sort is the most drying of wines. Of the same kind are the Ariusian produced in Chios and the fragrant Lesbian of Eresus and Methymna.

Next after these come all the old wines, when they have aged from white and astringent ones: in Italy the Signine, the Tiburtine and the Marsian; in Sicily the one they call Aminaean; in Asia the Aphrodisian [660] and the Misyan. It is enough for me to have named these as examples of the general powers. I also prepare cadmia in the same way with acrid vinegar, in the sun for many days in the summer season. Having dried it I store it, so as to be able to sprinkle it on ulcers that are turning malignant. A stronger drug than this is burnt chalcitis, first ground fine in the same manner as the cadmia; next after it, the unburnt chalcitis is so strong a drug as to produce eschars. It is therefore better to keep it washed and then dried. For the washed dries more weakly than the burnt, but it is much milder and less biting. A drug similar to it is burnt verdigris; the unburnt verdigris is a very strong drug, as is chalcitis too. But chalcitis has some share of astringency, and chalcanthum has much more of it than chalcitis does, being the most drying of the metallic substances. Verdigris, however, has no share at all of such a power. Of the same kind as chalcitis, as you have learned, are misy and sory.

For they are, as one might say, offshoots of a single root: misy is finer-particled [661] and less biting and caustic, while sory is thicker-particled and less drying than both, just as stimmi too has a more astringent and more drying power than sory. A drug most suitable for sores hard to cicatrise because of moisture is also the one named diphryges; for it dries strongly, although it bites only moderately, and it too has, in addition to its acrid quality and power, the astringent one. Both of these are stronger in raw chalcitis and in chalcanthum, whether one wishes to name it in the masculine, the feminine or the neuter. For always remember not to quarrel over names where the task before us is to learn a theory necessary for the works of the art. All the alums too dry sores sufficiently, astringing them violently. Hence one would not use them alone on a sore, just as one would not use raw chalcitis or verdigris alone either. But these, when burnt, and misy as well, are useful, as they are also when washed: they become non-biting, but they dry less.

It is therefore safer to use them washed, since most of the bodies which we are obliged to treat [662] have at least some one condition that does not tolerate strong biting. You have heard these things many times, but now too I shall remind you of them again, and I shall ask you to keep them in mind for the whole of the discussion that follows. All bodies, then, that are plethoric, and all that are cacochymic, and in addition to these those that are soft-fleshed and highly sensitive, are readily brought into inflammation when bitten. Included among the soft-fleshed are, evidently, the bodies of white women and those of children and eunuchs and of men white in complexion, and those who inhabit a cold land: the bodies of these too are moist and phlegmatic, and for this reason soft and white. Just so, those who inhabit a hot land, such as those in Egypt and Arabia, have a hard and dry habit of body. So, on the understanding that you always remember these things, I shall add some further material of simple drugs capable of treating malignant ulcers. Sarcocolla, then, and ichthyocolla, and more than these chrysocolla, are of this kind of power.

An excellent drug for such conditions is also burnt lead, [663] and after it sory and stimmi, these too burnt. The slag of lead also dries well, just as the flake of iron does too, and still more that of steel. That of copper, besides drying, also cleanses, which is why it also makes ulcers clean, the other flakes not having this property. So if you sprinkle all these drugs dry on malignant ulcers, you will see the ulcers dried wonderfully without biting. The same is true of the burnt shells of trumpet-shells, of purple-shells and of oysters, and of all other such things. The so-called transparent stone, which the Romans name specularium, is also among the things that dry without biting, when burnt. It is useful for ulcers that are hard to cicatrise, but not for malignant ones, for it dries more moderately than these require. Of the same power as it are also burnt glass and the fiery matter that forms in bronze heating-vessels.

Besides drying, the fruit of the Egyptian thorn, the omphacitis (unripe) gall, rhubarb, and pomegranate rinds also have an astringent power, as do not a few [664] roots and herbs. For birthwort, iris, acorus, mugwort, the root of panax, argemone, the root of the black chamaeleon, cyperus, dracontium and xiphium dry sufficiently, and centaury and polium dry still more than these. Slightly weaker than these is the earth called Eretrian, just as ampelitis is stronger. Such, then, is the material of the simple drugs that treat malignant ulcers. To them are added from outside certain things which are not applied on their own because of the vehemence of their power, but are mixed with others, such as unburnt verdigris, and unslaked and unwashed lime, and soft aphronitre, which is really aphrolitre. For the frothier it is, the better it is in both respects, both in biting less and in dispersing more. For you learned also in the works on simple drugs that, among all things of the same kind, the finer-particled have a power of this sort in comparison with the coarser-particled.

Nothing is so much to be guarded against as the drugs that Hippocrates calls 'softish' (malthakōdē), which belong to the [665] class of oil. Such are all the fats, and of these especially pig's fat, then next the resins, and after these wax. In another way the emollients of hardened parts are also unsuitable: galbanum, bdellium, ammoniac incense, storax, and the marrows. And in yet another way the acrid drugs: pepper, ginger, mustard, cachrys, and a great number of others of this kind. [How one must use the dry drugs just mentioned in ulcers that are difficult to cicatrize and malignant.] Ulcers of this kind are necessarily full of bad moisture, and not a few of them also have abundant filth. Whenever, therefore, we are about to sprinkle one of the dry drugs on them, one must first wipe them out with a piece of linen that is soft, clean and dry, and, having filled the hollow of the ulcer with the drug, lay over it on the outside a flat spread of a plaster that thins the lips, and over this again on the outside a piece of linen equal on every side, and over that a sponge out of water or wine.

One must make it of the utmost importance that the [666] sponge remains cold, which could easily be done if one continually pours cold water over it, without undoing the bandage. The bandage itself should be applied and wound round as Hippocrates taught in his works on fractures, since he held that the greatest harm would come from a bandaging that tends towards neat appearance and not towards benefit. If, then, there is a single bandage, it must be carried from below upwards, whether it is the shin, or the knee, or the ankle, or the elbow or the extremity of the hand, or any other part whatever. But if you wish to use two, as in the case of fractures, let the first be carried from the affected part towards the upper region only, and let the second be carried first from below, and next, ending above, let it come up to that very point to join the first. It is therefore evident that these bandages ought to be made of strips of linen, not of rag. One should undo them every third day, not every day, and, having undone them, should not apply water to the ulcer, but, in the manner described just now, wipe off the ichors with a soft, clean and dry linen cloth.

If the parts around the ulcer also show something phlegmonous, one should apply over the flat spread, on the outside, extending over a wide area [667], a liquid drug made from my palm plaster (phoinikinē), not simply melted, but having taken up as much astringent wine as possible. Nor indeed is it fitting to melt it with any oil that comes to hand. Rather, if some redness, or heat generally, prevails in the parts around the ulcer, it should be melted with one of the astringent and cooling oils; such are myrtle oil and quince oil; and if these are not available, the so-called omphacine oil and omotribes oil (oil of unripe olives). But if hardness appears to prevail, the same palm plaster is to be melted with old oil or with castor oil. It is safer, even if nothing bad appears in the place surrounding the ulcer, at any rate to apply the liquid drug to the region itself lying above it, so as to repel anything that flows in from before (i.e. from above), whether bad or in greater quantity than is fitting, and especially when the ulcer, being on the leg, has a varicose vein lying above it. If that vein is large and shows by its colour that it contains blood neither red nor good, but rather blacker and more melancholic, one must excise the vein.

It once happened, when such a vein [668] had been excised, that the ulcer at once cicatrised, although it was a year old, but in its place, at the incision from which the vein had been excised, a malignant ulcer arose which could not be brought to cicatrise. In such cases, then, it is better, after observing the strength of the patient under treatment, to begin with phlebotomy, and next to purge with a drug that evacuates the melancholic humour and, along with it, the phlegmatic as well, since this too sometimes flows in together with the melancholic in the generation of varices. Then, next, one should lance lengthwise the vein itself that lies above the ulcer and, having evacuated in abundance, first heal this very division made in the vein; and when it already appears to be cicatrising completely, only then undertake the treatment of the malignant ulcer, as has been said before. The spleen too, when it is in a bad condition, sometimes becomes the cause of such cacochymy, as indeed does the liver as well; one must first take care of these, and only then undertake the healing of the ulcer.

By the same reasoning, if the whole body is cacochymous or plethoric, one must first purge and evacuate it beforehand, before applying a drug to the ulcer [669]. And in the very course of treating the ulcer by means of the dry drugs, at each removal of the dressing one must attend to the action that the drug has produced on the part. One must know and remember that drugs which dry without deterging do not make the ulcer clean; such are those in which the astringent quality predominates. But those which, besides drying, also have the power to deterge render the whole ulcerated part not only dry but also clean. One must also know that clean ulcers are stung by drugs by which they were not stung at all before, when they were foul. One must therefore pass from the more strongly deterging drugs to the milder and less stinging kind at whatever moment the ulcer is found to be thoroughly clean. Conversely, in foul ulcers one must go back to the more detergent drugs, unless the ulcer has appeared foul because it has been stung.

For this has sometimes deceived even those reputed to be good physicians, so that they changed over to another drug, more cleansing and more acrid, by which the ulcer, eaten away again, [670] appeared at the next removal of the dressing equally foul, or even more so, the flesh melted down by the drug fouling it. For the flesh that is melted down dissolves into bad ichors; and of these, whatever part is finer-particled in consistency is dispersed by the drug, while the remainder, congealing right there around the ulcers, becomes filth for them. One must therefore attend to whether the ulcer was fouled because the underlying flesh was being eaten away and melted down, or because it needed a drug that removes the filth and the one applied was not of that kind. The distinction is made by the ulcer having at the same time become more hollow and having its lips reddish and hotter, when it is being fouled by the acridity of the drug. Perhaps, then, it would be superfluous in the present treatise to add the manner of use of compound drugs, for it has been stated in the Therapeutic Method; but things that are necessary, and that bring great harm if overlooked, it is better to say even twice and three times for the sake of reminder.

Let this, then, also be added to the account: in the treatment of such ulcers, if it should be [671] possible, without harm to the whole body, for the patient to go unbathed, being rubbed down at some length with linen cloths, and next with oil, and then exercising with jumping-weights, if the affected part is a leg, or by running in the case of the parts lying above. But if it should be impossible for the patient to go unbathed without harm to the whole body, one must not undo the bandaging; rather, when he has bathed bandaged as he is, one should squeeze the warm water out of the sponge and at once pour other, cold water over it, so that no heat is left behind in the bandaging. And if the treatment appears to be making progress, he may also be treated without the bandaging-on of a sponge, the moist phoenicine being laid on from outside as has been said; that is, without the application of a sponge, the drug being held in place by bandages wound round the treated part of the body in the fracture manner. [Composition of plaster-type drugs.] Since the chief point of the treatment of malignant and hard-to-cicatrise ulcers lies in the drug's drying without biting, and water and oil moisten most of all things,

[672] one must abstain from these, so as neither to apply them by themselves nor to mix them in with the dry drugs already mentioned. One must therefore select wax that is neither dry by nature nor has come to this state through age, but fresh and naturally oily, which a person, softening it in the sun, will be able to make take up into itself some of the dry drugs mentioned. When there is no sun, let it be softened by being warmed beside a fire and by being let down into hot water. For the water is not mixed in throughout, but runs off quickly from it as it is being softened, before it is applied to the ulcer. The due proportion of the mixture is as follows. If one wishes the drug to be moderate, let him add to the wax a fourth part of the metallic substances; it will be stronger if a third is mixed in. And since the metallic substances themselves are, in lesser and greater degree, non-biting and drying, the potency will be intensified in the more drying ones and relaxed in those that dry less; just as, again, the use will be safer with the more non-biting ones and more hazardous with the more biting ones.

For it has often been said that some natures of bodies have the skin and the flesh more sensitive, [673] while in others both of these are less sensitive. And according to the greater and lesser degree of sensation, the affection of pain also follows in greater and lesser degree, as does that of inflammation. No small difference also arises from whether the body is soft-fleshed or harder, euchymous or cacochymous, or plethoric or empty or in a middle condition between the states mentioned. It is therefore not possible to prepare one drug suitable for all people. But whatever drug of the same kind is prepared, one who has been trained in the art according to the method taught in this treatise ought to know how to use it. Take, for example, the material now before us: if you mix an equal amount of each, of verdigris and of burnt copper, and half of one part of split alum, so that the total made up from the three is either 2½ drachms or as many ounces, it will suffice to mix in 10 drachms of wax for the drachms, and 10 ounces for the ounces, to compose a drug that is moderate and middling in its power.

It will be better and at the same time less biting if it takes diphryges instead of the split [alum], and the drug will be finer if one whole drachm [of it] is put in, as of the [674] copper and the verdigris. If, suspecting the biting that comes from the verdigris, we should wish it to become perfectly free of biting, one must put in the verdigris burnt. And if [we wish it] also to remove filth, half a drachm of copper scale must be added, so that the whole proportion becomes as follows. ℞ Of copper, of burnt verdigris and of diphryges an equal amount of each, that is, 1 drachm each; of copper scale half a drachm. Let these be taken up in the fatty wax as it is being softened, as was said before. If [the wax] is too dry to receive the ingredients mentioned, one must, while softening it, mix in myrtle oil or quince oil or mastic-oil or castor oil or oil of cypros or old omotribes oil (oil of unripe olives) or the fresh Spanish [oil] or the [oil] prepared among us with olive shoots. And if we should not wish to add anything oily to the drug at all, one should mix in some of the larch resin; and if this is not available to us, one must use the terebinth [resin] in its place.

Those who read these things must always remember this too: to have recourse above all to what was mentioned first, as being best, [675] and after this to the second and the third, and then in order to the others that come after the third, since we have arranged the order of our account in proportion to the excellence and potency of the drugs. Anyone, then, who has heard this beforehand and knows the potencies of the simple drugs will be competent to judge the drugs that our predecessors wrote for malignant ulcers. For instance, Asclepiades, surnamed Pharmakion, wrote as follows in the third book of his External [Remedies]. [On the drugs written by Asclepiades.] A successful drug for chironian and hard-to-heal ulcers. ℞ Copper flake, 1 ounce; scraped verdigris, 1 ounce; wax, half a litra; larch resin, 1½ ounces. Pour the meltable ingredients over the dry ones, and when you have taken it up, use it, softening it carefully and laying a small plaster over the affected part alone, so as to cover only the ulcer. The surrounding parts must be covered with a drug that prevents inflammation.

In the treatment one must undo the ulcer every third day, then foment it beforehand and, washing off [676] the same small plaster, soften it and apply it again, until (ἔα; = presumably ἕως) cicatrisation begins. This, then, is the prescription of the drug, and he rightly added in the heading 'for Chironian ulcers'; for that is what they call ulcers that are not moderately malignant but extremely so. This drug is powerful, since it has the metallic ingredients in a third part of the wax: verdigris, a rather strong drug, and flake of copper, much more moderate than the verdigris but nonetheless powerful itself as well. If it had a well-proportioned mixture, so as to treat also moderately malignant ulcers, the wax would have been mixed with the other ingredients not threefold but fourfold; and it would be more moderate still if fivefold, so as to treat also ulcers that are not yet malignant but are otherwise hard to cicatrise. For so too (ὥσπερ γὰρ κἂν) if one were to make the wax sixfold the metallic ingredients, so that there is one drachm each of the verdigris and the flake, and of wax 12 drachms, and of the larch resin the proportional amount. And it will be proportional if there are three drachms of it.

Since the wax is fatty, the drug will have sufficient consistency [677] even if less of the resin is put in. For in drugs of this kind the resin is put in for the sake of the consistency, just as myrtle-oil or mastic-oil also is. I myself once also mixed in Attic oesypum, softening the wax with it. And in use the drug appeared to me to fall short either not at all or only very slightly of those prepared without these. It is quite clear that I say these things with regard to the strength of the drug that is to be produced. For the matter of benefit lies in the relation to something, since the softer drug is able to suit the more moderate of the malignant ulcers better than the more vigorous one. At any rate, where the ulcer itself is less malignant but its lips are callous, in these cases the oesypum is better. A good drug for these is also the marrow of the deer and of the calf. One must first triturate it and mix it with the wax, and then, once these have been united, take up into them the metallic ingredients, already triturated until they have become as fine as down. For such things are biting. And let all the drugs that are dry and earthy in consistency be thoroughly triturated beforehand, such as the gall-nut, the cytinoi, the pomegranate rinds and the fruit of the Egyptian thorn.

For all such things are hard to pulverise [678], just as those that come from dried juices or saps are easy to pulverise: myrrh, aloe, acacia and whatever is of the same genus as these. And at the end of the written recipe of the drug described above Asclepiades did well to add, in these very words: 'and unbind these every other day and foment, and having washed off the same small plaster, soften it and apply it again.' For unless the drug stays in contact with the skin for a longer time, it will accomplish nothing. This very point too has escaped most physicians, and they think that if they wipe away the ichors of the ulcer three times a day, they are doing something better than those who wipe them off twice. And those who unbind the dressing only once are often blamed by the patients themselves for neglecting them. But here too you ought to remember what we have often said in many of our treatises, that the qualities of all bodies that lie near one another act in some degree upon one another, even if one of them is much the stronger. For by this reasoning they become in time somehow of the same kind as one another, even if they differ very greatly.

And when the quality of the drug has become of like kind with the body being treated, a greater benefit [679] follows. For these reasons, then, the man who first conceived of using the flat spread that had been applied before would justly be praised, and it is fitting for us to follow him all the more, since we have learned that the idea is also attested by experience. Reasonably, too, he orders that it be fomented every third day, evidently at each unbinding; for since the drug is strong, it reasonably needs soothing. It is better, then, in cases that are not very malignant, for the wax to be fourfold or fivefold the two metallic ingredients taken together. Next after the drug written above, Asclepiades has written another drug, having the following composition: ℞ verdigris 2 oz., scale 2 oz., diphryges 1 oz., wax 1 lb., larch 3 oz. This proportion of the simple drugs is again the same as the previous one, exceeding it only in the diphryges. At any rate all the other ingredients are double those of the earlier one. For in that recipe he put in 1 oz. each of verdigris and of scale, and the wax threefold the two of them together, seeing that six ounces in all

he thought fit to put in of it; the resin, however, half an ounce [680] [more] than each of the metallic ingredients. In the second recipe, however, he orders three ounces of this to be put in instead of one and a half, and of the metallic ingredients two of each instead of 1 oz., and of the wax a litra, whereas in the first recipe he puts in a half-litra. It is quite clear, then, that in the second he added only the diphryges; and since he orders an ounce of it to be put in in proportion to the doubled amounts of the others, if anyone, mixing all the ingredients of the first recipe in single amounts, adds half an ounce of diphryges to them, he will make the composition of the drug as follows. Take: scale, 1 oz.; verdigris, 1 oz.; wax, a half-litra; larch resin, 1 oz. and a half; diphryges, half an ounce. This one too turns out to be in every respect the same as the first, except for the diphryges. Diphryges is so moderate a drug that even sprinkled on by itself it heals hard-to-cicatrise ulcers. Burnt copper behaves likewise. Verdigris, however, is considerably stronger, so much so that it is excluded from treating even very foul and moist ulcers, if one sprinkles it on by itself; for it eats away and bites violently.

But in the case of Chironian ulcers, when it is mixed with the other [681] drugs, it is itself relieved of the violence of its potency to such a degree, while it increases theirs, that the drug compounded from them all becomes excellent. On the same principle on which verdigris was mixed with the drugs mentioned, so too the unslaked lime (titanos) has been added by some, in a small proportion to many [ingredients]. Slaked lime, however, is a moderate drug, and if it is also washed, it is entirely non-biting. This plaster, then, he wrote [read perhaps 'I have written'] for the sake of example, because I think it right that the young should be trained on particulars and not be content with universals alone. Bringing the discussion back to the beginning again, I shall pass on to those written by Andromachus. [On the plasters written by Andromachus for malignant ulcers.] I shall therefore set out, for the sake of example, all those compound drugs that have been judged by experience to be suitable for malignant ulcers, making the beginning from those written by Andromachus. One might find fault with him for having written down the drugs without distinction.

For since this has been omitted, it comes about that most physicians use them badly, [682] and for this reason sometimes hit the mark wonderfully, but at other times miss it, falling very far short. So, though it was necessary to say 'this one is strongest', and again of this 'another is most moderate', and 'this one is weakest', Andromachus wrote them all one after another without adding any distinction. At any rate, he begins these very ones by writing the heading 'Cicatrizing [plasters]', and after this heading writes next: ℞ roasted cadmia, 1 litra; burnt chalcitis, 1 li.; wax, 4 litrai; dry resin, 3 litrai; myrtle oil, 3 litrai; wine, for the dry ingredients. After these he writes next, word for word, thus: 'The one with ladanum.' And having added the proportion he again wrote next: 'Otherwise, as Alcimion [makes it].' Then here too, having written the proportions of the simple drugs, he goes on to say: 'The one with barley.' And after composing this one he again wrote thus: 'Another cicatrizing one. ℞ dry resin, 18 dr.; diphryges, 4 dr.; litharge, 16 dr.; wax, 10 dr.; oil, 4 kotylai.' So that this drug is the sixth in his list from the beginning.

And after it he again writes six [683] others, prefixing to each 'another', evidently bidding us to supply 'cicatrizing'. Now five of these belong to the customary cicatrizing drugs, neither to those for ulcers hard to cicatrize nor to those for malignant ones, while the sixth belongs to those for ulcers hard to cicatrize, though not yet to those for malignant ones. But the recipes of the remaining six drugs suit malignant ulcers, differing from one another in strength. For these he ought to have done one of two things. Either, giving his teaching in a rational and methodical way, he should have added the difference in vehemence, so that we would understand that the stronger drugs are to be used on the more malignant ulcers and the weaker on the most moderate ones. Or, like the Empirics, he should have written that these particular drugs are suitable for phagedaenic ulcers and in general for those being eaten away and spreading, these others for hollow ones, these for very foul ones, and, for those with an inflammatory or scirrhous condition, or where the lips of the ulcer are hard or ridged or black or have some other colour, ones peculiar to each.

He did none of these things, but wrote, one after another, [684] six cicatrizing remedies, whose composition I shall state together with the appropriate distinctions. The first one written by him, then (the seventh from the beginning), is quite strong, inasmuch as it has taken verdigris and scale in equal bulk; but the admixture of the wax has slackened and reduced its strength, being eightfold of each and fourfold of both together. For he bids mix an ounce of each of the verdigris and the scale, and eight ounces of the wax, the one who compounded it having very rightly taken care not to mix in any of the emollient substances, I mean oil and fat, oesypum and butter and resin. But if the wax is not oily, it will have the metallic ingredients hard to mix in, and even if we force their mixing, doing it either by the fire or in hot sun, a little later the drug will become hard, so that when it is applied to the ulcer the patient will think a hard hide is touching him.

For all such drugs have a use of this kind: one who has warm hands takes up from them a portion of a size such as, once softened and spread flat, will be laid over the whole ulcer, [685] so as to cover the lips as well. When the ulcer is deep, its whole hollow is filled up besides, the drug being put into it. After this another flat spread is laid on, taking in the lips as well. Then over this a piece of linen soaked in cold water, again of such a size, is laid over the whole, so as to cover the drug. Then, on the outside, a soft sponge, held in place by a bandage of linen cloth wound in a circle around the affected part either once or twice, and of such a breadth that the whole ulcer is taken in together with its lips, and also something of the parts lying above and below them. Let the bandaging be done 'from two starting-points': they call it this when the whole middle of the band is laid upon the affected place, and each of the heads is led away towards the opposite side.

Then, if the linen strip is strong enough to hold the sponge securely with a single turn, it will be stitched together somewhere right there through its ends, the excess being cut away with scissors; but if it is weak, each of the two heads will be brought round again, drawn with equal tension towards the affected part. This must be guarded above all in the first turn, [686] and not least in the second as well. Nor indeed should you forget that which Hippocrates, first of those we know, discovered: an error committed formerly by all those before him, and now by those who have not learned the art in the proper way. For they think it better to keep the ulcerated part free from pressure and to wrap the bandage on either side of it; how harmful this is was shown by Hippocrates. When, then, you have done these things on the first day, on the second soak the sponge by pouring cold water over it. When the surrounding air is hot and dry, this should be done twice or even three times a day, and the bandage should be undone every third day; if it is winter, every fourth day. One must examine the alteration produced by the drug about the affected place, both in the hollow of the ulcer and at its lips, and indeed around them. Let the examination be made by you on the basis of what you learned in the treatises on temperaments; and these ulcers have also been discussed in the Therapeutic Method.

For the whole affected part, and each of its parts, appears either drier or moister or hotter [687] or colder than before. In addition one should examine whether any part of the lips has been reduced, or has become in some way softened or thinned, and should also look at the alteration in colour and at the quantity of the filth. From these you will know whether a stronger or a milder drug should be applied, or the same as the first. You will also be able easily to modify the first drug itself. If you wish to make it milder, mix in, while softening it, a little of one of the astringent oils: myrtle-oil, rose-oil, quince-oil, lentisk-oil, mastic-oil or oil of cypros. If you wish to make it stronger, mix in either the scale or the verdigris. For this purpose keep a small amount of each of these ready, ground very fine, so that you may add it while softening the drug. I, as you know, also sprinkle one of the mild drugs onto the ulcer, and on top of it apply the first, plaster-like drug. It is quite clear that by mild drugs I mean diphryges, sarcocolla and burnt chalcitis, and likewise burnt copper, burnt verdigris and chalcanthum.

For all these, when unburnt, are acrid; when burnt, [688] moderate; and when washed after the burning they become non-biting. It is better also to modify the plaster itself, as has been said, by admixture, and also to apply one of the other drugs which Andromachus mentioned next in order, attending not only to the powers of the ingredients being mixed but also to their quantities, as in the case of the drug just now spoken of. For the wax is mixed in fourfold to the two together, the verdigris and the copper scale. If, then, it is mixed in threefold, it will make the drug stronger, just as, if fivefold, weaker. One must proceed in this way in the other cases too, for instance in the case of the drug written after the one previously mentioned, the eighth in the sequence that follows, which has this proportion: ℞ chrysocolla 2 dr., scale 2 dr., wax 6 dr., diphryges 2 dr., litharge 8 dr., rose-oil or myrtle-oil, a little. In this drug, chrysocolla and diphryges, sprinkled on malignant ulcers by themselves alone, are sufficient to heal them.

The scale, however, is a stronger, more roughening and more biting drug, and for this reason the composer of the drug mixed in litharge, being wary of [689] the violence of the scale and wishing to relax it by the admixture of the softer drug. And if one should mix the four without wax in the stated proportion, he will have a dry dusting-powder drug that is not contemptible for the cure of malignant ulcers. But if you wish to make a plaster, it is necessary to mix in the wax as well. And because of the quantity of the metallic substances, Andromachus of necessity also mentioned liquids in the preparation under discussion, namely rose oil and myrtle oil. For the wax is very little in relation to the quantity of the metallic substances. Where, then, he directs that chrysocolla, scale and diphryges be mixed at two drachmas each of those named, and litharge at eight, plainly making fourteen in all, he needed either to mix in a very large amount of greasy wax or to add to the drug some of the oily substances. In the previously mentioned drug, by contrast, the wax was four times the metallic substances. It is therefore open to us to remove the litharge and compose the drug from the others, as I myself once did. For if one does this, he will not need the myrtle oil, since the wax, as I said, is greasy.

But if [690] it should be hard, it will be necessary to add something of the liquids as well. It is for this reason, then, that some, it seems to me, have also in such drugs added a qualification to the wax, some writing 'new', others 'fresh'. They were not, by Zeus, requiring its age, as in the case of other drugs, but its moistness. For new wax is indeed better, but not so much that one should already shun wax two or three years old. It is time to go on to the plaster written next after this one, which runs as follows. ℞ Diphryges, 84 dr.; litharge, 240 dr.; wax, 318 dr.; oil, 6 cotylae. This drug would be cicatrizing, for ulcers not yet malignant but already hard-to-cicatrise. For it dries, but not strongly, as does the one written after it. Nor, indeed, is it fitting to prepare it in so large a quantity. For this is the same as it: ℞ Diphryges, 14 dr.; litharge, 40 dr.; wax, 53 dr.; myrtle oil, 10 ounces. For the amounts written by Andromachus are sixfold of these. This, then, is truly cicatrizing, similar to the one made with cadmia and to the one called the Sweet [plaster], about which we shall speak in the following book.

The one written after [691] it is stronger, yet certainly not close to the first of these six, which is the seventh from the very beginning, into which he mixed both the scale and the verdigris with fourfold wax. For, mixing in addition to these 16 dr. of diphryges, he adds 48 dr. of litharge and 66 dr. of wax; then, because of the quantity of these, he was compelled to mix with them 1½ cotylae of myrtle oil. Let this one too, then, be counted by us among the cicatrizing drugs. And the one after it is of the same kind, but quite mild and non-biting, composed of burnt and washed lead, spodium, cadmia, diphryges and terebinth. He says that Zeno also mixes galbanum into it, which seems to me superfluous for the purposes at hand. At any rate, he writes its proportion as follows: ℞ washed lead 2 dr.; spodium 4 dr.; cadmia likewise 4 dr.; diphryges 1 or 4 [dr.]. He takes them up in 6 dr. of terebinth. He says that Zeno mixes in ½ dr. of galbanum; otherwise 4.

If he mixes it in with a view to softening the callous and hard lips [of the ulcer], which for this reason are called 'ochthōdē' (mound-like) [692] by some, he does well to mix it; but if with a view to the malignancy of the ulcer, he does not do so rightly. And even if it does not take the galbanum in addition, even so it still falls short of the strength required for malignant ulcers. It was therefore more reasonable that he wrote these twelve drugs one after another as cicatrizing. For apart from two among them, the seventh in order from the beginning and the one after it, all the others are curative of ulcers that are difficult to cicatrize, but not of malignant ones. For the twelfth, following these, is likewise cicatrizing, but too weak to treat malignant ones. Its composition is as follows. ℞ Molybdaena 100 dr., diphryges 16 dr., sory 10 dr., roasted Cyprian misy 8 dr., terebinth resin 8 dr., wax 40 dr., myrtle oil 40 dr. All such drugs should be compounded in a smaller quantity, in a proportion analogous to this one, since you know that they quickly become hard and stony. It is better, therefore, to prepare of each only as much as there is need for.

and especially if winter follows upon their use. [693] If you take a fourth part of each of the ingredients stated, there will be twenty-five drachmas of the molybdaena, four of the diphryges, two and a half of the sory, two of the roasted misy, and of the terebinth 9 dr. (otherwise, 2). Of wax and myrtle oil, an equal amount of each, 10 dr.; both together, evidently, making twenty. In all such drugs, melt the meltable ingredients and let them cool, then scrape them and mix them with the dry ingredients, which have been ground very fine. For if you pour the meltable ingredients down onto them, it often happens that wax-lumps (enkerides) form, especially when it is frosty. But if you do the mixing in hot sunshine, it is also possible to pour them down, stirring vigorously, at first with the spatula, and a little later with the pestle. In all such cases it is better for the spatula to be a branch of date palm. These, then, Andromachus wrote, as I said, without distinction: twelve drugs, prefixing to them in common only this, that they are cicatrizing. I myself have explained their difference clearly, as I think, so that it can guide an intelligent man to their skilful use in particular cases.

Apart from [694] these he mentioned other polychrest drugs which, just as they are suitable for many other conditions, are also suitable for that of hard-to-cicatrise sores. I too shall mention these in the following book, where I go through the polychrest drugs. For now my discussion concerns the drugs specifically suited to malignant and hard-to-cicatrise sores, and more particularly to the malignant ones, which some also call Chironian, as Andromachus himself does. At any rate, next after the twelve drugs I have just finished speaking of, he wrote two against anthrakes (carbuncles) and one against herpes, and after these three he wrote a fourth in the following words: "Cicatrizing plaster of Dioscorides for Chironian ulcers." He composed a drug more varied than the one written previously, though not stronger. In that earlier one he mixed in wax four times the amount of the two together, the scale and the verdigris. In the one now before us he put in less wax than the proportion of the metallic ingredients would require, and he directs that it be melted with a little myrtle oil or rose oil, without adding their quantity.

I shall now set down the whole of it in Andromachus' [695] own wording. Cicatrizing [plaster] for Chironian ulcers, of Dioscorides. ℞ Chrysocolla, 2 dr.; scraped verdigris, 2 dr.; [copper] scale, 2 dr.; wax, 6 dr.; diphryges, 2 dr.; litharge, 8 dr.; rose-oil or myrtle-oil, a little, enough to melt it. This drug is exactly the same as the one written above among the twelve cicatrizing drugs, the one that comes in order after the drug made with scale and verdigris, the eighth among them, as I said. It exceeds that one in one thing only, the verdigris. For this reason he recorded that one among the cicatrizing drugs, whereas for this one he made a greater claim, saying that it is suited to Chironian ulcers. And indeed at this point too he records a very fine drug, writing as follows: Cicatrizing [plaster], from the writings of Primion, for the despaired-of [ulcers]. By the term 'despaired-of' he means those ulcers which many have striven to heal without attaining their end, and have instead abandoned as incurable. One should have confidence in this drug, since it has been proved both in other respects and by experience. He writes its composition as follows: ℞ Sory, 24 dr.

of split alum [696] 16 drachms; of pomegranate rinds 16 drachms; of quicklime 16 drachms; of frankincense 32 drachms; of oak-gall 32 drachms; of wax 120 drachms; of calf's fat 160 drachms; of old oil 1 kotyle. This, then, is the proportion of the simple drugs that are mixed for the preparation of the compound drug before us. How it ought to be prepared he has left out, as he did also with many others that require an account of their preparation. In this case, indeed, it is quite easy, as will be said a little later. But above all I want you to know that if calf's fat is ever not at hand, old pig's fat, which they call axungia, should be mixed in instead of it. This must be unsalted and not of very many years. Now old oil is sufficiently discutient, and the fat is so too, both doing this without biting. Ox fat is likewise discutient, but not likewise free from biting. Calf's fat lies between the two: by as much as it is more acrid than swine's fat, by so much is it milder than ox fat.

Now the drug which it is our purpose to discuss has as its most powerful ingredients sory, the split alum, [697] the pomegranate rinds and the oak-gall, which, however, do not have a vigorous discutient power, but the one called astringent. It is quite clear that the gall one should always put in is the kind called omphacitis (unripe), and the alum the Egyptian and split kind. If we lack this, [one should use] the round alum, which is of coarser parts than the split, but no less astringent. That the rinds of the pomegranate are called sidia everyone knows. Yet the period of their prime is short, if one wishes to pound and grind them dry. For as they dry, the pomegranate rinds also come to have a weaker power, since it is lost together with their moisture as that is dispersed. It is therefore safer to take them while still juicy and boil them first in wine until they become easy to grind smooth. The wine must in every case be austere, but neither very new (for austere wines are of thick parts before they have aged) nor very old, so that it is already pungent. For the new wine does not penetrate into the depth of the body, while the old is pungent and biting. Better, then, is the one intermediate in age. This would in general be one between five and ten years old.

[698] It is necessary now too to call to mind what has often been said by many about austere and harsh and, in general, astringent wines, foods and drugs, and, even before that, about the things signified by the terms just mentioned. For by the term 'austere' (αὐστηρόν) the Greeks signify that which is moderately astringent, and by 'harsh' (στρυφνόν) that which is violently and intensely so. The genus common to both is indicated by the noun 'astringency' (στῦψις), when it is not further specified whether intensely or faintly. Now all astringent things draw together and condense the pores, and bind and constrict the substance of the parts with which they come into contact. They do this to a lesser or greater degree according to the quantity of the astringency. But while the surface of the body being astringed is constricted and condensed, the power of the astringent agents is shut out and prevented from going into the depth. And for this reason some of the physicians have well devised to mix with such drugs others that are fine-particled and have a pungent power, so that through them the powers of the astringent agents may be conducted into the depth of the body, guided along the way.

Having grasped this very point, then, the one who composed the [699] drug under discussion mixed unslaked lime (titanos) into it. In the book of Andromachus the designation 'lime' (titanos) has been left out, and only the word 'unslaked' (asbestos) is written, since physicians express many other things in this way too for the sake of concise wording. For instance, in the very drugs which they have composed for hard-to-cicatrise and malignant [sores], 'scale' (lepis) is written simply, without 'of copper' being added, and 'split' (schistē) without 'alum', and 'terebinth' without 'resin' being added. We supply mentally for them the words left out of the expression in this way, just as now, in the case of 'unslaked', we supply 'lime'. For they call this substance alone, par excellence, 'slaked' and 'unslaked', although the designation fits no less the other things that are burned. Having mixed the unslaked lime, then, into the harshly astringent (stryphna) drugs, the one who composed this plaster made the compound of all of them strong, so that its power reaches as far as the depth.

But since the composition had been made from the very strongest drugs, and it contained nothing assuaging or mitigating, nor [700] any of the concoctive material, he reasonably mixed into it a pus-producing drug, frankincense. Now if one were going to use the compound dry, sprinkling it on the ulcer, it would in that case be quite violent, and biting, roughening and erosive. But since the intention was to make it into a plaster, it is clear that resin or wax had to be mixed in, or in addition to these suet or marrow, and, if through these it did not yet take on a plaster-like consistency, some oil had to be added. When I add the word 'some', you must understand, besides what is called oil in the proper and unqualified sense, also the oil named with a qualification: rose-oil or myrtle-oil or oil of cypros or something of this sort. For it has already been distinguished many times how saying 'rose unguent' differs from 'rose-oil', and 'cypros unguent' from 'oil of cypros', and likewise with the others. Reasonably, then, the mixture of such drugs has not been the same for all who have composed such plasters. For that there are several causes of such a difference I found not from conjecture but from experience, since they have occurred in my own case.

For sometimes I was eager to compound the drug from simples few in number, [701] sometimes from more, and at times even from very many, or from all those of the same genus. And indeed also, because at that particular time I had some of them in abundance and others not at all or only very little, I turned to the composition of the drug from those I had, since need was pressing; then, having found it approved by trial, I always used it thus. Often, too, I deliberately set out to make some of the compound drugs stronger and some weaker, so as to have drugs suited to more conditions, and so I made the compoundings different. Indeed it was also because the part that has the ulceration needs more faculties, as when it is at once hollow and flabby and foul, raised and ridged at the lips, and receiving a flux from the parts lying above. For if one wishes to adapt oneself to all the things that have befallen parts ulcerated in this way, one must mix materials of differing (?) faculties. But if one wishes to treat first one thing, the one that is pressing, neglecting the others, there is no need to turn aside into a variety of drugs.

It is clear, then, that those before [702] me who compounded such drugs also differed for the reasons stated above. For instance, to take at once the drug now before us, its compounder chose calf's fat, since it is emollient of hardened lips. It was therefore going to provide him with a twofold use: the one, as being of a soft nature, for the uniting of the dry ingredients, which were the ones primarily beneficial; the other, that it might itself also treat one of the conditions attending the affected part. Still more beneficially, however, might deer's marrow be mixed in for hardened lips, or, if we should not have this, calf's marrow. And if none of these should be at hand, one of the liquid and non-acrid resins. For from their liquidity, and at the same time from the viscosity which all resins have as innate, there comes about a binding together of the dry drugs; and from their not being manifestly acrid, there comes their not exacerbating the ulcer. With good reason, then, some have mixed into such compositions of drugs either the terebinth or the so-called larch resin.

[705] Admirably, then, the one who composed it took on the one hand the astringent drugs, which have a repelling power, so that nothing might flow onto the affected part during the time of the cure, and on the other hand the discutient ones, for the sake of dispersing and evacuating the ichors contained in the affected part. As for their proportion, it stands thus. Of the split alum and of the pomegranate rinds, as being the most strongly astringent, he put in less, mixing sixteen drachms of each together; of the sory one and a half times the amount of each, that is, twenty-four, since it is less astringent but no less drying; and of the oak-gall he put in an amount equal to both together, the split [alum] and the pomegranate rinds, adding two to the thirty drachms, so that the total from the drugs comes to eighty-eight. Against these he set a strongly discutient and drying drug, quicklime, contenting himself with sixteen drachms, for these are sufficient to guide the power of the astringents.

At any rate, since one hundred and four drachmas had been gathered together from the metallic drugs, it would have been possible [706] to mix still more of the frankincense with them; and the drug would have become milder by as much as more had been mixed in. But since he wished to keep it strong, he mixed in less. You, however, may compound it in two ways. For after triturating the first five and mixing them all together, divide the aggregate that results into two portions, and mix with one portion sixteen drachmas of the frankincense and with the other double that amount; then, having melted, cooled and scraped the cerate made from the meltable drugs, divide this too in two, and mix one part with the portion that has the more frankincense and the other part with the remaining one. As for the proportion of the wax and the fat, the first estimate has a considerable latitude, since we do not know exactly what sort of consistency the drug will have. But once everything has been mixed it becomes clear whether it has turned out softer or harder than is proper, so that in the second compounding we may approach more precisely in our estimate both these very ingredients and, together with them, the oil.

For just as it is impossible to compose a drug without a rational method, so without experience it is not [707] possible to know its potency securely and precisely. Now, Andromachus himself said that this drug helps those who have been despaired of. Next after it he wrote down something for paronychiae, and after that he again wrote as follows, in these very words: 'For malignant [conditions], in the case of Valeria Secunda.' One must, of course, understand 'I used' in addition. The material of the drug shows that it falls short of combative treatment, but is able to soothe what has been exacerbated by the application of combative drugs. Its composition, then, is something like this: ℞ Tyrrhenian, 8 dr. (one must, of course, understand 'wax' in addition); bull's suet, 4 dr.; terebinth, 4 dr.; burnt lead, 4 dr. Use it on lint. This is what he wrote, word for word. But he did badly in neither making clear for which malignant [conditions] he says it is suitable, nor adding whether it is combative or soothing. For soothing drugs are of different kinds: some also benefit the conditions slightly besides, but some even harm them slightly.

and some neither benefiting nor harming, but only soothing the pains. These will be discussed again [708], and many such remedies, tested by long experience, will be written down. Some of them are indeed so wonderfully successful in their proportions that they are of benefit in every case, and sometimes even cure, on their own, the very conditions of what one might call 'wild' ulcers. But of the materials of those remedies, Tyrrhenian wax and burnt lead are among them, whereas terebinth and bull's suet are not. As I said, however, the discussion proper to such ulcers and drugs awaits us later. For now the task is to go through the hard-to-heal, or chironian, ulcers, or whatever one wishes to call them. To these belong also the following [plasters] recorded in the fourth book of Crito, the books being five in all. [On those written by Crito: the one with ladanum.] The one with ladanum, a most excellent cicatrizing [plaster], suitable for ulcers with raised edges and for hollow ones. It must be kept on without being undone for four days. ℞ Dry pitch 100 dr., scraped verdigris 24 dr., burnt copper 15 dr.

of red [copper] scale [709] 24 drachms; of ladanum 9 ounces; of litharge 3 pounds; of oil 1½ sextarii; of good wine 1½ sextarii. This plaster I too have prepared, having approved its materials, since it has nothing emollient in it. For that is what Hippocrates calls the whole class of drugs that have an innate moisture, such as fat, and all the oily drugs, and obviously oil itself and water. Resin and wax also have something emollient about them. Midway between them, I mean between those that are dry in temperament and the emollient ones, is pitch. For this reason it is mixed harmlessly with both classes, as is litharge too, and whatever other drugs lie about the middle temperament, even if at times they deviate slightly towards either of the excesses.

Pitch too is among such substances, at least with respect to the opposition between drying and moistening, though it has already clearly departed from the middle ones; with respect to the other opposition, that between heating and cooling drugs, it is no longer of this kind. For it heats moderately, and for this reason it is also mixed into drugs that bring to suppuration. So in the drug before us the dry [710] pitch is among the middle substances, and litharge still more so, as are the other drying substances. Since a misapprehension can arise here too, I shall discuss it, but first I shall recall a theorem useful for many purposes. I have stated it in other treatises as well, but it has been worked out sufficiently in the treatise On Simple Drugs and in that of the Therapeutic Method. We call a drug hot or cold, moist or dry, whatever is able to heat or cool or dry or moisten the body of a human being, making the reference to the best mixture in a human being. This mixture is a kind of middle among the faulty ones. For this very reason we call those hot or cold or moist or dry, naming them derivatively from whatever predominates in them, whether you wish to call it a quality or a power or a substance or a mixture. By the same reasoning, if you wish to speak of the whole mixture derivatively from the element that is in excess in the mixing, you will not hinder the knowledge of the matters themselves either.

For it has been shown in the therapeutic treatise that the discovery of remedies comes about through indication: [711] from the affections themselves comes the indication of the mixture contrary to them, and from the nature of each animal as a whole, and again of each individual part, the indication of what is proper and similar to it. So even if someone has a simple hollow ulcer, the treatment will be carried out with things that are the same in genus but differ considerably in their particular species. And for this reason it was shown that, among ulcers which are indistinguishably alike, some are cured by strongly drying drugs (root of panax, birthwort, acorus and iris), and some by frankincense alone, although it does not fill with flesh but rather brings to suppuration those natures which birthwort fills with flesh. And just as among the bodies being treated the particular difference is very great, so in the same way it is with ulcers. For a simple ulcer, hollow and clean, is treated by moderately drying drugs, but one that is foul and malignant, ridged at the lips and flabby in the flesh along the skin, requires the most vehemently drying drugs.

In the case of these ulcers, then, since it is about these too that our discussion is concerned, frankincense [712] is so weak a drug as not even to be able to bring about suppuration. Litharge is stronger than this, but it too is still below the middle ones. Dry pitch is among the middle ones, just as above it in drying stand burnt copper, chrysocolla and diphryges. Manifestly drying are burnt chalcitis, verdigris, misy, chalcanthum and flake of copper, and, in the other manner, the astringent things: oak-gall, omphacitis, pomegranate rinds, alum. Erosive before they are burnt are chalcitis, verdigris, misy and lime. Now, those that have the strongest powers seem to display the same action on all bodies, whereas the weak ones show the difference clearly; yet if you pay attention it will appear no less: even in the strong drugs there is no small difference in the action they exert on soft and on hard bodies, for they lay hold of the soft ones more quickly, cause more violent pain, and arouse greater inflammations.

Since, then, I have said these things usefully not only for the present matters but also for many others in this treatise, [713] I shall return again to the drug under discussion. For it, I said, Crito had written 100 drachms of dry pitch and 3 litrai of litharge. Neither of them is able by its own proper power to heal a malignant ulcer, but they were reasonably mixed with the beneficial ingredients so that the drug being compounded might become emplastic. Their quantity, arrived at by technical estimation, came to the weight just stated. The compounder took care neither to mix so little of each with the strong drugs that the biting and erosive ones would become painful to those being treated, nor so much in both bulk and weight as to slacken their power. For scale of copper dries and cleanses strongly, and verdigris still more than it; and both, besides doing these things, also eat through the flesh. Burnt copper, however, needs neither to be intensified nor to be slackened by anything, being moderate in power for the present purposes. And it is plain that the measure of the oil was estimated from the things mixed with it and from the amount of boiling.

For metallic substances that are being prepared so as to dry without biting need to be boiled for a longer time [714].
