And for this reason Crito also added the boiling for them, writing roughly as follows, in these very words: 'Boil litharge and oil until it thickens somewhat; then scale of copper and verdigris, until it thickens and becomes of good colour; then throw in the pitch; then, having cooled it, add ladanum made smooth with wine, taking care that it does not boil over once this has been thrown in; then, having united it over a gentle fire, pour it out and knead it.' This, then, is the written prescription for the boiling. It is also possible to put in more oil and to boil for a longer time: first the litharge, then, throwing in upon it the verdigris, the scale and the copper. For things that are boiled for a longer time acquire a twofold virtue, at any rate in ulcers of this kind, becoming both more drying and less biting. Concerning the other simple drugs, then, all those named by Crito in the plaster under discussion, I have said as much as is appropriate.

I have reserved the account of ladanum, because even by itself it suits hard-to-cicatrise sores when triturated with wine. This is not because it needs the power of wine, but because it is harder [715] than is right for the plaster. But if one mixes oil with it and boils it, one blunts the power of the drug. Yet it is not so strong as to need blunting, as verdigris or chalcitis or copper flake or some such thing does; and for this reason it is milder. Such is the fresh ladanum, for it is most suitable for the cicatrization of hard-to-cicatrise sores. In Cyprus, at any rate, where most of it is produced, a certain physician used to work it soft while it was still fresh and soft and apply it to such sores. If it had hardened even a little, he carried out the softening with myrtle-oil, and when myrtle-oil was not to hand, with oil of cypros or rose-oil. Another drug, not long after this one, in the fourth book, Criton wrote out in these very words, as follows: The [plaster] made with chamaeleon, effective for the same things as the Tyrian. It is most cicatrizing of intractable, callous and chronic sores. It also heals fissures in the anus, condylomata and indurations. Litharge, 1 mina; wax, ½ mina; verdigris, a quarter of a mina, and chamaeleon, an eighth; oil, a mina.

Boil the oil and the litharge, stirring [716] with a spatula, until it thickens and becomes quince-yellow. When this has happened, sprinkle on the verdigris. Then add the wax, having melted it carefully, and, lifting it from the fire, sprinkle on the chamaeleon; and when it has become united, pour it out into a mortar and, having softened it by kneading, take it up. This drug took chamaeleon in place of ladanum, since it is of the same power, for both are cicatrizing of hard-to-heal sores. The difference between them lies in this: the former has burnt copper and has no wax at all, whereas in this one there is wax but there is no copper. And he did this reasonably. For in the former he used ladanum instead of wax for the uniting of the drugs that lack moisture, whereas here, having nothing of that sort, he mixed in wax, which is a moderately emollient drug, though certainly not a cicatrizing one. It would have been possible here too to put in more oil, as indeed also old oil or castor oil. I, for my part, also put mastic-oil into such preparations, since it shares in several powers. For it has something emollient, something discutient and something astringent, all of which are required by hard-to-cicatrise sores accompanied by hardness of the lips.

[717] [On the remedies written by Heracleides.] It is time, then, now to make mention also of the remedies written by Heracleides of Tarentum in his book addressed to Astydamas. For he is a trustworthy man, if ever anyone was, since he writes only what has been judged by him through experience. This man, then, wrote word for word as follows: 'For old ulcers. Of scale one part, of scraped verdigris four parts. It is taken up in addition with an eightfold quantity of myrtle cerate.' Now Heracleides, as one writing notes for physicians, added 'take up in myrtle cerate'. But many of those of the present day are so rash that, before acquiring from teachers some medical proficiency, they set out from books of this kind to use fine drugs without method, and for this reason often fail. For instance, by mixing in less or more of the myrtle cerate, one may at one time use the drug moister and softer, at another harder and drier: at the first application by a broad conjecture, as was said earlier, but in the second use coming nearer to the mark, as was shown.

[718] For, looking at the ulcer, if it has been dried insufficiently, we shall make the drug more vigorous, so that it dries more; but if it has been dried more than it should, we shall make it milder by mixing in more of the myrtle cerate. For the potency of metallic substances is relaxed not only by this but by every cerate. Next after this he added the heading 'Another', and one must of course understand 'potency' along with it, and set down the following beneath it: 'Grind the scale fine, pour vinegar over it and triturate it under the Dog-star, bringing it to the thickness of honey, or boil it. When it has become dry, grind it fine once more, mix in eight parts of cerate, and use it for fresh wounds and old ulcers, and for abrasions, chafings and chilblains that are not very ulcerous.' You must also know the following about this drug. For the other conditions one would do well to mix eightfold cerate with the scale; but for very old ones, that is, the hard-to-heal ones, you will do no harm even if you mix sixfold or fivefold, for they need stronger remedies. Heracleides wrote the account of the drug as follows: 'It is also possible to use the scale after drying it over a fire.'

His [719] meaning is that, even if we compound the drug at some other season, we should use fire in place of the sun's heat. All such preparations, however, turn out finer when they are triturated in the summer sun over many days, some with wine, others with vinegar. Those triturated with vinegar become finer in their parts, and for this reason more reductive, more attenuating and more drying. For cicatrisations, however, those made with wine are better, and there is need of them once the hard-to-cicatrise sores have first been dried and then first cleansed. They will be dried beforehand by means of things that dry strongly, cleansed by means of detergent things, and cicatrised by means of astringent things. Another. Next Heraclides wrote another drug from the same material, but not a strong one, because he mixed much litharge with the diphryges. For he directs that thirty-five drachms of litharge be put into it, and eight of diphryges. And these too he takes up in a cerate containing 40 drachms of wax and 3 cotylae of oil.

I myself have often used diphryges alone with a cerate of this kind [720], though not even it against phagedaenic, chironian and putrefying ulcers, for it falls far short in power of the remedies that treat such conditions, but rather for ulcers that are hard to cicatrise without great malignancy. Hence if someone also mixes litharge with it, and that in large quantity, he will make the drug weak. After this, a drug of the following kind is recorded as belonging to the same declared purpose. Take: wax, 12 dr.; terebinth resin, 3 dr.; scale, 4 dr.; ladanum, 4 dr.; asphalt, 3 dr. Grind the ladanum by itself, and the scale as well; then melt the other ingredients with myrtle oil and mix. If the ladanum is soft, melt it. In this prescription Heraclides has clearly indicated that when the ladanum is hard one should grind it by itself in the mortar, but when it is moist and soft one should melt it down over the fire, either alone or with a little oil. You have seen me do this constantly, not only with this substance but also with ammoniac incense. The drug written after this one by the Tarentine is also of the same declared purpose, in the following proportion. Take: chalcitis, 25 dr.

[721] of cadmia 12½ dr. Having ground them separately and mixed them, boil unadulterated wine and pour it over, so that the mass is kneaded in due proportion; then grind until it has dried. Then, having melted wax 50 dr., terebinth resin 30 dr., myrtle oil 8 kotylai, mix into the cerate 20 dr. of the dry ingredients. This drug too contains none of the softening ingredients. In the mixing with the cerate, however, the one who has been rationally trained in the methods I set out would suitably produce the quantity of the mixture appropriate to each of the ulcers. He also does well to pour the unadulterated wine, that is, wine to which sea-water has not been added, hot over the chalcitis and the cadmia, as though wishing to remove the acrimony of the chalcitis through its heat. Another noteworthy drug is written next after this one, composed of simples of the following kinds and quantities: flake of steel 4 dr.; scraped verdigris 2 dr. (in some of the copies 1 dr. is written); chrysocolla 25 dr., or 15; wax 25 dr. In some copies we found neither the wax nor the verdigris.

Having ground the other ingredients fine, [722] melt the wax with a little resin, so that the drug is not too hard, and having mixed them, use it; and on top apply a sponge wrung out of vinegar. Demetrius the Bithynian said that he used the chrysocolla by itself, taking it up in very hot wax. In this drug too Heraclides showed that resin is not mixed into such drugs for a primary purpose, but in order to give them a certain viscosity towards a plaster-like consistency, and especially when the wax is neither oily by nature nor fresh, but hard and parched. The scale of steel, however, dries strongly, besides also having an astringent power. He said that Demetrius the Bithynian used it thus, taking up the chrysocolla alone in the wax. And Demetrius did well to use it in this way; just as I too, in such cases, often use not only chrysocolla but also each of the others on its own, softening it with soft wax.

It is clear that I said that each of the others which I went through earlier benefits such ulcers, and that I grind them, compounding such drugs with the wax, for each [723] of the intractable ulcers that I treat. For sometimes I take up chrysocolla in wax, sometimes burnt copper or the scale, and this either of steel or of iron or of copper; sometimes verdigris, unburnt or burnt, as also misy and chalcitis. And occasionally I also mix in one of the astringents, about which I spoke earlier, when I wish to repel what flows in; among these are alum, pomegranate rinds and the gall, the cytini and the balaustion, and all other such things. Trusting me, then, that of all the drugs mentioned up to this point none is to be discarded, practise the method of their use, so that you may succeed as I do. And since two other noteworthy drugs are written next by the Tarentine, it seemed reasonable to me to add these as well. The first of them, then, he wrote somewhat as follows. Rx: of scale, 4 dr.; of manna, 4 dr.; of split alum, 2 dr.; of misy, 2 dr. Having ground them with vinegar and made pastilles weighing 2 dr. each, store them away.

At the time of use, take of wax [724] 4 dr. (others: 40), pine resin 2 dr., bull's fat 4 dr.; melt them, let them set, and mix with the pastille. Use it for wounds, as it is agglutinative and anti-inflammatory. So much for the Tarentine. But I [say]: the preparation mixed in this way, he says, one ought to use for wounds; for malignant ulcers, however, one should not mix in a cerate of this kind, but the wax alone is sufficient, as we said in the case of the preceding drugs. And if it should ever be necessary to mix one of the emollient substances with it, let it be a little myrtle-oil or oil of cypros or rose-oil. Nor will you do any harm if you mix in the resin called larix, or the terebinth, which is less suitable for ulcers of this kind, yet certainly not to be rejected. The other resins, however, one should not mix in, unless there is a great lack of those mentioned before. So too with fat: one should not mix this in either, unless you also wish to soften the lips of the ulcer. That bull's fat is more drying than all the other fats that come from domestic animals, you have often heard.

For the fat of the lion and that of leopards [725] exceed it in fineness of parts, and so, evidently, does that of the hyena. It is better, then, when one must mix in fat, to put in goose fat, and preferably that of free-ranging geese; for it has sufficient fineness of parts and is soothing. One drug still remains, written immediately after the one written above. Heracleides began his instruction on it with these words: 'the ipōtērion, and especially for those with tender skin.' Since this drug belongs to the other class of material and power, which we said suits those who cannot bear the application of strong drugs but are stung, exacerbated and subject to flux, let the account of it be deferred; it will be given when I go through drugs of that kind. Now I shall pass on to those similar to the drugs written above, adding only this much more about them: Heracleides also wrote down the same drugs in another book, entitled The Soldier, and disagreed with himself only in the one that is third among them in order. For here 'wax, 40 drachms' is written without qualification, but in The Soldier there is added: 'but some, 16 drachms.' And this is indeed better.

[726] is. For a large admixture of wax destroys the potency of the drug. Heracleides also mentions these same drugs in the writings he addressed to Antiochis, and indeed the first of them first, writing thus in those just as in these: 'For those that are very long-standing and callous you will use this one. Of scale, 1 part; of verdigris,' and here in some of the copies the δ΄ is written marked off by a point, while in others it has a long line above it, so that it signifies either 4 parts or the fourth of one. In the same way I found it written differently in the aforementioned writings as well. So in this respect too there is need of the present treatise, so that one may know how to distinguish the differences between drugs, for only such a person would use them properly. At any rate, this very drug under discussion will be quite acrid if it takes four times the amount of verdigris. But if one puts in a fourth part of verdigris relative to one part of the scale, he will have a moderate drug for malignant [ulcers], especially if he makes the mixture of them not with wax alone but with cerate.

It has been said before that the wax must be both soft and fresh [727]; but if I am at a loss for such wax, then, warming by a fire or in the sun the wax we have and softening it with a little myrtle oil, we shall in this way mix in both the scale and the verdigris. It was also said at the beginning of this book that a most excellent drug is one composed of scale and verdigris with the addition of four times the amount of wax. For this reason I use it continually, mixing in as a rule an equal amount of burnt copper as well. The Tarentine, in the book he wrote to Antiochis, has added to the use of this drug things he did not add in those earlier writings of his that I mentioned. I shall therefore write out his whole statement, which runs thus: 'For very chronic and callous sores use this. One part of scale, a fourth of verdigris; having ground them fine, take them up in a hard eightfold myrtle cerate and use, having first washed the ulcer with cold water.' He added also that one must first wash the ulcer with cold water. Now, then, I shall write out the things I have passed over among those written by Andromachus under the same claim.

For earlier I went through only the plasters [728]. But I shall now add those drugs, prepared beforehand in the form of pastilles and mixed with cerates at the time of use, which he says are cicatrizing for ulcers hard to heal, and those that are dry dusting-powders. I begin from the one written in the section on dry drugs near the end. [Dry drugs from those of Andromachus: a dry cicatrizing drug.] Take: burnt bones (otherwise, burnt oyster-shells), 2 dr.; manna, 1 dr.; cadmia, 4 obols (in another copy, 4 dr.). Use finely ground; also for spreading ulcers. Another dry cicatrizing drug. Take: pine bark, 6 dr.; birthwort, 6 dr.; pumice, 4 dr.; dry resin, 4 dr.; manna, 6 dr. It is evident that by this he means the Colophonian resin. Illyrian iris, 2 dr. Use finely ground. Another, which cicatrizes even malignant ulcers. Take: pine bark, 6 dr.; burnt stag's horn, 4 dr.; cadmia, 18 dr.; manna (otherwise, white lead), 4 dr.; scraped verdigris, 2 dr. Use finely ground. Another. Take: oak-gall, 4 dr.; white lead, 8 dr.; myrtle, 4 dr.; litharge, 8 dr.; slag of lead, 4 dr. Use finely ground.

Of these four drugs the first is very simple, non-biting and drying, [729] and has a faint astringency. The second, because pine bark has been mixed into it, has a perceptible astringency, of the kind that drugs which are to cicatrize well must have. The third, because it contains not only the pine bark but also the verdigris, is suited to cases in which filth readily accumulates on the ulcerated parts, for it both removes their filth and does not hinder the cicatrization. The next has myrtle in place of the pine bark, together with the other ingredients, which dry without biting. After these he wrote three other dry drugs and added a fourth to them, word for word as follows: 'Another dry drug for hypersarcotic ulcers, cicatrizing, non-biting, as Harpocras made it. Sandarach, chrysocolla, arsenicon, an equal amount of each. This drug also works for malignant ulcers.' It is not at all like the preceding ones. Rather, it suits ulcers that grow excess flesh through much moisture, being also reductive of that flesh, for both sandarach and arsenicon are of such a power. One thing has been added to them from among the drugs that benefit malignant ulcers wonderfully: chrysocolla.

[On what was written by Archigenes.] [730] What Archigenes wrote about such ulcers in the second book On Drugs is set down here in his own diction, in the very words, as follows. On ulcers that are not callous, and old ones. Of ulcers, bring the old ones to cicatrisation thus: having cleansed them with some common [remedy], apply very old oil with lint plugs. Or take up scraped verdigris in a rose-oil cerate containing a little resin and apply it. Or take up as much as possible of the scale of red copper in a myrtle cerate and use it. Or: washed starch, 3 parts; calf's suet, 3 parts; Tyrrhenian wax, 1 part. Melt what can be melted, mix in the starch, and use. Or: diphryges and copper scale, 4 drachms each; manna, 8 drachms. Grind them well with vinegar to the consistency of honey, then melt 32 drachms of wax with 1½ kotylai of oil, pour it over, and, having worked it into one mass, use it as a dressing on lint plugs; or else make the oil less and make it into a splenion. Or: chalcitis and white lead, equal amounts; common salt, double; litharge, double the salt. Grind them with wine and oil alternately and use it as a liparon.

Or: of litharge, white lead and diphryges equal amounts, of quicklime [731] twice as much; use with myrtle cerate. Or: diphryges (the text has διφυγές), scale [of copper] and oak-gall in equal amounts, of verdigris half as much, with myrtle cerate. Some also mix in pine resin. Or sprinkle on root of wild cucumber, and over it [lay] lint [soaked] from cold [water]; it cleanses and cicatrizes. For ulcers that are hard to cicatrize, in whatever place of the body they may be. Seed of erysimum, ground smooth, mixed and brought to the consistency of a rhypodes, and applied in the manner of a pad, very quickly cicatrizes even malignant ones. Cicatrizing [remedy] for [the ulcers] of old people. For those of old people use slag of lead with myrtle cerate. If you wish to make it keep (παλαιῶσαι), mix in pig's fat as well. Ulcers that are turning black: first foment them with barley loaves freshly baked, then use butter and white lead in equal amounts, carefully combined.

[On putrefying ulcers and spreading ulcers.] For putrefying ulcers and spreading ulcers (νομαί): bitter-vetch meal, liquid alum, the inside of bread made from fine wheat flour (σεμιδαλίτης), unwashed flesh of old pork or of some other old salted meat, liquid terebinth resin, [732] good honey; work equal weights together and apply. Or equal amounts of birthwort and of the juice of castor-oil-plant leaves, half as much verdigris, with water; smear it on at the thickness of honey, adding a little of the liquid. If the eschar does not come away, mix in elaterium equal to the verdigris. Sory, finely ground and sprinkled on thickly with dry lint on top, works well for putrefactions. Or anoint round about with equal amounts of round birthwort and oak-gall with oil. Or wrap the root of wild cucumber in leaves of cabbage or of beet or of dock and bury it in hot ashes; when it has softened, pound it and apply; it cleans out vigorously. Or sprinkle on θαλλία boiled in wine, with honey; or sprinkle on chalkitis, and lay dry lint on top. Apply ground elaterium or linseed with chalkanthos; or sprinkle on thyme and stavesacre or the cultivated kind, with boiled figs; or ground fig leaves with honey; or nitre with cumin, and meal with honey; or the root of wild cucumber with honey; or boiled squill with honey; or hellebore with honey.

These are also effective for phagedaenas [733] and for melaniae and spreading ulcers (nomai); or: of sory 12 dr., of chalcitis 10 dr., of misy 4 dr.; triturate with half a cotyle of the sharpest vinegar until it dries, and take it up. Use it by dipping a probe and rolling it over the ulcer, and on top apply a single-layer linen cloth soaked in wine-and-oil (oenelaeum). If it becomes inflamed, sprinkle on henbane with barley-meal, or cabbage with honey. For those that have worms, smear on white lead and polium in equal parts with liquid pitch. [On cancerous ulcers.] For cancerous and malignant ulcers: of burnt river crab and of cadmia, equal parts, ground fine, sprinkle on; or apply the ash of the crabs with cerate; or apply erysimum seed ground very fine, making it to the consistency of lees with honey, as a pledget (plēnion). It is extremely effective for Chironian ulcers, for old ulcers and those hard to cicatrise, for the malignant black ulcers (melantria) on the shins, and for the malignant ulcers in the breasts. It is extremely effective for drawing out scrofulous swellings (choirades) and parotid swellings: of beef suet 3 lb., or, as some say, 5; of terebinth 5 oz.;

of manna [734] ½ ounce; of the earth called sardē, which the fullers use, 5 ounces. Pour the meltable ingredients over the dry ones, combine them into one, and use. Or sprinkle with boiled lentil with honey, or with thallia, or with both. [On callous ulcers.] For callused and ridged ulcers, the ones called 'sweet', the caustics known from experience will also be effective. Specifically, smear around them roasted nitron and quicklime with the urine of an uncorrupted boy; or smear around them verdigris, frankincense, salt and honey. [On the plasters written by Asclepiades for ulcers of this kind.] Asclepiades, surnamed Pharmakion, wrote best about ulcers of this kind.

For while one thing is common to all of them, namely that they are hard-to-cicatrise, some do not cicatrise because they are treated badly or because the patient under treatment follows a soft regimen, though they have no malignancy of their own; others are hard-to-treat on their own account, either because noxious humours flow in upon them [735] or because the ulcerated place has already acquired such a condition that, even if the blood flowing in is wholesome, it corrupts it. Asclepiades, then, having divided such ulcers into three kinds, gave his account of each one separately; I too shall set these out in order in his own words, adding explanation or judgement wherever there may be any ambiguity in the account. Concerning the first kind of such ulcers and drugs, then, Asclepiades writes word for word somewhat as follows. 'When the bodies are callused and are brought to a scar only with difficulty, the preparations written below are to be used. Andreas's, repressive of every protuberance. It is also an enhaemon, a wound plaster, anti-inflammatory. It acts on spreading sores and glues down sinuses. It acts on fluxional ulcers and on chronic and hard-to-cicatrise ones. Take: litharge, 3 pounds; flake of copper, chalcitis, scraped verdigris, 3 ounces of each; vinegar, 1 cotyle; old oil, 8 pounds. Prepare in the proper manner. The drug of Aster, successful for the aforesaid conditions. It is a good discutient.'

℞ [736] Litharge, 1 pound; old oil, 2½ pounds; verdigris, 1 ounce; chalcitis, 1 ounce; red scale, 1 ounce; vinegar, 1 cotyle. The plaster of Amphion, for the same conditions. ℞ Litharge, 2 pounds; old oil, 4 pounds; chalcitis, 9 ounces; copper scale, 4 drachms; vinegar, 1 cotyle. Prepare in the usual way. The plaster of Turpilianus, the one called 'of the philosophers'. It acts on fluxional sores, it acts on chronic and hard-to-cicatrise ones, it brings up corrupted bones. ℞ Litharge, 3 pounds; old oil, 3 sextarii; chalcitis, 2½ pounds; copper scale, 25 drachms; vinegar, 1 cotyle. Boil the litharge and the oil until they reach a consistency, then add the scale ground very fine and stir continuously; and when it is right, add little by little the chalcitis ground with the vinegar, the drug having been cooled somewhat; then, setting it on the fire, boil it again until it is non-soiling, and having emptied it out into a mortar, beaten it and kneaded it, take it up and use it for the conditions mentioned above.

The so-called tawny Isis, a successful drug for fluxional [737] and chronic and malignant and hard-to-heal [ulcers], and especially on the extremities. It must be prepared rather softer, for when stored it contracts and becomes drier. It is as follows. ♃ Litharge, 100 dr.; Sinopic red ochre (miltos), 8 dr.; diphryges, wax, burnt chalcitis, 1 ounce each (in another [copy], 4 dr. each); raw chalcitis, 2 dr.; oil, 2 cotylae. Boil the litharge and oil until it boils up a second and a third time. When this has happened, sprinkle it with a little water with the fingers; then sprinkle on the diphryges and the roasted chalcitis, ground smooth, little by little, sprinkling with the water, until the drug no longer crackles as it boils. When it has thickened, add the wax. Have lying ready the ingredients ground with a little oil, the raw chalcitis and the Sinopic [ochre]. When the drug is in good condition, add these and stir continuously; and when it is right, pour it out into a mortar, beat it up and knead it, then take it up and use it. Another, of Scribonius Largus, a successful drug. ♃ Wax, 100 dr. (others: 50); litharge, 50 dr.; myrtle oil, 1 cotyle.

of burnt misy, of burnt chalcitis, of burnt split alum, [738] of white lead, of terebinth resin, 2 dr. of each. Prepare in the customary manner. Another. It also reduces staphylomata in the eyes, and it is effective for hard-to-heal [ulcers]. ℞ Sinopic red earth 15 dr., litharge 100 dr., wax 40 dr., pine resin 20 dr., chalcitis 30 dr., ammoniac salt 1 dr., frankincense 1 dr., oil 1 cotyle. Prepare in the customary manner. Another, as Aphrodas [makes it]. It is effective also for condylomata and hard-to-heal fissures. ℞ litharge 48 dr., terebinth 28 dr., roasted misy, roasted chalcitis, 8 dr. of each, Sinopic red earth, chalcanthum, 4 dr. of each, old oil 1 cotyle, water 1 cotyle, wax 40 dr., castor oil 1 litra (others: half a cyathus). The dry ingredients are ground with the water. And so much concerning these. [On the second kind of hard-to-treat ulcers, about which Asclepiades wrote word for word as follows.] For the fluxional and hard-to-heal among ulcers one must use the preparations written below. The one with chamaeleon, which Philoxenus used for the fluxional and hard-to-heal among ulcers.

Take: of litharge [739] 1 litra; of old oil 2 litrai; of root of chamaeleon 4 ounces; of birthwort 4 ounces; of galbanum 2 ounces; of oak-gall 2 ounces; of frankincense 2 ounces. Prepare in the customary way. Another, the one called 'of the Theban'. Take: of litharge 1 litra; of old oil 1 sextarius; of chalcanthum 24 drachms; of chamaeleon 12 drachms; of birthwort 12 drachms; of galbanum 8 drachms; of frankincense 8 drachms. Prepare in the customary way. Another, the one made with the reeds, for fluxional and chironian ulcers; it is effective also against the bite of every creeping creature. Take: of litharge one litra, of old oil 2 litrai; of the root of black chamaeleon, of birthwort, of unripe oak-galls, 4 drachms of each; of galbanum, of ammoniac incense, of frankincense, 2 ounces of each. Prepare, stirring with roots of green reeds. The so-called gangrenous [plaster] of Castus, a successful drug. Take: of litharge 120 drachms; of oil 2½ sextarii; of root of black chamaeleon 16 drachms; of vinegar 2½ sextarii; of verdigris 8 drachms; of pine bark 8 drachms; of myrrh 4 drachms.

Prepare in the usual way. The black [plaster] called 'the one with pyrites' [740], of Damonicus. It acts on fluxional, hard-to-heal and phagedaenic [ulcers]. Inserted, it also acts on fistulas, and it softens every hardness. ♃ Of litharge and asphalt, 100 or 50 dr. each; of pitch and wax, 8 dr. each; of pyrites and terebinth, 25 dr. each; of propolis and split alum, 15 dr. each; of ammoniac incense, 12 dr.; of galbanum and aloe, 8 dr. each; of verdigris and manna, 5 dr. each; of old oil, 2 sextarii. Boil the litharge with the oil until it draws together; then add the asphalt, pitch, wax, resin and propolis; and when they have melted, let it cool and add the verdigris and the stone, then the ammoniac; then lift it off, cool it a little, and add the split alum, the galbanum and the manna; boil it a little, pour it out into cold water, leave it a day and a night, soften it by working and use it. It acts on hard-to-heal [ulcers]. Another. ♃ Of pitch, wax and pyrites, 12 dr. each; of ammoniac incense, 10 dr.; of asphalt, 50 dr.; of litharge, 40 dr.; of propolis, 8 dr.; of split alum, 5 dr.; of verdigris, 2 dr.; of oil, 1 sextarius. Another black [plaster], the one with willows, for the same conditions.

Take: of foreign misy [741], round alum, chalcitis, melanteria, scraped verdigris, split alum and unripe oak-galls, white lead, of each a half-litra; of wax, dry resin, Bruttian pitch and bitumen, of each 2 litrai; of acrid vinegar, half a xestes; of omphacine oil, 2 litrai; of the leaves of the tender shoots of the willow, 2 litrai. Put the willow leaves into the vinegar, set it on the fire and boil, stirring continuously, until a third of the liquid is left. Pound the dry ingredients and sift them through a very fine sieve, put them into a mortar, squeeze out the liquid and add it to them, and triturate diligently, as with the head preparations. Boil the meltable ingredients until they no longer stain. Then let them cool, scrape them off, add them to the triturated ingredients, pour the whole out into a mortar, take it up and use. The Indian plaster of Tharseus the surgeon, for the aforementioned conditions. Take: of wax, roasted resin, dry pitch, liquid bitumen and Zacynthian [pitch], of each 2 litrai.

of white lead, verdigris, chalcitis, foreign misy, melanteria, alum both split and round, unripe oak-galls, pomegranate rinds, sumac, frankincense, a half-litra of each [reading ἀνὰ for ἀκὰ]; of vinegar as much as [742] suffices. Boil the meltable ingredients until they no longer stain; and having pounded the dry ones and sifted them through a very fine sieve, knead them with vinegar and take them up with the meltable ingredients. Another, the Cyzicene. It acts against chronic affections and severances of the sinews. ♃ Of frankincense, the finest possible, wax, myrrh, aristolochia, chalcitis, Illyrian [iris], galbanum, 4 dr. each; of terebinth [resin], litharge, 8 dr. each; of oil, 1 kotyle. Putting everything into a copper vessel, boil it over soft ashes, stirring until, when dripped into cold water, it has the thickness of honey. After this take it off, stirring; spreading this on a small piece of leather, apply it, and undo it in winter after the seventh day, in summer after the fifth. Another, from those of Philoxenus. ♃ Of frankincense, myrrh, saffron, Illyrian [iris], bdellium, flake of copper, chalcanthum, chalcitis, alum round and split, foreign misy, ammoniac incense, propolis, oak birdlime, opopanax, closed pomegranate rinds, 4 dr. each; of aristolochia, 8 dr.; of wax, 100 dr., which he writes as a mina; of bull's suet, 100 dr.; of terebinth resin, 75 dr., which he writes as 'three-quarters' [τριατέτταρα].

Putting the resin into a new earthenware pan [743], boil it until it becomes odourless. Then, having shredded the suet and the wax, add them and melt them. Pound the dry ingredients and sift them through a very fine sieve; then, taking the meltable ingredients off the fire and letting them cool somewhat, sprinkle the dry ones over them, stirring carefully. One must have myrrh, frankincense, bdellium and opopanax ready ground with vinegar, and the contents of the pan are put into these and ground, so that wax-lumps (enkerides) do not form. When it is in good condition, take it up into a wooden box, having first smeared it inside with iris oil. [On the third kind of hard-to-treat ulcers, concerning which Asclepiades wrote the following, word for word.] In ulcers that do not close up at all, or that close up but break open again, either because the flesh is being corrupted or because the underlying bones too have become corrupted, one must use the preparations set out below. A successful drug for chironian and intractable ulcers. ℞ Copper flakes, scraped verdigris, 1 ounce each; wax, a half-litra; resin of larch, 1 ounce.

and a half. [744] [Pour] the meltable ingredients over the dry ones, take it up and use it, softening it carefully and laying a small plaster over the affected part alone, so that it covers only the ulcer. The surrounding parts must be covered with a non-inflaming drug. In the course of the treatment one must undo the ulcer every third day, then foment it first, wash the same small plaster, soften it and apply it again, until the ulcer begins cicatrisation. Another successful one. ℞ verdigris, copper scale, of each 2 oz.; diphryges 1 oz.; wax 1 lb.; larch 3 oz. Prepare and use as stated above. After these, concerning the so-called cephalics, as Asclepiades wrote, word for word as follows. Cephalic of Deileon. For chronic and hard-to-heal [ulcers]; it brings up corrupted bones. ℞ copper scale, manna, frankincense, dry resin, of each 100 dr.; vinegar 12 kotylai. Grind the copper scale with vinegar, and when it has been levigated add very finely ground frankincense and the resin, form pastilles, and dry them in the shade.

In use, in cases where you wish to remove callus, take one part of the drug and [745] an equal amount of cerate prepared with rose oil. In other cases let there be one part of the drug and three or four parts of the cerate, for the mixture must be made appropriate to the underlying conditions. The dark-green cephalic, which Tryphon the elder used. It is effective for chronic and hard-to-heal [ulcers], and brings up corrupted bones. Rx copper flakes 12 [unit not stated]; manna, frankincense, ammoniac incense, dry pine resin, treated calf's suet, terebinth resin, 16 dr. each; wax and oil, a quarter of a mina each; vinegar 1 kotyle. Prepare in the usual way. The cephalic of Philotas, for chronic and hard-to-heal [ulcers]; it brings up corrupted bones and melts away callosities. Rx Eretrian earth 100 dr.; copper flakes 50 dr.; isinglass 25 dr.; vinegar 12 kotylai. One must chop the isinglass into small pieces, put it into a glass vessel, pour vinegar over it and let it soak; when it has dissolved, add it to the prepared drug, and after mixing form pastilles. The use has already been explained. Of Dionysius of Samos.

Take: Eretrian earth, 1 mina [746]; copper flakes, half a mina; isinglass, a quarter of a mina; frankincense, an eighth of a mina; scraped verdigris, an eighth of a mina; myrrh, one-sixteenth of a mina; vinegar, 2 choes. Compound it during the heats under the Dog-star, grinding everything together with the vinegar in the sun. Cut the isinglass into small pieces and soak it with a little vinegar in a glass vessel; then mix it with the ingredients in the mortar and form pastilles weighing four drachms each, some eight, and dry them. In using the drug, take one part to three of cerate prepared with rose oil. Over the compresses he throws greasy wool soaked in vinegar. For fistulas, to one part of the drug, two parts of rose-oil cerate; make collyria and insert them. The drug made from herbs, as Lucius the Preceptor makes it. Take: anagallis, the kind that has the dark-blue flower, 56 drachms; wild poppy, 56 drachms; of the leaves of fresh henbane and of fresh leeks, 56 drachms each; copper flakes, 25 drachms; frankincense powder, 20 drachms; dry pine resin, 16 drachms; aloes, 6 drachms; split alum, 4 drachms, and round alum, 4 drachms; ammoniac salt, 4 drachms; wax, 1 mina.

of old oil [747] 2 kotylai; of vinegar a sufficient amount. Having pounded the herbs carefully and dissolved them in vinegar, squeeze out the liquid for the preparation of the drug. The Isis, cephalic, for Chironian and hard-to-heal [ulcers]. It is also good as an enaimos [plaster for fresh, bleeding wounds]. ♃ Of wax 100 dr.; of Colophonian resin 200 dr.; of ammoniac incense, of flake of copper, of burnt frankincense, of slender birthwort, of verdigris, of ammoniac salt, 8 dr. each; of galbanum, of manna, of myrrh, of aloe, 12 dr. each; of round alum 6 dr.; of old oil 1 kotyle; of vinegar a sufficient amount. Prepare it, and use the drug sometimes undiluted, sometimes diluted. [On the useful plasters written by Heras for the hard-to-treat among ulcers.] He wrote certain other polychrest plasters, which he says are also suited to [ulcers] hard to cicatrise and to malignant ones. But of one that excels especially for these alone he made mention, writing about it in roughly these very words: 'The [plaster] of Hygieinus himself, for many things, well-coloured, effective in [ulcers] hard to scar over and in paronychias; there is no finer plaster than this.'

Take: of litharge [748] of the golden kind, 1 mina; of wax, 1 mina; of the root of black chamaeleon, 36 drachms; of scraped verdigris, 18 drachms; of chrysocolla, 40 drachms; of oil, 3 cotylae. Boil the litharge and the oil over a gentle fire until it begins to boil up; then, having lifted it from the fire, sprinkle in the verdigris, and stir, boiling it again, until it recovers its proper colour; then add the wax; and when it is in good condition, the chrysocolla and the chamaeleon; and having poured it out into a mortar, sprinkle vinegar over it. For the conditions written above it is effective even with the chrysocolla mixed in. Without this, however, it is most soothing and extremely effective for punctures of the nerves, and wherever something needs to come away from muscles or nerves. Heras did well, at the end of his account of the plaster, to add in writing that with the chrysocolla it is not soothing; for this drug has something astringent about it, whereas the parts being soothed, evidently on account of pain, need relaxing agents. For in this case only the symptom needs to be soothed; and indeed the soothing agents often harm the painful affection itself.

But, taking our stand against what is [749] most pressing, we first assuage the pain, and only then proceed to the remedies capable of curing the condition itself. Now chrysocolla, as has also been said before, is one of the drugs of this kind that are wonderfully effective against hard-to-cure ulcers, as are many others among those that dry vigorously while at the same time having something astringent; but none of such drugs is soothing. And since he mentioned both a mina and a kotyle, directing that one mina of litharge be put in, and a kotyle of oil, it is necessary to make a determination about these too; for I have stated in the earlier treatises as well that some reckon the mina at twenty ounces and others at sixteen, just as some reckon the kotyle at 9 ounces and some at 12. The determination is made from the declared purpose of the drug and from the quantity of the metallic ingredients. For on account of its declared purpose it requires considerable boiling, and for this reason also more oil; and on account of the admixture of the metallic ingredients, which are not few, the drug needs an oily moisture.

Since, then, it takes neither suet nor marrow nor liquid resin, it is quite clear that one must increase [750] the oil. If, then, we reckon the mina as twenty ounces, we shall in any case put in three cotylae of oil, each of 12 ounces. But if as sixteen, it is possible to put in the cotyle of oil reckoned as nine ounces; but it is also possible to reckon it as 12, and, for the sake of the boiling, for this to be of benefit by its being carried on longer. For to such drugs this is most beneficial, also on account of the metallic ingredients, which are no small quantity. For if you reckon together the 36 drachms of chamaeleon with the 18 of verdigris and the 40 of chrysocolla, they would come to ninety-four drachms, and these too require the admixture of plenty of oil, and especially since he also directs that 100 drachms of wax be put in. For surely even so it will in any case need much oil. This plaster, then, Heras wrote down, attesting of it that it is suited to hard-to-cicatrise sores; but having written down other polychrest plasters in the same book, among their many effects he added also that they help hard-to-cicatrise or even malignant or chironian sores.

For all have praised both the plaster called by him the Aribarzanian, as treating malignant, spreading [751] and hard-to-heal [lesions], and the isis, as circumscribing gangrenes. And a third besides these, which he began with the following wording: 'Of good colour, for bloody wounds, cicatrizing', saying that it also helps Chironian [ulcers]. And a fourth, which he himself names panacea, and a fifth, that of Hicesius. My account of the polychrest plasters, then, will come in the book after this one, and in it I shall also write out these plasters praised by Heras. In this book, however, I shall add the remedies for hard-to-treat [ulcers], which some call Chironian, that have been tested through long experience both by our teachers and by ourselves. Some of them have also been attested by older men of repute, as indeed is the one written in the book entitled 'Mantias' Drug-Seller in the Surgery'. He wrote about them in these very words: Verdigris-coloured [plaster] of Mantias. ℞ Burnt copper, 4 minas; dry pine resin, 8 dr.; wax, 8 dr.; verdigris, 10 dr.; oil, 1 cotyle; Cimolian earth, 4 dr.; frankincense, 4 dr.; flake of copper, 4 dr.

Having ground the dry ingredients fine, leave them in the mortar; melt the wax with the oil and pour it [752] over the triturated ingredients, and let them soak it up for a short time; then add 1 kotyle of vinegar, and grind smooth for 3 days, adding as much vinegar as it will take, so that it comes to the consistency of a liquid cerate. Use it for every wound, for old and hard-to-cicatrise ulcers, and for those that are cancerous, with lint. Over the compress one should bind on lightly unwashed (greasy) wool soaked in wine and oil, undoing it every 2 days in summer and every three in winter, and wash the ulcers with lukewarm water. In deep wounds, lightly pack the openings themselves with lint; for the drug's property is that of a lint-applied remedy and pus-producing. When the ulcers have become clean and the eschar has fallen off, mix in wax equal to the verdigris and bring them to cicatrisation. It also expels carbuncles painlessly, and it arrests and heals completely every spreading malignant lesion. Use it also for herpes and for rotten nails. Likewise, for all of these one must use the wine and oil with the wool; and fill decayed teeth with the drug. Plaster of Galen. A fine one, our own.

Take: of wax, pitch [753] and asphalt, 1 litra each; of manna, verdigris and white lead, half of the aforementioned amounts, that is, a half-litra of each; of pomegranate rinds, oak-gall, Egyptian thorn, Illyrian iris, round birthwort and chalcanthum, of each of these a third of a litra, that is, 4 ounces; of long birthwort and burnt copper, a sixth of a litra of each, that is, 2 ounces each. Grind the dry ingredients with vinegar for several days, as was also said before. When they have been well worked up, melt the meltable ingredients with oil, a kotyle, and pour this over them while sprinkling in the manna; and having cooled and scraped the meltable ingredients, mix them in this way with the dry ingredients that have been ground with vinegar, so that you do not somehow produce wax-lumps (enkerides) in the pouring, especially when the surrounding air is cold. Another of ours. Take: of asphalt and liquid alum, 1 litra of each; of pitch, pine resin and wax, double of each, that is, 2 litrai each; of round birthwort, oak-gall and Egyptian thorn, 8 ounces each; and half of this weight

of each of these, namely of pomegranate rinds, burnt copper, manna and long birthwort, that is, [754] 4 oz each; of castor oil, or of old oil if you do not have the castor oil, 2 pounds, the pound containing 12 oz, so that there are 24 oz in all. Prepare this one too in the same way as the former: triturate the metallic ingredients with vinegar, after this add the dry ingredients and triturate again, and then, when these have a mud-like consistency, mix in the meltable ingredients as was said before. Another. Take: of asphalt, terebinth resin and Bruttian pitch, 1 pound each; of oil, 24 dr.; of litharge, white lead, manna, verdigris, scale and opopanax, of each an amount equal to the twenty-four drachms of the oil; of ladanum, two oz, which is 16 dr.; and two kotylai of vinegar. This drug too is prepared in the same way as the two before it. Another. Take: of chrysocolla, scale and stomoma, 4 dr. each; of verdigris and chalcanthum, half that amount of each, that is, 2 dr. each; of wax, 25 dr., that is, 3 oz and one drachm; of terebinth resin, 2 oz, that is, 16 dr.

Melt the wax with the terebinth, then mix it with the other ingredients. Prepare the [755] drug in two ways: sometimes, as with the preceding ones, triturating the dry ingredients with vinegar; sometimes without vinegar, mixing them, finely levigated, with the meltable ingredients. Let the terebinth be on the more liquid side, as for the most part is the kind called larch. In general, in all these drugs that are agreed to suit chironian ulcers, you will not go wrong if you mix in some of the larch resin instead of the terebinth. Another. ♃ Wax, 3 ounces, that is 24 drachms; burnt copper, scale and verdigris, 2 drachms each, so that the three together make 6 drachms. Let the wax be fatty, so that, when softened with a little rose oil or myrtle oil, it takes up the well-levigated dry ingredients, which is most necessary in all the drugs compounded for chironian ulcers. Moreover, after the dry ingredients have been mixed with the wax, it is better to pound them further in a mortar. Another. ♃ Wax, 6 ounces; verdigris, one sixth, that is 1 ounce; burnt copper and larch resin, 3 drachms of each, so that both together make 6 drachms. Let the wax be fatty.

and, having been put into hot water so as to become softer, let it be softened with the hands, the verdigris and [756] the burnt copper being taken up into it, and after this being pounded in a mortar, in which the mixing in of the resin will also take place, the resin being dripped in little by little. Another. ℞ Of cadmia 3 ounces; having mixed it with half its weight of chalcitis, that is 1½ ounces, and having ground them well, pour on astringent wine and grind again, and when you have made it honey-like in consistency, mix in the cerate made of wax and roasted resin. Let there be an equal amount of each, 1 ounce, so that both together are 2 ounces. And you will add to them a little myrtle oil while it is melting. Another. ℞ Of old oil or castor oil 1 kotyle; of wax, pitch and asphalt, 1 litra each; of manna, verdigris and white lead, half of the quantity just stated, that is a half-litra of each; of pomegranate rind, oak-gall, Egyptian thorn, iris, round birthwort and chalcanthum, a third of a litra of each, that is 4 ounces; of burnt copper and long birthwort, a sixth of a litra of each, that is 2 ounces. You will mix the meltable ingredients with the dry ones, previously ground fine in vinegar, as has been said before. Another. ℞ Of cadmia and chalcitis, 40 drachms each.

Having triturated them with wine [757] over several days, you will mix in a cerate made from oil and wax. Let there be 2 litrae of the oil and 200 drachmas of the wax. But it is better to prepare this in a smaller proportion, putting in 10 drachmas each of cadmia and chalcitis, and 50 drachmas each of wax and oil. Another. ℞ Burnt cadmia, burnt chalcitis, terebinth and wax, an equal amount of each; you will grind the dry ingredients in wine. Another, made with gall (κίκεως). ℞ Verdigris, one drachma; liquid alum, one litra; pomegranate rind, burnt copper and manna, a third of a litra of each, that is 4 ounces; oak gall, double that, that is 8 ounces; pitch and pine resin, 2 litrae each; and asphalt, half that, that is a litra, which is also the amount of liquid alum you have put in; round birthwort, as of the oak gall, 8 ounces; long birthwort, half that, that is 4 ounces; castor oil, 2 litrae. You will grind the metallic ingredients with vinegar, as with the preparations written above. Another. ℞ Wax, 3 ounces; burnt copper, [copper] scale and verdigris, 2 litrae (λι΄) each.

Having first warmed the wax in hot water, [758] you will soften it in the hands, mixing in rose oil; then, taking up the dry ingredients, you will pound them in a mortar for a long time, so that everything becomes truly unified, by the third or fourth day. Undo this and all other such plasters by placing a sponge on the outside, soaked in water or oxycrate. Another. ℞ Wax, 6 ounces; larch resin, half that amount, that is, 3 ounces; verdigris, a third of the amount of the larch, that is, 1 ounce; Bruttian pitch, 3 dr.; burnt chalcitis, likewise 3 dr. Prepare this one too in the same way as the one written above. Another. ℞ Burnt copper, scale and verdigris, an equal amount of each; mix them with one and a half times as much wax. Soften the wax as described before, first soaking it in hot water and adding either rose oil or myrtle oil while softening it, then putting it into a mortar. It is better, however, to mix in wax equal to the three weights together, wax as fresh, soft and fatty as possible, so that you will not need much of the oily liquid. Another. ℞ Verdigris and terebinth, an equal amount of each; wax, three times as much; split alum, cadmia and scale, four times as much of each, so that there is 1 part of verdigris

[759] and of terebinth 1 part, of wax 3 parts, of copper flakes, cadmia and split alum, of each four parts. Having pounded, sifted and thoroughly ground the dry ingredients, put the wax and the terebinth into a mortar and pound them, sprinkling on the dry ingredients and moistening the pestle with myrtle oil or rose oil, in warm air. In this it will be pounded easily, especially if it is pounded in the summer sun. The use is as with the others. First cleanse the ulcer with aphronitre, wash it with melicrat, and sponge it well so that it is without moisture. After this lay a flat spread of the plaster over the ulcer. Then, on the outside, put a double fold of linen cloth wetted from cold water, then a new soft sponge. You will, of course, undo it on the third or fourth day. Our own waxless plaster. Take: of litharge 3 pounds; of old castor oil 4½ pounds; of the sharpest vinegar 2 pounds; of black copper flakes, chalcitis and verdigris, of each of the three 2 ounces.

The litharge must first be boiled with the oil until it reaches a glutinous consistency; then the metallic ingredients are to be added, which have been ground [760] for several days with the vinegar, and in this way you will boil it until it is non-soiling. It is also possible, right at the outset, to mix the litharge thoroughly with the oil and the vinegar and boil it, and, when it has become half-boiled, to add the scale, the chalcitis and the verdigris. By a litra of oil and of vinegar I here mean the Roman one, which consists of twelve of its own ounces. I have sometimes put in as much as six litrai of oil to the three of litharge, and clearly with this proportion it will be boiled for longer. When you prepare this drug too, it is better for the litharge to have been boiled beforehand with the oil alone, and then for the metallic ingredients to have been added together with the vinegar. These being three, I said that 2 ounces of each are put in, to 2 litrai of vinegar, 3 of litharge, and of old castor oil the six litrai or, as I said before, the four and a half. This drug both agglutinates fistulas and, drying those that have already become callused, draws them together and closes them; and if the patient follows a proper regimen, they do not break open again.

But if a considerable plethos has accumulated, there is a danger that, when a flux supervenes, the part becomes inflamed and the fistula is opened. And on inveterate ulcers that are hard to bring to a scar, which are also called cheironian, [761] we not only apply the drug itself unmixed; melted in old oil or in castor oil and applied on lint (emmoton), even if no pus at all, not even the least, had ever formed in the ulcer before, it concocts the ulcer and makes pus, and makes the pus thick. You will undo this dressing too every third day, if nothing prevents it. If the scale is scale of steel (stomōma), it is better. If you have neither this nor the black scale, the scale of Cyprian copper will be put in. I once prepared this plaster mixing in also an ounce of Phrygian stone, and at other times an ounce of chrysocolla, and sometimes of both; it agglutinates even large wounds. Another, for those with soft skin and those whose ulcers heal badly, on the same ulcers. ℞ wax, 1 litra; rose oil, 1 litra; white lead, 8 oz.; sal ammoniac, 4 oz.; Cyprian scale, 2 oz.; frankincense, 1 oz.; quicklime, 1 oz.; split [alum], 1 oz.; verdigris, 1 oz.; pomegranate rinds, 1 oz. The use is the same as for those written above. The drugs compounded here are nine without the rose oil, for that is the tenth.

Of the nine, five [762] are equal in weight: quicklime, pomegranate rinds, frankincense, split alum and verdigris. The scale is of double weight, and the ammoniac salts are double this; and the white lead is double these. The wax in turn is one and a half times this, brought to 1 litra, which is also the amount of the rose oil.

[763] GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK 5. Here the polychrest drugs will be discussed. They call polychrest those that are suited to many conditions; and some of them [are suited to conditions that are] not only different in species but also different in genus. All of them, however, are compounded from drugs that are contrary not only in respect of their primary qualities and powers but also in respect of their secondary ones.

It is quite clear that by 'primary' I mean heat and cold and dryness [764] and moisture, together with the qualities compounded from these in any pairing whatever; and by 'secondary' I mean those that follow upon them. I discussed these at greater length in the fifth book of my treatise on simple drugs, where I showed that some drugs, not only among the compound ones but also among the natural ones, soften, while others harden. In the same way some block up the passages and others clear obstructions; some generate dirt in addition, while others even cleanse away the dirt lying on the surface; some make thin and others thicken; some condense and others rarefy; some regenerate flesh and others clean it away; some cicatrize and others ulcerate; some draw and others repel; and there are other such differences among them. I have also stated in the earlier treatises what the necessary mixing of drugs contrary in their powers is, and I shall recall it now as well, a little later. For it seems better to me to write out some two or three of the renowned polychrest drugs, and then to explain the rationale of their composition.

I shall begin from those known to all, which are written in the Narthex of Heras and in [765] others of those who have composed books of drugs. And since in the book before this my discussion concerned the powers that treat hard-to-cicatrise ulcers, it seemed good to me now too to explain first those of the polychrest plasters that were compounded for the sake of malignant ulcers, which some call Chironian; and as for the other plasters that are called polychrest because they suit many other affections, though not the Chironian ones as well, these I have decided to go through afterwards, one after another. [On those written by Heras.] Since, then, in the book of drugs by Heras the Cappadocian there is written a plaster that works supremely well on ulcers of this kind, I shall begin from it, setting down the man's text, which runs roughly thus: 'Of good colour, enaemon, cicatrizing; agglutinating when used unmixed, but filling up and cicatrizing when dissolved with cerate, and still more so for cicatrization. It also works supremely well on Chironian ulcers and on others similar to them.'

For it melts down callosities, and [766] after this it generates genuine flesh. Very white. ♃ [Take]: wax, 2 litrai; roasted resin, 3 litrai; scraped verdigris, 6 ounces; manna, 3 ounces; oil, 5 kotylai; vinegar, 1 xestes. The meltable ingredients over the dry. Use the plaster for wounds; and when it is let down with rose oil it produces pus and cleans out; dissolved with cerate, for cicatrization. Some, however, put in, of the resin, 2 litrai of the roasted and two litrai of the terebinth. Having prepared it in this way they took it up with scraped verdigris, so that it had the consistency of a collyrium, and they inserted this wherever they wished to melt away callosities. For it does this easily, so as even to detach bones. This plaster, then, Heras reasonably praises, since it has its efficacy from the large quantity of the verdigris and the vinegar, if we remember anything of what was said in the book before this one. He also praises the one he calls panacea, which I write out next in his own wording. Panacea of Heras, called by some Hygieia. For every spreading ulceration and malignancy. It halts spreading ulcerations, neither producing eschars nor hardening the surrounding bodies.

but breaking up and withering all [767] that is corrupted, so that it differs in no way from a moist raisin. When dissolved with myrtle oil it also checks a flux of blood, both the other kind and that through haemorrhoids, and it withers and consumes the haemorrhoids themselves. In addition to these it also heals fistulae, the so-called carbuncles (anthrakes), the aigilopes, the so-called Chironian [ulcers], and in general the whole class of hard-to-heal and chronic [ulcers]. For the hidden places, such as the uterus, it is melted down with unguent of cypros; for the external ones it is better to apply it in the same way as each of the other [plasters]. Applied to any ulcer, even if it is one of the wild ones, it will at once make it milder, and the pains and the sleeplessness gentler. The formula is this: chamaepitys, 4 dr.; symphyton, 4 dr.; chamaeleon, 4 dr.; prasion, 4 dr. (others, 6); polion, 6 dr.; fine centaury, 6 dr.; helenium, 4 dr.; birthwort, 4 dr.; frankincense, 12½ dr.; myrrh, 3 dr.; aloe, 6 dr.; galbanum, 6 dr., one and a half obols; oil, 180 dr.; honey, 30 dr.; propolis, 2½ dr.; split alum, 6 dr., one and a half obols.

Of terebinth [768], 6 dr., 1½ obols. Of chalcitis, 6 dr., 1½ obols. Of bitumen, 50 dr. Of ampelitis earth, 50 dr. Of litharge, 50 dr. Of oak-gall, 3 dr. Of fine powder of iris, 3 dr. One must pound the herbs and the roots on the day before and put them into the oil. When they have steeped through the whole night, in the morning one must add the litharge, the ampelitis and the bitumen, and boil them over a gentle fire. When the consistency thickens, lift the pot from the fire. Let the honey, the resin, the galbanum and the propolis be melted together in another vessel. These too must be mixed in by pouring them into the pot, and after these the dry ingredients. Boil it together with these until the drug no longer soils. Then, having again lifted it from the fire, sprinkle in the myrrh and the frankincense, ground smooth. One must take care that it never boils over, and boil it in as spacious a place as possible, for it becomes hard to extinguish if it should catch on anything. This, then, is what Heras says about the panacea.

But we must point out that the material itself differs from that of the drugs written up in the book before this one for the hard-to-treat [769] ulcers. For those were composed of metallic substances only, some of a few, some of more, only a few of them containing roots or herbs. With this panacea the opposite is the case: it takes both chamaeleon and centaury, each of them capable of benefiting malignant ulcers. It also takes birthwort and iris, which are weaker than centaury and chamaeleon as regards the healing of malignant ulcers, yet certainly not to be rejected. And it takes strong herbs, which are often able even on their own to treat malignant ulcers: ground-pine, polium and comfrey. Stronger than these are horehound and elecampane. Horehound, then, one might use even on its own in cases where the flesh in the ulcer is quite moist and rather foul; but elecampane is not suitable even in these cases when sprinkled on by itself, just as no other of the acrid drugs is either.

For you learned in the treatise on simple drugs the difference between acrid and bitter drugs: the acrid ones are irritant, biting and hot, and cause a flux into the affected parts [770]; the bitter ones are drying without biting and heating, and for this reason are suitable for ulcerated parts. But since the one who compounded these herbs intended to make from them a plaster, not a dry sprinkling powder, and for the composition of the plaster he was going to mix in either wax or resin, or at any rate litharge boiled for a fairly long time, by which the potency of the herbs was weakened, he mixed with them some drugs so strong that they cannot be applied on their own to ulcers. These strong drugs have a twofold general potency and quality: some an austere and acerbic one, others an acrid and acerbic one. For this reason, then, of those having an acrid potency he mixed in elecampane (helenion), and of those that are strongly astringent (for these we call austere and acerbic), alum and of course the oak-gall, the omphacitis. Chalcitis has both qualities strongly, as also the potencies that go with them, being both acrid and astringent.

For it brings to callus, more quickly and more safely, all recent fistulas, old burrowing ulcers (hypophorai), sinuses, phymata, parotid swellings, and the abscesses in the breasts and [775] armpits, either so that they do not arise or, having arisen, are treated. And when we are at the stage of the outflow (?), it further carries off scrofulous swellings (choirades) together with their tunics, bringing them very quickly to suppuration. Applied to the forehead, it also stops the flux of the eyes. It also removes livid bruises, circumscribes gangrenes and cleans out putrefactions, and in short it is good for everything. ℞ Wax, 100 drachms; terebinth, 200 drachms (others, 100); flakes of red copper, 8 dr.; scraped verdigris, 8 dr.; round birthwort, 8 drachms; frankincense, 8 dr.; ammoniac salt, 8 dr.; ammoniac incense, 8 dr.; burnt alum or round alum, 6 dr.; burnt copper, 8 dr.; myrrh, 12 dr.; aloe, 12 dr.; galbanum, 12 dr.; old oil, 1 kotyle; acrid vinegar, 2 kotylai. Pour the meltable ingredients into a mortar over the dry ones. This is how Heras wrote up the isis, without adding to it the entire detailed use, as he was accustomed to do in other cases.

Moreover, in calling it the plaster of Epigonus he also disagrees with many, who, I believe, have written more accurately about Epigonus, both on other matters and on how, having been shut up in prison [776] and having healed one of the very powerful men, he was released on that account. They say that he added the root of dracontium to the drug written above, and I too have always used it in this way, since one of my teachers also used it so, putting 8 dr. of dracontium into the proportion written by Heras. Moreover, he put in half a cyathus of the oil and 1 cotyle of vinegar, and he also put in the Colophonian resin, not, as Heras did, the terebinth. He also differed from Heras in the preparation of the plaster, working up the galbanum with the vinegar together with the other ingredients in a mortar. Having mixed these, just as Heras too says, with the meltable ingredients, he then softened the drug, kneading it for a very long time in his hands while applying the sharpest vinegar. After this he placed it in a bronze vessel and, having poured [vinegar] over it, kept it for a considerable time, and only then took it out and used it. He called it, as some others also do, the plaster of Hermon the sacred scribe. In other authors you may find it written that this one too comes from the inner sanctuaries at the temple of Hephaestus in Egypt, just like the plaster with dittany.

[777] The proportion of the simple drugs that compose it, however, almost all have recorded as the same, so that even if the title is different, you should not suppose that the sacred one from the inner sanctuaries, the one of Hermon the sacred scribe, and the one of Epigonus are each a different plaster. For it is called by all these names. Melted with liquid cerate it cleanses out and cicatrizes ulcers. Some have written that it should be diluted with three times as much cerate, others with double, both parties having fixed the proportion without qualification. For in those cases in which it renders the ulcer sufficiently clean if mixed with three parts of the cerate, one ought not to mix in double. But in those in which it cleanses less adequately, then one ought to take double the cerate. For we know that every such drug is more effective when it is not mixed with much cerate, and weaker when mixed with more.

It is not amiss also to say this much about dracontium: that in summer, when the stalk and the whole plant have dried, one must take up the root; then, having put it in a house that is dry but gets no sun, a little later, after six or seven days, one must cut the root into [778] little discs, and, threading these on a linen thread, hang them up again in a house that is dry but sunless; and so, whenever you wish to prepare the drug, pound the root. The root by itself, too, pounded and ground smooth well enough to become fine as down, is curative of malignant ulcers. [The plaster with dittany.] The plaster prepared with dittany they also call 'sacred', saying that this recipe too was found in the temple of Hephaestus at Memphis. And all of them record it with these same proportions, or with proportions differing a little. Concerning this one too it will suffice to copy out the text of Heras, which runs as follows: 'Sacred plaster, the one from the temple of Hephaestus at Memphis.'

It is effective for fresh bloody wounds and fluxing ones, for severances of sinews, old ulcers, burrowing ulcers, contusions, putrefactions, carbuncles, black lesions, fluxing ulcers and ulcers hard to cicatrise, parotid swellings, chilblains, abscesses, scrofulous swellings, boils and indurations; it draws out missiles, splinters, and bones from the head; it is effective for wounds from wild beasts and the stings of scorpions, of phalangia, [779] of the shrew-mouse, and human bites. For every pain of the neck, shoulder and joints, in place of an emollient. It stops fluxes of the eyes, not only fresh but also old ones, and is effective for headache when smeared on with rose oil; when thinned, it is also effective for pain of the womb, both rubbed on and used as a fumigation from below. The plaster, when burned as a fumigation, also drives away wild creatures. It consists of: old oil, 2 kotylai; litharge, 100 drachms; scraped verdigris, 8 drachms; scale, 6 drachms; liquid Colophonian resin, or as some have it, pine resin, 50 drachms; manna, 12 drachms; ammoniac incense, 16 drachms; burnt copper, 8 drachms; diphryges, 6 drachms; gentian, 6 drachms; aloe, 8 drachms; galbanum, 12 drachms; propolis, 8 drachms; wax, 25 drachms; birthwort, 10 drachms; Cretan dittany, 10 drachms.

Boil in a large pan over coals the litharge and the oil until it is entirely non-staining, or nearly so; then, lifting off the pot, mix in the verdigris and the scale and boil, and let it not stain at all; then, taking it off again, put in the resin and the ammoniac, sifted, stirring until it stops boiling; then, setting it back on and leaving it a little, take it off and sprinkle in the copper and the diphryges, and boil again until it does not stain, for sometimes, [780] when these have been thrown in, it slackens again; then, taking it off, add the wax and boil again until it becomes non-staining, and it becomes so quickly; then, lifting it off, you will add the propolis, and setting it on again and leaving it a little, lift it off and add the aloe, manna, dittany, aristolochia and gentian. When these have cooled sufficiently, you will sprinkle each one in separately, ground very smooth, and having stirred, if it is non-staining, you will take it off; if not, you will boil it over a light fire. This is what Heras wrote about the plaster. We ourselves have sometimes compounded it also without the burnt copper and the diphryges, and it becomes more drawing of what lies in the depth, and more emollient and more discutient, yet not suited to the hard-to-cicatrise sores. We have also made it without the dittany, adding in turn in its place, along with the others, 6 dr. of chrysocolla, so that it becomes more therapeutic of malignant sores. [The black plaster of Hikesios.] The one named the Hikesian; some, however, have written it in the genitive case, 'that of Hikesios', a polychrest drug. Heras at any rate writes the following about it.

The [plaster] of Hicesius, [781] for wounds and dog-bites, and dispersing indurations; for parotids and condylomata and for malignant [ulcers]. It is also attractive and agglutinative, and it works also for dropsies. Take: litharge 100 dr., Judaean asphalt 100 dr., ampelitis earth 100 dr., manna and propolis 25 dr. each, galbanum 12 dr., split [alum] 12½ dr., terebinth [resin] 12½ dr., iris 6 dr., omotribes oil 6 cotylae, honey 1 cotyle, chalcitis 7½ dr., omphacitis gall 6 dr., myrrh 6 dr. Boil the litharge, the asphalt and the ampelitis with the oil. When they are half-boiled, mix in the propolis, the resin and the galbanum, which have been boiled separately in the honey. When it sets, add the rest, and stir with a spatula of pine-wood. For this plaster not all have written the same weight of the ingredients, as will be shown in what follows. [The black [plaster] with the two birthworts.] A renowned plaster, and a polychrest one, is also the one made with the two birthworts, which Heras himself also wrote down in the following words.

[782] The black [plaster] made with the two birthworts, effective for old, callous, hard to cicatrise and spreading [ulcers]. It is also an enaemon cephalic; it draws up bones, it is agglutinant, effective for loosened joints; it cleanses parts affected by flux; when diluted it fills up [hollow ulcers]. Pitch, 1 pound; wax, 1 pound; asphalt, 1 pound; terebinth [resin], 1 pound; manna, half a pound or 7 ounces; scraped verdigris, half a pound; white lead, half a pound; chalcanthum, 4 ounces; long birthwort, 4 ounces; Illyrian [iris], 4 ounces; pomegranate rinds, 2 ounces; omphacitis gall, 2 ounces; burnt copper, 2 ounces; akantha, 4 ounces; round birthwort, 4 ounces [γο]; vinegar, 1 cotyle; castor oil or old olive oil, 1 cotyle. Having melted the meltable ingredients together, then drip on the white lead, the verdigris and the chalcanthum ground smooth with the vinegar; then, having set it on the fire until it becomes unified, sprinkle in the dry ingredients after withdrawing the fire; then pour it out and knead it. These things, then, are what both Heras and the others wrote about it.

The reasoning of the man who composed it is not obscure to those [783] who remember all that I have said, at least in this treatise and also in the preceding commentaries. For it is compounded of opposite faculties, drawing and repelling, which have drying in common. In it the repelling component predominates, the one belonging to the astringents: chalcanthum, pomegranate rinds, oak-gall, burnt copper and thorn. For this reason he also said that it is suitable for paralysed joints, that is, relaxed ones. He mixed the birthwort and the iris with the styptic agents, these being of a rarefying and dispersive faculty. And so that it might become a plaster and the drug not be a dry sprinkling-powder, oil and wax were mixed in: the wax merely as material, as also the oil, if this is the common oil and not castor oil or old oil, for we have learned that these heat and disperse. Terebinth resin, besides producing the plaster-like consistency in the drug (since wax alone cannot do this), also has something emollient, dispersive and detergent about it. Frankincense too has these properties, and manna has in addition taken on a wholly styptic faculty and quality.

For this is what they call [784] the siftings shaken off frankincense, which contain also a small amount of the bark. Asphalt, too, whether you prefer to call it feminine (ἡ ἄσφαλτος) or masculine (ὁ ἄσφαλτος), is sufficiently drying, a drug suited to the composition of a plaster. These ingredients, then, were sufficient for the composition of the plaster. But the one who composed this plaster, having set out to mix in drugs that have a strong power, added to them verdigris and vinegar, which are able to cut and to eat through, and both to be carried themselves into the depth of bodies and to guide the way for the other ingredients. These are mixed with the discutient drugs in order to thin in advance the thick moistures in the parts under treatment. It remains, then, to say something also about the white lead: it is quite clear that he mixed it in as being suitable for plaster-making, not as itself going to contribute anything to the effect. I, for my part, would rather have mixed in litharge, for it is both emplastic and cooling. White lead, though useful for certain other purposes, contributes nothing to the power of the plaster under discussion. [The plaster of Azanites.] The plaster of Azanites is polychrest and highly esteemed. Heras writes about it as follows.

The [785] [plaster] of the Azanite. ℞ Dry pitch, 1 oz.; wax, 3 oz.; pig's fat, 3 oz.; bull's fat, 3 oz.; oesypum, 3 oz.; pine resin, 5 oz. It is effective against all malignant [conditions], gangrenes, fistulas, fresh wounds, burns, and chillings, as an acopon. It is also an emollient pessary. It is suitable too for ulcers in the uterus, for phymata, and for parotid swellings. When the ulcers are hollow, use more of the drug; when [it is applied] for cicatrization, less. It is a peculiarity of the drug that it produces a dirty crust. It is also effective in those suffering from ophthalmia, when applied on the eyelids. Oil is antipathetic to the drug; therefore guard against it. When you prepare it, put in the pitch, the wax, and the bull's fat; and when these have melted, the pig's [fat], then the resin, and last the oesypum, after cooling [the mixture]. Melt the whole over fire and not over flame. It is most effective in cases where the wound is about the sinews or a muscle, and in malignant [conditions].

[The plaster of Halieus, made with Sinopic earth.] The plaster of Halieus, celebrated and polychrest no less than the preceding ones, recorded thus [786] by Heras. The plaster of Halieus, for old ulcers and those hard to cicatrise. It is also discutient, especially for indurations about the breasts. We use it as an excellent remedy for very many things. Wax, 1 mina; litharge, 1 mina; manna, 8 drachms; terebinth, 8 dr.; galbanum, 8 dr.; Sinopic earth, 8 dr.; old oil, 2 cotylae. Boil the oil and the litharge until it becomes non-staining, then add the wax and the resin. When these have melted, take the vessel off the fire and mix in the Sinopic earth and the galbanum, then the manna. This plaster also acts supremely well against the wounds of sea creatures. I once used it on a man who had been struck by a sea stingray and was suffering terribly, and it acted marvellously; likewise also on those stung by scorpions. This is what Heras wrote. Next let us look at Crito's prescriptions. [On what was written by Crito.] Heras composed a single book on the composition of drugs, entitled Narthex. Five such books of Crito survive, apart from his Cosmetics.

In the fourth [787] of these five he goes through the plasters of the same kind as those already written about: some, as Heras has them, identical in every respect; others besides these, which Heras did not mention. These I shall now write out in order, taking care also not to omit any of those written by Heras which he mentions in a different form, as he appears to have done in the case of that of Hicesius. For Crito wrote other weights and measures for this plaster, as did certain others too, not the same as those of Heras. I shall therefore begin with the first, that of Hicesius, since there is disagreement about it concerning the weight of the simple drugs from which they compose the plaster. [The plaster of Hicesius.] Concerning that of Hicesius, Crito wrote word for word as follows.

Hicesius' [plaster]: for every wound, fresh or old; for contusions, sprains and fractures; for inflammations and every pain, for it at once renders [the part] free of pain; for abscesses, phymata, choirades, carbuncles, parotid swellings, phygethla, condylomata, lichens, corns, melaniai, inflamed haemorrhoids, fistulas and burns, when it is softened with myrtle or rose oil; [788] for ulcers, splinters, barbs, dog bites, human bites and the wounds of wild beasts; it is also haemostatic. Use it also in place of a malagma for everything, but do not apply oil; and as an anacollema for those suffering from ophthalmia, on a linen cloth. Let the compresses always be larger. It is also effective for dropsical patients. ℞ Ampelitis earth, asphalt, litharge, 2 minas of each; wax, frankincense, terebinth, propolis, ½ mina of each; galbanum, split [alum], 5 minas of each; myrrh, oak gall, iris, 12 drachmas of each; chalcitis, 6 drachmas; honey, 2 kotylai; omphacine oil, 2 choes (some say 2 kotylai). Boil the ampelitis, the asphalt and the litharge with the oil, having first reduced them to a juice so that they become smooth. Boil over a gentle fire, stirring continuously with a spatula of pine wood so that it does not settle at the bottom, for it burns very quickly.
