Melt the meltable ingredients in another vessel, having first boiled the honey separately until it thickens, and mix them with the contents of the pot once these have thickened properly; for when these are thrown in, it dissolves again. Then sprinkle in the dry ingredients after cooling it somewhat, the frankincense last, and when you have unified it, use it.

This formula I received from [789] Herodotus. These things, then, Criton wrote about the [plaster] of Hicesius. He appears to differ from Heras on the proportion of the simple drugs of which the whole is compounded. Of this disagreement one part is clear, the other hard to decide. For Heras, rightly, reduced the weight of all the drugs to drachmas, whereas Criton did not write the vine-earth, the asphalt and the litharge by the weight in drachmas, but directed that 2 minas of each of them be put in. Now those who have written on weights and measures disagree about how great the weight of the mina is: some say that the mina is of sixteen ounces, some of twenty, and some even draw a distinction, asserting that the Alexandrian mina is of twenty ounces and the other of sixteen. And this is a still smaller matter. But among those who reduce the mina to drachmas, there are some who say that the mina is of a hundred drachmas, and some of more, since, as regards the ounce too, most say it is of seven and a half drachmas, but some of only 7, and others of 8.

Since, then, these things are so, it is difficult to find out how many drachmas [790] one ought to reckon the mina written in by Crito to be. He appears, however, in other places too, to be one who wants the mina to be 100 drachmas. And if this is so, one must understand that the composition of Hicesius was written by him at double the quantity, since Heras wrote, concerning these first three drugs, the ampelitis earth, the asphalt and the litharge, one hundred drachmas of each by weight, whereas Crito raises it to 200. Let us see, then, whether what follows agrees with the double; for some items appear to, and some do not. After the first three he mentions wax, frankincense, terebinth and propolis, requiring half a mina of each to be put in, that is, 50 drachmas; for we have supposed that the proportion was written on the basis that the mina is 100 drachmas. But if this is so, in the case of the frankincense, evidently written in place of the manna, there will be agreement between Crito and Heras; likewise also in the case of the propolis, but not, however, in the case of the terebinth. For twenty-five drachmas ought

to have been written by Criton, since Heras at any rate [791] wrote twelve and a half. In the wax, however, the greatest disagreement arose between the two men, since Heras did not put in wax at all; for we have learnt that the power of wax is moderately emollient. Next in Criton is written: of galbanum, of split [alum], a quarter of a mina each; in this the man agrees with Heras. For if the mina is taken to be 100 dr., the quarter would come to twenty-five dr.; and these are double the 12 and a half written by Heras. In what follows Criton abandons the term 'mina', and directs that myrrh, oak-gall and iris, 12 dr. of each of the three, be mixed with the aforesaid ingredients, agreeing in this with Heras, for Heras directed that six of each be put in. Next again Criton has written 6 dr. of chalcitis, differing not a little from Heras here. For since all the quantities are double, chalcitis too should have been written not as six drachms but as fifteen, since Heras at any rate wrote 7 and a half. In the honey, however, the men agree, Heras having written 1 kotyle.

while Crito [792] wrote 2 kotylai. There remains the oil, about which no small inquiry would arise for us, not only with regard to these two men but also with regard to others of those who have written up the drug, as we shall explain next. These two, at any rate, differ from each other on this point. Heras wrote 6 kotylai of omotribes oil (oil of unripe olives); and it is better to write it so than, as some have written, 6 kyathoi, since Heras requires that in the boiling one first make the litharge, the asphalt and the ampelitis earth half-boiled, and only then put in each of the other ingredients. But they would not become half-boiled if 6 kyathoi were put in. For we know that many of the men who compound drugs often require 2 kotylai to be put in for the 100 drachms of litharge. And indeed I have already said all this before, in the first of these commentaries: that, with the metallic substances too, the kotyle may be 9 ounces, as some have supposed; but it may also be 12.

to reckon it so, as others direct, being well aware that if the drug is boiled for a longer time (and this will be the case when more [793] oil has been put in), it will become more drying, whereas if it is taken off the fire quickly, on account of the small quantity of oil it will become less drying but more emollient and more soothing. So the six kyathoi must be rejected altogether, and six kotylai of nine ounces each must be put in. But if you wish to boil the drug for a longer time, so that it becomes more drying, nothing prevents the kotylai of twelve ounces from being put in as well. Since, then, six kotylai are written by Heras, it is clear that Crito ought to have put in twelve kotylai, so that in this respect too the measure would be double, as it is with the other ingredients. But in his text there stands written 'of omphacine oil, two choes'. Here too, again, those who wrote 'two kotylai' are to be condemned. Now as for the chous, if we reckon it at six kotylai, the agreement between the two men stands; but if it is not six kotylai but six xestai, no small disagreement will result. For the quantity will be large in relation to the proportion of the other ingredients, if one were to put in twelve xestai of oil.

So much for the present concerning the [794] disagreement of Heras and Criton over the drug before us. When we come to Andromachus, something will also be said about his agreement with both of them on some points and his disagreement on others. [The green isis.] This author too wrote down the isis, as did almost all the others. But since both its entire use and its preparation have been written up more carefully by him, and since he also differs slightly from Heras, I decided to transcribe below what he wrote as well, word for word.

The isis, which some call Epigonus' isis, is effective. Undiluted, it is for separations of scales and for thick exfoliations of bones. Applied on lint and as a compress, it treats splinters, the strikes and bites of all wild animals, and all punctures and wounds made by iron, in war or otherwise. It also treats fistulas, applied over them and inserted as a collyrium, removing their callus and agglutinating them. Mixed, it is applied on lint and as a compress for every wound, and for malignant and chronic wounds and those ruined by other practitioners; in these, scrape them first and then use the drug in its mixed form. [795] It works wonderfully also for the agglutination of sinuses, so long as they are large. For by drawing off their moisture and agglutinating them it puts them in good order, whether on lint, mixed or undiluted, in cases where we wish to melt away from beneath certain glands or membranes lying within. Use it also for fractures, with a wound and without a wound, for it forms callus very quickly and binds the affected parts together. And in cases where no other malagma is effective, this one is precisely effective: nails loosened by a stumble it either fixes or throws off, and teeth moved by a blow it fixes; and in general there are countless conditions for which it is effective when brought to different strengths. The relaxed form of it is one part of the undiluted drug to two parts of cerate; sometimes it is relaxed still further. For this, grinding and working are needed. For the cerate is sometimes also made with pine resin. The composition: ammoniac incense, 8 dr.; scraped verdigris, 8 dr.; ammoniac salt, 8 dr.; flakes of copper, 8 dr.; burnt copper, 8 dr.; round alum, 6 dr.; birthwort, 8 dr.; frankincense, 8 dr.

[796] of myrrh, 12 dr.; of aloe, 12 dr.; of galbanum, 12 dr.; of wax, 8; of Colophonian resin, 6 dr. (some use the same amount of terebinth instead); of old oil, 2 kotylai; of vinegar, 2 kotylai. Epigonus also adds 12 dr. of the juice of dracontium root, 12 dr. of the juice of prasion, and 8 dr. of the juice of seris. Having pounded and sifted everything carefully, put it into a mortar and, in the sun, pour in the vinegar little by little, until by triturating to smoothness the whole of the vinegar has been used up. When it has become smooth, melt the meltable ingredients and let them cool, then scrape them carefully, add them to what is in the mortar, knead, and take it up. So Crito wrote. I myself prepared it without the juice of seris, and sometimes also left out the alum, and used it on the nerve-wounded in the same way as the drug from metallic substances written in the treatise on the nerve-wounded. For it becomes stronger if it is stored drenched all round with the sharpest vinegar and kneaded at intervals of about fifteen days.

[That of Machairion.] It is at once renowned and polychrest; it is suited also to the conditions of ulcers, about which [797] this whole treatise is being written. Criton wrote it out thus, word for word: That of Machairion, effective for all fresh wounds, agglutinating them and keeping them free of inflammation, and especially those accompanied by contusion. For those bitten by rabid animals it is excellent, applied over a larger area and changed very frequently, and also taken as a pill, about the size of a bean, for 30 days. It is effective for every spreading ulceration, and especially the phagedaenic, and for ulcers in the ears and in the genitals; on denuded bones it makes flesh grow; and it is effective for ulcers in the nostrils. It is also green. It is dissolved with rose oil or omphacine oil. ℞ Round birthwort, 1 oz.; galbanum, 1 oz.; opopanax, 1 ounce; scraped verdigris, 1 oz.; Illyrian iris, 1 oz.; ammoniac incense, 1 ounce; myrrh, 1 ounce; terebinth, 7½ ounces; wax, 7½ oz.; omphacine oil, 7½ oz. Triturate half of the oil with the verdigris until smooth, and boil the rest with the wax and the terebinth.

[The Dysrhachitis, word for word as Damocrates (gives it).] This too [798] is among the celebrated and much-used drugs. Crito writes about it thus: Dysrhachitis, acting remarkably on callused sinuses and on fistulas when applied. If there is an opening able to receive a small piece of linen smeared with the drug, insert it, and it will act more quickly. Use the preparation on very moist, fluxional and chronic conditions, changing it for the most part every third day. It also acts wonderfully on gouty patients when plastered on at the beginning of the paroxysm and applied all round over a wide area. Let these patients also be released to their customary walks and the business of life, without the bath, until the third-day change, and let them persist with it for some days. For it does not give the matter passage towards an intensification of the affection. It is suitable also for every ulcer when mixed with six parts of cerate. As it ages the preparation becomes stronger. ℞ round alum, 8 dr.; scale, 12 dr.; burnt copper, 4 dr.; birthwort, 9 dr.; galbanum, 10 dr.; ammoniac incense, 12 dr. (others, 10 dr.); frankincense, 9 dr.; myrrh, 9 dr.; storax, 1 dr.; misy, 3 dr.

of chalcitis [799] 3 dr.; of the heart of squill 8 dr.; of liquid pitch 4 dr.; of Illyrian iris 9 dr., but some 4; of terebinth resin 10 dr., but some 7 dr.; of pine resin 10 dr., but some 6; of wax 75 dr.; of oil 1½ litrae. Some also add deer's marrow, 8 dr.; others 20. Grind first the scale, the burnt copper, the misy, the chalcitis and the squill with the sharpest vinegar in the sun, until they are reduced smooth. When they have been ground very fine, add the birthwort and the iris. Having first pounded these and sifted them through a fine-meshed sieve, pour vinegar over again and grind, and do this for as long as it still shows itself very rough, not sparing the expenditure of vinegar. When they have become smooth, put in the alum, and do the same until this too has been ground smooth. Then add the myrrh, after it the frankincense, then the ammoniac, and after these the storax, then the pitch. Let these be heated in the hot sun, so that the storax may be thoroughly worked in.

When all have become smooth and have taken on a grimy and glutinous consistency, melt the wax, the resins and the oil; and pour a little of the [800] decoction over the galbanum and, having made it into a single mass, grind it in a mortar; and, having let it cool a little, add the meltables; then, putting in the galbanum and dissolving it, strain it into an earthenware vessel and, scraping it up, mix it with what is in the mortar. [The plaster made with willows.] The one made with willows, which is itself also renowned and polychrest like those written above, Crito writes as follows. The one made with willows, suitable for bleeding wounds and for loosened joints, and inserted into fistulae, and for flabby flesh, especially that on the extremities. It is effective also for erysipelas and for very many other conditions, except burns. ℞ Misy, chalcitis, verdigris, white lead, oak-galls, split alum and round alum, melanteria, of each 6 ounces; wax, pine resin, pitch, asphalt, willow leaves, of each 2 ounces; oil, 4 cotylae, 4 ounces; chalcanthum, 6 ounces; pomegranate rinds, 6 ounces; vinegar, 6 sextarii. The willows with the vinegar, until 2 sextarii remain,

boil; then onto the verdigris, previously ground fine, and the white lead and the melanteria, put the leaves and grind them together; [801] then add the dry ingredients, ground fine, and again reduce to a juice; then pour the meltable ingredients over the top. Asclepiades prepares this one without the chalcanthum and the pomegranate rinds, as has been written in the preceding, second book. Next after this one Criton wrote another made with willow, roughly as follows. The simple willow plaster, as Herodotus makes it. ℞ melanteria, omphacitis gall, split alum, round alum, 6 ounces each; wax, asphalt, dry pitch, willow leaves, pine resin, 2 pounds each; oil, 1 pound; vinegar, half a sextarius. [On the plasters of the same kind written by Asclepiades.] Among these, of those already written above, are both the Fisherman's plaster, known to everyone, and the one made with dittany. But since Asclepiades wrote clearly about them, for this reason I shall now recall them as well. There is moreover a further benefit in what is written twice and three times: to learn in which of the ingredients put into them those who wrote them agreed with one another, and in which they disagreed; and likewise in the indications they promise for them.

[802] The [plaster] of Halieus. Tawny. It acts against bloody wounds and severances of sinews, and against old, hard-to-cicatrise and fluxional ulcers. It is also a good emollient, especially of the indurations that arise about the breasts. We use it in cases of dog-bites and human bites. It acts supremely well also against the strikes of sea sting-rays and of weevers and of the other dangerous fishes, and in general its potency is wonderful. ℞ Litharge, wax, of each 100 dr.; terebinth, manna of frankincense, galbanum, Sinopic red earth, of each 8 dr.; oil, 1 xestes. Prepare in the usual way. Galen's [plaster] of Halieus. ℞ Litharge, wax, of each 100 drachms; terebinth, myrrh, Sinopic earth, scraped verdigris, [copper] flake, of each 8 drachms; birthwort, 8 dr.; frankincense, 25 drachms; diphryges, 6 drachms; galbanum, 12 dr.; ammoniac incense, 12 drachms; oil, 2 cotylae. Prepare in the usual way. The [plaster] of the Huntsmen. A successful drug.

It is effective also against the wounds and bites of quadrupeds and of the other venomous creatures. [803] ℞ Litharge, 1 mina; old oil, scale of red copper, wax, roasted resin, 1 litra each; ammoniac incense, 4 ounces; galbanum and Sinopic red earth, 2 ounces each. Boil the litharge, the scale and the oil until they reach consistency, then add the wax and the resin. When this has melted, take it off the fire and add the ammoniac, having flattened it [πλατύνας, perhaps for πλύνας, 'having washed it']. When it has cooled, add the galbanum and the ammoniac, sprinkling on the Sinopic earth. Pour it out into a mortar, knead it soft, and use. The [plaster] of Chalcideus. Agglutinative, free from inflammation. It is effective also for divisions accompanied by contusion; it glues down sinuses, dries them up and prevents abscessions; it brings up corrupted bones; it is especially effective also on the extremities; and in general its power is wonderful. Litharge, copper scale, pine resin, wax, 100 drachms each; ammoniac incense and galbanum, 16 drachms each; diphryges, 12 drachms; birthwort ground very smooth, 40 drachms; old oil, three xestai.

Boil the litharge and the scale with the oil, and when it changes colour add the diphryges, then the wax and the pine resin [804] or fir resin. When it has melted and has become non-staining, lift it from the fire and add the ammoniac, having washed it. And when it has melted, sprinkle on the birthwort once the drug has become cold, and stir continuously; then pour it out into a mortar, knead it, take it up and use it. [The sacred plaster made with dittany, a wonderful potency.] For severings of sinews and muscles and for contusions. It works also for old and hard-to-heal ulcers; it draws up corrupted bones, and stakes and splinters, and it is also discutient. It works also for pains of the head and fluxes of the eyes; it is also a good emollient for pleuritics and hepatics. It works also against the strike of every venomous creature. Take: litharge, 100 dr.; Colophonian resin, 50 dr.; wax, 25 dr.; ammoniac incense and birthwort, 16 dr. each; manna and galbanum, 12 dr. each; verdigris, dittany, burnt copper, aloe and propolis, 8 dr. each; diphryges, copper scale and gentian root, 6 dr. each; old oil, in winter 2 kotylai, in summer 1½. Prepare in the usual way.

The recipe of this author [805] disagreed with that of Heras as regards the weights in the following points. Where he directs one to put in 8 dr. of dittany, Heras directed ten. And indeed also of birthwort and of ammoniac incense this author prescribes 16 dr. of each, but Heras twenty-six of ammoniac incense and 10 of birthwort. As for the oil, Heras wrote of it without distinction, prescribing only 2 kotylai, whereas Asclepiades prescribes that amount in winter, but one and a half in summer. [The plaster] of Diophantus the surgeon, which Phylax used. ♃ Litharge 150 dr.; white lead, pitch, flake of copper, wax, 18 dr. each; verdigris, dry pine resin, manna of frankincense, propolis, 12 dr. each; galbanum, birthwort, cyperus, 6 dr. each; dittany, trefoil, ammoniac incense, 3 dr. each; Illyrian [iris], artemisia, polion, prasion, 2 dr. each; old oil 2 kotylai. Prepare in the usual way.

[On the plasters of the same kind written by Andromachus.] In this book I set out to go through polychrest plasters that are at the same time effective for hard-to-cicatrise sores. [806] Among these, then, are also the ten finest of those written by Andromachus. Green plaster of Euangeus. ℞ Terebinth resin (others say dry), 50 dr. (others 100 dr.); wax 25 dr.; frankincense 3 dr.; flake 3 dr.; galbanum 3 dr.; aloe 3 dr.; myrrh 3 dr.; sal ammoniac 2 dr.; opopanax 2 dr.; scraped verdigris 2 dr.; burnt copper 2 dr.; birthwort 2 dr.; ammoniac incense 2 dr.; split alum (others say round) 2 dr.; isinglass 3 dr.; vinegar 4 kotylai; oil a quarter of a kotylē (others say an eighth). Use it without the insertion of scolex. The rhypōdēs ('dirty') plaster that I use. ℞ Isinglass 3 oz.; sarcocolla 3 oz.; Assian stone 3 oz.; Eretrian earth half a pound; Samian earth 4 oz.; myrrh 4 oz.; frankincense 6 oz.; copper flake 8 oz.; sal ammoniac 3 oz.; scraped verdigris 6 oz.; split alum 2 oz.; Indian aloe 4 oz.; galbanum 4 oz.; wax 2 lb.; terebinth resin 2 lb.; oil 4 lb.; vinegar, enough to soak the isinglass.

Sprinkle the dry ingredients, ground smooth, [807] into the meltable ingredients. Another green plaster. ℞ Pine resin, 200 dr.; ammoniac incense, 50 dr.; opopanax, 8 dr.; wax, 100 dr.; propolis, 8 dr.; galbanum, 8 dr.; copper flake, 12 dr.; verdigris, 12 dr.; round alum, 8 dr.; misy, 7 dr.; ammoniac salt, 8 dr.; chalcitis, 5 dr.; unfired sulphur, 8 dr.; frankincense, 12 dr.; dried bull's gall, 6 dr., or of liquid gall, 12; oil of cypros, 6 kotylai, others say 4; vinegar, a sufficient amount. The green plaster of Epicurus, which holds out great promise. ℞ Wax, 200 dr.; Colophonian resin, 300 dr.; flake, 16 dr.; burnt copper, 16 dr.; verdigris, 16 dr.; slender birthwort, 16 dr.; aloe, 24 dr.; round alum, 12 dr.; myrrh, 24 dr.; galbanum, 24 dr.; ammoniac salt, 16 dr.; vinegar, 4 kotylai; oil, 2 kotylai, sometimes less. A green plaster holding out great promise, that of Alcimion or Nicomachus. For fistulas and parts turning black, or spreading ulcers (nomai). It agglutinates bones, brings [flesh] up, and disperses scrofulous swellings. ℞ Galbanum, 16 dr.; burnt copper, 8 dr.; flake, 24 dr.; wax, 50 dr.; goat's or calf's suet, 30 dr.; frankincense, 25 dr.

[808] of dry resin 25 dr., of ammoniac incense 25 dr., of terebinth 25 dr., of natron 25 dr., of birthwort 25 dr., of bryony 12 dr., of the herb orchis 12 dr., of dry iris 4 dr., of Indian aloe 12 dr., of split alum 8 dr., of bull's gall 8 dr., of vinegar one cotyle, of oil 1 cotyle; but when it soils, use rose oil. A green plaster for herpes, as Andromachus gives it, and for chironian and hard-to-cicatrise sores. Rx: of burnt barley 10 dr., of verdigris 8 dr., of wax 80 dr., of oil of cypros 1 cotyle. This drug contains much verdigris relative to the proportion of the wax and the oil of cypros. For burnt barley, sprinkled on by itself, benefits chironian ulcers, neither intensifying the power of the wax and oil of cypros nor weakening that of the verdigris. If it is removed, the drug becomes similar to many of those written in the book before this one for the cure of such ulcers. One will not, however, take oil of cypros in abundance, especially if the wax is fatty, but only as much as is necessary for the wax mixed with the verdigris to be softened.

All the plasters written above have become polychrest [809] for this reason, that they have taken in emollient, drawing, discutient and concoctive drugs, and further those that dry without biting; and most of them also take in strongly astringent drugs, whose power is repellent of the humours flowing into the affected part. The materials of the drugs mentioned, written down by name according to their power, you have in the treatise on simple drugs, in the sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth and eleventh books. I have mentioned many of them by name in the present treatise and will mention them again. Indeed, I have also appended this drug here because I wanted to remind you of these very things I have just said, since it too is of the same kind as those written in the book before this one, and it would have been more fitting for it to have been written together with them. [The black Hicesian of Andromachus.] Andromachus wrote this plaster not in the section in which he wrote the green ones, but higher up, near the beginning. He wrote it also in a proportion that differs greatly, as I showed earlier, from the one in which both Crito and Heras wrote it.

The [810] prescription runs as follows. ℞ Bitumen, 300 dr.; ampelitis earth, 200 dr.; litharge, 60 dr.; galbanum, 36 dr.; terebinth, 36 dr.; split alum, 36 dr.; propolis, 72 dr.; manna, 50 dr.; myrrh, 12 dr.; iris, 12 dr.; chalcitis, 6 dr.; oak-gall, 10 dr.; olive oil, one and a half chous; honey, half a kotyle. He did well to remove the ambiguity about the mina and to write everything in drachms, so that we have to inquire only about the chous. In this respect those who wrote the six kotylai did better. They began the prescription with a tripled amount of bitumen relative to the one written by Heras: Heras wrote 100 drachms, he 300, and in one of the copies I found 200, which is not trustworthy [text uncertain]. The ampelitis earth, however, is clearly written as double the amount in Heras. But the litharge, which ought itself to be equal in weight to the ampelitis, he puts in at a much smaller amount: he mixes in sixty drachms of it, but of the galbanum thirty-six

drachmas, he does not keep to the proportion, at least relative to Heras and Criton, just as is also the case with the split alum; for in this [811] he departs slightly from the exact proportion, which comes out at thirty-seven and a half. In the terebinth he differs slightly from Heras, evidently by as much as in the galbanum and the split alum; but from Criton he differs very greatly, since Criton directs that a mina and a half be put in, which, relative to the proportion of his other ingredients, comes out at fifty drachmas. In the propolis, however, he departed slightly with respect to the double of the proportion. And in the manna, too, he differs from both Heras and Criton; for he ought to have put in 100 drachmas according to their proportion. In the chalcitis he took away a very great deal indeed from the proportion. In the other ingredients the disagreement is slight, except for the honey; for he ought to have put in 3 kotylai according to their proportion, but he has put in half a kotyle. So too in the oil: relative to Criton he ought to have put in three choes, and relative to Heras eighteen kotylai; but he prescribed a chous and a half.

[How Heracleides of Tarentum wrote the [812] black (plaster) of Hicesius.] For every wound, and especially those in the extremities, rendering them painless and agglutinating them; and for dog bites and boils (dothiēnes); and dispersing indurations, especially those about the breasts; and the condylomata in the anus. Take: litharge 100 dr., asphalt the same, ampelitis earth the same, manna 25 dr., propolis the same, galbanum 12½ dr., split alum, terebinth resin the same, iris 6 dr., chalcitis 7½ dr., oak-gall 8 dr., myrrh the same, honey 1 kotyle, omotribes oil (oil of unripe olives) 6 kotylai. Boil the litharge, the asphalt and the earth with the oil, stirring with a spatula of resinous pine-wood. When it has thickened, add the propolis, the resin and the galbanum; these should have been boiled beforehand in the honey. When these have been mixed in, at once take the pot off the fire and sprinkle in the dry ingredients. Since Heracleides wrote this in his books To Antiochis, I wonder how some of those after him did not preserve his text. Heras, then, appears to have followed Heracleides in everything, except in the myrrh and the oak-gall.

For whereas Heraclides puts in eight drachmas of each [813] of these, Heras took six of each of them. And in Asclepiades, in the second book of the External [remedies], everything is written in fourfold proportion relative to Heras, with the further point that twelve kotylai of omphacine oil are written, Crito having written two choes. And yet his composition had everything doubled, which is why some seem to me to have added two kotylai in writing. But this in turn conflicts still more with the truth and with the text of both the Tarentine and Heras. For Heras wrote 180 drachmas, reducing the oil to weight, not to measure, on the basis that the kotyle weighs 60 drachmas. And indeed the Attic kotyle does weigh this, being a kotyle of nine Italian ounces. For the nine Italian ounces, those on the graduated horns, weigh seven and a half ounces by weight, which come to 60 drachmas, since one ounce contains eight drachmas. So in this respect too Heras agrees with Heraclides, putting in three kotylai, while Asclepiades has written twelve, since everything in his composition is written at four times the amount.

Heras, since [814] the bulk of the drug became large according to the recipe of the Tarentine, for this reason seems to me to have written a quarter of all the ingredients. For he had to, as I said, deviate slightly in the myrrh and the oak-gall. And although others have also written up this plaster of Hicesius, those who prepared it more precisely have turned out to be in agreement both with the Tarentine and with the recipe judged by us to be truly correct by means of the boiling; but those who prepared it more carelessly appear to disagree with Heraclides either in only one or two of the ingredients mixed, or even in more. For this reason it seemed to me superfluous to mention them. For the drug is to be prepared as Heraclides directed or as Heras did, since the difference between them is very slight. Heraclides says that the simple plaster of Hicesius is as follows. ℞ Asphalt, 50 drachms; litharge, 50 dr.; oil, 10 kotylai. Boil, and when it thickens, add wax, 5 dr.; galbanum, 5 dr.; myrrh, 5 dr.

[The Cyzicene of Heras.] This too is one of the celebrated plasters, recorded by nearly everyone. In most respects they wrote it in agreement as to the proportion of the simple drugs, but in some points they also disagreed, [815] as will become evident when we set out below how each of them thinks it should be compounded. Heras, then, writes about the plaster before us as follows, word for word: 'Cyzicene, effective for fresh wounds and for old burrowing ones. It disperses above all the indurations in the breasts; it draws, cleanses out, fills up, agglutinates and cicatrises. It is effective also for cancerous indurations, λιποῦργα, and cases in which it is not possible to use the scalpel, as on the neck; use it in the form of a collyrium. It also soothes abscesses that are threatening, disperses phymata and ganglia, and brings collections to a head and ruptures them. It also draws out missiles, bones and splinters. It throws off eschars painlessly as well. In burrowing ulcers one must use large compresses. It also disperses choirades, checks haemorrhoids, and is supremely effective for conditions about the bladder. It contains: frankincense 4 dr., myrrh 4 dr., saffron 4 dr., Illyrian iris 4 dr., bdellium 4 dr., scale 12 drachms, chalcanthum 4 dr., split alum 4 dr., round 4 dr., ammoniac incense 4 dr., misy 4 dr., rinds of sweet pomegranate 4 dr.

of birthwort and of omphacitis gall, [816] 8 dr. each; alternatively 16; of chalcitis 4 dr.; of ammoniac incense 4 dr.; of oak birdlime 8 dr.; of opopanax 8 dr.; of scraped verdigris 8 dr.; of acacia 8 dr.; of rose flowers 8 dr.; of terebinth 1 mina, but others 50 dr.; of poppy juice 6 dr.; of wax 2 minas, but others 4 dr.; of prepared calf's fat 1 mina, but others 150; of common vinegar 2 cotylae; wine for the dry ingredients. Since Heras and Andromachus have written this about the Cyzicene, some will think there is a very great disagreement: Heras puts in 4 dr. of frankincense, saffron, myrrh and each item he lists after them, but Andromachus 8. But what I have already said before, that we must necessarily watch for, I shall say now as well: if all the simple drugs are put in at double the amounts written by others, the same proportion results, just as it does if all are tripled. So here too Andromachus has put in nearly all of them at double, while Heras has put them in at single amounts.

He differs, too, in adding aloe, Heras not having added [817] it, and moreover also the root of panax. For Heras wrote only opopanax, whereas Andromachus wrote not only this but also panax; for they customarily call by this name the root of the plant which they name panax. Andromachus has also added poppy juice for the sake of freedom from pain, and acacia and rose flower as astringent. The boiling Heras wrote out, as is his custom, but Andromachus omits it, since this too, again, is his custom: he rarely writes out the boiling. However, from his having added at the end 'common vinegar, 2 kotylai; wine for the dry ingredients', it is clear that he wants the dry ingredients to be ground smooth with the wine or the vinegar, and then the meltable ingredients, once melted, to be poured over them. Heras, on the other hand, made no mention at all of vinegar or wine, and at the end of the boiling added in writing as follows: 'Finally, put the dry ingredients and the opopanax into the cauldron and, having united them, pour out and knead, smearing the hands with iris oil.'

I myself prepare it in Andromachus' manner, grinding the opopanax in the mortar together with the dry ingredients. If I wish to make the drug stronger [818] and more discutient, I mix in the vinegar during the grinding; if I wish to make it more astringent and more repellent, I mix in the wine. So too, of the wine itself, I sometimes choose the austere and sometimes the tawny, and sometimes the old and sometimes the one of middling age. For the austere wine that is not old is more astringent, while the old wine that is not austere is more discutient. [The Cyzicene, according to Asclepiades.] This plaster has already been written down in the fourth book as well, where I wrote out in order all the drugs for malignancy that he advised keeping at hand in that book. Now, since he too disagrees with both Heras and Andromachus, it seems better to me to write out word for word what he wrote in the third book of his External Remedies, in these very words: The Cyzicene. It is effective for chronic conditions and for severances of the nerves. ℞ Frankincense of the finest quality, wax, myrrh, birthwort, chalcitis, Illyrian [iris], galbanum, 4 drachms of each; terebinth, litharge, 8 drachms of each; oil, 1 cotyle.

Putting everything into [819] a bronze vessel, boil it over soft ashes, stirring, until a drop let fall into cold water has the thickness of honey. After this, take it off while stirring; spread it on a small piece of leather, apply it, and undo it in winter after the seventh day, in summer after the fifth. [Another, from the writings of Philoxenus.] ℞ Frankincense, myrrh, saffron, Illyrian [iris], bdellium, flake of copper, chalcanthum, chalcitis, round and split alum, foreign misy, ammoniac incense, propolis, oak birdlime, opopanax, closed pomegranate rinds, 4 dr. each; birthwort 8 dr.; wax, bull's suet, 100 dr. each, which he writes down as a mina; terebinth resin 15 dr., which he writes down as three quarters. Putting the resin into an earthenware casserole, boil it until it becomes odourless; then grate the suet and the wax, add them and melt them. Pound the dry ingredients and sift them through a very fine sieve; then, taking the meltable ingredients off the fire and letting them cool somewhat, sprinkle the dry ingredients over them and stir carefully.

You must have ready myrrh, frankincense, [820] bdellium and opopanax ground with vinegar. Onto these put the contents of the earthenware pan, and grind so that no wax-lumps (enkērides) form. When it is in good condition, take it up into a wooden box, having first smeared the box with iris unguent. [The plaster made with the two birthworts, as Andromachus gives it.] Concerning this plaster Andromachus writes word for word as follows: The plaster made with the two birthworts. ℞ Roasted resin, 1 litra; wax, 1 litra; pitch, 1 litra; kiki oil or old olive oil, one kotyle, two kyathoi; white lead, 6 ounces; verdigris, 6 ounces; chalcanthum, 4 ounces; manna, 6 ounces; long birthwort, 4 ounces, and round birthwort, 4 ounces; Eretrian earth, 6 ounces; Illyrian iris, 4 ounces; oak-gall, 2 ounces; vinegar, 1 kotyle (I use more); pomegranate rinds, 2 ounces. Grind the dry ingredients smooth with the vinegar, then add the meltable ingredients. [The plaster made with dittany, as Damocrates gives it.] I have often said that recipes written in verse are more useful than those written in prose not only for memory but also for exactness in the proportion of the ingredients mixed.

For this reason, then, he has now also appended [821] the [plaster] made with dittany, which keeps its exact proportion in Damocrates' text. 'It is one of the celebrated plasters, and the only one that contains the so-called Cretan dittany. It heals the strikes of venomous reptiles and the bites of all quadrupeds, even if some of them have been rabid, and callused ulcers, and the corruptions of nerves, of muscles and of the cartilages that lie upon bones, when these already have corruption in depth. It treats ulcers about the breasts, the neck and the spine, even if they are of long standing, and everything that I said a little earlier the plaster called the Egyptian does. Since it is very good, some think it the only one better than all the good ones, because they have no experience of many drugs.'

It contains litharge, twice a hundred drachmas, [822] and of old oil a fourth of a litra; but some say rather a fourth of a kotyle. Twice twenty-five drachmas of Pontic wax, and of fine Colophonian resin double the wax, but some say rather the same quantity of terebinth. Of verdigris and of Indian aloe, of burnt copper and of fine diphryges, sixteen and a half of each ingredient of the mixture; twenty drachmas and 4 of galbanum; of manna and of frankincense equal amounts, twice 12; of ammoniac twice 5 and twice 20; sixteen drachmas of Attic propolis; of long birthwort twice 10 drachmas; twice 6 drachmas of scale of Cyprian copper, and an equal amount of very dry gentian root. To all these add further, of the herb dittany, dry and bearing its flower, 20 holkai, ground smooth.

Putting the litharge with the oil [823] into a new, wide-mouthed earthenware dish, boil it over a light and gentle fire, stirring with a spatula, until it takes on the thickness of Attic honey. Then add an equal amount of the scale as well and boil again more vigorously; next, when the drug has become tawny, add the copper and the diphryges, and, to make the drug non-staining and set, add the wax and the resin together. When these have melted together and you see that the plaster is blended, take the pot off the fire, and add some propolis and the galbanum, ammoniac, manna and aloe. Then, having cooled the fiery and seething heat of the drug, sprinkle in the aristolochia ground very smooth, and the gentian and the dittany herb. Beat the drug up further with the spatula, make it into rolls with your hands, and keep it, using it for the conditions I mentioned before.

[824] [On the troches of Asclepiades.] Just as some of the physicians named plasters from their colour, and not from what they promise to do by their power, calling them quince-yellow, white, grey and tawny, so they name troches (trochiskoi) from the shape given them in the moulding, although these differ from one another and are not for one affection but for a great many. Following them, then, we too shall write all of them in order, at least the approved ones, whether they are called little discs (kykliskoi) or troches (trochiskoi), for they name them in both ways. And they did well to write the promise above each one, especially Asclepiades, whose drugs written in the third book of his work on external [affections] I shall set out first. Troches of Asclepiades. Polychrest troches of Aristarchus of Tarsus.

It is effective against wounds (helkē), both recent and old; it is effective also against terēdones (caries) and kēria (honeycomb ulcers); it is effective against fistulae, ears discharging pus, and corrupted bones; it is effective against nomai (spreading ulcers); it represses every excrescence; it removes pterygia; it is effective against the affections of the uterus, against ozaenae, phagedaenae and condylomata; it is effective against chronic and intractable conditions; it is effective [825] for incipient phthisical patients, and for splenic, coeliac and dysenteric patients, given in the weight of three obols with the appropriate drink. It also benefits those suffering from synanchē and the spreading ulcers of the gums, and in general it is well suited to the affections both of the external and of the internal parts. ℞ Myrrh, 6 drachms; saffron, 3 drachms; crocomagma, 3 dr.; pomegranate flowers (kytinoi), 6 dr.; chalcanthum, 6 dr.; split alum, 6 dr.; aloes, 6 dr. Take up with Falernian wine, make into pastilles, and dry in the shade. In use, dissolve in a liquid appropriate to the underlying affections. That of the Neapolitan. ℞ Myrrh, 6 dr.; frankincense, 6 dr.; oak-galls, 8 dr.; lycium, 8 dr.; alum, 8 dr.; crocomagma, 8 dr.; aloes, 8 dr.; pomegranate flowers, 12 dr.; copper, 8 dr.; with Falernian wine. The one entitled 'Andronius'. ℞ Pomegranate flowers, 10 dr.; split [alum], 4 dr.; chalcanthum, 12 dr.; myrrh, 4 dr.; frankincense, 8 dr.; birthwort, 8 dr.; oak-galls (kykides), 8 dr.; sweet wine, 2 cotylae. In Heraclides it runs thus. ℞ Pomegranate rinds, 10 dr.; birthwort, 8 dr.; oak-galls, 8 dr.; ammoniac salt, 4 dr.; frankincense, 4 dr.; split [alum], 4 dr.; chalcanthum, 2 dr.; myrrh, 4 dr.

[826] Take up in sweet wine. The seal of Polyeides. ♃ Pomegranate rind 6 dr., myrrh 8 dr., split alum 5 dr., frankincense 4 dr., aloe 8 dr., chalcanthum 3 dr., bull's bile 6 dr.; take up in sweet wine. The raven-black (korakinē) seal. It is effective for inflammations of the tonsils and relaxed uvulae, and for putrefying gums; it is effective for spreading ulcers (nomai). It is effective for affections about the seat, and it removes the callus from fistulas. ♃ Round Cretan birthwort, pomegranate flowers, roasted chalcitis, frankincense, myrrh, chalcanthum, crocomagma, Indian aloe, bull's bile, 8 dr. of each; sweet wine, as much as suffices. A pastille for spreading ulcers. ♃ Savin 50 dr., myrrh 3 dr., sory 2 dr., cyperus 2 dr., chalcanthum 2 dr., frankincense 2 dr.; take up in wine. In other copies: olive leaves 2 dr., dried myrtle 4 dr., the plant orchis 4 dr., arsenicon 1 dr., myrrh 4 dr. From the writings of Heracleides. ♃ Orchis 2 dr., arsenicon 4 dr., oak galls 8 dr., scale 8 dr., scale 6 dr., sory 8 dr., myrrh 2 dr., frankincense 2 dr., inspissated juice of acacia 2 dr.; take up in wine.

The one entitled 'from the plants' [827]. ♃ Pomegranate rinds 8 dr., myrtle leaves 8 dr., dry nut-husks 8 dr., fruit of the thorn 8 dr., oak-galls 4 dr., rock salt 8 dr. All are crushed, then kneaded with vinegar and put into an earthenware vessel; then they are roasted and ground smooth with vinegar. When it is in good condition, add myrrh 4 dr. and frankincense 2 dr., and form troches. Use with vinegar. From Terentius; it is entitled 'astringent'. It acts against every spreading ulceration (nomē) and against affections about the anus. ♃ Sandarach, misy, chalcanthum and split alum, 2 dr. each; myrrh, copper flake, aloes and chalcitis, 3 dr. each; pomegranate flower-cups, rose blossom and oak-galls, 4 dr. each; acacia juice 8 dr.; pomegranate rinds 8 dr. Take up in a decoction of myrtle berries boiled down to half. A troche for creeping sores. Of Areius, for herpes. ♃ Cimolian earth 8 dr., roasted misy 16 dr., Sinopic red earth 3 dr. Grind each separately with water, then mix them together and form troches. Use with vinegar. Another, the one with origanum. ♃ Origanum 2 dr., olive leaves 2 dr., acacia 2 dr.

chalcanthum [828] 2 dr., Spanish salt 2 dr.; take up in vinegar. From the remedies of Largus, a successful drug: ℞ litharge or white lead 38 dr., split alum 12 dr., acacia 8 dr., saffron, frankincense, diphryges, opium, 2 dr. each. Grind with water and form pastilles. Use with water. Another, exceedingly excellent: ℞ round alum, chalcitis, melanteria or sory, 2 dr. each; misy, pomegranate rinds, 4 dr. each; quicklime 16 dr.; vinegar 1 xestes. Boil the pomegranate rinds with the vinegar, and when they have dissolved, grind them with the acacia and add them to the rest; and when it is in good condition, form pastilles. Use with water. As Threptus made it, for herpetic conditions and wherever a spreading ulceration (nomē) must be arrested. It acts also against affections in the mouth, against ears discharging pus, against exanthemata, overgrowths of flesh and ulcers in the nostrils, and against affections about the seat. ℞ pomegranate rinds 10 dr., omphacitis gall 8 dr., birthwort 8 dr., aloe 4 dr., myrrh 8 dr., split alum 2 dr., frankincense 4 dr., chalcanthum 4 dr. Take up in sweet wine.

[829] [Tawny pastilles of Hierax of Thebes, the one with halicacabus.] It is effective for psydraces, epinyctides, and ulcers in the nostrils. It is effective for fissures and for whatever you wish to cicatrise without pain. Rx white lead, one pound; litharge, ten pounds; split alum, bark of halicacabus, chalcanthum, Sinopic [earth], half a pound each; take up in vinegar. Of Lucius the Preceptor, a successful drug. Rx alum, Corinthian verdigris, Sinopic red ochre, an equal amount [of each] by the measure of a kotyle; take up in vinegar. From the [prescriptions] of Areius. For spreading psorae, herpetic [lesions], excrescences of flesh, pterygia, ears discharging pus, ulcers hard to heal. It is effective for fissures and condylomata. Rx split [alum], Sinopic red ochre, scraped verdigris, gum, oak-galls, pomegranate flowers, an equal amount of each; take up in vinegar. And as Magnus of Philadelphia used it for the conditions mentioned: Rx split alum, Corinthian verdigris, chalcitis, Sinopic red ochre, gum, equal by measure; take up in vinegar. A pastille for erysipelas. Rx saffron, 1 drachm; opium, 1 drachm.

white lead [830] 2 dr. Take up with sweet wine. In other versions it has 8 dr. of glaucium. The saffron trochisc of Andromachus, a successful drug. ♃ litharge 4 dr., that is ½ oz.; white lead 4 oz.; unfired sulphur 1 oz.; saffron, opium, 1 oz. each. Take up with juice of strychnos. At the time of use, dilute with sweet wine. Of Gaius of Neapolis. ♃ white lead, acacia, glaucium, opium, an equal amount of each. Take up with sweet wine; anoint continually. Another. ♃ white lead 8 dr.; acacia 8 dr.; ammoniac incense 4 dr.; saffron 2 dr.; opium 2 dr.; juice of polygonon or of seris or of strychnos or of hound's-tongue. From the recipes of Agathinus. ♃ white lead 6 dr.; manna, frankincense, 1 dr. each; crocomagma 2 dr.; unfired sulphur 2 dr.; yolks of boiled eggs 6 dr. Take up with sweet wine. For fissures and condylomata. Of Menestheus, for fissures in the anus; it is effective against spreading ulcers. ♃ aloe 6 oz.; saffron 3 oz.; split alum 3 oz. Take up with wine and make trochiscs.

But at the time of use let the [831] liquid be suited to the condition. Apollophanes' remedy for fissures and condylomata. ♃ Stibium 8 dr., acacia 6 dr., verdigris 1 dr., opium 2 dr., frankincense 1½ dr., myrrh 2 dr., gum 4 dr. With wine free of sea-water form pastilles. As Nicolaus has it: ♃ stibium 8 dr., acacia 8 dr., verdigris one drachm, opium 3 dr., myrrh 4 dr., gum 4 dr. Form with wine. From the remedies of Magnus, for fissures and condylomata; it arrests spreading ulcers. ♃ Aloe 8 dr., acacia 4 dr., oak-gall 2 dr., saffron 2 dr., frankincense 1 drachm, myrrh 1 drachm. Take up in wine. The one entitled 'from the juices', for spreading ulcers and psoric conditions. ♃ Indian lycium, Indian aloe, myrrh, copper, split alum, chalcanthum, pomegranate flowers, frankincense, of each 4 dr.; myrtle-berry juice half a kotyle. Compound and form pastilles. Petronius' 'Virtue', a successful drug for fissures and condylomata; even in the most severe violent pains it also brings swift relief.

℞ Stibium, acacia, burnt and washed lead [832], 16 drachms each; Cyprian spodium, fruit of heath, split alum, frankincense, chalcanthum, myrrh, opium, 8 drachms each. Take up with wine and make pastilles. In use, dilute with sweet wine. [The pastilles written by Andromachus in the book on external remedies.] Anal pastille of Darius. ℞ Stibium 16 drachms; acacia 16 drachms, but others 8; verdigris 40 drachms; poppy juice 3 drachms, but others 2 drachms; gum 4 drachms; myrrh 1 drachm; frankincense 3 drachms, but others 2 drachms. Wine, but others water. Polychrest, both pus-promoting and relaxing. ℞ Bark of frankincense 2 drachms; copper scale 4 drachms. Mould with wine; dilute with honey. The iatreion of Musa. ℞ Split alum, aloe, myrrh, chalcanthum, 6 drachms each; saffron 3 drachms; crocomagma 3 drachms; pomegranate flowers 4 drachms. Take up with oenomel made from Falernian wine. For erysipelas, from Agathocles. ℞ White lead 8 drachms; round alum 2 drachms; crocomagma 2 drachms; unfired sulphur 2 drachms.

To the ingredients, once ground smooth, juice of strychnos is poured in, and form [833] pastilles; at the time of use, [dissolve them] in astringent wine. Isidorus' [pastille] for spreading ulcers (nomai). ℞ Greasy wool, i.e. wool still containing its oesypum, 40 drachmas; lead filings 10 drachmas; [copper] scale 10 dr.; asphalt 10 drachmas; split alum 5 dr., and round [alum] 5; pomegranate rinds 5 drachmas; oak galls 5 dr.; misy 5 drachmas; chalcitis 5 dr.; frankincense 5 dr.; myrrh 2 dr.; amurca 8 kotylai, or, if dry, 5. The black pastille which I use. ℞ Pomegranate rinds 10 dr.; aristolochia 8 dr.; oak gall 8 dr.; split alum 4 dr.; aloe 4 dr.; myrrh 2 dr.; chalcanthum 2 dr.; frankincense 4 dr. Take up with wine. Use it with sweet wine. Pastille made with halicacabum. ℞ Litharge 24 dr.; white lead 12 dr., or 24; halicacabum root 8 dr.; chalcanthum 4 dr.; split [alum] 4 dr.; red earth (miltos), enough to colour it. Take up with water. Pastille made with origanum. ℞ Green olive leaves 8 dr.; pomegranate rinds 6 dr.; origanum 4 dr.; acacia 12 dr.; chalcitis 4 dr.; split [alum] 4 dr.; misy 4 dr.; astringent wine. The pastille made with sumach. ℞ Oak gall 3 dr.; acacia 4 dr.; chalcanthum 5 dr.

of chalcitis half a drachma, of split alum [834] 8 dr., of round alum 4 dr., of misy 3 dr., of pomegranate rinds 5 dr., of flake 4 dr., of myrrh 2 dr., of aloe 2 dr., of birthwort 2 dr., of frankincense bark 4 dr., of bull-glue 3 dr., of tanners' sumac the fourth part of a choenix (but some put half a choenix), of vinegar 1½ kotylai, for steeping and grinding the sumac smooth. Seal of Polyeides. Of split alum 3 dr., of frankincense 4 dr., of myrrh 4 dr. (or of myrrh 8 dr.), of chalcanthum 2 dr., of pomegranate flowers 12 dr., of bull's bile 6 dr., of aloe 8 dr.; take up with dry wine. The Andronian pastille. ℞ Of pomegranate flowers 10 dr., of oak-gall 8 dr., of myrrh 4 dr. (but some put 18 dr., others 28), of birthwort 4 dr., of chalcanthum 2 dr., of split alum 2 dr. (but some put 4 dr.), of Cyprian misy 2 dr.; take up with sweet wine. Use it for many things, as a drug of many uses. Pastille of Achillas. ℞ Of flake, misy, aloe, 2 dr. each; of birthwort 8 dr.; of split alum 4 dr.; of myrrh 2 dr.; of frankincense 4 dr.; of oak-gall 8 dr.; of chalcanthum 2 dr.; of pomegranate rinds 8 dr.; of bull's bile 2 dr.; take up with vinegar. Pastille for spreading sores (nomai), of Isidorus the pupil. ℞ Of manna and frankincense, 30 dr. each.

Pomegranate flowers [835] 8 dr.; split [alum] 8 dr.; oak-galls 8 dr.; chalcanthum, birthwort, myrrh, Cyprian misy, quicklime, 10 dr. each; acacia 8 dr. Take up in wine or vinegar, and use having ground it fine. Another pastille, polychrest. ℞ Oak-gall 8 dr.; pomegranate flowers 12 dr.; burnt copper 8 dr.; verdigris 6 dr.; split [alum] 8 dr.; chalcanthum, acacia, bull's gall, frankincense, aloe, lycium, myrrh, and in another [copy] also misy, 8 dr. each. Grind in much vinegar during the heats under the Dog-star. Pastille of Apollonius Archistrator, the 'smilinos', polychrest, as Alcimion [has it]. ℞ White lead 10 dr.; litharge 5 dr.; aloe 50 dr.; split [alum] 4 dr.; frankincense 4 dr.; myrrh 1 dr., but others 2 dr.; Cimolian earth 25 dr. Take up in wine; use sometimes with wine and rose oil. For erysipelas, the one I use. ℞ Litharge 7 pounds; white lead 1 dr.; opium 3 oz.; unfired sulphur 3 ounces; saffron 3 ounces. Take up with sweet wine, use with sweet wine. Polychrest of Glaucias. ℞ Liquid alum 100 dr.; myrrh 8 dr.; saffron 8 dr. Take up with sweet wine. Good for erysipelas.

℞ Acacia [836] 8 dr., misy 4 dr., opium 2 dr., frankincense 4 dr.; take up with vinegar. It is effective also for herpes. Another, effective for the same. ℞ Opium 4 dr., acacia 4 dr., diphryges 4 dr., split [alum] 4 dr.; take up with water, use with vinegar. Another for erysipelas. ℞ White lead 8 dr., unfired sulphur 4 dr., poppy juice 2 dr., leaves of rue 2 dr., split [alum] 4 dr., Cimolian earth 2 dr., starch 2 dr.; honey and vinegar. For herpes, that of Tiberius Caesar. ℞ Diphryges, poppy juice, split [alum], acacia, 3 oz. of each; use, taking up with vinegar or water. The keranitis (?), polychrest. ℞ Orpiment 32 dr., birthwort 32 dr. (others 8), iris 32 dr., oak gall 16 dr. (others 8 dr.), round alum 6 dr., chalcitis 6 dr., flakes of copper 16 dr., chalcanthum 8 dr., dry resin 8 dr., vinegar 4 choes; grind in the heats under the Dog-star, in a bronze mortar with a pestle. If you do not have a bronze mortar, put in 1 mina of the flakes, that is, 100 dr. A pastille called Bithynian, prepared in Sicily.

for spreading ulcers (nomai), fistulas, pterygia; with a double cerate [837] for herpetes, erysipelas and other things. ℞ Pomegranate rinds 6 dr., oak-gall 6 dr., Illyrian iris 4 dr., birthwort 6 dr., chalcanthum 3 dr., split alum 6 dr., chalcitis 6 dr., misy 3 dr., nitron 2 dr., frankincense 2 dr., cadmia 6 dr., copper flake 4 drachms, chrysocolla 2 dr., vinegar; prepare it in the [heats] under the Dog[-star]. A pastille for condylomata, inflammations in a finger, and pterygia. ℞ Frankincense, acacia, stibi, of each 2 dr.; verdigris, myrrh, opium, poppy, gum, Celtic nard, of each 2 dr. Grind with a dry wine and smear around. [The multiform dry powder, shown by means of what has been written above, for what each is suited. The [recipes] written by Andromachus at the end of the [book on] external [remedies].] A dry powder, septic, not biting. ℞ Sandarach 2 dr., arsenikon 2 dr., quicklime 4 dr., manna 4 dr.; use them ground fine. A haemostatic [powder] which I use. ℞ Chalcitis, misy, manna, 4 dr. each (others two); use them ground fine. The yellow [powder] which I use. ℞ Chalcitis 100 dr., chalcanthum 50 dr.

of roasted misy [838] 25 dr., of burnt copper 12½ dr. Use finely ground. The great blood-staunching powder. ♃ Cyprian misy 7 dr., chalcanthum 7 dr., pine bark 4 dr., manna of frankincense 4 dr., copper flake 4 dr., burnt copper 15 dr., chalcitis 15 dr., quicklime 8 dr. (others 40 dr.), roasted gypsum 4 dr. (others 5). Use finely ground. Blood-staunching powder of Aphrodas. ♃ chalcitis 6 dr., manna of frankincense 2 dr., roasted terebinth resin, 4 dr. of each. Use finely ground, for haemorrhoids. Another, as Harpocras makes it. ♃ sandarach 2 dr., arsenicum 4 dr., quicklime 8 dr. Make pastilles, grinding with water for 40 days, and in this way smear around. For haemorrhoids, which I use. ♃ arsenicum 8 dr., sandarach 8 dr., elaterium 4 dr., thapsia 2 dr., chrysocolla 4 dr., quicklime 4 dr. Use finely ground. A dry powder from those of Gallus, polychrest, for pterygia. ♃ litharge 8 dr., verdigris 10 dr. Use finely ground; it is praised. A good one for pterygia. ♃ chalcitis, burnt dried figs, pomegranate rinds, copper flake, an equal amount of each. At the time of use mix in boiled honey, and, making it plaster-like, apply it. Every day take it off, wiping around, and do not pour liquid over it, nor sprinkle powder on it.

[839] Anthera which I use. Take: sandarach, 32 dr. (some say 16); split [alum], myrrh, saffron residue (magma of saffron), 16 dr. each; iris, 16 drachms; cyperus, 66 dr. Anthera from Magnus. Take: cassia, 24 dr.; split [alum], 4 dr.; oak-gall, 4 dr.; sory, 4 dr.; misy, 4 dr.; sandarach, 8 drachms; pomegranate rinds, 1 drachm; myrrh, 4 obols; cinnamon, 4 obols; saffron, 2 dr.; tamarisk fruit, 2 dr. Use finely ground. A dry [powder] for the head. Take: iris, 4 dr.; frankincense, 2 dr.; panax, 2 dr.; birthwort, 2 dr. Use finely ground, also for spreading ulcers. A dry cicatrizing [powder]. Take: burnt oysters, 2 dr.; manna, 1 drachm; cadmia, 3 obols. Use finely ground, also for spreading ulcers. Another dry cicatrizing [powder]. Take: pine bark, 6 dr.; manna, 6 dr.; birthwort, 6 dr.; pumice, 4 dr.; resin, 4 dr.; Illyrian iris, 12 dr. Use finely ground. Another cicatrizing [powder], also for malignant [ulcers]. Take: pine bark, 6 dr.; burnt deer's horn, 4 dr.; cadmia, 22 dr.; white lead, 4 dr.; manna, 4 dr.; scraped verdigris, 2 dr. Use finely ground.

of the External [Remedies], which he entitles 'Marcellas'.] Andromachus [844] mixed together the dry [drugs] suited to an affection with those suited to the affected parts. But in Asclepiades they have been written separately, in the fifth [book]: those for an affection are marked by headings of their own, and those that go with an affected place likewise by headings of their own. Without reference to place he has written the cicatrizing and the escharotic [drugs], those suited to spreading ulcers and carbuncles, and the so-called haemostatics. With reference to an affected place, he has written those for polyp, ozaenae, haemorrhages from the nostrils, spreading ulcers in the mouth, sodden gums, the lumpy swellings on the chin, and those for paronychias, pterygia, fissures in the anus, and haemorrhoids. Some have also acquired their name from the affected part. Yet they suit other parts too. Such are the [drugs] called cephalic by the physicians: they are suited especially to the bones, but they are also able to incarn ulcerations arising in the whole body. For it is not as the head that they are by nature particularly suited to the head.

Indeed, when the bone has not been laid bare, we have no need of any of them; but in cases where it has been laid bare, [845] since we are wary of using greasy drugs, we use the dry ones alone, avoiding what physicians call emmota, that is, drugs applied by means of lint smeared with them. And just as their use is most suitable when the bones of the head have been laid bare, so it is likewise in all the other bones that have been laid bare, whether it be the upper arm, the ulna, the radius, the thigh or the shin. Therefore I too, being about to write out next the dry drugs written by Asclepiades, and having found that he wrote the cephalics first of all, will myself also write them first, because they are useful not only for laid-bare bones in the head but also for all the other bones affected in the same way. Second after them I shall write the cicatrizing drugs, passing over all those in between that concern an affected place. And after the cicatrizing drugs, all the rest in turn, in the order I have just stated. Some of these dry drugs, however, have a twofold use, so that one can use them both dry and mixed with certain other things, as Asclepiades himself also points out.

[846] [Dry cephalic powders.] A dry cephalic powder which Lucius my teacher used. It detaches scales, brings up corrupted bones and fills hollows with flesh. The drug is without fat. Take: Illyrian iris, 4 dr.; panax, 4 dr.; birthwort, 2 dr.; manna, 2 dr. Others make it without birthwort. Pound and sift everything; use it on its own and with honey. The one made with silphium. It melts away callused parts, cleans out foul parts and fills the hollows of ulcers; it melts away the little membranes (chitōniskoi) that remain behind. Take: dry pine resin, 12 dr.; pumice, or roasted sory quenched in wine, 8 dr.; Illyrian iris, 8 dr.; birthwort, 8 dr.; silphium, 50 dr.; copper scale, 2 dr.; frankincense, 4 dr. Use it dry and with honey. In other copies it does not contain silphium. The one made with bitter vetch, of Xenocrates. Take: meal of tawny bitter vetch, 8 dr.; Illyrian [iris], 10 dr.; manna, 5 dr.; birthwort, 5 dr.; scale, 5 dr. Use it finely ground, and also with honey. In other copies: bryony root, 8 dr.; manna, 12 dr.; scale, 12 dr.; iris, 12 dr.; bitter vetch, 10 dr.

of long birthwort [847] 15 dr. The one entitled 'the [remedy] with serapias': it detaches scales and produces flesh; it is among the strongly desiccating [drugs]. Of serapias, the orchis, 8 dr.; of Illyrian iris 8 dr.; of dry horehound 8 dr.; of bitter-vetch meal 10 dr.; of birthwort 50 dr. [Use it] dry and with honey. Tryphon's cephalic. It detaches scales. ℞ Of pine bark 6 dr.; of copper scale 6 dr.; of burnt pumice 6 dr.; of frankincense manna, birthwort, Illyrian iris, pine resin, of each 4 dr.; of myrrh, aloe, of each 2 dr. [Use it] dry and with honey. In the copies of Athenaeus the drug is without pine bark. It also has oak gall in an amount equal to the manna. [Dry cicatrizing drugs.] Concerning all ulcers, recent, old, easily treated, hard to treat, it has been said both in the books of the Therapeutic Method, in the third, fourth and fifth

book; and also in this treatise, in the earlier parts, where I showed that, of hollow ulcers without any complication at all, the flesh-producing drugs are of a [848] detergent, non-biting power; that the cicatrizing ones are more drying, together with being astringent without biting; and that those which remove overgrown flesh are hot and acrid. Moreover, which of the cicatrizing drugs I consider the best has also been stated by me before, in the Therapeutic Method, in which the methods of cure of all affections have been set out, and of those pertaining to ulcers earlier in this present [treatise] now before us. Asclepiades, however, wrote down drugs, as did Andromachus too, as cicatrizing, without further specifying whether they are for uncomplicated ulcers or for those properly called hard to cicatrize, which were shown to differ from one another by a number of differences, each having its own aim of treatment. In some cases, however, they have added in writing that it is also for malignant ones, or again, that it is for condylomata and fissures. And Asclepiades, although he is more accustomed than Andromachus to add the specifications, omitted them in the case of the cicatrizing drugs. But from what I have set out, both in the therapeutic treatise and in the present one, it will be clear to those who pay attention how each of the recorded drugs is to be used. Dry cicatrizing [powders].

[849] [Asclepiades' ash-coloured [powder], from the writings of Magnus.] ℞ Quicklime 6 dr.; manna of frankincense 4 dr.; scale 4 dr. Otherwise: quicklime 12 dr.; scale 4 dr.; manna 4 dr. As Archibius has it: ℞ scale 8 dr.; and manna 8 dr., or 4 dr.; in other copies, 8 dr. of quicklime. As Heliodorus has it: quicklime 8 dr.; manna of frankincense 8 dr.; scale 4 dr. Tawny cicatrizing [powder]. ℞ Roasted misy 8 dr.; copper scale 10 dr.; manna 6 dr. Use finely ground. [Magnus' cicatrizing [powder].] ℞ Diphryges 4 dr.; scale 4 dr.; Illyrian [iris] 2 dr.; manna 2 dr. Use finely ground. The [powder] made with pumice. ℞ Roasted pumice quenched in wine 8 dr.; scale 4 dr.; manna 4 dr.; iris 4 dr.; dry pine resin 4 dr. Use finely ground. Another, of Ptolemy, an acquaintance [of mine]; it also works for sores that are hard to heal. ℞ Pine bark 6 dr.; roasted cadmia 8 dr.; scale 4 dr.; burnt deer's horn 4 dr.; manna 4 dr. Use finely ground.

In other copies it has: burnt and washed lead, [850] 4 drachms; molybdaena, 8 dr. Dry escharotic [powders]. It has been said of these too that they are of acrid and caustic power, so that their use is both in cases [arising] from excessive moisture and dyscrasia of the affected part and on account of the putrefactions that arise in some parts. Escharotics of Asclepiades. The quince-yellow [drug] of Lucius the teacher, escharotic and excisive of calluses, sprinkled on and pressed in with the olive-tip of a probe. It is also repressive and cicatrizing of hard-to-heal [ulcers], if one were to use the drug on fine [ones], using what is called the 'down'. ♃ Raw chalcitis, 8 dr.; cadmia, 4 dr. While fasting, take it up with saliva only so far as just to moisten the drug; then gather it together and, having covered it, let it become quince-yellow; and having dried it in the shade, moving the pestle lightly round, take it up as was said before. Among others the drug is called 'the grey'. It is taken up with very sharp vinegar, and is dried and ground smooth.

In other copies, as Eunomus the Asclepiadean used it, [851] it runs thus. Take: of chalcitis 12 dr., of cadmia 6 dr., of realgar (sandarachē) 6 dr. It is taken up with vinegar. Another. Take: of roasted chalcitis, of roasted chalcanthum, of roasted cadmia, an equal amount of each, and take them up with fasting saliva. The one entitled 'Vigorous'. Take: of roasted chalcitis 8 dr., of chalcanthum 8 dr., of realgar 8 dr., of cadmia 8 dr. Sprinkle it on dry. The one made from the four. Take: of roasted chalcitis 4 dr., of roasted misy 4 dr., of diphryges 4 dr., of roasted chalcanthum 4 dr. Use it. A very powerful escharotic. Take: of split alum 16 dr., of chalcanthum 16 dr., of oak-galls 16 dr., of Cyprian misy 16 dr., of sory 4 dr. Use them finely ground. [A successful one, as Eunomus has it.] Take: of foreign misy 16 dr., of sory 12 dr., of burnt copper 2 dr., of burnt split stone 8 dr., of chalcanthum 4 dr., of realgar 4 dr., of split alum 4 dr. Use them finely ground, sprinkling them on and pressing them in with the button (pyrēn) of the probe. For spreading ulcers (nomai).

Putrefying ulcers, when they spread over the surrounding places, are specifically called nomai (spreading ulcers). It is clear that such [852] conditions require the most powerful drugs; indeed, we often use cauteries on them as well. For nomai, of Asclepiades. Of Lucius the teacher, for nomai. ℞ unfired sulphur 2 dr.; arsenicon 2 dr.; scale 2 dr.; burnt copper enough to colour it. Use dry, or with honey. [Of Publius the teacher.] ℞ Arsenicon 4 dr.; scale 2 dr.; elaterium 1 dr.; papyrus enough to colour it. As Eunomus used it: ℞ arsenicon 4 dr.; scale 4 dr.; unfired sulphur 2 dr.; elaterium 2 dr.; burnt papyrus enough to colour it. In other copies: sandarach 4 dr.; scale 6 dr.; arsenicon 4 dr.; elaterium 2 dr.; burnt papyrus 4 dr. From the [prescriptions] of Areius, for nomai. It also cleans out foul [ulcers] without biting when diluted with rose oil. It is also effective against erosions in the uterus. Theotropus gave it. ℞ arsenicon 4 dr.; burnt papyrus 4 dr.; burnt and washed lead 4 dr.; copper scale 4 dr. Grind each separately, then mix them together and use for the conditions mentioned above.

As [853] Ptolemy used it: ℞ burnt lead, orpiment, flake, burnt papyrus, 4 dr. of each; sulphur untouched by fire, 2 dr. Use finely ground. As Apelles used it: a successful drug, entitled 'the one with papyrus', for spreading ulcers. It not only arrests the spreading ulcer but also prevents it when it is beginning. It is also effective for dysenteric patients when infused with rose oil. But when, he says, on being infused in dysenteric patients it produces a biting sensation, the spreading ulcer is to be suspected. The composition is as follows. ℞ burnt papyrus, burnt lead, and burnt and washed copper, orpiment, flake of steel, an equal amount of each; sulphur untouched by fire, half that amount. Use finely ground, either with honey or with rose oil. Moschion's, for spreading ulcers. ℞ elaterium, 2 drachms; burnt papyrus, 2 drachms; copper flake, two drachms; orpiment, 4 drachms; worm verdigris, 1 drachm; ammoniac salt, one drachm. Use finely ground with rose oil. [The fragrant remedy of Lucius the teacher.] ℞ flake, 4 dr.; oak gall, 4 drachms; sandarach, 2 dr.; orpiment, 2 drachms; myrrh, 1 drachm; chalcanthum, 1 drachm.

of frankincense [854] 2 dr., of elaterium 1 dr., of burnt papyrus enough to colour it. As we ourselves make it: ℞ of flake 8 dr., of oak-gall 8 dr., of myrrh 8 dr., of realgar 4 dr., of orpiment 4 dr., of elaterium 4 dr., of frankincense 3 dr., of chalcanthum 3 dr., of papyrus enough to colour it. As Prasion makes it: ℞ of orpiment 2 dr., of flake 2 dr., of chalcanthum 1 drachm, of realgar 2 dr., of myrrh 1 drachm, of frankincense 1 dr., of oak-galls 1 drachm, of papyrus 4 dr.; [use it] ground very fine, and also with rose oil. Heracleides had this formula: ℞ of oak-galls 6 dr., of orpiment 4 dr., of realgar 4 dr., of flake 4 dr., of frankincense 3 dr., of chalcanthum 3 dr., of Minaean myrrh 2 dr., of papyrus 8 dr. As Cleobulus makes it: ℞ of flake 2 dr., of realgar 2 dr., of orpiment 2 dr., of myrrh 1 drachm, of frankincense 1 drachm, of chalcanthum 1 drachm, of oak-gall 1 dr., of papyrus enough to colour it.

[For carbuncles.] The carbuncle is an ulcer that quickly produces an eschar, with strong inflammation of the whole surrounding part, so that violent fevers also supervene [855] and extreme dangers. Hence one must place a strong drug on the eschar itself, and indeed of these drugs such as have been said to suit spreading ulcers, and plaster the surrounding parts with poultices having an even power, so as both to repel and moderately to cool and to disperse. But concerning poultices it has been said in the treatise on them; now we shall record those written by Asclepiades. For carbuncles, those of Asclepiades. That of the Massiliote. He set this one out publicly for the city, in proportion to its power (?), because carbuncles were rife and carried off many. ♃ Chrysocolla 4 dr., roasted nitre 4 dr., Assian stone 4 dr., arsenikon 4 dr., sandarach 4 dr., roasted misy 4 dr., chalcitis 4 dr., split alum 4 dr., diphryges 4 dr. Having ground them separately and together, we store them in a Cyprian copper vessel. At the time of use we apply it, pressing it on with the flat of the probe, until the carbuncle turns black; then we put on top the green salve written below. It is this: ♃ frankincense 1 dr., scraped verdigris 1 dr.

one drachm [856] of copper flake, four obols of split alum, four obols of ammoniac salt, 7 drachms 3 obols of wax, 15 drachms of dry pine resin, 1 kotyle of old oil. Grind the dry ingredients in the sun with vinegar. Melt the meltable ones, pour them in, and when you have beaten it up and taken it out, use it. In Demosthenes of Massalia, who also compounded the drug, it has two kotylai of oil. [Apion's, for carbuncles.] Take red natron, arsenic, sandarach, chalcitis, chalcanthum, diphryges, an equal amount of each; grind smooth with vinegar, dry, grind again, and use. Of Apollonius Organicus. Take 1 drachm of chrysocolla, 1 drachm of split alum and 1 drachm of round alum, 1 drachm of sandarach, 1 drachm of ochre, 1 drachm of raw misy, 1 drachm of chalcanthum. Use them finely ground. The 'flowering' remedy of Magnus, for putrefactions, spreading ulcers, carbuncles, pterygia and ears running with pus; it is also effective against spreading ulcers in the mouth. Take 8 drachms of split alum, 6 drachms of chalcitis, 3 drachms of sandarach, 2 drachms of dried pomegranate rinds, 1 drachm of chalcanthum.

[857] of misy, 2 dr.; of nitre, 2 dr.; of dry omphacine, 2 dr. Use it dry, and also with honey. Another, of Diodorus. ℞ Omphacine oak-gall, 4 dr.; misy, 2 dr.; chalcitis, 2 dr.; arsenikon, 2 dr.; sandarach, 2 dr.; split alum, chalcanthum, Assian stone, diphryges, red nitre, 1 dr. of each. Sprinkle on in powdered form, touching the place with the knob (pyrēn) of a probe. The blood-staunching remedy of Asclepiades; a successful drug of Lucius the teacher. ℞ Chalcitis, 16 dr.; manna, 12 dr.; terebinth kneaded with vinegar [no quantity given]. Sprinkle the bleeding places with the dry ingredients. In two other copies we have found instead (?): ℞ chalcitis, 8 dr.; manna, 16 dr.; roasted terebinth, 16 dr. And as Dioscorides of Tarsus gave it to Areius the Asclepiadean, wonderfully checking haemorrhages: ℞ Chalcitis, 8 dr.; manna, 16 dr.; dry resin, 8 dr.; gypsum, 8 dr. The other ingredients are pounded, sifted, mixed and stored in a bronze box; at the time of use an equal amount of the drug is mixed with the gypsum. From the writings of Heraclides, for haemorrhoids.

He used this for [858] haemorrhages of the nostrils, dipping wool into it and twisting it like a lamp-wick. Rx: rinds of sour pomegranate, 3 ounces; Egyptian alum, 4 ounces; chalcitis, 1 ounce. Use ground fine. For the nostrils, fill wool with the drug and insert it. The so-called 'Heracles', for haemorrhages. He used this in place of a cautery, and it is escharotic. It is also effective for pterygia, reduces every excrescence, brings up bones, and detaches scales. Rx: sory, 4 drachms; chalcanthum, 4 drachms; burnt chalcitis, 4 drachms; tanners' sumach, 4 drachms. Use ground fine. A successful blood-staunching drug. Rx: foreign misy, 6 drachms; chalcanthum, 6 drachms; pine bark, 4 drachms; chalcitis, 4 drachms; manna, 4 drachms (others: 20); gypsum, 4 drachms. Use ground fine. Another. Rx: frankincense, 1 ounce; foreign misy, 4 drachms; unripe oak-galls, 4 drachms; chalcitis, 4 drachms; burnt cork, 8 drachms; tanners' sumach, 4 drachms. Use ground fine.

[859] GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK VII. Having divided up the so-called polychrest plasters, since they suit many dispositions, in the book before this one I gathered together those that are able, along with the other things they promise, also to heal the hard-to-treat among ulcers.

Now I shall pass on to another kind of polychrest plasters, each of which acts against many other things and, indeed, also against the putrefying parts, [860] these being of a different condition from the ulcers specifically called hard-to-treat. For in the former the putrefaction spreads, and for this reason most physicians call these conditions nomai (spreading sores); in the latter, however, the condition is circumscribed in a single place without putrefaction, so that even the so-called phagedaenas eat away the contiguous parts, yet without making them putrefy and bringing on fevers, which usually follows the spreading conditions accompanied by putrefaction. The chief point of the cure, in the case of the aforementioned kind of hard-to-treat ulcers, which they also call Chironian, was to find drugs that, as far as possible, do not bite but dry strongly. But the drugs now to be written down are all biting if one uses them unmixed, without their being mixed with cerate. Mixed with cerate, however, they are able to cleanse a foul ulcer and fill it with flesh, and also to disperse some hardness and tension, but not to cure the hard-to-treat ones.

Their power is made plain by the affections for which they are trusted to be properly employed. And, as was said in the earlier discussion and as I shall say now as well, one must remember [861] what was written in the treatise on simple drugs: in its first books I stated the method by which the powers of drugs are discovered, and also exercised myself in it on a number of examples, while in the books that follow I recorded each drug by name. For whoever remembers those things will easily follow the reasoning of those who composed these drugs that are now before us, and he will clearly also compose others himself, at whatever time he lacks those already tested. For many such things happen to many people on journeys abroad, both on other kinds and above all on those by sea; indeed, even with some who stayed at home, the stock of drugs from which they treated those in need was lost, so that they wasted away from grief and died. Best, then, is to use drugs that have already given proof, in accordance with the method stated.

But if, as I said, we should at some time lack these, [it is best] that we ourselves have such a trained disposition as to be able to compound drugs similar to those that have already given sufficient proof by experience, as you often see me doing too, [862] at least on journeys abroad, and in other circumstances as well. At any rate, some of the drugs improvised in such circumstances, when tested by experience, proved in no way inferior to the most renowned. For we make their first composition from skilled estimation; after that, on the basis of experience, since some prove most excellent while others fall short of the aim, a second correction is made in turn; and sometimes a third as well, which brings them to the full accomplishment of what they promise. Without the method stated both in the earlier treatises and in the therapeutic treatise, it is impossible to use correctly the drugs described previously, and still more impossible to compound oneself drugs similar to them. Now then I shall begin on plasters of this kind. The plaster made with herbs has been written up by nearly all who have collected the renowned plasters in writings of one book or of several, and they do not differ much in the proportion of the simple drugs mixed in. Here too, then, I shall begin with those written by Crito, first mentioning, in his very words, the plasters that Crito wrote up in the fourth book On Simple Drugs.

[863] [The plaster from herbs of Criton.] The plaster from herbs, which I use, is effective against carcinomas and putrefactions; bringing choirades to suppuration and squeezing them out, it removes lepras and dissolves boils; it is suitable for gouty patients; it dissolves calluses; the same, as a cephalic, removes scales of bone without trepanation, brings up bones, and scrapes the bones to some extent; the same is for freshly inflicted wounds; for spreading ulcers, applied on lint, it cleans them out; it fills in with rose cerate, one part being mixed to two parts of cerate, and sometimes to three or four. With myrtle cerate, in two or three parts, it brings to a scar. ♃ Herbs from waterless places by the sea: pimpernel, the kind that has the dark-blue flower, 56 dr.; horned poppy 56 dr.; horehound 56 dr.; tender leaves of henbane 56 dr. Throw these into a mortar and pound until they are crushed and broken down, only do not waste their juice; then throw them into a grinding-mortar and triturate. In another grinding-mortar have: scale of red copper 25 dr.; manna 8 dr.; dry pine resin 16 dr.; aloe 16 dr.; split [alum] 4 dr.

[864] round [alum], 4 dr. Grind these in the sun with vinegar until they have the thickness of gloios (strigil-scrapings); then mix in the herbs and grind until they are well united. Then make a cerate from Chian wax, 100 dr. (others say 1 mina), and old oil, 2 kotylai; boil it and mix it in. Thus Heras. Some put in both kinds of anagallis, and some also add chrysocolla, Eretrian earth, ammoniac salt, and fissile arsenikon, 4 dr. each. What Asclepiades wrote about this plaster has also been set out in the book before this one; it is somewhat similar to this, and so it seemed superfluous to me to write it out again, especially as I am now about to go through the common account of these things. For the man who first composed this drug used acrid herbs to disperse vigorously the bad humours in the affected parts. That is why he directs that they come from waterless and seaside places. Opposite to these he used others of a cold power, to soothe the vehemence of the acrid ones; such are henbane and the poppy.

For they also have something mitigating of pains, implanting a numbing chill [865] in whatever they come near. 'Moderate numbness is a resolver of pain,' says Hippocrates. Of the metallic substances he also added the scale of copper and the split alum, about which I spoke earlier, namely that each of these two drugs suits malignant ulcers. Aloe he mixed in from among the drugs that are astringent and dry without biting, and manna from among those that concoct, soothe and bring to suppuration. The pine resin he added as material for the making of a plaster, just as he did the wax and the oil; at the same time it also comes about through these that the vehemence of the acrid drugs is tempered. The pine resin, however, also has a drying property, and the drier it is, the more it is of the kind he requires to be put in.
