He says that some have also mixed into the drug chrysocolla and Eretrian earth, since both heal the hard-to-treat ulcers. Conversely to these, ammoniac salts and what is called arsenikon are by nature such as to irritate ulcers on account of their acridity, but they are also suited to putrefying ones.

And for this reason the drug under discussion [866] is not at all useful for Chironian ulcers. But in those in which some putrefaction is present, it is suited to stopping this, since it disperses the ichors that produce it. The same faculty of the drug also cures choirades. And since some of the ingredients put into it are detergent, for this reason it also cleanses lepras. For the aim in this affection is, as it were, to peel off the hardened part of the skin, and this is accomplished by things that dry excessively while also being detergent. For if the condition of the skin were able to return to its natural state, no one would excessively dry what has already been dried out. But since it is not possible for what is already leprous to be cured, the second aim would be the one that is common to all incurable conditions: to cut out the incurable part of the body. It is cut out sometimes with iron, sometimes with fire, and sometimes with a drug, either with caustics or with drugs that are at once discutient and detergent, such as the one now under discussion. Just as, then, this account is common to every lepra, so too is the account concerning the generation of flesh.

For since, as was shown in the third book of the Therapeutic Method, the drugs called flesh-producing are of a non-biting [867] detergent faculty; and since those of this class of material that go into the drug now set before us in the discussion have the detergent property but do not have the non-biting one, for this reason we mix with them a liquid cerate composed of wax and resin melted in oil. For wax and oil, just as they blunt acridities, are likewise emplastic, and for this reason generative of filth. Resin, on the other hand, though it has the non-biting property, does not have the emplastic one, being of a detergent faculty that is biting to parts already ulcerated but non-biting to unulcerated ones. The due proportion in the mixture we shall find conjecturally before trial, but scientifically after trial, knowing at the same time that the clean ulcer requires a detergent of an exactly non-biting faculty, the dirty one a stronger detergent. For in the latter the filth serves as a protective covering, whereas the clean ulcer meets bare whatever touches it. And moreover, of the bodies themselves, some have a more sensitive substance, others a less sensitive one, and some a softer, others a harder.

For this reason, then, Criton too, in the case of the drug under discussion, directs that to one part [868] of it one should mix sometimes two parts of the cerate, sometimes three or four. He did not, however, specify when two parts and when more should be mixed, as though whoever was going to use the drug already had some practice in the art and were able to work out for himself what is now being said by me. It is better, however, for the cerate to have been prepared with rose oil, though the advantage in such ulcers is not great even if it were melted with olive oil. For rose oil is better than olive oil in cases that have something phlegmonous, but ulcers that are to be filled with flesh are entirely free of phlegmone. Criton did well to add in writing that for ulcers needing cicatrization the cerate should be prepared with myrtle oil, for these have need of astringency. This is enough to have been said, for the present at least, about both the flesh-producing and the cicatrizing drugs. For the method of their use and composition has been stated in the books of the Method of Healing, while the exercise on the particular materials, which belongs to the present treatise, will be set out in the book after this one.

[869] [Plaster with squill.] Next after this one Criton wrote down another plaster of the same power in kind, in these very words: ℞ chalcitis, round birthwort, of each 30 dr. (others, 15 dr.); iris, 30 dr. (others, 15 dr.); dry pine resin, 30 dr. (others, 15 dr.); ammoniac, 15 dr.; myrrh, 15 dr.; storax, 15 dr.; flake of red copper, 15 dr.; roasted squill, 108 dr. Pound in the sharpest vinegar for 40 days, in the heats under the Dog-star. First the flake and the storax, a little of each of them at a time; then add the ammoniac and the copper and the squill, so that it may be thoroughly worked; then the resin, a little at a time; after these the myrrh; then, when these are smooth, the remaining dry ingredients. When the days have been completed, make a cerate as follows: wax, 5 litrai (others, 240 dr.); terebinth resin, 1 litra (others, 30 dr.); oil, 2½ sextarii (others, 6 kotylai); galbanum, 30 dr.; liquid pitch, 30 dr. Add the galbanum last; then, having cooled it, take it up carefully. This, then, is the composition of the drug.

Concerning its use Criton writes the following [870] word for word: 'In use, employ the drug unmixed for fractures in the head, for fistulas, spreading ulcers (nomai) and fleshy excrescences, for widening openings and for drainage (hypophora). When you wish to make it milder, so that it becomes flesh-producing and cicatrising, add 12 parts of rose-oil cerate to one part of the drug. For burns, add 8 parts to one part.' Criton wrote well about the use of the drug. He used it as acrid, as opening (anastomotic), as discutient and for that reason also as drying, for fistulas, for fleshy excrescences and for putrefactions, that is, spreading ulcers, and for widening openings, as is the case with narrow-mouthed sinuses. He used it also for fractures in the head, when we attempt to treat them without trepanation; such fractures are those that have not penetrated as far as the meninges. For the sake of producing flesh he mixed in 14 parts of the rose-oil cerate, 'until cicatrisation'; but it would be better to say 'until the filling up of the cavity in the ulcers'.

For of necessity the spreading (nomōdē) ulcers, which I said is the same thing as the putrefying kind, when they are treated by strong [871] drugs, such as the present one is, first have the putrefying parts cleansed away, and in this way they become hollow. After the putrefaction has ceased they need cleansing and filling, and once they have been filled, then also the cicatrizing drugs. The drug itself, when it has not yet been mixed with cerate, being acrid, is not only unable to produce flesh but also cleans away the overgrowing flesh, just as Criton himself said. And it is especially fitting to remember this point, which was also stated in connection with the plaster before this one, the one he named 'from herbs': that all compounds made up of heating and detergent ingredients, even if they are strongly acrid, become flesh-producing when mixed with cerate. Some, however, give up on them when, having mixed in either a double quantity of cerate, they see the plaster still biting so much that it cannot produce flesh, as is the case with this plaster. For being much more acrid and more biting than the one from herbs, it is useless for producing flesh, even if it is mixed with four times as much cerate.

There is need, then, of an intelligent man, practised in the use of such [872] drugs, one who considers straightaway at the outset how many times its amount of cerate the drug needs to be mixed with, and who, if after the first application the drug still appears too pungent to be able to make flesh grow, estimates how much more of the cerate must still be added, just as Criton did with the plaster before us. For do not suppose that he found at his very first estimation that the cerate must be mixed in twelvefold; rather, he knew that more was needed than what is mixed with the plaster of herbs, but how much more he found after the first estimation. For if, when eightfold had been mixed in, it still appeared biting, he mixed it in tenfold, just as, if it was still so at tenfold too, he went on to twelvefold.

Since, as I said, the quantity of cerate mixed in must be varied according to the amount of the filth and the moistness of the ulcer, the sensitivity or insensitivity of the parts that suffer along with it, and further the softness and the hardness of the habit of the body, as has been said many times, we must bear in mind and consider that in such recipes it is the quantity used that is written down, since for everyone the way from there towards the other cases in either [873] direction is easy, as far as the extremes. By extremes I mean the full concurrences of all the indications of the same kind. Concerning these I am now giving one example, and you must remember it always and no longer expect to hear about it many times. I say, then, that the indications of the same kind for mixing in the greatest amount of cerate are that the ulcer is clean and dry, and that the body of the patient being treated is sensitive and soft. The indications for mixing in the least are much moisture and filth in the ulcer, and a hard and insensitive body in the patient. It was, however, well done that copper flake was mixed with all the ingredients composing it, which are discutient, since it is a drying drug and has no little astringency in it. Not only in the case of this plaster must you recognise that the plaster becomes flesh-producing and cicatrizing for ulcers that are not malignant through the admixture of much cerate. The same holds for all the others that are of the same power, which Criton wrote down next after them, for instance the one made with whetstone, which he says he himself uses and which he directed to be compounded as follows.

[874] [The plaster made with whetstone.] The plaster made with whetstone, which is in use among us, is effective against all chronic conditions, and specifically against headache when applied to the forehead, and against chronic pains of the side, for gouty patients, sciatic patients, pains of the shoulders, and toothaches, when placed on the parts after they have been rubbed. It also draws down the menses when applied above the pubes. It also helps those who have pain in the stomach, those who suffer from flux, and those who do not retain their food. It is also all-purpose, being without burning, even for those who do not tolerate an acrid drug. It is suitable also for hardness of the liver and spleen, for scrofulous swellings, and for sciatic patients. In their case specifically, let the application be made for seven days, or, if they are delicate, for five. Let the part not be touched by water or oil until it breaks out in small blisters and draws out thick ichors. Then, having taken it off, use the white cerate made with water, or, if you want something more effective, the whetstone plaster made with pepper. ♃ Wax, galbanum, terebinth, roasted pine resin, laurel oil, old oil, of each 1 litra; flake of copper 1½ litrae.

[875] of verdigris, 6 oz.; of ammoniac incense, 1 oz.; of mustard, adarce and sulphur, 1 oz. each; of southernwood, centaury, chalcanthum, ammoniac salt, frankincense, common salt, round alum, litharge, propolis and Cnidian berry, 3 oz. each. Pound and sift all together, and take them up with the astringent ingredients together with the oils. This, then, is the composition of the plaster now under discussion, which differs not slightly in heat from the one written above. It contains, at any rate, mustard and adarce, and sulphur and Cnidian berry, which reach such a degree of heat that they ulcerate whatever they are in contact with for a longer time. Laurel oil, too, is among the substances that heat considerably, and after these chalcanthum and the salts. You have learned that these also have a share of astriction, the salts a slight one, chalcanthum a great one. But the mixing of astringent drugs with discutient ones has also been discussed earlier, in connection with the polychrest plasters. For in general nothing can become polychrest unless it also has a share of the opposite power.

For if the faculty is simply discutient and nothing else, it will suit one kind of affection, the kind that ought to be dispersed; and if [876] astringent, it will suit one other kind, in which it is proper to check what flows in. For this reason astringents suit affections that are beginning to arise from an influx of fluids, while discutients without the admixture of astringents suit those bodies into which nothing can flow because they have been evacuated beforehand. For if there is some superabundance of humours, not only is the fluid contained in the affected parts dispersed, but more fluid also comes to them, since discutients naturally draw to themselves not only those of the fluids that lie around and in contact, but also those that are in the depth of the body. With good reason, then, the drugs called checking and repellent are mixed with the discutients: the man who arrived at their composition used this reasoning, and experience bears witness to the reasoning.

Reasonably, then, in the drug before us, although its aim is to heat and to dry and for this reason also to produce psydraces [pustules], something of the astringents too was mixed in. But since these two, chalcanthum and salt, are not sufficient against many violently heating drugs, copper flake too was mixed in by the same [877] reasoning, and so was alum, which also took this very name because it astringes violently. Another. Crito recorded another, very celebrated plaster, which he names the Mesian. Its material is of a different kind from that of the plaster written above, and from that of the one I am about to write next, which Crito himself names the invincible and which is composed mostly of acrid drugs. The Mesian is not of this sort, as will be shown later at its own proper occasion. Moreover, he also names certain others 'cephalic', whose general property will be stated a little later. Having written these next after the Mesian, he afterwards writes the one he himself calls the invincible, which is of a property closely similar to the one written above, the one he called 'the whetstone plaster'. Crito's text about it runs roughly thus, in these very words: 'The invincible, which is in use with us. It is all-purpose: it draws out, it ruptures, it cleanses out, it conglutinates, it squeezes out, by means of a compress and the application of tubes; and when it is dissolved it always has the consistency of mud, with oxelaeum.'

It also disperses indurations and helps contractions of the sinews, being applied without [878] moistening, so that the parts are not chilled. And, when diluted, it acts as an unguent in the manner of an anti-fatigue remedy. For it also stops the lassitudes that come at the beginnings of diseases and those that arise from an obscure cause. It is also an emollient for the extremities, applied on large compresses. It is also agglutinative of bloody wounds, once a wound has been sutured or fastened with clasps, a folded pad soaked in vinegar alone being laid on top of the compress, cold in summer and warm in winter. It is effective also for lesions on the soles of the feet and for cuts, for putrefactions and affections about the fingers, and for fractures accompanied by wounds. One may use no other flesh-producing or cicatrizing drug, but trust in it alone. It is effective also for human bites, dog bites and bites of wild beasts. Its greatest promise is that it does not allow hidden abscesses in the colon and the peritoneum to form, provided they have not already suppurated; or, if they have formed, it thins them and makes them break into the intestines. One must apply a compress to the place, and over it a felt pad soaked in warm oxelaeum, and moisten it twice a day.

Do not undo it except after three or four days; then, after fomenting, [879] apply the vapour (?) again. It was named 'the Invincible' on account of its many marvellous effects. Take: flakes of copper, 58 dr.; pellitory, stavesacre, Cnidian berry, mustard seed, cachrys, pigeon dung, slender birthwort, verdigris, cyperus, rocket seed, cumin, of each 16 dr.; natron, 32 dr.; ammoniac salt, 32 dr.; laurel berries, 120 dr.; manna, 120 dr.; iris, 120 dr.; acrid vinegar, 16 sextarii; boiled-down liquor of dried figs, 4½ cyathi. Pound and sift everything together and triturate it with the vinegar in the heat of the Dog-days. When it has become dry and green, add the decoction of the figs, and, having kneaded it together, take it up and store it in a copper pot of red copper. The boiled-down liquor of the dried figs is made thus. Take: rich dried figs, 5 lb.; water, 6 sextarii; boil until 2 sextarii remain. The use is: one part of the drug, thinned with vinegar so that it becomes glutinous, to six of the resin-wax.

The undiluted resin-wax is one part of wax and three parts of roasted resin, melted together with a little oil. The medium [880] is one part of wax and two parts of resin. The relaxed and well-tempered is one part of wax and one part of resin. The weakened is two parts of wax and one part of resin. The over-relaxed is three parts of wax and one part of resin. It is also reported to have been suitable for a wild lichen when applied undiluted. Crito wrote these things in these very words. I shall begin my discussion with the last of the things he said. They call lichens 'wild' when they see that they are not benefited at all by weakly drying drugs, but are irritated by strongly drying ones. In their case, therefore, there is need of a drug that is sufficiently active but not violently biting. Such a drug, as I said, is composed by technical estimation and then tested by experience. The drug set out above is composed of many acrid, fine-particled and discutient ingredients. It also contains some of those that cleanse without biting and some of those that are slightly astringent.

Now the acrid ingredients in it are pellitory, mustard, Cnidian berry and pigeon dung, verdigris, laurel berry and nitron, then the so-called Ammoniac [881] salts, and in addition to these acrid vinegar; for he requires that vinegar of this kind be put in. Of the detergent ingredients, those that are entirely without biting are iris and birthwort, and, still more so than these, so much so as to belong already to the class of concocting drugs, manna; cachrys and wild stavesacre are more vigorous. Still more vigorous than these are cumin and the seed of rocket. Cyperus is drying without biting, but it also has something astringent, just as copper flake does, which is a strong drug. For, as was shown earlier, this drug had to share to some degree in the astringent faculty as well, and for this reason flake was mixed in abundantly. And if the manna is really manna and not frankincense, this too would have something astringent. This too has been put in, in much greater quantity than the flake, and reasonably so, in order that it may soothe the violence of the acrid drugs, besides concocting the fluids in the affected place. Most soothing and most concocting, while at the same time in some way dispersing, is the decoction of dried figs. All these, then, being mixed together, have reasonably made the drug polychrest.

But the vinegar contributes most of all to their efficacy [882]; he directs that the drugs be ground in it under the summer sun. For all things prepared in this way become fine-particled, and for this reason their power sinks down into the depth of bodies. [On the plasters of the same kind written up by Heras.] The plaster made with herbs, whose preparation by Criton I wrote out above, Heras himself also prepares in the same way, as Criton too recorded of him. But he differs in the preparation with squill. For of the ammoniac, the myrrh, the pine resin, the storax, the flake and the squill, Criton mixes in with the other ingredients as much as Heras does. But in the case of the birthwort and the iris he differs. For whereas Heras wrote: round birthwort 30 dr., dry iris 30 dr. (others, 10), Criton in turn afterwards wrote as follows: ℞ birthwort 30 dr., iris 30 dr. (others, 40). At the end of the preparation Heras wrote: 'When the days have been completed, make a cerate as follows: ℞ wax 5 pounds (others, 40 dr.), terebinth 1 pound (others, 30 dr.).'

of old oil [883] 2½ sextarii; others, 6 kotylai. But I do not approve of mixing into the drug 240 drachms in place of the 5 litrai of wax. For sometimes they themselves write 100 drachms in place of the litra, and sometimes in place of the mina, but no one has ever written a litra so small as to be 48 drachms; for that is what results when 240 drachms are put in in place of the 5 litrai. Likewise I do not approve of 30 drachms in place of the litra of terebinth either. [The plaster of Serapion.] This one too Criton wrote down in his pharmaceutical book, in these very words: The plaster of Serapion, which some call the Egyptian, others the Aphrodite. It is effective for every wound, and one must persevere with it without despairing. It is effective for punctures, splinters and parotid swellings; it perforates phymata and, having pressed out their contents, agglutinates them. It is effective also for every induration, for epinyctides, for fluxion to the joints and for contusions of the ears; it is effective also for senile, chironian and thick-lipped ulcers. ℞ Old oil, 3 kotylai; litharge, 200 drachms.

of ammoniac [884] incense, 168 drachms; of Colophonian resin, of pine resin, 68 drachms; of wax, 168 drachms; of galbanum, 20 drachms; of verdigris, 50 drachms (others, 20 drachms); of myrrh, 4 drachms (others, 8 drachms). Boil the litharge and the oil until it seems to have thickened moderately; then, lifting off the pan, add the ammoniac, then the resin, then the wax. Having melted each one of them attentively, so that it does not burn onto the pan, lift it off again and add the galbanum and the verdigris; then, setting it on the fire, boil until it becomes quince-yellow and of good consistency. Lastly, lifting it off, add the myrrh, stir, and pour it out; taking it up, store it in a skin. [How Andromachus wrote the aforementioned plasters.] Andromachus wrote three compositions of this plaster: the first differing slightly from Crito's written above, and after it two others showing a greater disagreement. The promised effects of the drug and its preparation have been written well earlier by Crito; Andromachus, then, wrote as follows about it. The one made from herbs.

[885] ℞ Of the pimpernel that has the dark-blue flower, 56 dr.; of horehound, 56 dr.; of wild poppy, 56 dr.; of green henbane, 56 dr.; of flake, 25 dr.; of frankincense, 8 dr.; of dry resin, 16 dr.; of aloe, 16 dr.; of split alum, 4 dr.; of wax, 1 mina; of old oil, 2 kotylai; of vinegar. Many used to put both the pimpernels into the [plaster] made with herbs, while Theocritus also [adds] Eretrian earth and chrysocolla and ammoniac salt and arsenic, 4 dr. of each. [Other plasters of the same kind, about which Andromachus wrote.] For gangrenes and putrefactions and old and malignant spreading sores, that of Isidorus of Antioch. ℞ Of litharge, 4 dr.; of scraped verdigris, 8 dr.; of oil, 6 cyathi. Talius Aelius [gives] 12 cyathi, and worm-verdigris.

Put the litharge and the verdigris, ground smooth, into a pot, pour on three cyathi of oil, and boil over a gentle fire, stirring with a wooden spatula, until it becomes greenish-yellow; then take it off the fire, pour it out into a mortar and triturate it while it is hot [886] for a longer time. Then pour it back into the pot, add 3 cyathi of the oil, and boil, stirring so that it does not burn on, until it becomes quince-yellow; and again empty it out and triturate it as for collyria. Then take it up again into the pot and boil it, stirring, until it becomes red; empty it into the mortar again and for the third time triturate it for a longer time. For the fourth time boil it again in the pot, so that it draws together; and again, while it is hot, pour it out, triturate it, take it up, store it in a red box, and use it for the conditions mentioned. Immediately after the one written above, Andromachus wrote about another plaster, word for word, as follows. A moist plaster for spreading ulcers, which I use also for many other things. ♃ Wax 8 dr., terebinth resin 8 dr., prepared bull's suet 4 dr., chalcitis 2 dr., copper scale 3 dr., manna of frankincense 2 dr., omphacine gall 4 dr., myrtle oil 5 cotylae. The dry ingredients are combined with vinegar and honey, and then the meltable ones are poured over them. [Polychrest grey plasters.

…that for the works of the art there is need both of method and of practice.] That of the remedies [887] some are found by reason alone, some by experience, and this without any need of reason, while some require both, working together with one another, has often been shown to you; and in addition to this, that those found through reason and experience use a conjectural path towards the discovery of what is sought, but what has been anticipated by reason is confirmed by experience; and indeed also that within conjectural expectation there is no small difference in respect of the more and the less, just as in the whole of life. For we do not expect rain in the same way at the winter solstice and at the rising of the Dog. For at the winter solstice it rarely fails to occur, whereas at the rising of the Dog it rarely occurs. And since all the works in the arts are brought to exactness by continuous practice, it is not enough to learn only the universal in them; one must also often be active in the particulars. For practice by means of imperfect activities is the road to the acquisition of the perfect ones.

For this reason, then, I too, in all the treatises that I composed for you, my companions, at your request, was not content with the universal theorems alone, but also added [888] many exercises, through which I hoped that your knowledge of them would become clearer and more secure. Just as, then, in all the other parts of medicine, so also in the treatment of the nerve-wounded I wrote, first showing you the rational way to the discovery of remedies, and next after this the materials in which you learned that the powers discovered by reason are contained. For in the commentaries On the Power of Simple Drugs, eleven in number, I wrote down all, or at any rate most, of the most useful powers in the particular materials.

For it was shown that this is necessary for a ready supply of remedies, and not only so that you yourselves may be able, without prepared drugs, to be well supplied with remedies in situations of want, as Erasistratus once supplied himself with the juice of herbs when his mouth-drug was not at hand in that place on his journey, but also so that, even if you lose the written recipes of what you yourselves have compounded, you may nevertheless be able yourselves to [889] compound drugs closely similar to those that were lost. Moreover, the training gained through the present treatise is also useful for making good use of what has been discovered by others. What need is there to say that it is useful too for being able to distinguish both the ingredients superfluously put into compound drugs and, conversely, whatever has been left out by those who first compounded them? Just as I showed in the third book, when I discussed the remedies suited to the nerve-wounded, so likewise I shall now demonstrate it, exercising you on what was discovered by physicians older than I. For the general method was written by none of my predecessors, neither precisely, with distinctions, nor even defectively, without distinctions. Nor did anyone so much as write down a drug professing to heal those pricked in a nerve by something sharp, such as needles and children's styluses, a drug able to do excellently this one thing alone, whereas I went through a number of them not easily counted in the aforementioned book.

Some of them, however, having written up noteworthy polychrest drugs (those, at least, who were more careful), added, besides the other things which they profess [890] these do, sometimes that they are also beneficial to the nerve-wounded, at other times that they are so for severances of the nerves and muscles, and there are times when they said that they also help punctures or contusions of these. But you, from what you have learned, are able to recognise before trial whether someone professes possible or impossible things concerning what he has written. And you are able also, with drugs written down without a statement of what they are by nature able to do, to recognise in which cases they are to be used. So, to begin, by way of example, with a certain polychrest plaster drug, written second in order in Andromachus' pharmaceutical book (φαρμακωνῖτιν), which he composed on the remedies applied to the body from outside, without his having indicated for what it is chiefly to be used, you may again exercise yourselves in how one must recognise, from the simple drugs written down, the faculty of the compound. [The grey Egyptian of Andromachus.] For Andromachus wrote thus, word for word: The grey Egyptian. ♃ Of litharge, 44 drachms; of castor oil, 6 kotylai; of wax, 144 drachms; of ammoniac incense, 72 drachms; of terebinth resin, 36 drachms.

of burnt wool [891] 18 dr.; of scale of hardened iron 8 dr.; of copper flake 8 dr.; of birthwort 8 dr.; of frankincense 8 dr.; some add myrrh 4 dr.; of opopanax 2 dr.; of sea water 50 dr., for soaking the wax. This is the prescription of the drug, which is in truth a fine one and of many uses; but he himself omitted to say in which cases it is to be used. Now if, after first stating the potency of each of the simple drugs, as we have done in eleven treatises, and after writing some general method for the composition of drugs, as I have done in the book before this one, he had then set such prescriptions before others still living for the sake of exercise, so that they might answer for what affections the drug can be useful, we would truly have praised his teaching. But since he did none of these things, one might find fault with him in every respect. For this reason, then, his pharmaceutical books, although they contain the compositions of very many excellent drugs, have with good reason been neglected by physicians.

For among a thousand, some one person seems to possess the end of the art, while the others [892], just like laymen, are content if they are able to use correctly the drugs that have been clearly written down. And what need is there to speak about physicians of this sort? Where even some of those called Empiricists, although they have been seen to be noteworthy through the works of the art, nevertheless say that they do not know by what reasoning each of the compound drugs has been discovered. And why do I say 'by reasoning'? For they say that none of such things was discovered by reasoning in the first place. To them, then, the recipe of this grey plaster is useless, since in its heading it conveys only the colour, without the claim regarding its power, which would better have been written before the colour. Since, then, Andromachus omitted to state its power, let us try to discover it from the nature and the power of the drugs that are mixed in. Now as for litharge, you have learned that, while it is of a mean temperament as regards heating and cooling, it has departed a little toward drying.

And indeed you also learned that its use in plasters is twofold: if it remains unmelted, it serves only as material; but if it is melted, it serves also as something able to dry, [893] and the more so if it is boiled longer. Now, however, the question is to what extent it is to be boiled, since Andromachus wrote that 6 kotylai of kikis must be mixed in, that is, of castor oil. For he did not make clear of how many ounces of the Roman litra he means the kotyle to be. And yet it would have been better for one who had lived in Rome to mention litrai, xestai and ounces, and to leave aside the name of the kotyle, which is in use in the Greek cities outside Italy. Now if the name of the kotyle denoted the same thing in all of them, there would be no question. But as it is, since there is a very great difference in quantity among them, he ought to have said either 'I mean the Attic kotyle', or the Alexandrian, or the Ephesian, or some other. Most of those who have written on measures and weights say that the kotyle written by physicians in pharmacological books is one of 9 ounces of the Roman litra. Others say that the kotyle meant by them is the one of 12 ounces, just as in Rome they customarily give the name 'litra' to the litra of oil.

I have also heard someone say that [894] the kotyle recorded by the physicians in their books on drugs holds 16 Roman ounces (γο ιστ΄). And it makes no small difference to the potency of the drug whether one puts in large or small kotylai. I, at any rate, once weighed at Rome the so-called litra of oil, which they measure by means of graduated horns, wishing to learn how much it amounts to in weight. And I found that the twelve ounces of oil by measure were equal to ten ounces by weight. Therefore the physicians ought to have written more carefully in their books on drugs what sort of ounces or litrai of the liquid ingredients they direct to be put in, whether those by measure or those by weight. For it is plain that among these liquid bodies, just as among the solid ones, some are heavier and others lighter. The weight of each of the liquids put into drugs has been stated by me in another treatise, but for now let us take up again the matter before us. For the three kotylai, if one sets each at nine ounces by measure, will make the three come to twenty-seven ounces.

And since each [895] of them is divided into eight drachmas, they will contain two hundred and sixteen drachmas. But if one supposes each cotyle to consist of twelve ounces, there will be thirty-six ounces, and two hundred and eighty-eight drachmas, each ounce being divided into eight drachmas. I myself have often found by trial, when I boiled litharge in oil, that its well-proportioned mixture comes about when a pound by weight of litharge is set equal to a pound by measure of oil. But if one puts in more oil, and boils it, obviously, for a longer time, it becomes more drying. In the white plasters, for the sake of the colour, we also mix white lead with the litharge, as a rule equal to equal by weight. Those who wish to preserve the colour put in the cotyle of nine ounces relative to the pound by weight of litharge, because longer boiling makes the litharge darker; but the drug becomes less adhesive when only a little oil has been put in.

For this reason some have mixed in either terebinth resin or the translucent kind called Colophonian, trying as far as possible to harm neither the colour nor the potency of the drug, and, by the admixture of the resin, to give it the property of not readily falling off; for the drug becomes friable if this much litharge and white lead is boiled in this much oil. Others, on the same reasoning, have added white wax to the drug once it has been boiled. Litharge that has double its amount of oil, however, will acquire adhesiveness from the boiling even if you add nothing resinous or waxy, and much more so if you mix triple the oil with the litharge, that is, if you mix three measured [pounds] of oil with three [pounds] by weight of litharge. It is likely, then, that Andromachus means the castor oil to be put in by the [cotyle] of 9 measured ounces, so that the six cotylae come to 54 measured ounces, which is the same as 4½ Roman measured pounds. It is plain that if castor oil is at any time not available to us, we shall take old oil in its place.

I too have often put Sicyonian oil into discutient plasters; and when that was not available, I improvised another oil and made it similar to those, by boiling down in it roots of wild cucumber, of bryony [897] and of marsh-mallow. That Andromachus wants the drug before us to be both discutient and emollient is quite clear from his putting into it castor oil and a very great quantity of ammoniac incense. For he wants the wax to be equal in weight to the litharge, and the ammoniac half. And yet in many of the renowned plasters this drug is put in not at half but at a fourth part or a fifth, and often at a seventh and an eighth, and sometimes at a tenth, by weight, relative to the litharge. Concerning the wax, we have learned that in the compositions of such drugs it holds the rank of material, not the contribution of an active power. It too has some slight emollient power, but it was not for this that it was taken into the drug before us, just as the terebinth resin was not either, although it is much more plastic in power than the wax. For it softens more than wax, and in addition warms and disperses, whereas the wax has neither of these. But the ammoniac incense, put in alone, will make the drug dry and rough.

But as regards [898] plaster-making (for it is no worse to name it so), both the wax and the resin are useful. For the capacity to soften and to disperse belongs to the drug even from the ammoniac alone, which holds first place among the emollients and is also a rival to the dispersive ones. If you recall what was said in the fifth book of On the Capacity of Simple Drugs about what sort of mixture such drugs ought to have, you will need no further, newer instruction. For the first active capacities in drugs lie in heat and cold and moisture and dryness; second are the emollient, dispersive, repellent, drawing, concoctive, detergent and putrefactive capacities; just as, third, are those that are agglutinative of wounds, cicatrizing and flesh-producing. So the drug compounded of oil of kiki and ammoniac incense is able to disperse and to soften and, plainly, also to dry, having taken on as suitable material the wax, the resin, and the litharge boiled for a longer time.

He directs that one also throw into it [899] some of the burnt wool and of birthwort, drugs that are very strongly discutient and very strongly drying; after these he mentions frankincense, a concoctive and soothing drug. And if we should also throw in some myrrh and opopanax (for he says that some people also mix some of these into the drug), we know that myrrh heats and dries in no ignoble fashion, and that opopanax does both of these things still more vigorously, and is moreover of an attenuating and discutient faculty. But of this a very small amount is thrown in, because, I think, the one who added it feared the acridity of the drug and wished to make the plaster not only discutient and emollient but also suitable for wounds. For this reason, then, he also mixed into it the flake of copper and that of steel, drugs having an astringent faculty together with drying strongly. At any rate, because of the admixture of these, the Egyptian plaster set out above becomes, reasonably enough, a good drug for bleeding wounds and for not a few other ulcers.

And indeed, for abscesses and for everything [900] that needs to be dispersed, you have often heard that those remedies which, together with the discutient drugs, contain something of the astringent ones as well become safer, whereas those without the astringents are more effective, but not safe. For they often draw fluxes when the body under treatment is plethoric or cacochymic. But if the body is empty and free of superfluities, the more discutient drugs, used alone without the astringent ones, reach their end more readily. But since drugs are applied to bodies of this kind in only a few cases, for this reason it has seemed safer to mix in something of the repellent ones as well. Thus indeed some have added a little chalcanthum to the discutient plaster made with salts, even though the salts themselves have something astringent.

The drug before us, then, has been found to be powerfully discutient, so that it is able to disperse even pus already formed, at least when it is not very much, without perforating the skin; and to be emollient of parts that are becoming scirrhous and of those hardened in any way whatever; and agglutinative of large wounds, just as it is also cicatrizing of ulcers that have already turned malignant, [901] and of all the other affections that are measured by (? μετρεῖται) a faculty at once discutient and repellent. Among these are also the applications placed on the forehead for eyes suffering from flux, which physicians call anakollēmata. This same drug will also be suitable for nerves that have been laid bare, even if they happen to have been cut in some part of them. For nerves that have been cut right through no longer carry the danger that arises from sympathy, and they also take away sensation from the bodies lying beneath them, into which they are distributed (? κατίσχεται). Yet these too need a drug of this kind. For moistening drugs readily putrefy them. For this reason the drying little discs too, although they are considerably astringent, nevertheless suit nerves that have been laid bare, at least those that have not yet arrived at the peak of the inflammation. For these are irritated and exacerbated by such drugs. But these matters will be discussed as the account proceeds; concerning the plaster before us, let us add to the account what remains.

Since most physicians, in their ignorance, apply such plasters hard, it is better to make them suitable for application on lint (ἐμμότους) by melting them, [902] or else to make them soft straight away in the preparation. Then, when they have tried them on large divisions in which nerves have been laid bare, they expect them to be much more beneficial in punctures, being ignorant here too of a very important principle, about which I have already discoursed in teaching you, which I first discovered by reasoning and then recognised as confirmed by experience; for this reason I remind you of it now as well. For punctures of the nerves need much hotter and more discutient drugs than when a nerve is laid bare entirely, a considerable wound having occurred. For nerves that have been laid bare do not bear the application of acrid and very hot drugs, because of the biting, but need relaxing and discutient drugs mixed in due proportion with astringent drugs. But I have also taught that it is better to cover the parts around the wound with drugs that are acrid, fine-particled and strongly discutient, such as the one made with euphorbium. I, then, inferred that the plaster under discussion was capable of doing what I have said above, and having prepared it I found experience bearing witness to this.

Later [903], at some point, when I came upon the books on drugs of Asclepiades and of Crito as well, I found that they had written, not without distinctions as Andromachus did, but with distinctions, clearly what power it has. For this reason, then, and because on certain points they disagree with Andromachus in the preparation, it seemed better to me to add also their own words, and then to say something about their disagreement in the composition of the drug. [On what Asclepiades and Crito wrote about the plaster under discussion.] Concerning the Egyptian plaster written up by Andromachus, Asclepiades wrote as follows. Andromachus' Egyptian, bloodless, a wound plaster. It works for severings of nerves and muscles; it works for punctures, contusions, abrasions, sprains. It is also an adhesive application (paracollema) for those suffering from ophthalmia. It works for those with headache, and the drug is useful for many conditions. ℞ Litharge, wax, of each 144 dr.; ammoniac incense 72 dr.; terebinth 36 dr.

of burnt greasy wool [904] 18 dr.; flake of copper 8 dr.; flake of steel 8 dr.; frankincense 8 dr.; round birthwort 8 dr.; castor oil 3 kotylai. Having set these out first, Asclepiades next writes the method of boiling. Andromachus did not preserve this part of the composition either in the case of the plasters, for it has been omitted in almost all of them. But concerning the boilings, a good deal was said in the fourth book, and something will be said now shortly. It is worth examining the matter of the disagreement which Asclepiades made with Andromachus in the quantity of the simple drugs. For he thinks fit to put in not six kotylai of the castor oil, as Andromachus does, but three. In the case of the birthwort, where Andromachus had specified nothing beforehand, he himself added 'round', just as, in the case of the burnt wool, he added 'greasy'. The weight, however, he puts in equal to that of Andromachus. At any rate he writes thus: Take of burnt greasy wool 18 dr.; round birthwort 8 dr.

What Andromachus added at the end, Asclepiades did not write at all. He said nothing about the [905] myrrh or about the opopanax, and much less about the sea-water, although Andromachus had clearly written these down beforehand: 'sea-water for moistening; wax, 50 drachmas.' For neither Asclepiades nor Crito added this. Crito, however, puts in the round birthwort just as Asclepiades does, and likewise the 18 drachmas of greasy wool, and of castor oil, for he wrote it thus word for word, 6 kotylai. The boiling of the plaster is written by Asclepiades in this manner: 'Boil the litharge and the castor oil until it thickens, then the flakes, and when it takes on a good colour, add the rest.' By Crito it is written in this manner: 'Boil litharge with castor oil until it has the consistency of honey. When this has happened, sprinkle on the flakes and boil them together for a sufficient time, until it becomes non-staining. Then add the terebinth and the wax, and when these are united, the ammoniac, softened beforehand with the fingers by the fire. Then, lifting it from the fire, sprinkle in the powder of the greasy wool, and after that, at the end, the frankincense, and then take it up thus.'

And concerning [906] the declared uses (ἐπαγγελία) of the drug, too, Crito wrote more carefully, verbatim as follows: "The Egyptian [plaster], keeping every division and every contusion free from inflammation. It is also suitable for every bite of venomous creatures, and it also benefits inflammations that arise without ulcers. It is good also for pains of the nerves and muscles that arise without an evident cause." [Another grey plaster of Andromachus.] Andromachus also wrote down other grey plasters, somewhat of the same kind as the one written above. He calls the one 'Athena', the other 'for punctures' (nygmatikē). The Athena is suited to more conditions than the nygmatikē, and especially to those accompanied by ulcers, since it is more complex and contains a still greater share of astringent drugs. The nygmatikē, for its part, is more relaxing and more anodyne than this one. Concerning the first of the drugs mentioned, then, he wrote verbatim as follows: "Grey Athena. ℞ Litharge 100 dr.; terebinth resin 36 dr.; wax 25 dr.; Sinopic red ochre 24 dr.; ammoniac incense 36 dr.; galbanum 12 dr.; aloe 8 dr.; diphryges 8 dr.

of burnt copper [907] 6 dr.; of mastic 6 dr.; of birthwort 5 dr.; of propolis 5 dr.; of manna 6 dr.; of flake of copper 6 dr.; of Assian stone 3 dr.; of seed of trefoil 2 dr.; of root of comfrey 1 dr. and four obols; of oil 4 kotylai. About the other grey [plaster] Andromachus wrote thus, in these very words: Grey [plaster] 'for punctures' (nygmatikē). ℞ of ammoniac 8 dr.; of new wax 8 dr.; of terebinth 3 dr.; of burnt copper 8 dr.; of dry pitch 40 dr., or, as Zeno [has it], half a mina [and] a quarter; of litharge 4 dr.; of Indian aloe 2 dr.; of birthwort 2 dr.; of galbanum 2 dr.; of verdigris 1 dr., but others [give] 2 dr.; of frankincense 2 dr.; of oil in winter 4 kotylai, in summer an eighth; of vinegar half a kotyle, for the dissolving of the ammoniac.

Andromachus also wrote, together with these, many other plasters, adding nothing else to them but the name of the colour, composed of drugs contrary in their powers. Some of them, however, have the relaxing and anodyne as the predominant quality, some the discutient and detergent, and some astringency. So we too must use all [908] of them with confidence, each in its appropriate way: for hard-to-cicatrise and malignant ulcers, those that have more of the astringent; where the aim is to soothe and relax, those that have the relaxing quality; and where it is to draw and discuss, those that contain heating ingredients and draw to themselves the noxious moistures of deep-seated affections. To some of them this too has been added in writing: 'Grey plain plaster which I use.' For he wrote three such plasters in succession, not of many ingredients, whose composition it also seemed better to me to add in his own wording. Grey plain plaster which I use. ℞ Litharge 24 dr., castor oil 1 kotyle, burnt copper 4 dr., manna 4 dr., resin 4 dr., Colophonian resin 8 dr. Another, anodyne, of Isidorus. ℞ Litharge 36 dr., wax 36 dr., oil 1½ kotylai, Colophonian resin 15 dr., copper flake 9 dr., manna 50 dr. Boil. Another which I use. ℞ Litharge 144 dr., dry resin 144 dr., flake 24 dr., oil 3 kotylai.

One [913] of them he calls that of Phtheirographos, which he says is composed of the following. ℞ Litharge 100 dr., resin 50 dr., ammoniac incense 30 dr., wax 50 dr., scraped verdigris 12 dr., flake of copper 2 dr., birthwort 8 dr., root of centaury 8 dr., oil 2 kotylai. The other, that of Irion, he says is composed thus. ℞ Litharge 144 dr., dry pitch 144 dr., terebinth 72 dr., ammoniac incense 72 dr., manna and frankincense, of each 102 dr., calf's suet 144 dr., wax 36 dr., birthwort 9 dr., burnt copper 9 dr., scraped verdigris 9 dr., galbanum 9 dr., opopanax 9 dr., vinegar half a kotyle, oil 1½ kotylai, castor oil an equal amount. It is evident that he wants the litharge, the pitch and the calf's suet to be double in weight to the terebinth, the incense and the frankincense, and fourfold to the wax, and sixteenfold to the birthwort, the burnt copper, the verdigris, the galbanum and the opopanax.

This drug too is quite polychrest, as are the others [914] written above, and one should use all of them with confidence. The Hellespontine, as Andromachus gives it. Andromachus recorded this plaster too, it being a celebrated one, among the grey plasters, in the following proportion: ♃ litharge 100 dr., pitch 50 dr., ladanum 25 dr., scraped verdigris 8 dr., burnt copper 8 dr., scale 2 dr., old oil 200 dr. [The Hellespontine of Heras.] Since Andromachus differs from Heras in the compounding of the drug, it seemed good to me to add also what was written by Heras, which reads word for word as follows. The Hellespontine, diapneustic, keeping free of inflammation. For choirades, phygethla, parotid swellings: applied on a compress it draws out, makes pus, ruptures, agglutinates, and in general it acts in all burns; it also soothes gouty patients. ♃ old oil 100 dr., dry pitch 50 dr., ladanum 25 dr., litharge 100 dr., scraped verdigris 8 dr., galbanum 4 dr. Having ground the litharge smooth with the oil, boil it.

When it thickens, add the pitch [915] and the verdigris, then ladanum and the galbanum, and having poured it out in this way into a mortar, knead it and use it. Some, so that it may become of good colour and grey, also mix in 8 drachms of scale; for otherwise it becomes very black. I have often used this one also for gout, and it worked excellently. One should use pine-splinters instead of logs. It is plain that the men disagree slightly in the other ingredients, but very greatly in the proportion of the oil; for Andromachus puts in double what Heras does. It can also be prepared otherwise, since we know that if more oil is put in, the boiling becomes, clearly, more prolonged, and the drug itself will become more drying; but if less, that the boiling will †hold out† and the drug will be less drying. [The polychrest plasters written by Damocrates. The Tyrian, requiring no bandage.] Following on these, I would like to set out the uses and the compositions of plasters requiring no bandage.

They are effective for divisions that are not large, [916] and for the larger wounds of the flesh itself, and for the superficial bites of quadrupeds; they also disperse recent boils. And they open those that already contain pus as well, and, bringing away the eschars upon them, they will very quickly cicatrize them without surgery. And when applied to the forehead, they alone most easily check the fluxes of those suffering from ophthalmia. First I shall describe a plaster superior to others of this kind, easily procured, of good colour, efficacious; I call it Tyrian, for it takes on the colour of Tyrian purple, if it is made in the proper manner. Prepare it thus: of litharge of good quality put in 5 pounds, and of wax 1, and of pine resin 3, the oily kind, free of wood.

And of good verdigris and of galbanum, and of burnt copper and of good scale, [917] put in four ounces of each ingredient, and of rich oil fifteen pounds and one. You will boil the plaster carefully in this way: having put the litharge, ground very fine, with the oil into a rather large, new earthenware pot, rub it down with the hands, then stir it also with a spatula, and boil it over a fierce and continuous flame. When it takes on the consistency of honey, add the verdigris and the scale and let it boil for a sufficient time; then add the copper. And having again let it boil for a short time, pour off a little of the drug from the pot. Having cooled it, rub it with the hands and with the fingers, and when you see it is of good colour and hard, then add the pine resin and the wax. Then, when everything has been carefully united, again drip off a little.

And if you see that it is of good colour and well blended, lift the pot off the fire at once, [918] and add galbanum softened beforehand. But if the drug is a good deal too hard, add oil to it until it is well tempered, straining it in this way; then, into another, cold vessel, knead it with the hands and so store it away. I shall set down another, of the same kind as the one before this. It acts against the affections I spoke of earlier; this one cicatrizes better than all drugs ulcers that are hard-to-heal, callous and chronic. The eruptions that arise on the face this one treats without any harmful biting, and the fundament when it has fissures; and condylomatous indurations and calluses it casts off. Prepare it thus: a mina of good litharge (a mina is a litra and a third part of a litra); of good Pontic wax half a mina; of verdigris a fourth of a mina, a portion of the good scraped kind; of black chamaeleon an eighth part.

[919] The good root is the Cretan, in the first place; next the Cilician. And of old oil a mina, weighed a little on the heavy side; if it is not to hand, use fresh. You will boil the litharge, ground smooth, putting it and all the oil into a pot, stirring with a spatula. When it thickens and becomes quince-yellow, sprinkle in the verdigris, then add the wax; and when you have melted this and lifted the pot from the fire, sprinkle in a little of the chamaeleon. When everything has united and has cooled somewhat, pour it out into a mortar, and so store it away. The Egyptian [plaster]. The Egyptian, keeping free of inflammation every division [of tissue] and all contusions, and the bites of all quadrupeds and of creeping creatures, and whatever inflammations have arisen without ulcers, and pains of the nerves and muscles without [evident] cause.

[920] Andromachus, who had the greatest proficiency in drugs, praised this one and used to give it to his friends. He said the quantities were: of litharge three times 40 drachmas, and another twice 12; of white Pontic wax amounts equal to these; of pure ammoniac three times 20, and twelve more; of frankincense twice 4; of flake of copper and flake of steel, again of each ingredient of the mixture twice 4; of pure terebinth three times 12; of castor oil eighteen cotylae by measure; of burnt unwashed wool 18.

He said that they are to be burnt in this manner: placing a plentiful quantity of greasy wool in a new dish or a wide-mouthed pot, having first smeared its body with gypsum or with dust, or with potter's earth mixed with water, and burning it on a fierce fire, when it is easy to do so, [921] pound it and sift it. It seems, at any rate, to be fine to burn them likewise also in baking-ovens and in furnaces that have been very strongly heated; and, grinding them fine in this way, take the weight that is needed. He orders that the litharge, ground very fine, be boiled together with all the castor oil, after mixing them in a new pot; when the drug has become of the thickness of honey, sprinkle in the flake and boil it together long enough, until it becomes non-staining; then add the turpentine and the wax, and then, once these are united, the ammoniac softened with the fingers. When you are about to lift the pot from the fire, sprinkle in ground frankincense, and throw in also the ash of the greasy wool at the very last, a little later, but before the frankincense.

Some, however, wishing this drug to be called their own, having taken away the one [922] of a single scale, put in the sixteen, and they use scale of copper, not of steel. Another. In no way worse than the former Egyptian one, doing the same things, and sometimes even better, if one prepares the drug carefully, thick, and uses it, not perfunctorily, for the same purposes. It contains: of oil 5 litrai, of castor oil an equal amount, of golden litharge four, of copper scale 48 drachms, of fine terebinth three times 12, of manna and of frankincense the same as of the terebinth, of pure ammoniac 2 litrai, of white Pontic wax 2½ litrai.

Boil the oil, the scale and the litharge until it comes together and becomes of a very good colour, and a sufficiently hard plaster; then, in this way, put in the terebinth and the wax, then [923] the ammoniac softened with the fingers; then, lifting the pot boiling from the fire, you will then put in the manna, the drug already cooling. I have often made this without the litharge, putting in an equal amount of good molybdaena, and used it most gladly for the things we mentioned before. And it was made of a better colour. [On dispersing and attractive plasters.] Those who wrote on the powers of compound drugs called some of the plasters attractive, just as others dispersing; and to some of them they attested both, that they draw and that they disperse. For the powers are close to one another: the power that draws things from the depth, and the power that disperses what has been drawn. For those that draw also certainly disperse something, and those that disperse also draw. But in the dispersing drugs the dispersing power prevails, and in the drawing drugs the drawing power.

Drawing plasters, then, are compounded from those simple drugs which [924] have the power to draw the surpluses of the fluids from the depth to the skin, and the dispersive ones from those that are by nature apt to disperse what has been drawn. But in order that a plaster may result, as was said in the earlier sections, there is mixed in, for one, some litharge, for another resin, for another wax, for another oil, for another pitch, such substances having no noteworthy power either dispersive or drawing, as propolis has, or 'lime' (titanos), or marrow, or galbanum, or the 'flower' of the Asian (Assian?) stone, or foam of nitre, or aphronitre, or vinegar, or strained lye, and pepper and mustard and strouthion, and the edible salts and the ammoniac ones, and besides these many others, concerning whose power I have spoken in the treatise on simple drugs. Now, however, I shall describe the plasters that have already given sufficient proof in trial, saying only this much more about them: that some have also mixed some of the astringent drugs into the attractive ones, guarding against what happens in those cases in which there will be a surplus of humours.

For they sometimes draw more than is fitting, so as to make the drawing not only from the deep parts of the region being treated but also from all the [925] surrounding parts. I have also said earlier, in the discussion of flesh-producing powers, that the drawing and the discutient powers, just as indeed all those that cleanse more than they should, become flesh-producing by the admixture of cerate: more of it in those whose power is strong, less in those whose power is weak. But if the compound drawing or discutient drug already happens to contain something astringent as well, one should not use such a drug as a flesh-producing one, because astringent powers are useful for the agglutination of wounds and of sinuses and for the cicatrization of ulcers, but useless for the production of flesh. For enough has already been said by us about this. [The discutient and drawing plasters written by Andromachus. The saline one, for many conditions.] ℞ Common salt, 4 lb; flake of copper, 4 oz; magma, half a pound; manna, 1 lb; wax, 14 lb; oil of cypros, 16 lb; vinegar. Another, of Theudas, a flesh-eating one, for malignant conditions, fistulas, caries, scrofulous swellings. ℞ Terebinth resin, 4 oz.

[926] frankincense, 4 oz.; wax, 4 oz.; litharge, 1 oz. (some use an equal amount of orpiment instead of the litharge); red flake, 4 oz.; scraped verdigris, 8 oz.; ammoniac salt, 6 oz.; vinegar, 1 kotyle. I add in addition: oil, 1 kotyle; wine, 1 kotyle; squill vinegar, a kotyle. Another, a discutient of Candidus, which I use. ℞ Terebinth, 3 lb.; wax, 50 lb. [sic; the singular λίτραν suggests the numeral may be corrupt]; galbanum, 2 ounces; nitre, 2 ounces; Assian [stone], 2 ounces; frankincense, 4 lb.; deer's marrow, 4 oz.; ammoniac incense, half a lb.; propolis, 3 ounces; laurel oil, 6 ounces; bull's suet, half a pound; the dry ingredients onto the melted ones. Another, for choirades, from Nymphodotus. ℞ Assian stone, 8 dr.; aphronitre, 8 dr.; quicklime, 16 dr.; calf's suet, 16 dr.; wax, 24 dr.; terebinth, 32 dr. Another, a discutient for bronchoceles, with which Clemens Sertorius was treated; also for indurations. ℞ Litharge, 50 dr.; pine resin, 40 dr.; old oil, 10 kotylai; galbanum, 4 dr. (in another [copy], 1 oz.); burnt copper, 20 dr.

of ammoniac [927] incense, 40 dr.; of split alum, 4 dr.; of manna of frankincense, 4 dr.; of wax, 50 dr. Add the galbanum and the manna last. Another, the one made with asps, discutient of scrofulous swellings (choirades) and for gouts of the feet (podagra). ℞ Of terebinth, Asian stone and bitumen, 360 dr. each; of aphronitre, calf's [suet], wax, bay berries and ammoniac incense, 340 dr. each; of pyrites stone, 80 dr.; of quicklime, 108 dr., otherwise 1 mina; of ash of asps, 140 dr.; of old oil, 2 kotylai. Add the ash last, once the drug has cooled; otherwise it is lost. Another, drawing, the one of Sarkeuthites. ℞ Of terebinth, 1 mina; of wax, 1 mina; of nitre, 2 minas; of bdellium, 32 dr.; of ammoniac incense, 32 dr.; of oil, 2 kotylai; of sea-water or brine, 2 kotylai; of red ochre, 32 dr. Another, the one of Ctesiphon, dissolving some things, while drawing together and cleansing others. ℞ Of aphronitre, 1 litra; of manna of frankincense, 1 litra; of percolated lye, 1 litra; some add also 1 litra of vinegar. Another, drawing, made with salts. ℞ Of common salt, 80 dr.; of white lead, 80 dr.; of old oil, 40 kotylai, otherwise 3.

of chalcanthum [928] 24 dr., of vinegar half a cotyle. Another (version of) the one with salts, otherwise. ♃ Of ceruse 8 dr., of common salt 50 dr., of old oil 8 cotylae (otherwise 2), of birthwort 8 dr., of propolis 10 dr. Silo used to praise this one. Another, the discutient one with sea earth. ♃ Of litharge 4 minas, of sea earth a quarter, of sal ammoniac a quarter, of ceruse a quarter, of wax a quarter, of vinegar 1 cotyle, of oil 4 cotylae. Another, the drawing plaster of Kyrtos. ♃ Of Illyrian iris 50 dr., of manna 50 dr., of turpentine 50 dr., of aphronitre 50 dr., of pumice 50 dr., of ammoniac incense 25 dr., of galbanum 16 dr. (otherwise 6), of cachrys 12½ dr., of wax 100 dr. (but some say 8), of oil 1 cotyle. Another, the one with bay berries. ♃ Of resin, of tawny nitre, of fresh wax, of bay berries, of Colophonian resin, of calf suet, of ammoniac incense, 70 dr. of each; of oil of cypros one-sixteenth of a cotyle; and some add 50 dr. of birdlime. Another, the drawing plaster of Harpalus. ♃ Of ammoniac incense 8 dr., of wax 4 dr., of iris 4 dr., of manna 4 dr., of pepper 4 dr., of unfired sulphur 4 dr., of pumice 4 dr.

[929] terebinth 8 dr., a little oil. Another drawing [plaster] of Harpalus. ℞ terebinth 8 minas, pumice 15 dr., nitre 16 dr., ammoniac incense 16 dr., wax 4 dr., a little oil, and red ochre, enough to colour the dry ingredients, with vinegar. Another. ℞ mustard 4 dr., nitre 4 dr., wax 8 dr., terebinth 30 dr., laurel berries 4 dr., quicklime 4 dr., oil one-sixteenth of a kotylē, oil of cypros 8 dr. Another, dispersing pus. ℞ wax, terebinth resin, dry pitch, calf suet, red nitre, laurel berries, quicklime, pumice, ammoniac incense, an equal amount of each. Another, of Codamus or of King Nicodemus. ℞ wax 100 dr., red nitre 100 dr., roasted resin 100 dr., ammoniac incense 25 dr., propolis 25 dr., oak mistletoe 12½ dr., oil 1 xestēs, percolated lye 1 xestēs. Another, discutient, for melicerides. ℞ old oil 100 dr., litharge ??1 dr., ammoniac incense and galbanum, 19 dr. each. Another. ℞ litharge 100 dr., common salt 60 dr., old oil 6 kotylai; otherwise 1.

Another, drawing [930] and discutient, polychrest. Rx litharge 1 litra; white lead 1 litra; galbanum 1 litra; rock salt ½ litra; scraped verdigris half a litra; oil 3 sextarii; chalcanthum 2 ounces. Another discutient, the one made with struthion. Rx litharge 2 litrae; oil 3 litrae; white lead 4 ounces; pitch 4 ounces; terebinth 4 ounces; wax 2 ounces; manna 3 ounces; aristolochia 2 ounces; struthion 2 ounces; oak-galls 3 ounces; good wine 3 cotylae. Sprinkle the wine in last. Another discutient, as Scribonius has it. Rx litharge 5 litrae; oil 5 litrae; dry pine resin 5 litrae; propolis 8 litrae; of the oak [kind] 3 ounces. Another, drawing and discutient. Rx new wax 100 drachmas; dry pine resin 100 drachmas; natron 100 drachmas; oil 3 cotylae; some [add] frankincense 100 drachmas; percolated lye 3 cotylae. For indurations there is mixed in ammoniac incense 12 drachmas, an equal amount of galbanum, and of scraped verdigris, propolis and the oak [kind] an equal amount. Another, for choerades, of Minucianus, which I use for girls. Rx terebinth 1 litra; wax 8 litrae; propolis 1 litra; galbanum 8 litrae; oak mistletoe 8 litrae.

Having melted these, [931] sprinkle in 2 ounces of burnt lees and 8 pounds of aphronitre. Then, setting it over the embers, add 3 kotylai of oil. Then, taking it off, sprinkle in 1 ounce of root of wild cucumber, 4 ounces of root of xiphion, and 4 ounces of flower of Assian stone. Another, of Antipater. Take: 1 pound of nitre, 1 pound of terebinth, 1 pound of old oil, 1 xestes of water, and more. When, as it boils, it no longer bubbles up, add 2 ounces of ammoniac incense, 1 ounce of galbanum, 1 ounce of bdellium, 2 ounces of frankincense, 2 ounces of sandarach, and 2 ounces of Assian stone. The Assian stone and the sandarach are ground smooth with a little oil; the meltable ingredients are scraped up and mixed with the dry ones. Another discutient, of Antipater. Take: 300 drachms of molybdaena, 150 drachms of wax, 30 drachms of terebinth, 6 drachms of chalcitis, 8 drachms of galbanum, 8 drachms of myrrh, 8 drachms of manna, and of oil 4 kotylai in winter, 3 kotylai in summer. Another, of Xenocrates, anodyne, discutient, as Castus gives it, the plaster of Polystomus for gouts. Take: 150 drachms of white lead, 3 pounds of wax, 30 drachms of terebinth, 30 drachms of aphronitre, and 3 kotylai of old oil. Another discutient, for meliceris, of Alexander. Take: 1 pound of Spanish salt, 1 pound of litharge.

[932] of white lead 1 litra; of wax 1 oz.; of terebinth 1 oz.; of galbanum, or else of opopanax, 2 oz.; of mustard 6 oz.; of old oil 3 litrae; of vinegar 8 sextarii. Another, the Hygieia, discutient and attractive, for the breasts, made with birdlime. ℞ of litharge 2 litrae; of oil 2 litrae; of oak birdlime 4 oz.; of oak-galls 4 oz. Another, evacuant of pus, as Asclepiades has it, without rupture. ℞ of resin 2 litrae; of wax 2 litrae; of natron 8 litrae; of butter 1 litra; of lion's fat 6 litrae; of old oil 1 litra. Melt together; use it daily, plastering on some of the drug. Another, which presses out fluids and abscesses, especially in the knees and joints, drawing them out without incision; it does not inflame and is a wound plaster. ℞ of slag of lead 100 dr.; of terebinth 100 dr.; of old oil 2 cotylae; resin last. Another, discutient, rupturing and cicatrizing, and provocative, which I use. ℞ of oak birdlime 60 dr.; of pitch 50 dr.; of ammoniac incense 100 dr.; of wax 50 dr.

of roasted resin [933] 15 dr.; of pyrites stone 10 dr.; of galbanum 8 dr.; of manna 4 dr.; of Illyrian iris 4 dr.; of cachrys 4 dr.; of pigeons' dung 4 dr. In some copies also 4 cotylae of honey; in some also 20 dr. of propolis. Having melted the meltable ingredients, sprinkle in the dry ones. [The drawing plasters written by Asclepiades.] A white drawing plaster. It is effective for scrofulous swellings and parotid swellings and abscesses in particular parts; it is effective for fistulas and aegilops, so as to clear them away without incision; it is effective for fluxional and hard-to-heal conditions; it is effective for dropsical patients. Rx of litharge 80 dr.; of white lead 80 dr.; of salt 80 dr.; of old oil 1 sextarius. Grind the salt, the white lead and the litharge, pouring the oil onto them; then, having mixed carefully and put the mixture into an earthenware vessel, boil it, stirring continuously, until it no longer stains; and having poured it out into a mortar and beaten it up, take it out and use it. Another. Rx of litharge 100 dr.; of white lead 10 dr.; of salt 50 dr.; of oil 3 cotylae; of wax 50 dr.; of turpentine resin 12 dr.

prepare in the [934] usual way. Another. ♃ Of manna, 16 dr.; of split alum, 8 dr.; of old oil, 2 kotylai. Another. ♃ Of litharge, 1 litra; of white lead, 1 litra; of mined salt, 1 litra; of wax, 50 dr.; of terebinth resin, 25 dr.; of manna, 16 dr.; of split alum, 8 dr.; of old oil, 1½ kotylai. Another, of Lucius, for the aforementioned conditions, a successful drug. It acts on the fluxional among ulcers and on the chronic and hard-to-heal ones. ♃ Of litharge, 100 dr.; of white lead, 100 drachmas; of ammoniac salt, 100 dr.; of chalcanthum, 100 dr.; of pine resin, 100 dr.; of old oil, 3 sextarii; of vinegar, 1 sextarius; of wax, 50 dr. Prepare in the usual way. Another, the Hygieinē, a successful drug for the aforementioned conditions. ♃ Of litharge, 100 dr.; of white lead, 100 dr.; of salt, 100 dr.; of liquid alum, 100 dr.; of old oil, 10 sextarii; of vinegar, 1 sextarius; of wax, ½ litra; of terebinth resin, ½ litra. Prepare in the usual way. Another, a black drawing plaster: it acts on scrofulous swellings, parotid swellings and local abscesses, and dissolves all hardness.

It is also a good emollient [935], as Antonius the root-cutter used it. It acts against conditions about the joints. ℞ Rock salt, 1 litra; litharge, 1 litra; gloios of the purest kind, 4 litrai; and galbanum, 50 dr. Grind the salt and the litharge, then add the gloios and beat it up diligently; put it into an earthenware vessel, set it on the fire and boil it, stirring continuously. When it becomes non-staining, take it off the fire and add the galbanum, pounded with a wooden pestle. When it has dissolved, pour it out into a mortar, beat it up, and use. Another, which Andromachus used. It acts against choirades, parotid swellings, indurations of the breasts, and local abscesses; it draws out the surrounding fluid and glues down sinuses. It acts against fistulae and aegilopes, and against fluxional ulcers that are chronic and hard to heal. ℞ White lead, 80 dr.; rock salt, 80 dr.; chalcanthum, 12 dr.; old oil, 3 kotylai; vinegar, 4 kotylai.

Boil the salts and the white lead, ground as fine as possible, with the oil, and stir until non-soiling; and when it is right, take it off the [936] fire and add the chalcanthum ground fine with the vinegar, sprinkling it in a little at a time continually and taking care that it does not boil up; then pour it out into a mortar, beat it up, take it up and use. [The discutient (plasters) written by Asclepiades, in his own words.] When the swellings have been dissolved and given off into fluid, the preparations written below are to be used. The wax plaster of Ctesiphon, for choirades, ganglia, parotids and the abscessions in the breasts: like no other of the drugs it both dissolves the swellings and carries off all the adjacent fluid through the porosities, and it glues together the sinuses. It is effective for fistulae and aegilopes, so as to rid the patient of them without incision. It is also a good emollient for sciatic, gouty and arthritic patients, applied after the paroxysms, so as to rid them of the whole affection. The particulars of the preparation are as follows. ℞ Wax, 1 litra; terebinth, 1 litra; nitre, 1 litra; old oil, 1 litra; water, 1 kotyle.

Grind the nitre and the water so that it is completely dissolved, and, putting it into an earthenware vessel and setting it [937] on the fire, boil it, having covered the vessel with a lid and stirring at intervals. When the loud crackling noise ceases, add the meltable ingredients, stirring continuously until it no longer stains; pour it out into a mortar, pound it, take it up and use it. Or prepare it in this way: the meltable ingredients (τηκνὰ, read τηκτὰ) are melted, and when they have dissolved, we add to them the nitre ground with the water, adding it little by little, stirring continuously and taking care that it does not boil over. Another, which Menecrates used, specifically for choirades and for the indurations in the breasts; for it perforates them, discharges the surrounding fluid, makes the sinuses adhere, and brings them to a scar. ℞ wax, 1 litra; terebinth resin, 1 litra; woody resin, 1 litra; galbanum, 1 litra; old oil, 1 litra; aphronitre, 1 litra; myrrh, ashes, 1 xestes; ὃς ἄγγει (text corrupt), 3 ounces.

Putting the resins into a bronze or earthenware vessel and setting it on the fire, melt them; and having dissolved the galbanum with as much of these as suffices to dissolve it, then mix the meltable ingredients together and boil until it no longer stains. Then take it off the fire, let it cool, and add to these [938] the aphronitre, stirring continuously; and having beaten it up, add it to the ashes ground very fine, and having mixed it, take it up and use it, undoing the dressing every fifth day, then every third day, until the parts around the swellings are perforated; then undo it daily and so treat. Another, the one made with aphronitre, called by some 'Dionysia', a drug that succeeds for the aforementioned affections, which Largus used. ♃ Wax, 1 litra; terebinth, 1 litra; manna, 1 litra; aphronitre, 1 litra; oil, 1 sextarius; potter's water, 1 sextarius; raw misy, 2 ounces. Compound it in the usual manner. Another, the one made with Assian stone, a drug that succeeds for the aforementioned affections. ♃ Wax, 1 litra; terebinth, 1 litra; nitre, 1 litra; frankincense, a half-litra; flower of Assian stone, a half-litra; oil of cypros, a half-litra; potter's water, as much as suffices. The dry ingredients are dissolved in the potter's water so as to have the consistency of gloios (strigil-scrapings), and are ground diligently. The meltable ingredients are melted, cooled, and added to the ground ingredients; having beaten it up and taken it up, we use it. Another, an Asian one of Neapolites; it is effective for the aforementioned affections.

℞ Wax [939] 1½ litrae; red nitre, 1 litra; flower of Assian stone, 1½ litrae; manna, a half-litra; myrrh, 3 ounces; old oil, 1 litra; potter's water, 1 kotyle. Prepare in the usual way. Another, which works for the aforementioned conditions. ℞ Wax, 100 drachmas; terebinth, 100 drachmas; foam of nitre, 1 litra; old oil, 1 litra; manna of frankincense, 1 litra; flower of Assian stone, a half-litra; galbanum, 12 drachmas; propolis, 12 drachmas; ammoniac incense, 12 drachmas; potter's water, as much as suffices. Another, tawny, from the [preparations] of Damocrates, which works for the aforementioned conditions. ℞ Litharge, 1 litra; white lead, 1 litra; rock salt, 1 litra; Sinopic ruddle, a half-litra; wax, 2 ounces; galbanum, 2 ounces; terebinth, 2 ounces; old oil, 3 kotylai; vinegar, enough to dissolve the Sinopic [ruddle]. Prepare in the usual way. Another, which works for the aforementioned conditions. ℞ Litharge, 1 litra; white lead, 1 litra; rock salt, 1 litra; Sinopic ruddle, a half-litra; wax, 4 ounces; galbanum, 2 ounces; terebinth resin, 2 ounces; old oil, 3 kotylai.

of vinegar, enough to dissolve the Sinopic earth; prepare in the usual [940] manner. Another, the one with mastic; it acts against the aforementioned conditions. ℞ Wax, 1 litra; mastic, manna of frankincense, Sinopic earth, aphronitre, a half-litra of each; myrtle oil, 3 ounces; sea water, 3 kotylai. Another, that of the Neapolitan; it acts against the aforementioned conditions. ℞ Litharge, 1 litra; white lead, 1 litra; rock salt, 1 litra; Sinopic red earth, a half-litra; wax, a half-litra; pine resin, a half-litra; galbanum, 2 ounces; oil, 3 kotylai; vinegar, a sufficient quantity. [The discutient plasters written by Damocrates.] A good discutient plaster, quince-yellow: it disperses the choirades of children that are not of long standing, the indurations about the muscles and the skin, and the inflammations that persist for a longer time; and it fills up flesh and brings to cicatrization.

It is prepared thus: of fine litharge at most a litra, of white lead a half-litra; to these he adds a litra of new [941] rich oil. Having put in the litharge, boil it with the oil and, making it dirty-looking in its thickness, then add the white lead, ground smooth. When you see it non-soiling and very well tempered, rather a little harder, throw in wax and pine resin; and when these have melted, lifting the pot boiling from the fire, then put in ammoniacum, flattened with the hands and the fingers beside the fire, as wax usually is; then stirring the drug with the spatula, and again softening it with the hands: in this way store it away. Another. Another for all these things; but it disperses scrofulous swellings more, and it benefits sufferers who are apprehensive of an abscession of the hypochondrium accompanied by some swelling and fear. Being black, it has this preparation: of very moist pitch and of dry pitch, 2 litrae.

[942] and add two [pounds] of dense, glassy bitumen; four of roasted pine resin; three of wax; one pound and a third part of frankincense; twice four ounces of copper scale; five ounces of fresh common oil. Grind the frankincense and the scale, pouring in a moderate amount of vinegar, and when you have ground them carefully and brought them to the thickness of honey, then boil the wax and the remaining ingredients with the new oil, and so pour it hot over the ground ingredients. When you have mixed everything carefully and vigorously with the hands, store it, keeping it covered with a skin, for it forms a crust and becomes rough. The dispersing [plasters] of Damocrates made with salt. Prepare this one too, as a most excellent drug: of good white lead and of good litharge, a pound of each, and ten ounces of salt.
