Any salt that is white is [943] serviceable enough for a drug, but much better are ammoniac and clean sea salt; and three times the weight of a pound of oil many years old. Boil the oil and the rest, ground smooth, in the same way, until they become harder than an emollient, for when they are stored they become softer. Another. Another, better, for it disperses indurations. Better than all, [it disperses] those that have become very chronic, and bronchoceles and large melicerides, scrofulous swellings that are hard to alter, and ankylai. Prepare it thus: a pound of very finely ground salt, and two of plain white lead, and of galbanum 2 ounces; the same of clean propolis, of aristolochia, of galbanum an equal part, and 2 pounds of good oil many years old. If it is very thick, add another one; and boil it in the same way, and well mixed.

[944] Lift it off the fire, and then you will sprinkle in finely ground birthwort, adding also the softened propolis and the galbanum. Another discutient of Damocrates, made with quicklime. Very good, dispersing choirades, repressing every oedema, and healing the watery conditions of the liver or of the spleen, bringing on abundant excretions of urine; and it resolves chronic sciaticas. Ulbianus, a naturally gifted young man, used this and benefited very many people. It contains one litra of Pontic wax, one of the roasted and one of the pine resin, one ounce of fresh quicklime, one ounce of split alum, and an amount equal to one of these of Pontic orpiment.

Pouring fragrant vinegar over these a little at a time, grind them sufficiently in a larger mortar; [945] and adding a little oil to the wax and the resin, melting them over a fire of vigorous flame, and mixing everything carefully, and making emollients (malagmata) of the thickness of the amolyntos ('non-soiling' plaster), keep it in store, using it, in the cases where it is needed, on a fresh pad. The most excellent man, the father of the drug, said that the drug is also serviceable and good for the riddance of long diseases, and that in those in whom a chronic inflammation of one of the viscera has made the hypochondrium hard or large it helps greatly; for it brings on sweats and dissolves the hardnesses of the hypochondria, and quickly effects the riddance of the diseases; and the suppressions of the natural menses it brings on when it has lain applied for a few days. But I, removing the 'lime' (titanos), used to put in double the alum, and found the drug acting better, not producing the pustules (psydrakia).

[946] GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK VIII. Physicians call malagmata ('emollients') those drugs that soften bodies which have been hardened contrary to nature. All of them are of a moderately hot krasis, yet they are not drying, just as they are not clearly moistening either. For those that are emollient in the strict sense are in some way intermediate between moistening and drying agents, and they bring about, as it were, a kind of melting of the substance of the parts that are being hardened.

But drugs are also called emollient even if in other cases they deviate [947] slightly towards drying or moistening, provided only that they possess the property of melting the underlying substance of the parts they touch. This evidently comes about because their heat is moderate. That after the hardness has been melted there is need of discutient drugs has been stated both in the fifth book of On the Power of Simple Drugs and in the fourteenth of the Therapeutic Method. The best treatment, then, of parts that are becoming hardened, which indeed also become scirrhous if they are not treated by medicine according to method, comes about when the practitioner considers how far the substance of the body under treatment has advanced in its nature beyond the well-proportioned moisture and dryness, and likewise the constitution of the affection itself, to what extent it has increased, and in addition to these, the more and less in the softening drugs themselves. For if you look to these things, your first use of the emollient drug will be conjectural, but with art. After one or two

…days you will perceive whether it is fitting to intensify or to slacken the potency of the drug, as has been said both in the preceding cases and [948] in the Therapeutic Method. Now the physicians have compounded emollient and discutient drugs with a view to both aims together: that of the liquefaction of the hardened and scirrhous part, and that of discussion. They do not use each in alternation, as you often see me doing; they always accomplish the two by means of the compound drug. It is quite clear that in the mixture either the emollient ingredients are the more numerous or the discutient ones, and the more and less among them is no small matter. It is quite clear too that they are often mixed in equal potencies. Just as with the other drugs, so with these, the one who wishes to treat well must have prepared several drugs of the same kind, or at any rate two to be mixed, the strongest in the kind and the most moderate, so that from their differing mixture, made at the opportune moment, he may produce a great many drugs between the extremes.

For fat does not have the same power as bdellium, storax and ammoniac incense, just as among the fats themselves goose fat and [949] fowl's fat do not have the same power as that of the leopard or the lion or the hyena or of any other animal. For the fat too is according to the temperament (krasis) of the animal: that of the hotter animals is more heating, that of the drier more drying. And indeed most physicians know that the strongest in both respects, I mean heating and dispersing, is the fat of the lion. Close to it is that of leopards, so that it has little emollient quality. Goose fat has a weaker power in heating and dispersing, but it has somewhat more in softening. And that of hens stands at a proportionate remove from this one. Now all of these also have the property of being finer-particled than those in four-footed animals. Among those, in turn, there is a very great difference: pig's fat is the softest and moistest and for this reason the weakest of the others, so that it suits soft bodies, such as are those of women and children and eunuchs and of men of delicate living, made effeminate by rearing in the shade, lack of exercise, and frequent baths of drinkable water.

That of goats and oxen, by as much as it is stronger than that of swine, by so much is it suited to bodies [950] that are harder, also by nature, and to the more scirrhous among the harder [conditions]. That of bulls and he-goats is for the stronger bodies and affections. The same difference also obtains among the others in relation to one another, according to the more and the less. I shall begin from the weaker ones, having first spoken about the affection that consists in hardness and scirrhosis. For since the resistance to the pressure of the fingers is an attribute common to parts that are inflamed and to parts that are hardened, the affections are distinguished by the painful and the painless; for this is no longer common to both.

Just as in all other things whose nature is to pass over into one another there is a borderland between the two that shares moderately in both, so also between phlegmonous swellings and the scirrhi without phlegmone, such as are those of parts that have become hardened, there exists a certain intermediate condition. It is painless unless you press the fingers on it, but painful when people do so. For the sake of clear and concise teaching it must be called either a scirrhous phlegmone or a phlegmonous scirrhus, without attending here to the [951] magnitude of the swelling. For 'phlegmone' and 'scirrhus' are names of the form of the affections, not of the quantity in either of them. A phlegmone is large either because of the magnitude of the part affected by phlegmone or because of that of the swelling contrary to nature, and small when it has either occupied a small place or has a slight swelling. I shall now speak of the treatment of a small phlegmone and a small scirrhus, as also of a large one of each, according to the forms of the affections. For from these the treatment of the other things called large and small will also be understood. The cure of a large phlegmone, then, comes about through poultices and certain liquid drugs. The cure of a small one, when it has been mixed with scirrhous hardness, comes about sometimes through poultices, but also through cerate-like and liquid drugs, and further through the emollient plasters. Through such means the cure of a small hardness also comes about. In its case the aim is simple, as also when a phlegmone is forming. But in the case of a hardness that has something phlegmonous in it, the aim too becomes compound.

[On the parhygros.] And for this reason [952] the drug too is in a way compound, such as this one known to everyone and highly praised by certain others and above all by Heras, the so-called parhygron. For this heals a part that still has slight inflammation, when it is applied not long after its preparation but immediately. But when the affected part acquires a painless hardness, it is useful even if it is a little older than the freshly prepared. Just so, if the affected part has been entirely freed from the inflammatory condition, the older drug is better for it. Clearly the age of the drug ought to increase in proportion to the intensification of the hardness; a part that is excessively hardened, however, not even the aged drug will soften. For this so-called parhygron has a mixed promise and power, because it also has mixed material. Pig's fat and wax are the weakest of the emollients, while litharge and white lead have nothing emollient, as we have learned.

Heras, who praised this drug most of all, composes [953] it from the following ingredients, in these words: ℞ fresh pig's fat, with the fibres removed, 44 ounces; wax, 24 ounces; white lead, 6 ounces; litharge, 6 ounces. Pour the meltable ingredients over the dry ones; it sets with time. Just as I said that wax and pig's fat are of weak emollient power, so too, if you mix a little wax with oil, you will make what physicians call cerelaeum (wax-oil). The oil, clearly, must be neither the so-called omphacine and omotribes oil (oil of unripe olives), nor oil that has taken up olive shoots in its preparation. [The differences by kind, and the powers, of emollient drugs.] Now, emollients that are weak in this way also treat small inflammations; those that are feebler than these treat slight hardnesses without inflammation.

Those that are stronger still than these treat the greater ones, just as those that cure a hardness which has come close to a scirrhus are the most drastic; of this sort is the class of the marrows, which differ from one another by more and less, as I shall distinguish next, [954] and that of both bdelliums, the Arabian and the Scythian, and that of the storaxes. For of these too the most drastic is the one pale yellow in colour, which is also produced finest in Pamphylia. The one that has departed from this towards the duskier is produced in many places and falls far short in power of the pale one. Yet this very one too, as it ages, inclines towards a golden colour. This one, then, we use for antidotes on account of its scarcity, so that when preparing anything with storax for an emperor you will always use this. And if any of those near you is lavish in expenditure on drugs, for him too you will compound the drug from storax of this kind. For the others, you will select the best of the duskier, judging chiefly by its smell and its colour; for the blacker is inferior. Among the things that strongly soften parts that are becoming scirrhous is the so-called ammoniacum incense, and more than it the kind that is fatty and fresh. Less than these, but themselves also active, are goat's and ox fat.

Among these themselves, that of he-goats and bulls is stronger, while that of oxen and she-goats is weaker than these, though not inactive either [955]. That of kids and calves is weaker still than even these, but is nevertheless more active than pig's fat. The fat of the lion and of the leopard, and that of the hyena and of the goose, have a more discutient, not a more emollient, power than these, inasmuch as they also have a substance of finer parts than goat's and ox fat. That of hens is ranked between the goose's and the pig's. Just as, among the marrows too, the best is that of calves. And resins, as many as do not have a pungent smell, when mixed with one of the aforesaid, supply the adhesive quality to the drugs being compounded and do not destroy their emollient quality. Most suitable are the so-called Chian and the larch resin. After these comes the resin of the pine (peukinē), and after that the fir resin. The strobiline is violently pungent, and the pine resin (pityinē) is without fat and greatly drying; they call it by the special name physēma. These, then, are to be avoided. The Chian and the fir resin are to be used not on their own, but with wax and some one of the others, whichever seems to suit the condition. And Bruttian pitch has the same power, as having something adhesive and fatty.

The [956] other pitch, however, is not to be mixed in, just as asphalt is not either; for they go further in dryness. And we have learned that drying things are contrary to softening ones. Since they are accustomed to call the pine resin, that is, the roasted resin, also Colophonian, one should know that there is also another Colophonian resin, closely resembling Chian mastic, which has something emollient, as that mastic and frankincense also do. Egyptian mastic too has something emollient, but the greater part of its power is concoctive and discutient. Frankincense likewise has some emollient quality, but it is useful when boiled, as is fenugreek seed; for this too softens well when boiled, and still more if it is mixed with fat. Things that, without boiling, need to be relaxed, melted, moistened and dissolved because of the dryness of their consistency require one of the oily substances. Such are oil itself, when it has no astringency, the gloios from the baths, further the so-called susinon, and, still much more than it, the Commagenian.

And further, butter too is of the same class [957], as are the decoction of marsh-mallow and that of fenugreek. Between things that are mild in this way and the strongest, such as bdellium and storax, lies ammoniacum incense, which has the same power that propolis also has. Concerning bdellium, however, this distinction too must be drawn: the Scythian is far better for these purposes than the other, the Arabian, and especially when it is fresh and soft, which they also call 'fatty'. For this too is a custom among the more recent physicians, in the case of such drugs, to call the more emollient one also 'moister'. And this one is plainly also moister. Galbanum too, and what is called opopanax, have, besides dispersing, something emollient as well. Opopanax excels in dispersing, galbanum in softening and concocting. Such, then, is the power of emollient drugs. And you, whenever you either examine and judge one of the remedies written in the pharmacological books, or compound one yourself, having just heard of the differences of more and less among drugs, and having heard also of the differences of bodies and of affections, will apply the strong ones to the strong and the weak ones to the weak.

[958] In the interval of applying another [drug] after the one applied before, it is fitting to pour simple oil over the affected part, and something oily suits it. Of the drugs called echekolla ('adhesive'), none should be removed before it comes away of its own accord; rather, even if the patient bathes, one should let it stay in place. One should also avoid baths in medicinal waters, and especially those that are chalcanthous, aluminous and sulphurous. These things suffice for intelligent men who have also acquired some practice in the works of the art.

[The differences by species, and the potencies, of emollient drugs.] But since not all are of this kind, and since what is proposed in this treatise is not, as in the Therapeutic Method, to state the method alone, but to state it together with an example of the particulars, one or a second, and the drugs established by experience must also be added, those set down by the men before us who were renowned in the pharmaceutical part of the art, I shall come to the differences by species among the emollient drugs, making my beginning from the mildest of them, which also cure small inflammations. [959] Of the compound emollients, some are, as one might say, weaker, in the first order; some, not much stronger than these, in the second; certain others in the third; and, besides these, others in the fourth. One should use, as has been said before, for slight indurations and for soft bodies those of the first order; for bodies and affections stronger than these, those of the second; and likewise those of the third and of the fourth in proportion. They also describe separately the drugs belonging to each of these orders. [Emollient drugs of the first order.] Butter or Colophonian resin and white wax that is not old, the three in equal weight, melted together, are emollients of the first order. So too is the parhygros, when it is fresh; when it has aged it becomes more discutient. And the weakest of the emollients is wax melted with butter, or with susinum or Commagenum.

And weaker than these is what is called wax-oil (kerelaion), when twelve or sixteen ounces of wax are put into a litra of a relaxing oil that has no [960] astringency. The cerates made with eggs also have a slight relaxing quality. Stronger than these, but these too still weak, are the cerates made of oesypum, resin and wax, melted together in equal weight. If these ingredients are somewhat old, the mixture will need an admixture of one of the relaxing oils, either the lily oil (susinum) or the Commagenian, or of pig's, fowl's or goose fat. Emollient drugs of the second order. As in the case of the simple drugs, we made four orders of things of the same kind, defining the more and the less among them. Of some I said that their power is ambiguous, that is, whether their power is to be placed at the end of the first order or at the beginning of the second, and likewise also concerning the second and third orders and those that follow them. But in some cases I ventured to make a declaration and said that some belong at the beginning of this order and others at the end of that order, just as I said that some, without qualification, belong either to the first, or the second, or the third, or the fourth order.

Pronouncements of this kind require much particular experience over many bodies and [961] affections. Therefore, even if someone after me should prove, as I am, industrious and zealous for truth, let him not rashly pronounce on the basis of two or three uses. For through long experience it will often appear to him, as it has also appeared to me, that what was stated under the second order must be transferred into the third at its beginning, or simply to the beginning of the third. For since the bodies to which the drugs are applied, and the affections themselves, show no small excess in the more and the less, it is most difficult to make a single pronouncement for all cases; and, in addition, the simple drugs themselves have no small difference among themselves. And since I pronounced on the power in the case of the best of each species and genus, if someone makes this examination through experience on the worst, he will make it falsely, and he has not determined the orders of their power.

It is therefore safest to set down accurately the difference of the drugs themselves relative to one another in respect of the more and the less, [962] as I have done in the other cases and shall do now. [That various differences in respect of the more and the less arise in the emollient plaster of Mnasaeus, according to the differing quantity, age and boiling of the simple ingredients.] For in the second order of emollients one might quite justifiably place the plaster composed by Mnasaeus. All who have recorded it agree with one another that it is made of old oil, litharge and pig's fat. They differ, however, both in the quantity of each of these and in that some compose it from fresh fat and others from old, the fat which is now customarily called by everyone axungia. On these premises the weakest would be the one made of litharge, pig's fat and oil, neither of the two being old. The stronger is the one in which the oil is old and the other ingredient, the fat, is put in new. The one stronger than this is the one in which both are old. So, according to whether the oil and the fat are put in new or old, there are four differences.

[963] the differences will be four: sometimes when both are new, sometimes when both are old, sometimes when the oil is old but the fat fresh, or the reverse, when the oil is fresh but old fat is put in. According to the proportion of the three simple drugs to one another, however, there are several others. For either the three are mixed in equal amounts by weight and measure (and many say that the plaster composed by Mnasaeus himself consists of three equal parts), or two are equal and the third not equal but less or more, or the three are mixed unequal. It is quite clear, then, that many differences will arise. For when more of the litharge is put in, the drug will become softer in its power, and when less, stronger. It will also be more emollient if we put in more of the fat, and more discutient if more of the oil. For when more oil has been put in, something else in turn comes in as well, having great power to make the drug more discutient. This is, as I said in the first book, if you boil it for longer. At any rate, if you boil the litharge alone in a larger quantity of oil, the drug will be more drying.

[964] And you will boil it for a longer time if you have put in more oil, that is, if it is to have the consistency of a plaster. So if someone pays no attention to this, but boils the preparation having less oil and the one having more for an equal time, it is evident that the one in which more oil has been mixed will be more emollient in its power, just as if someone should wish to use the litharge raw and unground, mixed with oil. For this reason I bid you always remember what I have often said already: that we should not, as some make their pronouncements about drugs without qualification, act in this way ourselves, saying without qualification that this composition of the drug is better than that one. For each of the two can be well composed for affections that differ in kind, and sometimes for the same affection at different times. Therefore anyone who has heard beforehand all these things I have now said, being not only diligent or retentive of memory but also naturally intelligent, will read with profit what has been written, and will be written, by me with distinctions.

And I shall tell you that the distinctions in the case of the drugs before us come about by the addition of three or four syllables, [965] the kind of addition which Andromachus appears to have made in the case of the drug of Mnasaeus that is before us in the present account. For in the catalogue of the quince-yellow plasters, having written it eleventh in order, he was not content to name it simply, as in the case of those mentioned earlier, prefixing to them 'another' and 'another', but he added the word 'soft'. This, then, I would have expected him to have done for all of them, and, in the case of the quince-yellow plasters themselves, to have begun from the softest and, passing from it to the one a little stronger, to have made this clear, adding in writing that the second is stronger than this one by some small amount, and again that the third is stronger than that one, and then the fourth than that one.

just as, again, if he thought that some had equal potency, he should have added this very fact in writing; or, if he was wary of running a risk in such pronouncements, he should at least have taught beforehand the simple emollient drugs, distinguishing the more and the less among them, so that one reading in sequence the many emollient plasters he wrote might recognise as stronger the one compounded of storax, ammoniac, bdellium, propolis and galbanum, and of [966] bull's and goat's suet and the marrows, and as weak the one containing none of these, but either ingredients all weak in potency, or ingredients stronger than these themselves but intermediate in their temperaments and potencies, or with one or two of the strong ingredients mixed in with the weak ones. For it is clear that the intermediate latitude in all drugs is not small in respect of the more and the less, with reference to a potency common to all of them conceived generically, according to which drugs are said to be of the same genus and of the same species, just as others are said to differ by generic or specific differences. Since, then, these distinctions have been made by me, and anyone starting from them will without difficulty be able to discern those having a stronger potency and those having a milder one, I shall now give the record of them, writing out in sequence those recorded by the men most experienced in drugs, whether you wish to call them plasters or malagmata ('emollients'). I shall begin with those written by Asclepiades in the fourth book of his External Remedies, which he entitles Marcellas.

[967] [The emollients (malagmata) recorded by Asclepiades.] The emollient of Amythaon, for distensions of the hypochondria. It dissolves all hardness, and it is also effective for joints that move with difficulty. Take: of ammoniacum incense, 36 oz.; of wax, 36 oz.; of terebinth, 8 oz.; of bdellium, 8 oz.; of frankincense, 4 ounces; of myrrh, 4 oz.; of galbanum, 8 oz.; of oil of cypros, 4 cotylae. The myrrh, frankincense and bdellium are steeped in wine, and the ammoniacum is dissolved in vinegar. Everything is pounded, the pestle being smeared with the oil of cypros, until it is completely dissolved. This drug is one of the old and esteemed ones, as is also the one written after it by Asclepiades, in the following manner. The myrrh preparation (diasmyrnon) of Apollophanes (?), a successful drug. For distensions of the hypochondria; it dissolves all hardness; it is effective for those with liver complaints, those with spleen complaints and those with kidney complaints; it is effective for every sympathetic affection of the sinews; it is effective for pains and fixations of the joints. Take: of wax, 16 oz.; of terebinth, 16 oz.; of ammoniacum incense, 16 oz.; of bdellium, 16 oz.; of myrrh, 16 oz.; of propolis, 16 oz.

[968] of iris, 16 ounces; of storax, 16 ounces; of the dregs of iris unguent, as much as suffices; of fragrant wine, a sufficient quantity; prepare as stated above. The drug written by Asclepiades after this one is more noteworthy than those written below it, but inferior to those [above] for the resolution of hardened parts. Another drug, of Dioscorides, a successful one, for limbs that are hard to move and for ankylai; it dissolves every hardness, and is effective also for affections of the internal parts and for deep-seated abscesses. ℞ Of wax, 1 mina; of roasted resin, half a mina; of galbanum, half a mina; of Illyrian iris, half a mina; of dregs of iris oil, a sufficient quantity; of wine, as much as suffices. The drug is a pounded one; prepare as stated above. The drug written by Asclepiades next after the one just mentioned is the same as the one written by Heras at the end of his pharmaceutical book, but it has a slight difference in the proportion of four of the simple drugs, as will be clear when both have been written out.

But first I shall record the one written by Asclepiades, [969] which reads word for word as follows. 'Entitled "Of Lucius the preceptor, for ankylai".' It acts on deep-seated abscessions; it also acts on contractions of the sinews and on the fixations of the joints which we call ankylai. It acts for the opisthotonic and against every sympathetic affection of the sinews. It is also a good akopon, dissolved in iris oil or cyprinum or laurel oil. It acts on chronic and hard-to-heal indurations. ℞ Of bdellus 16 dr.; of calf's suet 16 dr.; of ammoniacum incense 16 dr.; of Illyrian iris 16 dr.; of opopanax 8 dr.; of galbanum 8 dr.; of cachrys 8 dr.; of storax 8 dr.; of frankincense 8 dr.; of pepper 160 grains; of the dregs of iris unguent as much as suffices; of wax and of terebinth resin a half-litra each; of wine a sufficient amount. The drug is a pounded one; prepare it as stated before. Where, then, Heras disagreed with Asclepiades in the proportion of the simples, I shall now show, as I promised. As the very first ingredient Asclepiades wrote bdellus, 16 holkai; but Heras wrote not bdellus but bdellium, 80 holkai.

These are fivefold [970] of the 16, clearly. Next, where Asclepiades had written 16 drachms of calf's fat, Heras wrote five times as much, as he also did for the bdellium; for 80 drachms are clearly fivefold of 10 and 6. Third, after those already written, Asclepiades wrote a drug, ammoniac incense, requiring that 16 drachms of this too be put in. By the proportion of the preceding ones, then, Heras too ought to have written 80 drachms. But he wrote not so many, but 100, so that he put in 20 more. Another drug, after the drugs written before, Asclepiades wrote, speaking thus: 'of Illyrian iris 16 dr.' Heras preserved the proportion of this, writing 80. After the drugs written before, Asclepiades wrote 8 drachms of opopanax; and Heras preserved the proportion with respect to this too, writing 40. As the sixth drug Asclepiades mentioned galbanum, putting in 8 drachms. Heras preserved the proportion with respect to it as well, requiring that a fivefold amount be put in; for 40 are fivefold of 8. The seventh drug Asclepiades wrote thus:

of cachrys [971] 8 dr. So Heras too, if indeed he was preserving the proportion, ought to have put in 40; but as it is, he did not do so, but put in double, for he himself has written 16. As the eighth, Asclepiades mentions storax, putting in 8 dr. Heras preserved the proportion of this, putting in fivefold. The ninth drug Asclepiades wrote was frankincense, putting in 8 dr. of it; but Heras requires not fivefold but double. As the tenth, Asclepiades mentioned pepper, putting in 160 grains, for which Heras again, in agreement, put 500. In some of the copies, I do not know how, 20 are written, just as in others 108. As the eleventh, Asclepiades wrote wax, as also, as the twelfth, the terebinth resin, requiring a half-litra of each to be put in. So Heras too, if indeed he was preserving the proportion, ought to have put in fivefold of each, which was 2 litrai apiece with a half of a litra further added. But he did not do so; instead he requires three litrai and 4 ounces of each to be put in.

It is therefore quite clear that Heras puts in [972] double the proportionate amount of cachrys, as also of frankincense. Of ammoniac incense he has exceeded by a fourth part, as indeed also of terebinth resin together with the wax (3). For in these too he exceeded by a third part, and in this way he made the whole composition of the drug closely similar to that of Asclepiades. For, having exceeded in the measure of cachrys, which has nothing softening but is only discutient, he increased along with it the emollient ingredients as well: the frankincense, the wax and the terebinth. Asclepiades names this drug as that of Lucius his teacher, and I have gone through the points in which he differs from Heras. It is of the highest rank among the emollients, for you would not find one more emollient than it for parts becoming scirrhous. Whoever composed it also aimed at dispersing what is contained in the parts becoming scirrhous. The other drugs before it surpass those written earlier by a little. Among them are also included the agents that cut thickened and viscid humours, which are often useful for scirrhous swellings, when their scirrhous induration is produced by viscid humours.

Moderately, [973] then, does opopanax thin. They call by this name the root of the panax, from whose stalk they make opopanax by drawing off its juice; for it is of a detergent, not an incisive, faculty. Vinegar together with goat's dung cuts, cleanses and disperses powerfully not only thickened and viscid humours but also the solid bodies themselves; these are added to the drug written next after the one under discussion, which he says is entitled 'of Alcimion'. About the former, then, he writes in this manner: Another emollient of Marcus Telentius Asclepiades, very excellent for the aforementioned conditions. It acts especially against inflations of the womb; the drug is entitled 'Asclepiadeion' because it is ascribed to Asclepiades the Bithynian. Take: myrrh, 3 drachms (otherwise, 3 ounces); opopanax, a half-litra; wax, 1½ litrae; galbanum, 3 ounces; manna, a half-litra; ammoniac incense, a half-litra; roasted resin, 1½ litrae; vinegar, 1 kotyle. It is to be used also for every sympathetic affection of the sinews. Another, entitled 'of Alcimion'. Take: wax, 1 litra

[974] and a half; Colophonian resin, 1½ pounds; ammoniacum incense, 1½ pounds; galbanum, 3 ounces; myrrh, 3 ounces; frankincense, 3 ounces; opopanax, 1½ pounds; propolis, 3 ounces; vinegar, 2 sextarii; goat's dung, 3 ounces. Pound the ammoniacum, adding 1 sextarius of vinegar; then add to these the myrrh, the frankincense and the opopanax, and grind smooth again. Pound the propolis together with the galbanum. Boil the wax and the resin, adding 2 cotylae of oil; and when it has drawn together, add the propolis and galbanum, stirring continuously. And when it has melted, take it off the fire and let it cool, and having scraped it off, add it to the ingredients that have been ground smooth, and having mixed, take it up and use. After the emollient plaster written above, there is written in the book of Asclepiades another, which has little emollient power but more heating power. It contains not only the juice of gentian but also the saps, both that of peucedanum and that of sagapenum, drugs that heat strongly.

Mixed into it are also aphronitre and flower of Asian stone, drugs of attenuating [975] and cutting power. That unfired sulphur heats, everyone knows, as indeed they know it of pitch-wine too. I shall write out this drug as well in Asclepiades' own words. An emollient entitled 'Pharmianon', for the aforementioned conditions. It works best for pleuritics, for it resolves the pains at once when applied during the paroxysms themselves. After the application of the drug, once redness has arisen about the affected places, one must lift off the compress and, after leaving an interval, apply it again. It also resolves chronic conditions. Take: wax, 5 pounds, or 1 pound; ammoniac incense, 3 pounds; roasted resin, 3 ounces, or 1 pound; terebinth resin, 1 pound; frankincense, 1½ pounds; myrrh, 6 ounces; aloes, 6 ounces; oesypum, 3 ounces; juice of gentian, 3 ounces; sap of peucedanum, 3 ounces, or of opopanax, 6 ounces; sagapenum, 4 ounces; aphronitre, 6 ounces; flower of Asian stone, 6 ounces; propolis, 3 ounces; unfired sulphur, 4 ounces; pitch-wine, 5 sextarii. Boil the pitch-wine and the juice of the gentian; melt the meltable ingredients and let them cool.

Grind the ammoniacum, the frankincense [976], the myrrh and the aloes together, put them into a mortar, and pour the liquid over them. When they have dissolved, grind industriously. Pound and sift the dry ingredients and add them to what has been ground smooth; pound again carefully, then add to these the meltable ingredients, boiled up, without the wax residues (ἐγκηρίδων). Mix, take up, and use. Directly after the aforementioned, Asclepiades wrote another malagma similar to it, in these words: Another, that of the Neapolitan; it was prepared for Aquilia Secundilla. ♃ Pitch wine, 6 sextarii; wax, 6 pounds; ammoniacum incense, 3 pounds; roasted resin, 3 pounds; terebinth resin, 1½ pounds; frankincense, 1½ pounds; myrrh, 6 ounces; aloes, 6 ounces; aphronitre, 6 ounces; flower of Assian stone, 6 ounces; juice of the root of gentian, 6 ounces; sagapenum, 4 ounces; unfired sulphur, 4 ounces; propolis, 4 ounces; root of panax, 3 ounces; sampsuchum, 3 ounces; white pepper, 3 ounces. Prepare and use as stated above. [The malagmata (emollients) written by Andromachus.] A hard and dry malagma. ♃ Pitch, 3 pounds.

of wax [977] 2 pounds; of resin 1 pound; of galbanum 2 ounces; of ammoniac incense 2 ounces; of manna 4 ounces; of vinegar 3 sextarii; of the juice of the root of peucedanum 6 ounces; of oesypum 4 ounces. Otherwise: ℞ of pitch 4 pounds; of wax 2 pounds; of resin 1 pound; of ammoniac incense 1 pound; of manna 1 pound; of galbanum 6 ounces (others: 1 pound); of vinegar 3 sextarii. Another, that of Aristocles: ℞ of pitch 4 pounds; of wax 8 pounds; of roasted resin 4 pounds; of terebinth 4 pounds; of ammoniac incense 2 pounds, 8 ounces; of galbanum 1 pound, 4 ounces. Another, the one for ankylae: ℞ of bdellium 16 drachms; of frankincense 16 drachms; of ammoniac incense 8 drachms; of opopanax 8 drachms; of galbanum 8 drachms; of calf's suet 16 drachms; of pepper 160 grains; of storax 8 drachms; of cachrys 16 drachms; of Illyrian iris 16 drachms; of terebinth half a mina, of wax half a mina, of cyprinum 4 cotylae; of wine a sufficient quantity. The one made with melilot: ℞ of Celtic nard 10 drachms; of cyperus 8 drachms; of cardamom 8 drachms; of Illyrian iris 8 drachms; of myrrh 8 drachms; of saffron 4 drachms; of melilot 25 drachms.

of ammoniac incense [978] 8 dr.; of terebinth 50 dr.; of fresh wax 100 dr.; of oil of cypros half a cotyle; of vinegar a sufficient quantity. Some put ammoniac incense at 100 dr. For all internal [conditions]. The [plaster] from seeds. ℞ Ammoniac incense 50 dr.; wax 50 dr.; terebinth 50 dr.; fenugreek 25 dr.; treated bull's suet 25 dr.; Illyrian iris 25 dr.; nitre 25 dr.; honey 6 cotylae; vinegar 1 cotyle; panax 25 dr.; oil of cypros, a little. As Philonides [has it]: ℞ Fenugreek seed, anise seed, storax, crude bdellium, manna, frankincense, cardamom, fresh cyperus, panax root, Illyrian iris, aphronitre, of each 25 dr.; ammoniac incense and terebinth, 50 dr. each; bull's suet 60 dr.; melilot 60 dr.; wax 2 dr., otherwise 100; honey half a cotyle; wine 1 cotyle. Another, as Harpocras [has it]: ℞ Fenugreek, nitre, panax, iris, 8 drachms each; terebinth, ammoniac incense, wax, 100 dr. each; bull's suet 100 dr., otherwise 50; honey 1 litra; vinegar 2 sextarii.

Of celery seed, of cumin, of fennel or anise, [979] 50 drachms each; of melilot 50 drachms, but some say 25; of sampsuchum 50 drachms; of cardamom and of ammi, 50 drachms each. Take up with cyprinum. The one with sampsuchum, for many conditions. ♃ Of new wax, of laurel berries, of finely ground fenugreek, of sampsuchum, 100 drachms of each; of turpentine 150 drachms; of nitron 32 drachms; of pepper 32 drachms, but some say sixteen; of cyperus 16 drachms; of cyprinum 2 cotylae, or of storax oil. The one with laurel berries. ♃ Of wax 75 drachms; of Bruttian pitch 75 drachms; of laurel berries 75 drachms; of nitron 75 drachms; of roasted resin 75 drachms; of galbanum 12 drachms; of ammoniac incense 12 drachms; of cachrys 12 drachms; of ammi 12 drachms; of white pepper 16 drachms; of cyprinum 6 drachms, or 6 cotylae. Another emollient (malagma), of good colour, of many uses. ♃ Of wax 1 litra; of roasted resin 1 litra; of ammoniac incense 6 ounces; of liquid alum 6 ounces; of flower of salt 6 ounces; some add of mistletoe 6 ounces. That of Apollophanes. ♃ Of wax 80 drachms; of ammoniac incense 80 drachms; of bdellium 80 drachms; of Illyrian iris 80 drachms; of terebinth resin 40 drachms; of frankincense powder (manna) 40 drachms. It is pounded together with iris oil.

The [plaster] with alum, [980] another way. ℞ Wax, 100 dr.; pitch, 50 dr.; liquid alum, 25 dr., but I [use] 50 dr.; birdlime, 50 dr. Good for those suffering from ischias. ℞ Seed of wild rue, silphium, laurel berries, aphronitre, southernwood, colocynth, cardamom, ammi, 4 dr. each; fresh rue, pitch, terebinth [resin], ammoniacum incense, wax, suet, 8 dr. each; galbanum, 6 dr.; opopanax, 4 dr.; unfired sulphur, 4 dr. For splenics. ℞ Wax, 1 mina; resin, 1 mina; ammoniacum incense, half a mina; liquid alum, 50 dr.; gloios (strigil-scrapings), 1 cotyle; root of caper, 50 dr.; root of calamint, 50 dr.; residue (magma) of myrobalan, 50 dr. Use vinegar for the dry ingredients, oil for the meltable ones. A plaster of many uses. ℞ Mustard, 4 dr.; manna [of frankincense], 2 dr.; rue, 4 dr.; aphronitre, 4 dr.; root of caper, 6 dr.; ammoniacum incense, 4 dr.; myrobalan, 25 dr.; the slender centaury, 4 dr., or 7; flower of Assian stone, 4 dr.; fenugreek, 4 dr.; cardamom, 4 dr.; wax, 75 dr.; resin, 100 dr.; honey, 6 cotylae; sediment of iris oil, 1 cotyle.

Of vinegar for the ammoniacum, 2 kotylai. [981] The Polyarchion, from the letter. Take: of cyperus 1 mina; of cardamom an equal amount, of manna an equal amount, of wax an equal amount; of roasted terebinth resin 1½ minae; of liquid [terebinth] 3 minae; of oil of cypros a sufficient amount. I add bdellium, 1 mina. The second version. Take: of cyperus 1 mina; of cardamom an equal amount, of bdellium an equal amount, of frankincense an equal amount, of balsam an equal amount; of wax 1½ minae; of roasted resin 4 minae; of oil of cypros 6 kotylai; of fragrant wine 1½ kotylai. And as I myself use it. Take: of cyperus 1 mina; of cardamom an equal amount, of amomum an equal amount, of bdellium an equal amount; of wax 1½ minae; of roasted resin [and] of terebinth resin, 4 minae; of oil of cypros 1 kotyle; of cassia, cinnamon, ammoniacum incense, Indian nard, saffron, myrrh, 4 minae each; of fragrant wine as much as suffices. An emollient of Apollonius, effective for many conditions. Take: of wax, pitch, roasted resin, 125 drachmas each; of natron and frankincense, 50 drachmas each; of calf's and bull's suet and of butter, 75 drachmas each; of oesypum 15 drachmas; of water 6 cyathi. An emollient good for those suffering in the liver. Take: of ammoniacum incense 144 drachmas (others 102 drachmas); of bdellium 144 drachmas; of saffron 12 drachmas; of myrrh 12 drachmas; of wax 144 drachmas.

[982] others 100; of vinegar 4 kotylai; of oil of cypros 1 kotyle, but I use 10 kotylai. Emollient (malagma) for flux (rheumatism) of the stomach and intestines. ℞ Of oenanthe 1 ounce; of the flesh of the date 2 ounces; of acacia 1 ounce; of roses one ounce; of omphacium 4 ounces; of aloe 4 ounces; of oak-gall 4 ounces; of round alum 4 ounces; of pitch 4 ounces; of wax 3 ounces; others add frankincense; of myrtle oil 3 ounces. Wine for the dry ingredients. For dropsical patients and those who are flatulent. ℞ Of liquid pitch 1 litra; of wax 1 litra; of nitre 6 ounces; of unfired sulphur 6 ounces; of split alum 6 ounces. Another emollient for sciatic patients and many other things. ℞ Of wax 72 drachmas; of turpentine 48 drachmas; of ammoniac (incense) 32 drachmas; of propolis 43 drachmas; of galbanum 36 drachmas; of bdellium 25 drachmas; of saffron 5 drachmas; of opopanax 12 drachmas; of foam of nitre 30 drachmas. Pound with iris unguent and use. Another emollient, of Andreas, polychrest. ℞ Of pellitory 8 drachmas; of Cnidian berry 8 drachmas; of ammoniac salt 8 drachmas; of the root of wild cucumber 8 drachmas; of pine resin 8 drachmas; of turpentine 8 drachmas; of wax 30; of the juice of the sycamine 12 drachmas, others 10 drachmas.

of rose-oil [986] 4 kotylai; of fenugreek unguent 1 kotylē; of good olive oil 1 kotylē. Melt these over a gentle fire, stirring lightly. Have ready, pounded smooth: of Illyrian iris 2 choinikes; of birthwort 1 choinix; of hypocistis, smooth, half a choinix; of oak-gall, smooth, 2 choinikes; of manna 1 choinix; of bdellium 1 choinix; of cinnamon, Cilician saffron, myrrh, cassia, Indian nard, flower of schoinos (rush), aromatic calamus, amomum, pepper, juice of sumach, blood of the sea-turtle, the herb androsaemum, pellitory (pyrethron), of each 35 drachmas; of old vinegar 1 kotylē. Having mixed all the ingredients together, soften and pound until it becomes ductile and thoroughly worked, and store it away. It is effective also for fluxions of the chest and lung and for those who have pain in the bregma of the head; it makes them free of pain at once. The preparation is called 'Asclepius'. A sciatic remedy, very good for sciatics, from Heras the Cappadocian. Rx: of liquid pitch 3 or 2 kotylai; of wax 1 litra; of pine resin 1 litra.

of unfired sulphur [987] 1 litra; of nitron 1½ litrae; of wild raisin (stavesacre) 1 xestes; of pellitory 1 litra; of burnt lees 2 litrae; of cardamom 1 xestes; of galbanum half a litra. Pour the meltable ingredients over the dry ones. Another emollient, of Baccheius, which Caesar used. ℞ Of pig's fat 2 minae; of wax 2 minae; of elecampane, aromatic reed, root of panax, rock salt or ammoniac salt, 10 drachmas each; of translucent bdellium and ammoniac incense, 2 minae each; of flower of schoinos and iris, 1 mina each; of frankincense, pepper and galbanum, 25 drachmas each. The boiling is as for the Cardamelian (emollient). Another emollient, the golden one, for arthritics. ℞ Of strobiline resin 2 litrae; of axunge and galbanum, 12 drachmas each; of wax 24 drachmas; of laurel oil 12 drachmas. Boil as you know. Another emollient for pain of the sides. ℞ Of cyperus, cardamom, manna, ammoniac incense, terebinth resin, wax and iris oil, 1 litra each. Boil the ammoniac (incense) separately; grind smooth the meltable ingredients, having melted them with a cyathus of iris oil; sprinkle the ammoniac on; then mix in the dry ingredients, dipping your hands in iris oil. Another emollient, of Kloniakos, of good colour.

♃ [988] Arsenic 3 oz.; split alum the same; quicklime the same; roasted resin 3 litrae; wax the same; vinegar for the dry ingredients, oil for the meltable ingredients, 8 oz. Use it also for splenic patients. [Malagma of Damocrates.] Since what is written in metre is useful for memory and preserves the proportions of the drugs exactly, for this reason I am accustomed to add the prescriptions of Damocrates as well, among which this one too is written. "There will surely often be need of a good malagma (emollient) too for those who are very devoted to medicine, for great strains of muscles and for ruptures of joints, and further also for sprains, thickenings of sinews and hardnesses of muscles accompanied by inflammation, and moreover for bites: for these this is most effective. It also removes lichens and lepras, being kept applied for ten days at most, changed at intervals of one or two days."

[989] Of translucent, very dry pitch, 2 pounds; one of pine resin and one of good wax; of ammoniac and of liquid alum, again, make one; and, having measured out 2 sextarii of the most acrid vinegar, keep it prepared. Occasionally some used to add 2 ounces of galbanum, wishing to soften more quickly the indurations that are also of long standing. Prepare it thus: taking a third of the vinegar, pour it over the ammoniac and the alum, and, making them smooth in a rather large mortar, bring them to the thickness of fresh liquid honey. The pitch and the remainder boil in a new pot, so that the whole is all but fried out; then pour it over the things well ground in the mortar, and beat it up until it takes on a yellow colour resembling quince-yellow. If you wish by all means to mix in galbanum as well,

[990] Add this [galbanum] together with the wax and the pine resin (pityinē), lifting the pot from the fire shortly afterwards. Some add an equal weight of manna, removing the alum from the drug. Using it for such conditions, they also glue together fresh divisions with this preparation. Use it from the very first day as well, in the cases I mentioned before, when they are in a state calling for caution (?), for scarifications and what follows on them. On top of the compress lay a sponge soaked through with vinegar and bind it on tightly; in this way you will also apply it to splenic patients. In those in whom you suspect that a scirrhus is going to form in some viscus, use the emollient without fear. After this drug Damocrates wrote the one made with salts, beginning it thus: "If it persists in any of these for longer periods, prepare this one too, as a most excellent drug."

[991] Then after this he also writes another drug made with salts, and after both of them yet another, which professes to disperse scrofulous swellings (choirades) and dropsical conditions of the liver and spleen. To me, however, it seemed better to write these drugs up among the discutient plasters. [On relaxing drugs.] Certain drugs are called 'relaxing' (chalastika) in the customary usage of almost all the more recent physicians: drugs by which, as the name itself also shows, the parts that have been stretched are relaxed. For 'being relaxed' is said as the opposite of 'being drawn tight'. At any rate, it has been written somewhere by Hippocrates as follows: 'of hard skin, softening; of tightened skin, relaxation.' If, then, one were to use the words in their proper sense, one will say that certain drugs are emollient of bodies that have become hardened, namely those that dissolve their hardness, just as certain drugs are relaxing, namely those curative of tension.

It happens that in inflammations the skin is stretched, sometimes acquiring this symptom from the underlying swelling, and sometimes also being itself inflamed along with it; yet the essence of inflammation [992] is not the hardness of the inflamed part but, quite the contrary, as we show in our discussions of it, moistness. In parts becoming scirrhous, however, it is not moistness that predominates in the affected part, but hardness. The generation and the cure of both affections are in some way of the same kind. For they are generated from an influx, and are cured when they have been evacuated. Yet the mode of evacuation is not the same in both. Rather, as has been shown in the treatise on the Therapeutic Method, in which the method of cure of all the other affections has also been set out, in inflamed parts the repellent quality of drugs is beneficial in the first stages, and the discutient quality throughout. In scirrhi, however, the discutient alone is beneficial, without the repellent. Now parts that have become completely scirrhous are completely incurable. One must recognise them by the fact that no sensation at all remains in the affected parts.

But those in which sensation is present, though faint, are treated by means of drugs that do, clearly, disperse the thickened fluid, yet do not do this strongly and all at once [993], as the discutient drugs do. Such drugs are called drawing (epispastic) and squeezing-out (exipōtic). One should not be surprised at the change into hardness that takes place from inflamed parts when, at the same time, the fluid that has flowed in is rather thick and viscous and the cure is effected by drugs that dry vehemently. For just as, in external things too, many bodies are parched when in contact with fire itself, but are softened again by means of water, in the same way, in inflamed parts, the fluid in the affected place, under drugs that heat and dry rather strongly, retains something viscous and thick left behind, the thin part having been dispersed. And it is in this way that the chalk-stones (pōroi) form in arthritic affections and the stones in nephritic affections. But if ever the flux that is going to produce an inflammation is thin in consistency, and its cure is effected by drying and heating drugs, nothing scirrhous is left behind. Not least, drugs that cool and astringe vehemently are also wont to produce scirrhi.

And we see many who, from erysipelases that were immoderately subjected to these [i.e. strongly cooling and astringent applications], have scirrhous [994] swellings, through the ignorance of the physicians who treated them. The first difference, then, between the drugs that treat inflammations and those that treat scirrhi is the one that has been stated. Another is the difference arising from the pain conjoined with inflamed parts, which does not tolerate a strong drug being applied to the affected part. For these [strong drugs] act with pain, while the inflamed parts are already in pain because of the affection and on this account require the mildest drugs. The more vigorous ones, besides not resolving or soothing the pains, also exacerbate them and so make the inflammations greater. The first use, then, in painful inflammations is that by means of sufficiently moist drugs, together with moderate warming. Next comes that by means of drugs slightly thicker and more drying. The third is by means of the so-called relaxing (chalastic) drugs, which some record among the malagmata (emollients). Of these the most emollient are those that are cerate-like in consistency, when they are compounded from butter, wax and fats, and relaxing oil.

With these is mixed a little oesypum and resin and [995] pitch, as also frankincense and galbanum and some Illyrian iris. The drug called 'the one made from juices' (dia chylōn), a remedy curative of inflammations that are no longer severely painful, was discovered by Menecrates, as he himself says and as certain others also testify on his behalf. The book in which the drug is written bears the title 'Autokrator Hologrammatos': 'Autokrator' because it is addressed to him, and 'Hologrammatos' because two and three and four and five and each of the other numbers, whether of resin or pitch or of any other drug, are written in full syllables without numerical signs. Menecrates did this because it often happens that errors are made in the writings not only by people acting unintentionally but also by some acting deliberately out of envy: they make the letter ο into θ by drawing another, transverse line through the middle of the round line, and alter the letter iota by adding another, likewise transverse, line; just as, when one line is scraped off from the letter [gamma?] and from rho, the result is that the character of iota is left.

In the same way, in the case of many letters, it comes about that the characters indicating them are altered, by addition in some cases, by combination in others, and by removal in others. [996] Yet Menecrates achieved nothing further with respect to later times, since those who copy his book write the names of the numbers not in full letters but by means of the characters that indicate them. It is reasonable, then, that the books of Damocrates on drugs, written in metre, have won esteem; and had all of them been written in this manner, it would have been best. But since not a few of the approved drugs have been left out, we also need the other pharmacological books, in which some have written down the compositions of varied drugs. Now the drug made from juices, discovered by Menecrates, has been written by Damocrates in the following trimeter lines, together with certain others as well, two of which have been written before it in the same manner as itself.

[The drug made from juices, of Damocrates, (devised) by Menecrates.] Having, then, said earlier how wounds that remain without inflammation will be conglutinated, we shall next say how it will be possible to treat well with drugs those that are severely inflamed. [997] When, after a muscle or some nerves have been wounded, or a membrane near a bone has been pricked, there come after the fourth day frequent pains and inflammations, and fevers with symptoms; when there is an increase of much sleeplessness, delirium, violent thirst and dryness of the tongue, inclining day by day towards the worse; when the ichor is lees-like and thin, the wounds red, and all the parts near them have turgescences, distensions, inflammations and oedemas: then do not apply varied poultices. For it is the custom of the young to do this, so that, having escaped the peaks of the inflammations, they may not give the slanderers cause for accusation. But one who has confidence in his own practice must also go down with the patients into their fears, not waiting upon fortune and nature.

[998] Prepare, then, for the affections mentioned before, a drug that is also fitting for the gouty, one laid upon the patients at every stage: for in the intervals it affords a ready ease of movement, and the security of not being quickly or easily troubled by chalk-stones (πῶροι) and frequent attacks; in the beginnings it does not allow the affections to take on magnitude, and at the peaks it quickly brings about the declines, provided one does not lightly shift to other remedies. Prepare the drug in this way: put in 2 litrai of golden litharge ground very fine, four of very old lard, and one litra and a third of a litra of oil many years old and very thick, not ill-smelling, not dark, not harsh; for thus the drug will be efficacious.

Having carefully melted the lard in a shallow pan, take off from it the membranes and the salts, [999] straining it through a strainer into another, larger pot; and, having added the oil, bring it to the boil again. Not all the oil, however, but two parts of it; leaving the third part aside, keep it lying in readiness, so that, if you are pressed to add it, you may have it to hand. And there will certainly be need of it, in winter at any rate, when the oil being put into the drug has become thick through long keeping. Then sprinkle the litharge over the boiling ingredients, and boil over a gentle and continuous fire, stirring with a spatula; it would be better if it were one of pine.

When the drug, boiled for a moderate time, takes on the thickness of a plaster, and likewise takes on the foul smell of a drug, lift the pot quickly from the fire, making it a little harder in summer, but soft in winter, yet nevertheless non-soiling; and stir it likewise until it has cooled moderately; [1000] then again with rather firm hands sprinkle (?) the whole, once softened, and in this way transfer it from the pot. When there is need, soften it again vigorously, and, having spread it carefully on soft leather, in this way apply the pads of good size. But if you wish at some time to make this plaster more effective for thick sinews and muscles, and hard breasts, and swollen joints, put in a litra of the roots of wild mallow, clean and fresh, and, having cut them into finger-sized pieces, in both length and thickness, throw the pieces onto the contents boiling in the pot. And when, being charred, they have given up all their moisture and potency to the drug, lift out the little roots of the mallow with a strainer, and, having sprinkled on the litharge ground smooth, then boil it, as I said before, and again store it away likewise and use it in the same manner.

[1001] This one, says Menecrates, who first discovered the drug, possesses the virtues of both; he was a most excellent man, of settled proficiency in the art. For it keeps freshly inflicted wounds free of inflammation, and it has persuaded us that it agglutinates what has been divided and treats ulcers that are excessively inflamed, and wounded muscles, without any other of the cataplasms, sponges and embrocations able to give help. It does everything that I said earlier the one made with litharge and axungia does. He says it is best as a pessary in chronic and in fresh inflammations of the uterus, and for filling hollow ulcers, and, dissolved in rose unguent or in good myrtle unguent, for cicatrizing. And in general, he says, every cataplasm and drug applied over them from outside is superfluous for those who use this one.

[1002] The drug is worthy of being recorded. It is by now trusted even by the envious, and he says to make it in this way. Of oil, in summer, seven litrae by weight. (In another copy I found half of the oil [replaced by] rich and fresh axungia.) In winter, as he says, you will put in nine, but only six of very finely ground litharge. Of fenugreek, he said, half a sextarius, and the same of burnt linseed. Of wild mallow he said three litrae by weight, of the root still holding its fresh juice. Boil it in water, eight sextarii by measure, in a new, wide-mouthed earthenware pan, putting in the mallow root, cleaned, cut up, fine and bruised, the washed fenugreek, and the linseed, carefully.

And when it has turned into juice and taken on thickness, [1003] squeeze the juice out through a linen cloth and keep it; and weighing out four litrae of it by weight and mixing in the oil, boil it all over coals. When, in place of larger bubbles, small and close-set ones rise up on the contents of the pot, then sprinkle on the ground litharge and boil over a gentle and continuous fire, until the juice, fried off together with the fat, ... the drug will be a quince-yellow plaster, of good colour, not soiling, yet not very hard. Having devised this as an addition to the old drugs, he called the drug, reasonably, 'the one made from juices' [diachylon]. Another. This drug too is of the same kind, even if it is prepared from different mixtures.

For indeed it acts upon the things I mentioned before, quite simply all things that are raw and difficult to concoct and hard to change, [1004] the large wounds in muscles and membranes. For it readily resolves their wounds (scars), and, applied to all arthritics, it will soothe the chronically affected places. It contains: of very dry pitch, 2 litrae; of clean Pontic wax, 2 litrae; again, of terebinth, the very liquid kind, 2 litrae; of manna of unadulterated frankincense, a litra; and half a litra, or something a little lighter in weight, of fresh butter, white and preferably fatty. Melt the rest for a long time over a fierce fire, continuously, watching whether the drug turns out to be non-soiling when rubbed between the fingers. When this happens, lift it off the fire and in this way sprinkle the manna over the melted ingredients, stirring the drug for a long time with the spatula.

When it has thus cooled and been softened, store it away. [1005] And when you have mixed a good deal of fresh rose oil into this preparation, you will use it also for very hollow and fleshless ulcers, for inflammations of tendons, and for those that are slow to change toward white pus. [On akopa (anti-fatigue remedies).] The very name of the akopa drugs makes plain what they claim to do. People call kopoi (fatigues) the conditions that arise in bodies from many or vehement movements, either in the whole body or in the parts that have laboured more. These conditions are painful, chiefly to those who are moving, but also to those at rest, in the case of the more vehement ones.

Later, however, it also became customary among physicians, even if the drug they had compounded was not for fatigues but for a pain lingering chronically in the depth of the body, or for difficulty of movement, or impaired sensation, or hardness of a part, or tension, or a scirrhous swelling, to call all such things likewise akopa (anti-fatigue remedies), provided only that it has a consistency, in respect of fluidity, similar to the akopa; this consistency is close [1006] to the liquid cerates, such as we use also for dislocations and fractures. For of such a consistency the most liquid is what the more recent physicians call kerelaion (wax-oil). Next after it come the akopa ointments, and after these, having a thicker consistency, that of the liquid cerates, then that of the cerates named tender and soft. Last is that of the amolynta (non-soiling ones), similar to that of the things specifically called epithemata (applications). Next after these is the consistency of plasters, and these too have no small difference among themselves in degree, more and less, so that some physicians gave the name kerotomalagmata (cerate-emollients) to certain preparations, naming them thus from their consistency alone: namely those of the applied drugs which are no longer liquid, yet not yet hard to the same degree as plasters. Since, then, all the differences mentioned indicate not the power of the drugs but the form of their consistency, the name of the akopa formerly signified the power of the drugs, but later their consistency.

And for this reason they were compelled to name them together with distinctions, [1007] calling this one an anti-lassitude remedy (akopon) that is relaxing, and that one emollient or warming or anodyne or metasyncritic, and likewise as suited to this or that particular affection, such as ischias, paralysis, or pain of the sides, or in common to all pains. Now there is a natural simple drug that helps against every kind of lassitude, namely oil, which we name even without any qualifying addition, since in ancient times it was also the only one. Later castor oil was added to it, at least among you; for in Egypt this too was ancient, and after castor oil again others, radish oil, mustard oil and sesame oil, and other such, just as among us lily oil, mastic oil and lentisk oil, and those still more elaborate than these, right up to the perfumed unguents.

It is quite clear, then, that the drugs called akopa (anti-fatigue remedies) by the ancients must all be liquid in their consistency, since oil alone treats the superficial fatigues, while those that are deep and more severe [are treated by oil] together with one of the relaxant drugs put into it, which are by nature moderately warming, such as galbanum and terebinth [1008] resin, and besides it the one called colophony and the roasted [resin]. Warmer than these are fir resin and strobiline, and larch resin is a little warmer than terebinth. All such things are mixed with relaxant oils, of the sort that Sabine oil is, wax sometimes being added as well. Also an anti-fatigue ointment for those already in pain deep down is the one made with the seed of the fir, with chamomile, dill and poplar flower, concerning which we shall say next how it is prepared. Lily oil (susinum), must oil (gleucinum) and the Commagenian are also among the anti-fatigue ointments, as are all those compounded with soft fat and fat; pig's fat relaxes most moderately, hens' fat more than these, and goose fat still more than that. Stronger is the fat of the lion and of the leopard, so that it warms more violently and for this reason also disperses sufficiently. Between these, along with ox and goat fat, lies that of foxes and of the hyena.

All these, then, belong by kind to the remedies properly called akopa [anti-fatigue remedies], differing from one another in heating more and less, so that some of them will seem to have fallen outside the whole [1009] kind of akopa ointments when they are tested on soft bodies, although they prove most beneficial for harder bodies, such as those of country people. For it has been said many times that hard bodies tolerate stronger drugs, whereas those that are soft and moist, like those of children, women and eunuchs, do not bear the power of such drugs. It is quite clear, too, that the so-called myrakopa [perfumed akopa] come about when akopa are mixed with perfumes; they are in no way better than the others, except in fragrance. As, then, I am accustomed to write down the remedies that have been tested by the older physicians through long experience, so too now I shall do, making my beginning from those written by Asclepiades. [The akopa and myrakopa written by Asclepiades in the fourth book of the External Remedies.] An akopon: it works against the discomforts arising from fatigues, and for nervous sympathetic affections. Themison used it. The drug is very fine. Take: sampsuchum, 1 xestes; libanotis, 1 xestes; fenugreek, 1 xestes.

of cardamom [1010] half a sextarius, of savin half a sextarius, of sweetish wine 3 sextarii, of Venafran oil 3 pounds, of wax 2 pounds. Put the dry ingredients into the wine and leave them to steep for 3 days; on the following day put in the oil, stir carefully, set it over coals, and boil it while stirring. When it has boiled up repeatedly, press out the liquid; grate the wax, throw it into this, set it on the fire again, and boil. When the wax has melted, take it off the fire and leave it to cool; once it has cooled, store it in a vessel of glass or of tin and use it, sometimes unmixed, sometimes diluted with one of the perfumed oils. Another. Take: of sampsuchum 1 sextarius, of libanotis 1 sextarius, of fenugreek 1 sextarius, of shoots of laurel six pounds, of flower of schoenus 3 ounces, of old wine 3 sextarii, of sweet olive oil 3 sextarii, of the root of wild cucumber and of Celtic nard half a pound each, of wax 3 pounds. Prepare and use as stated above. Another drug, a successful one. It is effective also for the paralysed and the tremulous, and against every sympathetic affection of the sinews. Menius Rufus indeed used it.

It is effective for sufferers from podagra, from arthritis and from sciatica, [1011] so that it frees them from the whole condition. It is used in the intervals; in the paroxysms we use the drug diluted. ℞ Sampsuchum, 2 xestai; fenugreek, 1 xestēs; libanotis, 1½ xestai; melilot, 1 xestēs; Illyrian [iris], 1 litra; cyperus, 1 litra; savin, 1 litra; cachrys, 1 litra; cardamom, a half-litra; flower of schoinos, a half-litra; cassia, a half-litra; southernwood, a half-litra; fruit of myrtle, a half-litra; fruit of bay, a half-litra. Crush all of these and put them into a double perfumer's vessel, then pour on 8 xestai of Tmolite wine. Leave to steep for 3 days. Then add 16 litrai of Sabine oil; of iris oil, 1 litra; of mastich oil, 1 litra; of Syrian [ointment], 1 litra; of must oil, 1 litra; of myrtle oil, 1 litra; of bay oil, 1 litra. Set it on the fire and boil, then press out the liquid from the boiled ingredients, pour it off into another vessel and boil it again, without the decocted residue, adding a half-litra of wax, 1 litra of larch resin, and of percolated myrrh 1 litra each. When these have melted, use as was said before. Another. ℞ Sampsuchum, 2 litrai; fenugreek, 2 xestai; libanotis, 2 xestai.

of savin [1012] 2 litrai; 2 sextarii; of melilot 2 litrai; of cyperus 1 litra; of Macedonian iris 1 litra; of cachrys 1 litra; of cardamom 1 litra; of aromatic calamus half a litra; of the flower of schoenus half a litra; of cassia in pipes, of costus, of elelisphacus, half a litra of each; of laurel berries half a litra; of the root of wild cucumber half a litra; of myrtle sprigs half a litra; of fragrant Tmolite wine 8 sextarii; of Sabine oil 24 litrai; of iris oil 1 litra; of cyprinum oil 1 litra; of mastic oil 1 litra; of gleucinum 1 litra [Greek 'κι.', read as 'λι.']; of myrtle oil 1 litra; of ammoniac or amaracinum 1 litra; of hedychroum 1 litra; of malabathrinum 1 litra; of percolated myrrh 1 litra; of opobalsam 1 litra; of wax 15 litrai. The dry ingredients are steeped, as was said before, for three days, and the oil and most of the unguents are poured onto them. But the malabathrinum, the amaracinum, the hedychroum, the stacte and the opobalsam are kept back to the last, so that in the preparation of the drug they are added when the wax has already melted. How the drug ought to be prepared and in what manner it is to be used has already been shown.

The akopon called 'the one with honey' [1013]. It is effective against fatigue-like discomforts and contractions of the nerves. It is effective for opisthotonics and for those convulsed in the canine manner. It is called tetramyron. Take: honey 3 oz.; iris oil 3 oz.; rose-oil 3 oz.; oil of cypros 3 oz.; must-oil 3 oz.; wax 3 oz.; terebinth 3 oz. Boil the honey separately. Melt the meltable ingredients, put them into a mortar and pound all together; having ground them fine, take the mixture up and use it. Another. Take: oil of cypros, iris oil, rose-oil, must-oil, 6 kotylai of each; wax 24 dr.; terebinth 8 dr.; honey 6 dr. Prepare and use as described above. Another, called lexopyreton. Take: rose-oil 4 kotylai; iris oil 4; must-oil 4; oil of cypros 4 kotylai; wax 12 dr.; terebinth 14 dr.; percolated myrrh 4 dr.; boiled honey 16 dr. Prepare as described above. Another, from the remedies of Aphrodiseus. Take: rose-oil 4 kotylai; iris oil 4 kotylai; oil of cypros 4 kotylai; wax 12 dr.; must-oil 4 kotylai; goose fat 12 dr.; terebinth 4 dr.; stakte 4 dr.; opobalsam 2 dr.; boiled honey 8 dr. Prepare in the usual way.

Another acopon, called the 'foul-smelling', for the [1014] conditions mentioned above. ℞ Wax, 8 dr.; terebinth, 8 dr.; galbanum, 6 dr.; ammoniac incense, 6 dr.; old oil, 2 kotylai; deer marrow, 8 dr. Prepare in the usual way, and use it both undiluted and thinned. Another, for every sympathetic affection of the sinews. ℞ Terebinth resin, 56 dr.; wax, 28 dr.; ammoniac incense, 32 dr.; galbanum, 32 dr.; deer marrow, 24 dr.; boiled honey, 24 dr.; old oil, 2 kotylai. The ammoniac is dissolved in vinegar. Another. ℞ Wax, 24 dr.; terebinth, 24 dr.; galbanum, 6 dr.; ammoniac incense, 6 dr.; old oil, 2 kotylai; deer marrow, 8 dr.; storax, 16 dr. Prepare in the usual way. Another. ℞ Wax, 24 or 28 dr.; terebinth, 16 dr.; galbanum, 6 dr.; storax, 8 dr.; old oil, 2 kotylai; honey, 1½ kotylai; deer marrow, 8 dr.; flower of salt, as much as suffices. Dissolve the ammoniac in vinegar. Another, for sciatic patients, for those with opisthotonos, and for every sympathetic affection of the sinews. ℞ Wax, 6 oz.; terebinth, 1 litra; ammoniac incense, 1 oz.

opopanax [1015], 2 oz.; galbanum, 2 oz.; deer marrow, 2 oz.; bull marrow, 2 oz.; oesypum, 2 oz.; iris oil, 1 cotyle; honey, 3 oz. Prepare in the customary way. Another, for conditions of extreme lassitude and for contractions of the sinews. Take: wax, 50 dr.; terebinth, 25 dr.; aphronitre, 6 dr.; oesypum, 6 dr.; boiled honey, 6 dr.; ammoniac incense, 6 dr.; deer marrow, 6 dr.; galbanum, 6 dr.; bull suet, 6 dr.; dried laurel berries, 6 dr.; oil, 1 cotyle; wine unmixed with sea-water, 1 cotyle. Prepare in the customary way. Another, entitled 'the Acuntian'. Take: wax, 2 oz.; galbanum, 3 oz.; nitre, 3 oz.; liquid terebinth, 3 oz.; oesypum, 2 oz.; bull suet, 2 ounces; oil of cypros, 4 oz.; quince-oil, 4 oz.; iris oil, 4 oz.; honey, 4 oz.; common oil, 6 oz.; old oil, 4 oz.; ammoniac incense, 1 oz.; frankincense, 1 oz. Prepare in the customary way. Another. Take: old oil, 1½ xestes; terebinth, 1 litra; ammoniac incense, 2 oz.; wax, a half-litra; galbanum, 3 oz.

[1016] of oesypum 2 oz.; of frankincense 1 oz.; of verdigris 2 oz.; of honey 2 cotylae (otherwise: 4 oz.); of deer's marrow 3 oz.; of goose fat 2 oz.; of wine 2 cotylae; of aphronitre 2 oz. Prepare in the customary way. Another, a green acopon. It is effective for opisthotonics, sciatics, the paretic, and those afflicted with tremor. ♃ Of myrrh 4 dr.; of ammoniac incense 4 dr.; of frankincense 4 dr.; of nitre 4 dr.; of verdigris 4 dr.; of opopanax 10 oz.; of galbanum 4 oz.; of turpentine 2 lb.; of wax 2 lb.; of malabathrum unguent half a sextarius; of cypros unguent half a sextarius; of vinegar as much as suffices. Dissolve the ammoniac, the myrrh and the nitre, and when they have dissolved, add to them the opopanax and the galbanum. When these have been ground smooth, add the meltable ingredients, and having mixed, take it up and use it. Another. ♃ Of myrrh 4 dr.; of turpentine 2 lb.; of wax 2 dr.; of ammoniac incense, frankincense, nitre and verdigris, of each 4 dr.; of quince unguent half a sextarius; of cypros unguent 3 oz.; of iris unguent 3 oz.; of old oil 3 sextarii; of opopanax 3 oz.; of galbanum 4 oz.; of vinegar a sufficient quantity. Prepare as stated above.

Another, for chronic conditions, [1017] very excellent. ℞ Wax, 1 mina; old oil, 4 sextarii; terebinth resin, 1 pound; myrrh, 4 ounces; frankincense, opopanax, root of wild cucumber, verdigris, nitre, 4 ounces of each; white pepper, 2 ounces; galbanum, 4 ounces; deer marrow, 4 ounces; unguent of cypros, 4 ounces; iris unguent, 4 ounces; quince unguent, 4 ounces; of the shoots of green rue, 3 ounces; vinegar, a sufficient quantity. Boil the roots of the wild cucumber and the rue with the vinegar, then squeeze out the liquid and pour it onto the dry ingredients; and having ground them carefully, take them up with the meltable ingredients, and use the drug sometimes undiluted, but at times also diluted. This is done according to the nature of the conditions present. Another, a successful drug of Bassus. By using this very drug he recovered when he had formerly been paralysed. ℞ Myrtle oil, 4 ounces; oil of cypros, 4 ounces; old oil, 1½ pounds; chalcanthum, 1½ pounds; wax, 1 pound; terebinth resin, 1½ pounds; galbanum, 3 ounces; manna, 4 ounces; opopanax, 2 ounces; bryony root, 4 ounces; verdigris, 4 ounces; aphronitre, 4 ounces.

of pepper [1018] 2 ounces; of pellitory 4 ounces; of kid's suet 6 ounces; of euphorbium 4 ounces; of vinegar a sufficient quantity. Boil the bryony and the pellitory with the vinegar, then squeeze out the liquid, add it to the dry ingredients, grind carefully, and take up with the meltable ingredients. The use has already been explained. Another, the one made with castoreum, for paralytics and for chronic conditions. ℞ Of oesypum 3 ounces; of deer's marrow 4 ounces; of turpentine 3 ounces; of ammoniac incense 2 ounces; of galbanum 2 ounces; of castoreum 2 ounces; of white pepper 2 ounces; of euphorbium 2 ounces; of adarce 2 ounces; of foam of nitre 2 ounces; of opopanax 2 ounces; of storax oil 1 ounce; of iris oil 2 ounces; of old oil 1 cotyle; of wax 1½ pounds. Compound in the usual manner. Another, which Bassus used when he had been paralysed for a long time, and he was rid of this disease. ℞ Of myrtle oil 4 ounces; of quince oil 4 ounces; of cyprus oil 4 ounces; of old oil half a pound; of wax one pound; of turpentine half a pound; of galbanum 5 ounces; of frankincense 4 ounces; of opopanax 2 ounces; of verdigris 2 ounces; of bryony root 4 ounces; of aphronitre 4 ounces.

of pepper [1019] 2 ounces; of pellitory 2 ounces; of kid's suet 6 ounces; of euphorbium 1 ounce; of vinegar a sufficient amount. The compounding is that common to such drugs. Another liniment for the gouty and the arthritic, the one made with salts; it frees from the whole condition. The use is daily. ℞ Of dirty salts, that is, of the earth itself, 1 pound; of split alum 1 pound; of lees of Italian wine 1 sextarius; of the flower of Assian stone 4 ounces. Grind the dry ingredients assiduously, and having added the lees and having ground them carefully fine, add to the ground ingredients 1 sextarius of old olive oil, and having beaten it up, take it up and use it. In other copies it is taken up with Attic honey. Another. ℞ Of dirty salts 3 ounces; of split alum 3 ounces; of the flower of Assian stone 3 ounces; of frankincense half an ounce or 6 ounces; of myrrh half an ounce or 6 ounces; of lees of Italian wine half a sextarius; prepare as stated before. Another liniment, the one composed for Patroclus, the freedman of Caesar; it frees from the whole condition. The use is daily, both in the morning before the bath and after the bath and towards evening.

One must take as much of the drug as suffices, dissolve it, and anoint [1020] the feet and rub them down without crushing pressure. ℞ Frankincense 10 dr.; white pepper 10 dr.; aphronitre 8 dr.; myrrh 4 dr.; ammoniac incense 6 dr.; vinegar, a sufficient amount; oil of cypros 1½ cotylae.
